These results demonstrate that fingerprint-centric self-supervised learning effectively improves hit prioritization under distribution shift, enabling practical DEL virtual screening. Code is available at \hyperlink{https://github.com/GenerativeDrugDiscovery/DELBERT-2}{DELBERT-2}.

title: Randomized Caches in Hardware: Challenges and Trade-offs
abstract: Randomized caches protect against side-channel attacks by obfuscating the mapping of memory addresses to cache locations. Existing proposals typically describe architectural behavior, leaving practical hardware implementation challenges largely unexplored. We implement four prominent designs, CEASER-S, ScatterCache, SassCache, and MIRAGE, and integrate them as the last-level cache (LLC) of a multi-core out-of-order RISC-V system-on-chip (SoC). We identify common and design-specific implementation challenges and develop practical solutions. We evaluate complete FPGA implementations by running SPEC CPU 2017 rate and GAPBS workloads to completion, providing, to our knowledge, the first comparative evaluation of these designs on a common full-system hardware platform. Pipelining the index derivation function (IDF) alone is insufficient: in three of the four variants, other components become the frequency bottleneck, reducing frequency by up to 35% relative to the baseline set-associative cache. Redesigning the critical paths while preserving mappings, rekeying, and victim-selection policies brings the three affected variants to no more than 10% below the baseline frequency, at the cost of added latency or reduced concurrency. Increased LLC access latency, rather than additional misses, dominates IPC degradation, reducing instructions per cycle by up to 5% for SPEC and 11% for GAPBS. Hardware overhead depends on the design and implementation technology: FPGA lookup-table usage increases by 10-35%, while ASIC area increases by 1-14%.

title: Does Validation Loss Predict Real-Robot Success? Evidence from Four Imitation-Learning Policies on a Low-Cost Arm
abstract: Held-out validation loss is the standard offline signal for choosing checkpoints and comparing models, but its relation to closed-loop success on a real robot is rarely measured. We measure it for ACT, Diffusion Policy, SmolVLA and $π_{0.5}$ (action expert only), trained on nested subsets of 12 to 200 demonstrations of a pick-and-place task on an SO-101 arm. We score 82 checkpoints on 25 held-out demonstrations, with each policy's training loss and with the error of the actions it outputs, and compare the scores with 930 bench rollouts. We also score all 700 intermediate checkpoints of 70 training runs, and recover the ball positions of every training, held-out and bench episode from the front camera. Within each policy, hold-out action error correlates with bench success (Spearman $ρ$ from -0.23 to -0.88), but no more strongly than the number of training episodes alone, and not at all among seeds trained on the same data. Across policies the ranking is inverted ($ρ$ = +0.90 at 200 episodes): the policy with the lowest hold-out error succeeded in 3 of 110 rollouts. The most common failure, the arm never leaving its rest pose, ended 96% of rollouts for Diffusion Policy trained on untrimmed demonstrations and 47% for SmolVLA, and cannot occur in a hold-out set made of demonstrations. Among rollouts in which the arm moved, SmolVLA's hold-out action error predicts success well ($ρ$ = -0.81). For the diffusion and flow-matching policies, hold-out loss rises two- to five-fold during training while hold-out action error falls by up to 29%. Held-out metrics are a sound diagnostic of learning but no substitute for evaluation on the robot, and we recommend reporting initiation failure and success among started rollouts as separate bench outcomes.

title: OCELOT: Planetary-Scale Species Distribution Modeling with Satellite Foundation Embeddings
abstract: Large-scale repositories of species observations now contain billions of occurrence records from around the world, but these sightings cluster heavily in human-accessible areas. Existing models use only a small fraction of these records and are not evaluated on extrapolating to remote, unvisited regions--where species distribution models can be used as geographic priors to help classify data from camera traps and acoustic recorders. We scale relative occurrence species distribution models by training a multimodal implicit neural representation network called OCELOT that fuses spatial coordinates with satellite foundation embeddings on two orders of magnitude more observations than previous work: 2 billion GBIF records across 100,000 taxa. Scaling to this regime requires co-designing the data pipeline, taxonomic representation, loss formulation, and model architecture: spatiotemporal thinning and sub-linear cell sampling correct for spatial redundancy and observer bias, while an additive taxonomic readout shares representations across species, genera, and families to improve predictions for rare taxa. To evaluate performance in remote areas, we benchmark geographic extrapolation using the NDCG metric on spatial block holdouts up to 600 km. Satellite foundation embeddings improve extrapolation by 51% over coordinate-only models and outperform classical bioclimatic rasters. The resulting model also matches or outperforms existing baselines on established interpolation benchmarks, demonstrating that optimizing for geographic extrapolation does not compromise in-distribution accuracy.

title: Quantitative spectral rigidity for negatively curved manifolds and Outer Space
abstract: Let $M$ be a closed manifold with fundamental group $G$. A subset of conjugacy classes $E \subset \text{conj}(G)$ is said to be spectrally rigid if when two negatively curved Riemannian metrics have the same marked length spectra on $E$, then their length spectra agree on all conjugacy classes. In this work we study spectrally rigid subsets from a quantitative perspective. We show that, if the density of $E \subset \text{conj}(G)$, measured with respect to a fixed reference metric, decays more slowly than $T^{-1/2}$ then $E$ is spectrally rigid. We establish analogous rigidity results for Culler-Vogtmann Outer Space and show that the $T^{-1/2}$ threshold is sharp in this setting.

title: Quantization of Large Models with Weight Outliers and Sparsity
abstract: Post-training quantization (PTQ) reduces the memory burden of large model deployment by casting the high precision trained weights to fewer bits. While this promotes memory-efficient inference, it also incurs quantization error that impairs model performance. To compensate for quantization error, the present contribution decomposes the original trained weights into a quantized matrix, a low-rank component, and a sparse matrix that accounts for outlier rows in the weights. Due to analytical intractability and the discrete structure of the decomposition, a simulated annealing search is employed to explore candidate decompositions while avoiding poor local minima. Numerical tests demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach across a broad suite of large language models, including Llama 3.2 1B, Llama 3.2 3B, Llama 3.1 8B, and Qwen2.5 7B, evaluated on natural language generation benchmarks using 4-bit NF4 and FP4 quantizers. The novel method can markedly outperform direct quantization while incurring minimal memory overhead.

title: VerusWeave: A Benchmark for Proof Repair in Concurrent Verus Programs
abstract: Concurrent software underpins critical infrastructure, including operating systems and databases, yet thread interactions can have bugs that bypass conventional testing. Verus extends Rust with formal verification capabilities, enabling developers to specify, implement and prove the correctness of concurrent code in the same language. Although coding agents have been explored for automated proof construction, existing Verus benchmarks offer limited coverage of concurrency-specific examples that connect atomic operations to abstract protocols. To address this gap, we introduce VerusWeave, the first benchmark dedicated to concurrent proof repair, derived from four open-source projects. It comprises 75 focused tasks and 17 full-module variants that exercise features used to verify low-level concurrent code. Tasks remove selected proof annotations and require agents to fill gaps, while preserving executable code and specifications. The evaluation harness validates repairs using Verus and a change checker, recording solutions, execution traces, and resource usage. An initial evaluation of four general-purpose coding-agent harnesses achieved 75-85% success on focused tasks and 29-47% on full-module variants, highlighting the challenge of autonomous module-wide repairs. VerusWeave provides a reusable foundation for evaluating automated proof construction for concurrent software.

title: Seeing Less in a Sparse World: Cross-View Geolocalization from Limited Field-of-View Observations
abstract: Cross-view geolocalization aims to determine the geographic location of a ground-level image by retrieving its corresponding satellite image, offering a promising alternative for localization in Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS)-denied or degraded environments such as urban canyons, dense forests, and disaster scenarios. Despite recent progress, existing approaches remain limited by the lack of globally diverse training datasets and benchmarks that are often geographically restricted. Furthermore, most benchmarks rely on panoramic ground views, which do not reflect the limited field-of-view imagery captured by real world cameras. To address these challenges, we introduce Cross-View World 500k (CVW500k), a large-scale globally distributed dataset containing over 500,000 ground-satellite image pairs collected across diverse geographic regions and environments. Unlike previous datasets, CVW500k uses limited field-of-view ground images, providing a more realistic and challenging setting for cross-view geolocalization. In addition, we propose GeoQueryNet, a query-based cross-view fusion transformer framework designed to bridge the viewpoint gap between ground and satellite images. The model leverages a CLIP-based visual encoder with parameter-efficient LoRA adaptation and introduces a Cross-View Alignment Module that uses learnable query tokens to extract geographically consistent features across viewpoints. Our code can be found here: https://github.com/Fahim17/Cross_View_World_Dataset.git .

title: The Complexity of Choosing Parity Projections
abstract: Cube attacks in cryptanalysis seek small sets of Boolean variables (cubes) whose parity sum is constant. We study the bounded constant derivative problem introduced by Smirnov (2026), which seeks a smallest cube with sum 1, and its sum-0 analogue. Despite their similarity, the problems differ sharply in parameterized complexity: the sum-1 problem admits a $2^{O(k^2)}\operatorname{poly}(N)$-time algorithm, where $k$ is cube size, whereas the sum-0 problem is not fixed-parameter tractable unless $\mathrm{FPT}=\mathrm{W}[1]$. Without a bound on cube size, both problems are $Σ_2^{\oplus\mathrm{P}}$-complete and NP-hard to approximate within $N^{1-\varepsilon}$ for every fixed $0<\varepsilon<1$. Our hardness proofs use a crown construction that embeds maximal monomials of parity-projected circuits into positive 2CNF. This yields completeness and inapproximability results, as well as a dichotomy for Boolean constraint languages of arity at most two: the bounded constant derivative problem is in P when all relations are affine and $Σ_2^{\oplus\mathrm{P}}$-complete otherwise. We also give algorithms parameterized by the number of quadratic rounds, treewidth, or ordered branching-program width, with lower bounds for the first two unless $\mathrm{NP}\subseteq\mathrm{SUBEXP}$. The treewidth lower bound holds for circuits; the case of 2CNF remains open.

title: Quantifying Local and Global Fidelity of Nonlinear Embeddings
abstract: Dimension reduction rests on a claim: t-SNE and UMAP preserve local structure, PCA global structure. Our DLP curve is the share of each point's k nearest neighbors a map keeps. Corrected for chance, it gives L at k=10 and G over 30 to 50% of the data, local and global fidelity. At the midpoint the curve is provably a rank correlation of distances. The LG reversal test decides, with a stated error rate, which of two maps is local and which global. On twelve datasets of up to 1.38 million points, G agrees with established global scores at 0.84 and 0.93, and the area under R_NX at 0.22 and 0.30. The entity fidelity E, read at each point's entity size, predicts which entities a map loses beyond L and G where entity sizes differ. In an agent memory of one million passages, t-SNE and PCA cross at 150,000 passages (p=2.6e-5).

title: When AI Agents Act on Our Behalf: A Taxonomy of Human-Agent Interaction Failure
abstract: AI agents write and execute code, manipulate user interfaces, and transact on their users' behalf. We ask what forms failure takes in human-agent interaction, and how those forms change as agents act with greater autonomy. From 695 documented incidents in two public repositories, we developed 12 failure modes bottom-up within three interaction stages adapted from Amershi et al.'s guidelines, coding the autonomy at which each arose. What a person can do when an agent fails depends on how much the agent completes between points of user involvement--a property fixed at deployment. Therefore, the same model on the same task can fail differently under different configurations. All 12 modes appear at both low and high autonomy, and rising autonomy changes the form each failure takes. Users need controls between full delegation and full manual work, and neither incident records nor agent benchmarks reach the interaction where these failures occur.

title: TADA: Technology Aware DNN Accelerator Performance and Energy Estimator
abstract: Deep neural network (DNN) accelerators for edge inference must meet tight energy, latency, and area (EDP) constraints, and their optimal hardware architecture and dataflow configuration is typically identified through design space exploration (DSE). However, on-chip memory technology including cell type, bank organization, and process node, is rarely treated as a first-class citizen in DSE. For example, increasing memory capacity can reduce memory accesses through greater data reuse, but at the cost of higher area and access energy, thereby limiting the compute units budget. Consequently, memory technology can fundamentally shift the optimal accelerator architecture for a given area and EDP budget. Existing machine learning (ML)-based DSE methods require repeating simulation, data generation, and model training for each new memory technology. We present TADA, a memory technology-aware DNN accelerator performance and energy estimator that predicts system latency and energy for a given workload, hardware configuration, and memory technology. TADA is trained on a synthetic dataset that generalizes across memory technologies. The dataset spans current and future technology trends while enforcing physics-based guardrails to preserve realistic area-energy trade-offs. Each memory technology is represented by a technology signature, a vector of read energy, write energy, and storage capacity across a range of areas, provided as input alongside the workload and hardware configuration. Across 21 unseen technology curves spanning SRAM, STTRAM, ReRAM, PCM, FeFET, eDRAM, and CTT, TADA predicts system energy and latency with 1.5-4.4% and 0.7-1.2% mean absolute percentage error, respectively. In three pairwise case studies, it matches the simulator-selected memory technology at 98.7-100% of area budgets, with a mean EDP loss of at most 0.21%, while achieving over 10^4x higher evaluation throughput.

title: Seeing the Unseen: Unified Visible--Invisible Motion for Physically Consistent Video Generation
abstract: Recent advances in video generation have achieved impressive visual quality, yet they often fail to produce physically consistent dynamics due to the lack of explicit modeling of underlying physical processes. Existing approaches either rely on simulators with strong assumptions or use coarse semantic guidance, and further struggle to effectively inject physical priors into generation models. In this work, we propose Seeing the Unseen, a unified framework for physics-grounded video generation. Our approach decomposes the problem into two stages: learning physical dynamics and injecting them into video synthesis. First, we introduce a lightweight Particle-based Graph Dynamics Simulator (PGDS) that learns generalizable physical interactions from data and predicts plausible 3D motion trajectories. Second, we propose a Visible--Invisible Motion Field (VIMF) that captures both motion observable in the input frame and motion that emerges over time due to object dynamics. This representation enables more complete and structured motion guidance compared to conventional physical signals. By integrating these trajectories into a diffusion-based generator, our method produces videos that are both visually coherent and physically consistent. Extensive experiments demonstrate improved motion accuracy, interaction consistency, and reduced physical artifacts compared to strong baselines.

title: Software Change Request in AI-Orchestrated Software Evolution: Literature Review and Research Agenda
abstract: In the emerging paradigm of holistic AI-orchestrated software maintenance and evolution, large-scale app stores continuously generate exponentially vast Software Change Requests (SCRs) streams through user feedbacks. These streams enable intelligent software evolution. Automating SCR extraction and classification is crucial with rapid growth of Mobile Apps (MA). However, significant challenges exist such as scare large-scale datasets, inconsistent classification schemes, limited data sharing and insufficient research. This study presents a first and thorough systematic survey of SCR identification from MA Reviews (MAR). In particular, we investigated how Machine Learning (ML) and Deep Learning (DL) enhanced identification and classification of SCR. This study has found pertinent datasets varying sizes from 5,000 to more than 18 million reviews. The key findings highlight the dominant use of Random Forest and Support Vector Machines, limited adoption of deep learning techniques, inconsistent F1-score results ranging from 0.08 to 1 and partial automation in existing SCR tools such as SURF and ChangeAdvisor. Finally, we have performed a synthesis of the studies to presents a comparative taxonomy of SCR methodologies, identify research gaps and annotation frameworks. We contend that classification schemes, shared datasets and annotation frameworks are essential for advancing SCRs and thereby improving the maintenance of mobile applications.

title: Sharp transitions between optimal therapy regimes reveal robust dosing strategies against drug-induced persistence
abstract: Anti-cancer drug treatment can induce tumor cells to adopt reversible drug-tolerant persister states, facilitating resistance evolution and eventual treatment failure. Although low-dose and intermittent therapies have been proposed as alternatives to maximum tolerated dose (MTD) therapy in this setting, it remains unclear when and why these strategies are optimal. To address this question, we develop a mathematical model of drug-induced persistence where the drug can promote switching to a drug-tolerant state or inhibit reversions to sensitivity in a dose-dependent manner. We uncover sharp transitions between qualitatively distinct therapy regimes, including intermittent high-dose and continuous low-dose therapy, driven by the relative dose sensitivities of cell death and phenotypic switching. In particular, intermittent treatment is optimal when the drug inhibits reversions at doses too low to effectively kill the sensitive cells. We finally exploit the simple regime structure of optimal therapies to show that robust alternatives to MTD therapy can be identified under incomplete knowledge of the underlying dynamics

title: Hardware-Aware Conditional Code in Android Apps
abstract: Android OS runs on a highly diverse set of devices, spanning entry-level phones and flagships with substantially different hardware characteristics, including memory capacity, processors, displays, cameras, and sensors. Through APIs, apps can query device information at runtime, such as memory, hardware features, and manufacturer, among other device properties, allowing developers to execute different code paths on different devices. Existing studies cover only specific compatibility bugs or brand-specific behavior; however, the broader use of hardware information in app logic has not been comprehensively explored. We address this question with a large-scale empirical study of hardware-related if statements in Android apps. We statically analyze 50,000 apps to identify the if statements whose conditions depend on the values of hardware-related APIs, and extract their conditions together with the code of their branches. Our results show that 95% of successfully analyzed apps contain at least one such statement, with an average of 74 per app, which suggests that hardware-related logic is widespread. We then apply an LLM-assisted open-coding process to the extracted code to build a structured taxonomy of the purposes behind hardware-related conditional code. The resulting characterization shows that developers use hardware information for feature availability checks, UI adaptation, emulator detection, device tiering, and resource management, among others.

title: Teach, Abstract, Apply: A Framework for Dialogue-Driven Task Learning with Collaborative Robots
abstract: Collaborative robots (cobots) are designed to be safer and more interactive than traditional industrial robots, share the same workspace as humans, and assist them in a range of shop-floor tasks such as palletization, joint assembly, and part inspection. Many of these tasks involve repetitive workflows that may evolve with changes in production environments and task specifications. These requirements motivate the need for intuitive interfaces that allow workers to modify workflows on the shop floor and generalise these routines for future use. This work introduces the Teach-Abstract-Apply (TAA) framework, which enables human operators to (a) teach new workflows to cobots in natural language, (b) abstract the taught workflows into skills for later use, and (c) apply these skills in different settings. As a case study, we apply the TAA framework to a collaborative structure-building task and evaluate it with both open-weight (Qwen3-Coder) and closed (GPT5.2-Codex) models in self-play and cross-model configurations. Our results show that skill abstraction improves task success rates and reduces interaction cost. Beyond automated evaluation, a preliminary human-in-the-loop study suggests that the pipeline also works with human instructions.

title: A Framework for Task-Agnostic Counterfactual Fairness in Transformers through Activation Steering
abstract: Bias in transformer-based models is a growing concern as these architectures become more prevalent in automated decision-making systems, such as prediction models for hiring, lending, and clinical treatment recommendation. Mechanistic interpretability (MI) is a growing body of work that measures meaningful causal effects of activations on model output by identifying human-interpretable features encoded in model activations. When such features correspond to sensitive attributes, they provide a direct way to quantify the bias those attributes introduce and to causally intervene to mitigate it. However, counterfactual fairness (CF) methods have not been systematically adapted to this setting of intervening on interpretable mechanisms in transformers. We propose a framework, Mechanistic Interpretability for Counterfactual Fairness (MICF), that utilizes MI tools to reformulate CF constraints in terms of transformer activations, unifying former approaches into a single pipeline for fairness analysis in transformers. MICF does not require a prior causal model or specific transformer architecture. We evaluate MICF on real-world tabular data and show that CF can be improved across different prediction tasks.

title: The Agentic AI Kerr Lab: LLM Agents for Kerr Microscopy Experiments with Magnetic Skyrmions
abstract: Magnetic skyrmions are topological spin textures that can be observed directly by magnetic microscopy and driven by fields and currents, which makes them a model system for fundamental physics and candidates for spintronic devices. Magneto-optical Kerr microscopy is a method to image them in real time; however, most experiments use an inefficient cycle of consecutive imaging, analysis and excitation in which every step requires the judgement of the experimentalist operating the setup. Here we present the Agentic AI Kerr Lab (AgentKerr), in which an agent based on a large language model operates this cycle automatically and efficiently on a Kerr microscope. Rather than relying on pattern detection by a language model, a convolutional neural network trained on Kerr images turns live images into skyrmion observables such as position, size and shape, on which the agent bases its decisions. The architecture lets agents operate the instruments safely, as every hardware action is checked deterministically against an action policy, independently of the agent that issues it. With no procedure given, the agent determines by itself how to create, tune and move skyrmions, and writes its own analyses. The approach can be transferred to other spin textures and points towards magnetic imaging experiments in which the researcher poses the question and the agent finds the way to realize the experiments that yield the answer.

title: Cross-Lingual Persona Effects in LLM Negotiation
abstract: Tell an LLM negotiator to be "headstrong" and it should hold firm on price, but does that instruction retain the same behavior in every language? To test this, we use identical buyer and seller instances of Gemini 3.6 Flash to negotiate the same 12 CraigslistBargain scenarios in English and Korean. The pilot-scale 2 x 2 x 3 design crosses interaction language, seller urgency (none or strong), and buyer persona (cooperative, neutral, or headstrong), yielding 432 attempted negotiations. We call this property cross-lingual social-policy fidelity: whether a prompt-defined social policy produces the same behavioral effect regardless of interaction language. It often does not. Korean negotiations reached agreement far more often than English (77.3% vs. 52.5%, a 24.8-point gap, Holm-adjusted p = .0039), but only for neutral and headstrong buyers; cooperative buyers were already near-ceiling in both languages. Buyers' opening offers barely differed by language; the gap instead emerged later, through larger seller concessions and a smaller final gap in Korean, and agreed prices were also lower in Korean. Repeating the full design with Qwen3.7 Flash as both agents gives directional support: agreement was again higher in Korean (+13.9 points vs. Gemini's +24.8, with an interval whose lower bound is near zero), and sellers again conceded more. Pragmatic analysis reveals why: while both languages frequently featured face-threatening acts like rejections and counter-offers, Korean dialogue softened these threats with substantially more politeness mitigation, especially among sellers (11.7% vs. 3.6%). These results show that such a policy can produce different simulated negotiation behavior, not just different wording, when only the interaction language changes.

title: The Rise of Low Precision Floating Point
abstract: Floating point computing has dominated scientific computations since the 1950s because of its versatile ability to approximate real numbers with both sufficiently high precision and sufficiently great range. Since 1985, two specific formats have become standard across the industry, one with 32 bits which is adequate for many purposes and one with 64 bits which allows numbers with both much higher precision and much greater range for applications where these are needed. However, during the past decade, deep learning has come to dominate computation, and narrower floating point formats with lower precision and reduced range have steadily become more common. In this article we discuss this phenomenon, why it is happening, how various 16-bit, 8-bit and even 4-bit floating point formats have been developed, and efforts to standardize these formats.

title: Fourier analysis on a class of Schwartz spaces and applications
abstract: The study of regularity and solvability of partial differential operators on non-compact manifolds requires the construction of adapted functional spaces. In this work we introduce $\mathcal{S}(\mathfrak{M}\times\mathbb{R}^n)$, the Schwartz space on the product of a homogeneous space $\mathfrak{M}$ and the Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^n$. We characterize $\mathcal{S}(\mathfrak{M}\times\mathbb{R}^n)$ and its topological dual by employing discrete Fourier analysis in terms of eigenfunction expansions associated with a class of anisotropic elliptic operators on $\mathbb{R}^n$. We provide a characterization via partial Fourier coefficients and via full coefficients, that is, with respect to both components of $\mathfrak{M} \times \mathbb{R}^n$ simultaneously, which is achieved by studying the Fourier analysis on $\mathfrak{M}$. Our results provide new tools for the analysis of operators in this broader setting. As an application, we investigate the global existence and regularity of solutions for a class of partial differential equations on $\mathfrak{M}\times \mathbb{R}^n$.

title: Application a quantum machine learning algorithm to the applied problem of modeling the thermal regime of a servers
abstract: Quantum computing is a rapidly developed field of science. In the NISC era, quantum machine learning stands out, potentially outperforming classical machine learning. In this paper, we explore the applicability of quantum machine learning to a real-world application. We solved the problem of prediction of the temperature of GPUs in a high-performance computing cluster. We trained a quantum circuit to predict the temperature of each of the eight GPU of each cluster node based on 16 physical parameters. We demonstrated that quantum machine learning performs on this task just as well as classical machine learning. Furthermore, using model problems, we demonstrated that quantum machine learning can potentially outperform classical machine learning.

title: Quantum dynamics of ultrasmall magnetic skyrmions in atomic-defect landscapes
abstract: Magnetic skyrmions are prime candidates for future information technology, and their fate in devices is settled by the defects they encounter. In ultrathin films, skyrmions can be as small as a couple of nanometers, carrying only a few tens of magnetic moments, while atomic defects reshape their energy landscape on the atomic scale. Here, we demonstrate that such ultrasmall skyrmions can behave quantum mechanically and that their quantum dynamics is unusual. Since the gyrotropic force dominates, the two coordinates of a ferromagnetic skyrmion are canonically conjugate and the skyrmion behaves as a particle in the lowest Landau level of an effective magnetic field, with a magnetic length of 0.6~Å. Utilizing skyrmion-defect interaction profiles of Cr and Fe adatoms and dimers in PdFe/Ir(111), obtained from atomistic spin simulations parametrized from first principles, we unveil quantized gyrotropic orbits with level spacings of 20--85~$μ$eV, bound not only by pinning defects but also, counter-intuitively, by repulsive ones. Saddle points of the energy landscape act as quantum beam splitters for skyrmions, and quantum depinning reaches rates of 1--100~Hz below the critical current. Embedded impurities, in contrast, bind the skyrmion so strongly that it ceases to behave as a rigid particle, defining a strong-coupling regime. For the Gilbert damping typical of ultrathin films, the quantized levels remain well resolved. The thermal-to-quantum crossover lies between 40 and 160~mK, which is within reach of millikelvin scanning tunneling microscopy, where tip-induced escape statistics and electron spin resonance STM can reveal the quantized gyrotropic motion of skyrmions pinned at defects crafted atom by atom.

title: Distortion of Random Max Filters over Reflection Groups
abstract: A max filter with Gaussian templates $a_1,\dots,a_D$ is a $G$-invariant map $\R^d\to\R^D$, where $G$ is a finite reflection group. As $D\to\infty$ its distortion converges a.s to the condition number of $M_G^{1/2}$, where $M_G$ is the second-moment matrix of a standard Gaussian vector moved into a fundamental chamber of $G$. We compute this limit exactly for the sign and dihedral groups, and show it grows as $Θ(\sqrt d)$, $Θ(d^{3/2})$ and $Θ(k)$ for the sign, symmetric and dihedral groups of order $2k$. The symmetric case bound uses a lower bound on the covariance of order statistics. For any finite $G$ we also show that the infimum defining the optimal lower Lipschitz constant of a piecewise-linear $G$-invariant map is a minimum.

title: Proposal for the resolution of the disagreement between DAMA and other Underground Dark Matter Experiments
abstract: It is a great mystery still needing a solution that the underground experiments looking for dark matter disagree, in tIt is a great mystery still needing a solution that the underground experiments looking for dark matter disagree, in the sense that DAMA/LIBRA has found dark matter with a confidence level of several standard deviations, while neither the xenon based experiments nor even the experiments using the same target material NaI(Tl) as DAMA see the same amount of dark matter. We propose to solve this enigma by postulating that the dark matter gets excited during its passage through the mountain shielding from outer space down to the experimental halls; the DAMA experiment is namely about twice as deep as the ANAIS and COSINE-100 experiments, so that there is longer passage time for DAMA, which thus gets more excited dark matter particles. The xenon-scintillator experiments have their strong limits for dark matter making itself felt via nucleus recoils, and thus we can just assume that the excited dark matter mainly emits e.g. electrons, and the xenon-experiments would hardly see such dark matter. The single event recently seen by LUX/ZEPPELIN could be due to a low rate of nucleus emission in addition to the hypothesised electrons.

title: Spectral unions of intervals with few rational relation tile the real line
abstract: We prove that every spectral finite union of pairwise disjoint bounded intervals whose lengths satisfy at most four linearly independent rational relations tiles the real line, and that each of its spectra has at most five cosets modulo its least period. This includes every spectral union of at most five bounded intervals. The proof combines specialization preserving subset-sum equalities with rigidity of exchanges between finite spectral fibers. We also obtain common tiling complements for all spectra of primitive sets of at most seven elements in finite cyclic groups, and establish the sharp eleven-point range in which consecutive pairs force periodicity of the dual set.

title: Ewald summation of doubly periodic 2- and 3-dimensional Stokes multipoles
abstract: In spite of the qualitative differences between Stokes flows in 2 and 3 dimensions, most particle-resolved computational studies of microswimmers and other colloidal systems dominated by low-Re hydrodynamic interactions are carried out in triply periodic geometries, while the corresponding continuum descriptions are frequently solved in 2-dimensional doubly periodic domains. Furthermore, most experimental examples of biological and synthetic microswimmers are realised in confined, quasi-2-dimensional geometries with a finite thickness in one of the three dimensions. To enable studying the non-trivial differences between these system geometries, in this paper we systematically derive Ewald representations for periodic Stokes force multipoles in geometries with two periodic directions, treating both three-dimensional Stokes flow with one unbounded coordinate and intrinsically two-dimensional singularities. Starting from the periodic Stokeslet, we obtain explicit expressions for force dipoles and quadrupoles and analyse the non-trivial zero-wavevector contribution arising under partial periodicity. The analytical expressions are independently validated by comparing with results from an explicit lattice Boltzmann solver in each geometry.

title: Zero mode, Zero influence: Spatial-derivative coupling in particle detectors
abstract: It is common in particle detector models in cavity QED to often omit zero modes or assume their state, compromising causality or introducing ambiguity in their predictions. We show that spatial-derivative coupling eliminates both problems. For free massless scalar fields in static periodic or Neumann cavities of any spatial dimension, cavity-frame spatial derivatives annihilate the zero-mode operator while preserving microcausality. Detector dynamics and entanglement harvesting then depend only on the reduced detector-oscillator state, nonperturbatively and even with initial correlations with the zero mode. Time derivatives and moving-detector rest-frame spatial derivatives can retain zero-mode state dependence not compromising causality. Realized through current coupling in superconducting circuits, spatial-derivative coupling thus makes zero-mode state assumptions unnecessary.

title: Evidence for topological flat band magnetism in Co$_3$Sn$_2$S$_2$
abstract: Correlations and topology are central pillars in the study of emergent electronic phases. Topological flat bands near the Fermi level unite these concepts, providing a route towards correlated topological phenomena and unconventional magnetism. Despite theoretical predictions, momentum-resolved observation of a topological flat band at the Fermi level has remained elusive. Using angle resolved photoemission spectroscopy, we observe a flat band at the Fermi level within the topologically non-trivial electronic structure of the magnetic kagome Weyl semimetal Co$_3$Sn$_2$S$_2$. We further uncover a strong temperature dependence in which the flat band shifts across the Fermi level, accompanied by a reconstruction of the Fermi surface. Strikingly, this evolution occurs on the same temperature scale as previously reported anomalies in the magnetic response. Together, these results provide evidence for topological flat band magnetism in Co$_3$Sn$_2$S$_2$, establishing a microscopic setting in which topology, electronic correlations, and magnetism become intertwined.

title: On potential density of rational points on hyperkahler varieties
abstract: In this paper, we prove that the rational points on hyperkähler varieties in each of the four known deformation families admitting a rational Lagrangian fibration are potentially dense. Furthermore, we give several applications and construct examples of hyperkähler varieties beyond these families satisfying the potential density property. Our approach is first to prove that rational points on hyperkähler varieties admitting two rational Lagrangian fibrations with distinct associated isotropic rays are potentially dense. We then construct a projective Shafarevich--Tate twist admitting two such fibrations, together with a dominant rational map from the twist to the original variety.

title: RaMMOBO: Random Max-Margin Multi-Objective Bayesian Optimization
abstract: Multi-objective Bayesian optimization (MOBO) maximizes $M$ expensive black-box objectives with the goal of approximating the Pareto set, whose objective vectors cannot be improved in one component without sacrificing another. A common quality measure is hypervolume, the volume in objective space dominated by these vectors relative to a reference point. Expected hypervolume improvement (EHVI) directly targets this metric and is one-step Bayes-optimal, but its standard computation scales exponentially with $M$, making it prohibitively expensive for many-objective problems. We introduce random max-margin multi-objective Bayesian optimization (RaMMOBO), whose acquisition function lower-bounds EHVI while requiring only linear cost in $M$ to evaluate. RaMMOBO measures the volume of a max-margin box contained in a candidate's hypervolume-improvement region and averages over random reweightings of the objective space, yielding a utility that is strictly Pareto-monotone on hypervolume-improving outcomes. It naturally handles noisy observations and different probabilistic surrogates and supports efficient gradient-based optimization. Across synthetic and real-world benchmarks, RaMMOBO matches or outperforms state-of-the-art methods, with largest gains at higher $M$, with acquisition optimization up to two orders of magnitude faster than qLogNEHVI. Our implementation is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/rammobo.

title: Quasi-polynomial valuations of lattice polytopes
abstract: We prove that for any valuation $φ$ of lattice polytopes in ${\mathbb R}^m$, which is quasi-polynomial with respect to ${\mathbb Z}^m$-translations, and any lattice polytope $P$, the function $φ(nP)$ is quasi-polynomial in $n$.

title: Decentralized Multi-Agent Coordination and Communication in Shared Codebases
abstract: Coding agents working in shared repositories may receive separate, independently-motivated requests from human developers, creating a setting that is multi-agent by necessity. When this scenario happens, their individual implementations may work separately but conflict when combined. To study this setting, we introduce ParallACT, a benchmark of orchestrator-free multi-agent coding tasks. ParallACT contains both complementary and contradictory tasks. In complementary tasks, each agent's task is separately useful and implementations must share an interface to be productively combined. In contradictory pairs, both agents' tasks require editing the same code in incompatible ways, and naively combining independent solutions fails to produce a useful implementation. We compare a single-agent oracle given the combined set of tasks against multi-agent settings that vary execution order, visibility, awareness of other agents, and access to a communication channel. We find that the oracle solves most tasks while parallel agents perform substantially worse. Their performance drop is notable for complementary tasks, and particularly sharp for contradictory tasks (e.g., from 62% to 16% for Claude Code with Claude Opus 4.8) where merged code typically satisfies only one specification, and the same gap appears in all six further configurations pairing two agent harnesses with three open-weight models. Simply telling an agent that a peer exists does not help significantly, and giving agents access to a communication channel recovers only a small part of the performance, at an additional token cost. ParallACT thus identifies and isolates a core challenge that will become more common as multi-agent coding by independent principals becomes standard, and provides a controlled test of which coordination strategies help, and at what cost.

title: Isomorphism classes and geometric classification of three-dimensional Jordan algebras and the length function
abstract: We investigate the algebraic classification of Jordan algebras of dimensions at most three over arbitrary fields with more than two elements. Our approach combines the theory of nilalgebras and radicals with Peirce, Wedderburn decompositions and the length function. In characteristic two, we adapt the Peirce decomposition to organize the classification, including the field-dependent isomorphism conditions among parametrized families. We also study the varieties of Jordan algebra structures up to dimension three over an algebraically closed field of characteristic two. Besides explicit degenerations and standard arguments, we introduce the alicyclic and characteristic conditions as geometric obstructions to degeneration. We determine the rigid algebras and irreducible components in both dimensions. In dimension three, one component is the nine-dimensional affine space of square-zero products; unlike the other three components, it contains no open orbit.

title: Cyber-physical attack detection approaches in the wide-area measurement system
abstract: Improving situational awareness within the Smart Grid is an effective preventive measure to detect potential anomalies, and avoid their adverse consequences. A wide area measurement system (WAMS) based Phasor Measurement Unit (PMU) can assist in improving visibility within the grid by collecting relevant measurements including magnitude, phase angle, frequency, voltage, and current, with a precise GPS-based timestamp. So far, there are more than 2500 PMUs deployed in the North American power grid, where each of which generates between 30 and 60 samples/s, roughly 1.5 TB/month of streamed data. Thus, processing such large PMU streams requires expensive computational resources and faster algorithms. This paper provides state-of-the-art cyber and physical anomalies in the WAMS and analyses their impact on the integrity and availability of the system. Next, it investigates the current anomaly detection approach in historical and streaming PMU data, including conventional machine learning and hybrid approaches, and assesses their advantages and main drawbacks. Lastly, it sheds light on the importance of handling missing PMU data and concept drifts.

title: Variance-reduced First-order Methods for Finite-sum Function Constrained Convex Optimization
abstract: This paper studies finite-sum convex optimization with convex function constraints, where both the objective $f(x)=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^m f_i(x)$ and the constraint mapping $g(x)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^n g_j(x)$ may have a large number of components. We propose a variance-reduced anchored constraint extrapolation method (VaRAn-ConEx), which combines stochastic component sampling with primal--dual extrapolation for nonlinear function constraints. Relative to stochastic approximation schemes such as ConEx, VaRAn-ConEx~method reduces gradient complexity by using epoch-wise full-gradient correction and variance-reduced estimators for both the objective and constraint components. In the semi-finite case where $n=1$, the method attains gradient complexities $O(\sqrt m/ε)$ under constant steps and $O(m/ε^{1/2}+1/ε^{3/2})$ under nonconstant steps. In the fully finite-sum case, we establish boundedness of the Lagrange multiplier sequence and derive convergence and gradient-complexity bounds for constant and nonconstant step-size policies. Under these policies, we then prove similar gradient complexity with $m$ replaced by $\max\{m,n\}$. We also show acceleration when the finite-sum objective $f$ is strongly convex, irrespective of components $f_i$.

title: Multistable elastic pixels: nematic elasticity for non-volatile positioning of colloidal optical scatterers
abstract: Non-volatile reconfiguration of optical devices, in which a configuration persists without continuous energy input, remains a challenge. We introduce multistable elastic pixels (MEPs), lithographically defined pores filled with a nematic liquid crystal, whose curved ends capture a scattering inclusion in one of two mechanically stable sites. Simulations and experiments show that pore geometry and homeotropic surface anchoring define the energy minima and the height of the barrier between them. This barrier far exceeds thermal energies, stabilizing a scatterer location absent an external field. Colloidal inclusions switch reversibly between sites under transient electric fields. Using arrays of static scatterers, we show that the two positional states produce distinct responses at visible wavelengths, demonstrating the potential of MEPs for reconfigurable devices and metasurfaces. Unlike phase-change and liquid-crystal-tuned approaches, which switch a material surrounding fixed scatterers, MEPs use the nematoelastic energy landscape to move the optical element itself.

title: GAVAGAI: Referential Alignment for Infant-Scale Vision-Language Models via Balanced Optimal Transport
abstract: A child learns which words name which things from roughly 100 million words of input. Vision-language models trained at a comparable scale bind words to referents far less reliably, and we argue that part of the gap is structural: the usual next-token captioning objective has no variable standing for "this word refers to that region," so training applies no direct pressure to ground words. We add such a variable by treating each scene as a small assignment problem between the content words heard and the regions seen, solved as entropic optimal transport under two constraints. First, a word may be assigned to a special NOTHING column instead of any region, which matters because most content words in caregiver speech do not name anything visible. Second, no region may receive more than a bounded share of the assignment mass, a capacity constraint that encodes mutual exclusivity. The alignment step costs about eight Sinkhorn iterations, small next to the vision encoder. In controlled simulation, the naive version of the idea, a row-wise softmax that forces every word onto some region, collapses to 0.000 word-to-picture accuracy under realistic non-reference rates, below the 0.058 of captioning alone, while our two constraints reach 0.075 in that regime and 0.700 on clean input. A one-parameter version of the model reproduces adult cross-situational learning accuracy across three ambiguity conditions (RMSE 0.024). On the SAYCam infant video corpus, adding the alignment loss to a next-token captioning model raises word-to-picture accuracy from 32.4% to 48.7% and localization IoU from 0.18 to 0.38. A contrastive model trained on the same child's data remains stronger on its own benchmark, so our claim is that the loss improves a captioning objective under high non-reference rates, not that it sets a new best.

title: Quantum Dipolar Magnon Drag in Conducting Magnetic Bilayers
abstract: We predict electrical drag between two electrically isolated metallic ferromagnets mediated by quantum dipolar magnon coupling. A charge current in one layer generates a nonequilibrium magnon current whose momentum is transferred across an insulating spacer through interlayer dipolar interactions. The resulting magnon current in the passive layer produces a measurable voltage through electron-magnon scattering. We show the combination of resonant quantum momentum transfer and magnetic tunability through the control of magnetization configurations distinguish quantum dipolar drag from conventional drag mechanism.

title: Spherical Schubert varieties in $GL_n / P$
abstract: Let a general linear group act on a partial flag variety transitively, and consider the induced action of a Levi subgroup $L$. A Schubert variety is $\textit{$L$-spherical}$ if it is stable under the $L$-action and contains a dense open orbit of a Borel subgroup of $L$. It is $\textit{toric}$ if, in addition, $L$ is a torus. In this paper, we give a combinatorial classification of $L$-spherical Schubert varieties in partial flag varieties. This is achieved by applying Lakshmibai-Seshadri paths forming crystal graphs of Demazure modules. Previously, Hodges and Lakshmibai classified $L$-spherical Schubert varieties in Grassmannians. $L$-spherical Schubert varieties in complete flag varieties were treated independently by Gao-Hodges-Yong and Can-Saha. Our classification generalizes and unifies these results.

title: Painlevé VI superintegrability and Heun-Racah algebras
abstract: We study the two fourth-order quantum superintegrable systems in the Euclidean plane that separate in polar coordinates and whose angular potentials are determined by the general four-parameter sixth Painlevé transcendent. One system has an oscillator radial term and the other an extended-Coulomb radial term. For both systems we give the fourth-order quantum integral explicitly, derive the cubic symmetry algebra and its Casimir, and construct a deformed-oscillator realization. At fixed energy the two algebras are specializations of the Heun--Racah algebra. Their structure functions contain the same quartic angular factor, determined by the Painlevé~VI parameters, while different radial factors distinguish oscillator and Coulomb dynamics. The Coulomb integral is obtained by transforming the Cartesian Hermitian symmetry at the operator level. The lower-order terms generated by the polar coordinate change are essential for commutation with the Hamiltonian. The two quantum systems are also related by the Levi-Civita transformation and coupling-constant metamorphosis, which gives a direct correspondence between their Painlevé parameters, algebras, Casimirs and representations. Earlier exceptional-Jacobi models arise at special rational parameter values, whereas the results here apply to the full four-parameter Painlevé~VI family. We also compare the quantum results with the corresponding classical Poisson algebras.

title: Beyond Semantic IDs: Atomic Creator Tokens for Large-Scale Generative Recommendation
abstract: Recommending creators that a user does not yet follow is a cold-start problem: from hundreds of thousands of popular creators and only a short trail of prior engagements, the system must predict the next creator worth surfacing. The prevailing generative recommendation recipe tokenizes each creator into a \emph{Semantic ID} (SID) by quantizing a frozen embedding and trains a language model to generate SIDs. We show that this SID layer, not the language model, is the binding constraint. The creator-to-SID map is many-to-one, so colliding creators must be resolved by a popularity tie-break that caps creator-level recall and favors already-popular creators, and the frozen quantizer stops the training gradient from reaching the creator representation. We propose Atomic Creator Token (ACT), which gives every creator its own vocabulary token trained end-to-end. The map is bijective, so collisions are impossible and inference is a direct top-$k$ over creator logits. In a controlled comparison on production data in which the token layer is the only variable, ACT improves creator-level Recall@15 by 19.8 points ($1.84\times$) over a matched SID baseline, still leads when the SID codebook is enlarged $64\times$, and serves at ${\sim}2.7\times$ lower per-user latency. The advantage carries over to the public KuaiRand dataset, where ACT is the only method that beats a global-popularity baseline, provided each creator token sees enough training examples. In a live A/B test, ACT is directionally positive on every reported metric against both the SID-enhanced and the classic production rankers.

title: Catenary Visibility: A Geometric Framework for Planning with Tethered Robots
abstract: This paper introduces \emph{catenary visibility}, a new geometric visibility concept for a robotic system consisting of a ground robot tethered to an aerial drone. The tether is modeled as an extensible catenary curve with bounded length, providing sustained power and significantly extending operational range. We define a point on the ground plane as \emph{catenary-visible} from a target point in 3D if there exists a collision-free catenary connecting them, given a set of obstacles. This paper introduces a geometric framework for visibility-aware planning of a tethered marsupial system, addressing the computational challenge of determining the feasible deployment locus: the collection of points in the ground plane that are catenary-visible from a given target in 3D space. We begin by solving the 2D subproblem, where the obstacles, target, and the ground vehicle's line of motion are all constrained to a single vertical plane. Our algorithm for this case computes the complete set of feasible launch points along the motion line and simultaneously determines the range of viable cable lengths for each. We also consider the query problem of finding all collision-free length ranges for a given location of the ground robot. Building upon this planar solution, we then generalize the approach to three dimensions, deriving a 3D solution for a constrained class of obstacles.

title: One Waveform, Two Stories: Benchmarking Speech-Acoustic Conflict in Audio-Language Models
abstract: Audio-language models (ALMs) are evaluated on their understanding of both speech and environmental sounds. What remains underexplored is how they respond when spoken claims contradict acoustic evidence within the same recording. We introduce SAC-Bench, a benchmark of intra-audio speech--acoustic conflict comprising 616,031 unique clips from 188 sound-event classes across seven semantic, temporal, and spatial tasks. It pairs environmental recordings with compatible or contradictory synthesized spoken claims and includes audio-only controls where applicable. Across five open-weight ALMs evaluated on semantic and temporal tasks, high audio-only accuracy often coexists with large losses under conflicting claims; Event Identity accuracy is 24.8--46.5 percentage points lower in conflict than compatible conditions. Temporal Order failures persist even when speech follows the complete event sequence, so simultaneous speech--event masking cannot fully explain them. A spatial case study with Spatial-Omni finds lower motion accuracy associated with both spoken claims and the speech source's physical trajectory. Prompt interventions sometimes restore acoustic accuracy, but can also reduce claim-aligned answers without improving grounding or worsen performance. SAC-Bench thus separates acoustic competence, conflict robustness, and intervention effects.

title: Robust Estimation of Prior Parameters in Normal-Normal Empirical Bayes
abstract: Many large-scale A/B testing systems leverage normal-normal empirical Bayes models to improve estimates of treatment impacts and launch decisions. We show that in these models maximum likelihood estimates of the variance of true impacts can be sensitive to a small number of extreme observations. We propose a bounded influence maximum likelihood estimator (BIMLE) that downweights such observations in proportion to their inconsistency with the model, reducing sensitivity while retaining the full sample in estimation. Absent extreme observations, BIMLE coincides with the standard MLE. In an application to A/B tests run at Amazon, BIMLE reduces instability in the estimated prior variance by over 50 percent while downweighting less than 0.1 percent of observations.

title: Quantum superposition of Cosmic String spacetimes
abstract: Since the quantum nature of spacetime is anticipated by a theory of Quantum Gravity, the possibility of spacetime superposition would be a natural consequence. This spacetime interference phenomena could bring us some clues about what effects could be expected over quantum fields and their interaction with matter. In this article, we investigate the effect of the superposition of a Cosmic String spacetime on the Unruh-De Witt detector. This is of interest as the spacetimes possess flat geometry but non-trivial topology. We analyze the effect of the interference of a Cosmic String with different topological charge over the Unruh-De Witt detector response function to vacuum fluctuations. We obtain some quantum interference effects, due to the superposition of spacetimes, which would be absent if a classical probabilistic mixture of spacetimes would be considered. In this manner, we obtain real physical consequences that would be indications of a Quantum Gravity phenomena.

title: Déjà Vu: Cycle-Consistent Re-ranking for Semantic Correspondence
abstract: We propose \emph{Déjà Vu}, a test-time decoding module for semantic correspondence. Matching semantically equivalent keypoints across images of the same object category is challenging due to variations in appearance, viewpoint, and scale. While features from large pretrained vision models carry strong zero-shot correspondence ability, existing methods reduce final matching to greedy top-$1$ nearest-neighbor selection. We show that the correct correspondence appears among the top-ranked candidates far more often than top-$1$ matching achieves: with $30$ candidates, zero-shot features exceed the top-$1$ accuracy of a supervised model. This reveals a \textit{decoding bottleneck} rather than a limit of the representation. Motivated by this observation, we formulate semantic correspondence as a \textit{recall-then-rerank} problem. Our method first nominates an adaptive candidate set, larger when the similarity distribution is ambiguous and smaller when it is confident, then re-ranks the candidates with a graded cycle-consistency score: each candidate is matched back to the source image and penalized by how far its reverse match lands from the original keypoint. The module operates entirely on the similarity matrix already computed by the base method. It consistently improves three representative baselines on SPair-71k, its geometric subset, and PF-Pascal under both unsupervised and weakly supervised settings, with gains of up to $+1.8$ PCK@0.10 on SPair-71k and $+3.4$ PCK@0.15 on PF-Pascal, and $+4.9$ under Keypoint Average Precision.

title: Slowly rotating white dwarfs in f (R, T ) = R + 2λT gravity: structure and stationary tidal response
abstract: We calculate the structure and stationary tidal response of cold carbon fluid white dwarfs in $f(R,T)=R+2λT$ gravity through second order in uniform rotation. Equilibria are compared at fixed baryon number, with angular momentum also conserved during each aligned electric quadrupolar tidal perturbation. Negative coupling increases radii and dimensional tidal deformabilities over the common mass range. For the baryon sequence studied, background readjustment accounts for 95.8--97.5\% of the rotational enhancement at 40\% of each model's Kepler reference frequency. The explicit mixed rotational tidal contribution is positive and numerically resolved, but subdominant. At that spin, the enhancement relative to each coupling's static model decreases from 107.4\% in general relativity to 14.2\% at the most negative coupling, despite its larger absolute deformability. This reduction reflects less relative background expansion and a different Love-number variation.

title: Transient subtraction method: An alternative approach for variance reduction in dissipative particle dynamics
abstract: The efficient and accurate computation of transport coefficients remains a numerical challenge in dissipative particle dynamics (DPD), which can require substantial sampling to control statistical uncertainty. We extend recent results obtained in Langevin dynamics to consider the transient subtraction method for reducing the variance of transport coefficient estimations in DPD. The system is initialised by perturbing equilibrium samples, and its relaxation towards equilibrium is monitored under the reference dynamics. A reference trajectory, initialised at equilibrium and driven by the same Brownian noise, provides a control variate for the transient response. We apply the transient subtraction method to the computation of the mobility and the shear viscosity in a Lennard-Jones fluid in DPD. The shear viscosity is obtained from the time-integrated response of a Fourier observable associated with the longitudinal velocity. Numerical comparisons with the naive transient estimator show that the transient subtraction method reduces the variance at various integration times, and the reduction is more pronounced with a higher friction coefficient. These results indicate that the transient subtraction method is able to improve the statistical precision of transport coefficient estimations in DPD and reduce the number of trajectories needed to attain a prescribed standard error.

title: A Koszul-Type Splitting Theorem for Complex Supermanifolds
abstract: We study the splitting problem for complex supermanifolds using formal exponential maps and Ehresmann connections. We show that every formal exponential map induces a splitting of the underlying supermanifold. Furthermore, we establish that every Ehresmann connection determines a linearization of the infinite jet space, extending the corresponding construction for ordinary manifolds to supermanifolds. For Ehresmann connections preserving the zero section, we construct a formal exponential map in two ways: via the linearization of the infinite jet space and directly from the connection operator. We prove that both constructions yield the same map and induce the same splitting, thereby generalizing Koszul's splitting theorem from linear connections to zero-section-preserving Ehresmann connections. Finally, we provide examples showing that, without this assumption, the two constructions may yield different splittings, or one or both of them may fail to induce a splitting.

title: Dataset and Experimental Testbed for Deep Learning-Based Bluetooth Device Fingerprinting
abstract: AI-enabled wireless networks have emerged as vital components of future-generation wireless communication systems. Among various wireless architectures, Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) networks have attracted significant research interest due to their widespread adoption and low cost. In these networks, deep learning (DL) models can be integrated directly into the physical-layer infrastructure to perform diverse tasks, including environment sensing, localization, radio frequency fingerprinting (RFFP), and signal denoising. While highly effective under their original training configurations, these DL models often fail significantly when deployed in unseen environments---such as different rooms, varying temperature conditions, or altered carrier frequencies. Addressing this limitation requires rigorous benchmarking of models and algorithms against unseen configurations to evaluate their generalization and robustness. To bridge this gap, this paper makes two key contributions: i) we introduce a comprehensive, large-scale wireless BLE dataset consisting of raw IQ transmissions from 31 distinct commercial devices captured across diverse days, locations, environments, temperatures, receiver hardware, and frequency channels; ii) we present a case study evaluating state-of-the-art techniques for domain-robust RFFP to advance real-world AI reliability.

title: C3: Speech-Guided KV Retrieval for Long-Context SpeechLLM Inference
abstract: Speech language models encode audio at a much higher rate than text, causing the KV cache to dominate the memory, bandwidth, and decoding cost of long-form generation. KV retrieval can reduce per-step access by attending to only a query-dependent subset of the cache, but existing methods are designed primarily for text and do not account for the structure of audio attention. We first show that retrieval errors may compound autoregressively into generation drift. We then analyze full audio attention during long-form generation and identify three properties relevant to retrieval: unequal attention concentration across query heads, non-contiguous audio support, and temporal continuity across decoding steps. Guided by these observations, we propose $C^3$(Cluster-Compete-Compete), which organizes audio KVs in a hierarchical key-space index, lets query heads sharing a KV head compete for a common retrieval budget, and adaptively reallocates retrieval resolution through paired split-merge updates. Across long-form speech recognition, translation, and summarization on four SpeechLLMs, $C^3$ achieves the strongest overall performance among retrieval methods under comparable final-KV access budgets, with particularly large gains in the tight-budget regime, while improving long-context decoding efficiency and accelerator-memory scaling.

title: Optimistic Gradient Algorithms with Randomized Coordinate and Variance Reduction Strategies for Composite Inclusions
abstract: In this paper, we consider a class of possibly nonmonotone finite-sum composite inclusions in which evaluating all components or updating all coordinates at every iteration can be computationally expensive. We develop two optimistic gradient frameworks that combine variance reduction with randomized block-coordinate updates. The first framework applies under a blockwise average Lipschitz continuity condition and the existence of a weak-Minty solution. It achieves an $\mathcal{O}(1/k)$ convergence rate for the expected squared residual, and its iterates converge almost surely under mild additional conditions. The second framework relies on a backward-forward reformulation under average co-coercivity and co-hypomonotonicity. It achieves faster $\mathcal{O}(1/k^2)$ and $o(1/k^2)$ rates for the expected squared residual, as well as $o(1/k^2)$ almost-sure rates. For both frameworks, we provide a generic condition on the stochastic estimator that covers mini-batch, loopless SVRG, and a generalized JacSketch-type estimator, and we derive the corresponding oracle complexities under importance-based block sampling. In particular, in highly heterogeneous regimes, the L-SVRG and JacSketch variants attain $\mathcal{O}\big(n + n^{2/3}ε^{-2}\big)$ and $\mathcal{O}\big(n + n^{2/3}ε^{-1}\big)$ oracle complexities for the nonaccelerated and accelerated methods, respectively. Numerical experiments illustrate the effects of variance reduction and block-coordinate sampling, and compare the proposed methods with existing baselines.

title: The Valence and Inner Shell Ionization Properties of Sr I - III by Non-Thermal Electrons in Kilonovae
abstract: The presence of strontium (Z = 38) was identified from spectra of the first multi-messenger kilonova transient, AT2017gfo, with the evolution of its spectral signature indicating a rapidly changing ionization balance. Interpretation of spectra at later times requires a more detailed understanding of recombination and ionization processes, including ionization by `non-thermal' electrons produced by beta decay. Published measurements of the ionization cross sections of Sr I and Sr II show complex structures likely arising from excitation autoionization. Using the Flexible Atomic Code we report calculations of the valence and inner shell ionization cross sections for Sr I, Sr II, and Sr III, and recover similar structures in the ionization cross sections. Though no measurements exist for Sr III, the calculations suggest negligible contributions from excitation autoionization. These new data are incorporated into Spencer-Fano models of non-thermal electron degradation and coupled to an ionization balance solver. The effects of excitation autoionization, treated as excitation with the additional production of an Auger electron, on the degradation spectra of non-thermal are explored. Calculations at both level- and configuration-average resolution return ion fractions that agree within 5-20%. The calculations probe the impact of including final-charge-state-resolved branching ratios for inner shell ionization which result in multi-ionization events from successive Auger cascades. Omission of these branching ratios is shown to have large impacts on the ionization balance. The calculated cross sections will be provided on Zenodo.

title: The L1157 filament as traced in HNCO by the LMT
abstract: Context. The L1157 outflow is a prototype of chemically active outflows where to look for molecular species linked to complex chemistry. Aims. With the aim of imaging the large (parsec) scale structure of key prebiotic molecules, we have mapped the whole blue-lobe of the L1157 outflow with the Large Millimeter Telescope (LMT), proving the potential of this facility to detect weak and extended molecular emission. Methods. Isocyanic acid, HNCO, an important precursor of complex chemistry, was chosen to be observed in its (4_0,4-3_0-3) transition at 87.925 GHz with the SEQUOIA focal-plane array, covering an area of 3x3 arcmin2 centered at the position of the main shock L1157-B1, which included a large portion of the vicinity of the protostellar region. Results. The HNCO emission was detected not only from the outflow but it also was found tracing a structure of about 0.3 pc in length, corresponding to the filament from which the protostellar system was born. Conclusions. The HNCO molecule was found to be a tracer of the densest part of filaments in molecular clouds, and given its importance in the formation of more complex molecules, its presence in the cold, quiescent filamentary gas indicates that the building blocks of complex chemistry are already well established in stages prior to protostellar warming or shocks. By allowing the detection of structures related with the filament, these observations proved the LMT potentialities to map weak and extended components in molecular clouds.

title: Decomposing Irregular Time Series into Interpretable Temporal Patterns with Mixture-of-Experts
abstract: Irregularly-spaced sequential data, such as transaction logs, encode multi-scale temporal structure that is critical for prediction but difficult to recover explicitly with standard sequence models, which often trade interpretability for performance. We introduce MoTIF, an interpretable framework using mixture-of-experts (MoE) attention to decompose irregular time series into temporal patterns spanning minute-to-year scales. Each expert is trained via temporal alignment that induces attention specialization to a designated cyclical or within-range pattern, with label-free routing supervision that learns to activate the correct expert from patterns present in the data. On synthetic data with known temporal structure, MoTIF recovers correct routing well above chance (0.389/0.829 for range/cyclical patterns vs. 0.091 random) and outperforms all baselines, including a standard transformer and an unspecialized MoE, on next-value prediction. On a public credit card transaction dataset, MoTIF achieves higher macro-F1 than all baselines for next-amount prediction. Its learned routing reveals structure a black-box model cannot: transactions are governed primarily by intraday and short-interval rhythms, while fraudulent transactions show bursty, calendar-agnostic timing versus the steadier periodicity of legitimate ones. On downstream fraud detection, MoTIF matches standard transformer and MoE baselines and clearly outperforms recent sequential recommendation models used as embedding baselines. These results show that decomposing temporal structure into interpretable, expert-specific patterns need not sacrifice predictive accuracy, offering a practical route to sequence models that are both accurate and auditable in high-stakes settings. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/MoTIF-82E4.

title: Reading the Count: Prediction Markets and Brazil's 2026 Presidential Election
abstract: We rebuild the public count of Brazil's 2026 presidential runoff minute by minute from the electoral court's section-level records and compare it with every trade on Kalshi and Polymarket. A projection published live on the night gave the eventual winner, Lula, a probability of 0.998 from 19:15, with 1.6% of sections counted. The markets reached 0.9 at 20:24, with 46% counted. Read as the projection's central estimate with a wider uncertainty, their prices imply a standard deviation of the final margin about four times the live projection's, and about twice that of a section-level projection calibrated on the 2018 runoff, the earlier night with the largest errors. Valued at these projections, takers' purchases of Lula after the count resumed had an expected profit of 4 to 18 cents per Kalshi contract after fees; valued at a state-level extrapolation of the count, it was zero. During a two-hour suspension of the count the markets gave Lula 0.25 to 0.44, below every reading we compute afterwards from the sections then public, none of which was available live. On the first-round night, when the headline count showed the eventual leader ahead from its first file, the same markets were faster than our projection.

title: Efficient NPN Classification for Large Functions using Graph Neural Network
abstract: Two Boolean functions are considered NPN equivalent if one can be transformed into the other by negating inputs, permuting inputs, or negating the output. Efficient NPN classification is valuable in fields such as logic synthesis, quantum computing, and information theory. However, exact NPN classification demands exhaustive enumeration of all possible input permutations and negations. Its complexity grows exponentially, making it impractical for larger functions with more inputs. In this paper, we introduce the first learning-based formulation for NPN classification by recasting it as NPN action prediction. Our method represents Boolean functions as AND-Inverter Graphs (AIGs) and applies a bidirectional heterogeneous graph neural network to predict input negations, output negation, and input permutations. To mitigate the non-canonicity of logic networks, we further introduce graph rewriting techniques that reduce structural ambiguity and recover useful symmetries before prediction. Experimental results show that NPN action prediction is learnable, that the resulting canonicalization quality improves over heuristic baselines, and that on practical benchmarks our method approaches exact methods on tractable cases while scaling to functions with up to 16 inputs.

title: Autoformalization for Ambiguous Inputs: Precision, Coverage, and Cost across SQL and Logical Forms
abstract: Agentic systems translate natural-language requests into executable artifacts while managing ambiguity and inference cost. We evaluate seven autoformalization workflows on SQL and first-order logic benchmarks for ambiguous inputs. Across five SQL workflows, the raw model leads with F1 of 53.35% on AMBROSIA and 60.85% on AmbiQT. On AmP, DRIFT gains 15.98 F1 points over the raw model at 2.03 times its token cost, whereas LoC uses 18.65 times the raw model's tokens with lower F1. Within AutoCedar, structured interpretation lowers F1 by 6.44-6.95 points and raises AMBROSIA token use 2.2-fold. Paired reviewer comparisons show modest Kimi K3 gains of 1.93 points on AMBROSIA and 2.04 on AmbiQT. Clear-ambiguous AMBROSIA analysis shows greater relative stability for AutoCedar, with a smaller F1 drop than the raw model (11.46 vs. 16.68 points), alongside lower aggregate F1 (50.16% vs. 53.35%). Autoformalization alone does not guarantee robustness to ambiguity: the tested additions offer no uniformly effective remedy, making accuracy, ambiguity handling, and inference cost joint design requirements.

title: CHIME All-sky Multiday Pulsar Stacking Search (CHAMPSS): Power Spectrum Injections and Survey Sensitivity
abstract: Artificial signal injection into real data is a key tool in time-domain radio astronomy, with particular import to the study of pulsars and Fast Radio Bursts (FRBs). Many surveys inject into the time series to probe observational biases impacting the detection of radio transients. In the case of the CHIME All-sky Multiday Pulsar Stack Search (CHAMPSS), the computational demands of both hardware and software time series injections force an alternative approach.
