However, existing approaches typically rely on a single policy trained with outcome-reward reinforcement learning (RL), which often suffers from long-horizon plan failures where the implicit plan drifts from valid strategies, especially for small LMs with limited capacity. To address this, we propose Multi-Level Reasoning (MLR), which reformulates long-CoT generation as a two-level stochastic process. A high-level planner generates structured step descriptors specifying both the reasoning mode and the semantic subgoal. The low-level executor then produces detailed reasoning conditioned on these descriptors, forming an alternating plan--execute loop. To maintain scalability, we adopt a minimal design where the base model serves as the low-level policy and a lightweight LoRA module implements the high-level policy. For training, we observe that outcome-reward RL provides sparse and delayed feedback for long trajectories (e.g., several thousand tokens), hindering credit assignment. We therefore introduce iterative Step-DPO, a process-level preference optimization scheme that leverages Twisted Sequential Monte Carlo (TSMC) to provide scalable stepwise supervision. This yields more effective training, improved stability, and higher accuracy. Extensive experiments on challenging math, science, and logical reasoning benchmarks show that, under the same reduced data budget (10% SFT and 5% preference relative to the DeepSeek-R1 distillation setup), MLR outperforms both SFT-based distillation and strong RL/preference-optimization baselines across multiple base models and tasks. Moreover, MLR exhibits slower performance degradation on long-horizon reasoning, demonstrating stronger robustness under extended CoT generation.

title: Words Caught in the Heart: Simulating Person-Specific Expression for Self-Opaque Clients in Psychotherapy
abstract: Psychotherapy clients may experience distress before they can coherently describe it, and their expression changes with emotion, perceived safety, and trust. Large language model-based client simulators often rely on clinically organized case descriptions, which can encourage responses explaining the client's difficulties more clearly than their current understanding warrants. We propose Pandora, a psychotherapy client simulation framework that models how psychological experience becomes situated, individual expression. Pandora updates psychological and relational states in response to therapist interventions, constructs subjective appraisals and attributions, and plans response content and strategy. A separate expression planner combines these decisions with language patterns distilled from the client's utterances to guide linguistic realization. We evaluate Pandora against five baselines on 115 cases from four counseling and motivational interviewing datasets. It achieves the highest expression similarity and overall disclosure-alignment score among the compared systems. In a four-evaluator study of 45 matched disclosure items, Pandora receives AI-like judgments in 7.2% of ratings, compared with 43.3--67.2% for the baselines and 35.6% without expression planning. The ablation also reduces expression similarity. These results support explicit expression planning in client simulation to improve alignment with individual language patterns and reduce perceived AI-like expression in the evaluated setting.

title: Kinetics of Self-Organization in One Component Active Matter Systems
abstract: We study an inherently nonequilibrium system consisting of self-propelled particles using molecular dynamics simulation in $d=2$. The system self-organizes through quorum-sensing interactions characterized by an interaction range $λ$ and a parameter $c_{\mathrm{th}}$. When the local concentration sensed by a particle, represented by an auxiliary variable $c_i(t)$ exceeds $c_{\mathrm{th}}$, its self-propulsion velocity abruptly drops to zero, leading to the emergence of particle rich domains. For small $λ$, we observe a droplet-like morphology of clusters, which crosses over to a bicontinuous structure as $λ$ increases. We confirm this transition by computing the eccentricity of the domains. Next, we characterize the evolving domain morphologies using equal-time correlation function $C(r,t)$ and structure factor $S(k,t)$ of the density field. For a fixed $λ$, the scaled $C(r,t)$'s at different times are indistinguishable from each other, indicating dynamical scaling. However, at a fixed time $t$, the scaling functions differ for different values of $λ$, confirming a $λ$-dependent morphological transition. In the large-wavevector limit ($k\rightarrow\infty$), the tail of $S(k,t)$ consistently follows the Porod's law: $S(k,t)\sim k^{-3}$. Furthermore, the average domain size $L(t)$ exhibits a power-law growth, $L(t)\sim t^{1/3}$, independent of $λ$.

title: LM6-CastBench: A Geometry-Aware Simulation Dataset for Transient Thermal Prediction in LM6 Sand Casting
abstract: Transient thermal fields during solidification connect casting process conditions and cooling behaviour to the formation of defect-prone regions in aluminum cast ings. Repeatedly solving this thermal problem across geometries and process conditions is computationally expensive, motivating data-driven surrogate models. However, existing machine-learning studies on casting thermal behaviour rely on study-specific simulation databases that do not support reproducible geometry-level benchmarking. We introduce LM6-CastBench, an open simulation dataset for geometry-aware learning of transient thermal fields in LM6 aluminum sand casting, combining three geometry families, ten variants per family, five pouring tempera tures, and three mould temperatures (450 geometry-process cases in total). Each case retains CAD geometry, unstructured mesh connectivity, spatial descriptors, process metadata, and time-resolved nodal temperatures. We benchmark a point wise MLP against a spatially structured U-Net under geometry-level data splits; the U-Net reduces temperature-field errors by a large margin, with the biggest gains on geometries with localized features and abrupt section changes. LM6-CastBench gives researchers a reproducible dataset and benchmark for geometry-aware surro gate modelling of casting thermal behaviour.

title: Discovering Models for Experimental Quantum Systems with Agentic AI
abstract: A central obstacle in realizing color center cavity-QED-based quantum technologies is inhomogeneity, or disorder, among individual emitters. As the number of emitters increases, so does the complexity of the experimental data, making it difficult to quantify the present physical mechanisms of disorder. Here we introduce an artificial intelligence-driven model discovery framework in which a large language model (LLM)-based agent, equipped with tools and a structured workflow, proposes candidate Hamiltonian and Lindbladian models, generates computational tools, and quantitatively evaluates competing physical hypotheses. We apply the workflow to three previously published experimental cavity-QED datasets collected from color centers in diamond and silicon carbide. Across the experiments, the agent successfully identifies physical models for the system and characterizes the disorder. In assessing reproducibility, we find that run-to-run variability is concentrated primarily in the research plan generation step, while the computational analysis itself is substantially more consistent. Our results suggest that structured LLM agent workflows can support model discovery from quantum optical experimental data while simultaneously allowing for human expert supervision and collaboration.

title: Log-Driven Semantic Tuning for Mixed Integer Programming Solvers
abstract: Automated configuration of mixed-integer programming (MIP) solvers largely relies on black-box optimization. Each trial requires an expensive solver run and provides only a scalar outcome, so tuning can require many such evaluations. Human experts take a different approach. They inspect solver logs, identify performance bottlenecks, and adjust the parameters that address them. We propose Log-Driven Semantic Tuning (LDST), which uses a large language model (LLM) to automate this process. LDST extracts compact diagnostics from solver logs, uses the LLM to propose sparse edits to the current best configuration based on parameter meanings and observed solver behavior, and validates each proposal before execution. A regime-adaptive objective selects the tuning signal according to the information available from a time-limited run, while a log-based completion signal estimates completion time from branch-and-bound tree growth recorded in ordinary solver logs, so that solved and unsolved runs share one time scale. On 215 instances from five benchmark sets, LDST reduces geometric-mean loss by 43.9% on easy instances and 16.7% on intermediate instances relative to the best of SMAC3, RBFOpt, and random search. In both regimes, LDST achieves a lower loss with 10 proposals than any of these baselines achieves with 50. Configurations that LDST tunes on a single instance also transfer better than baseline configurations to unseen instances of the same family.

title: X-ray magnetic circular dichroism in altermagnets: insights from symmetry
abstract: Altermagnets are a unique subset of antiferromagnets possessing ferromagnet-like responses that are odd in the Néel vector, making X-ray magnetic circular dichroism (XMCD) a natural probe of ground state altermagnetic order. Because the relativistic ingredient of XMCD at the $L$-edge is supplied predominantly by core-level spin--orbit coupling (SOC), the dichroic signal can reflect the non-relativistic order of the valence electrons. Here we develop a complete symmetry framework for XMCD in altermagnets (AMs) preserving the crystalline unit cell. We tabulate the symmetry-allowed optical Hall vector, anisotropic magnetic dipole (AMD), and underlying octupolar components for all magnetic point groups, thereby identifying the experimental geometries that maximize the XMCD signal. We show that only twelve magnetic point groups, none with a rotation axis of order three or higher, are compatible with both altermagnetism and finite XMCD. By extending the Landau theory of collinear AMs, we connect these relativistic constraints to the spin--orbit-free order. We show that the AMD is forced to vanish at zero valence SOC in conventional antiferromagnets, and that every AM sublattice structure allows the Hall vector and AMD at linear or cubic order in the Néel vector; whether the resulting XMCD is nonzero depends on the Néel vector orientation at finite SOC. The Landau theory thus fixes the Néel-vector dependence of the XMCD for all AM candidates, and separates $d$-wave AMs, whose signal is inherited from a non-relativistic AMD, from $g$- and $i$-wave AMs, whose signal requires valence SOC or core--valence multiplet effects. We illustrate these predictions with first-principles Bethe--Salpeter calculations of $L$-edge XMCD for five representative altermagnetic materials and one conventional antiferromagnet.

title: The distribution of $απ$ modulo one in $\mathbb{F}q(T)$: beyond Matomäki's exponent
abstract: Let $α$ be an element of $\Fq((1/T))$ which is not in $\Fq(T)$. We ask how small $\nrm{απ}$ can be made when $π$ runs over irreducible polynomials, and write $θ(α)$ for the largest exponent $θ$ such that $\nrm{απ}<|π|^{-θ}$ has infinitely many solutions. The analogue of Matomäki's exponent, $θ(α)\ge\frac13$, was proved by Baier and the author, and it is the natural limit of \chg{methods based on} the Riemann Hypothesis. In this paper we go beyond it. For odd characteristic $p$ and $q$ large in terms of $p$ and $θ$, we prove that $θ(α)\geθ$ for every $α$ and every $θ<\sqrt2-1=0.414\ldots$, and for every $θ<\frac12$ when $α$ has bounded partial quotients. The main tools are an exact count of points in affine subspaces of $\Fq[T]$, a splitting of these subspaces into long arithmetic progressions, and the results of Sawin and Shusterman on the Möbius function along such progressions.

title: XLA from the Trenches: Correctness on TPU Workloads at Scale
abstract: Accelerating modern foundational models has pushed domain-specific compilers toward increasingly complex, multi-tiered optimization pipelines. However, this heavy optimization focus introduces delicate tradeoffs between peak execution performance and correctness. Subtle codegen defects can trigger numerical degradation and memory or buffer corruption, invalidating multi-million-dollar training runs and degrading live serving quality without raising obvious compiler errors. In this paper, we present a battle-tested methodology for verifying and triaging Google's XLA:TPU compiler at hyperscale. We leverage fuzzing techniques, combining synthetic program generation with real production traces, while orchestrating AI agent swarms to autonomously generate stress tests, reproduce failures, and draft fixes. To pinpoint root causes in full workloads, we pair this with a hierarchical differential pipeline that bisects large graphs down to individual failing operations inside fused kernels. Deployed in production, our framework has already driven the resolution of over 142 compiler bugs (with 103 additional findings under review), from which we distill pragmatic lessons learned.

title: Communication-Efficient Model-Distributed Inference for CBRS Radar Detection at the Edge
abstract: The Citizens Broadband Radio Service (CBRS) shares the 3550-3700 MHz band between incumbent radar systems and commercial LTE/5G users, so radar activity must be detected accurately and promptly. Spectrogram-based YOLO detectors can localize coexisting radar and cellular signals, but running them on resource-constrained edge devices is challenging. Model-distributed inference (MDI) can increase throughput by partitioning a model across edge devices. Using an end-to-end pipeline from raw I/Q samples to on-device detection, we show that partitioning recent YOLO generations incurs high activation-transfer costs due to their multi-scale structures. To reduce these costs, we propose CEDAR, a communication-efficient, edge-distributed architecture for radar detection. Its RF-aware detector, CEDAR-YOLO, removes YOLO's multi-scale neck and two of its three detection scales, leaving a single-scale path with independently configured frequency and time resolutions, which lowers the communication cost of partitioning. Its compression-aware MDI framework, CEDAR-MDI, integrates lightweight activation compressors and selects, for each compressor, the partition that minimizes the pipeline bottleneck. On an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano testbed with real-world over-the-air data, CEDAR-YOLO reduces the parameter count by 35-57% and model inference time by 16-33%, and CEDAR-MDI achieves up to $3.27\times$ the throughput of single-device inference, with detection quality preserved in both cases.

title: Lorentzian entropy, subgaussian matrix concentration, and sharp functional inequalities for all matroids
abstract: We prove complete entropy contraction for homogeneous Lorentzian laws and derive subgaussian matrix concentration and sharp functional inequalities for every matroid. Uniform retention of $\ell$ out of $r$ particles contracts matrix entropy by the optimal universal factor $\ell/r$, in every finite matrix dimension and positive field, including repeated labels. The matrix Laplace comparison retains matrix variance and arbitrary Hermitian offsets. It gives subgaussian bounds for arbitrary Hermitian observables with bounded exchange differences, and Chernoff and Bernstein bounds for basis sums. Every unit-edge matroid basis graph satisfies the cube's small-set and Gross inequalities, with equality classified and optimal universal complete entropy-decay rate four. Its spectrum lies in $\{0,2\}\cup[3,\infty)$, with binary direct-factor contrasts spanning the eigenspace at two. We classify extremal down-up eigenfunctions, resolving Alaniz Pintos's degree-one conjecture and the equality problem for the Feder--Mihail walk. For degree at least two, every matrix entropy extremizer extends uniquely from its two-particle marginal. Equality depends only on the normalized pair law, with noncommutativity confined to mutually exclusive labels. We classify power-entropy extremizers for $1<p<2$ and give a fourth-order criterion for affine equality. Retained-level Gibbs reconstruction has sharp dimension-independent stability. For multiaffine laws whose generating polynomial and complement are Lorentzian, we determine the exact simultaneous all-field quantum marginal and matrix Hölder regions and classify the sharp half-marginal fields. Connected sharp laws are determinantal through rank three; stable nondeterminantal examples exist in every higher rank.

title: Autonomous Analysis of Thermoelectric Materials Big Data by Multi-Agentic AI and Construction of a Knowledge Base and Specialized AI
abstract: Large databases of paper-derived experimental materials data hide essential information on materials. Their analysis is demanding, large-scale and complex, making manual knowledge extraction very difficult. To address this challenge, we developed Multi-Agentic AI (MAA) for automated, autonomous analysis of materials experimental big data and a specialized AI built on the obtained knowledge. MAA's nine role-specific AI agents, under predefined instructions and quality checks, autonomously perform data extraction, compositional feature generation, machine-learning modeling, feature-importance analysis and knowledge-base recording, iterating while inheriting previous knowledge. Delegating numerical processing to code makes large-scale data tractable; recording every choice and result enables later tracing to sources. In four thermoelectric-data experiments varying theme and cycle counts, the knowledge graph grew: knowledge clustered by theme and vocabulary was shared across themes. The specialized AI, searching and reading these records, answered materials questions citing sources. Retrospective verification also revealed errors, traced through the records to their sources.

title: AgentPRO: Coordinating Compiler Optimizations for LLM Agent Workflows
abstract: LLM agents repeatedly return to a model to generate actions and interpret tool results, incurring repeated context processing and generation overhead. Yet a value needed to execute an action need not be observed by the model to generate that action. This distinction creates an optimization opportunity: reconsider where model decisions are necessary, together with the work performed between them. We present AgentPRO, a compiler framework for optimizing agent workflows as execution information becomes available. AgentPRO organizes planned duties, generation regions, and concrete operations in a hierarchical representation, distinguishing execution dependencies from observations required for generation. Region transformations combine compatible duties into fewer model requests, while operation transformations reduce redundant context and tool work. These scopes interact: eliminating a redundant read can remove an observation requirement that otherwise separates generation regions. AgentPRO coordinates transformations using initial plans, current observations, and historical execution profiles through just-in-time, adaptive, and profile-guided optimization. Runtime guards check state-dependent assumptions and retain fallback paths. We implement guarded workflow transformations for AppWorld agents. On 115 tasks selected by successful historical baseline executions, automatic AgentPRO reduces all-attempt mean token consumption by 41.85% and mean component time by 6.61% relative to those baselines, successfully completing 110 of 115 tasks.

title: Multivariate diagonal harmonics: character polynomials and proofs of two conjectures of Bergeron
abstract: We prove Bergeron's Hook-Components and Coefficient-Length conjectures for the Vandermonde polarization module and full diagonal harmonics in every rank and number of alphabets. Hook-label characters are elementary skewings of the alternating character, and the maximal Schur length in label $μ$ is $n-μ_1$. We compute character and dimension polynomials of diagonal coinvariants in every bosonic--fermionic superspace for $D\ge3$, $n\ge\max\{D,2D-6\}$, answering Church--Ellenberg--Farb's character and dimension questions. For augmented commutative algebras in characteristic zero, we construct natural two-Schur presentations and filtered free resolutions with one Schur generator in each homological degree. For polynomial algebras, specialization to orthogonal idempotents identifies the first unstable correction for every nonempty tail $τ$ and degree $D>|τ|$. The stable threshold $n\ge D+τ_1$ is sharp when the row dimension is at least $\ell(τ)$. First parabolic algebras recover finite jets, their multiplication and their maps. Selected-label lifts give uniform Vandermonde generation through degree $D$ for $D\ge3$, $n\ge2D-3$, and disjoint-label products generate every first occurrence for positive integral row weights. Constructive degree reflection determines all two-column moment homology and generates its first syzygies from degree $n+1$; two-column Vandermonde generation reduces to degree $n-1$. Invariants and harmonics separate through the character range and through degree $n$ in two alphabets. The hook identities also give the fully graded sign component of the $t=0$, $(1,2)$-superspace Theta conjecture.

title: Accessibility to Higher Education and Inter-regional Mobility
abstract: We develop an equilibrium model of the undergraduate higher education market that incorporates interregional mobility for enrollment. An individual chooses a college to attend, seeking to maximize utility depending on the quality of education and the costs of attendance. Costs include tuition fees, the effort required to pass the entrance exam, and moving costs from one's hometown to the region where the college is located. Each college admits students whose entrance exam scores exceed a certain threshold, which we call the college's qualifying score. In our model, the qualifying score of each college is determined endogenously as the shadow price of the constraint that the number of enrolled students must not exceed capacity. We structurally estimate the model's parameters by simulating equilibrium using Japanese data. Based on empirical results and counterfactual experiments, we evaluate the welfare costs of disparities in access to higher education due to uneven spatial distribution of colleges among regions.

title: TopoQuant: Topological Framework to Characterize Behavioral Shifts in Quantized Large Language Models
abstract: Post-training quantization (PTQ) reduces the com putational cost of large language models (LLMs), but it can introduce internal structural and behavioral changes that are not captured by traditional metrics such as accuracy and per plexity. We present TopoQuant, a topological framework that uses topological data analysis (TDA) to quantify structural drift in self-attention weights and relate it to behavioral changes in quantized LLMs. Across four LLM families and multiple quantization levels, we show that topological drift remains stable at moderate compression levels but increases sharply below 4 bit precision, closely tracking declines in attention agreement. Our results reveal a strong relationship between topological drift and attention agreement, indicating that structural changes in model parameters closely reflect behavioral degradation under quantization. We further demonstrate that topological features can accurately predict attention consistency using lightweight machine learning models, achieving R2 scores of up to 0.85. Predicting attention agreement enables efficient assessment of be havioral consistency in quantized LLMs, allowing quantization induced degradation to be detected without running expensive downstream tasks. The results indicate that topological drift pro vides an efficient early-warning signal for quantization-induced degradation and can help identify safe compression limits without extensive downstream evaluation.

title: Completing the classification of Hopf superalgebras of dimension up to 10
abstract: We introduce a family of semisimple Hopf superalgebras obtained from abelian extensions. Using this family and bosonization, we complete the classification of Hopf superalgebras of dimension up to 10 over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero. We also determine the duals of the semisimple classes with nonzero odd part and give tables of the complete classification.

title: Evidence-grounded large language models guide perovskite solar cell design and optimization
abstract: Using large language models to interpret experimental evidence, design discriminating experiments and formulate well-supported mechanistic explanations remains a central challenge in materials research. Here we establish PSM-Bench, an 800-question benchmark developed by perovskite researchers to evaluate scientific reasoning in perovskite photovoltaics. We also introduce OpenPerov, an expert-informed language-model framework that learns from expert-calibrated evidence records reconstructed from 4,035 training articles; these records link experimental strategies, controls and observations to mechanistic interpretations. Structured-evidence adaptation outperformed conventional question-answer training, and OpenPerov Flash ranked first among 13 closed-book systems. OpenPerov Pro raised Scientific Mastery further, from 87.6 to 89.1, by revising selected passages with retrieved evidence. On questions derived from subsequent studies, both models also outscored expert-authored answers. In an experimental test of self-assembled monolayer design, OpenPerov selected a K analogue that outperformed the Na analogue preferred by experts. Devices incorporating the selected contact reached a power conversion efficiency of 27.05% and retained 96.74% of their initial efficiency after 1,000 h of dark thermal ageing at 85 $^\circ$C. These results show that reconstructed scientific reasoning provides an effective basis for building domain models that interpret experiments and inform materials design.

title: PREM: Prediction-Regulated Memory for Robot Manipulation
abstract: A robot's next action can depend on recent motion or earlier visual evidence absent from its current observation. A recurrent visual-memory architecture can retain this history in a visual state, but its usefulness depends on what the state represents and how it is updated with new observations. We introduce Prediction-Regulated Memory (PREM), a framework that uses action-conditioned future prediction to guide both memory learning and updating in vision-language-action policies. During training, predicting future visual features provides temporal supervision for memory learning. During execution, PREM compares current visual features with the prediction made at the preceding decision and uses the spatially normalized prediction discrepancy to regulate updates to the visual state at each spatial location. The updated visual state supplies temporal context for action generation alongside current observations. Built on $π_{0.5}$, PREM improves average success rate from 9.63% to 20.74% on DOMINO dynamic manipulation tasks and from 14.4% to 83.8% on the RMBench M(1) memory-dependent setting. Further evaluations on LIBERO and LIBERO-Pro show improvements in general manipulation and robustness to spatial perturbations. PREM incurs a mean inference overhead of 7.7 ms on a single NVIDIA H800 GPU.

title: From Confounding to Counterfactuals: A Cross-Layer Causal Model for RAN Scheduling
abstract: Data-driven control in radio access networks (RANs) selects resource allocations using associations between control actions and key performance indicators (KPIs) learned from network telemetry. Because the shared radio environment influences both the scheduler's decisions and the resulting performance, a bias known as confounding, such associations overstate the effect of an allocation and misdirect resources toward user equipment (UEs) that cannot benefit. Moreover, individual UEs respond heterogeneously to the same decision, so even a corrected average effect does not identify which UEs gain from additional resources. While causal inference has recently been applied to RANs, existing approaches do not model the cross-layer mechanisms that connect an allocation to its outcome. In this paper, a hierarchical structural causal model (H-SCM) spanning the PHY, MAC, and network layers is proposed that separates cell-load confounding from UE-specific response heterogeneity. In particular, a counterfactual scheduling problem is formulated in which physical resource block (PRB) allocations are selected using per-UE counterfactual goodput rather than observational conditional averages. This problem is solved via a pipeline combining constrained causal discovery, structural-equation fitting, and abduction-action-prediction. Simulations demonstrate that naive observational estimation overstates the full-PRB response by 73.3%, whereas adjustment for cell-load confounding reduces the relative error to 9.8%. Held-out interventions are predicted with a coefficient of determination of 0.988. Counterfactual scheduling achieves a mean relative loss in total cell goodput below 0.5% against the ground-truth optimum, compared with 2.0-2.9% for a neural-network baseline.

title: Structural Dual Adaptation for Safe Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Primal-dual methods enforce safety constraints in reinforcement learning through Lagrangian relaxation. For a fixed policy, the exact bounded multiplier response exhibits bang-bang switching at the constraint boundary. Practical gradient updates can oscillate through coupling with policy optimization. We propose Structural DuaL Adaptation (SDLA), which replaces this bang-bang response with a unique continuous response through current-cost centering, trajectory weighting, and quadratic regularization. We characterize activation thresholds and response sensitivity. Ternary search computes multipliers without a dual gradient stepsize. For entropy-regularized tabular policies, we bound equilibrium constraint violations alongside reward gaps. We establish convergence of delayed updates under mild assumptions. Neural PPO/SAC experiments on OmniSafe and HASARD demonstrate competitive rewards with improved constraint tracking. On HASARD, PPO-SDLA achieves higher reported mean reward than the human baseline in six of eighteen settings while meeting the respective mean-cost budgets, including four with lower mean cost. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first report of higher mean reward at lower mean cost than the human baseline across multiple HASARD settings.

title: Equal Hamming Weights at Fixed Root Order and Applications to Constacyclic MDS Codes
abstract: For a fixed positive integer $n>1$, we study the prime powers $q$ coprime to $n$ for which all monic irreducible factors of $Φ_n$ over $\F_q$ have the same coefficient Hamming weight. Cyclotomic orbit coefficients give a finite, effective classification of these fields. Outside finitely many computable characteristics, every factor has the support of its characteristic-zero orbit polynomial; the uniform condition $p>2^{φ(n)}$ suffices. In each remaining characteristic, extension exponents reduce to divisors of $\ord_n(p)$, and an integer variance identity expressed by polynomial gcd degrees decides equal weight. The same coefficient data determine the full weight distribution. As an application, we prove that an MDS constacyclic code with an irreducible generator forces every irreducible polynomial of the same root order to have full support, including factors associated with different constacyclic constants. This yields a uniform gcd and norm obstruction. We develop its short-multiplier extension, give a prime-order cubic family, and establish an explicit quadratic-residue exclusion without a prime-square alphabet or a near-square length hypothesis.

title: ElectroChemLLM: A Multimodal LLM Pipeline for High-Fidelity Electrochemical Informatics
abstract: Electrochemistry is central to solving many modern-day challenges, including energy storage systems for a sustainable future, and its advancement relies heavily on the data from past findings. Existing automated pipelines are limited by text-only architectures, context fragmentation, and numerical hallucinations - collectively preventing accurate, large-scale curation of property databases. We introduce ElectrochemLLM, a multimodal information extraction pipeline that jointly identifies structured electrochemical records encompassing electrolyte compositions, electrode materials, cell configurations, and their measured physicochemical properties from unstructured scientific PDFs at scale. By combining hybrid document parsing with vision-capable LLM orchestration, the pipeline extracts verifiable, structured data across text, tables, and figures. Evaluated on the battery-electrolyte subset of our manually annotated benchmark of 232 papers, ElectrochemLLM achieves an F-1 score of 0.97, and has been applied to curate ElectroChemDB, a structured database spanning 15,000 electrochemical research articles. We demonstrate the utility of this resource by training machine learning models for electrolyte property prediction, illustrating a complete pathway from unstructured literature to predictive materials discovery.

title: Doubly-periodic instanton via the ADHM method and the self-dual monopole-center vortex chain
abstract: Calorons, i.e., instantons on $\mathbb{R}^3\times S^1$, with nontrivial asymptotic holonomy decompose into $N$ fundamental monopole constituents. This suggests that a doubly-periodic Yang--Mills instanton on $\mathbb{R}^2\times T^2$ may admit a description in terms of a periodic array of monopole constituents. Starting from the Atiyah--Drinfeld--Hitchin--Manin (ADHM) construction, we derive the $2$d Abelian Hitchin system with impurities as a dual description of the doubly-periodic instanton. We then give a prescription for reconstructing the instanton from the Green's function of this system, assuming a scaling ansatz for the ultraviolet divergences induced by the delta-function impurities. In the far-field limit with strongly anisotropic torus periods, we extend the analysis of Bruckmann and van Baal for multi-calorons and identify an alternating chain of BPS and Kaluza--Klein (KK) monopole constituents: The monopole-center vortex chain arises from the non-Abelian self-dual field especially when an 't Hooft twist cuts the torus into the $1/N$ fragment.

title: Bridging Singular Learning Theory and Mechanistic Interpretability at the Billion-Parameter Scale
abstract: Mechanistic interpretability (MI) explains a computation in a trained network by identifying the components and variables that implement it and testing them with interventions. Singular learning theory (SLT) describes the same network through the geometry of the loss around its parameters, summarized by the local learning coefficient. In pretrained language models the two have not been compared: SLT's estimates at this scale concern whole models or components whose roles were not independently established, and the estimator, which averages the loss over parameter settings drawn near the trained ones, has had no reference for how far those draws may move the parameters. We show that both are functions of one object, the map from a component's parameters to the model's predictions under inputs and interventions, whose first derivatives determine the Fisher information, the learning coefficient, and intervention effects, and whose higher derivatives add a quartic correction and pairwise terms. We test this correspondence in Pythia-1B on Dyck bracket matching at all 154 training checkpoints, against a five-stage circuit identified by interventions. We measure the local geometry of all 144 components inside the region where predictions are preserved, with the Fisher spectrum at every checkpoint, which gives the quadratic part of the learning-coefficient estimate at every temperature. Changes of the Fisher trace track changes of causal effect (median partial rank correlation 0.51), largely as a trend shared across the model, whereas the gain Fisher of a component's output and the large-temperature count are specific to the component. The count follows causal change across the population but not the growth of a formed circuit component. The quartic part is what a sampler that leaves the region registers beyond curvature. Pairwise interaction curvature tracks joint-ablation interactions.

title: Representative Learning for Distributed Support Vector Machines
abstract: Distributed support vector machine (SVM) learning is challenging under heterogeneous local data and limited communication. We develop a Representative Learning framework based on Lifted Empirical Risk Minimization, replacing each covariate by a local Gaussian distribution. For linear SVMs, the resulting expected hinge loss has an exact closed form, is smooth for nondegenerate lifting covariances, and converges to the ordinary hinge loss as the covariance vanishes. The lifted formulation enables clouded representatives that encode both location and covariance. We study a model-independent Mean Representative (MR) and a Score-Matching Representative (SMR) that matches the class-wise lifted gradient at its construction parameter. We show that SMR covariance scaling is stable with respect to within-group heterogeneity and that the gradient discrepancy between full data and frozen representatives is controlled by the maximum within-group diameter. Under strong convexity and smoothness, this yields an inexact-gradient convergence guarantee. Experiments under heterogeneous class allocation show that lifted representatives remain competitive with centralized solutions, while SMR more closely recovers the centralized lifted-SVM optimizer. We further extend the framework to nonlinear SVMs through a shared kernel dictionary, with experiments on Ionosphere and Australian Credit Approval showing analogous behavior. These results provide a distributional representative framework for communication-efficient distributed SVM learning under heterogeneity.

title: Spectral and convex geometry of $α$-harmonic maps and sharp Morse index rigidity
abstract: We develop a weighted scalar spectral geometric description of Sacks-Uhlenbeck $α$-harmonic maps into round spheres and identify its convex geometry realization for $α$-harmonic diffeomorphisms onto the round $2$-sphere. More precisely, we establish a one-to-one correspondence, modulo orientation preserving isometries of $\mathbb{S}^2$, between orientation preserving $α$-harmonic diffeomorphisms onto the round $2$-sphere and positive Codazzi tensors satisfying a determinant bound and a compatibility condition with the prescribed metric on $\mathbb{S}^2$. These tensors are the radii tensors of auxiliary strictly convex surfaces, and the weighted scalar forms in spectral geometry equal $-α$ times the second variations of the enclosed volumes with respect to the support functions. Using these spectral geometry and convex geometry results, we prove a sharp Morse index characterization of isometric equatorial parametrizations among $α$-harmonic $2$-spheres in the round $n$-sphere. We also prove that every $α$-harmonic diffeomorphism between unit round $2$-spheres is orthogonal for all $α>1$. Equivalently, the only admissible positive Codazzi tensor whose reconstructed metric on $\mathbb{S}^2$ has Gaussian curvature $1$ is $(κ+2)^{α-1}\bar{g}$, where $\bar{g}$ is the unit round metric.

title: Selecting LLM-Generated Hypotheses Raises Truth Beyond What an LLM Panel Expects: A Pre-registered Study on NAS-Bench-201 and HPOBench
abstract: LLM research-ideation systems aim for hypotheses that are both true and non-obvious, yet neither property can normally be checked. We build a testbed in which both can. Generators propose conditional interaction claims about two fully tabulated benchmarks, NAS-Bench-201 and HPOBench; every claim is verified exactly against the tables, and its non-obviousness is scored against a calibrated blind prior elicited from other LLMs. Excess truth measures how much more often a run's claims hold than this panel expects. Across a series of pre-registered stages with Claude and GPT generators, our main positive result is a simple two-stage step found by a harness optimizer: draft a large pool of claims, then select a subset in a separate call. For Sonnet on NAS-Bench-201, this step raised excess truth in every pre-registered test, including against a same-pool ablation that keeps only likely-true claims, without lowering precision. The gain comes both from credit for true claims and from avoiding near-miss false ones. In post hoc checks it held under every calibration, panel and truth rule we tried, and it exceeded random and type-filter selection from the same pools. Because kept claims recur across runs, the evidence weakens when runs and claims are resampled jointly, and it is not significant against Sonnet's own prior. Two secondary findings are also pre-registered. GPT makes real use of the results of cheap probes, beating shuffled and withheld controls, though not more efficiently than asking for more claims. Optimizing the harness for an LLM judge raised judge scores while sharply cutting precision for every generator.

title: A unifying view of averaging for wave-mean flow decomposition
abstract: Geophysical flows are routinely decomposed into mean flow and waves, and the procedure used determines how the motion is divided between the two. Ideally, the wave and mean motions of interest evolve on distinct timescales, in which case they can be separated by taking an infinite-time average over all wave periods. Individual waves average away, while exactly resonant interactions contribute to the averaged dynamics because they are steady on the fast timescale. We generalize this averaging to finite windows, yielding a family of decompositions that additionally retain near-resonant interactions whose phases do not fully cancel over the time window. Such averaging necessarily invokes a choice of reference frame; the same flow averaged in two frames may yield mean flows differing by a drift. The averaging formulation developed here enables us to express Stokes drift through resonant and near-resonant interactions, confirming the intuition that it is a slow quantity generated by fast waves and revealing a coherent near-resonant contribution generally present in Stokes drift calculated over finite time from broadband wave fields. We use the fast-wave evolution underlying the exact average to define both the wave reference frame, in which the fast phase is steady, and a wave-frame average. We cast familiar Eulerian and Lagrangian averages and this wave-frame average in a common form to further illustrate how the chosen frame determines which motions enter the mean. This view of averaging provides a common basis for comparing decompositions and choosing among them according to the physical processes one seeks to isolate.

title: FastAgent: A Physics-Aware FastFluent-to-Fluent Workflow for Rapid CFD Screening and Industrial Steam Dewaxing Design
abstract: Industrial computational fluid dynamics (CFD) becomes costly when complex geometries, long transients and coupled physics must be evaluated across large design spaces. We introduce FastAgent, a physics-aware campaign controller built around FastFluent, a lightweight numerical engine for rapid physical screening. FastFluent supplies stage-specific fields and diagnostics; FastAgent allocates physical models, numerical resolution and simulation horizons by the active quantities of interest (QoIs), while returned Fluent discrepancies update subsequent decisions. Across six public CFD benchmark campaigns, the framework reduces normalised worst-QoI error by 5.68-99.14% and accelerates decision-relevant computation by factors of 1.53-15.36 relative to a matched Generic Agent control. Applied to high-pressure steam dewaxing in investment casting, FastAgent identifies nonuniform condensation heating as the dominant startup mechanism and separates rapid risk-window localisation from high-fidelity melt-completion confirmation. The rapid route requires 81.39% fewer cell-time updates than a fine-grid, small-time-step reference. Structural analysis localises fracture at the observed blade edge. Screening 131,072 outlet layouts and selectively evaluating candidates with Fluent and Abaqus identifies Sparse-6, which reduces simulated crack opening by 96.0% and connected crack extent by 66.7% relative to the Original design. These results demonstrate how rapid numerical evidence and adaptive fidelity control connect large CFD search spaces to mechanism-guided industrial design.

title: When Shards Fly: Cross-Tensor In-Flight Conversion for Low-Latency, Low-Memory Weight Updates in Disaggregated RL
abstract: Disaggregated LLM reinforcement learning (RL) repeatedly synchronizes policy weights between training and rollout GPU pools. Existing systems reduce communication through shard delivery and replica forwarding, yet separate conversion passes and staging buffers still add latency and GPU-memory overheads to synchronous updates. We present ShardFly, which coordinates reusable transfer planning with streaming GPU execution for synchronous, in-place weight updates. ShardFly introduces two components. The Planner compiles native shard mappings, quantization dependencies, and replica routes into cross-tensor schedules, reserving payload buffers only for scheduled transfers. The Executor runs each rank's schedule in one persistent transfer kernel, fusing memory-layout conversion, quantization, GPU-initiated communication, and destination writes while forwarding transformed bytes across replicas. Plans and communication state are reused under stable configurations and replaced between updates for coordinated rollout scaling. On up to 32 H20 GPUs, ShardFly achieves complete BF16 weight-update speedups of 1.26--27.92$\times$ across five models and four baselines: veRL NCCL, Awex, veRL NIXL, and WeightBridge. In end-to-end Qwen3-30B-A3B GRPO across four rollout configurations, ShardFly improves response-token throughput by 5.49--6.71\% over veRL NCCL.

title: Cyclotomic polynomials with trinomial irreducible factors over finite fields
abstract: We classify the pairs $(q,n)$, where $q$ is a prime power, $n>1$, and $\gcd(n,q)=1$, for which every irreducible factor of $Φ_n(x)$ over $\F_q$ has exactly three nonzero terms. The positive support exponents of these factors have a common greatest common divisor, which gives a unique reduction by a power substitution. The reduced degree is two in odd characteristic and belongs to $\{2,3,4\}$ in characteristic two; the cubic and quartic cases arise by scalar substitution from the layers of orders $7$ and $15$. This yields necessary and sufficient arithmetic conditions on $(q,n)$ and explicit factorizations. Among the classified families, precisely those arising from quartic bases have a divisor layer containing an irreducible factor with more than three terms.

title: Synergy-Aware Symbol Allocation for Distributed Semantic Communication
abstract: Distributed semantic communication enables spatially separated terminals to support collaborative inference over wireless links for 6G edge intelligence. In multimodal sensing and cooperative perception, a single terminal captures only a partial view, and full task semantics emerge only when complementary observations from multiple terminals are fused at the receiver. However, under tight uplink budgets, existing task-oriented joint source--channel coding (JSCC) and distributed information bottleneck (IB) methods evaluate rate--distortion trade-offs per terminal, tending to undervalue cross-terminal synergistic features and prune them prematurely. To address this issue, we propose a synergy-credited distributed JSCC (\method{}) framework that introduces a differentiable, post-equalization matrix Rényi synergy credit as a surrogate to reward complementary task evidence surviving the wireless channel and backpropagates its gradients to local symbol gates. At deployment, the credit branch is removed and binary symbol masks are frozen, allowing each terminal to encode independently without inter-terminal signaling or extra inference overhead. Experiments show that \method{} recovers the analytical symbol-selection threshold on parity sources and reduces payload symbols by 28.4\% on AV-MNIST and 32.9\% on PAMAP2 over an uncredited gated baseline, while achieving a 6.2-point accuracy gain at $-6$~dB under 3GPP TDL-C fading with pilot-aided channel estimation for low-overhead wireless cooperative sensing.

title: Weighted $L^q$-$L^r$ estimates of a generalized Oseen evolution operator in exterior domains, with applications to the Navier-Stokes flow past a rigid body
abstract: We consider a generalized Oseen evolution operator arising from time-dependent rigid motions in 3D exterior domains. Hishida and the present author established the regularity theory of the evolution operator by use of the $L^q$-$L^r$ smoothing estimates with a weight function $(1+|x|)^α$. The objective of this paper is to develop the weighted $L^q$-$L^r$ estimates globally in time. These estimates are applied to the study of the large time behavior of the Navier-Stokes flow around a time-periodic solution in weighted spaces.

title: Heirloom: Carrying a Phone's Personalization Across Base-Model Generations
abstract: On-device language models can learn a user's preferences through adapters trained on private data. However, a base-model upgrade may change the layers or vocabulary, leaving the personal adapter incompatible. Replacing it with a non-personal adapter loses much of the personalization, while retraining requires retaining the user's labeled history. We present Heirloom, a system that transfers a personal adapter to a new base model on the phone without retaining labels. Heirloom uses the old personal model as a teacher, collecting its predictions on stored unlabeled inputs, vendor-provided prompts, or prompts generated by the new base. It then unloads the old base and trains an adapter for the new model to match those predictions, keeping only one base model in memory at a time. We evaluate Heirloom across three generation upgrades from two model families, an architecture-preserving refresh, and three personalization tasks. On movie tagging, migration from stored inputs maintains pre-upgrade accuracy and differs from labeled retraining by at most 1.7 percentage points across the three upgrades. On a phone's neural processing unit (NPU), a fixed-length migration for the 4B upgrade takes 38 minutes and consumes 20% of the battery end to end, making the stored-input setting feasible during overnight charging.

title: The Testability Gap: A Pre-Registered Census of Naming versus Implementation in 59 Cognitive-Architecture LLM Systems
abstract: A companion line of work audited individual cognitive-architecture LLM systems in depth and found that module names and module computations are empirically independent claims. This paper asks how far that gap extends across the system class. We pre-registered a census protocol (sample frame, metrics, and acceptance criteria frozen before any sample was downloaded) and surveyed the 59 most-starred Python repositories declaring cognitive architecture on GitHub, plus five classic architectures as a historical control. We measure a testability gap. First, an auditability gap: 22% of repositories document no code reference whatsoever. Second, an integrity gap: 42% of repositories have at least one dangling reference, and within that subgroup the median fraction is 8%, the top quartile 19.6%, and the maximum 79.5%; one 148-star system documents paths of which a majority do not exist. Three of four pre-registered hypotheses were falsified: the integrity gap is not universal (58% of repositories either offer no checkable references or offer references that all resolve); claim density does not predict dangling rate (rho = -0.10); and the classical-architecture control does not significantly outperform (p = 0.059 with five controls, all at zero dangling). Exactly one repository in 59 (1.7%) ships executable falsification criteria for its own claims. A second pre-registered round classified every dangling path by git lifetime: 85.5% of dangling references (159 of 186) are ghosts - paths that never existed at any commit - against 14.5% that were once real and later removed.

title: Inference First, Training Underneath: Layer-Granular LoRA Co-Serving with LayerLoom
abstract: Serving and fine-tuning a large language model on the same GPUs can turn the idle capacity between inference bursts into training progress, and low-rank adaptation (LoRA) makes this co-location cheap because both workloads read a single frozen copy of the base weights. The difficulty lies in the fine-tuning backward pass, which has no counterpart in inference. Current co-serving systems schedule backward work per serving iteration: each iteration carries a fixed backward budget, and requests that arrive in the meantime wait for it to finish, so fine-tuning dictates inference latency whenever load spikes. We observe that the backward pass of a LoRA microbatch decomposes into per-layer tasks over the same weights that the inference forward pass visits, which allows backward work to be scheduled at layer rather than iteration granularity. Building on this observation, LayerLoom attaches same-layer backward tasks to the inference forward pass and, at each layer, runs only as many of them as the latency slack of in-flight requests permits. To keep a ready task at every layer, LayerLoom maintains a wavefront of fine-tuning microbatches staggered across layers, and it bounds the wavefront's activation memory by offloading microbatch state to host memory and prefetching it ahead of the layer where the scheduler plans to use it. A fused kernel serves the paired forward and backward GEMMs from a single read of each base weight. Because all backward work of an iteration finishes within its forward pass, new requests join the next iteration as in continuous batching. On an RTX 4090 GPU running Llama-3.1-8B under a bursty production trace, LayerLoom raises joint SLO attainment by 13.5-21.8 points over prior works with fine-tuning throughput that is comparable or up to 12% higher, and it reaches the same training losses.

title: Regularized Wasserstein Distance for Discrete Generative Modeling and Clustering Analysis
abstract: In this paper, we formulate clustering analysis as discrete generative modeling. Specifically, when the generator is restricted to a finite candidate space, the generated samples naturally emerge as the most representative prototypes of the underlying data distribution. To model such a discrete candidate space, we employ a Discrete Distribution Network (DDN). However, DDN suffers from unstable training due to its hard nearest-neighbor selection. To stabilize training and encourage geometric consistency, we replace DDN's l2 loss between images with regularized Wasserstein distance between the empirical distributions of real and generated images. The resulting framework, termed Discrete Generative Clustering (DGC), offers four notable advantages: 1) the learned cluster centers are directly interpretable, as they are realistic synthetic samples; 2) the inference cost scales logarithmically with the number of clusters, i.e., O(log K), making the method scalable to extremely large K; 3) the regularized Wasserstein distance provides a smooth and well-behaved optimization objective that facilitates stable convergence, whereas DDN's l2 loss tends to converge to poor local optima; and 4) DGC replaces DDN's nearest-neighbor selection with random-neighbor selection, which avoids the density shift problem during multi-step forward. Extensive experiments on several benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness and desirable properties of DGC. The code is publicly available at GitHub.

title: GateTrim: Adaptive-Rank Quantization for Large Language Models
abstract: We introduce GateTrim, an adaptive-rank post-training quantization method for large language models that learns matrix-specific ranks through gate optimization and threshold-based rank selection. GateTrim standardizes the low-rank factors of a quantized low-rank--residual representation, learns a separate gate vector for each target weight matrix, and uses a shared threshold to automatically determine its retained rank. The resulting ranks can differ across matrices, and the compact quantized representations are subsequently reconstructed. We evaluate GateTrim under W4A8 on Qwen3-4B/8B/14B, Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Across all five models, we observe a counterintuitive finding: increasing the threshold from $τ=0.3$ to $τ=0.7$ reduces the mean retained rank by 46.60%--67.89% while simultaneously lowering WikiText-2 perplexity by 0.59%--5.17%. Threshold 0.7 achieves the lowest mean retained rank and final perplexity among the three tested thresholds, 0.3, 0.5, and 0.7, and reduces measured target-export size by 1.50%--4.25% relative to 0.3. GateTrim uses an $8\times512$-token fitting pool and a separate development pool of the same size. Its Qwen3-4B/8B/14B perplexities at $τ=0.7$ are numerically below TwinQuant's published W4A8 values, reported with a $128\times2048$-token calibration pool, in a cross-study comparison. On Qwen3-8B, the threshold-0.7 configuration already has the lowest perplexity before reconstruction under both tested initialization seeds; reconstruction improves it further without increasing retained rank or export size.

title: Zeeman Spin Photocurrents without Spin Textures
abstract: Inversion symmetry forbids bulk second-order spin photocurrents driven solely by electric-dipole coupling. We show that interference between the electric-dipole and spin Zeeman couplings of light enables Zeeman spin-shift and spin-injection currents in centrosymmetric magnets. Our microscopic theory and systematic symmetry analysis establish the allowed responses and polarization selection rules for both spin-degenerate and spin-split antiferromagnets, with and without spin--orbit coupling (SOC). In collinear magnets without SOC, spin injection vanishes, whereas a pure spin-shift current survives independently of the carrier scattering time. This response arises from transverse electronic spin coherences generated by the optical magnetic field, while the ordered moments remain collinear and fixed. Model analyses validate the mechanism, and first-principles calculations for $\mathrm{MnF_2}$ predict experimentally accessible spin photocurrents. These findings establish a general framework for optical spin-current generation in centrosymmetric magnets, including a SOC-free pure-spin mechanism particularly relevant to altermagnets.

title: Parameter Bounds and Inverse Approximation for Linearized ReLU$^k$ Networks on the Sphere
abstract: We study direct and inverse approximation for linearized shallow ReLU$^k$ networks on $\mathbb S^d$ with quasi-uniform hidden parameters. For $0<α<\frac{d+2k+1}{2d}$, under the coefficient growth condition $\bigl(n\sum_{j=1}^na_{j,n}^2\bigr)^{\frac{1}{2}}\leq n^αM$, we prove that approximation at the order $n^{-\frac{d+2k+1}{2d}+α}$ is equivalent to membership in the parity-compatible Besov space $\mathcal B_{2,\infty,*}^{\frac{d+2k+1}{2}-αd}(\mathbb S^d)$. Mere convergence under the same coefficient budget does not imply this regularity. For unconstrained approximation along a nested parameter sequence, a single ridge function gives a counterexample when $α<\frac{1}{2}$, whereas for $α>\frac{1}{2}$ the endpoint Besov inverse conclusion follows from a Bernstein inequality under antipodal quasi-uniformity. The inverse conclusion is also recovered when the prescribed rate holds for two quasi-uniform parameter sequences whose union is antipodally separated.

title: Spatial DJ: Spatial Audio Control for Arbitrary Loudspeaker Layouts
abstract: Object-based spatial audio promises render-anywhere playback, yet deploying it in a new venue still requires two tasks that are rarely addressed together: acquiring the physical loudspeaker geometry and enabling creators manipulate spatial audio while listening through the target loudspeaker system rather than a headphone proxy. We present Spatial DJ, a system for on-site loudspeaker layout acquisition and real-time spatial audio rendering and control, using head-worn AR in a coordinate frame aligned to the physical loudspeakers. In an 18-loudspeaker room, we evaluate calibration accuracy, repeatability, and control latency, and conduct an 18-participant listener study comparing diffuse and orbiting point-source rendering configurations applied to vocal and instrumental layers. Orbiting point-source conditions received higher ratings of perceived immersion, energy, and novelty than the diffuse baseline. Beyond this controlled setting, four representative deployments illustrate reuse of the same system across heterogeneous loudspeaker venues.

title: SE-Mem: Semantic-Episodic Memory for Scene-Consistent Generative View Synthesis
abstract: Generative view synthesis aims to synthesize novel-view videos from reference observations along user-defined camera trajectories. Maintaining global scene consistency throughout this process remains challenging for camera-conditioned interactive video generators. Existing approaches typically select reference frames based solely on camera poses, overlooking whether the content remains semantically relevant or even visible. To address these limitations, we draw inspiration from semantic and episodic memory in human cognition, in which semantic memory captures generalized knowledge across experiences, whereas episodic memory preserves information tied to specific past events and contexts. Motivated by the complementary roles of semantic and episodic memory, we introduce SE-Mem, a Semantic-Episodic Memory framework that organizes historical observations in a structured 3D representation and augments its elements with semantic importance scores. A two-stage memory retrieval strategy is designed to identify the most informative frames to provide contextual guidance. Taking into account both semantic significance and geometric visibility, SE-Mem preserves semantic coherence and fine-grained visual details during novel view synthesis. Extensive evaluations show that our approach improves visual quality and achieves competitive geometric consistency across multiple benchmarks.

title: Confinement Geometry Regulates Fluctuations, Densities, and Collective Escape in Interacting Active Matter
abstract: Active matter exhibits non-equilibrium signatures such as the violation of the fluctuation-dissipation theorem, giant number fluctuations, and non-Gaussian velocity distributions. We investigate how confinement geometry and particle number influence the steady-state behavior of sterically interacting Active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck Particles (AOUPs) in a double-well potential. Unlike bulk active systems, increasing particle number suppresses non-equilibrium fluctuations through crowding, making the steady-state density profiles increasingly resemble those of passive systems. Nevertheless, instantaneous active density profiles exhibit both unimodal and bimodal distributions, even at large particle numbers, whereas passive profiles remain bimodal. The local velocity and position distributions are unimodal in the concave regions of the potential but become bimodal in non-concave regions. Confinement suppresses long-range correlations while producing spatially localized fluctuations governed by potential geometry. Velocity fluctuations are suppressed in the densely populated wells but enhanced near the barrier, where non-equilibrium effects are strongest. At large persistence times, correlated barrier crossings and strong velocity-alignment correlations emerge, which are absent in passive systems. These results demonstrate how confinement geometry, crowding, and persistence jointly control density fluctuations, velocity correlations, and collective escape in interacting active matter.

title: A Mixed-Precision CNN-LSTM Accelerator Featuring Long-Kernel Memory Reuse and Dynamic Quantization for Sleep Staging
abstract: This letter presents a mixed-precision CNN-LSTM accelerator for EEG-based sleep staging. To efficiently execute long temporal convolutions, a serpentine dataflow propagates activations between neighboring processing elements, reducing memory accesses by 6.2 times and 2.25 times compared with output- and weight-stationary dataflows, respectively. A hybrid quantization scheme applies runtime dynamic quantization to the LSTM and MLP layers and assigns mixed precision on a layer-by-layer basis, reducing model size by 4.16 times. Combined with a bit-flexible MAC architecture and channel-grouped memory scheduling, the accelerator supports INT2/4/8/16 inference. Fabricated in 65 nm CMOS, the accelerator consumes 0.40 mW and achieves a 258 times speedup over an iso-frequency 32b RISC-V processor. Evaluated across all 62 subjects in the public MASS-SS3 dataset using 31-fold leave-two-subject-out cross-validation, the mixed-precision approach with hybrid quantization maintains 5-class accuracy within 0.15% of the floating-point baseline when optimized for general sleep staging and N3 sensitivity within 0.51% when optimized for deep-sleep detection. The developed techniques are broadly applicable to EEG-based DL workloads.

title: Designing Behavioral Profiles for Language Model Simulation of Out-of-Distribution Human Behavior
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to simulate human behavior, but which descriptions of people improve prediction when experimental designs change remains unclear. We develop a framework that draws candidate behavioral features from the literature and constructs profiles from earlier human experiments. An LLM-based profile generator assigns feature values from observed actions, messages, and surveys; a separate LLM simulates behavior using these profiles. By comparing simulated and observed outcomes in the training data, we select profile contents through forward feature selection, adding features while they improve prediction. We then evaluate the selected contents without modification against outcomes from new participants under new designs. Across 616 public-goods games, 144 multi-party bargaining games, and 1,480 generalized 11--20 money-request designs, leading one-feature profiles predict human outcome distributions better than no profile or general-purpose personas. Profiles with more features provide no clear additional benefit, and features' relative predictive value largely persists across learning and validation. Using profiles from one game family to simulate another produces uneven gains and can make predictions less accurate than simulations without profiles. The framework makes the choice of behavioral information a testable part of simulation design, helping researchers assess which descriptions remain useful as experimental conditions change.

title: Large $N$ limit of the ratio of Lukyanov integrals
abstract: We study the large-$N$ asymptotics of ratios of Lukyanov integrals for fixed real coupling $b\geq1$. Our approach uses their biorthogonal ensemble structure and vector Riemann--Hilbert techniques. Under stated analytic hypotheses, we derive the logarithmic ratio through its constant term, which is expressed by a Fredholm determinant. The expansion is locally uniform in the real parameter $α$ and is formulated separately for even and odd particle numbers. We verify the hypotheses for the correction defined by the physical ground-state thermodynamic Bethe ansatz. The relation to quantum-field-theoretic one-point functions is discussed separately.

title: $K_h$-Minor-Free Graphs Have Balanced Separators of Size $O(h\sqrt{n})$
abstract: We show that every $K_h$-minor-free graph with $n$ vertices has a balanced separator of size $O(h\sqrt{n})$ for any parameter $h \in \mathbb{N}$, resolving the conjecture posed by Alon, Seymour, and Thomas [AST90] in 1990. The proof is elementary, building on the combinatorial framework by Le [Le26]. A key new idea of the proof is the existence of a short hitting walk on vertex expanders: given $k$ large (not necessarily disjoint) subsets of vertices, there is a walk of length $O(k/ψ(G))$ hitting every subset, where $ψ(G)$ is the vertex expansion. This technical result substantially improves on an analogous lemma by Alon, Seymour, and Thomas [AST90] in an important parameter setting, where the previous lower bound [Kot00] does not apply.

title: Curvature-Driven Density and Fluctuations in Interacting AOUPs under Confinement
abstract: We investigate interacting active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck particles (AOUPs) confined in harmonic and double-well potentials, combining mean-field theory, analytical approximations, and numerical simulations. We derive the stationary density, position and velocity correlations, correlation length, dynamical structure factor, and leading-order entropy production. Unlike established harmonic normal-mode descriptions, our framework incorporates steric interactions, persistent forcing, and spatially varying confinement curvature through the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the many-body Hessian. Within a locally homogeneous approximation, the correlation length is controlled by persistence and local curvature, increasing as the effective restoring stiffness decreases and formally diverging at the instability of the linearized description. Entropy production, at leading nontrivial order in persistence, is governed by gradients of the effective curvature. Harmonic confinement provides a constant-curvature reference, whereas double-well confinement creates equilibrium-like regions near the minima and strongly nonequilibrium regions near the barrier. The barrier exhibits enhanced velocity and density fluctuations, soft collective modes, long-lived correlations, and increased entropy production. Persistence amplifies these effects, while steric crowding suppresses collective fluctuations. The dynamical structure factor reveals enhanced low-frequency contributions from soft modes. Our results establish how confinement geometry, active persistence, and interactions jointly regulate collective fluctuations and irreversibility in active matter.

title: Audit at the Precision You Deploy: Quantization Reshapes a Subliminally Learned Preference
abstract: Subliminal learning allows AI models to inherit hidden preferences from seemingly unrelated training data, such as number sequences. Safety audits may evaluate models at standard 16-bit precision, while deployments may use compressed, quantized weights. We ask whether quantization changes the expression of a subliminal preference and what drives any resulting change. To investigate, we implant a "favourite animal: panda" preference into Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. We define its net strength as the difference in mean panda-answer probability between subliminal models and neutrally trained controls under the same quantization setting. Applying this metric across different compression levels reveals a stark contrast. While behaviour remains stable at 8 bits, 4-bit quantization triggers severe, opposing shifts depending on the quantizer. Half-Quadratic Quantization (HQQ) amplifies the preference, raising the subliminally trained model's panda probability from roughly 55% at 16 bits to 64% at 4 bits, while the controls stay near 17%. This raises the trait's net strength ~1.3 times its 16-bit value. In contrast, NormalFloat (NF4) at 4-bit suppresses it, shrinking the net strength to just ~0.3 times its 16-bit value, despite producing rounding errors of the same size to within 4%. We examine the structure of the rounding errors and find that their arrangement drives the divergence. Randomly shuffling HQQ's errors within each quantization group, without changing their magnitude, shifts the trait's net strength between 0.2 and 1.6 times its 16-bit value. Despite these opposing shifts, the underlying fine-tuning signal remains largely intact. Because a model's internal state and outward behaviour diverge so unpredictably under compression, a 16-bit audit cannot reliably bound real-world risks. Safety evaluations must test the exact quantized weights intended for deployment.

title: Exploring the properties of low-lying excited $Ξ_c$ and $Ξ_c'$ baryons
abstract: Motivated by the rapidly accumulating experimental data, we systematically calculate the $Ξ_c$ and $Ξ_c'$ mass spectra for the $1S$-, $1P$-, and $1D$-wave states and investigate the strong decay properties of the $1P$- and $1D$-wave states, thereby interpreting the internal structure of the currently controversial excited states and providing useful guidance for future experimental searches. The main conclusions are summarized as follows. $Ξ_c(2790)$ and $Ξ_c(2815)$ can be well explained as $Ξ_c1P\big|J^P=1/2^-,1\big\rangle_λ$ and $Ξ_c1P\big|J^P=3/2^-,1\big\rangle_λ$, respectively. $Ξ_c(2882)$ may correspond to $Ξ_c1P\big|J^P=1/2^-,0\big\rangle_ρ$ or $Ξ_c1P\big|J^P=1/2^-,1\big\rangle_ρ$; under this interpretation, $Ξ_cπ$ and $Ξ_c'π$ would be promising channels for its detection. $Ξ_c(2923)$ might be assigned to $Ξ_c'1P\big|J^P=3/2^-,1\big\rangle_λ$, but further confirmation is required. $Ξ_c(2939)$ is very likely to be $Ξ_c'1P\big|J^P=3/2^-,2\big\rangle_λ$ and has a good potential to be observed in the final states $Ξ_cπ$ and $Ξ_c'^{*}π$. $Ξ_c(2965)$ can be explained as $Ξ_c'1P\big|J^P=5/2^-,2\big\rangle_λ$ and $Ξ_cπ$ decay channel is a promising additional mode for future experimental searches. $Ξ_c(3055)$ and $Ξ_c(3080)$ can be assigned as the quark configurations $Ξ_c1D\big|J^P=3/2^+,2\big\rangle_{λλ}$ and $Ξ_c1D\big|J^P=5/2^+,2\big\rangle_{λλ}$, respectively. $Ξ_c(3123)$ is possibly state $Ξ_c'1D\big|J^P=1/2^+,1\big\rangle_{λλ}$ or $Ξ_c'1D\big|J^P=5/2^+,3\big\rangle_{λλ}$, with the latter being more favorable. Decay channels $Λ/ΣD$ are very likely to serve as a criterion for distinguishing between these two possible candidates.

title: Characterizing and Predicting the Longest CI Builds in Machine Learning Projects
abstract: Continuous integration (CI) builds in machine learning (ML) projects tend to run longer than in other projects, yet little is known about the longest builds, which consume most CI time. This paper characterizes the longest builds in ML projects, analyzes how CI workflow properties are associated with them, and evaluates whether they can be predicted before execution. We study 269,930 GitHub Actions builds from 107 open-source ML projects. The top 18% longest builds account for 80.30% of total build time and fail in 39.09% of cases. Build duration differs significantly across ML project types. The framework and infrastructure ML projects have the longest upper tail and produce 98% of the longest builds, whereas projects that use existing ML libraries have the lowest median build duration. The longest builds are most strongly associated with the recent history of the same workflow, as the duration of its last build and the median duration of the project's last 20 builds show large effect sizes. The longest builds are more consistently associated with CI workflow structure than with configuration. The number of jobs, control flow complexity, coupling complexity, and maximum steps per job show medium effect sizes, whereas caching, matrix settings, and Docker builds show small or negligible effects. Framework-specific workflows have the largest percentage of builds among long builds. Platform-specific workflows produce the largest number of the longest builds. Finally, 47 features describing build history, workflow structure, and the ML project outperform a traditional baseline with all four classifiers. In a chronological evaluation, the best model (XGBoost) reaches an F1-score of 0.775, compared with 0.682 for the baseline, and an AUC-ROC of 0.955. These results show that build history and CI workflow structure help identify the longest builds in ML projects before they run.

title: Deep Reinforcement Learning with Smith-Predictor Delay Compensation
abstract: Time delays can degrade feedback performance and destabilize a closed loop that is stable without delay. This paper studies Smith-predictor-assisted reinforcement learning for systems with constant input delays. A deep deterministic policy gradient (DDPG) actor is trained on a nominal delay-free environment and deployed with a Smith predictor using a fixed nominal delay. For linear controllers, we derive exact closed-loop maps under plant and delay mismatch and provide small-gain and $ν$-gap robustness conditions. A separate delay-independent Razumikhin condition gives a sufficient stability test for a fixed Lipschitz state-feedback policy. We also study output-error delay identification from a fixed input--output record, deriving the loss gradient and establishing projected-flow descent and local exponential convergence under exact model matching and an excitation condition. These identification results do not imply stability of an online adaptive predictor. Numerical experiments retained from the conference study compare PID, LQR, and DDPG controllers on stable and open-loop unstable first-order plants with valve stiction. The results illustrate the benefit of predictor compensation in the tested configurations and the sensitivity of standalone DDPG to delay and plant changes.

title: FPGA Acceleration of CNN-BiLSTM for EEG-Based Sleep Staging Featuring FFT-Based Non-Unit Stride Fast Convolution
abstract: Deep learning (DL) models for real-time wearable sleep staging often rely on long-kernel temporal convolutions, a requirement that current accelerators struggle to support efficiently. To overcome this, we present an FPGA-based CNN-BiLSTM accelerator that incorporates several algorithm-hardware co-design techniques to enable efficient edge inference. Central to this design is an FFT-based non-unit stride fast convolution, which performs accumulation in the frequency domain to enable a single IFFT per block, reducing post-processing complexity to $O(N\log N)$. On the target long-kernel convolution layer, this yields a 20.5$\times$ reduction in arithmetic operations. Power-of-two quantization is applied across the pipeline, including FFT-based convolution and BiLSTM activations, with an average accuracy degradation of only 0.11% relative to the floating-point baseline across all subjects on the public MASS-SS3 dataset. Additional optimizations, including block convolution, depth-first execution, and hardware engine reuse minimize memory access and enhance resource utilization. The accelerator, implemented on a Xilinx Zynq-7000 FPGA, operates at 10 MHz and consumes 11 mW of dynamic power including data handling and configuration overhead from a microcontroller. The design achieves a DSP power efficiency of 0.91 GOPS/W/DSP using only 4 DSPs, demonstrating scalable and energy-efficient DL acceleration for sleep staging that can be extended to other wearable applications.

title: Versatile Graph Foundation Models from Frozen Time-Series Foundation Models via Parallel Flows
