The analysis uses proton-proton collision data at $\sqrt{s}$ = 13 TeV, corresponding to an integrated luminosity of 138 fb$^{-1}$, recorded with the CMS detector at the CERN LHC. The observed data do not exhibit any excess over the standard model predictions. Constraints are derived on chargino, top squark, and slepton pair production in the context of simplified models with $R$-parity conservation. In these models, the neutralino is taken to be the lightest supersymmetric particle. For chargino production, an exclusion region in the chargino-neutralino mass plane is determined, which extends to chargino masses of 1120 GeV and neutralino masses of 490 GeV. For mass splittings between the lighter top squark and the neutralino ranging from the W boson mass to the top quark mass, top squark masses up to 500$-$540 GeV are excluded. Slepton masses are excluded up to 700 GeV for a massless neutralino.

title: Modeling Crystallization in Concentrated Suspensions of Compressible Microgels
abstract: Soft colloidal particles, such as microgels, made of cross-linked polymer gels that can swell by absorbing a good solvent, have internal degrees of freedom that allow them to respond to external stimuli by changing size. Sensitive responses to variations in temperature and concentration have inspired many practical applications, e.g., to drug delivery, biosensing, filtration, and photonic crystals. At sufficiently high concentrations, mutual crowding can drive microgels to interpenetrate or deform by faceting. To explore the influence of particle softness and compressibility on thermodynamic phase stability, we develop a coarse-grained model in which spherical microgels interact via the Hertz elastic pair potential and can respond to crowding by deswelling and faceting or interpenetrating, as governed by the Flory-Rehner theory of polymer networks. In our model, faceting reduces the volume available for swelling, while interpenetration affects polymer solvent mixing entropy. By performing Monte Carlo simulations that incorporate novel trial changes in particle size and shape, we compute equilibrium swelling ratios and Lindemann ratios to determine the fluid-solid phase stability boundary over a range of particle softness, tuned by varying cross-link fraction. Predictions from our facet model are in qualitative agreement with experiments and molecular-scale simulations. In contrast to the phase behavior of incompressible Hertzian spheres, we find that suspensions of compressible microgels crystallize at significantly lower volume fractions when accounting for the free energy costs of faceting and interpenetration. Our results extend previous studies of microgel phase behavior and can help to interpret experiments.

title: Extrapolation and explainability in hadron mass predictions with machine learning
abstract: In this work, we study the predictive performance of four machine learning (ML) models for hadron masses, with particular attention to extrapolation beyond the conventional hadrons represented in the training data. Calculations are performed using a multilayer perceptron (MLP), eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM), and Gaussian process regression (GPR). ML models are trained on conventional hadrons, using features that describe valence quark content and quantum numbers. Then, we evaluate their performance on test sets and on a separate extrapolation set of 39 states, including exotic candidates and heavy baryons, none of which appear in the training or test sets. We find that the MLP achieves the lowest extrapolation Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) on the $30$ states with measured masses at $294.2 \pm 57.9$~MeV, roughly one-third that of the other models. We also show that the MLP reproduces the overall mass scale of nine unobserved doubly heavy baryons predicted by theoretical calculations, although it underestimates the doubly bottom masses. We use SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analysis and show that heavy quark content is the most significant factor in the MLP's mass predictions, with the remaining features contributing differently across hadron types. Our results quantify the extrapolation accuracy of ML models for hadron masses and identify the features that drive the MLP predictions.

title: Recursive Reasoning Exploration: Mathematical Research through Evolving Reasoning Graphs : case study: An Exact Certificate-Degree Theorem for Two-Term Tensor Decompositions : Phase III of the Math Instruments Program
abstract: Large collections of manuscripts and research notes offer ways to reuse arguments, while making it harder to retain hypotheses, check claims, and understand how results were obtained. We propose Recursive Reasoning Exploration (RRE), a framework for cumulative mathematical research through evolving reasoning graphs. RRE links claims and jointly required premises to research targets, attempted arguments, counterexamples, checks, and revisions. Each investigation can generate further targets, and its supported outcomes become available to subsequent investigations. This is Phase III of the Math Instruments program: identifying mathematical instruments, reconstructing reusable reasoning, and organizing recursive research from that reasoning. The framework supports human-directed, collaborative, and goal-directed autonomous exploration, with open-ended exploration as a further mode. Its records also provide material for learning how mathematical investigations develop. A complexity research case study establishes an exact theorem: for every complex tensor of order n >= 2 and rank greater than two, the minimum Nullstellensatz certificate degree for its original two-term decomposition equations is 3n. This includes an infinite family whose every flattening has rank at most two. The exploration develops an explicit boundary certificate, a balanced transfer lemma, and an exhaustive argument using classical rank-two geometry. A parallel branch gives bounds 3m + 3 <= delta_m(I_m, N) <= 3m + 6 for every nonzero nilpotent m by m matrix. Six graph revisions record the progression from inherited results to these theorems, with exact arithmetic checks and a replayable exploration history. We present the RRE representation and protocol, the mathematical proofs, visualizations of graph evolution, and a research agenda for shared human-AI exploration, cumulative reuse, and education.

title: An $L\log L$ theory of sparse graph convergence
abstract: Borgs, Chayes, Cohn and Zhao developed a limit theory for sparse graphs based on $L^p$ upper regularity with $p>1$, where Holder's inequality controls small sets. We develop the analogous theory in the Orlicz class $L\log L$, replacing Holder by the Young-Fenchel inequality for $Ψ(u)=(1+u)\log(1+u)-u$ and $Ψ^*(v)=e^v-1-v$. We prove a weak regularity lemma for upper $Ψ$-regular graphons with $4^{O(1/\varepsilon^2)}$ parts, using the modular $\intΨ$ as the energy; that upper $Ψ$-regular sequences have cut-metric convergent subsequences; that convergent sequences with $L\log L$ limits are upper $Ψ$-regular; and that $L\log L$ balls are cut-metric compact. The class strictly contains every $L^p$ class with $p>1$, and we give sparse $W$-random graphs that are upper $Ψ$-regular but not upper $L^p$ regular for any $p>1$. For graphs with a given degree sequence we prove, by Stein's method of exchangeable pairs with switchings, that if the average degree tends to infinity, the density to zero and the degree profile converges in $L^1$ to $φ$, uniformly random graphs converge in the normalized cut metric to $φ\otimesφ$, with no condition on the maximum degree; the sequence is upper $Ψ$-regular when $φ\in L\log L$. We also show that the maximum-entropy $β$-model is entrywise Chung-Lu when $d_{\max}^2=o(M)$, and that cut-closeness to it follows from a lower bound $e^{-o(M)}$ on its probability of having the prescribed degrees. Finally, $Ψ$ is the large deviation rate function of sparse Erdos-Renyi graphs up to a factor $1+O(1/\log\frac1p)$.

title: Fuzzy-Enhanced Machine Learning Approach for Type 2 Diabetes Diagnosis
abstract: Accurate diabetes prediction is critical for early clinical intervention, yet existing machine-learning pipelines often fail due to class imbalance, noisy physiological measurements, and redundant or weakly informative features. To address these unresolved limitations, this study establishes a unified fuzzy-evolutionary-ensemble framework designed to uncover a more discriminative feature space for type 2 diabetes prediction. The workflow integrates selective fuzzification of nonlinear clinical variables, SMOTE-ENN-based balancing and noise filtering, and Bat-Algorithm-driven evolutionary feature selection prior to training a Random Forest classifier. Applied to the Pima Indians Diabetes Dataset, the framework compresses the expanded fuzzy-numerical space into an optimized 10-feature subset and yields substantial performance gains: 96.11% accuracy, 95.14% precision, 98.00% recall, and a 98.23% F1-score. Relative to a baseline Random Forest using all 16 features (74.45% accuracy; 59.86% F1), the system achieves more than a 1.6-fold improvement in F1-score while preserving over 99% stability in majority-class detection and surpassing earlier published 16-feature models impacted by imbalance and weak feature relevance. Collectively, these results demonstrate that the integrated pipeline produces an enhanced fuzzy-numerical representation space that improves diabetes risk stratification and provides a scalable, uncertainty-aware foundation for diagnostic modeling across broader clinical datasets.

title: Directional Bounded-Confidence Matrix Alignment in Vicsek Flocking
abstract: This paper proposes a directional bounded-confidence variant of the discrete-time Vicsek multiagent model, in which pairwise heading alignment is modulated by a state-dependent, positive semidefinite matrix that independently gates orthogonal radial and tangential components in the instantaneous line-of-sight frame. We analyze the normalized, matrix-weighted system dynamics, proving a uniform non-vanishing bound on proposal vectors that guarantees global well-posedness across arbitrary network states. For local small-spread states under complete metric interaction, we prove linear geometric contraction of the heading diameter and establish an offline-verifiable spatial bootstrap condition that guarantees metric contact preservation and coincidence avoidance a priori. A counterexample demonstrates invariant polarized states on connected matrix graphs, delineating systemic structural limits. Numerical experiments against unfiltered Vicsek averaging, scalar tied confidence, trace-matched scalar baselines, and restricted-angle rules demonstrate component-selective filtering without rejected-channel leakage, along with improved fixed-bound alignment on multi-seed benchmarks across varying population densities.

title: A Singularity Theorem for Quasi-Topological Gravities
abstract: Quasi-topological theories of gravity have recently attracted substantial attention as several theories in this class have a non-singular black hole as a vacuum and spherically symmetric solution. This motivates the expectation that these theories can provide a resolution to the singularity problem and a description of black holes cores. The known solutions, however, possess a Cauchy horizon which denotes the end of predictability of the theory, as the initial data do not determine a unique continuation past this type of horizon. In this paper, we show that Penrose singularity theorem can be extended to all the known classes of quasi-topological theories that have non-singular black holes as solutions. We prove that spherical collapse satisfying the null energy condition necessarily leads to future null geodesic incompleteness once a trapped sphere forms. This implies that the lack of predictability of the theories is not an artefact of vacuum solutions and these theories are as problematic as general relativity for the dynamical studies of black hole interiors.

title: Graphs versus loopless digraphs with a given degree sequence, and convergence of uniformly random graphs at every density
abstract: For a degree sequence d on n vertices with M edges, let G(d) be the number of simple graphs and D(d) the number of loopless digraphs with in-degree = out-degree = d. We conjecture that G(d) >= sqrt(D(d)) exp(-C n log(2+M/n)) for every graphical d, a single inequality across all densities, and prove it up to an extra factor log n: G(d) >= sqrt(D(d)) exp(-C n log n log(2+M/n)) for every graphical d. The proof compares pairs of graphs with Eulerian digraphs by alternately colouring closed trails; the failure of injectivity is measured exactly, shared edges cancel against 2-cycles, and parity is handled by merging trails and by a parity argument on Eulerian circuits of odd components. No asymptotic enumeration and no bound on the maximum-entropy multipliers is used. When the maximum-entropy edge probabilities lie in [delta, 1-delta], the same method gives the conjecture itself, G(d) >= sqrt(D(d)) exp(-C n log n / delta). Combined with the exact identity G(d) = exp(g*(d)) pi(d), where pi(d) is the probability that the maximum-entropy beta-model has degrees exactly d, and a van der Waerden-type bound for D(d), this shows that uniformly random graphs with degree sequence d are close in the normalized cut metric to their beta-model whenever M >> n log n log(M/n), at every density, with no tameness and no cap on the degrees. We also record the conjecture in the sparse regime and, with constant 1/2+o(1), in the dense tame regime, from the asymptotic enumerations of McKay-Wormald and Barvinok-Hartigan.

title: Concatenation Locality under Successive Adjacent Transpositions
abstract: We study codes correcting up to $t\geq1$ successive adjacent transpositions, using block concatenation to support blockwise encoding and decoding. A fixed set $P$ of words of length $b$ over a $q$-symbol alphabet generates, for every $m$, the length-$mb$ code of all concatenations of $m$ words from $P$. For our explicit constructions, the prepared encoder and decoder depend only on the block parameters and are reused at every concatenation length. We first prove that correction at every concatenation length is certified by a single finite test at $2t+1$ blocks, and this test is tight over a $q$-symbol alphabet exactly when $\binom q2\geq2t$. For binary words and $b\geq2t+1$, we give an explicit construction with total redundancy at most $mt\log_2 b+O_t(m)$, matching the optimal per-block redundancy $t\log_2 b+O_t(1)$ among block sets correcting at every concatenation length. Among all binary $t$-correcting codes of length $mb$, the optimal total redundancy is $t\log_2(mb)+O_t(1)$. Using all concatenations of one block set makes our total redundancy grow linearly in $m$ and buys independent block encoding, with one encoder and decoder at every length. The construction encodes and decodes in time linear in $mb$ for fixed $b,t$, and recovers the $j$-th source block from the first $jb$ received symbols. We also prove that, whenever the length-$mb$ code corrects $t$ transpositions, the $j$-th source block is determined within $2tb$ received symbols beyond position $jb$, and that explicit binary block sets with rates tending to one as $b$ grows with $t$ fixed attain this bound in the worst case. Finally, we prove that every ordinary correcting code contains a constant fraction of its words whose arbitrary concatenations retain correction, for fixed $q,t$.

title: Increasing the security of advanced metering infrastructure using dynamic defense methods
abstract: With the increase in Internet usage over the last half century, technology has also benefited from the growth and development of the Internet. It is no wonder that smart grids are emerging as one of the most popular technologies of today. As smart grids are connected to the internet, they are constantly vulnerable to cyberattacks. It is always possible for attackers to gain access to metering system infrastructure which is a major and critical part of smart grids. When this system is not working properly because of some security threats, irreparable damage is in the place for a country and its industries. This article suggests utilizing dynamic Applications that Participate in Their Own Defense defenses to secure such systems and infrastructures.

title: The real eigenvalues of the non-backtracking Laplacian
abstract: Let $G$ be a simple graph on $N$ nodes and $M$ edges, with minimum degree at least $2$. We prove that the non-backtracking Laplacian of $G$ has at least $2M-2N+2c+2b$ real eigenvalues, counted with algebraic multiplicity, where $c$ is the number of connected components of $G$ and $b$ is the number of bipartite ones. More precisely, at least $M-N+2c$ of them lie in $[0,1)$ and at least $M-N+2b$ lie in $(1,2]$. We show that the bound $2M-2N+2c+2b$ is sharp, and that a connected $d$-regular graph attains it if and only if it is strictly Ramanujan, i.e., every adjacency eigenvalue $μ\ne\pm d$ satisfies $|μ|<2\sqrt{d-1}$. For completeness, we also show that the non-backtracking Laplacian has at most $2M-2c-2b$ real eigenvalues.

title: The multivariate Berry-Esseen theorem with an absolute constant
abstract: We prove that the multivariate Berry--Esseen inequality for sums of independent random vectors holds with the same constant in every dimension. For independent centered random vectors $X_1,\ldots,X_n\in\mathbb{R}^d$ whose covariance matrices sum to $I_d$, we show that the distance between the distribution of their sum and $N(0,I_d)$, measured uniformly over convex sets, is at most $C_0\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbb{E}\|X_i\|_2^3$ for a universal constant $C_0$. The bound requires only finite third moments and holds uniformly in the dimension, the number of summands, and their distributions. It also yields the corresponding bound for independent and identically distributed vectors. In particular, $C_0$ can be chosen to be $980$.

title: Higgs boson decays into gauge bosons: theoretical predictions in RNS
abstract: We discuss recent results on the loop-induced decays $h\to Zγ$, $h\toγγ$, and $h\to gg$ in the Radiatively Natural Supersymmetry (RNS) framework. These processes are sensitive to contributions from particles beyond the Standard Model and provide complementary probes of supersymmetric effects. We evaluate the decay amplitudes and partial widths for parameter points consistent with a Higgs boson mass near the measured value of 125 GeV, and examine their dependence on the model parameters. Across the parameter space, the predicted $h\to Zγ$ width can reach about 7.5 keV, while the $h\toγγ$ and $h\to gg$ widths remain close to their Standard Model predictions. We compare the $h\to Zγ$ predictions with the available ATLAS and CMS measurements and discuss the prospects for distinguishing RNS from the Standard Model with improved experimental precision.

title: Conditional Diffusion-Based Generation of T2-Weighted Prostate MRI for Clinically Significant Prostate Cancer Classification
abstract: Scarce and unrepresentative training data limit the performance of prostate MRI prediction models. Synthetic T2-weighted (T2W) MRI may augment training data containing clinically significant prostate cancer (csPCa) and transition zone (TZ) lesions. In this retrospective, single-center, ethics-committee-approved study, we developed a conditional generative model for T2W prostate MRI extending MAISI-v2 with csPCa class, zonal, and lesion-mask-guided conditioning, incorporating a relative advantage weighted loss fine-tuned on 1,303 patients (1,654 lesions). Fidelity was assessed by incremental ablation, and downstream utility was evaluated with T2W-based csPCa classifiers across five simulated training-data scenarios, each testing 18 synthetic-data configurations. The proposed model reduced Fréchet inception distance (FID) from 13.28 (pretrained MAISI-v2) to $2.04 \pm 0.06$ internally (PI-CAI: $3.83 \pm 0.51$). Synthetic augmentation significantly increased AUC in all five scenarios (+0.027 to +0.088; adjusted $p = 0.016$--$0.043$), though cross-institutional augmentation of PI-CAI yielded a non-significant gain (+0.013; $p = 0.397$). Overall, our model improved T2W MRI fidelity, and synthetic images improved csPCa classification under simulated data constraints, although benefit did not transfer significantly across institutions.

title: Eunoia: Area-Proportional Euler and Venn Diagrams in Rust, Julia, Python, R, and JavaScript
abstract: Area-proportional Euler diagrams visualize sets and their intersections through regions whose areas represent their sizes. Because many set specifications have no exact geometric representation, constructing these diagrams requires numerical optimization and diagnostics that quantify the remaining discrepancies. Eunoia is a Rust library for fitting area-proportional Euler diagrams and constructing canonical Venn diagrams. It supports circles, ellipses, squares, and rectangles, computes region areas analytically, and provides exact analytical gradients for several shape families. Its fitting pipeline combines multidimensional scaling initialization with local refinement, global optimization when needed, and seeded restarts. Fitted layouts include residuals and goodness-of-fit statistics that help users assess how faithfully a diagram represents the data. Shared plotting routines extract region polygons, place labels, and pack unit glyphs and member names within regions. The same core implementation powers packages for R, Python, Julia, and JavaScript, a C interface, and a web application that fits diagrams entirely in the browser through WebAssembly. By centralizing fitting, geometry, diagnostics, and annotation in an independent library, Eunoia provides consistent set visualization across programming languages and interactive applications.

title: Current Sheets and Magnetic Reconnection statistics by Solar Orbiter at few to tens of Ion Inertial Lengths II: Conditions for Reconnection, and Current Sheet Planarity
abstract: We present a statistical study of magnetic reconnection and current sheet (CS) properties at scales from the ion inertial length ($δ_i$), up to 86.4 $δ_i$. We analyze 103 hours of high-cadence (4 samples/s) in-situ Solar Orbiter ion data, collected from July 2020 to September 2022, which correspond mainly to slow and Alfvénic solar wind. We applied an automatic detection algorithm to find CSs of thicknesses near and above the ion inertial length ($δ_i$), and classify them as Alfvénic or reconnecting. The orientation of the CSs is consistent with an isotropic distribution of the discontinuities. The median ratio of reconnection jet velocity to theoretical outflow velocity is 0.71. We find that the diamagnetic drift reconnection suppression mechanism has no impact on the cataloged CSs, due to the symmetry of their upstream conditions. We find that a flow shear in the reconnection direction suppresses magnetic reconnection, and it is consistently greater for Alfvénic than for reconnecting CSs. Flow shear in the guide-field direction is too small to suppress magnetic reconnection in ion scale solar wind CSs.

title: ZeroGraph: Compositional Blockwise Training via Materialized Boundary Supervision
abstract: Blockwise learning can remove online gradient dependencies across depth, but independently optimized blocks need not compose into a useful model. We present ZeroGraph, a systems transformation for pretrained-model conversion and distillation that materializes a frozen teacher's coherent boundary trajectory as a versioned dataset. Each partition then trains with disjoint parameters, optimizer state, random state, and checkpoints, replacing live cross-depth dependencies with persistent supervision. Experiments separate learning quality from systems behavior. On GPT-2 Large, an unanchored objective reduces denoising error by 99.44%, yet assembled held-out cross-entropy worsens from 3.63 to 10.48 and context use becomes negative. A six-arm TinyLlama study identifies clean teacher-boundary regression as the successful interface; the tested noisy objective fails with cached or online targets. The clean recipe passes quality and context-use gates across three Qwen2.5-1.5B seeds and on a 3.086B Qwen2.5 model. In an objective-matched comparison, cached and online targets are bitwise identical. Cached jobs are faster after materialization, but a 618.31 s cache-build cost prevents wall-time break-even through 16 measured reuses. Boundary-shift tests show tolerance to intermediate representation mismatch, and an interrupted block resumes to a bitwise-identical final state without rerunning unaffected blocks. In the tested pretrained-model conversion and distillation setting, cross-depth semantic dependence can move from online optimization into persistent data.

title: Angle-dependent emission from evolving accretion layers
abstract: Photon propagation through an evolving atmosphere can change the angular distribution of emerging radiation even when its integrated optical column remains constant. We quantify this effect in an irradiated, internally heated, expanding plane-parallel layer using grey, special-relativistic similarity solutions. The full angular radiation field determines both the source function and the acceleration of a pressureless flow in prompt radiative balance. We compare each evolving solution with two frozen transport calculations on the same density and velocity profiles, holding the source fixed in one and allowing it to relax in the other. Heating produces the familiar transition from limb darkening to limb brightening, while the temporal correction to the angular contrast changes sign with optical column. For an upper boundary moving at $0.04c$, an injection speed of $0.06c$, and heating four times the reference incident flux, the intensity ratio between direction cosines $0.1$ and $1$ exceeds the frozen, fixed-source result by $18.8$ per cent at column $τ_0=0.15$, but is smaller by $2.53$ per cent at $τ_0=0.55$. Source relaxation preserves this reversal. The corresponding direct photon flight times are one third and three per cent of the flow age in the oblique and normal directions, respectively. These solutions provide a controlled local benchmark for temporal angular transfer in evolving disc atmospheres and reprocessing layers; application to a specific accreting system requires thermal, spectral, and geometrical physics beyond the present model.

title: Thermodynamic Underpinnings Affecting Compressive and Tensile Plasticity in Refractory Compositionally Complex Alloys
abstract: Refractory compositionally complex alloys (R-CCAs) show great promise as next generation structural materials for extreme conditions, but alloys with excellent high temperature mechanical properties most often exhibit virtually zero room temperature tensile ductility, hindering potential commercial application. Several semi-empirical metrics have been employed for predicting plasticity in R-CCAs, including valence electron concentration, Pugh ratio, Rice criteria, and the D-parameter. While many currently available ductility metrics correlate very well when compressive plasticity is considered, only the density functional theory (DFT) based D-parameter shows a strong correlation in tension. A new ductility metric is developed using CALculation of PHAse Diagrams (CALPHAD) thermodynamics, Gamma, with includes the free energy difference between the body-centered cubic (BCC) and hexagonal close-packed (HCP) phases, the interfacial free energy of a (110) BCC surface, and an electronegativity-corrected lattice distortion. The Gamma parameter exhibits better correlation with tensile ductility than D-parameter and performs equally well in compression. While this improvement is modest, a thermodynamically grounded ductility metric is clearly required to capture intrinsic ductility behavior. Extrinsic contributions to brittle behavior in R-CCAs, namely interstitial oxygen content, are also briefly discussed. Combining the Gamma ductility parameter with CALPHAD-calculated oxygen solubility is proposed as a first order attempt to capture both intrinsic and extrinsic contributions to ductile behavior in R-CCAs.

title: Depth Anyviewpoint? Evaluating Monocular Depth Over Viewpoint Sequences
abstract: Monocular depth estimation aims to predict depth maps from single RGB images (forgoing the need for stereo camera pairs) and has seen impressive leaps in performance in recent work due to the introduction of affine-invariant losses and the use of foundation model features. These monocular depth models predict affine-invariant depth, which describes the relative positions of objects in the scene instead of absolute depth. While these models demonstrate strong performance on single image benchmarks and qualitatively consistent predictions in video, their effectiveness at preserving consistent spatial structure has been less thoroughly explored. Many potential real-world applications, such as handling video streams as input, rely on coherent three dimensional consistency in scenes. Further, anchoring relative depth predictions to a metric reference for a given scene is a key challenge for applying monocular depth models to real-world situations. We develop a novel evaluation protocol for monocular depth models using video sequences with moving camera positions to test the consistency of prediction across variation in viewpoint. We demonstrate this methodology over diverse, real-world video sequences where we are able to anchor depth model output to metric depth values using structure from motion. Our work demonstrates open challenges in the development of broadly applicable monocular depth foundation models, particularly with their ability to provide temporal consistency over long time frames. We also identify challenges in the straightforward adoption of structure-from-motion as a metric grounding tool for monocular depth estimation models.

title: Learning from high-resolution 2D images to reconstruct 3D microstructures
abstract: High-resolution three-dimensional (3D) microstructure characterization remains difficult to undertake at scale because volumetric imaging at the required spatial resolution is expensive, time-consuming or destructive. In many settings, however, fine-resolution two-dimensional (2D) imaging and lower-resolution volumetric measurements are both readily available. We introduce a Privileged Cross-modal Relational Distillation (PCRD) framework that leverages fine-resolution 2D observations during training to improve specimen-specific 3D reconstruction from lower-resolution volumetric imaging alone. We demonstrate PCRD on pultruded carbon fiber-reinforced polymer composites, using scanning electron microscopy as the privileged modality and micro-CT as the inference input. The framework transfers spatial organization by matching similarity distributions defined around corresponding spatial anchors in the teacher and student representations, avoiding direct alignment of heterogeneous feature vectors. In 2D cross-sectional reconstruction, PCRD improves mAP by 1.66 percentage points over direct micro-CT training. Independent 3D validation against high-resolution synchrotron X-ray CT data shows close agreement in fiber volume fraction, diameter and local spacing. The PCRD reconstruction matches 89.97% of the reference fiber centerline length, compared with 75.08% for the interpolated low-resolution volume.

title: Fisher--Hartwig asymptotics and critical moments for the circular beta ensemble
abstract: We determine the joint moments of real powers of the absolute value of characteristic polynomials in the circular beta ensemble, for every $β>0$. At fixed distinct prescribed points, the Fisher--Hartwig formula holds for every exponent greater than $-1$, with explicit constants and a relative error bounded by a negative power of the matrix size $N$. For approaching points in the same integrable range, the error is bounded by a negative power of $Nδ_N$, provided that $Nδ_N\to\infty$ and the sum of the absolute values of the negative exponents is less than two. Here $δ_N$ is the minimum distance between the prescribed points; this range includes every integrable pair of root exponents. For $q>0$ at the critical relation $pq^2=2β$, we prove the Keating--Wong asymptotic for the $p$th moment of the integral of the $q$th absolute power of the characteristic polynomial, for every real $p>1$. The leading asymptotic extends to every complex spatial weight in $L^p$. The proofs combine the recursion for orthogonal polynomials on the unit circle with conditional expectation identities for Gaussian multiplicative chaos and quantitative estimates for approaching singularities.

title: Hardy transitions on product lattices
abstract: Boundary conditions can change the dimensional scale of a sharp functional inequality. We determine this change for inverse-square Hardy inequalities on the product lattices $\mathbb N^k\times\mathbb Z^{N-k}$. Their sharp constants satisfy $C_{N,k}\sim N^2Ψ(k/N)$ uniformly for $1\le k\le N$, where $Ψ(α)\sim2α$ at zero. The law gives linear growth for a fixed number of positive coordinates, every intermediate power for suitable sublinear choices, and quadratic growth for a positive proportion. We develop a method that connects exact uncertainty inequalities with Hardy inequalities through logarithmic localization, and combines this transfer with a block decomposition to cover all proportions. The transfer holds on weighted graphs with an explicit geometric error and controls the variational problem over arbitrary functions. A mixture of two Mathieu ground energies determines $Ψ$. At the fully positive endpoint, the variational problem defining $κ=Ψ(1)$ has a unique nondegenerate minimum and a unique positive energy--moment minimizing profile. We also prove strict comparison with the continuum coefficient in every sector for $N\ge9$, the optimal uniform dimension.

title: Built on Broken Assumptions (BOBA): Why Coding Agents Cannot Be Left Alone
abstract: Coding agents are autonomous developers. Given a request, they change the code and report back when done. As such, they can handle not only independent requests but whole chains of them, each request built on the last. Agents are known to report wrong work as done, yet benchmarks still test them one request at a time, on human-written code, checked once. We build BOBA-Bench, 280 chains of 20 consecutive requests drawn from 140 real open-source projects, and evaluate ten coding agents on both. All ten do far worse on chains. On average, they complete 95% of requests taken one at a time, but when requests are chained together, they complete 51%. Worse code is not the cause. Once checked, agent code is nearly as good a base for later requests as human code. The cause is the mistakes agents miss. Coding agents declare a request done once their own tests pass, even when those tests miss a mistake. The next request then builds on broken code and fails about twice as often. The mistake is rarely found later. Nor can agents catch such mistakes by reviewing code. Asked whether an implementation is correct, they are right 53% of the time, barely better than a coin flip. Coding agents are therefore heavily dependent on access to verification. A single external ``that's wrong'' after a failed request and one repair round lift chain completion from 51% to 59%, and a repaired mistake no longer hurts the requests that follow. In simpler terms, coding agents are only as reliable as the checks they can reach: without verification, every request that follows is built on broken assumptions.

title: Test-Time Scaling for Open-Ended Reasoning at Small Model Scale
abstract: A vote over a model's samples can only help when the samples disagree. For open-ended generation the binding question is therefore not how to combine samples but whether a model produces samples worth combining, a question test-time scaling has answered for math but not for free-form text. We study it at small scale with semantic cluster voting, a judge-free aggregator that groups a small instruct model's samples by meaning and returns the largest cluster's representative, with no reward model or self-judging. On a 250-prompt benchmark with three tiers of answer checkability, the same pattern holds across three model families (Qwen2.5-3B, Llama-3.2-3B, Gemma-2-2B) and two generation seeds: voting raises accuracy on the math control, where samples vary but stay checkable (a gain of +10 to +29 points across the three models), yet adds at most +0.30 judge points on open-ended text. On a larger 200-problem MATH-500 run with the primary model, the math gain is +8.5 points (95% CI [+4.0, +13.0]). Almost every open-ended sample falls into one meaning cluster, so there is little to select over. The collapse is consistent with instruction-tuning rather than model size, and raising decoding temperature does not recover usable diversity, because it costs more quality than it adds (net -0.64 judge points, 95% CI [-0.93, -0.37]).

title: From Fabrication Disorder to Quantum-Protocol Yield in Inverse-Designed Silicon Photonic Beam Splitters
abstract: Telecom-band silicon spin-photon qubits offer a promising platform for scalable quantum networks and distributed information processing, but their fixed emission wavelengths require compact, low-loss beam splitters with precise splitting and fabrication robustness. Conventional designs can face trade-offs between footprint, optical performance, and wavelength-specific operation. Here, we employ adjoint-based inverse design to optimize photonic geometries beyond conventional layouts, developing 1*2 Y-splitters and 2*2 directional couplers for the silicon T (1326 nm) and Al1 (1482.44 nm) spin-photon qubits. The devices achieve footprints of 2.9 and 26 um^2, respectively, with excess losses of 0.14-0.44 dB and back-reflection below 5*10^-4. We assess fabrication tolerance using 100-realization Monte Carlo simulations incorporating etch bias, line-edge roughness, thickness, and refractive-index variations. Mirror symmetry reduces the splitting-ratio spread of the Y-splitter by a factor of seven to nine relative to the directional coupler. We translate these variations into dual-rail fidelity, ideal splitting-ratio-limited Hong-Ou-Mandel visibility, and random-number min-entropy. All realizations satisfy a protocol-performance threshold of 0.95. At 0.99, the tolerated splitting-ratio deviation shrinks from 0.035 for visibility to 0.0035 for min-entropy, and the simulated yields are 68% (T) and 91% (Al1) for coupler visibility and 90% (T) and 66% (Al1) for Y-splitter min-entropy. The tolerance of the target protocol, rather than the device alone, therefore sets the fabrication requirement for silicon spin-photon beam splitters.

title: A Quasisymmetric Analogue of the Bruhat Order
abstract: We define a quasisymmetric analogue of the Bruhat order on indexed binary forests using the multiplicity-free Monk rule for forest polynomials. For the finite window $\mathcal{P}_n$ of forests supported in $[1,n]$, we construct an explicit partition into saturated chains terminating at the top rank, proving that $\mathcal{P}_n$ is strongly Sperner. We also recover the known Catalan ballot formula for its rank numbers. For principal lower intervals, we prove that $[\varnothing,F]$ is a lattice if and only if it is Boolean, and characterize this property by the avoidance of a bent corner in $F$, a path of three internal vertices that changes direction. This gives a forest analogue of the pattern-avoidance characterization of Boolean principal Bruhat intervals. We also conjecture that every principal lower interval is shellable, providing computational evidence and proving the conjecture for a family of hook intervals.

title: Forecasting Earth Surface Change in Embedding Space
abstract: Repeated satellite imagery permits understanding of how our planet changes over time, letting us predict its future and plan mitigating actions. Most existing studies that rely on a time series of satellite observations forecast the spectral values at each pixel for a future target date. However, clouds, shadows, and sensor noise often corrupt these observations, so that spectral forecasters waste much of their capacity on low-level features or noise rather than real change. With the advent of Earth foundation models, we argue that forecasting in embedding space is a feasible and more effective alternative. To this end, we design a token space that handles irregular histories from different sensors and foundation models and supports forecasts at any query date. Tokens from this space are inputs to our proposed forecaster, E$^2$Forecast, which is a transformer with two branches: a Gaussian branch that directly predicts a mean point forecast and per-dimension standard deviations, and a rectified-flow branch that generates forecast ensembles. On Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 benchmarks, forecasting embeddings instead of spectral values halves the cosine distance (from 0.20 to 0.10) and greatly reduces overconfidence, lowering the z-score standard deviation from 2.63 to 1.22. By comparing new observations with its forecasts, E$^2$Forecast can also detect anomalous changes without labels or retraining, raising F$_1$ from 41.58 to 48.70 on a global benchmark. This consistent superiority is validated on nine remote sensing foundation models. Beyond change detection, we believe our approach advances the field by permitting effective reuse of diverse pretrained task heads. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/ucam-eo/e2forecast.

title: Empirical rather than simulated spectral band adjustment of MODIS to Sentinel-3 OLCI for European vegetation monitoring
abstract: Spectral band adjustment derived from convolved spectra describes sensor differences under controlled conditions, but its applicability to operational products requires assessment. We compare this approach with adjustment estimated directly from MODIS and Sentinel-3 OLCI observations for European vegetation monitoring. Both streams undergo atmospheric correction and Ross-Thick/Li-Sparse Reciprocal BRDF normalization to nadir viewing and local solar noon. Using observations from 2019-2024, we derive annual OLCI/MODIS reflectance-ratio relationships with unadjusted MODIS NDVI. The operational correction uses quadratic red and linear near-infrared (NIR) functions. We compare these relationships with irradiance-weighted canopy simulations and assess the empirical correction at 460 locations. Simulated and empirical relationships differ, particularly for red reflectance at high NDVI. Background-dependent simulated ratios also demonstrate the limitations of a single NDVI-based function. The empirical correction reduces red and NIR root-mean-square error (RMSE) at 66.3% and 71.1% of locations, with median paired reductions of 5.98% and 13.67%. Median paired RMSE decreases by 0.86% for NDVI but increases by 0.95% for EVI2, 0.74% for NIRv and 7.07% for the Plant Phenology Index (PPI), calculated with stream-specific historical references. This study establishes an operational empirical adjustment and shows that the specified spectral simulation does not reproduce the relationship between the normalized products. It provides evidence for improved reflectance consistency while demonstrating that vegetation-index benefits require separate assessment.

title: The nucleon is not a hard sphere: screening fifth forces with Skyrmions
abstract: Laboratory searches for chameleon and symmetron fifth forces increasingly rely on individual nucleons as sources or probes, but model them as uniform spheres. Motivated by the Skyrme picture, we instead consider a nucleon profile with a constant-density core and an $r^{-6}$ pion tail, together with its exponential truncation at the physical pion mass. We derive analytic screening charges for the uniform sphere and the $r^{-6}$ profile, and extend the comparison to the exponential truncation at the physical pion mass using numerical solutions. Because the outer tail is too dilute to be screened at any coupling strength, the $r^{-6}$ tail produces a power-law enhancement over the sphere charge in strong screening, and the exponential tail has a weaker, logarithmic enhancement. Propagating this difference through the published analyses, nucleon-sourced exclusion regions extend systematically further into the strongly coupled regime. For example, symmetron constraints from neutron interferometry at $μ=1\,\mathrm{keV}$ reach maximal self-couplings about $1.4$ orders of magnitude higher than for a uniform-sphere neutron ($3.0$ orders of magnitude in the chiral limit),and at the dark-energy scale the hydrogen $1s$--$2s$ chameleon bound reaches couplings $1.8$ orders of magnitude weaker than for a uniform-sphere proton ($2.4$ in the chiral limit), overtaking the muonium bound.

title: Clock Offsets and Ranges from Optical Pseudoranges
abstract: This note describes the estimation of ranges and clock offsets from measured pseudoranges in the context of the Kepler Navigation System. The latter system continuously adapts the frequency of its clocks to ensure that they all show the same time independently of where they are. In Medium Earth Orbits, the joint problem of estimating ranges and clock offsets can then be factorized.

title: Discrimination, Calibration, and Ranking: A Unified Matrix Framework
abstract: Discrimination, calibration, and ranking are the three pillars of classifier evaluation, yet no single algebraic language spans all three. A recent indicator-matrix account unifies discrimination measures (precision, recall, F1, Matthews correlation) across binary, multiclass, multilabel and related settings, using Boolean cell operations on indicator label matrices, generalised to soft labels by t-norms. Calibration measures (Brier score, log-loss) and ranking measures (nDCG, AUC) fall outside it. We close the gap with two further classes of cell operators: deviation operators phi(y - yhat), which give a Calibration Framework, and rank- and slice-dependent operators (positional gains for DCG, column concordance cells for AUC), which give a Ranking Framework. Both inherit the micro/macro/exemplar aggregation architecture. For calibration, the three Brier aggregations collapse to one scalar; the Murphy decomposition holds in matrix form (unbinned, binned and isotonic); and, within the Brier-type class-indexed family, a measure is skew-invariant if and only if it depends only on the class-conditional errors alpha_j and beta_j, the calibration analogues of recall and specificity. For ranking, raw DCG collapses across aggregations while nDCG does not; per-class nDCG and per-class AUC are related by a row-column duality; micro-AUC differs from pooled ROC-AUC; raw positional scores are never strictly proper, and nDCG and AUC need not be proper. The skew-invariant per-class building blocks share one class-conditional expectation template. Experiments on two multilabel benchmarks illustrate the distinctions. Many of the results are machine-checked in Lean 4; the proofs, the experiments and the aggmetrics.scores package are public: https://github.com/rcprati/discrimination-calibration-ranking

title: Do agents need to sleep?
abstract: LLM-based agents, which increasingly operate persistently across sessions and accumulate memory through interaction, already exhibit the familiar symptoms of unchecked plasticity: semantic drift, degraded retrieval precision, propagation of stored errors, and saturation of memory capacity. Drawing on the selectionist "ringing, resonance and renormalization" (RRR) account of sleep, we propose that each of its three phases maps onto an operation feasible in digital memory architectures. Engineers building stateful agents, meanwhile, are independently rediscovering the problems sleep evolved to solve: what to forget, and when to do the forgetting. From this we derive the falsifiable prediction that selectionist consolidation will outperform instructionist alternatives as memory stores grow large. The core claim concerns the nature of continuous learning itself: plasticity has a price, and for any system that learns continuously under finite capacity while coupled to its environment, that price is sleep.

title: A converse theorem for GL(2) over global fields without root numbers
abstract: We prove a converse theorem for GL(2) over global fields in which the root numbers in the twisted functional equations need not be prescribed. Instead, we allow nonzero scalar factors that are invariant under unramified twists. We show that these scalars are independent of the twisting character and obtain a unique isobaric automorphic representation with the prescribed unramified local components.

title: Beyond Ensemble Disagreement: Predictive STL Monitoring of RL Locomotion under Distribution Shift
abstract: RL locomotion policies trained under nominal simulation conditions may encounter distribution shifts that compromise safety. Predictive monitors could anticipate violations, but their world-model forecasts may become unreliable under shift, and ensemble disagreement is not calibrated. We evaluate predictive Signal Temporal Logic (STL) monitoring for frozen Ant-v5 and HalfCheetah-v5 policies using closed-loop world-model rollouts and a three-model ensemble. Across external-force, observation-noise, and mass shifts, predicted robustness ranks HalfCheetah's future STL violations strongly, whereas disagreement does not reliably track observation prediction error or violations. Under severe noise, violations remain common ($64.2\pm24.4\%$ at $K{=}20$ across three PPO seeds), yet current-state robustness without prediction comes within $0.03$ AUROC of predictive robustness. Penalizing predicted robustness by disagreement does not consistently improve ranking. Ant provides complementary per-specification evidence, but its composite target has no positive violations and its any-violation target is single-class in most evaluated seed-condition slices. Overall, predictive robustness provides useful STL-specific ranking but little demonstrated additional ranking value over the current state; these findings caution against treating ensemble disagreement as a reliable indicator of safety uncertainty.

title: What is the connection between quantum relationality and symmetry-based relationality?
abstract: Although it has often been noted that both quantum mechanics and relativistic physics involve significant forms of relationality, the nature of the connection remains unclear. In addressing such a question it makes sense to start from the simplest possibility, so in this article I set out to consider the viability of the hypothesis that the two types of relationality are ultimately the same: that is, quantum states always characterize degrees of freedom which can be changed by a symmetry transformation, so they are relativized for exactly the same reason as partial observables in general relativity. I use the idea that we only measure partial observables to argue that this suggestion is compatible with all existing empirical evidence for quantum mechanics, and then I consider the consequences for ongoing debates about the nature of measurement in quantum mechanics.

title: Statistical mechanics of spontaneous behavior
abstract: Why do a few behaviors fill most of an animal's time? The usual answer is that these behaviors are started more often, because learning and reinforcement favor them. Here we show that how long a behavior lasts can, by itself, explain much of what is observed. We consider a system that runs until it meets a constraint, such as a wall, and then resets. The fraction of time it spends in each behavior then follows the Boltzmann law, and the partition function is the mean time between resets. The four laws of thermodynamics follow as theorems from four postulates, and critical points that act as bottlenecks become the most occupied states. In 47 multi-day recordings of fruit flies, the dominant behavior accounts for only $13\%$ of bout starts yet fills $49\%$ of the time, and its typical duration identifies the individual fly. These results lay the groundwork for a statistical mechanics of behavior.

title: Solving the Mystery of the Electron Radiation Belt at Uranus: Leveraging Knowledge of Earth's Radiation Belts in a Re-Examination of Voyager 2 Observations
abstract: Voyager 2 provided the only direct measurement of the radiation environment at Uranus and established the well-accepted characterization of a system with a weaker ion radiation belt and surprisingly intense electron radiation belt. Recent re-analysis of the flyby, however, suggests that these observations were not taken during normal solar wind conditions, and instead occurred while a large solar wind transient, a corotating interaction region, was passing over the system. With this context, this study compares the Voyager 2 observations to a similar event observed at Earth. This comparative approach, along with an expanded contextual interpretation of the Voyager 2 flyby, suggests that solar wind-magnetospheric interactions at Uranus may have driven enhanced lower band chorus wave emissions capable of accelerating electrons to relativistic energies. This motivates new, more expansive questions to be explored at Uranus and highlights the need for a Uranus orbiter mission.

title: A Data-Driven, Gain-Scheduled Equivalent Circuit for the B-H Behavior of Power Ferrites
abstract: An equivalent circuit for the dynamic B-H behavior of power ferrites is identified from measured transients. It consists of classical elements of hysteresis modeling: a nonlinear inductor for the reversible curve, six viscous play branches (inductors in series with diode-bridge sliders) that form a Prandtl-Ishlinskii model, two R-L branches for the magnetic after-effect, a mean-field feedback of H as in the Jiles-Atherton model, and a measurement path. All elements are positive apart from the feedback sources, and the circuit can run in SPICE. Discretized at the sampling step, the circuit is a difference equation with 32 parameters per material, fitted by backpropagation through time. On the 15 materials of the MagNet Challenge 2, the mean sequence relative error is 7.33 % against 7.77 % for the challenge-winning recurrent network with 336 parameters, and the circuit is more accurate on 12 of the 15 materials. The accuracy can be scaled up by gain scheduling, where a small network per material sets the element values at every step from the excitation, while the hysteresis memory stays in the circuit, such that the error drops to 5.25 % with 656 parameters per material. Thus, an interpretable model is demonstrated that achieves state-of-the-art accuracy.

title: On the probability that the integer parts of polynomials are coprime
abstract: We prove that for any $s\ge 2$ and polynomials $f_{1}(x),\dots,f_{s-1}(x)\in \mathbb{R}[x]$ satisfying a certain equidistribution condition, the natural density of the numbers $n\in \mathbb{N}$ such that $n,\lfloor f_{1}(n)\rfloor,\dots,\lfloor f_{s-1}(n)\rfloor$ are mutually coprime is $1/ζ(s)$. This generalises a recent result of Champagne, in which this was proven under the assumption that $f_{1}$ is linear.

title: Radial Evolution of a CIR: Observations From a Nearly Radially Aligned Event Between Parker Solar Probe and STEREO-A
abstract: The addition of Parker Solar Probe (PSP) to the Heliophysics System Observatory has allowed for the unprecedented ability to study Corotating Interaction Regions (CIRs) at multiple radial distances without significant temporal/longitudinal variations. On September 19, 2019, PSP observed a CIR at $\sim$0.5 au when it was nearly radially aligned with the Solar Terrestrial Relations Observatory-Ahead (STEREO-A) spacecraft at $\sim$1 au, allowing for an unambiguous assessment of the radial evolution of a single CIR. Bulk plasma and magnetic field signatures of the CIR evolve in a fashion characteristic to previous observations; however, the suprathermal ions are enhanced over a larger longitudinal range at PSP than at STEREO-A, although at much lower intensities. The longitudinal spread appears to be largely a consequence of magnetic field line topology at CIRs between the compressed slow solar wind upstream and high-speed stream following the CIR, underscoring the importance of the large-scale topology of these structures.

title: Nondestructive 3D Metrology of Through-Glass Via Geometry and Internal Wall Texture Using Holotomography
abstract: Through-glass vias (TGVs) are increasingly important for semiconductor packaging, yet their internal geometry and wall texture remain difficult to characterize nondestructively. Here, we use holotomography (HT) to inspect the three-dimensional (3D) geometry and internal wall texture of intact, unfilled TGVs before metallization. HT reconstructs the refractive index (RI) distribution of the glass and via. Maps of RI and spatially filtered RI then localize the internal boundary. Geometric fitting quantifies via dimensions and taper, while spatial filtering separates slowly varying wall form from finer texture. The reconstructed surface supports volumetric visualization, dimensional measurements and spatial characterization of wall texture within one optical inspection workflow. These measurements reveal internal features inaccessible from surface views and provide quantitative descriptors to evaluate TGVs

title: Modeling and Experimental Validation of Bubble-Induced Performance Losses in Microstructured Copper Electrodes for Alkaline Water Electrolysis
abstract: Water electrolysis is a promising technology for sustainable hydrogen (H$_2$) production. However, gas bubble formation significantly degrades the electrochemical surface area ($A_{\rm EC}$) and the electrocatalytic activity of microstructured electrodes in water electrolyzer cells. Existing theoretical models fail to connect computational fluid dynamics (CFD) and electrochemistry to analyze how bubble dynamics affect the performance of gas-evolving microstructured electrodes. This work develops a multiphysics-based theoretical model that couples two-phase CFD with Butler-Volmer and Faradaic kinetics, incorporating exchange current density, cell current, gravitational acceleration, surface tension, and fluid properties such as density and viscosity. The model quantifies essential electrochemical parameters, such as the enhancement in $A_{\rm EC}$ and the overpotential ($η$), which deviate by less than 7\% and 15\%, respectively, from the experimental results. Evaluations of the fabricated microstructured electrodes using polarization curves, cyclic voltammetry, electrochemical impedance spectroscopy, and linear polarization resistance techniques demonstrate reduced $η$ by 2.49--21.39\% and 9.55--24.32\% for oxygen (O$_2$) and H$_2$ evolution, respectively. Furthermore, the model reveals the interplay between enhanced geometric surface area and bubble-transport limitations, facilitating the optimization and analysis of structural parameters. These findings establish a physics-informed roadmap for designing optimal, robust, and industry-scalable microstructured electrodes for efficient H$_2$ generation via water electrolysis.

title: Quantum Temporal Marginal Problem
abstract: Experiments on a multi-time quantum process may reveal its responses only on selected, possibly overlapping, sets of times. We ask whether these partial descriptions admit a common underlying process, and formulate this process tensor marginal problem as a semidefinite feasibility test. Agreement on overlaps is necessary but insufficient: three locally consistent qubit marginals can have no common extension. Another family is incompatible as a time-ordered process even though a single quantum channel satisfies both its channel and temporal marginal constraints. This isolates temporal causality as the obstruction. We quantify incompatibility by the mixing needed to restore compatibility and derive finite tests using separate interventions at each time and final measurements. We further show that incompatibility is equivalent to an advantage over every compatible family in a multi-time process-discrimination task. Together, these results test whether process descriptions obtained in different experiments can arise from one causally ordered quantum process.

title: Integrating Data Center Flexibility into Power System Operations: A Framework for Temporal Redispatch
abstract: Rapid growth in data center electricity demand, driven by artificial intelligence (AI) training and inference, is expected to increase stress conditions for power grids. Operational flexibility from data centers offers a near-term lever to relieve such stresses. Existing models of data center flexibility tend to bundle economic incentives with physical constraints, obscuring the tradeoff between economic willingness to shift load and technical limitations to do so. This paper proposes a temporal-redispatch focused framework that decouples data center demand flexibility into two independently parameterized dimensions: (1) systematic flexibility, capturing the economic environment through penalties for temporal shifting of data centers' scheduled demand, and (2) operational flexibility, capturing the physical envelope through the demand shifting time window and the limit on shifted data center demand. The framework relies on a direct current optimal power flow (DC-OPF) linear program which enables annual parametric analysis at hourly resolution. The framework is studied using a synthetic grid mimicking the Texas transmission system populated with the 2026 Adjusted Forecast from ERCOT (Electric Reliability Council of Texas). Results show that operational flexibility imposes a physical lower bound on unsatisfied demand that no economic incentive can overcome; longer shifting windows and higher limits on shifted data center demand reduce operational cost with different impacts on grid utilization; and, temporal redispatch shaves system-wide net load peaks while partially compensating for localized transmission bottlenecks that emerge under modeled coal retirement scenarios.

title: Generalized Quasi-Symmetric Nets: A Constructive Approach to the Equimodular Elliptic Type and to Flexible $m \times n$ Nets
abstract: Quadrilateral meshes that flex with rigid planar faces are of interest to transformable architecture, rigid-foldable origami, and mechanical metamaterials. Their building blocks are flexible $3 \times 3$ nets, that is, Kokotsakis polyhedra with a quadrangular base, classified by Izmestiev. We study one of his types, the equimodular elliptic type, defined by three conditions on the flat angles, the third of them through Jacobi elliptic functions. We turn these conditions into equivalent algebraic ones, free of elliptic functions, which lead to the generalized quasi-symmetric nets (GQS-nets), polyhedra of this type that include the known elliptic quasi-symmetric nets. For every polyhedron of this type, we give a flexible polyhedron with the same flat angles and its flexion in closed form. From the simplest GQS-nets, we assemble arbitrarily large flexible $m \times n$ nets. Examples include nets that, at one position, form letters; further nets in the supplementary materials form digits or, seen along their rows, approximately follow the side silhouettes of a bunny and a fish. Unlike numerically computed mechanisms, these nets are exactly flexible. As an application, we design three such nets as transportable arch halls of 80 mm sandwich panels, which fold to fit through the door of a standard container or into the well of a low-bed semi-trailer, and we check them numerically under snow load and build a 1:20 model of one. Supplementary Mathematica notebooks verify the symbolic computations, a Python tool constructs the nets and checks them numerically, including for self-intersections, and further scripts recheck the halls.

title: Who Should Score the Cache? Mid-Depth Layers Are the Best Judges of KV-Cache Eviction
abstract: Key-value (KV) cache eviction methods rank tokens by attention scores, and each layer scores its own cache. To our knowledge, no eviction method asks which layer should score. We find, across twenty-one models, that the depth of the scoring layer governs eviction quality. On the eighteen models with per-layer caches, spanning 0.5B to 109B, long-context retrieval accuracy collapses at shallow layers, peaks between 0.4 and 0.75 of depth, and degrades at the last layer. The curve arises because a layer judges tokens well only once it has used the question to find the answer, which takes several layers. Modeling eviction as a top-$k$ cut, we compute answer survival probability from prefill attention and reproduce the measured curves. This approach selects the scoring layer using calibration prompts with known answers, and the selected layer is the best layer measured on most models and never significantly below it. It improves on the own-layer default on sixteen of the eighteen models, with significant gains on seven, all at 14B or below, while on larger models the default is already close to the best mid-depth layer. Scoring every cache from the selected layer while keeping one set of tokens for all heads also beats per-head SnapKV by 18 to 43 points on five models up to 14B under tight budgets. This gain carries over to financial filings at 32K context, all at the same memory budget, with no extra forward pass. The same curve explains a penalty in shared-cache models, where several layers read one cache and the layer that writes it scores by default. On Gemma-4-E2B the writer is shallow and loses 28 points to a mid-depth reader at a 10% budget. We also find that in open-book question answering (LongBench) no mid-depth layer beats the own-layer default.

title: Nonlinear adiabatic theorem for the Gross-Pitaevskii equation
abstract: We prove a nonlinear adiabatic theorem for the repulsive Gross-Pitaevskii (GP) equation with a time-dependent trapping potential $V(x,t)$. If either (i) $V(\cdot,t)$ is smooth, subquadratic in space and with uniformly bounded spatial derivatives of order $\geq 2$, or (ii) $V(\cdot,t)$ is a uniformly bounded perturbation of a fixed non-negative potential which is asymptotically $|x|^m, m\geq 2$, then the GP equation has a global solution, which remains uniformly close to the instantaneous minimizer of the time-independent GP functional, provided the initial condition is a ground state. In fact, we show that the existence of a solution of the GP equation is the real bottleneck: If existence is assumed, then adiabaticity holds under very minimal assumptions.

title: Weak and Sharp Stretched-Exponential Flocking in the Kinetic Cucker-Smale Model with Noncompactly Supported Initial Data
abstract: We study the long-time behavior of the kinetic Cucker-Smale model under initial data with unbounded support in both position and velocity. Such data invalidate classical diameter-based flocking arguments and make sustained spatial cohesion difficult to establish. We prove an estimate for spatial characteristics under a finite spatial second moment and a sufficiently high velocity moment, without any requirement on coupling strength. We also prove weak flocking, i.e. control of spatial variance and integrability of velocity fluctuations in time. Under stronger assumptions on the initial tails, we establish uniform propagation of spatial exponential moments of explicitly determined order, a substantially stronger conclusion than bounded spatial variance. These estimates lead to explicit stretched-exponential rates of velocity alignment and convergence of the centered spatial distribution toward a limiting profile. Another contribution is the construction of countably atomic solutions that show optimality of the decay exponent in the spatial-tail-limited class. Together, the results clarify how initial phase-space tails govern spatial confinement and quantitative flocking for kinetic distributions without compact support.

title: Ferroelectric Switching in x-cut MgO-doped Thin-Film Lithium Niobate: Implications for Periodic Poling and Domain-Wall Electronics
abstract: Thin-film lithium niobate (TFLN) revives a mature ferroelectric as a wafer-scale platform for integrated photonics and, increasingly, for domain-wall electronics such as nonvolatile memories and memristors. Both applications rely on controlled ferroelectric switching, which is poorly understood in TFLN: periodic poling consistently requires electric fields above 30~kV/mm, far above the coercive fields of about 21~kV/mm and 4.5~kV/mm of bulk congruent and 5~mol\% MgO-doped lithium niobate, respectively. Here, we present systematic ferroelectric hysteresis measurements on x-cut, 5~mol\% MgO-doped TFLN with coplanar electrodes as used for periodic poling, combining the positive-up-negative-down (PUND) method with second-harmonic microscopy (SHM). We obtain a spontaneous polarization of $(0.72\pm0.02)$~C/m$^2$, consistent with bulk values, while the coercive field varies between 24 and 40~kV/mm with the voltage ramp rate and depends on the electrode geometry. We identify three contributions to the high coercive fields: (i) fast voltage ramps, (ii) finger electrodes, and (iii) the coplanar surface-electrode geometry. Together with bulk data, the coercive field follows a single power law of the ramp rate over five orders of magnitude, showing that the high fields are dominated by switching dynamics rather than by intrinsic thin-film properties. Moreover, the apparent internal field depends on the electrode geometry, and reverse switching leaves buried, electrically isolated domains. These results provide guidelines for scalable, fab-compatible periodic poling---one of the principal bottlenecks of TFLN device integration---and for the write and erase operation of TFLN domain-wall devices.

title: TIGER: Learning from Researcher Taste to Generate Tailored Research Ideas
abstract: In pairwise comparisons where each judge chooses between an idea generated by its corresponding TIGER-8B policy and one generated by GPT-4.1, the three LLM researchers select the TIGER-8B idea in 56.6%-68.4% of 76 comparisons per researcher. PhD1 and PhD2 select the TIGER-8B idea in 19 of 30 pairs (63.3%) and 17 of 30 pairs (56.7%), respectively. All six directed cross-policy comparisons likewise favor the judge's matched TIGER-8B policy over an off-target policy, supporting the use of individual preference feedback for tailored research ideation.

title: High Frequency Safeguard and Weighted Objective Scoring Bandwidth Extension
abstract: Speech Bandwidth Extension (BWE) reconstructs missing high frequencies from a band-limited signal. Please note that perceptually important information is often concentrated in short high-frequency (HF) events. Therefore, an effective BWE requires both accurate HF generation and explicit control over where, how often, and in what spectral form HF energy should be produced. To address the above HF supervision, we present HFSWO, a compact complex-spectral Swin-based dual-stream adversarial framework with two newly proposed specialized discriminators: 1. High-Frequency Safeguard Discriminator (HFSD) converts excessive framewise HF-energy ratios into a differentiable safeguard-constraint penalty optimized through a projected primal--dual augmented-Lagrangian update; 2. Weighted Objective Scoring Discriminator (WOSD) learns an interpretable convex objective scoring over spectral flatness, centroid, and rolloff. Our rigorous experiments on VCTK English and MLS French datasets across multiple frequency ranges, including noisy conditions, show significantly improved perceptual scores with 74.6% fewer parameters than the existing baseline AP-BWE, establishing a new baseline in the BWE task in multilingual and multispeaker setups.

title: Iterative Gumbel Planning for Continuous Control
abstract: Search-based planning remains a powerful policy improvement paradigm in reinforcement learning, driving milestone successes in discrete domains. However, extending this paradigm to continuous control exposes a structural mismatch: search evaluates a finite set of action candidates, whereas continuous RL typically relies on Gaussian policies. We show that winner-action distillation into a continuous Gaussian induces a \textit{projection error} and a stepwise variance-expanding gradient tendency when the selected action is sufficiently far from the current mean. Empirically, this tendency is associated with elevated terminal variance and a return gap on the evaluated tasks. To address this, we propose \textbf{Iterative Gumbel Planning (IGP)}. By adopting a per-dimension factorized categorical policy, IGP naturally aligns the policy support with the search candidates, eliminating the projection error and reducing the residual approximation to a bounded discretization error. To bypass the combinatorial explosion of high-dimensional discrete action spaces, IGP pairs Gumbel Top-$K$ candidate sampling with an MPPI-style multi-round iterative search to refine the policy at each state. Empirically, IGP achieves state-of-the-art aggregate performance and sample efficiency on DMControl and HumanoidBench. Furthermore, it produces more stable action sequences with lower temporal variance, demonstrating its practical potential for real-world robotic deployment.

title: Nonreciprocal Spherical Attention and Retrieval: Sharp Coarsening Clocks and Certified Score Correction
abstract: We develop nonreciprocal spherical attention as a mathematical framework for coarsening and compressed nearest-neighbor retrieval. For two shrinking acute blocks whose centers have zero skew pairing and whose total mass ratio is subexponential in inverse temperature, we prove $\lim_{β\to\infty}β^{-1}\log T_β=1-\cosϕ$, without restricting particle-count growth. An explicit three-body flow has two rigorously separated metastable exponents. For finite compression, mass centering yields a sharp $O(r^2)$ attention-output error bound at fixed temperature, with an explicit spherical-normalization correction. We formulate skew query-side score calibration as a strictly convex moment problem and derive a unique normal equation, residual-based optimization certificates, and bounded low-rank projections. A norm-aware margin objective calibrates native squared-distance rankings. Experiments use semantic retrieval data, one million visual descriptors with three codebook seeds, and a ten-million-vector FAISS IVF-PQ index with recomputed exact cosine ground truth. On SIFT1M, skew margin calibration raises native-L2 hit@10 from 0.8926 to 0.8948; symmetric calibration reaches 0.8996. The ten-million-vector index reaches 0.8827 hit@10 at 0.1794 ms per query in a four-thread batch benchmark, while validation selects no skew update. Exact streamed attention over ten million keys evaluates compressed memory on 1,024 held-out queries. Independent matrix solves, automatic differentiation, finite differences, interval arithmetic, full-flow tests, and nine Rocq-checked algebra lemmas support reproducibility. Directionality alone does not establish retrieval superiority.

title: User Engagement in Visualization: A Scoping Review of 243 Research Articles
abstract: User engagement is well studied in other domains. Work to date has proposed conceptual models and definitions, approaches to measurement, and factors that influence engagement in digital interactions. However, of the articles in the visualization literature that refer to engagement, few of them make evidence-based, generalizable claims, and research that does is challenging to locate due to inconsistent reporting and often lacks connection to the broader engagement literature. To address these issues and promote the consideration of the broader engagement literature, we conduct a comprehensive scoping review of visualization literature and engagement. Using scoping review methodology, we identify and analyze 243 articles that make claims about engagement with visualizations. We coded the studies conducted, literature cited, definitions provided, and claims made in these articles and analyze the codes to evaluate the quality of the work in the field and to synthesize existing findings. We find that, despite frequent references to engagement and apparent interest in the topic, the overall quality of visualization engagement research is poor, often with weak evidence, inconsistent conceptualizations, and infrequent citation of existing models, methods, or claims. We report the evidence-based claims about what engages people with visualization, including the factors of animation, interaction, and immersion, additionally describing both corroboration and apparent contradictions between these claims. Finally, we propose the COMFI framework and mnemonic for reporting important information in future engagement studies.

title: A General Approach for Assessing Sensitivity to Violations of Causal Assumptions
abstract: Although causal sensitivity analyses are widely used to assess the robustness of conclusions, a key limitation is that existing methods are typically developed for specific designs. This paper develops a general sensitivity analysis framework that applies to a wide range of discrete causal models and estimands by deriving sharp bounds on causal estimands as a function of the maximum proportion of the population for which the assumption is relaxed. The framework is built on the generalized principal strata approach, which allows the translation of assumptions, estimands, and data into polynomial programs. In this approach, three classes of assumptions can be relaxed: a) functional restrictions, which limit the ways that one variable can respond to another, e.g. strong monotonicity; b) exclusion restrictions, which rule out direct causal effects; c) unconfoundedness, which rules out unobserved common causes of variables. The approach produces both sharp sensitivity curves and robustness values, i.e., the smallest sensitivity level at which the sign of a causal effect stops being identified. The applicability of the method is demonstrated by generalizing existing proportion-of-violations approaches, deriving new sensitivity analysis methods for instrumental variable and selection-on-observables designs, and reanalyzing empirical results.

title: When to Probe and When to Act: Clarity-Aware Risk-Adaptive Control for Interactive Driving
abstract: Safe navigation in interactive traffic requires autonomous vehicles to reason about unobservable human characteristics and the reciprocal nature of multi-agent interactions. Traditional architectures often decouple prediction from planning, leading to the "Frozen Robot Problem" or unsafe maneuvers under high ambiguity because they treat risk assessment and information acquisition as independent objectives. We argue that the notion of safety should not remain static but must instead dynamically co-evolve with the system's internal confidence: the robot should actively clarify ambiguity when necessary while also recognizing the diminishing returns of information, and naturally transition toward task execution. We introduce a unified belief-space Model Predictive Control (MPC) framework that couples multistep information planning with a clarity-adaptive Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) barrier mechanism.
