This improves the previously known $O(\varepsilon^{-4})$ upper bound and matches the known lower bound. The same guarantee holds also for importance sampling, where vertices are sampled proportionally to their weighted degrees, and we further prove a matching lower bound for this sampling method. Our analysis extends directly to metric Max-Cut, showing that importance sampling of $O(\varepsilon^{-2})$ vertices yields $(1\pm\varepsilon)$-approximation to the Max-Cut value, and to Max-Cut in graphs with edge weights in $[0,1]$ and average weighted degree $\bar d$, achieving the same $(1\pm\varepsilon)$-approximation by either uniform or importance sampling of $O(\varepsilon^{-2}n/\bar d)$ vertices. We additionally show how to use this coreset to recover a cut of expected value at least $OPT-\varepsilon n^2$, by making $O(n\varepsilon^{-2})$ additional edge-weight queries. Finally, our result extends to Max-$r$-Cut, giving an additive $\varepsilon n^2$-approximation using a sample of $O(\varepsilon^{-2}\log(2r))$ vertices.

title: Neumann problem for Hessian equation and geometric inequalities in hyperbolic space
abstract: We establish the existence of solutions to the Neumann problem for the Hessian equation on a smooth, bounded strictly static convex domain in hyperbolic space. The boundary condition determines a unique compatibility constant, and admissible solutions are unique up to a multiple of the static potential. As an application, we give a direct analytic proof of some weighted geometric inequalities for the static convex domain in hyperbolic space.

title: Spin SYK-dot chains: entanglement bound and resource estimates towards a quantum advantage
abstract: Ground states of Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev (SYK)-type models are volume-law entangled, which makes them costly both for tensor networks and for quantum hardware simulations. Thus, it remains unclear where quantum hardware could outperform classical simulation of such models. In this work, we study a spin SYK-dot chain, in which q dense SYK dots of p qubits are joined by single ZZ bonds of strength K. The entanglement across any cut is then bounded by floor(p/2) ln 2 plus the inter-dot entanglement, and the two-qubit depth of one Trotter step is set by p alone. A resource estimate shows that a quantum advantage for the ground state could appear only for dots of about 15 to 21 qubits or more. There, a single Trotter step already requires two-qubit error rates of order 10^{-6}, beyond the reach of noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) hardware. We test the assumptions of this estimate with an imaginary-time matrix product state (MPS) that applies each dot as one block. It agrees with exact diagonalisation at (p, q) = (6, 2). At (5, 2), a variational circuit with the same dot-plus-link layout comes within 3.6% of the exact energy, and noisy simulations show that its fidelity decays as assumed in the resource estimate. At (8, 5), i.e., N = 40 qubits, the energy converges at bond dimension chi = 768, far below the exact value 2^20, and the inter-dot entanglement stays small and is set mainly by K. Out-of-time-order correlators across the links decay on a time scale that shrinks rapidly with |K|. Thus, the dot size p and the inter-dot coupling K together set the entanglement of the chain, and with it where a quantum advantage could appear.

title: A Stieltjes representation of order $p$ for $ \mathrm{tr}[(A+tB)^{-p}]$: Heinävaara's measure, B-splines, and Stahl's theorem
abstract: For $A$ positive definite, $B$ positive semidefinite and $p\ge1$ we show that $\mathrm{tr}[(A+tB)^{-p}]=\int(1+t\ell)^{-p}\,dρ_p(\ell)$ for a positive measure $ρ_p$ on the spectral interval of $L=A^{-1/2}BA^{-1/2}$, and we identify the measure: it has atoms $\mathrm{tr}[(P_sA^{-1}P_s)^p]$ at the eigenvalues of $L$ and a continuous density, an integral of Heinävaara's tracial joint spectral measure along rays. For integer $p$ the positivity of $ρ_p$ follows from the positivity of Heinävaara's measure alone, and the density is a sum of Curry-Schoenberg B-splines; for real $p$ the representation is obtained by inverting Heinävaara's transform. For $0<p<1$ the function is a Stieltjes function of order $p$ only if $[A,B]=0$, but a positive representation of order one holds, with an explicit density. Along $A_p=pI+A_0$, $p\to\infty$, the measures converge to the measure of Stahl's theorem (the Bessis-Moussa-Villani conjecture) for $\mathrm{tr}\,e^{-(A_0+tB)}$.

title: DynSL: Resource-Adaptive Model Training across Heterogeneous Edge Devices
abstract: Training models over data distributed across edge devices presents a trade-off: centralizing data simplifies training but raises privacy and regulatory concerns, while full local training may exceed the devices' compute and memory capacity. Split learning addresses this challenge by partitioning the model between clients and the server, allowing part of the computation to be offloaded. However, existing approaches typically rely on static split configurations or simplified assumptions that fail to capture the heterogeneity and complex dynamics of real deployments. We present DynSL, a framework that dynamically allocates model layers between clients and the server by continuously monitoring system metrics and periodically solving an optimization problem that accounts for client and server computation and communication. When beneficial, the system reconfigures the split, enabling the offloading strategy to adapt to changing device capabilities and system conditions. Extensive experiments on a testbed of 24 heterogeneous edge devices show that DynSL reduces training time by up to $\sim\!$30% over the strongest adaptive baseline and by more than 50% over a suboptimal uniform split, with no loss -- and sometimes a gain -- in accuracy.

title: CFD-driven symbolic regression of RANS transition models
abstract: Laminar-turbulent transition governs skin friction, heat transfer and losses in turbomachinery, yet Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes (RANS) transition models rely on empirical correlations and hand-calibrated activation functions whose structural deficiencies cannot be resolved by recalibration. We propose a CFD-driven sparse symbolic regression framework to learn interpretable, closed-form corrections to the production and destruction activation functions in the intermittency equation of the local, Galilean-invariant $k$-$ω$-$γ$ model of Ge et al. Each correction combines a polynomial of a local pressure-gradient parameter, controlling amplitude and sign, with a bounded exponential of local flow features, controlling spatial support. This construction bounds the corrections without ad hoc limiters. Coefficients are identified by gradient-free optimization with the RANS solver in the loop, accelerated by POD-Kriging field surrogates, using mean-velocity data from wall-resolved large-eddy simulations (LES) of the ERCOFTAC T3 flat-plate cases. Elastic-net hyperparameters are selected automatically through bi-level optimization with leave-one-case-out cross-validation. The resulting model retains 11 of 21 candidate terms, compared with 20 under conventional grid-search tuning, while achieving comparable or slightly better accuracy on training and unseen cases. Both approaches recover the same leading-order correction. Applied without retraining to the transonic LS89 turbine cascade, far beyond the training envelope, the augmented model remains numerically robust and improves heat-transfer predictions at all four operating points, reducing errors by up to 70% where the baseline predicts premature transition under high freestream turbulence. Residual errors in transition onset and length highlight the limits of training on flat-plate data alone.

title: The quantum magic of top quarks
abstract: In recent years, a growing community of researchers has been applying ideas from Quantum Information theory to high energy physics. Entanglement is one such quantity, but there are by now many others. This contribution will examine the property of ``magic" (also known as ``non-stabliserness") which, roughly speaking, measures whether quantum systems have a genuine computational advantage over their classical counterparts. We will review the origin of this concept, before describing recent applications in collider physics, including top quark production.

title: Approximating Submodular Orienteering via Rooted Subgraph Decomposition
abstract: The Submodular Orienteering problem asks for an $s$-$t$ walk in a directed graph that maximizes a monotone submodular function over the visited vertices subject to a bound on its length. We give a deterministic polynomial-time approximation algorithm with subpolynomial approximation rate $2^{O(\sqrt{\log n\,\log\log n})}$. This improves over the $O(n^\varepsilon)$ approximation rate that was previously known for every fixed $\varepsilon>0$. We prove a decomposition lemma that partitions a directed graph into rooted subgraphs such that every path intersects only polylogarithmically many such subgraphs. Our algorithm uses this decomposition to construct its recursive subproblems.

title: Reducing SNAP Payment Errors at Lower Cost With AI: A Simulation Study
abstract: New federal legislation will require states with high payment error rates in the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) to pay a share of benefit costs, potentially costing some states over a billion dollars per year. These costs create substantial pressure to improve payment accuracy. One strategy to improve payment accuracy is preauthorization review, in which staff double-check applications and correct mistakes before benefits are issued. But limited staff capacity makes it important to target these reviews effectively. One leading targeting approach uses statistical risk models to prioritize cases likely to contain errors. Another novel approach uses AI to flag specific potential discrepancies for reviewers to check. For states under pressure to reduce error rates, it is unclear which approach-or combination of approaches-would reduce payment error rates most effectively. We compare these strategies through simulations using public SNAP quality control data. Under our main assumptions, risk-based review alone costs about seven times as much as combining AI flags with risk scores. This cost advantage persists across a wide range of plausible assumptions. Our findings suggest that AI-assisted preauthorization review could be a key tool to help states avoid substantial cost-sharing obligations.

title: The Dirichlet problem for quaternionic Monge--Ampère equations on flat quaternionic quotients
abstract: We prove smooth solvability of the Dirichlet problem for quaternionic Monge--Ampère equations on smooth relatively compact domains in ${\mathbb H}^m/Γ$, where $m\ge2$ and $Γ$ is a discrete additive subgroup: for a smooth positive density, the existence of a smooth strictly plurisubharmonic subsolution guarantees the existence and uniqueness of the smooth admissible solution. The technique of the proof is a simple adaptation from the Ph.D. Thesis of Jingyong Zhu [25] in 2017, supervised by Xinan Ma, which is a joint work of Ma and Zhu. The claim [22, Theorem A.1] by OpenAI on Sogge's local smoothing conjecture is a special case of our theorem.

title: Lower bounds for Riesz interaction functionals
abstract: Motivated by the pressure formation problem for hydrodynamic models with nonlocal interactions, we classify strong Lebesgue lower bounds for the Riesz energy functional and for a determinant functional arising from the theory of compensated integrability. The classification covers all integrability exponents in $(0,\infty]$ within the class of confined log-concave densities. These geometric assumptions are motivated by counterexamples for general densities. On the whole space, neither functional controls any fixed Lebesgue quasi-norm. Under confinement, lower bounds fail for exponents greater than one, whereas $L^1$ bounds hold for the energy in every dimension and for the determinant only in dimension one. The log-concave estimates hold at sharp integrability exponents and follow from endpoint Lorentz bounds for confined quasiconcave densities and a weak-to-strong lemma. In particular, the energy estimates provide a geometric lower-bound counterpart to the classical Hardy-Littlewood-Sobolev inequality.

title: Towards end-to-end co-design for one-shot printable task-specific soft robots
abstract: Soft robot co-design methods can jointly optimise morphology and control, but the resulting designs are often difficult to manufacture, while manufacturable approaches typically restrict actuator placement or require manual assembly. We present a simulation-based co-design framework that jointly optimises material distribution, pneumatic actuator placement and orientation, and control, while producing designs that can be fabricated monolithically using fused deposition modelling. The framework uses a differentiable 2D plane-stress Material Point Method simulator, incorporating an experimentally validated material model and an empirically derived surrogate model of a 3D-printed inflatable actuator. We demonstrate gradient-based optimisation soft robotic arms for prescribed tip trajectories. Optimised designs are transferred directly from simulation to one-shot monolithic FDM fabrication, with integrated actuators and no post-assembly. Physical experiments demonstrate that the resulting arms reproduce the behaviour predicted in simulation. This framework provides a path from task-level objectives to physically realisable soft robots while retaining substantial freedom over both morphology and actuation.

title: What crossing symmetry forbids just above $c=1$
abstract: What does a unitary two-dimensional conformal field theory look like just above $c=1$? Using the numerical conformal bootstrap, we study the four-point function of a scalar Virasoro primary $ϕ$ such that no primary lighter than $ϕ$ appears in its operator product expansion with itself. Slightly above $c=1$, crossing symmetry excludes the interval $0.17\lesssimΔ_ϕ\lesssim1$, although the compact boson realizes every such $Δ_ϕ$ at $c=1$. Combining this exclusion with results from the modular bootstrap, we show that the lightest primary of a compact unitary conformal field theory at $c=1.0005$ or $1.001$ has dimension $Δ_{\rm gap}<0.17$. Further from $c=1$, the largest excluded central charge at fixed $Δ_ϕ$ has two sharp minima near $Δ_ϕ=1/2$ and $4/7$. At these values it lies within $2\times10^{-7}$ of $c=8/7$, where the $\mathbb{Z}_5$ parafermion and its charge-conjugation orbifold have scalars of exactly these dimensions.

title: Probing aQGCs from dimension-eight operators via neutral triboson production at muon colliders
abstract: We investigate the sensitivity of a future high-energy muon collider to neutral anomalous quartic gauge couplings (aQGCs) through neutral triboson production processes, specifically $μ^+μ^- \to γγγ$, $γγZ$, $γZZ$, and $ZZZ$. Within the Standard Model Effective Field Theory (SMEFT) framework, we focus on genuine dimension-eight transverse operators ($\mathcal{O}_{T_0}$--$\mathcal{O}_{T_9}$). The analysis is performed at prospective center-of-mass energies of $\sqrt{s} = 3\text{ TeV}$ and $10\text{ TeV}$ with integrated luminosities of $1\text{ ab}^{-1}$ and $10\text{ ab}^{-1}$, respectively. Employing an optimized cut-and-count analysis and a $χ^2$ statistical framework incorporating a $5\%$ systematic uncertainty, we derive projected 95\% confidence level bounds on the corresponding Wilson coefficients. Our results demonstrate that the triphoton channel yields the most stringent constraints, particularly for the $f_{T_8}$ and $f_{T_9}$ coefficients, while channels involving $Z$ bosons exhibit reduced sensitivity owing to leptonic branching ratio suppressions. Furthermore, we report constraints on the $f_{T_3}$ and $f_{T_4}$ coefficients, established here for the first time in this neutral triboson context, highlighting the powerful physics reach of multi-TeV muon colliders in probing electroweak gauge sector interactions.

title: Can Coding Agents Sustain Continual Evolution without Forgetting?
abstract: Recently, harness self-evolution has emerged as an important paradigm for improving agent performance. Prior studies show that evolving the agent harness can effectively enhance agent capabilities without modifying the foundation model's parameters. We find that existing approaches largely study agent evolution on a single task. In practice, coding agents may need to handle multiple task types over time. Whether an agent harness can continuously evolve across multiple tasks without suffering from catastrophic forgetting remains an important open question. In this paper, we investigate this open question through a comprehensive empirical study of continual harness self-evolution. We organize three software engineering task datasets into six different evolution directions and apply two representative harness evolution methods to perform continual evolution along these directions. Our experimental results show that evolution on a subsequent dataset can substantially undermine the performance on previously seen datasets. For example, with DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731, Meta-Harness improves its performance on SWE-Bench to 94.0% after evolution. However, after further evolution on FeatureBench, its performance on SWE-Bench drops to 32.0% by the fifth round, corresponding to a 66% relative decrease. Finally, based on our experimental findings, we identify several insights, providing directions for the continual self-evolution of agent harnesses. Code is available at https://github.com/THU-Agent/continual-harness-evolution.

title: Dynamics of Fock states in traveling pulses
abstract: The quantum state of a traveling light pulse can qualitatively change the excitation dynamics of a two-level atom. We investigate this dependence for coherent and Fock input states using a virtual-cavity formulation with matched input and output temporal profiles. Analytical treatment of the master equation and numerical simulations show that coherent pulses produce damped Rabi oscillations, whereas Fock pulses can exhibit a partial recovery of the oscillation amplitude in the trailing part of the pulse. We examine how coupling to an auxiliary temporal mode and radiative loss shape this recovery. We also establish a connection with stimulated Raman adiabatic passage through an exact many-photon dark state and derive the associated adiabaticity condition. The observed recovery occurs away from ideal dark-state following. These results distinguish transient recovery in traveling-pulse scattering from conventional cavity collapse and revival, and clarify the scope of an adiabatic-transfer interpretation.

title: A new toric ALF gravitational instanton
abstract: We construct a new explicit toric ALF gravitational instanton. The instanton has Euler characteristic $χ= 4$ and Hirzebruch signature $τ= 1$. The topology at infinity is a lens space $L(3,1)$. The solution depends on one parameter and is constructed from the Belinski--Zakharov four-soliton solution. We prove that the instanton is smooth and positive definite on and away from the axis. This is the first example of a non-Hermitian ALF (not AF) gravitational instanton.

title: CERBO: Certified Recourse at a Requested Rate for Gradient-Boosted Trees
abstract: Recourse-aware learning trains models so that people who receive an adverse decision can reverse it with an affordable change. For gradient-boosted decision trees (GBDTs), the existing method, RABIT, exposes a single recourse weight whose effect on the recourse rate is abrupt and data-dependent, and its training bound cannot certify recourse for any rejected individual. We present Certified Recourse Boosting (CERBO), which takes a requested recourse rate and returns a GBDT with certified actions: it tracks exact additive effort along tree paths, trains against committed boxes (a family of bounds that contains RABIT's and certifies a within-budget action for each training sample) and adjusts the weight after every tree until the certified rate meets the request. A calibration step guarantees the rate on new individuals, and the certifier runs on any tree ensemble, including XGBoost and LightGBM, in milliseconds per person without a solver. In RABIT's own experimental protocol, at equal accuracy, CERBO raises the recourse ratio from 0.90 to 0.99 on FICO and from 0.64 to 0.77 on Bail. Under additive costs on six data sets, it raises the area under the accuracy-recourse frontier in all 12 settings, and in simulated deployments it guarantees recourse to 70% of rejected individuals in 11 of 12 settings, against 2 for RABIT.

title: Do Agents Still Follow the Rules? Benchmarking Rule Compliance under Agent Context Compaction
abstract: LLM agents compact long histories to fit their context windows, but the compacted context must still carry the operating rules that govern later actions. Prior work shows that violations rise after compaction, but measures compliance outside a complete agent harness and does not identify where each violation comes from. We introduce ARCBench(Agent Rule Compliance Benchmark), a configurable benchmark built on the open-source pi agent harness. Its tool-calling agent loop lets us measure rule compliance from actions taken during execution, bringing the evaluation closer to deployed agent workflows. Using ARCBench, we examine where violations after compaction come from, and how different compaction configurations and adversarial settings change their sources. We find that compaction rarely deletes the rule: most violations after compaction occur while the rule is still in the compacted history, with the agent treating a later request as permission, ignoring the rule, and proceeding anyway. Where violations come from depends on the configuration: how the rule is delivered decides whether the agent would break it even without compaction, while the compaction strategy and budget decide whether the rule survives. The strongest compactor-targeted attack more than doubles violations by corrupting the rule in the summary and changing how the agents behave, whereas the strongest defense restores the rule in most summary but still violates. Finally, retaining a rule does not guarantee compliance: compacted runs that retain the rule violate more than twice as often as runs with the full history.

title: Global Stability and Decay for the 2D Anisotropic Navier-Stokes Equations with Fractional Horizontal Dissipation
abstract: Although the classical Yudovich theory guarantees global existence and uniqueness of two-dimensional Euler solutions with bounded vorticity, their higher-order norms may still grow in time. This raises a fundamental question: how much dissipation we need to ensure global stability and decay? While the full Laplacian dissipation is sufficient, the stabilizing effect of weaker, anisotropic dissipation is considerably more subtle. In this paper, we investigate the global stability and long-time decay of the two-dimensional incompressible Navier-Stokes equations with fractional horizontal dissipation $Λ_1^{2s}u$, where $s<1$. A central challenge is to recover sufficient decay of the second velocity component, whose weak dissipation obstruct the closure of conventional anisotropic energy estimates. Previous work by Wang-Wu-Zhu [arXiv:2601.16110] resolved this difficulty whereas the spatial weighted energy functionals must be used when $s$ approaches $1$. The main purpose of our manuscript is to remove this restriction. We introduce a hierarchy of carefully designed time-weighted anisotropic energy functionals which captures the interplay between horizontal fractional dissipation and the decay of velocity components. Under such initial assumptions, the characteristics of anisotropic dissipation is presented more straightforwardly, which also reveals the more essential intrinsic structure of fluid stability.

title: Human Variations on AI Mathematics
abstract: This article is motivated by the OpenAI manuscripts "Minimal metrics and interior injectivity for nef adjoints" and "Log abundance in characteristic zero". We establish a jet comparison for metrics with minimal singularities and use it to prove a dlt-type extension theorem. Combined with geometric arguments from the latter manuscript, this yields an alternative analytic proof of its Theorem~3.1.

title: A Cepheid-based Distance to the Type 1 Seyfert NGC 3783
abstract: We present a Cepheid-based distance to the Type 1 Seyfert NGC 3783 using the Hubble Space Telescope. Images were obtained over 15 visits using nonredundant time spacing, with ten observations in the F350LP filter and eight observations each in the F555W and F814W filters. We found 1541 unique point sources across all observations, and we fit Cepheid templates to analyze these light curves. From these data, we determined a full sample of seven Cepheid candidates. Of these seven candidates, four are the most convincing and comprise our "strong" sample of Cepheid candidates. We fit the period$-$luminosity relationship to the total sample and to our "strong" sample using the LMC calibration by Riess et al. (2019). Adopting an independent distance constraint to the LMC given by Pietrzynski et al. (2019), and correcting for the potential effects of metallicity, we determine a distance modulus of $μ= 33.118 \pm 0.154$ mag using our strong sample. This value is formally consistent with the value derived using our full sample and corresponds to a distance of $D = 42.03 \pm 2.98$ Mpc. NGC 3783 is therefore among the farthest galaxies with a Cepheid-based distance measurement.

title: What Structurally Breaks an Agent? Auditing Difficulty in Stateful Tool-Use Workflows
abstract: An aggregate task score does not distinguish failures of scheduling, state retention, and candidate selection. We develop a small executable instrument that varies dependency depth, candidate count, active state width, and access to current-state snapshots while holding the number of required operations fixed. Two dependency-graph families show that increasing depth at fixed work changes both scheduling freedom and the number of reachable completion states, so these controls are coupled, and we quantify the coupling. The primary study contains 49,152 generated tasks and 393,216 reference-controller rollouts. A separately frozen follow-on design adds 295,936 rollouts covering retention strategy, snapshot cadence, hidden state resampling, recovery, query locality, candidate indexing, and relabeling. Residue caches and precomputed plans solve tasks that defeat limited raw-value caches, and indexed selection removes the serial-scan branching deficit. Hidden resampling imposes an exact success ceiling that additional state tracking cannot overcome. The contribution is an executable diagnostic instrument, analytic calibration, and an audit of its assumptions. A small local CPU study with a 0.5B model completed no workflows, and a 16-episode Copilot-routed fractional factorial is descriptive only. Neither supports general capability claims.

title: AnchorComplete: Recovering Complete Scene Meshes from Partial Point Clouds
abstract: Most image-based 3D reconstructors primarily recover visible surfaces, producing partial point clouds with large holes and leaving unobserved geometry unresolved. To address this limitation, we introduce AnchorComplete, a framework that reconstructs complete scene meshes from partial point clouds while preserving observed geometry and supporting scenes of varying scales. Building on TRELLIS.2, our method combines partial-point conditioning, which integrates global scene tokens with local spatial evidence to anchor generation to the input, and metric-scale coarse-to-fine generation, which progressively refines scene geometry within fixed-size windows while maintaining global structural consistency. Experiments on Replica and SCRREAM demonstrate that AnchorComplete consistently outperforms strong baselines in complete-scene reconstruction, particularly under sparse-view settings.

title: CL3DOD: Understanding the Stability-Plasticity Dilemma in Outdoor Class-Incremental 3D Object Detection
abstract: Class-incremental learning (CIL) for outdoor 3D object detection remains largely underexplored. Existing outdoor studies are limited to single-benchmark evaluations, with SDCoT++ considering KITTI and CL2OD considering nuScenes under different incremental settings. This makes it difficult to assess whether observed continual-learning behavior generalizes across autonomous-driving benchmarks. To the best of our knowledge, we provide the first unified cross-benchmark analysis of outdoor class-incremental 3D object detection across multiple autonomous-driving benchmarks, covering both two-task and multi-stage settings. We investigate: (1) how severely existing 3D detectors forget previously learned classes, (2) how incremental training exposes the stability-plasticity dilemma between knowledge retention and new-class acquisition, and (3) which forms of supervision are most effective for balancing these objectives. We introduce CL3DOD, a class-incremental 3D detection framework that restores missing supervision for previous classes using predictions from the previous-stage detector, preserves old-class responses through query-wise knowledge distillation, and employs EMA-based temporal consistency regularization. Experiments on KITTI and nuScenes reveal a consistent stability-plasticity dilemma across both benchmarks. CL3DOD generally achieves a more favorable stability-plasticity balance than controlled incremental baselines and improves upon published prior methods in the reported benchmark comparisons. This advantage persists across multiple incremental stages, demonstrating strong retention of previously learned knowledge while maintaining effective new-class acquisition. Our code, evaluation setup, and incremental task splits will be publicly released.

title: Bagel: A Fast Bayesian Online Changepoint Detection Algorithm for Linear Models via Posterior Merging
abstract: Bayesian online changepoint detection provides a natural framework for quantifying uncertainty about whether and when a change has occurred. It also enables the use of prior information which can increase detection power. Exact Bayesian inference sequentially updates the posterior of whether and when a change has occurred. We present a unified approach to calculating and updating this posterior for a class of regression models covering standard changepoint scenarios, such as changes in mean and slope, whilst also allowing common structure such as seasonal effects. However, naive implementation has a computational cost that increases linearly over time. We, further, introduce approximate updates that keep this cost constant. These are based on novel ideas of merging changepoint times, and are an alternative to existing pruning approaches. We show that merging enables better approximations of the posterior of when a change occurs. Furthermore, we introduce a novel condition for merging that accounts for both the posterior probability of the changepoint times and the similarity of their corresponding post-change parameters. We show that this is more accurate than conditions that only consider the former. We demonstrate the advantage of our approach on simulated data, and the Azure LLM inference traces.

title: Specification-Driven Governance for Fairness-by-Design in Agentic Software Engineering: How Far Can We Go?
abstract: Agentic AI is shifting developers' responsibilities from software implementation to software governance. While this paradigm improves productivity, it also raises challenges in ensuring that autonomous coding agents preserve developers' intentions. Among these, operationalizing fairness-by-design is largely unexplored, as existing approaches provide limited support for representing and propagating fairness requirements throughout agentic development workflows. In this paper, we investigate whether specification-driven development can operationalize fairness-by-design in the agentic development of machine learning systems. We study three coding agents on four machine learning applications, using four prompts that progressively operationalize fairness through nine Fairness Specification Elements, and analyze the traceability of fairness requirements across the generated artifacts, the fairness-accuracy trade-off of the resulting models, and the agents' design decisions and rationales. The results show that when fairness is operationalized, agents capture almost all fairness requirements in the specification (97.22%) and preserve most of them in the code (82.41%). However, the resulting models are not significantly fairer, as agents implement fairness as a post-hoc audit that neither shapes training nor prevents model delivery. Specifications thus make fairness traceable, but not enforceable, calling for fairness specifications that state what agents should do when requirements are not met, and for workflows that make the fairness decisions agents delegate to developers explicit.

title: Calibrating Multimodal Test-Time Adaptation under Reliability and Availability Modality Shifts
abstract: Multimodal test-time adaptation (TTA) enables pretrained multimodal models to accommodate distribution shifts during inference using only unlabeled test data, without recourse to the original training data. Compared with unimodal adaptation, multimodal adaptation is further complicated by the coexistence and interaction of multiple representation perspectives. This complexity is particularly pronounced under modality reliability shifts, which preserve modality availability but degrade information quality, and modality availability shifts, which render the corresponding modality entirely inaccessible. Category-conditional Gaussian modeling offers a natural starting point for handling such distributional variations, having proven effective in unimodal test-time adaptation for characterizing representation distributions, yet its extension to multimodal settings requires a more elaborate formulation. To this end, we propose Adaptive Probabilistic Gaussian Calibration (AdaPGC), which extends category-conditional Gaussian modeling across modality-specific and multimodal fusion representations for probabilistic calibration under multimodal distribution shifts. AdaPGC continuously updates category-conditional Gaussian models over modality-specific and fusion representations, using the resulting probabilistic predictions to calibrate source model predictions and guide reliability based rectification, while exploiting their joint distributions to recover unavailable fusion representations. Extensive experiments under diverse modality corruption and missingness conditions demonstrate that AdaPGC effectively improves robustness under both modality reliability and availability shifts. Our source code will be released at https://github.com/XuJinglinn/AdaPGC-plus.

title: Axion 1.0: Open Agent Foundation Models, Simplified
abstract: We introduce Axion 1.0, a fully open agent foundation model that combines strong and broad agentic capabilities with a remarkably simple training recipe. Axion 1.0 is trained in only three stages: two lightweight supervised fine-tuning stages followed by reinforcement learning, without dedicated mid-training, direct preference optimization (DPO), or on-policy distillation (OPD). The first SFT stage develops strong self-contained reasoning through model-aware data construction, where we synthesize challenging problems and adversarially strengthen them based on the base model's own successful solution strategies. The second stage extends these capabilities to tool-dependent reasoning through a scalable pipeline for constructing diverse and automatically verifiable tasks grounded in real-world data sources and deterministic computation. Finally, reinforcement learning further strengthens long-horizon reasoning and interaction with external tools and environments. Despite this compact training recipe, Axion 1.0 achieves strong performance across a broad suite of agentic benchmarks and is competitive with leading commercial models on several of them. Equally importantly, Axion 1.0 is open beyond model weights: we release the complete recipe, including data construction, generation, filtering, verification, prompts, and training code, enabling the entire development process to be reproduced and extended. Axion 1.0 demonstrates that strong agent foundation models can be both open and simple, offering a practical and reproducible path toward advancing open agentic intelligence.

title: SHAPE: Solar Heliospherical Analysis and Prediction of Eruptions A machine learning approach to solar flare forecasting
abstract: Solar flares are the most energetic impulsive events in the solar system, and reliable operational forecasting of the rarest and most destructive M- and X-class events remains an open problem. We present Solar Heliospherical Analysis and Prediction of Eruptions (SHAPE), a two-phase deep-learning pipeline that bypasses sunspot proxies in favour of direct soft X-ray observations from the GOES X-ray Sensor (XRS). Phase 1 forecasts monthly flare counts, aggregated to annual totals, with a hybrid model: a cycle-shape curve anchored to published solar-cycle minima fixes the timing and mean profile, and a compact gated-recurrent-unit network with Monte Carlo dropout models the residual variability. Trained on the science-quality NOAA GOES Flare Report for 1995--2020 and validated on 2021--2025, it achieves a mean absolute error of 204 flares yr$^{-1}$, although it underestimates the 2024 solar maximum. Phase 2 forecasts the next day's strongest flare class (C, M or X) with a shared-trunk, dual-head LSTM operating on a 12-day rolling window of five intensity features, with an optional blend against an active-region physics score and a decision threshold tuned to favour recall of M-or-above (M+) events. On a 100-day chronological backtest, the classifier attains a true skill statistic of 0.351, a Heidke skill score of 0.335 for M+ events, a Brier skill score of 0.163 relative to climatology, and an expected calibration error of 0.023. A day-to-day persistence baseline is, however, competitive on both skill scores, showing that much short-term predictability in flare class is autocorrelation rather than learned structure. SHAPE shows that competitive flare forecasting is achievable with compact architectures that retain in minutes on standard hardware, without sunspot proxy inputs.

title: Microscopic Origin of the Equation of Motion for Open Thermodynamic Systems
abstract: In my previous work (arXiv:2609.07810) \cite{Aydiner_2026}, I derived a second-order equation of motion for open thermodynamic systems from the First Law of Thermodynamics and established its dynamical equivalence with mechanical oscillators and electrical RLC circuits. In the present study, I independently recover the same mathematical structure of the equation of motion from a mesoscopic model of particle transfer between two reservoirs connected by a channel. Starting from collective momentum balance, particle conservation, and reservoir chemical-potential response, I derive the inertial--dissipative--restoring dynamics and obtain explicit expressions for its effective coefficients in terms of the physical parameters of the system. The resulting equation predicts distinct damping regimes, characteristic relaxation time scales, and resonance under periodic driving. The natural frequency and resonance conditions are explicitly determined by the physical parameters of the particle-transfer system. In the slow-transport limit, the model recovers the conventional Onsager-type linear flux--force relation. The independent emergence of the same dynamical structure from two distinct physical approaches provides theoretical support for the previously proposed thermodynamic equation of motion. By identifying the physical mechanisms underlying its effective coefficients, the present study strengthens the physical foundations of the proposed framework and supports the possibility of describing open thermodynamic systems within a common dynamical framework shared with mechanical and electrical systems.

title: The strong fractional choice number can exceed the choice number by an arbitrarily large amount
abstract: Erdős, Rubin and Taylor asked whether $(a,b)$-choosability implies $(am,bm)$-choosability for all positive integers $a,b,m$. Dvořák, Hu and Sereni disproved this for $(a,b,m)=(4,1,2)$ and asked whether a $3$-choosable graph can fail to be $(6,2)$-choosable. Following Jiang and Zhu, Li and Zhu asked whether every $k$-choosable graph is $(kb+1,b)$-choosable for all positive integers $k,b$. Equivalently, Xu and Zhu asked whether $\operatorname{ch}_f^s(G)\le\operatorname{ch}(G)$ for every graph $G$. Here $\operatorname{ch}(G)$ is the choice number, and $\operatorname{ch}_f^s(G)$ is the strong fractional choice number, defined as the infimum of real $r$ such that $G$ is $(a,b)$-choosable for all positive integers $a,b$ with $a/b\ge r$. We prove that, for all integers $t\ge0$ and $b\ge7t+2$, there is a planar graph $G$ with $\operatorname{ch}(G)=3$ that is not $(3b+t,b)$-choosable. This answers all these questions and gives a lower bound of $1/7$ on the supremum of $\operatorname{ch}_f^s(G)-\operatorname{ch}(G)$ over planar graphs of choice number three. For all integers $k\ge4$, $t\ge0$ and $b\ge3t+2$, we construct a graph $G$ with $\operatorname{ch}(G)=k$ that is not $(kb+t,b)$-choosable, using the six-vertex wheel $W_5$ as its core gadget. This gives the corresponding lower bound $1/3$ for each $k\ge4$. The case $t=0$ and $b=2$ recovers the main result of Dvořák, Hu and Sereni. Finally, for every integer $t\ge1$, there are a positive integer $k$ and a $k$-choosable graph that is not $(8k+4t-1,8)$-choosable. Thus the difference between the strong fractional choice number and the choice number is unbounded, even with multiplicity fixed at eight. We further prove $k+Ω(\log k)\le\sup\{\operatorname{ch}_f^s(G):\operatorname{ch}(G)=k\}\le2^{(1+o(1))k}$ as $k$ tends to infinity.

title: Differential measurement of global polarization of $Λ$, $Ξ$, and $Ω$ hyperons in Au+Au collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\mathrm{NN}}}=7.7$--$27~\mathrm{GeV}$ from the RHIC Beam Energy Scan-II
abstract: We present high-precision differential measurements of the global polarization of $Λ$, $Ξ$, and $Ω$ hyperons in Au+Au collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\mathrm{NN}}}=7.7$, $9.2$, $11.5$, $14.6$, $17.3$, $19.6$, and $27~\mathrm{GeV}$ from the RHIC Beam Energy Scan Phase II (BES-II) using the STAR detector. The results show a clear centrality dependence, with polarization increasing toward more peripheral collisions. Within the present experimental precision, no significant dependence on transverse momentum is observed for $Λ$ and $Ξ$, and no significant rapidity dependence is observed for the $Ξ$. The polarization of $Ξ$ hyperons is comparable at the current precision to that of $Λ$ hyperons, consistent with a picture in which all hyperons acquire polarization from the same global angular momentum source, with differences arising from quark content and hadronization dynamics. These high-precision, differential measurements across centrality and $p_T$ over the measured energy ranges provide a unique test of spin--vorticity coupling and sensitivity to spin--spin correlations among hyperons with different quark content (uds, dss, and sss). The results are consistent, within current precision and under the stated spin-transfer assumptions, with a common vorticity-driven polarization mechanism across strange and multistrange hyperons. Consequently, they constrain the interplay of vorticity, magnetic fields, and quark-flavor dynamics in the produced medium.

title: ScienceCUA: Resource-to-Skill Construction and Execution-Guided Skill Evolution for Scientific Computer Use Agents
abstract: Computer-use agents for scientific software require application-specific expertise. Much of this expertise is documented in human-authored software manuals and web pages. However, turning these resources into executable, reusable skills remains challenging due to mismatches between documented and deployed software versions and differences in scope between documentation coverage and task requirements. We introduce ScienceCUA, a two-stage framework combining resource-to-skill construction with execution-guided skill evolution. First, ScienceCUA identifies tasks supported by the software from its documentation, infers operational trajectories, and generalizes them into reusable Skills. Command catalogs, syntax constraints, and shortcuts are organized separately as References for on-demand lookup. Then, ScienceCUA uses execution feedback to drive skill self-evolution by contrasting successful and failed trajectories for the same task, identifying deficiencies, revising existing skills or adding new ones, and updating the skill library only after repeated validation in real environments. To enable reliable evaluation without benchmark noise or task leakage, we introduce two improved benchmarks. ScienceBoard-Verified provides an audited and corrected basis for measuring task performance, while ScienceBoard-VE separates skill evolution from final testing through disjoint evolution and test tasks and further supports native-agent evaluation. Experiments show that the initial Skills and References improve average task success rate by up to 7.23 percentage points over the base model, while skill self-evolution increases the total gain over the baseline to as much as 17.12 percentage points. ScienceCUA turns software documentation into an evolving set of executable skills and queryable references, offering a practical way for general-purpose agents to use scientific software reliably and at scale.

title: Mechano-chemical control of enzymatic activity in crowded environments
abstract: Macromolecular crowding has long been known to alter biochemical equilibria and enzyme kinetics, with reported catalytic activities that may increase, decrease, or vary non-monotonically with crowder concentration. Classical Michaelis--Menten kinetics does not by itself identify which of these responses should occur for a conformationally active enzyme. Here, we develop a minimal non-equilibrium mechano-chemical theory for a fueled enzyme embedded in a bath of passive crowders and uncover a fluctuation-induced effective force dipole acting on the enzyme subunits, akin to a generalized form of dispersion or depletion interaction. Since the preferred conformation of the model enzyme varies through the catalytic cycle, the fluctuation-induced mechanical load affects the relevant kinetic activation barriers and is sufficient to produce both monotonic inhibition and non-monotonic modification of turnover. The framework provides a thermodynamically consistent route for linking crowded environments to catalytic currents, suggesting how mechanical design principles could be leveraged to control enzymatic pathways.

title: Susceptibility optimization for wisdom of crowds: A social power reformulation and realization framework
abstract: Whether social influence makes a crowd wiser or more biased hinges on who yields to others and who holds firm. Such heterogeneous susceptibilities to social influence, together with the influence network, determine the weight each agent's initial estimate carries in the collective estimate, known as social power. This paper studies susceptibility optimization for maximizing the wisdom of crowds under the Friedkin-Johnsen model. Minimizing the squared collective bias over susceptibilities leads to a nonconvex problem. To overcome this nonconvexity, we develop a social power reformulation and realization framework, which decomposes the problem into two stages: first characterizing the social power that minimizes the collective bias, then determining the susceptibilities that induce such social power. Social power reformulation yields a quadratic program over the probability simplex. Under uniform-sign biases, the optimal social power concentrates on the least biased agents and immediately determines the optimal susceptibilities; under mixed-sign biases, its geometry enables a linear-time construction algorithm. For social power realization, we introduce the notions of susceptibility realizability and establish necessary and sufficient conditions for them, under which we derive all optimal susceptibilities in closed form using the Laplacian pseudoinverse and eigenvector centrality. These results yield a unified algorithm that solves the original problem globally, with worst-case complexity cubic in the number of agents when realizability holds. Finally, we develop a fully distributed implementation with linear communication complexity, illustrating how collective intelligence can emerge from local interactions.

title: Establishing Néel order in the square-lattice antiferromagnetic Heisenberg model: a bootstrap proof
abstract: Rigorously establishing spontaneous symmetry breaking (SSB) in the thermodynamic limit is generally challenging. This is exemplified by the two-dimensional (2D) $S = 1/2$ antiferromagnetic Heisenberg model where the existence of Néel order is not rigorously established despite overwhelming evidence from a variety of methods. We show that a bootstrap approach can be used to rigorously establish SSB and use it to prove the existence of Néel order in the 2D $S = 1/2$ XXZ model by deriving a strictly positive lower bound on the Néel order parameter for a set of discrete values of the anisotropy parameter $Δ$ in the range $[0,2]$ including the isotropic (Heisenberg) point $Δ= 1$. Our approach employs a generalization of the Kennedy--Lieb--Shastry inequalities, which use an infrared bound to reduce the existence of long-range order to bounds on certain finite-distance correlators. We compute these bounds for all sufficiently large systems with periodic boundary conditions using the bootstrap. An important ingredient in our proof is a novel method for obtaining exactly certified variational upper bounds on the energy density in the thermodynamic limit from matrix product states. Our approach can be readily generalized to other local lattice models for which infrared susceptibility bounds can be obtained.

title: When will androids outnumber humans?
abstract: Humanoid robots are increasingly discussed not only as machines but also as a potential technological population. We develop a nonlinear population-dynamical framework to examine their possible diffusion relative to humans, without assuming that large-scale adoption or numerical crossover is inevitable. The human population $H(t)$ is calibrated to the United Nations World Population Prospects 2024 median trajectory. The android population $A(t)$ is represented through the normalized stock $a=A/A_s$. A conventional, human-organized manufacturing and adoption channel is calibrated to a conditional scenario spanning approximately $10^4$ humanoids in 2025 to $10^9$ in 2050 and follows $\dot a=(q_M+r_Ma)\exp(K_Ma^γ)$. We separately introduce a hypothetical autonomous channel in which installed androids contribute materially to producing additional androids. Under the minimal canonical TZ closure, the corresponding production--feedback number is $\mathcal{P}(a)=(r_A/δ_A)\exp(K_Ra)$, where $r_A$ is the gross robot-mediated production coefficient, $δ_A$ the retirement rate, and $K_R$ the autonomous feedback parameter. This channel is locally self-amplifying if and only if $\mathcal{P}>1$, whereas numerical human--android parity, $A=H$, is a separate cumulative condition. Global uncertainty analysis shows that crossover dates remain strongly scenario-dependent, while the production--feedback threshold is more robust. An extreme early-autonomy stress test can produce parity by 2050, but this represents a conditional dynamical boundary rather than a technological forecast.

title: Dynamics of a two-dimensional microswimmer near a slippery boundary
abstract: Microswimmers near walls and interfaces can switch between qualitatively different modes of motion depending on the slip properties of the neighbouring boundaries. To study this theoretically, a two-dimensional point-singularity model of a microswimmer, which does not self-propel in unbounded fluid, is placed near a flat viscosity discontinuity between two fluids with viscosity ratio $σ$, and also near a partial-slip wall with Navier-slip length $λ$. Using complex-variable methods, the dynamical systems governing the swimmer motion are derived explicitly in both scenarios. Near the viscosity discontinuity, below a universal critical viscosity ratio $σ_c=1/2$, the swimmer is trapped at a fixed height with its stresslet axis normal to the boundary. When $σ=σ_c$ it glides parallel to the boundary at a speed selected by its orientation, with a terminal speed determined by its initial state. For $σ>σ_c$ it oscillates periodically in height and orientation while drifting along the boundary. The dynamics near a partial-slip wall depend on the ratio of the slip length to the length scale of the singularity and are similar in exhibiting an analogous transition at a critical slip length. It is found, however, that the dynamics near a viscosity discontinuity for $σ$ above $σ_c$ are richer than those near the partial-slip boundary, including the existence of a hydrodynamic bound state with zero net displacement over one period. Although the study is limited to two dimensions, these results show how a single boundary parameter organises qualitatively distinct modes of locomotion, in close analogy with slip-induced transitions reported for three-dimensional swimmers.

title: Forecasting How RLHF Responds to Reward-Model Edits Before Training
abstract: Responses with headers, lists and greater length receive high scores from reward models (RMs), and RLHF policies learn to produce these features even when true quality does not improve. Practitioners therefore edit their RMs, but they learn whether an edit works only after an RL run. We show that the response of a policy to an RM edit can be forecast before training, from samples of the current policy and the scores of the old and new RM. If we read the RM as a set of prices, the first-order theory of KL-regularized RL implies that each feature moves in proportion to its within-prompt covariance with the change in reward. We implant controlled price changes into retrained RMs under a 2^(4-1) fractional factorial design with a self-distilled placebo, run 54 RL runs from six parent policies, and fix every forecast before the runs. With the covariance predictor, we predict the direction of all 20 changes in supply whose forecast has the same sign at every parent and explain 82% of the standardized change. With counterfactual prices, the classical alternative, we explain 50%. The forecast also holds under GRPO and for real RM upgrades, where we explain 66% out of sample with a coefficient frozen from the factorial runs. For rent, the gap between the proxy reward and a gold reward from stronger judges, we rank RM edits correctly with the same covariance over the first 30 steps (Spearman 0.94). This measures the horizon of the forecast: by step 200, the ranking of the factorial edits reverses under both RLOO and GRPO, while the real upgrades keep their order. When we vary the KL coefficient beta, the initial response does not depend on beta, and the response saturates below the KL equilibrium. In one experiment, the long-run response to a price rise is consistent with an additional implicit regularizer beta_0 of about 0.003 to 0.007.

title: HyperFlow: Class-Incremental Semantic Change Detection via Hyperbolic Flow
abstract: Semantic change detection in remote sensing aims to identify and characterize land-cover transitions observed in pairs of satellite or aerial images. Existing methods assume a fixed set of change categories, limiting their applicability in real-world scenarios where changes of interest may vary, for example across geographies or over time. In this work, we tackle the problem of class-incremental semantic change detection, where a model progressively learns to detect new types of semantic change. To do so, we exploit the hierarchical structure of land-cover semantics, where newly introduced categories correspond to fine-grained refinements of existing ones, and represent said semantic categories in hyperbolic space, which is particularly well suited to represent such hierarchical relationships. To capture semantic changes, we introduce HyperFlow, a method relying on Busemann prototypes, modeling change as an anomaly in a learned semantic flow within the hyperbolic embedding space induced by segmentation. HyperFlow couples change detection to class-incremental semantic segmentation, enabling class-incremental semantic change detection. We also present HiChange, a new large-scale, high resolution remote sensing dataset with detailed, fine-grained hierarchical labels. Experimental results demonstrate that HyperFlow achieves both strong change detection and semantic segmentation performance across incremental steps. In particular, we show that progressively refining semantic categories, rather than considering them all directly, yields improved change detection, highlighting the benefits of incremental learning for semantic change detection.

title: A Common Language for Dynamic Graphs: Interaction Tokenization Enables Foundation Models
abstract: Dynamic graphs capture evolving interactions in Web systems, including online communication, user engagement, and recommendation. Graph foundation models aim to reuse predictive capabilities across networks, but extending this capability to dynamic graphs faces two challenges. First, node identities are graph-specific, and similar interaction patterns can appear at different temporal and activity scales, making histories difficult to represent consistently across networks. Second, the predictive roles of historical patterns vary across interaction dynamics, limiting transfer from a narrow range of training processes. In this paper, we show that a common interaction language, combined with learning across diverse interaction processes, offers a basis for dynamic graph foundation modeling. We propose CL-DGFM, a Common Language Dynamic Graph Foundation Model for temporal link prediction. Its Dynamic Interaction Tokenizer encodes interaction memory, historical connectivity, and ordered destination transitions into calibrated tabular inputs, making dynamic histories accessible to existing predictors without an additional trainable graph encoder. Its Dynamic Interaction Prior trains a pretrained tabular foundation predictor across diverse synthetic dynamics. Labeled historical context guides prediction, with a Contextual Value Adapter modulating attention values. The model transfers to real graphs without target-graph parameter updates. Experiments on TGB and TGB-Seq demonstrate competitive performance. Further comparisons show that the common language supports basic machine learning and neural models, and enables direct use of frozen tabular foundation models on dynamic graphs.

title: R$^2$-Omni: Reducing Structural and Precision Redundancy in Omni-LLMs for Long-Form Generation
abstract: Omni-modal large language models (Omni-LLMs) typically process large numbers of multimodal tokens from audio-visual inputs, incurring substantial computational costs and a large memory footprint for the key-value (KV) cache. Aggressive token pruning can alleviate this problem while maintaining competitive performance on multiple-choice tasks, which require only a single option as output. However, we observe substantial quality degradation when generating long-form, open-ended responses. We attribute this gap to query-guided selection, which can retain sufficient evidence for answer selection while discarding details needed for comprehensive generation. This motivates reducing overlapping information across tokens, termed structural redundancy, while preserving diverse content. However, the retained representations may still contain precision redundancy due to unnecessarily high numerical precision in their cached values. To address these two levels of redundancy in token representations, we introduce a training-free framework named R$^2$-Omni. First, Structure-Aware Token Consolidation (STC) consolidates redundant representations using spatiotemporal similarity in video and local continuity in audio. Then, Semantic-Sensitivity Guided Precision Allocation (SSPA) allocates value precision to the retained representations according to the estimated reduction in attention-output error under quantized keys, with query attention and audio-visual alignment providing a semantic prior. Extensive experiments on long-form generation benchmarks demonstrate an average 5.0$\times$ reduction in the memory footprint while preserving 97.98% of baseline generation quality and achieving a 1.48$\times$ end-to-end speedup, highlighting the benefits of jointly reducing structural and precision redundancy.

title: A Multi-messenger Study of the Cygnus bubble
abstract: We perform a comprehensive investigation of particle acceleration at the termination shocks of massive star clusters, with a particular focus on the Cygnus region. Building on the particle-acceleration model for cluster-driven winds, we use recently available spectral and spatial measurements of ultra-high-energy $γ$-rays from the Cygnus bubble to place stringent constraints on the physical conditions in the acceleration zone. By jointly modelling the observed $γ$-ray spectrum and spatial morphology, we derive quantitative limits on key parameters such as the maximum particle energy, acceleration efficiency, magnetic-field strength, and shock geometry, and assess their consistency with a hadronic origin of the emission. These data allow us to refine the target gas profiles within and around the bubble, thereby improving estimates of the expected hadronic $γ$-ray and neutrino fluxes. Using this revised gas model, we compute the neutrino emission associated with the Cygnus bubble and evaluate the statistical significance of a potential neutrino signal from this region for current and near-future high-energy neutrino observatories. Taken together, these results provide a more precise characterisation of the particle-acceleration environment at cluster termination shocks and help clarify the role of young massive star clusters as potential Galactic PeVatrons and contributors to the observed diffuse high-energy neutrino and $γ$-ray emissions.

title: Entropy and round-point convergence for the $σ_k$-curvature flow
abstract: We prove that every smooth closed strictly convex hypersurface in $\mathbb R^{n+1}$ contracts to a round point under the $σ_k$-curvature flow for $2\leq k\leq n-1$, without additional pinching or symmetry assumptions. After rescaling about the extinction point to mean width two, the hypersurfaces converge smoothly and exponentially in normalized time to the unit sphere. The proof is based on an entropy which is invariant under translations and dilations and admits a representation by weighted boundary areas of orthogonal projections. A strengthened Codazzi inequality yields its monotonicity. An upper bound for the entropy controls the inradius relative to the mean width, while its dissipation controls the spatial variation of the normalized speed. We also obtain two-sided curvature bounds at the natural extinction scale.

title: Anomaly-ranked confirmation slows new-class learning
abstract: Anomaly detectors rank unfamiliar examples for expert confirmation, and the confirmed examples teach a classifier to recognise a new class. Across five benchmarks from physics, medicine and computer vision, the members flagged by the detector are those the classifier learns first. In three systems, confirming the highest-ranked members of a new class gives lower recognition than confirming the same number of random members. Handing subsequent selection to the promoted classifier recovers part of this loss in two systems. A paired intervention further shows that replacing nearby known classes with distant ones sharply reduces the confirmations needed for recognition. These results distinguish finding a new class from selecting examples that teach its extent: within the tested classes, concentrating confirmations at the top of the anomaly ranking makes learning less efficient.

title: On the difficulty of characterizing top trading cycles with identical houses
abstract: We study Shapley-Scarf housing markets (Shapley and Scarf, 1974) in which houses come in types and agents are indifferent between houses of the same type but rank the types strictly. On this domain of objective indifferences, top trading cycles (TTC) rules with fixed tie-breaking regain Pareto efficiency and group strategy-proofness (Sandholtz and Tai, 2026), properties that need not hold under general weak preferences. We ask whether the characterization of the TTC rule for strict preferences by Ma (1994) and the characterization of TTC rules with fixed tie-breaking for weak preferences by Ehlers (2014) extend to this domain. They do not. With five agents and two types of houses, we construct a rule that satisfies individual rationality, Pareto efficiency, group strategy-proofness, non-bossiness, and consistency, but whose restriction to the five-agent population is not welfare equivalent to any TTC rule with fixed tie-breaking. With two types, five agents are minimal for this fixed-population result. The same rule shows that several other characterizations of TTC for strict preferences do not extend either.

title: Conformal dimension of Bedford-McMullen carpets
abstract: We show that the Hausdorff dimension of a Bedford-McMullen carpet with non-uniform fibres can be lowered with a quasisymmetry, provided that the defining iterated function system does not have a full column. We prove this by constructing explicit dimension lowering metrics which are quasisymmetrically equivalent to the Euclidean metric.

title: Normalizers in the category of topological groups
abstract: We show that the category of morphisms of topological groups admits split extension classifiers and hence the category of topological groups admits normalizers. We give explicit descriptions of both normalizers and of split extension classifiers of morphisms of topological groups in terms of split extension classifiers of topological groups.

title: TRAILS: Trajectory Generation for Automated Indoor Locomotion Studies
abstract: Virtual reality experiments involving navigation and simulated robot motion often require large, realistic environments and numerous distinct trajectories to avoid repetitive navigation while providing sufficient variation for controlled experiments. Designing such scenarios manually is labor-intensive, particularly when trajectories must satisfy predefined geometric and kinematic constraints while remaining diverse and comparable across experimental conditions. This paper presents TRAILS, an automated framework for generating complete virtual navigation scenarios consisting of an environment layout, a path, and a time-parameterized motion profile. The framework combines a constraint-based procedural environment generator inspired by Wave Function Collapse, trajectory generation using optimized cubic Bézier curves, and speed-profile generation subject to kinematic constraints. The generated scenarios provide diverse indoor environments with corridors, open spaces, and obstacles, together with trajectories of identical duration that vary in path geometry, wall proximity, and velocity profiles while minimizing systematic dependencies between these characteristics. The framework is designed as an easy-to-use tool requiring only a small number of intuitive user-defined parameters to automatically generate large sets of distinct navigation scenarios satisfying prescribed geometric and kinematic constraints. By relying on explicit, seed-controlled algorithmic procedures rather than data-driven models, the generated scenarios remain transparent, reproducible, and configurable, making the framework well suited for telepresence and human-subject experiments. The code is available at https://github.com/JucciK/Trails .

title: Conditional independence testing through marginal permutation
abstract: Marginal permutation is exact for testing marginal independence but generally invalid for conditional independence because it breaks the dependence between the exposure ($\bm X$) and covariates ($\bm Z$). In this paper, we show that empirical studentization can nevertheless make this deliberately misspecified resampling scheme asymptotically valid for important conditional independence tests based on scores. The resulting procedures are novel in the sense that they are valid in finite samples when the exposure is marginally independent of the outcome ($\bm Y$) and covariates, and asymptotically valid under the broader conditional independence null, $\bm X\indep \bm Y\mid \bm Z$, subject to method-specific conditions. For generalized linear model scores, separately studentizing the observed and permuted scores yields validity under a correctly specified null mean despite \emph{arbitrary} conditional variance misspecification. Moreover, the permutation calibration also applies to tests based on generalized and projected covariance measures. Their validity accommodates machine learning nuisance estimates under a condition on the stability of refitting after permutation, for which we provide sufficient conditions for common regression learners. Permutation calibration preserves first-order local power while better capturing the finite-sample discreteness and skewness induced by sparse observations. Simulations and single-cell CRISPR screen analysis show substantial calibration gains with our methods when effective sample size is small.

title: Poisson Super Learning For Survival And Competing Risks On A Discretized Time Scale
abstract: We introduce the Poisson Super Learner, a scalable ensemble method for survival and competing risks prediction with right-censored data. The approach exploits the correspondence between the likelihood of piecewise-constant hazard models and the Poisson likelihood. After expanding the data over a chosen time partition, candidate hazard learners are trained under a common Poisson loss, and cross-validated log-hazard predictions are combined by a Poisson meta learner. The resulting ensemble is a geometric combination of candidate hazards, and can be used to estimate survival probabilities and cause-specific absolute risks. The Poisson Super Learner framework is modular and can in principle incorporate any learner that can estimate interval-specific hazards, including parametric, penalised, additive, and other machine-learning hazard models. Training targets the cause-specific hazard directly and does not require explicit modelling of the censoring distribution. For competing risks, separate cause-specific ensembles are fitted and subsequently combined to obtain individualised cumulative incidence predictions. We illustrate the approach using data from the Steno Diabetes Center collected between 2005 and 2022 to predict cardiovascular disease risk in patients with type 1 diabetes from detailed covariate information. The applied analysis is complemented by simulation studies designed to reflect key features of the data and to examine the behaviour of the method under controlled settings. All analyses were implemented using the freely available R software package poissonsuperlearner.

title: Rethinking Fairness Metrics for Multi-Class and Multi-Group Assessment: Not Everything is Binary
abstract: Artificial Intelligence, and Machine Learning in general, is becoming pervasive across all domains and disciplines. By means of this data-driven approach, algorithms can learns complex task just by learning from samples. However, if the data-set is biased, they might lead to the development of unfair computer systems, that is, characterised by a prejudice towards specific individuals or groups, which might get an unmotivated output from the system. This circumstance lead to the development of multiple metrics designed to quantify the level of unfairness of an algorithm. However, a generalised assumption in the literature is that the sensitive features and the output labels are binary. When the data is not binary, it is forcefully binarized using a one-versus-the-rest simplification. In this work, we discuss the limitations of existing metrics and propose novel, mathematically sound, and generalized multi-group and multi-class formulations of the metrics. Ultimately, our results highlight the empirical assessment distortion caused by binarization strategies, which reveals the limitations of binary fairness metrics in the multi class setting.

title: Persistence of $C^2$ regularity for aggregation patches
abstract: We prove persistence of $C^2$ boundary regularity for patch solutions of the two-dimensional aggregation transport equation, in contrast with the known $C^2$ ill-posedness of Euler vortex patches. More generally, we consider transport equations with kernels of the form $L(\nabla N)$, where $N$ is the fundamental solution of the Laplacian and $L$ is a linear map. We show that $C^2$ regularity persists for every $C^2$ initial patch if and only if $L$ is a scalar multiple of the identity. Our approach builds on the curvature formulation introduced by Kiselev and Luo.

title: Output-feedback controller design for switched systems under graph-constrained switching
abstract: Switched systems operating under a switching constraint are commonly paired with a digraph encoding the possible mode switches. Thereby, edges are associated with the modes of the switched system and the vertices encode the mode switching history. To control those switched systems under graph-constrained switching, an established method is to design vertex-dependent controllers, that is one controller gain per vertex of the graph, which has lead to various results for static feedback controllers. In this paper, we explore the design of edge-dependent controllers. Edge-dependency allows to synthesize dynamic output feedback controllers in a convex manner by means of a Linear Matrix Inequality problem with the additional requirement that the active mode is known. Further, we show that edge-dependency offers a potentially less conservative static output feedback controller design compared to vertex-dependent controllers. We illustrate our results by a numerical example.

title: The Cost of Mismatch: Noise Amplification in Zeroth-Order Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Zeroth-order (ZO) optimization has emerged as a promising approach for memory-efficient large language model (LLM) post-training, yet its reliability in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) remains largely unexplored. Motivated by the distinct data regimes of on-policy RL and fixed-data optimization, we develop a generic variance-theoretic framework to investigate what limits the reliability of ZO gradient estimation. Our analysis reveals that estimation reliability is structurally determined by whether the two finite-difference evaluations are performed on matched data. On-policy reinforcement learning (RL) under the mismatched-data regime produces a $1/μ^2$ oracle-noise amplification that sets an irreducible noise floor as the perturbation scale $μ$ decreases, whereas Boltzmann Targeted SFT (BOLT) under the matched-data regime eliminates this amplification via noise cancellation. We further derive convergence guarantees with explicit constants that cleanly separate the two regimes. These results motivate the ZO-BOLT algorithm, which builds on BOLT's matched-data advantage for reliable ZO optimization of an RLVR-aligned objective. Controlled perturbation-scale sweeps and matched-versus-mismatched end-to-end comparisons validate the predicted effect of data matching. Experiments across three models and two mathematical reasoning benchmarks further show that ZO-BOLT consistently improves over the pretrained baseline while retaining a near-inference memory footprint. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/lianmin-chen/the_cost_of_mismatch.

title: Exact Agreement Expansion up to the Top via Non-polarity
abstract: Agreement expansion asks whether local assignments to faces of a poset that usually agree on a sampled common face must agree with a single global function on most faces. Agreement expansion is exact (approximate) if local assignments need to exactly (approximately) agree with the global function. We suggest a new proof technique for agreement expansion that enables agreement expansion in settings which were previously beyond reach, such as: exact agreement expansion for Grassmannian posets (before only simplicial complexes support exact agreement expansion); agreement expansion based on assignments to top faces of the a complex (before agreement expansion is generally proven only for assignments to low dimensional faces); agreement expansion from one-sided spectral expansion (before, two sided spectral assumption was needed in general settings). Specifically, for down-closed simplicial and Grassmannian complexes, we prove an exact agreement theorem between any two layers assuming one-sided spectral expansion in links of singletons. As an application, we show that full bases of every rank-$k$ matroid admit exact agreement with soundness $O(k^2/[h(k-h)])$ when tested through $h$-element independent sets. We also obtain exact agreement on Grassmannian posets under one-sided spectral expansion, with stronger soundness under a local distance guarantee. Our key proof ideas center around non-polarity of the distributions of local assignments, probed via a random exposure of elements.

title: Qyantram: A Transparent and Verifiable Quantum Computing Platform
abstract: Most quantum circuit platforms focus on idealized circuit assembly and simulation, hiding hardware compilation, error identification, and variational model training behind black-box operations. QYANTRAM addresses this gap through an open platform comprising four subsystems, built around evidence-backed results and independent verification. Its staged compilation pipeline makes every transformation traceable, while the router publishes rejected SWAP candidates and their scores for transparent decision-making. Verification exploits inactive qubits remaining in the |0> state, reducing complexity from 2^N to 2^k for k active qubits. This mathematically exact reduction enables full pre-compilation verification on 127- and 156-qubit layouts, achieving approximately 10,000x speed-ups with execution times below one millisecond. The error identification engine exhaustively evaluates all Pauli error patterns without sampling, matching closed-form predictions within 2.8e-17. Its machine-learning engine achieves numerical agreement within 2.0e-15 of qiskit.quantum_info while training 25-50 times faster. The router introduces approximately 1.27x more SWAP gates than Qiskit's SABRE due to its omission of optimization, trading routing efficiency for complete decision transparency and traceability.

title: Kernelized Stable Fluids for simulating physically accurate solutions
