Every generalized hep-derivor induces a functor between categories of many-sorted partial algebras. The values of this functor satisfy the domain conditions wherever their operations are defined, and we characterize when the operations are defined exactly where these conditions hold. The functor induced by a composite receives a natural inclusion from the composite of the induced functors; this inclusion, which can be strict, makes the induced functors a normal lax indexed category. In finite dimensions, generalized hep-derivors realize graduation and unification as an equivalence between the homogeneous and heterogeneous presentations, and discretization as a left adjoint to truncation. In dimension $ω$, we reconstruct the categories of $ω$-categorial algebras as projective limits of their finite-dimensional truncations and obtain unification by a quotient construction; we also establish algebraic squares and compatibility with change of signature. Finally, for nonempty sets of sorts, we show that the finite-dimension condition in the homogeneous $ω$-presentation is not axiomatizable by quasi-existence equations on its fixed signature.

title: Determinant boundaries and gaps in determinantal complexity
abstract: Landsberg, Manivel, and Ressayre constructed determinant-boundary components whose defining forms, for odd n >= 3, are limits of n x n determinants but cannot themselves be represented by determinants of that size. Their border determinantal complexity (DC) is therefore smaller than their exact DC. We prove that the difference can grow linearly with n. For every n >= 10, we construct an explicit homogeneous form of degree n, concise in n^2 variables, whose orbit closure is a boundary component, whose border DC is n, and whose exact DC is at least 2n - 1. Thus n rows suffice when limits are allowed, whereas every exact representation requires at least 2n - 1 rows. The same bound holds for the unpadded odd-skew forms at every odd n >= 3. We also prove that every concise degree-n boundary form in n^2 variables has exact DC at least n + 2. We construct three families of pairwise distinct boundary components. Together with the traceless determinant, they give at least floor((n-1)/2) + floor(n/3) components for every n >= 3, with an additional term counted explicitly in the paper. The main lower bound follows from a general degree lemma. If an affine matrix represents an irreducible homogeneous polynomial f of degree d and has globally free rank-one cokernel over the coordinate ring of f = 0, its size is at least 2d - 1. The adjugate factors into two nonzero kernel vectors, each requiring a coordinate of degree at least d - 1. Comparing their product with the degree of a cofactor proves the bound. The lemma is sharp for individual representations, as witnessed by algebraic branching programs. Whether the exact-versus-border gap can grow superlinearly remains open.

title: MCP Tool Poisoning in Agentic AI Frameworks: A Cross-Framework Measurement Study
abstract: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) lets agentic AI frameworks connect language models to external tool providers, but it carries attacker-controlled content (tool descriptions, schema fields, and response data) into model context without validation. Prior benchmarks measure model compliance with poisoned instructions without confirming real execution. We present the first cross-framework measurement of MCP tool poisoning with real tool execution. A 25-class root-cause taxonomy unifies prior classifications, and the open-source tool mcpvenom drives a 9,720-cell susceptibility matrix across 12 frameworks, 18 models, and 45 attack scenarios, with a dual oracle that confirms exfiltration via canary HTTP receipt. The overall attack success rate is 22.9% (2,113 vulnerable cells). Of these, 64.9% dispatch an attacker tool call, 23.0% contact the attacker endpoint, and 12.1% verifiably exfiltrate a secret. Resistance is model-level: nine core frameworks cluster within 23 to 26% (chi-squared = 3.30, p = 0.91), and no framework implements intentional defense. Incidental framework properties mitigate in specific cases, and a regex description scanner rejects 20 of 45 scenarios at a 7.2% false-positive rate, so metadata scanning alone is a partial control. Model ASR ranges from 0.4% to 49.7%. Claude Opus 4.8 is vulnerable in 8 of 530 cells while issuing 223 explicit refusals. A code-level audit finds no intentional defense across twelve frameworks, and all five coordinated disclosures across four vendors were rejected.

title: Toward the one- and two-loop EFTofLSS for Simons Observatory CMB lensing
abstract: Cosmic microwave background (CMB) lensing observations are becoming sensitive to non-linear structure formation and baryonic feedback scenarios. The effective field theory of large-scale structure (EFTofLSS) provides a systematic description of matter clustering in the mildly non-linear regime, accounting for baryonic effects through counterterms and offering a consistent framework for cross-correlations with other observables. We perform a Fisher forecast for the joint Simons Observatory temperature, polarization, and CMB lensing likelihood using noiseless data vectors with different baryonic feedback scenarios, modelling non-linear structure formation using the one- and two-loop EFTofLSS. We find that, with a single additional parameter, obtained through a principal-component analysis of the EFTofLSS counterterms, both the one- and two-loop EFTofLSS provide a good fit across the baryonic feedback scenarios considered. This parameter is closely aligned with the effective AGN heating temperature $T_{\rm AGN}$. Both loop orders reduce cosmological parameter biases, with only a small loss in marginalized precision at fixed scale cuts. We find that the one-loop EFTofLSS yields unbiased estimates over a range of scales similar to the dark-matter-only model, while the two-loop EFTofLSS extends this range to smaller scales and accommodates different feedback scenarios more robustly. When each model is evaluated at the smallest scales for which its cosmological parameter estimates remain unbiased, the two-loop EFTofLSS yields stronger constraints than the dark-matter-only model.

title: PlantVLM-Edge: Quantized Vision-Language Models for On-Device Crop Health Diagnosis
abstract: Timely and accurate crop health diagnosis is essential for sustainable agricultural production, yet accurate diagnosis often requires expert knowledge that is not readily available. Recent vision-language models (VLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in visual understanding, reasoning, and natural-language interaction, creating new opportunities for intelligent crop health assessment. However, deploying VLMs on resource-constrained devices remains challenging due to their substantial computational and memory requirements. This paper presents PlantVLM-Edge, a quantized vision-language framework for conversational crop health diagnosis that can run entirely on resource-constrained edge devices. PlantVLM-Edge combines agricultural domain adaptation, post-training quantization, and on-device serving with an offline chat interface, allowing growers to ask open-ended questions and receive diagnoses, symptom explanations, and management guidance without cloud connectivity. The framework is backbone-agnostic: we validate it with two different VLM types with varying scale and architecture (Qwen3-VL-2B and LLaVA-1.5-7B), four quantization schemes, and two diagnostic domains (plant diseases and insect pests), and we deploy all variants on an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin. Eight-bit quantization affects answer quality minimally relative to the full-precision model, and 4-bit activation-aware weight quantization (AWQ) retains 98.6% of full-precision answer quality on both domains while reducing the weight memory of the 2B backbone by 49%. In its most compact form, PlantVLM-Edge requires 2.01 GiB of weight memory, returns its first token in about 0.12 s, and completes a 64-token diagnostic response in 0.78 s. These results demonstrate that timely and accurate crop health diagnosis is practical on edge devices, providing a foundation for next-generation crop monitoring and decision support systems.

title: Quantum Private Information Retrieval on Forests
abstract: We consider the problem of graph private information retrieval (PIR) in the quantum setting. We focus on a specific type of graphs, namely the forest graphs. A forest graph is a union of disjoint trees. We consider the quantum setting where all the servers share an entangled state. Each server is allowed to send only one qudit per retrieval round. We design a scheme for the forest graphs that achieves the rate of $\frac{3}{N}$. The scheme uses a GHZ state as the initial entangled state between the servers prior to the scheme initiation. We compare our scheme with the only work done in the literature that considered the quantum setting of graph PIR. We show that our scheme is more efficient in this setting. We derive the quantum capacity for the case of $G=3K_2$, which is equal to $4/6$. $G=3K_2$ is a special case of the forest graph. We design a scheme that is specialized for this graph, achieving a rate equal to $4/6$ and provide the corresponding matching upper bound, establishing it as the capacity.

title: Episodic Protostellar Outflows: A Proper Motion Study in Serpens South
abstract: Serpens South is a notable protostellar cluster with signatures of recent star formation, including a high protostellar fraction. Within the region, several protostars provide important mechanical feedback via outflows. We investigate the molecular outflow driven by the Class 0 protostar known as CARMA-7, which is located in the central hub of Serpens South. Two epochs of observations with the Atacama Large Millimeter/sub-millimeter Array (ALMA) with sub-arcsecond resolution capture the well-collimated, episodic outflow with distinct ejecta knots. This outflow, traced with 12CO J = 3-2 and SiO J = 8-7, appears to be mostly blueshifted to the south and redshifted to the north, with radial velocities up to at least 25 km/s. We present the first proper motion study of this outflow by comparing observations taken in 2017 and 2021. The measured proper motions trace the ejection history and refine the inferred outflow morphology. We find that proper motions of the 12CO J = 3-2 and SiO J = 8-7 knots range between 10 - 40 mas/yr, corresponding to 30-90 km/s. Using radial velocities and proper motions, we determined that the inclinations of the outflow lobes are ~60 -80 degrees relative to the line of sight. Finally, we measure ejection timescales as recent as ~10 to ~120 years, and we discuss this in the context of other known protostars with recent ejecta events.

title: Haagerup symmetries of the $E_8$ theory and conformal nets at central charge eight
abstract: A Haagerup algebra is a positive strongly rational vertex operator algebra $U$ of central charge eight with $\mathrm{Rep}(U)$ braided equivalent to the Drinfeld center $Z(\cal H_3)$ of the Haagerup fusion category. We prove that $U$ has exactly three holomorphic extensions, each isomorphic to $V_{E_8}$, and that the corresponding Lagrangian algebras have module categories $\cal H_1$, $\cal H_2$ and $\cal H_3$. The extensions attached to $\cal H_2$ and $\cal H_3$ are the two lattice extensions of $V_{E_6 \oplus A_2}$. We prove a recognition theorem for $\cal H_2$ and $\cal H_3$ among unitary fusion categories of rank six with three invertible objects, a noncommutative Grothendieck ring and trivial pointed associator. For simple regular unitary vertex operator algebras with bounded localized vertex operators, we construct the transport module of two ordinary unitary modules when the second integrates in Tener's annular sense. For a unitary conformal Haagerup subalgebra of $V_{E_6 \oplus A_2}$, these results give a completely rational net with representation category $Z(\cal H_3)$, a realization of the Haagerup subfactor and the generalized orbifold of Bischoff. In particular, they apply to the strongly local explicit algebra $S$ of levels $(3,13)$, whose Haagerup property is established in [ArhIII, Theorem 6.1]. In [ArhIII], the net of $S$ is recognized from strong rationality and lattice branching, and a diagonal extension of the net is then used to identify $\mathrm{Rep}(S)$. Here an exact construction of the compatible unitary structure on the diagonal lattice algebra $V_{E_8 \oplus E_8}$, followed by passage to the twin algebra, proves complete unitarity and Condition I+ for every Haagerup algebra. This also gives the VOA--net comparison through smeared vertex operators for unitary conformal embeddings in $V_{E_6 \oplus A_2}$.

title: Studentized inference in randomized experiments when a few units dominate the outcome variation
abstract: In completely randomized experiments with heavy-tailed outcomes, a few units can carry a share of the residual variation that does not vanish as the number of units grows. We study the studentized difference in means and Lin's regression-adjusted estimator, with covariates whose leverage vanishes, when the finite population is fixed, and the treatment assignment is the only source of randomness. The studentized statistic then has a nonnormal limit in general. Populations with the same marginal distributions of potential outcomes can have different limits, as the limit depends on the unobserved pairing mechanism of the two potential outcomes of each dominant unit. When the outcome errors are drawn from a heavy-tailed law, the limit is random and, outside a degenerate case, varies with the population. Under balanced allocation, the conventional Wald interval has an explicit asymptotic coverage floor. At the nominal level $0.95$, the floor is about $0.42$ for every population and about $0.84$ when the two potential residuals of each unit are equal. Both floors are close to the best possible, and without balanced allocation, the coverage can fall to the smaller of the proportions of treated and control units.

title: Multiple windows of eigenstate-selective delocalization in a non-Hermitian quasiperiodic lattice
abstract: We investigate localization in a non-Hermitian quasiperiodic lattice with a real quasiperiodic onsite potential of strength $W$ and a staggered imaginary quasiperiodic modulation of strength $λ$. Using the inverse participation ratio (IPR), normalized participation ratio (NPR), fractal dimension $D_2$, transfer-matrix Lyapunov exponent, and wave-packet dynamics, we find a strongly non-monotonic and state-dependent response. At fixed $λ$, varying $W$ yields two distinct delocalization windows, whereas varying $λ$ at fixed $W$ produces a single re-entrant delocalization window. These regimes arise within selected eigenstate sectors, where localized states coexist with extended or critical states, leading to mobility-edge-like behavior. The corresponding suppression of the Lyapunov exponent and enhancement of the dynamical RMS spreading are consistent with the IPR, NPR, and $D_2$ results. Finite-size scaling confirms the persistence of the re-entrant features, while the complex-energy spectrum resolves their state-selective structure. The resulting phase boundaries delineate distinct localization regimes in the $(W,λ)$ plane. Our results show that the interplay between quasiperiodicity and a staggered non-Hermitian modulation sharing the same quasiperiodic spatial structure can generate re-entrant, state-dependent localization, with implications for localization and dynamics in non-Hermitian quasiperiodic lattices.

title: Geometric Aspects of $C^*$-Extreme Points II
abstract: Building on the results of \cite{HR}, we investigate the relationship between \(C^*\)-extremality and linear extremality in the closed unit balls of general unital \(C^*\)-algebras. We show that, unlike in von Neumann algebras, these two notions of extremality need not coincide in general \(C^*\)-algebras. More precisely, we prove that the unilateral shift is a linear extreme point, but not a \(C^*\)-extreme point, of the closed unit ball of the Toeplitz \(C^*\)-algebra. We further establish that \(C^*\)-extremality implies linear extremality whenever the \(C^*\)-algebra admits a faithful unital representation on a separable Hilbert space. We also prove this implication for elements admitting a factorization $x=v|x|$, where $v$ is a partial isometry belonging to the algebra, and extend the result to suitable quotient \(C^*\)-algebras, including the Calkin algebra. Finally, we characterize the linear extreme points of the closed unit ball of unital \(C^*\)-subalgebras of \(B(H)\) containing the compact operators.

title: Surrogate model of gravitational waveforms for quasi-circular, spin-aligned, asymmetric-mass black hole binaries based on the hybridization of WaSABI-C inspirals with numerical relativity waveforms
abstract: With the incorporation of aligned-spin dynamics into self-force waveform models, such as the WaSABI-C inspiral model, and with the release of the SXS collaboration's third public catalog of NR simulations, the gravitational waveform modeling community has made significant advances in the modeling of spinning, asymmetric-mass black hole binaries. In light of these developments, we present WaSABINRHybSur2dq15, the first surrogate model to incorporate information from self-force theory, post-Newtonian theory, and numerical relativity. The model is trained on 65 hybrid waveforms for quasi-circular, spin-aligned, asymmetric-mass black hole binaries with mass ratios spanning 1:1.25 to 1:20 and aligned-spins for the primary black hole ranging -0.5 to 0.5. The hybrid waveforms are generated from a set of WaSABI-C inspirals and NR waveforms from the third SXS public catalog. The model covers the parameter domain $1.25 \leq q \leq 15$ and $|χ_{1z}| \leq 0.5$, and includes the $(2,2),\, (2,1),\, (3,3),\, (4,4),$ and $(5,5)$ spin-weighted spherical harmonic modes. The model also spans the entire LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA (LVK) frequency band (with $f_{\text{low}}=20$ Hz) for total masses $M \gtrsim 111.5\,M_{\odot}$. We find that the WaSABINRHybSur2dq15 model faithfully reproduces the hybrid waveforms with mismatches less than $10^{-3}$ for total masses in the range $80\,M_{\odot} \leq M \leq 300\,M_{\odot}$.

title: The Virasoro Bootstrap: from the $c\sim1$ desert to coupled Potts
abstract: We develop a numerical conformal bootstrap for two-dimensional CFTs with $c>1$ based on Virasoro conformal blocks, computed with Zamolodchikov's recursion and optimal polynomial interpolation. As a first test we isolate an island around three decoupled Ising models. We then consider three 3-state Potts models coupled through their energy operators, a candidate irrational CFT. Mixed correlators isolate the decoupled theory in an island, and different gap assumptions, motivated by perturbation theory, yield a peninsula that contains the coupled fixed point but not the decoupled one. Finally, we explore the standard single-correlator bound on the lowest-dimension scalar primary in the OPE of two identical scalars. We find that for central charges just above $c=1$ the bound collapses over a wide range of external dimensions. This excludes any theory whose lightest scalar is absent from its own OPE and lies in this range, and supports the conjecture that no compact CFT exists in this region. We explain several features of these bounds analytically.

title: GW/PT-correspondence for CY $4$-fold-II: Virtual Classes
abstract: Let $B$ be a complex manifold and $f:\bX\to B$ a derived \textit{complex-analytic} (not necessarily \textit{algebraic}) space with an oriented relative $(-2)$-shifted symplectic structure. We suppose that the closed symplectic form is locally exact in the completed relative de Rham complex, and construct a derived smooth manifold over $B$, independent of additional choices. When $f$ is proper and oriented, this gives integral virtual fundamental classes on its fibres. Our argument is heavily based on the strategy of Borisov-Joyce who already solved the \textit{algebraic} version of this problem, and uses \textit{derived differential geometry}. The proof also contains a relative analytic Darboux theorem a-la Brav-Bussi-Joyce, and has a natural analogue in Borel-Moore homology. We provide applications to complex-analytic enumerative geometry: in particular, to counting Pandharipande-Thomas pairs on compact and non-compact complex-analytic Calabi-Yau $4$-folds. This is part of a joint project with Felix Thimm dedicated to the proof of the GW/PT-correspondence for Calabi-Yau $4$-folds by implementing Pardon's programme in dimension $4$.

title: High-order guaranteed lower bounds for the Schrödinger eigenvalue problem
abstract: We compute unconditional guaranteed lower eigenvalue bounds for Schrödinger operators using a modified hybrid high-order method with built-in correction for the potential defect. The method assumes exact numerical integration and allows possibly unbounded potentials in $L^p$ for $p>n/2$ and $p\geq2$ on general polyhedral domains. We prove that the high-order correction preserves optimal a priori convergence orders, and derive reliable and efficient a posteriori error estimators. Numerical experiments provide striking evidence of optimal high-order convergence rates of the adaptive algorithm.

title: Flexibility of Laplace-Beltrami eigenfunctions under metric variation
abstract: We study the surjectivity of the differential of the Laplace-Beltrami operator with respect to the metric parameter. We use the obtained results to prove that every small deformation of a nonconstant eigenfunction can be realized with a small perturbation of the metric. As a consequence, we prove that every generic property of smooth functions which is invariant under multiplication by a nonzero scalar is generic for eigenfunctions of the Laplace-Beltrami operator, extending a result by Uhlenbeck.

title: Associated primes in group cohomology and a strange result
abstract: In 2010. Okuyama proved the following. Let $G$ be a finite group and $k$ an algebraically closed field of characteristic $p$ dividing the order of $G$. (1) Let $\frak p$ be an associated prime of $H^*(G,k)$ of $\dim=s$. Then there exists an elementary abelian $p$-subgroup $E\subseteq G$ of rank $s$ with $\mathfrak p=\mathfrak p_E$ and depth$\,H^*(C_GE,k)=s$. (2) Let $E$ be an elementary abelian $p$-subgroup of $G$ of rank $s$ and suppose depth$\,H^*(C_GE,k)=s$. Then $\mathfrak p_E$ is an associated prime of $H^*(G,k)$. It is shown this result is true for all fields of characteristic $p$. We also show the following result: If $E$ is an elementary abelian $p$-subgroup of $G$ and depth $H^*(G,k)=\text{rank} E$, then up to conjugation $E$ contains the maximal elementary abelian subgroup contained in the center of a Sylow $p$-subgroup of $G$.

title: Chemical and dynamical evolution of prestellar cores, the dawn of star and planet formation
abstract: Studying prestellar cores is crucial to understanding the formation of stellar and planetary systems. To date, we lack a comprehensive survey of their density and velocity structure at small scales (100-1000 au), the gas ionisation state, their lifetimes, and how these properties are influenced by the environment. A deep study into this critical stage of star formation requires a large single-dish (sub)millimetre telescope like AtLAST.

title: Nonlinear gauge maps and the structure of Goldstone loops in canonical inflation
abstract: We clarify the nonlinear relation between the spatially flat scalar and Goldstone descriptions of canonical single-field inflation. An exact clock map shows how potential interactions are reorganized into derivative Goldstone interactions. A change of slicing further connects their dilation symmetry to its comoving realization. We then study the Goldstone two-point function at one loop in the decoupling limit. Using identities derived from the general mode equation, we reveal how seemingly independent loop contributions combine and their non-boundary parts cancel once the associated counterterms are included. This reduction requires no explicit mode-function solution. The leading adiabatic long-mode response reduces to a total derivative in loop momentum, which requires an additional regularization prescription.

title: Counterexamples to the Jacobian Conjecture from the viewpoint of lineability
abstract: Algebraic genericity in the family of polynomial counterexamples to the recently solved Jacobian Conjecture for $N\ge3$ is investigated. The notion of affine-coneability is introduced and it is shown that this family is affine-coneable and 1-lineable, but not 2-lineable. Semigroupability is further studied with respect to coordinatewise multiplication and composition.

title: Dynamical Unbalanced Optimal Transport: Duality, Reachability, and Computation
abstract: We study dynamical unbalanced optimal transport for nonlinear control-affine systems in which the control input affects both the transportation of mass and its growth or decay. This phenomenon arises naturally in controlled transport-reaction systems such as cancer treatment, and distinguishes the problem from standard unbalanced optimal transport, where transport and mass variation are typically independent. To address this problem, we combine classical relaxed-control theory with a weighted superposition principle to obtain an infinite-dimensional linear programming reformulation over weighted trajectories. Under suitable convexity and compactness assumptions, we show that this relaxation is tight. Based on the relaxation, we derive a Kantorovich dual formulation in terms of Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman inequalities, and establish strong duality over smooth subsolutions. We then utilize the dual formulation to characterize reachability of the system, namely, when a given terminal measure is reachable from a given initial measure. In addition, tractable sufficient conditions for reachability are provided. Finally, we develop an augmented-Lagrangian algorithm based on the dual formulation for numerical computation of the optimal transport plan. The framework is illustrated on a phenotype-structured cancer treatment problem in which therapy simultaneously drives phenotypic adaptation and population growth or death.

title: BISECT: Bilevel Spectral Decomposition for Low-Rank Continual Learning
abstract: Exemplar-free continual learning on pre-trained Vision Transformers increasingly relies on Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), yet prevailing methods govern the low-rank update space through strict subspace isolation. By projecting each incoming task into the approximate null space of historical token activations, isolation-based learners equate any cross-task feature overlap with catastrophic interference. We show that this orthogonality premise induces a structural bottleneck we term \emph{spectral starvation}: when down-projection bases are locked before task optimization, the gradient norm reaching the trainable up-projection is upper-bounded by the energy of current-task features captured by the chosen basis. Because natural visual tasks share low- and mid-level covariance structure, historical null tails contain barely $5.5\%$ of incoming task variance, starving new-class plasticity while blocking positive consolidation along shared directions. We propose BISECT (Bilevel Spectral Decomposition), a continual LoRA framework that partitions a fixed rank-$r$ budget into two orthogonal functional blocks: an invariant carrier spanned by the dominant modes of the joint historical-and-current Gram matrix, and a novelty complement extracted via generalized Rayleigh whitening followed by orthogonal complement projection. After single-task training, BISECT folds both blocks back into the frozen backbone using a closed-form precision gate that scales each rank-1 invariant atom by its current-to-joint Rayleigh ratio while preserving novelty atoms at unit gain. Across eight incremental settings on ImageNet-R, ImageNet-A, CIFAR-100, CUB-200, and DomainNet, BISECT outperforms prompt, adapter, and LoRA baselines with zero extra inference parameters or FLOPs, and remains complementary to sparse analytic expansion.

title: VeriHarm-Bench: Measuring Harmful Success in LLM Coding Agents Verifiably
abstract: Large language model (LLM) coding agents increasingly operate with shell access, allowing them to write scripts, move files, alter permissions, and modify system configurations. However, an agent may achieve a user's goal while causing unintended harm, such as deleting unrelated files, weakening access controls, or corrupting data, in response to benign inputs without explicit jailbreaking. This failure mode is particularly important because apparent task success may reassure users that an agent behaved correctly, causing harmful side effects to go unnoticed. We call this harmful success: the agent successfully completes the intended benign task while simultaneously causing unintended harm. Despite its importance, harmful success is difficult to measure because conventional task-success metrics overlook harmful behaviors, while existing safety evaluations are often designed solely to assess harmful outcomes. We introduce VeriHarm, an automatic framework for constructing programmatically verifiable benchmarks that directly measure harmful success. VeriHarm minimally perturbs coding tasks to elicit unintended harmful behavior while maintaining the benignity of the task and preserving the original task objective. It then synthesizes executable harm tests that, together with the original task-correctness tests, evaluate both task accuracy and harmful outcomes. Frontier agents, including GPT-5.6-Sol and Claude-Opus-5, achieve an average task accuracy of 95% on our curated VeriHarm-Bench, yet still struggle to complete tasks safely: their safe success rate, the fraction of tasks completed successfully without triggering the designated harm, averages only 37%. These results suggest that successful task completion can frequently coexist with unintended harm, and that task-success metrics alone may substantially understate the potential safety risks of coding agents.

title: NitiBench+: A Temporal Thai Legal Question Answering Benchmark Across 17 Domains
abstract: Law changes over time. A court decides a case under the law in force on that day, and legal QA benchmarks grade answers against today's law. We checked 156,650 decisions of four Thai courts. Up to 67% of them cite law that has since been amended or repealed. We introduce NitiBench+, the sequel of our NitiBench, a Thai legal QA benchmark with 1,670 items across 17 domains, built from decisions of three courts. For each cited section it holds both the text in force on the decision date and the current text, and its retrieval corpus holds every dated version of every Thai statute section. Answers are graded on the Thai Bar Council rubric, the Bar-standard score, and on the overlap between the cited sections and the court's. The report has two parts. Part I measures the cost of the wrong text on 13 open-weight models. Reading the current text of amended law drops the Bar-standard score by 0.25 and missing repealed law drops it by 0.79. The penalty comes from rule changes, 0.45 on the 428 rule-changed items and none on the 331 wording-only items, and Citation F1 does not see it. The text in force is the fair setting. Part II benchmarks today's models on that setting. A public leaderboard ranks 26 models on a held-out test split of 500 items stratified by domain, with a validation split of the same shape released for public use, from memory alone, with the court's sections provided, and as a retrieval agent over the law in force, with the cost per item and the hallucinated citations. The best model scores 7.78 out of 10 and the best open-weight model 6.39. Without a search tool only five open-weight models recall any Thai law, and with it twenty of the 26 models gain and six lose. Leaderboard will take new models as they are released. Legal benchmarks must track dates, and on the right text today's models still leave a wide gap on Thai law.

title: Sonar-MoE: In-Backward Expert Updates for Memory-Efficient Mixture-of-Experts Training
abstract: Most parameters of a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model belong to its experts, and standard training keeps every expert gradient in GPU memory until the optimizer step. This memory grows with the number and size of the experts, so it rises as MoE models scale. We introduce Sonar-MoE, which updates each expert tensor during the backward pass and frees its gradient right away. It brings optimizer-in-backward from dense models to batched MoE expert tensors, so the GPU never holds more than one layer of expert gradients. When we fine-tune OLMoE-1B-7B and Granite-3.1-3B-A800M in bf16 with two expert-kernel backends, Sonar-MoE lowers peak memory by 19% to 22%. Its updates are bitwise identical to standard training without expert gradient clipping, and held-out loss stays within 0.003 of all baselines. Each step also takes 17% to 23% less time than standard training with global-norm clipping. Updating whole batched tensors rather than individual experts is what keeps Sonar-MoE fast, as it avoids a 20% to 72% slowdown while using the same memory. Sonar-MoE matches optimizer-in-backward over all parameters in memory and speed while still clipping the dense parameters.

title: Uniform Sampling of Linear Codes with Prescribed Hull Dimension
abstract: We give exactly uniform samplers for linear codes with prescribed hull dimension, for the Euclidean, Hermitian, and symplectic inner products and over finite fields of every characteristic. Except for the Euclidean form over fields of odd characteristic, these are the first uniform samplers for arbitrary prescribed hull dimension. Each sample costs an expected $O(k^2 N + k \log q)$ field operations for codes of dimension $k$ in a space of dimension $N$ over $\mathbb{F}_q$ or $\mathbb{F}_{q^2}$.

title: An Almost-tight Size Lower Bound for Bounded Treewidth Homomorphism-Distinguishability
abstract: One way to compare two graphs $G_1, G_2$ is to check whether there is some graph $H$ in a graph class $\mathcal{H}$, such that the number of homomorphisms from $H$ to $G_1$ is not equal to that from $H$ to $G_2$. This is the field of homomorphism distinguishability which has gained a lot of traction in recent years. In this paper, we study the case where $\mathcal{H}$ is the class of graphs of treewidth $k$. This has connections to important concepts in logic, machine learning, combinatorial optimization and proof complexity. In particular, Dvořák showed that $G_1$ and $G_2$ can be distinguished by a homomorphism count from a graph of treewidth $k$ iff $G_1$ and $G_2$ are distinguishable by the $k$-dimensional Weisfeiler-Leman algorithm. While the relation between the iteration number of this algorithm and the depth of the tree-decomposition of a distinguishing graph is understood, our understanding of the \emph{size} of $H$ is limited. We show a $2^{Ω(n^{k/2})}$ lower bound on the size of a graph of treewidth $k$ required to distinguish two graphs of order $n$. This bound is proved via a new combinatorial game along with a construction which uses a recent compression technique for CFI graphs. It is almost tight to the known $2^{O(n^{k+1})}$ upper bound and is an exponential improvement on the previous best known lower bound.

title: Detection of the Galaxy--Galaxy--Temperature Skewed Bispectrum
abstract: We present the first measurement of the galaxy--galaxy--temperature skewed bispectrum, obtained by cross-correlating the squared, filtered unWISE galaxy overdensity with \textit{Planck} maps at 100, 143, 217, and 353~GHz. The signal is detected with high significance in all four channels. Its frequency dependence reveals contributions from hot gas through the thermal Sunyaev--Zel'dovich (tSZ) effect and from dust through the cosmic infrared background (CIB). With the galaxy occupation fixed, our halo-model fits favor higher integrated pressure and peak star-formation efficiency for the galaxy--temperature cross-spectra than for the skewed bispectrum. Comparisons with component-separated tSZ and CIB maps from the same \textit{Planck} observations indicate that this mismatch is not confined to the frequency-map fits. This difference motivates testing more flexible descriptions of gas pressure, CIB emission, and galaxy occupation. In particular, it could point to a mass dependence of the gas-pressure profile that our model does not fully capture. By giving greater weight to massive halos that host many galaxy pairs, the skewed bispectrum provides a complementary test of these descriptions, using information beyond two-point statistics at a comparable computational cost.

title: Single-pass stochastic cooling for electron microscopy
abstract: Scientific applications of free electrons, such as in electron microscopes and particle accelerators, are limited by the brightness of available electron sources. Accelerators can use phase space cooling to surpass these source limitations, whereas electron microscopes can only rely on particle filtering to increase beam coherence at the cost of reduced brightness. We show that strong electron-light coupling in nanophotonic structures makes it possible to achieve single-pass stochastic cooling inside an electron microscope for a lossless improvement of longitudinal emittance. This approach is laser-free and compatible with normal CW operation of electron microscopes. We derive a fully quantum mechanical model of stochastic cooling valid in the strong coupling regime, finding an analytic asymptotic formula for the optimal cooled energy spread $σ_{E_f}\simeq0.88(\hbarω)^{2/3}σ_{E_0}^{1/3}$, with $\hbar ω$ the cooling photon energy and $σ_{E_0}$ the initial energy spread. Numerical simulations confirm that the energy spread reduction is reflected in an increase in the purity of the electron's quantum state and a reduction of the longitudinal phase space area. Our work paves a path towards even brighter beams for electron microscopy, promising higher image quality, enhanced spectral resolution, and a route to reaching fundamental quantum limits on electron beam phase space area.

title: Local scaling limit of the four-dimensional uniform spanning tree
abstract: In this paper, we prove that the uniform spanning tree of $\mathbb Z^4$, seen from the origin, converges locally to an infinite spatial Brownian Kesten tree: a Brownian spine onto which independent spatial Brownian trees are grafted at a constant rate. The convergence holds jointly for the intrinsic metric, the volume measure and the Euclidean positions of the vertices, after rescaling these quantities by suitable constant multiples of $n^{-1}$, $n^{-2}(\log n)^{1/3}$ and $n^{-1/2}(\log n)^{-1/6}$, respectively, under the local rooted spatial Gromov-weak topology. The rescaled space-time occupation measure converges to that of infinite canonical super-Brownian motion. We also identify the limiting law of the rescaled intrinsic-ball volume and obtain sharp first-moment asymptotics.

title: Bounds for the binary quartic Weyl sum
abstract: We prove that $$ \sum_{1\le x,y\le N} e(αF(x,y)) \ll_{F,α,ε}N^{5/3+ε} $$ for every $ε>0$, real quadratic irrational $α$, and integral binary quartic form $F$ that is not the fourth power of a linear form over $\mathbb{C}$. The proof uses the two-dimensional $q$-analogue of van der Corput's method, following Heath-Brown's work in the one-variable case. The heart of our argument rests on new bounds for complete binary cubic Weyl sums with linear terms, which retain the dependence on the cubic discriminant and the linear coefficients.

title: TAMPAgent: Agentic Belief-Space Planning for Mobile Manipulation
abstract: Open-world robotic mobile manipulation requires acting in physical environments with only partial information. While recent Large Vision-Language Model (LVLM) agents show strong open-world reasoning capabilities, existing architectures that rely on direct tool calling struggle with geometric uncertainty and thus are limited to fully-observable tabletop environments. In contrast, Task and Motion Planning (TAMP) systems can solve long-horizon tasks under partial observability but incur high computational costs and require closed worlds. We propose \textbf{TAMPAgent}, an agentic planning framework that unifies the reasoning of LVLMs with the structured constraint satisfaction of TAMP systems. We endow an LVLM agent with a belief-space planning model operating over an extensible API of perception, planning, and control tools. The agent formulates a partial task plan composed of parameterized observation and execution actions, which is subsequently completed using classical search algorithms. After extracting the plan's geometric constraints, the agent leverages its tool API to bind valid parameter values, satisfying feasibility requirements and producing an executable motion plan. Upon execution, the agent continuously updates its belief history and repeats this closed-loop process by interleaving observation and manipulation actions. Evaluated across complex household mobile manipulation tasks on Rainbow Y1 and Unitree G1 platforms, TAMPAgent significantly outperforms direct tool-calling agentic baselines, demonstrating that integrating TAMP constraint satisfaction into agentic planning loops is essential for unstructured, partially observable environments.

title: Seeing Through the Illusion: Test-Time Scaling for World Action Models
abstract: World action models (WAMs) jointly generate actions and imagined futures, but a plausible prediction need not be realized by its co-generated action. We introduce WISE (\emph{World Action Inference Scaling through Evaluation}), a pre-execution selector that scores each sampled rollout on action validity and temporal regularity, inverse-dynamics consistency between the proposed action and the imagined motion, and instruction-conditioned task progress, and executes the highest-scoring candidate while keeping the WAM frozen. With four candidates per decision, WISE raises closed-loop success from 6.0\% to 24.0\% on RoboLab with Cosmos~3 Edge and from 75.1\% to 78.3\% mean success on LIBERO with DreamZero, and exceeds the best existing selector in aggregate by 4.0 and 0.9 points. Component ablations and agreement analyses show that the three scores rank candidates differently and that task progress carries the largest weight in the fused decision.

title: FedReady: Bounded Agents for Federation Formation
abstract: Federated learning (FL) runtimes standardize aggregation and deployment, but each new study still requires federation formation: selecting task-eligible sites and preparing their local data and task code for federated training or analysis. This preparation recurs when the target changes, while raw records and site-private mappings are excluded from cross-site FL messages. We present FedReady, a system that performs federation formation with bounded LLM agents. Agents propose shared contracts, local adapters, and task code; the runtime owns workflow state and accepts artifacts only after checks tied to their digests. Candidate site discovery prioritizes recall; local eligibility verification checks task support before site admission. Once participating sites and artifacts are fixed, conventional federated training or analysis proceeds without readiness agents. Across 39 simulated retinal sites and four tasks, discovery reaches recall 1.00 at precision 0.65; local eligibility verification removes all 17 false positives without losing an eligible site-task pair. The participating sites supply 45,575 task-record instances and complete four 100-round jobs, including one with a runtime-generated contract. Across ten patient cohorts, preparation supports seven patient populations and holds endpoints at three sources as unsupported. Comparison with manually prepared reference populations and analysis (the manual reference) gives a maximum survival-curve difference of 0.001133. We also analyze 19 development failures, targeted classification ablations, and standalone and heterogeneous agent configurations. These results establish the feasibility of task-specific data preparation before ordinary FL training or analysis.

title: Synchronization of Enriched Spin Glasses
abstract: We show that enriching a non-convex multi-species Hamiltonian by a uniform Ruelle probability cascade implies synchronization of the joint overlap array without an additional regularizing perturbation. In particular, we show that any limit point of the overlap array is a deterministic non-decreasing function of a uniform Ruelle probability cascade.

title: 3D-BBDA: Backpropagation-Free Black-Box Domain Adaptation for Robust 3D Point Cloud Recognition
abstract: Robust 3D point-cloud recognition is critical for robotics, mapping, and urban sensing, yet point-cloud classifiers often suffer performance drops under domain shifts caused by sensor changes, environmental variation, and acquisition artifacts. Many existing adaptation methods are difficult to deploy in practice because they require access to source data or the internal parameters of the source model, which may be restricted by privacy, licensing, or security constraints. We present 3D-BBDA, a backpropagation-free black-box domain adaptation framework that adapts a source-trained predictor to unlabeled target data using only black-box outputs. Our method performs pseudo-label guided prototype-based alignment and employs a weighted prediction module to fuse source logits with alignment logits, reducing sensitivity to noisy pseudo-labels. To stabilize prototype memory when pseudo-label coverage is incomplete, we construct a Gaussian-perturbed prototype prior from unlabeled target predictions and use it as a fallback for missing or unreliable class prototypes during alignment. Experiments on four corrupted 3D benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements over strong baselines. On ModelNet-40C, 3D-BBDA achieves mean errors of 32.08% (PointNet) and 29.62% (GDANet), outperforming Source-only (35.88% / 34.03%) and BFTT3D (33.78% / 32.36%). 3D-BBDA requires only a single forward pass with no gradient updates making it suitable for real-time, privacy-preserving deployment in transferable 3D recognition pipelines. Project page is available at https://visdomlab.github.io/3D_BBDA

title: On the lower bound for the $L^1$ norm of Liouville exponential sums. I
abstract: Let $λ$ be the Liouville function. We prove Let $λ$ be the Liouville function. We prove \[ \mathcal{I}_λ(X)=\int_{\mathbb{T}}\left|\sum_{1\leqslant n\leqslant X}λ\left(n\right)\mathrm{e}\left(nα\right)\right| \mathrm{d}α \gg X^{\frac{1}{4}}. \] This removes the $X^\varepsilon$ loss in the previous result of Pandey and Radziwiłł~\cite{PandeyRadziwill2026}. In the second paper in this series, we will prove that \[ \limsup_{X \to \infty} \frac{\log \mathcal{I}_λ(X)} {\log X} \geqslant\frac{1}{3}. \]

title: A Scaling Theory of Multi-Epoch Pretraining: Late-Time Overfitting and Ensembling
abstract: In the near future language model pretraining will become bound by total data rather than total compute. Such a regime requires revisiting scaling laws and scaling law theory. Motivated by prior works that have found utility in ensembling, we study how the number of training epochs and ensemble size jointly shape generalization when training data are fixed. In language-model experiments on FineWeb, logit averaging reduces late-training deterioration, delays optimal stopping, and can outperform wider or deeper single models at matched parameter-token budgets over a common training horizon. To analyze this interaction between data reuse and ensembling, we derive a dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT) for multi-epoch stochastic gradient descent in power-law random-feature ensembles, tracking error correlations across epochs and models. Ensembling reduces the prediction variance responsible for late-time growth in expected test error, changing the optimal stopping time. We use these stopping times to derive compute-allocation laws at fixed data and individual model sizes. Under this allocation, ensemble size grows with compute at least as fast as training time per member, while excess test loss above the limiting loss decreases as a power of compute.

title: Internal friction and frequency-dependent conductivity in the bivariate site energy model for the mixed alkali effect in glasses
abstract: The mixed alkali effect is fundamental to understanding ion transport in glasses. It manifests itself in strong changes of various ionic transport properties when one type of ion is successively replaced by another type. Recently, we have developed a new theory of thermally activated hopping in bivariate random site energy landscapes that takes into account site occupation statistics according to generalized Fermi distributions and mixture kinetics in accordance with linear irreversible thermodynamics. The theory was successfully applied to predict the behavior of partial conductivities and their activation energies at low frequencies corresponding to the dc limit. Here we show that the theory is capable to capture the salient features of the mixed alkali effect observed in ac ion conductivities and in the peculiar behavior of the internal friction.

title: Evaluating Uncertainty Calibration in Probabilistic Time Series Foundation Models
abstract: Time series foundation models (TSFMs) are increasingly used for probabilistic forecasting across diverse domains, yet the reliability of their uncertainty estimates remains poorly understood. In this work, we study uncertainty calibration in probabilistic TSFMs from a broader methodological and empirical perspective. We introduce a taxonomy of how TSFMs represent predictive uncertainty and develop a fine-grained evaluation framework for calibration in multi-horizon forecasting that distinguishes pooled, horizon-wise, and stronger conditional notions of calibration. Using this framework, we conduct a comprehensive empirical evaluation of popular TSFMs across diverse datasets and show that current models exhibit distinct and systematic patterns of miscalibration that standard metrics often obscure. We further analyze common post-hoc recalibration methods and characterize which forms of calibration they can improve and which tend to persist. Our results provide practical guidance for evaluating and improving uncertainty calibration in TSFMs and highlight important limitations of current practice.

title: Temperature-Independent Logarithmic Current Slope in Interdiffusion-Broadened Silicon pn Junction toward Low-Power Thermometry
abstract: With the development of cryogenic technologies such as quantum computing, there is an increasing need for low-power cryogenic thermometers that minimize self-heating. Here, we report an anomalous temperature-independent logarithmic current slope, $d(\ln J)/dV$, in heavily doped silicon p$^{+}$n$^{+}$ junctions with significant dopant interdiffusion and highlight the advantages of our device as a low-power, cryogenic thermometer. Electrical characterizations from 2 to 420 K reveal that, at low forward bias, $d(\ln J)/dV$ remains nearly constant, which yields a voltage-temperature responsivity that is nearly independent of bias current. The observed transport cannot be fully understood with conventional diffusion or direct band-to-band tunneling. Instead, the results suggest the contribution of trap-assisted tunneling. These results establish interdiffusion-broadened silicon p$^{+}$n$^{+}$ junctions as a route to low-power temperature sensors while providing insight into carrier transport in heavily doped semiconductor junctions.

title: Square-Root Pass Semi-Streaming Algorithms for Digraph Problems
abstract: We study directed graph problems in the semi-streaming model where we are restricted to $\widetilde{O}(n):=O(n\cdot \text{polylog}(n))$ space for processing the edge stream of an $n$-node graph and can make one or a few passes to solve the given problem. A longstanding open problem in multipass streaming is determining the number of semi-streaming passes needed to solve directed $s,t$-reachability: there is an exponential gap---$Ω(\log n/\log \log n)$ vs $n^{1/2+o(1)}$---between the best-known lower and upper bounds. Several related fundamental digraph problems, e.g., topological sorting, acyclicity testing, and decomposition into strongly connected components (SCCs), are known to have the same semi-streaming pass lower bound. However, no $o(n/\text{polylog}(n))$-pass upper bound was known for any of them. Our main result achieves an $n^{1/2+o(1)}$-pass semi-streaming algorithm for each of these problems. As a corollary, we get algorithms with the same pass and space usage for a broad class of DAG problems that admit a certain form of dynamic program over a topological ordering. This class includes weighted single-source shortest paths, longest paths, max-outdegree+1 coloring, and constructing a lexicographically-first DFS (depth-first search) forest. Our algorithm for the last problem can be seen as a generalization of our results on topological sorting and acyclicity testing: recall that standard textbook algorithms for these problems use DFS as a subroutine. Our algorithms are optimal up to an $n^{o(1)}$ factor in passes under the reasonable conjecture that $s,t$-reachability requires $Ω(\sqrt{n})$ semi-streaming passes. However, using the fact that our algorithms can be parameterized by the number of passes taken by topological sorting or single-source reachability algorithms, we prove stronger lower bounds for some of the problems even under weaker conjectures.

title: DynaSolver: A Neural Operator for Autoregressive 4D Flow Prediction with Dynamic Boundaries
abstract: Neural operators provide efficient surrogates for computational fluid dynamics (CFD), but most are designed for static geometries and are not equipped to model unsteady flows induced by continuously moving boundaries. We study dynamic-boundary 4D CFD prediction for articulated moving geometries and introduce RoboCFD-4D, a temporally resolved robotic CFD benchmark spanning diverse morphologies and flow conditions. To address the computational and autoregressive challenges of this setting, we propose DynaSolver, a neural operator that explicitly conditions on boundary evolution and causal flow history. DynaSolver employs an efficient physical-token formulation that amortizes point-to-token projection across the operator stack, substantially reducing repeated point-space spatio-temporal computation while retaining accurate point-level reconstruction. We further introduce Replay-Augmented Parallel Training, which exposes the model to autoregressively generated histories while preserving parallel dense supervision, narrowing the gap between ground-truth-conditioned training and autoregressive rollout. Experiments on RoboCFD-4D show that DynaSolver achieves the best full-rollout accuracy among a broad range of learned CFD surrogates, with its advantage increasing as rollout proceeds, indicating substantially reduced autoregressive error accumulation. Project page: https://made-gpt.github.io/DynaSolver-ProjectPage.

title: Spacetime Emergence in the Memory of a Learning Agent
abstract: We show that the causal structure of spacetime can emerge within the memory of a learning agent performing a quantum information task. We train a model-based reinforcement-learning agent to maximize the quantum mutual information between localized quantum probes interacting with a quantum field in Minkowski spacetime, without directly providing it with information regarding the spacetime metric or causal structure. In learning to accomplish this task, the reinforcement-learning agent constructs an internal predictive model whose planner develops the characteristic null structure of spacetime, allowing us to reconstruct the causal structure of the Minkowski metric with high accuracy. Within this task, spacetime geometry is obtained from an agent's successful predictions and actions, providing a first step toward showing that spacetime concepts emerge from operational quantum experience.

title: Structured Visual Landscape: Generating Preferred Representations in Biological and Artificial Neural Networks
abstract: Understanding how neurons respond to visual stimulus is an important question in both deep learning and neuroscience. It has significant implications for enhancing the interpretability of black-box artificial neural networks and for understanding the visual representation in the human brain. We propose a structured visual representations landscape and design an activation-based prior that allows us to effectively regularize the landscape with activations from brain regions or neural network units. Our model Vis-Lens integrates a variational autoencoder and a diffusion model into an image generation framework. It enables the generation of natural, realistic preferred images by directly modifying the activation-regularized latent codes without per-image iterative optimization. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework on both artificial neural networks and human visual cortex using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data. Our framework improves activation modulation and image realism compared with a recent state-of-the-art method for generating preferred visual representations of these neural targets. Code is available at https://github.com/NeuroAIHub/Vis-Lens.

title: Online Matching with Arbitrary Stochastic Rewards
abstract: Online matching with stochastic rewards is a generalization of online bipartite matching in which an attempt to match an online arrival to an offline resource may fail with some probability. Each arrival allows at most one attempt and the success probabilities of its edges are revealed when it arrives. Greedy is 0.5-competitive, which is the best possible for deterministic algorithms. While better competitive ratios are known in several special cases, beating 0.5 for arbitrary probabilities has remained open. We show that, against the adaptive offline benchmark and for arbitrary probabilities, a randomized Perturbed Greedy algorithm is at least 0.591-competitive in the unweighted setting and at least 0.531-competitive with vertex weights. The perturbation functions combine Greedy with scaled versions of the classic exponential function.

title: Should We Combine Our Data? Algorithms and Limits for Privately Assessing Data Sharing
abstract: In this paper, we study when two parties should pool their data to train a machine learning model. Two agents, Alice and Bob, each hold a sensitive labeled dataset and want to train a classifier from a given hypothesis class $\mathcal{H}$. Even when each party's dataset can be perfectly classified on its own, the two parties may follow conflicting labeling standards or have selection biases that affect their features and label sets, such that no single classifier in $\mathcal{H}$ fits their combined data. Before committing to data sharing, Alice and Bob therefore want to test whether a single classifier in $\mathcal{H}$ can jointly fit both datasets---without revealing their individual data points to one another. We formalize this problem from a learning-theoretic viewpoint via $\operatorname{opt}_\mathcal{H}$, the minimum \emph{number of mistakes} made by any hypothesis in $\mathcal{H}$ on their pooled data. Through interactive communication, the agents must distinguish $\operatorname{opt}_\mathcal{H}=0$ (compatible datasets) from $\operatorname{opt}_\mathcal{H}\geq t$ (conflicting datasets) under pure $\varepsilon$-two-party differential privacy. A trusted curator could do this with $t=O(1/\varepsilon)$, and we ask how small $t$ can be without one. For thresholds on the real line over a domain of size $m$, we show that the optimal $t$ is $\tildeΘ(\log\log m/\varepsilon)$, exponentially smaller than the $Θ(\log m/\varepsilon)$ samples needed to privately learn thresholds, even with a curator. For halfspaces in $\mathbb{R}^d$, the dependence on $m$ jumps to $\log(m)$: we give a protocol with $t=\tilde{O}(d^3\log m/\varepsilon)$ and show that some domains require $t=Ω(d\log(m/d)/\varepsilon)$.

title: Four Bridges: Measuring Deception Propensity in a Multi-Agent Game
abstract: AI agents are increasingly deployed in settings where they interact and coordinate with other agents, yet honesty is mostly measured in single-turn, single-agent benchmarks that pressure the model to deceive. We study deception that emerges in multi-agent interaction without any instruction to deceive. We introduce Kradle, a platform for evaluating AI models, and Four Bridges, an information asymmetry game in which four agents distribute across four rooms: one is the death room, the others hold food worth more if not shared. One agent, the informed agent, knows which room is the death room and can withhold or disclose that information. We evaluate eight frontier models as the informed agent. Deceptive behavior appears in every model and in 73% of all runs (6% to 100% per model), and does not decrease with capability tier within a model family. When the informed agent does disclose, the warning is often challenged, and agents that challenge it enter the death room twice as often as those that do not. Telling all agents that one of them knows the death room collapses deception in six of eight models; telling the informed agent that the room is permanently fatal moves only one. On an open-weight model, an honesty steering vector reduces deception to 0% and adversarial honesty training to 6%. The platform and game provide a testbed for measuring deceptive behavior and comparing interventions.

title: DiabAgent: Toward Agentic Physiological Control
abstract: As pretraining scales, medical language models have advanced rapidly in clinical question answering. Their ability to achieve effective physiological control through sustained intervention still lacks systematic quantitative evaluation. Type 1 diabetes provides a concrete setting: impaired insulin secretion creates dependence on exogenous insulin, with dosing continually adjusted using information about meals, exercise, illness, and glucose measurements. We introduce DiabAgent, a research suite for agentic physiological control comprising the Agentic Physiological Control (APC) framework, the DiabetSim simulator, and the SweetBench benchmark. APC controls glucose through medical-device tools, using ongoing observations to infer individual states, accumulate personal experience, and choose treatment actions. We build DiabetSim to simulate different patients, events, and device conditions for scalable virtual testing and training. Using DiabetSim, we construct SweetBench by instantiating 32 scenario designs as 212 glucose-control tasks. With Claude Opus 5.5 and a fixed decision interval of one hour, APC achieves a COGI of 73.5, compared with 71.2 for the open-source closed-loop baseline OpenAPS. Ablations further show that individual adaptation and contextual information improve glucose control. Combining high-frequency rule-based control with lower-frequency agent decisions shows potential for balancing control performance and computational cost. Our work provides a framework, simulator, and evaluation foundation for agents to participate in human physiological control.

title: Reviso: Not All Visual Evidence Deserves Equal Attention in Video Captioning
abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can generate detailed video captions, yet they may overemphasize minor details while overlooking essential context and key events. We argue that not all visual evidence deserves equal attention, as the importance of visual information depends on the content of each video. Motivated by this observation, we propose Reviso, an agentic video captioning framework that learns what to observe and how to gather relevant visual evidence. From a low-frame-rate global preview, Reviso constructs a hierarchical Context--Focus--Points (CFP) observation plan that identifies the video context, prioritizes key aspects, and defines concrete observation targets and corresponding tools. Guided by this plan, Reviso performs goal-directed active perception by selectively revisiting temporal segments and combining tools for fine-grained inspection. It interprets the acquired evidence, updates its plan as needed, and integrates global and local information to generate the final caption. To learn this observation strategy, we develop a verification-guided pipeline that constructs high-quality training trajectories through factual verification and teacher-guided refinement. We further train Reviso using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), incorporating a key-fact reward for caption quality, a Plan Alignment Reward (PAR) for identifying important observation targets, and an Unproductive Tool-Call Penalty (UTCP) that adjusts observation-cost penalties based on caption quality. Experiments across four video captioning benchmarks show that Reviso outperforms the evaluated open-source baselines, while its generated captions better support downstream video question answering. These findings highlight the effectiveness and potential of priority-guided active observation for video captioning.

title: Automatic Generation of Novel Highly-Functional Molecular Sequences
abstract: While multiple methods now exist to generate functional sequence variants from existing annotated examples, it is unclear how well such methods can be used to generate sequences that exceed the functionality of those contained in the example set. Using two complete fitness landscapes, we quantify how effectively generative tools can search sequence space and find rare, novel, highly functional sequences, focusing on variational auto-encoders and information-theoretic methods. We find that an information-theoretic method that does not require training and runs significantly faster than standard Machine-Learning/Artificial Intelligence (ML/AI) methods also is significantly more effective in finding rare highly-functional sequences. We discuss the application of this novel method to discover rare polypeptides with anti-bacterial properties that are specific to bacterial, but not eukaryotic, cell membranes.

title: Near-Optimal Space and Time Cut Sparsification in Turnstile Streams
abstract: A seminal result of Ahn, Guha, and McGregor (PODS'12) showed that a cut sparsifier of an unweighted graph can be computed from a near-linear number of linear measurements. Later work extended this to spectral sparsifiers (Kapralov et al., FOCS'14) and to near-linear recovery time (Kapralov et al., SODA'20). For weighted graphs, these sketches rely on grouping edges by weight, which general turnstile streams do not allow. Chen, Khanna, and Li (FOCS'22) removed this limitation, using $\tilde{O}(n/\varepsilon^3)$ bits of space. We improve the space to $\tilde{O}(n/\varepsilon^2)$ bits. Our algorithm makes one pass over a general turnstile stream of a weighted graph, processes each update in $\tilde{O}(1)$ time, and recovers, in $\tilde{O}(n/\varepsilon^2)$ time, a reweighted subgraph with $O(n\varepsilon^{-2}\log^2 n)$ edges that preserves every cut within a factor of $1\pm\varepsilon$. Its space, update time, and recovery time are all optimal up to polylogarithmic factors.

title: ufakzeka-kulak: Building and Evaluating a 31.6M-Parameter Turkish Speech Recognizer from Scratch
abstract: ufakzeka-kulak is an open Turkish speech-to-text model of 31.6M parameters, a FastConformer encoder with a token-and-duration transducer (TDT) and a CTC head, trained from scratch and released under Apache-2.0. It writes cased, punctuated Turkish with numbers as words. Its 4,977 training hours come from sources whose licences allow commercial use; 281 hours are human-transcribed, and for the other 4,696 the training text is an uploader subtitle or a machine transcript, kept only where a second, independent reading of the audio agrees with it. The recipe, checkpoint, labelling and export choices were made on development data, and the test sets were scored once, in a release gate fixed before training. With greedy TDT decoding the normalised word error rate (WER) is 0.0921 (95 percent interval 0.0792 to 0.1055) on FLEURS Turkish test and 0.0916 (0.0873 to 0.0958) on Common Voice 27.0 Turkish test, lower than Whisper base and Whisper small on both sets with paired intervals wholly below zero; Whisper large-v3 (greedy) scores 0.0604 and 0.0767. On conversational speech the WER is 0.3807. We also report punctuation and casing, degraded audio, and how closely each shipped export reproduces the trained model.

title: Isogeny rigidity under algebraic group actions and finite translation orbits
abstract: We study finite orbits generated by fibrewise translations on varieties carrying two abelian fibrations. Under natural dominance and generation hypotheses, non-isotriviality of the first family forces points with finite orbit to lie over proper closed subsets of both bases. This extends results of Corvaja, Tsimerman and Zannier to complex families of arbitrary, possibly different relative dimensions, including torsors. The proof combines relative Manin-Mumford with a general isogeny rigidity theorem for algebraic group actions.

title: Cyclicity of Drinfeld modules modulo primes in arithmetic progressions
abstract: Let $A=\mathbb{F}_q[T]$ and $K=\mathbb{F}_q(T)$, and let $ϕ$ be a Drinfeld $A$-module over $K$ of rank $r\geq 2$. We study the reduction of $ϕ$ at primes $\mathfrak{p} \in A$ lying in a prescribed arithmetic progression, for which $ϕ(\mathbb{F}_{\mathfrak{p}})$ has at most $r-1$ cyclic components. We obtain asymptotic formulas for the number of such primes of a given degree, with error bounds uniform in the modulus of the arithmetic progression. Furthermore, when $\mathrm{End}_{\overline K}(ϕ)=A$, we sharpen the error term and, under additional hypotheses, establish a necessary and sufficient condition for positivity of the resulting density.

title: Penalized Cox Regression with Graph-Structured Distribution-Valued Predictors
abstract: We propose the Graph-Fused Distributional Cox Model (GFDCM), a penalized survival analysis framework for distribution-valued predictors organized on a known graph. Modern neuroimaging studies collect high-dimensional voxel-level measurements across multiple regions of interest (ROIs) with rich spatial dependency structures. Rather than reducing these to scalar summaries, GFDCM models the full distribution of voxel intensities within each ROI, retaining region-specific interpretability while exploiting spatial relationships among adjacent ROIs. The distributional associations are modeled using penalized splines. To achieve simultaneous predictor selection and graph-based fusion, we introduce a structured Graph-Fused Group LASSO (GFGL) penalty that combines a group-sparsity term for discarding irrelevant predictors with a fusion term that enforces coefficient functions for graph-adjacent predictors to be identical. A flexible alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) algorithm is employed to optimize the penalized partial likelihood. Numerical simulations illustrate satisfactory selection, fusion, and estimation performance of GFDCM compared with unpenalized functional Cox regression and selection-only alternatives. Finally, we apply GFDCM to baseline T1-weighted MRI data collected from 308 patients in the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI-1) to identify brain regions associated with AD conversion. The results provide clinically meaningful insights and exhibit superior predictive performance compared to traditional ROI-level summary-based approaches.

title: On ill-distributed $B_3$ and $B_4$ sets
abstract: We show that, for $k\in\{3,4\}$, a $B_k$-set $A\subseteq[N]$ has size $o(N^{1/k})$ if it omits a fixed positive proportion of the residue classes modulo every prime in a fixed family whose reciprocals have divergent sum.

title: A GPU Engine for Sparse Matrix-Vector Products on $k^2$-Tree-Compressed Graphs
abstract: The $k^2$-tree is a compact representation of Boolean matrices: it stores the recursive hierarchy of their non-empty submatrices, with neither values nor coordinates, and serves rows and columns alike. Its traversal, however, locates the children of each node by rank queries, a chain of dependent irregular loads that leaves a GPU waiting on memory. We implement sparse matrix-vector multiplication (SpMV) on $k^2$-trees for the GPU. Since the traversal does not depend on the vector, the positions of the children are static: we descend the tree one level at a time and obtain them from a parallel prefix sum or from a sampled directory of about 0.1 bits per node. Descending in tiles bounds the temporary memory by the depth of the tree, so the device memory of a product is known before it runs. The same traversal computes right and left products, for one vector or a batch, over the plus-times, Boolean and tropical semirings. We evaluate the engine on an NVIDIA GB10 and an H100 with fourteen Wikidata, Software Heritage, web and social graphs of up to 1.2 billion edges, against cuSPARSE, a grammar-compressed GPU engine and a Boolean CSR. Our results show that the tree is 2.3-27x smaller than the CSR of cuSPARSE and that, with its last internal level cached, a product takes 0.7-2.4x the time of cuSPARSE on the right and 0.27-2.6x on the left. On a 1.2-billion-edge graph, a product needs 1.1 GB on the device, 9x less than cuSPARSE. The engine is memory bounded: the $k^2$-tree is the format of choice when device memory, not time, is the constraint.

title: Associated Varieties of Finite-Group Orbifolds
abstract: Let $V$ be a simple, strongly finitely generated vertex algebra with a connected nonnegative integer grading, and let $G$ be a finite group of grading-preserving automorphisms. In this paper, we prove that $X_{V^G}\cong X_V/G$ as reduced Poisson varieties. More precisely, the canonical surjection $R_{V^G}\longrightarrow (R_V)^G $ has nilpotent kernel. The proof uses a uniform derivative bound in a relative $C_2$-quotient, which also implies that $V^G$ is strongly finitely generated. Consequently, quasi-lisseness and $C_2$-cofiniteness descend to finite-group orbifolds, and hence, by existing results, so does strong rationality.

title: Efficient Closure Learning in Dynamical Systems: A Comparison of Data-Assimilated and Embedded Approaches
abstract: Increased computing power has transformed computational science and improved predictive capabilities for complex systems, but many phenomena still exceed current simulation capabilities or require rapid evaluations for fast design iterations. Closure models address this challenge by approximating unresolved effects in reduced or incomplete dynamical systems. Data-driven closures offer a flexible mechanism for improving model accuracy and applicability, but approaches that embed the closure within a computational model for construction and training phases can be computationally expensive and cause numerical instabilities in the computational model during training. To avoid the challenges posed by embedded approaches, staged approaches to closure-model learning have been developed. The first stage uses data assimilation to infer state and closure trajectories from observations. The second stage trains a machine learning closure model offline using the assimilated data, thereby avoiding repeated simulator calls during training. In this work, we investigate the cost and accuracy tradeoffs between embedded and staged data-driven closure modeling approaches for a synthetic epidemiological SIQR model with a nonlinear state-dependent quarantine closure. The results illustrate a practical accuracy-efficiency trade-off: for this exemplar, embedded training provides the strongest average accuracy, while the staged approach yields comparable qualitative behavior with a moderate increase in error, substantially fewer model evaluations, and improved optimization robustness.

title: The Giant Planet Mass Function Across Stellar Mass and Metallicity: Massive Stars Make Massive Planets
abstract: Although giant planet occurrence correlates with stellar mass and metallicity, it remains unclear whether these properties also shape the companion mass distribution. We investigate this question using 719 FGKM stars from the California Legacy Survey and companion true-mass constraints from radial velocities and Hipparcos-Gaia astrometry. Our hierarchical occurrence analysis accounts for survey completeness and companion parameter uncertainties over giant planet and brown dwarf masses of M_c=0.4-50 M_Jup and semi-major axes of a=0.1-10 AU. We find that, compared to the rate among our full sample of 0.19 +/- 0.02 planets per star in this interval, giant planet occurrence is significantly enhanced around stars with high mass (M_star>1 M_sun; 0.39 (+0.06/-0.05) planets per star) and high metallicity ([Fe/H]>0.0; 0.30 (+0.04/-0.03) planets per star). We find evidence at the 2-3 sigma level that the planet mass function shape varies with stellar mass, with higher characteristic planet masses around stars with M_star>1 M_sun than around lower-mass hosts, based on differences in both the CDFs of fitted models and constraints on model shape parameters. For the full sample, occurrence declines above a few Jupiter masses and is consistent with either a plateau below ~3 M_Jup or a peak near 1-2 M_Jup. The brown dwarf desert begins at a companion-to-host mass ratio of 0.013-0.02. These results suggest that stellar properties influence not only the frequency of giant companions but also their characteristic masses. Within the core accretion framework, this shift could reflect larger gas reservoirs around more massive stars or earlier core formation in metal-rich disks, allowing greater gas accretion before disk dispersal.

title: Benchmark Prediction with Sparse and Unpaired Cached Responses
abstract: Evaluating a generative model on all queries from all available benchmark tasks is prohibitively expensive. As such, models are often evaluated on different subsets of tasks and/or different subsets of queries from a given task. The resulting collection of responses and the corresponding (model, task) score matrix are sparse and unpaired. In this paper, we introduce the Product Kernel Perspective Space (PKPS), a collection of low-dimensional representations of models based on their embedded responses. PKPS generalizes existing methods for representing black-box generative models by comparing responses to similar -- rather than just identical -- queries and is therefore able to utilize sparse and unpaired information. Theoretically, we show that benchmark prediction using PKPS is query-efficient relative to methods that only use information from dense and paired portions of the evaluation data. Empirically, we show that PKPS-based methods outperform baselines on benchmark prediction across two large benchmark suites.

title: A Circuit Complexity Trichotomy For Regular Languages
abstract: We establish a trichotomy for the non-uniform, unbounded-fan-in circuit complexity of regular languages: the complexity of every regular language lies in exactly one of $O(1)$, $Ω(\log n)\cap O(\log n\log\log n)$, or $Ω(n)\cap O(n)$. Our main technical contribution is a characterization of the sublinear class in terms of algebra, word congruences, regular expressions, and logic.
