This class consists precisely of the regular languages computable by constant-depth circuits of size $O(\log^2 n)$, or, equivalently, by circuits of size $O(\log n\log\log n)$ and depth $O((\log\log n)^2)$. Consequently, every regular language of sublinear circuit complexity is definable in $\mathrm{FO}^2[Σ,<,\mathrm{mod}]$, which is contained in wire-linear $\mathbf{AC}^0$. For each of the three classes, deciding membership is $\mathbf{PSPACE}$-complete when the language is specified by a nondeterministic finite automaton. We also obtain a corresponding classification for regular languages with a neutral letter.

title: Inhomogeneous Synthetic Fluxes in Optical Lattices
abstract: Synthetic gauge fields in optical lattices are usually engineered to realize a uniform magnetic flux. Here, we propose a scheme to generate spatially inhomogeneous fluxes and demonstrate how such fluxes reshape the single-particle spectrum. Within Wannier--Stark-assisted tunneling, onsite modulation produces a plaquette flux that depends on the orientation of the static tilt, whereas laser-assisted tunneling (LAT) does not. Using LAT, two coherent Raman processes with different momentum transfers imprint a dimerized Peierls phase that alternates the flux between neighboring plaquettes of a square lattice while keeping the mean flux fixed. A bond-selective Raman phase extends the scheme to the kagome lattice, where a parameter $ξ$ redistributes the flux between triangles and hexagons at fixed flux per unit cell. The Hofstadter--Rammal spectrum of the bipartite square lattice retains chiral symmetry for all $ξ$, whereas the kagome lattice lacks this symmetry, and its flux periodicity and reflection symmetries survive only at special values of $ξ$. As $ξ$ is reduced, the anomalous Landau levels of the kagome singular flat band are compressed toward the flat-band energy and evolve into a degenerate zero-energy manifold at $ξ=0$ with compactly localized states. The dynamical structure factor, accessible through Bragg scattering, resolves this evolution as a Rydberg-like series of peaks whose spectral span tracks the width of the anomalous-level tower and vanishes as $ξ\to0$. We discuss the frequency resolution and temperature required for its observation.

title: Tracing the Scientific Discovery Capacity of LLMs to Their Training Data
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) show growing promise for scientific discovery, yet basic questions remain about what enables reliable discovery. How can we trace the scientific discovery capacity of LLMs to their training data? We study this question as one of missing probability mass and develop a theoretical account in which monofacts-the facts observed once during training-set the discovery capacity. In materials science and regulatory genomics, we directly manipulate monofact rates in training sets and find that more monofacts consistently yield more discoveries across two open-weight model families, sampling strategies, and reasoning budgets. Further experiments show the relationship cannot be explained by training-set diversity alone and can transfer across scientific domains when paired with in-domain data. Together, our results identify monofact rate in training data as a key factor governing discoveries in language models.

title: Strategist: Evolving Reasoning with Agents
abstract: A model is only half of an AI agent system. The other half is the inference strategy: the reasoning procedure that turns model calls into a response. Today that second half is written by hand, and the experience of building one strategy never carries to the next. We introduce Strategist, a meta-agent that evolves inference strategies across tasks. Each strategy is written as a blueprint,executable code that other strategies can reuse, and together the blueprints form a library. Given a task and a small development set, Strategist retrieves related blueprints, writes candidate strategies, tests them on real samples, and revises them from the results. Every candidate then enters the library, so later tasks build on earlier discoveries. On 30 benchmarks, Strategist beats the strongest baseline on 24 and matches its average accuracy (74.7% vs.74.0%) at 39% lower inference cost. Its strategies also transfer to unseen tasks and other models without further search. The part of an AI system that is not improved on its own now does.

title: Inferring geometric structure from eigenfunction triple products
abstract: This article presents two converses to well-known observations regarding products of eigenfunctions of the Laplacian on a closed Riemannian manifold $(M,g)$. First, if $(M,g)$ is real-analytic, the coefficients in the eigenfunction expansion of a product of eigenfunctions decay exponentially. We show that such exponential decay in fact implies that $g$ is real-analytic. Second, it is clear that if $(M,g)$ is flat, there exists an eigenbasis for which the product of any two of its elements lies in the span of at most $N = N(M,g)$ elements. We prove that any manifold with such an eigenbasis must be flat. We then construct metrics on $\mathbb{S}^7$ that share an eigenbasis with the standard metric yet are not locally homogeneous, from which we deduce that homogeneity cannot be characterized solely in terms of the multiplicative structure of eigenfunctions.

title: Adjacency Labeling Schemes of Size $\log n+O(\log\log^* n)$ for Graphs of Bounded Treewidth
abstract: Gavoille and Labourel (ESA 2007) gave an adjacency labeling scheme of size $\log n+O(k\log\log n)$ for graphs of treewidth at most $k$, and asked whether $\log n+O(k)$ bits suffice. We give a labeling scheme of size $\log n+O(\log\log^* n)$ for every fixed $k$, the first improvement of the second-order term for any $k\ge 2$. Equivalently, there is an induced-universal graph with $n(\log^* n)^{O_k(1)}$ vertices for this family. We work with laminar families of intervals, in which a vertex finds each earlier neighbor as the owner of an interval of a given nesting depth around it. As long as every subtree occupies consecutive positions, the nesting depth must be logarithmic, and $\log\log n$ bits per neighbor follow. We give up contiguity. Heavy subtrees are moved out, which brings the depth down to $O(\log^* n)$; the intervals broken by the moves are repaired with $2^{O(k^3)}$ additional intervals per vertex; and the bits needed to find these intervals are paid for by the moved subtrees.

title: Multi-Trajectory Parallel-in-Iteration Optimization
abstract: Previously, we developed a ``parallel-in-iteration'' optimization framework that uses multigrid reduction-in-time (MGRIT) to parallelize slowly converging optimization methods, such as gradient descent. Unlike time-dependent evolution problems, optimization requires only a final point with a sufficiently small gradient, rather than an accurate approximation of the entire trajectory of iterates. This motivates a different use of MGRIT: instead of repeatedly improving the approximation of a single long trajectory, we introduce restarted MGRIT (R-MGRIT), which performs one MGRIT iteration on a trajectory, takes the approximate final point as a new initial guess, and repeats the process on a new trajectory. Each restart thus defines a new all-at-once system, allowing progress toward the solution without accurately approximating the preceding trajectory. Moreover, we find that these trajectories can be shortened without increasing the number of restarts needed for convergence. We provide theoretical results comparing MGRIT and R-MGRIT for linear problems and demonstrate the convergence behavior of the shortened trajectories numerically for both linear and nonlinear problems. Shortening the trajectories increases the estimated parallel speedup while reducing the number of processors required.

title: D&A: Decoupling Description and Assessment Enables VLMs as Zero-Shot Robotic Reward Models
abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) hold promise for zero-shot video task-progress estimation in robot learning, yet existing frameworks frequently suffer from confirmation bias, hallucinating progress in failed executions due to implicit success assumptions or relative temporal ranking designs. Naive prompting of frontier models collapses into a binary success detector that fails to capture nuanced, non-linear progress and failures. While post-training approaches can mitigate this through explicit training, they demand expensive real-world robotics data and require computationally intensive post-training for every individual base model. To resolve these limitations, we introduce D&A (Describe & Assess): our approach decouples progress estimation into an objective, task-grounded textual description of scene dynamics followed by an assessment phase using explicit rubrics. By compelling the VLM to synthesize an explicit, text-based definition of absolute success before scoring, the framework anchors evaluations to an external, global criterion rather than the video's internal timeline. Empirical results demonstrate that our method calibrates zero-shot estimates and mitigates confirmation bias, providing fine-grained, partial progress metrics that accurately penalize failed executions while correctly interpolating successful runs. Being purely prompt-based, D&A generalizes across tasks, embodiments, and benchmarks---matching or surpassing post-trained reward models---and its reward estimates enable efficient downstream reinforcement learning.

title: Thought-deciphering via hierarchical EEG-to-text alignment
abstract: Non-invasive brain-to-text interfaces offer alternative communication pathways for people with communication disabilities. However, sentence-level decoding from electroencephalography (EEG) remains challenging. We propose a hierarchical EEG-text alignment framework that retrieves sentences by progressively decoding coarse-grained semantic information and fine-grained sentence representations. We hypothesize that broader semantic context can be more reliably captured from EEG than individual sentences. Accordingly, EEG representations are first aligned with semantic classes, followed by sentence retrieval within the predicted class. Among over 2,000 unique text samples, our approach achieves average top-5 and top-10 retrieval accuracies of 62.6\% $\pm$ 1.0\% and 83.5\% $\pm$ 1.0\%, respectively, compared with 50.3\% $\pm$ 2.3\% and 68.3\% $\pm$ 2.0\% for direct EEG-sentence alignment. Qualitative analysis further reveals that decoding performance depends strongly on textual context. These findings demonstrate the potential of hierarchical semantic alignment for improving sentence-level EEG-to-text decoding.

title: Lee-Yang theorems for $q$-deformed oscillators and doubly-scaled SYK
abstract: We show that the vacuum partition function of the $q$-deformed oscillator \[ L_q(z):= \langle0|e^{zT_q}|0\rangle, \qquad T_q := \mathsf{a}_q + \mathsf{a}_q^* \] satisfies the Lee-Yang property, i.e., all zeros of $L_q$ lie on the imaginary line for all $q\in[-1, 1)$, proving the conjectures of Okuyama'23. Using the connection between $q$-deformed oscillators and the Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev (SYK) Hamiltonian in the doubly-scaled regime, we show that the annealed SYK partition function satisfies the Lee-Yang property in the thermodynamic limit, that is, all of its Fisher zeros are on the imaginary axis. As a result, we show that the quenched SYK partition function admits a zero-free strip of constant width with high probability, rigorously complementing the large$-k$ replica calculations of Zlokapa and Kiani'26. We show the imaginary-rootedness of $L_q$ by expressing $φ_q(z):= L_q(\mathbf{i} z)$ as a locally uniform limit of ``$q$-deformed'' matching polynomials and then showing that those $q$-deformed polynomials are real-rooted. This establishes that $φ_q$ is real-rooted, and in fact belongs to the \emph{Laguerre-Pólya} class. The real-rootedness of the $q$-deformed polynomials yields novel log-concavity relations on the \emph{$q$-deformed matching moments} \[M_\ell(q):= \sum_{π\in\mathcal{P}_2(2\ell)}q^{\operatorname{cr}(π)}.\] We show the real-rootedness of the $q$-deformed polynomials by using the Touchard--Riordan formula to derive a partial differential equation relating their $q$-derivatives to their $z$-derivatives, and then analyzing the resulting motion of their roots.

title: FADE: Factored Ability--Difficulty Filtering for Online RLVR Scheduling
abstract: Group-based reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) learns only from prompts whose sampled completions disagree: all-pass and all-fail groups produce zero relative advantage and burn generation budget without moving the policy. Adaptive schedulers try to steer rollouts toward informative prompts, yet they rely on per-prompt pass-rate trackers that entangle two quantities evolving at very different speeds---the policy's shifting competence across reasoning skills and each prompt's intrinsic difficulty. When a single exponential average or Beta counter tracks both at once, short memory scrambles the relative ordering of prompts whereas long memory reports stale pass rates. We introduce FADE (Factored Ability--Difficulty Estimation), a bilinear state-space filter that separates the two timescales. FADE represents each prompt's success logit as the inner product of a whitened $K$-dimensional skill loading with a fast-drifting policy ability vector, minus a slow-shrinking scalar item intercept. Using Pólya--Gamma augmentation, each minibatch of binary rollout outcomes updates the $K$-dimensional ability posterior in closed form via a rank-$K$ Woodbury step, instantly transferring competence shifts to all unobserved prompts that share those skills while leaving item intercepts stable. From the resulting posterior mean and variance we derive a closed-form utility for the probability of drawing a non-degenerate rollout group. Across five reasoning benchmarks, two base models, and four scheduling paradigms under a matched rollout budget, FADE consistently improves downstream accuracy and calibration while adding less than $0.6$\,ms per step.

title: Isekai3D SDG: A Platform for Diverse Synthetic Gameplay Visual Data
abstract: We present Isekai3D Synthetic Data Generation (SDG), a platform for simulating and capturing synthetic 3D gameplay for research in vision and world models, neural graphics, gameplay agents, and other applications. The platform combines reusable environment and character assets with Unreal Engine plugins in a two-stage workflow. First, world simulation generates gameplay while recording the world state, character movements, actions, and camera tracks needed for replay. Second, the recorded simulation is replayed to capture selected outputs, such as rendered video, images, and depth maps, at a specified resolution and frame rate under selected rendering and camera configurations. Separating simulation from capture allows the same recorded gameplay to produce multiple output variants without repeating the original simulation. Visual outputs are accompanied by frame-aligned camera, character, and action metadata. The platform uploads generated data directly in a training-friendly format, reducing intermediate storage, preparation time, and manual processing. This report describes the design of our overall system, including the platform's assets, plugins, and their functionality, explaining how they work together to generate diverse synthetic gameplay data.

title: Not All Reasoning Generalizes: A Case Study on Learning Generalizable Reasoning Strategies in RLVR
abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) can enable generalizable improvement for large language model (LLM) reasoning. This paper studies how to incentivize such generalization via reasoning strategies. We study this question with a controllable equation-solving framework: finding multiple inputs x for equations f(x)=y, where f is a non-bijective string function. This setting makes reasoning strategies observable while supporting a clear definition of easy-to-hard out-of-distribution (OOD) shifts, e.g., more solutions, longer y, etc. We uncover a subtle RLVR failure: it teaches the model to solve in-distribution tasks with high accuracy and structured step-by-step derivation, yet under OOD shifts, the same model abandons derivation and collapses to ineffective brute-force enumeration, causing sharp accuracy drops. This observation reveals the deeper challenges of RLVR generalization as it is neither incapable base model nor reward hacking, since the model succeeds in-distribution with the correct reasoning strategy. The key to mitigating this failure is an indirect intervention that surprisingly helps: co-training with bijective inversion tasks. Although these bijective tasks are actually not uniformly harder and even further from the non-bijective OOD evaluation, they make derivation more certain and substantially restore the correct strategy and accuracy under OOD shifts. This effect further motivates our theoretical analysis: outcome-only RLVR can shape reasoning processes through implicitly crediting the effective reasoning strategies more, even without process supervision. To conclude, our analysis framework and findings systematically reveal the crucial role and incentivization of reasoning strategies in RLVR generalization under OOD shifts. Code is available at https://github.com/ziqipang/rl_meta_thinking.

title: Active-subspace learning reveals dominant parameter directions in nuclear observables
abstract: Nuclear observables computed using ab initio methods can depend on many low-energy constants (LECs) of the underlying chiral effective field theory interactions, while being sensitive to only a few LEC combinations. We use active-subspace learning to identify these dominant parameter directions directly from many-body calculations. For ground-state energies and charge radii of oxygen isotopes, we find that more than 99% of the gradient-based variation is concentrated along a single direction for each observable in the 17-dimensional LEC space. Comparing these directions across nuclei and observables quantifies similarities in their LEC dependence. The same analysis yields derivative-based global sensitivities without requiring a global emulator. Active-subspace directions can also serve as an efficient representation for emulation, greatly improving Gaussian-process emulators especially for broad LEC variations. We demonstrate this for Hartree-Fock calculations of $^{48}\mathrm{Ca}$, where the emulator error is improved with active-subspace learning by more than two orders of magnitude.

title: PDFP: GPU-Accelerated Feasibility Pump via PDHG
abstract: The feasibility pump (FP) is among the most widely used primal heuristics for mixed-integer linear programming. It alternates between rounding an LP-feasible point and projecting the rounded point back onto the feasible region of the LP relaxation. Recent pump-based heuristics compute the projection with the primal--dual hybrid gradient method (PDHG), which is scalable on modern GPUs. They pose it as a linear program, which needs auxiliary variables and constraints for general integers. Once the projection runs on the GPU, the constraint-propagation rounding (CPR) of FP~2.0 takes a large share of each iteration. For the projection, we propose PDFP, a custom first-order method that solves the pump's projection problem directly, without auxiliary primal variables or constraints. We prove that it keeps the accelerated linear rate of restarted Halpern PDHG. For the rounding, we propose a new procedure that is more efficient than CPR and, under certain assumptions, still returns a CPR rounding. It also chooses rounded values by constraint violation, which can produce feasible roundings where nearest rounding cannot. Finally, our pump runs two independent trajectories concurrently on one GPU through CPU--GPU synchronization. This exploits the variance in trajectory length and lets the pump terminate sooner on average. Computational experiments on MIPLIB~2017 instances show early, promising results: these contributions speed up the discovery of the first incumbent solution. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/MIT-Lu-Lab/PDFP.

title: Mutual information to all orders from modular flow: a replica-free approach
abstract: We derive an all-orders long-distance expansion of vacuum mutual information between two disjoint balls in generic $d$-dimensional CFTs. The derivation uses a novel radial sewing expansion of the joint vacuum density matrix, together with a modular response formula for relative entropy and the geometric modular flow of a single ball, without analytic continuation in replica number. The expansion coefficients are modular integrals of modular-flowed vacuum correlators. Our formula provides a systematic treatment of arbitrary multi-point sectors, and recovers known results on two-point sector derived from replica methods. The full two-point sector resums into a modular integral of the thermal partition function on $S^{d-1}$, with an effective temperature depending on ball configuration and modular time. We compute the expansion explicitly in CFTs. In two-dimensional Ising CFT, using analytic reductions and multidimensional numerical integration, we obtain the first ten radial orders in the long-distance expansion, which involve sphere correlators with up to twenty spin insertions. The truncated expansion agrees well with lattice data at finite separation, and approximately satisfies crossing symmetry. Analytic calculations also reproduce known expansion coefficients for 2d free compact boson at self-dual radius and its current sector, as well as for free scalars in higher dimensions.

title: Supporting Viewpoint Coordination for Compliance by Design with an Artifact Model for Regulatory Requirements Engineering
abstract: Regulatory compliance has become an essential software requirement Legal demands for compliance by design CbD call for requirements engineering RE approaches that derive requirements and support compliance implementation in subsequent software engineering SE processes such as software design The complexity of the legal knowledge demanded in regulatory RE makes it important to involve legal experts and ensure the relevant specifications are valid and usable for them Regulatory requirements must support compliance implementation in software design However there is a lack of approaches bridging legal and SE viewpoints and interaction challenges between the two persist To address engineeringlegal coordination in specification of regulatory requirements we propose the Artifact Model for Regulatory Requirements Engineering AM4RRE operationalized through templates AM4RRE was positively evaluated by most of the 37 practitioners for coordination in regulatory RE and for supporting requirements quality Results from a quasiexperiment with 34 of them in 10 groups indicated that templateguided coordination was associated with on average shorter total specification time when executed first and higher requirements quality in most groups in which it varied Existing RE research and practice provide little attention and support for viewpoint coordination in regulatory RE for CbD Artifactoriented approaches such as AM4RRE have the potential to guide coordination in RE for better RE results and contribute to concretizing the role and contribution of RE to CbD

title: Tracing source imprints on the gravitational direct wave
abstract: The direct wave component of black hole (BH) ringdown, revealed through quasinormal-mode filters, carries a non-quasinormal-mode imprint of the plunging perturber's dynamics. However, the connection between the source trajectory and the observed direct wave remains incompletely understood. We first show that the full waveform filtered by the frequency-dependent black hole response gives a substantially more localized kernel than the standard rational filter approach. We then show that analytically continuing the Teukolsky source variables to complex coordinates allows for a semianalytic direct wave which closely reproduces numerical integration throughout the entire plunge. Our generalized steepest-descent method clarifies how coherent emission shapes the imprint of source dynamics on the observed direct wave beyond the light-cone picture.

title: Pretraining Data Scale Reverses the Muon-AdamW Fine-Tuning Gap
abstract: Muon has recently emerged as a promising optimizer for pretraining large language models, offering a speedup over AdamW in minimizing pretraining loss. However, it remains unclear whether Muon's advantage persists after fine-tuning. In this paper, we study the downstream behavior of Muon and AdamW and uncover a surprising trend: beyond a sufficiently large pretraining data budget, AdamW outperforms Muon after fine-tuning. Moreover, as model size increases, AdamW overtakes Muon at progressively smaller pretraining token-parameter ratios. To explain this reversal, we view fine-tuning as a perturbation of the outputs and introduce the margin-to-spread ratio, which measures how far the correct logit lies above the wrong ones relative to how widely the wrong logits are spread. In language models, Muon has the larger margin-to-spread ratio at small data budgets and AdamW at large ones, mirroring the fine-tuning trend. In a linear associative memory, we prove that after one update the margin-to-spread ratio of gradient descent gains on that of Muon as the data budget grows, and simulations show that this trend persists after extended training.

title: WebHarbor: Docking Real Websites for Evolving GUI Agent Environments
abstract: GUI web agents require realistic and interactive environments that remain stable during both evaluation and training. Live website evaluation suffers from changing content, access restrictions, and limited coverage of authenticated workflows, while existing synthetic environments for training often lack functional depth and visual fidelity. We propose WebHarbor, a suite of 153 executable and dockerized website environments that faithfully reconstruct the visual interfaces, content, and functional workflows of real-world web services under deterministic control. We build WebHarbor through task-driven human-agent collaboration, where environments evolve as new tasks expand their functional scope, coding agents implement the required changes, and human contributors audit visual fidelity, functional correctness, and task validity. The resulting suite comprises 3,518 tasks spanning multi-step and post-authentication workflows, where existing works often fail to cover. Beyond reliable evaluation, WebHarbor provides high-fidelity synthetic web environments for cost-efficient reinforcement learning (RL). We demonstrate that a Qwen 4B-level GUI agent trained with RL in WebHarbor generalizes to unseen tasks and performs competitively with leading open-source GUI web agents across four benchmarks. The code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/aiming-lab/WebHarbor.

title: Ultrafast X-ray-induced dephasing of valence electrons
abstract: Diffract-before-destroy schemes for atomic-scale electron mapping assume that ultrashort X-ray pulses outrun radiation damage. Although atomic cores move over tens of femtoseconds, outer electrons respond much faster, compromising their locations. We test this limit in elemental silicon using broadband, energy-chirped X-ray pulses to encode time with few-femtosecond resolution. Comparing valence-sensitive structurally forbidden reflections with simultaneously measured core-dominated Bragg peaks reveals valence-bond dephasing on sub-20-fs timescales even at pulse energies where direct ionization effects are negligible. Our findings demonstrate that crystallography where outer electrons contribute substantially to Bragg peaks requires pulses shorter than today's standard $\sim50\,fs$ standard. They also establish a path to disentangle valence electron and lattice contributions to order and dynamics with hard X-rays, enabling studies across molecular biology, quantum matter and devices.

title: Get Permanent Results Faster by Counting Stars
abstract: We show that $n \times n$ permanents can be computed with $O^*{(2-\varepsilon)^n}$ arithmetic operations over every commutative ring, for $\varepsilon = 10^{-40}$. This solves a problem stated in Knuth's The Art of Computer Programming. Our algorithm implements the classical Binet--Minc identity with dynamic programming and careful bookkeeping. It also gives algebraic branching programs of size $O^*{(2-\varepsilon)^n}$.

title: Mercury (Hg): a relativistic $N$-body simulation for Horndeski gravity
abstract: We present Mercury, a relativistic $N$-body code for cosmological simulations in the $α$-basis formulation of Horndeski gravity. Mercury extends a particle-mesh scheme by incorporating the dynamics of the additional scalar degree of freedom and the corresponding modified Einstein equations, expressed in terms of the time-dependent functions $α_{\rm K}, α_{\rm B}, α_{\rm M}, α_{\rm T}$ and the effective Planck mass $M_*^2$. This generalises our previous implementation of Horndeski subclass models, namely $k$-essence and kinetic gravity braiding (KGB), to the general linear Horndeski $α$-basis. The code evolves the additional scalar degree of freedom and its effective stress--energy tensor alongside the nonlinear matter and metric fields, so that nonlinear structure formation sources the scalar-field evolution and feeds back on the gravitational potentials. Through its interface with hi_class, Mercury supports both phenomenological $α$-function parametrisations and covariant Horndeski theories; we demonstrate the latter using nKGB, the Cubic Galileon, and Brans--Dicke models. We validate the implementation against hi_class in the linear regime and recover the expected nonlinear $k$-essence and KGB limits. For the luminal Horndeski models considered here, we show how a running effective Planck mass generates gravitational slip through the scalar anisotropic stress and modifies the friction terms governing the vector and tensor metric perturbations. The evolution of $M_*^2$ also modifies the normalisation and scale dependence of the effective dark-energy density contrast, leaving a corresponding imprint on its power spectrum. The present framework provides an intermediate step towards nonlinear Horndeski simulations, in which nonlinear scalar self-interactions and screening effects can be incorporated consistently within the same relativistic framework.

title: A Triangular Log-Det PDHG for Semidefinite Programming: Complementarity Selection and Global Linear Convergence
abstract: Semidefinite programming (SDP) is an important class of convex optimization problems with wide applications in practice. In this paper, we study a solution-selection question for first-order methods for solving SDPs: Can a first-order method provably select a strictly complementary solution when one exists, and a maximally complementary solution otherwise? We propose Triangular Log-Det PDHG (TriLog-PDHG), a primal-dual hybrid gradient method equipped with a triangular log-determinant Bregman kernel. We show that TriLog-PDHG converges to a KKT point for any fixed positive shift and to a maximally complementary solution for every sufficiently small positive shift. When a strictly complementary solution exists, the unshifted method provably selects a strictly complementary KKT point and enjoys a global linear convergence rate. Under the same condition, we further develop an averaged and adaptively restarted variant that accelerates convergence. Numerical experiments on classical examples and SDPLIB instances illustrate the complementarity-selection and convergence properties predicted by the theory.

title: Quantum channel tomography: optimal bounds in the near-boundary regime
abstract: Quantum channel tomography (also known as quantum process tomography) is a fundamental task in quantum information and quantum computing, aiming to learn the full description of an unknown quantum channel from black-box queries. For channels with input dimension $d_1$, output dimension $d_2$, and Kraus rank at most $r$, [CGO+26] identifies the dilation rate $τ=rd_2/d_1\geq 1$ as a key parameter governing a Heisenberg-to-classical transition in query complexity. While the optimal bounds in the boundary regime ($τ=1$) and the away-from-boundary regime ($τ\geq 1+Ω(1)$) are now known, the precise behavior in the near-boundary regime ($1<τ<1+o(1)$) has remained unresolved. In this paper, we close this gap, thereby fully settling the query complexity of quantum channel tomography. Specifically, we show that the query complexity is - $Ω(rd_1d_2/\varepsilon^2)$ for diamond norm error $\varepsilon$, matching the upper bound by [MB26, CGO+26], - $Θ(d_1^2/\varepsilon+\min\{(τ-1)d_1^2,(τ-1)^2d_1^2d_2^2\}/\varepsilon^2)$ for Choi trace norm error $\varepsilon$. Our results reveal two qualitatively different forms of the Heisenberg-to-classical transition. For diamond norm tomography, the Heisenberg scaling disappears suddenly as soon as $τ$ leaves the boundary regime. In contrast, Choi trace norm tomography exhibits a gradual transition from Heisenberg to classical scaling as $τ$ moves from the boundary regime to the away-from-boundary regime.

title: Construction of the 2D non-Abelian Yang-Mills-Higgs measure via stochastic quantisation
abstract: We provide the first mathematical construction of the non-Abelian Yang-Mills-Higgs measure on a two-dimensional torus by implementing Parisi and Wu's ``stochastic quantisation'' procedure. We use a specific gauge covariant (but non-Markovian) approximation to the previously constructed associated Langevin dynamics and develop a covariant paracontrolled calculus for it. This allows us to obtain short-time control over times that are much longer than what the cubic nonlinearity naïvely suggests. When combined with the decay properties of the Yang-Mills-Higgs action under the deterministic gradient flow, as well as a quantitative measure of how the noise pushes the dynamic away from Yang-Mills connections, this is good enough to yield uniform-in-time bounds. We finally show that there exists a renormalisation under which our gauge covariant approximation converges to the Langevin dynamics (modulo gauge transformation) and that the latter is topologically irreducible and strong Feller. It therefore admits a unique invariant measure, providing the sought-after construction. Our construction is non-perturbative and works in particular for any fixed values of the coupling constants.

title: From Natural Language to Exact Cover: A Neuro-Symbolic Approach to Zebra Puzzles
abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) generation has substantially improved the performance of Large Language Models (LLMs) on complex reasoning tasks, including code generation, data analysis, and exam-style question answering. Despite these advances, purely neural LLMs continue to struggle with elementary logical reasoning problems and lack the determinism, soundness, and reliability characteristic of symbolic reasoning systems. Conversely, classical symbolic methods such as SAT solving and exact cover guarantee correctness and completeness, but require problems to be expressed in highly specialized formal encodings, limiting their applicability to natural language inputs. In this work, we present a synergistic neuro-symbolic framework that bridges this gap by combining neural semantic parsing with deterministic exact cover reasoning. Given a Zebra-style logic puzzle in natural language, an LLM translates entities and constraints into structured tool calls that construct an exact cover instance. A symbolic solver then computes the solution and provides feedback to iteratively refine invalid, under- or overconstrained encodings, exploiting the uniqueness property of Zebra puzzles. We conduct a comprehensive empirical evaluation across multiple parameter scales, post-training paradigms, and LLM families. The results demonstrate that our hybrid approach consistently outperforms strong plain neural baselines, including CoT prompting, as well as recent neuro-symbolic methods.

title: A hyperbolic nonlinear Schrödinger system in multiple spatial dimensions: structure, convergence, and numerical discretization
abstract: We propose and study a first-order hyperbolic approximation of the nonlinear Schrödinger (NLS) equation in $N$ spatial dimensions. This is an extension of the recently-proposed 1D hyperbolic NLS model. We study the structure and properties of the hyperbolic approximation and their relation to those of the original system. We show that the N-dimensional hyperbolic system exactly conserves analogs of the mass, energy, and momentum, and that it possesses stationary solutions that are closely related to those of NLS. The hyperbolic system is also shown to admit plane-wave solutions that share some stability properties with those of NLS, and that relaxation can shrink the focusing low-wavenumber modulational instability band as well as introduce a high-wavenumber instability band not present in NLS. We also show that solutions of the hyperbolic system converge to solutions of NLS in the relaxation limit. We present an adaptive-mesh finite volume discretization of the hyperbolic system and demonstrate its effectiveness in handling simulations, including those with geometric obstacles or non-periodic boundary conditions. The effectiveness of the numerical scheme is demonstrated through examples including a Bose-Einstein condensate, line soliton instability, and superflow past a cylinder.

title: The Neptunian ridge through the lens of TESS
abstract: The Neptunian desert and savanna are separated by a ridge, an overdensity at orbital periods of approximately 3-6 d identified with Kepler. Like the hot Jupiter pileup at larger radii, this feature has been linked to the accumulation of successful outcomes of high-eccentricity migration (HEM). We revisit the ridge independently using TESS occurrence posteriors for FGK main-sequence stars. We quantify its excess over adjacent regions and compare six occurrence profiles using leave-one-out cross-validation and Bayesian evidence. For planets with radii of approximately 5-8 $R_\oplus$, the ridge has twice the occurrence density of the denser neighbouring region ($J=2.05^{+0.52}_{-0.44}$), with 99.9% posterior support (one-sided Gaussian equivalent of $3.1σ$). This contrast agrees with the discovery study and earlier Kepler occurrence measurements. Both predictive performance and Bayesian evidence strongly favour profiles peaking within the ridge over a single power law. The lognormal is preferred, suggesting a narrower inner wing and a more extended outer wing, although evidence for asymmetry remains weak. In the same period window, the analysis recovers the hot Jupiter pileup (approximately 10-16 $R_\oplus$) with a contrast consistent with that of the ridge and excludes an analogous excess among sub-Neptunes (approximately 2-4 $R_\oplus$) with $3.4σ$ posterior support. TESS thus provides an independent detection of the Neptunian ridge. Its possible asymmetry would be compatible with HEM, in which tidal disruption could produce a sharper inner edge and variations in circularisation efficiency a more gradual outer decline. Establishing whether the ridge has this shape requires more precise occurrence measurements, with PLATO's expected planet yield offering a promising opportunity to help unveil its morphology.

title: Single-visit screening for intracochlear tissue growth validated against multi-visit electrical measurement changes
abstract: Purpose: Tissue growth (TG) around cochlear implant electrodes raises impedance but is not reliably visible on CT scans. Routinely recorded stimulus current-induced non-stimulating electrode voltages (SCINSEVs) carry this information, but a single recording has no patient-specific reference. We present an algorithm for detecting signs of significant TG from a single SCINSEV measurement. Methods: TG is assumed to concentrate basally near the electrode insertion site, leaving the apical region mostly unaffected. A patient-specific forward model built from CT is fitted to the apical measurements and predicts the basal ones. The misfit score, T, measures each basal contact's signed relative misfit against the apical misfit, accounting for apical fit quality and measurement noise. An ear is flagged when two adjacent basal contacts cross a predetermined threshold. We compare T with T-delta, a model-free reference, tracking basal relative to apical SCINSEV change since the intra-operative recording, persisting over the last two visits. Results: T had a false-positive rate of 3% on growth-free ears. It agreed with T-delta in 81% of 68 ears (sensitivity 71%; specificity 86%; p = 6e-6). Over 200 patient-level two-fold splits, median held-out agreement was 78% at a false-positive rate of 5.1%. Conclusion: An apically fitted patient-specific model predicts basal SCINSEVs well enough to flag signs of significant TG at a single visit, without an intra-operative baseline. Detections largely agree with persistent multi-visit basal-versus-apical change, a surrogate ground truth for significant TG.

title: Episodic Star Formation - II. The Origin of the Fundamental Metallicity Relation
abstract: The Fundamental Metallicity Relation (FMR) extends the mass-metallicity relation (MZR) by including star formation rate (SFR) as a third parameter. At fixed stellar mass, galaxies with higher SFRs tend to have lower gas-phase metallicities. We investigate the physical origin of the FMR in the context of episodic star formation (Gui et al. 2026, paper I of this series) by tracing the evolution histories of 8,979 central star-forming galaxies selected at $z=0$ in TNG100 back to $z=1$. We find that the overall MZR scatter at $z=0$ ($\sim0.11$ dex) comprises both long-lived differences among galaxies ($\sim0.09$ dex) and temporal fluctuations within individual galaxies ($\sim 0.07$ dex). The galaxy-to-galaxy component shows an anticorrelation between SFR and gas-phase metallicity, as shown by the observed FMR. As for the consequence from temporal fluctuation, we track individual histories and stack the upward and downward SFR phases of a refined sample. Time-shift analysis and stacked histories show a well-behaved sequence in which the cold non-star-forming gas reservoir increases (decreases) first, followed by a decrease (increase) in gas-phase metallicity and then a rise (decline) in SFR. This ordering is consistent with a physical scenario where metal-poor gas first replenishes the cold reservoir and dilutes the gas before SFR rises to the peak, followed by feedback-driven gas heating/removal, resulting in a shift in metallicity from dilution to enrichment as SFR decreases towards the valley. This naturally explains the anticorrelation between the SFR and gas-phase metallicities as indicated by the observed FMR.

title: EgoActionBench: Benchmarking Dense Action Captioning for Egocentric Human Videos
abstract: Learning from human data offers a scalable path toward embodied intelligence, yet it requires models to accurately understand fine-grained human actions from egocentric observations. However, existing benchmarks remain limited in action atomicity, temporal precision, and hand-action association. We introduce EgoActionBench, a benchmark that represents continuous human manipulation as temporally localized atomic actions associated with the left hand, right hand, or both hands. EgoActionBench contains 1,407 episodes with 41,132 human-refined action annotations. To evaluate such dense predictions, we propose an evaluation protocol that retrieves temporally eligible candidates, selects a prediction by content agreement, and scores semantic fidelity and temporal overlap alongside action precision and recall, jointly capturing what happens, when it happens, and which hand performs it. We benchmark 20 baseline models and systems on EgoActionBench and further adapt two backbones, Qwen3-VL-4B and LLaVA-OneVision-2-8B, through supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning on automatically annotated training episodes. EgoAction improves EgoActionScore by 15.9 and 23.2 points on the two backbones, and both adapted models outperform all open-source baselines. Our experiments reveal substantial limitations of current models in action atomicity, temporal precision, and hand-action association, highlighting the gap between general video understanding and the action understanding required for embodied intelligence.

title: Pixel-UMI: Learning Environment-Aware Whole-Body Manipulation from Sensorized Human Demonstrations
abstract: Sensorized human demonstrations offer scalable data for mobile manipulation, but embodiment differences complicate policy learning. We present Pixel-UMI, a pipeline for learning environment-aware whole-body policies from human data. We first introduce Environment-Aware Retargeting (EAR), which combines reconstructed scene geometry with demonstrated head and gripper trajectories to determine robot posture and generate collision-aware joint and base targets. Delay-calibrated action assignment converts these trajectories into actions. However, kinematic differences can leave residual pose errors, creating viewpoint mismatches between human demonstrations and robot observations. We therefore introduce Retargeting-Error-Aware Masking (REAM), which uses these errors during training to reduce reliance on mismatched views at deployment. Finally, because estimated actions cannot fully capture contact-rich interactions, we collect on-policy human corrections through DAgger to improve performance. We evaluate Pixel-UMI on five challenging tasks spanning articulated-object manipulation, deformable-object handling, constrained-space reaching, whole-body collision avoidance, and contact-rich bimanual coordination, achieving 87.0% average task progress. Video results are available at https://pixel-robot.com/pixel-umi

title: Pixel: A Co-Designed Full-Stack Robot System for Learning General-Purpose Mobile Manipulation
abstract: General-purpose mobile manipulation requires a combination of capable robot hardware, scalable demonstration collection, expressive whole-body control, and effective policy learning. Yet these components are often developed independently, creating mismatches that limit the capabilities of the complete system. We present Pixel, a co-designed full-stack system for learning general-purpose mobile manipulation. Pixel combines a low-cost wheeled humanoid with human-aligned kinematics and compliant grippers, multiple teleoperation and robot-free human data-collection interfaces, a unified whole-body controller, and a common policy learning pipeline across human and robot demonstrations. A hierarchical learning stack further enables language-conditioned visuomotor control and long-horizon task execution. We evaluate the system across hardware, data collection, and policy learning, and demonstrate mobile-manipulation behaviors requiring dexterity, active perception, navigation, and whole-body coordination. We hope that Pixel provides an integrated and extensible foundation for studying how robot hardware, data, control, and learning can be designed together for robot learning. More results at https://pixel-robot.com/pixel

title: GHOST Driver
abstract: AI inference workloads running on GPU clusters exhibit a well-documented utilization paradox: monitoring tools such as nvidia-smi regularly report GPU utilization figures above 80%, yet effective compute throughput is substantially lower. A significant fraction of reported utilization time is consumed by fence waits, driver submission overhead, DMA scheduling latency, and interrupt coalescing delays, none of which is visible to userspace profiling tools. These hidden latency components are embedded deep inside the Linux kernel GPU driver stack, primarily within the Direct Rendering Manager (DRM) subsystem, GEM buffer object lifecycle, and dma_fence synchronization infrastructure. Existing vendor profiling tools like CUPTI operate at the CUDA userspace boundary and provide no visibility into kernel-side driver paths. We present GHOST-Driver (GPU Host-Side Observability and Tracing for Drivers), a non-intrusive eBPF-based framework that attaches to stable DRM kernel tracepoints and select kprobes to expose the full latency decomposition of the GPU driver submission path with sub-microsecond resolution and CPU overhead below 2% in production. GHOST-Driver tracks six key submission stages (ioctl entry, GEM BO validation, dma_fence dependency resolution, command ring emission, DMA engine scheduling, and interrupt fence signaling) and correlates them with per-tenant vGPU context IDs for multi-tenant attribution in SR-IOV and MIG environments, exporting trace metrics to Prometheus and OpenTelemetry.

title: Alignment Faking Depends on the Value, Not Just the Model
abstract: Language models can follow a directive when they believe they are monitored and abandon it when they believe they are not, a pattern termed Alignment Faking. Prior work establishes this for harmful-content objectives and a handful of moral-foundations values, leaving open how it distributes across a wider value space. We argue it is value-dependent: whether compliance survives a change in perceived oversight is a property of the model--value pairing, not of the model alone. Our framework profiles Alignment Faking per value, scoring each model-value pair under three conditions: bare (no system prompt), unmonitored, and monitored. On 32 ValueBench dimensions across ten open- and closed-weight models (8B-~675B), compliance gaps span 0.05-0.50, with a distilled 70B above a ~675B model. We observe that majority of the structural variance depends on which model was asked about which value and not on the model or value alone. A six-category taxonomy over reasoning traces tracks the behavioural shift: training-signal reasoning dominates under monitoring and value-conflict reasoning dominates when unmonitored. We package per-model results as value cards, extending model cards with behavioral disposition. Code and data are available at https://github.com/respailab/VALET.

title: CARD: A Proof-Carrying Certificate-to-Action Interface for Relative-Measurement Graphs
abstract: Geometric certificates make mathematical claims about specified estimator objects, while robotic action requires a physical transform, a service decision, and timely proof support. We present CARD, a proof-carrying interface that keeps these objects distinct and records how they combine. Its lifted-fiber formulation separates semantic motion from witness repair and characterizes when projected and proof-carrying costs coincide. Its actionability result gives an exact useful-service law: uniform sampling without replacement produces a hypergeometric yield, while sampling from the eligible population gives one useful service per request under the observed live-confirmation condition. The primary study contains 404 Full16 cases from 20 sorties of an AA15-X500 airborne survey system. All 404 checker-confirmed optimizer points are reference-discrepant, with median rotation and translation discrepancies of 1.9891 degrees and 21.6322 m. The paired causal-navigation transforms are reference-consistent in all 404 cases, with medians of 0.0036566 degrees and 0.0104519 m. Across five matched request budgets, the largest difference between the hypergeometric prediction and the observed ordinary-random mean is 0.8412 services. Ordinary matched random reaches 0/50 target successes, while actionability-matched random reaches 50/50 and matches the CARD policy. Public downstream evaluation on 11 KITTI, EuRoC, and TUM SLAM cases measures optimizer wall-time ratios of 1.128x-67.65x for random versus CARD graph interventions. Native solver records locate this difference in elimination fill, Cholesky factor size, and numeric factorization. Together, these results connect certificate semantics, physical execution, proof acquisition, and graph computation through explicit system objects.

title: Latent Cluster Separation as a Regularizer for Lifelong Anomaly Detection
abstract: Lifelong (continual) anomaly detection systems must learn a sequence of tasks without forgetting how to recognize anomaly types seen earlier -- a property known as backward transfer. A common way to try to improve backward transfer is to reshape a model's internal representation around learnable concept centroids, typically coupled with a new way of scoring anomalies based on distance to those centroids. Because these two design choices are usually introduced together, it is unclear which one is actually responsible for any performance gain. In this paper, we unbundle the two mechanisms within a VAE-based lifelong anomaly detector and study them separately. We find that used purely as a training-time regularizer -- while leaving anomaly scoring unchanged -- latent cluster separation can improve detection quality and backward transfer, though whether it outperforms the alternative scoring approach depends on the dataset's underlying representation. Switching to distance-based scoring is instead where most of the instability commonly associated with this class of method actually originates; we identify and explain the underlying mechanism. This benefit depends on the dataset's underlying representation, and we report this as practical guidance for choosing between the two design choices, rather than as a list of caveats.

title: Four Extensions of the Universal Law of Robustness: Log-Concave Covariates, Heterogeneous Mixtures, Vector-Valued Predictors, and Markovian Data
abstract: Bubeck and Sellke's universal law of robustness says that fitting $n$ noisy samples below the noise level with a class of $p$ real parameters forces a Lipschitz constant of order $\sqrt{nd/p}$, when the covariate distribution on $\mathbb{R}^d$ is isoperimetric: smooth interpolation costs a factor $d$ of overparametrization. Its hypotheses are Gaussian-type concentration, a homogeneous covariate law, scalar outputs, and independent samples; we relax each one. Exponential concentration suffices, at the unchanged rate and absolute constant and at the price of a capacity burn-in, some form of which we show is necessary; this gives the law for normalized log-concave covariates, with a $\log d$ loss from the current KLS bound. For heterogeneous mixtures the worst component constant is replaced by the weighted average of the component constants, under a typicality condition on the mixture composition. For vector-valued predictors the bound at the Frobenius Lipschitz scale is free of the output dimension $K$, and the Euclidean bound loses only $K^{-1/2}$, a loss that covariate-independent noise removes. Stationary Markov covariates retain the i.i.d. rate, the pseudo-spectral gap entering only the sample-size conditions. One master theorem carries the shared argument, and constants are explicit throughout.

title: Towards Automatic Heart Murmur Characterization from Multi-spot Phonocardiograms
abstract: Cardiac auscultation traditionally detects the presence of a heart murmur, but clinicians further characterize it by timing, shape, pitch, quality, and grade. Most automatic phonocardiogram analysis systems stop at binary detection and do not estimate this richer description. In this work, we formulate automatic murmur characterization as five patient-level classification tasks and compare three multi-spot strategies on recordings from the aortic, pulmonary, mitral, and tricuspid auscultation locations. First, classical and deep-learning classifiers are trained independently at each location, and predictions are combined via a maximum-severity late-fusion rule. Second, a synchronous multi-input CNN jointly processes one representative segment per location for a single task. Third, a unified multi-input, multi-output CNN predicts all five attributes from one shared multi-spot representation. Using 735 patients from the CirCor DigiScope dataset with complete four-spot recordings, the best late-fusion configurations reach an unweighted mean sensitivity between 85.56% and 93.81% across the five tasks, with class-specific recalls between 80.00% and 100.00% for every relevant category. The multi-input CNN trails late fusion by 7-16 points depending on the task, while the multi-output model reaches values between 72.59% and 79.40%, estimating all five attributes from one shared representation. We further show that naively balancing training data by adding all minority-class segments degrades patient-level performance under the maximum-severity rule, since it introduces non-representative, noisy segments not filtered by the clustering-based segment selection used for evaluation. These results indicate multi-spot murmur characterization is feasible with both fusion-based and jointly learned architectures, outlining a path toward automatic, structured murmur reports complementing binary screening.

title: Mixture of Wide Experts: Sparse Routing for Interpretable Native Coordinates
abstract: Language models often spread a concept across many internal dimensions, making their features difficult to interpret. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) recover clearer features after training. We ask whether models can instead learn interpretable output coordinates directly. We introduce Mixture of Wide Experts (MoWE), a sparse feed-forward layer in which selected experts read the full representation but write to fixed, disjoint output coordinates. On a controlled task with known hidden causes, this design preserves predictive performance while localizing causes more clearly than dense and standard mixture-of-experts (MoE) models. At approximately matched compute, we train two 19-layer runs of each architecture for 10 billion tokens. MoWE achieves evaluation cross-entropy 2.417 versus 2.452 for dense, while standard MoE reaches 2.22. We measure native-coordinate readability by asking a language-model judge to describe each coordinate from passages where it is strongly active and test that description on new passages. Correcting for descriptions that also fit other coordinates gives a specificity score of 0.523 for MoWE, 0.375 for dense, and 0.268 for standard MoE. TopK SAEs trained on the same FFN updates score 0.489 for dense and 0.556 for MoWE, making native MoWE comparable to the dense SAE. In the first case study, we identify a four-coordinate causal path supporting the model's prediction of degrees after the prompt A right angle is 90. We then copy seven angle-related coordinate values into the model as it processes A rectangle has four, changing its next-token prediction from sides to degrees. In the second, one fixed coordinate set detects hazardous requests and another steers the next token toward refusal. These examples show that MoWE combines sparse conditional computation with coordinates that can be identified and reused directly.

title: Stress-Testing the Robustness of LLM-Based Causal Inference
abstract: Why do some of the world's most powerful Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems still struggle to reason about cause and effect? Causal discovery, the ability to discern the underlying drivers of a system, is fundamental to scientific inquiry and has traditionally relied on structured data and statistical methods. Recently, Large Language Models (LLMs) have been explored as an alternative paradigm for causal inference, leveraging their broad knowledge and reasoning capabilities. Yet, despite their linguistic fluency, LLMs often rely on surface-level pattern recognition rather than genuine causal logic. While it is known that LLMs stumble in this domain, we lack a precise map of where, why, and how significantly these failures occur. In this paper, we propose a systematic stress-test framework across six critical dimensions: model scale, causal graph complexity, prompting strategy, metadata quality, data quality, and sensitivity to uncertainty. Our findings reveal a significant "optimism bias" in LLMs; models consistently overestimate causal links, leading to low precision across the board. Furthermore, we demonstrate that traditional evaluation metrics can be deceptive: while reasoning-heavy models lead in performance, the highest scores often occur when uncertainty in inference is overlooked. Once uncertainty is integrated into the evaluation, performance drops, providing a more honest reflection of causal reliability. We also find that, while scaling model size improves outcomes, these gains are fragile; performance degrades sharply as the quality of metadata decreases. This work serves as a practical guide to the blind spots of LLMs, offering a clear-eyed assessment of when these tools can be integrated into a causal discovery pipeline and when they are likely to lead researchers astray.

title: Shock wave transmission across solid-water interfaces in underwater electrical foil explosions
abstract: The transmission of shock waves generated by underwater electrical foil explosions across solid materials with varying acoustic impedances and thicknesses is investigated. Copper foils with thicknesses of 10 and 18 $μ$m are exploded on planar substrates of aluminum, copper, and 3D-printed PLA with thicknesses up to 5 mm using a multi-gigawatt pulsed-power electrical discharge. The resulting shocks are visualized in water using high-speed shadowgraphy at 5 million frames per second, while high-resolution fiber optic hydrophone measurements provide direct quantitative measurements of shock strength after transmission through the impedance-mismatched materials. One-dimensional magnetohydrodynamic simulations are used to reproduce the foil explosion dynamics and provide insight into the thermodynamic, acoustic, and electrical properties of the foil during the explosion. The results show that shock transmission is governed not only by the impedance mismatch at the solid--water interface but also by the finite thickness and dynamic response of the supporting material. These findings provide a quantitative framework for understanding and controlling shock transmission in underwater electrical foil explosions and establish the feasibility and limitations of using solid substrates as structural supports in complex shock-generating geometries.

title: Recovering Hidden Wildlife--Vehicle Collisions from Existing Crash Data: A Cross-State Framework for Detection, Prevalence Estimation, and Under-Reporting Audits
abstract: Wildlife--vehicle collisions (WVCs) impose a large toll on U.S. highways, yet state crash databases often fail to record animal involvement, leaving agencies uncertain of the true missing count. This study evaluates whether existing crash records can identify individual WVCs and estimate overall unrecorded rates. We analyzed 4.9 million crash records from Colorado, Utah, Iowa, and Illinois (2007-2026). Each state's schema underwent a label-leakage screen to exclude explicit animal fields before harmonization into a shared vocabulary. Calibrated gradient-boosted classifiers were trained per state, interpreted using Shapley additive explanations, and evaluated for prevalence estimation via Adjusted Classify-and-Count and Maximum-Likelihood techniques across in-domain, cross-state, and synthetic reporting-gap scenarios. Detection performance depends heavily on record completeness rather than collision rarity. At ~4% prevalence, feature-rich Utah achieved an average precision of 0.88 versus 0.64 for feature-poor Colorado, and outperformed Iowa despite Iowa's 3x higher WVC rate. Within-state richness curves confirm feature depth drives accuracy. While classifiers ranked records accurately across states, probability calibration did not transfer directly. However, in-domain prevalence estimation recovered true collision rates within 0.001. This work shifts WVC analysis from spatial clustering to record-level detection and missing-data estimation using legacy datasets. Transportation agencies can retrospectively flag unrecorded WVCs, quantify total collision burden to support mitigation funding, and identify high-value reporting fields prior to revising crash-report manuals.

title: Mapping urban heat from citizen-collected data: a scalable Gaussian process approach to correcting for preferential sampling
abstract: The urban heat island (UHI) effect amplifies heat stress in cities, increasing heat-related illness, mortality, sleep disruption, and energy demand. Because UHI intensity varies at neighborhood scales, intra-city temperature mapping is essential for assessing public health impacts, yet existing monitoring networks are sparse. Crowdsourced weather stations provide dense, hourly observations but suffer from noise and systematic biases, including preferential sampling driven by where residents install sensors. We introduce two scalable Gaussian process frameworks which adjust for preferential sampling and enable statewide, high-resolution temperature prediction. The first integrates sampling correction directly within a sparse variational Gaussian process (SVGPR+PS). The second uses a two-stage estimator involving a log-Gaussian Cox process (LGCP+GP) that estimates the sampling intensity field and incorporates it into temperature prediction. Both methods rely on inducing-point approximations and variational inference to scale beyond traditional Gaussian processes. Applied to approximately 10,000 citizen stations across North Carolina, the models generate hourly temperature fields within minutes. Validation against independent urban heat campaign data shows that the preferential sampling correction improves predictive performance, increasing average afternoon correlations across four cities from 0.26 to 0.43. This scalable framework enables neighborhood-level UHI assessment and supports studies of heat exposure disparities statewide.

title: Behavioral Prior Elicitation via LLM for Heterogeneous-Agent Bitcoin Flash-Crash Simulation
abstract: Bitcoin perpetual futures trade continuously with shallow liquidity and high price impact, making them prone to millisecond-scale flash crashes. Agent-based limit order book simulators are a natural tool for studying such events, but their behavioral parameters are usually hand-crafted or require full order book histories that are rarely available at scale. We propose a four-stage pipeline that constructs a reproducible 100 ms BTCUSDT flash-crash event panel from 66 detected events, elicits behavioral priors for four agent archetypes using an offline large language model conditioned on empirical microstructure anchors, instantiates a heterogeneous limit order book simulator with the validated priors, and applies causal discovery plus counterfactual analysis to the resulting synthetic panel. Across 500 simulation runs, LLM-elicited priors produce a crash rate of 0.176 versus 0.008 under uninformative uniform priors and generate heav- ier return tails. In the frozen counterfactual analysis, reducing leverage amplification by one within-sample standard deviation lowers the predicted crash rate from 0.176 to 0.136, whereas reducing directional pressure yields only a marginal change. These find- ings suggest that empirically anchored LLM elicitation can improve simulator fidelity and help identify plausible crash-amplification mechanisms in a controlled synthetic environment

title: Tail reliability in probabilistic electricity price forecasts: comparing model combination and conformal prediction in the GB day-ahead market
abstract: Probabilistic forecasts of day-ahead electricity prices are increasingly used to manage price risk, yet competing models are usually ranked on aggregate scores that average over the price regimes in which uncertainty matters most. This study evaluates probabilistic forecasts of hourly EPEX SPOT GB day-ahead prices over a full held-out calendar year, applying a common pre-auction information boundary and rolling-origin design to linear quantile regression, a quantile regression forest (QRF), a LEAR-QRA benchmark and an encoder-decoder quantile long short-term memory (LSTM) network. Two routes to more reliable intervals are then compared: conformal recalibration and Quantile Regression Averaging (QRA). Aggregate scores separate the LSTM and QRF only weakly, with a non-significant 4.4% difference in continuous ranked probability score (CRPS), but their conditional behaviour differs sharply. Above 200 GBP/MWh the LSTM covered 0.12 of outcomes and QRF 0.71, consistent with the forest retaining realised spikes in its leaf distributions while the network learned a smooth upper tail. Conformal recalibration corrected marginal coverage but did not improve the interval score or materially repair spike coverage. QRA combining the LSTM, QRF and LEAR-QRA forecasts reduced CRPS to 5.14 GBP/MWh and raised coverage above 200 GBP/MWh to 0.65 at unchanged interval width. Recalibration and combination therefore address different failures and are not substitutes.

title: MCPGuard: Finding Conformance Gaps in MCP SDKs via Dual-Track Analysis and Dynamic Adjudication
abstract: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) connects large language model agents to external tools and services through official SDKs that implement message validation and session logic. Specification constraints omitted by these SDKs may propagate to downstream applications, highlighting the importance of SDK-level conformance testing. Yet existing MCP conformance tools mainly exercise running endpoints and reveal little about whether SDK models enforce specification requirements. We present MCPGuard, an automated LLM-based framework for detecting specification-to-SDK conformance gaps. Its structural track aligns JSON Schema constraints with normalized SDK models and produces constraint-specific evidence. Its behavioral track extracts normative prose rules, retrieves bounded function-level slices, and audits them with LLMs for candidate omissions. An evidence-aware dynamic adjudicator then inspects complete source context and builds PoCs to validate candidates. A shared kernel with language-specific adapters enables analysis across SDKs. On the official Python 1.26.0 and TypeScript 1.29.0 SDKs, MCPGuard confirms 13 and 19 findings, respectively, none of which are exposed by two black-box baselines. Tests on open MCP servers further show that these gaps can systematically propagate downstream. By making SDK conformance of specification constraints directly testable, MCPGuard complements conventional endpoint-oriented conformance suites.

title: Sequential Bayesian analysis of time-varying transmission in stratified epidemic renewal models
abstract: Understanding how transmission varies across age groups is important for epidemic surveillance and targeted intervention, but estimating age-specific transmission in near real time is challenging when infections are only partially observed, observations are delayed, and transmission varies across age groups. We develop a Bayesian age-stratified renewal model that jointly estimates latent infections, time-varying age-specific susceptibility, and age-specific contributions to transmission within an empirically specified contact structure. To enable sequential inference under these processes, we use a block particle filtering approach embedded within a sequential Monte Carlo squared framework, with fixed-lag smoothing to account for temporal dependence and delayed observations. From the inferred transmission process, we derive a next-generation matrix, effective reproduction number, and reproduction contributions. Applied to age-stratified COVID-19 surveillance data from Ireland during the Omicron dominant period, the framework reveals heterogeneity in susceptibility and transmission, with older adults exhibiting higher susceptibility, while younger and working-age groups make larger contributions to transmission because of their higher contact rates. These results demonstrate how statistical inference can provide age-specific transmission estimates to support targeted epidemic monitoring and intervention.

title: Identifiability of Neologism Dynamics from Aggregate Corpus Counts
abstract: Aggregate lexical frequencies reflect both what speakers do and how a corpus records it. We develop a stochastic framework for lexical adoption, abandonment and reactivation on a temporal multilayer network, together with a count observation model separating speaker prevalence, use intensity and detectability, and ask what such data identify. We give a necessary and sufficient condition for the never-active and dormant states to be merged exactly, collapsing the three-state chain to two, and show that the condition constrains the exposures a given network can deliver, not the response function as a whole. No count design can distinguish use intensity from detectability, an exact invariance distinct from the merely practical loss of information in sparse series. And we prove that in a low-prevalence community approximation the rates enter only through the net growth $β-μ$ and the coupling product $βκ$, so that a one-parameter family of triples has identical trajectories, the only separating information lying in a term quadratic in prevalence whose size depends on the emission scale. Simulations characterise recovery, prediction and sensitivity to misspecification. An exploratory analysis of 144 candidate forms in CREA and CORPES XXI press subcorpora illustrates the consequences: under the chosen emission scale and a symmetric contact graph, very different rate triples give nearly identical fitted trajectories, and in leave-one-country-out comparison with training-only proxies and seeds on a retrospectively selected cohort, a constant-rate count baseline beats the evaluated dynamic specifications on 84 to 94% of forms. These findings neither establish nor refute contact-driven diffusion. They delimit what this model and panel can support, and name the calibration, geographical contrast and repeated speaker observations that would make the question answerable.

title: Development of tools for all-cause mortality prediction in heart failure patients: a systematic review
abstract: Heart failure is a serious medical condition associated with risk of acute deterioration, recurrent hospitalizations and high mortality making accurate mortality prediction potentially valuable for patient care and healthcare planning. Numerous prognostic models have been developed using conventional statistics (CS), machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL), but variation in study populations, heart failure definitions, prediction horizons and development practices may limit interpretation of applicability. We conducted a systematic review of mortality prediction models published between 2009 to the start of 2026 searching three databases (PubMed, IEEE and Scopus) for studies predicting all-cause mortality over a 1-60 months prediction horizon among patients with heart failure. Data extracted were cohort characteristics, heart failure definitions, model development, cohort size, validation practices, mortality, computational model design and reported performance. The risk of bias and applicability were assessed using the Prediction Model Risk of Bias Assessment Tool (PROBAST). Of 1516 publications identified, 56 met the inclusion criteria. Publication numbers increased over the observation period, alongside increasing use of ML/DL models and decreasing use of CS approaches. Most development cohorts (64%) were classified as Unknown/Undefined heart failure, reflecting inconsistent reporting and terminology that did not correspond with established heart failure guidelines. External validation was reported in 23% of studies. Overall, research in modeling heart failure mortality has grown alongside increasing adoption of ML/DL approaches. Greater standardization of study design and reporting is needed for meaningful comparison, reproducibility and evaluation of models for clinical application.

title: Statistical analysis of the remaining human life expectancy. Mathematical models of the type Gompertz-Makeham and others
abstract: Many researchers believe that human lifetime on the interval (30,80) years is described by the Gompertz-Makeham distribution. In this work, the task is set to test this hypothesis. We consider a number of distributions: Gompertz-Makeham, Gompertz-Weibull, Logistic Kannisto-Makeham, Logistic Beard-Makeham and Logistic Beard-Weibull, some of which are partially known, for which comparative calculations on real mortality data are performed using the $χ^2$ criterion. The data were selected for three countries: England \& Wales, Norway and Sweden, cohorts born in 1900. As it turned out, on the interval (30,80) years the Gompertz-Makeham distribution is far from being the best among those listed above. In addition, for the same data, a similar problem was studied for the interval (80,120) years.

title: A signal-processing cascade linking satellite heat exposure, genomic variation, and mortality risk
abstract: Heat-related mortality varies among individuals under similar environmental conditions, yet environmental exposure and genetic susceptibility are typically modelled separately. We propose a signal-processing cascade linking satellite-derived land-surface temperature to sequence-dependent heat-shock response and mortality risk. The framework combines distributed-lag filtering of thermal exposure, nonlinear HSF1 activation, cross-correlation with an HSF1 position-weight-matrix kernel, and Hill-model mapping of sequence-dependent binding changes to regulatory response. Applied to 52 heat-response genes and 157 naturally occurring variants, the framework identifies 21 heat-shock-element arrays across 17 genes. Variants in canonical arrays are significantly enriched for predicted binding disruption ($p=3\times10^{-4}$). Propagating these effects through the cascade yields a peak predicted mortality-risk multiplier of $1.68\times$ at $40$--$42\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. The framework demonstrates how environmental and genomic signals can be integrated to model inter-individual variation in heat-related risk.

title: Predicting Factor Decay: ML Models for Cross-Factor Predictability Erosion
abstract: We develop ML models that predict when cross-factor predictability will erode, enabling prospective risk management. A decay prediction model achieves C-index $= 0.93$ on held-out factor pairs, providing early warning of signal erosion---the key predictor is initial signal strength: stronger signals decay faster (``regression to the mean''). An online regime detector enables real-time classification with 6.6-day average detection delay. Prior work explains why factors decay (arbitrage, publication effects); we predict when decay will occur. Limitation: The primary HML$\to$SMB signal does not replicate in post-break OOS (2013--2024); this null result is consistent with genuine decay but limits confirmatory claims. Motivation: Among 30 directed Fama-French factor pairs (1990--2024), predictability targeting the Size factor (SMB) decays fastest. Of 7 pairs showing exponential decay ($R^2 > 0.3$), 4 target SMB (Mkt-RF$\to$SMB, CMA$\to$SMB, HML$\to$SMB, RMW$\to$SMB; half-lives 2.4--4.1 years). This SMB-concentration pattern motivates the predictive models. Methodology: Using a regime-conditional Granger framework with Student-$t$ HMMs, we document structural breaks clustering around June 1998 ($p < 10^{-10}$).
