The proper procedure, and a much safer one in terms of accuracy, is recommended here: first derive the dynamics and the necessary regularizations within a fully covariant relativistic framework. Only after the exact, internally consistent equations of motion are established should low-velocity limits be extracted from them. Only in this way can all the relativistic effects which matter: time dilation, aberration, non-inertial mass shifts, be systematically preserved, and accurate results obtained.

title: Variational Learning with Lie Group Exponential Families
abstract: Variational Bayesian learning for deep neural networks offers many potential benefits. The difficulty in implementation arises from constraints on the parameters of the variational distributions, as well as the need for low-variance gradient estimators. Our recent work proposes Lie group methods for multiplicative or affine groups that naturally overcome such difficulties. Lie groups are essentially parameter spaces with a binary operator such as addition or multiplication, which allows for natural updates within the parameter space. In this article, we streamline and extend our Lie group framework to any general Lie group, and give an explicit relation to standard natural-gradient variational learning methods such as the Bayesian learning rule (BLR). In particular, we prove that linear approximations of the Lie group algorithm give generalizations of the BLR. The key ingredient is the harmonic exponential family, a general class of Lie group exponential families associated to representations of Lie groups. Our work provides a systematic method to construct from such representations efficiently implementable algorithms for variational learning.

title: On the Irreducibility of Locally Analytic Vectors in Certain Banach Representations of $D^\times$
abstract: We investigate the structure of locally analytic representations of $p$-adic groups, and establish a sufficient condition for the irreducibility of locally analytic vectors in certain Banach representations of $D^\times$, where $D$ is the quaternion division algebra over $\mathbb{Q}_p$. As an application, we prove that $\mathrm{JL}(ρ)^{\mathrm{an}}/\mathrm{JL}(ρ)^{1\text{-}\mathrm{alg}}$ is a topologically irreducible locally analytic representation of $D^\times$ under certain genericity conditions on $ρ$. Here $\mathrm{JL}(ρ)$ is the $ρ(-1)$-multiplicity space in the image of $Π(ρ)$ under Scholze's functor, and $Π(ρ)$ is the representation associated to $ρ$ by the $p$-adic local Langlands correspondence.

title: Learnings and Pitfalls from AI-Assisted A/B Experimentation at Scale
abstract: A/B testing underpins product decisions by providing trustworthy, reproducible quantification of proposed changes' effects. Growing large language model (LLM) capabilities have motivated efforts to automate experimentation workflows. Yet LLMs are nondeterministic and prone to hallucination, properties that conflict with the trust experimentation systems must provide. Experiments are also operationally messy: diagnosing anomalies, debugging configurations, and conducting bespoke follow-up analyses require flexible reasoning and manual effort. These tasks let agents accelerate experimentation without replacing its deterministic statistical foundations. We report lessons from building and operating such an agent. Our central finding is that this tension is resolved not by making the model deterministic, but by bounding where its nondeterminism can reach; the model selects and sequences procedures, while deterministic code computes every quantity it reports. Three consequences surprised us: withholding information from the model improved its answers, demand concentrated on mundane retrieval rather than the autonomous decisions we anticipated, and the agent's eagerness to help threatened statistical validity.

title: Uniqueness in an incompressible fluid with objective heat conduction model
abstract: In the context of heat conduction, the equations of Maxwell-Cattaneo is a successful alternative to the Fourier's law. In 2009, Christov proposed a frame-independent (or objective) generalization of Maxwell-Cattaneo equation. For a more general class of objective heat conduction Maxwell-Cattaneo-Christov equations proposed by Angeles, a uniqueness result is proved, applied to an incompressible fluid.

title: GeoSim: Benchmarking Multi-Field Neural Operators for Geodynamics
abstract: Learning reliable surrogates for geodynamic models requires benchmarks that resolve coupled fields and temporal stability. We present GeoSim, a benchmark of high-resolution two-dimensional mantle-plume simulations generated with I2VIS, comprising 237 trajectories across two parameter regimes, with six coupled fields, physical timestamps, and trajectory-level splits. GeoSim defines short-window prediction and autonomous rollout, and evaluates representative neural operators field by field. Across models, we observe a pronounced scalar--velocity gap: scalar fields are reconstructed accurately while velocity errors remain large, and short-window accuracy does not imply stable rollout. We also evaluate MFGNO (Multi-Field Graph Neural Operator), a joint multi-field graph baseline designed for this benchmark; on GeoSim-Plume1, under a fixed per-field objective, it reduces horizontal and vertical velocity errors by 58.4% and 38.5% relative to an independent-field graph baseline, while an explicit field-difference input shows no measurable benefit at this scale. GeoSim provides a reproducible benchmark for field-wise diagnosis and long-horizon evaluation of geodynamic surrogates.

title: LLM-Assisted Planning with Distributed Onboard Behaviour Tree Execution for Multi-AUV Missions
abstract: Coordinating autonomous underwater vehicles requires translating operator intent into feasible assignments while preserving autonomous execution when communication is limited. We present a hierarchical framework that couples Large Language Model (LLM) interpretation of natural-language mission instructions with Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) and distributed Behaviour Tree (BT) execution. The LLM extracts assignment and ordering constraints, which the MILP optimizer combines with vehicle capabilities and temporal requirements. A BT-LLM Bridge distributes the resulting allocations to onboard BT Mission Managers. Per-vehicle Robotic Agents assess local faults and request selective replanning, allowing unaffected vehicles to continue their assigned tasks. Evaluation in a ROS-based AUV simulator compares Qwen-3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B on constraint extraction and tests recovery from sensor degradation and critical vehicle faults. Qwen-3-8B provides more accurate constraint extraction, and all tasks are completed in the tested failure scenarios. These simulation results support the feasibility of combining language-based mission specification with structured allocation and distributed execution.

title: Order-Dependent Complexity of Enumeration and Direct Access for Conjunctive Queries on Dynamic Data
abstract: This note studies the fine-grained complexity of ranked enumeration and ranked direct access of conjunctive query answers over a dynamic database. We focus on lexicographically sorted answers, defined by an ordering on the query's free variables. From the literature, when no particular order is required, we know that when the query is self-join-free and q-hierarchical, we can build a data structure for enumeration (resp. direct access) with linear (resp. linearithmic) preprocessing and constant (resp. logarithmic) update time in the size of the database. For enumeration (resp. direct access), this data structure yields an algorithm that enumerates all query answers (resp. that returns the $k$-th query answer) with constant delay (resp. logarithmic access time). Our goal is to extend these results to ranked enumeration and ranked direct access, with the ranking function defined by a lexicographic order. We define a property on the order over the variables of $Q$, which we call being hierarchy-consistent. Given a user-specified query and hierarchy-consistent order, we first propose, for ranked enumeration under updates, an algorithm with linear preprocessing and logarithmic update time that enumerates all the query answers according to the user-specified order with constant delay. Moreover, for ranked direct access under updates, we propose an algorithm with linear preprocessing and logarithmic update time that returns the $k$-th tuple according to the user-specified order with logarithmic access time. In contrast, given a user-specified query and non-hierarchy-consistent order, we show a lower bound for ranked direct access under updates.

title: A remark on singular solutions of semilinear elliptic equations in two dimensions
abstract: We study positive radial singular solutions of $-Δu=f(u)$ in two space dimensions. Fujishima, Ioku, Ruf, and Terraneo constructed such solutions under asymptotic assumptions on $f$ and an additional convergence-rate condition, denoted by $(f_3)$. We prove their local existence result, with the same approximate solution and remainder estimate, under the original assumptions $(f_1)$ and $(f_2)$ alone. The proof combines a contraction on finite intervals with a nonlinear energy estimate uniform in the terminal point and requires only $C^2$ regularity of $f$ near infinity. We also obtain derivative asymptotics and, under additional global assumptions, a singular Dirichlet solution which solves the equation distributionally across the origin. An analytic oscillatory example satisfies our hypotheses but violates both $(f_3)$ and the derivative assumptions of Kikuchi and Kumagai. For every fixed finite iterate of the exponential of order at least two, we verify the hypotheses and quantify the remainder; condition $(f_3)$ fails for all iterates of order at least three.

title: Estimating the generator of matrix exponential time-series
abstract: The achievable precision in estimating the spectrum of a time-series signal that is promised to be sparse in Fourier space deteriorates rapidly as the spectral peaks get closer together, as soon as we introduce noise. Here, we study the related task of generator estimation: estimating the generator of a matrix exponential time-series and its eigenvalues. We obtain rigorous non-asymptotic precision guarantees on genESPRIT, a practical algorithm solving generator estimation, and show that this task can be solved with precision independent of the spectral spacing. The guarantees are complemented by a Cramér--Rao analysis of a relaxation of the problem. In particular, in the case of unitary data with bounded additive noise with effective entrywise variance $σ^2$, we show that genESPRIT estimates the associated propagator matrix in Frobenius norm with precision scaling as $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(σNL^{-\frac12})$ in the length of the time-series $L$ and matrix dimension $N$, matching the corresponding spectrum-independent Cramér--Rao standard deviation scaling up to logarithmic factors. We prove that the matching distance error in the spectrum estimated by genESPRIT scales as $\tilde{\mathcal{O}} (σ^2 N^3 L^{-1} + σN^{\frac32} L^{-\frac32} )$, which we compare to the lower bound on the corresponding Cramér--Rao bound with the asymptotic standard deviation scaling $\mathcal{O}(σL^{-\frac32})$. These guarantees provide the first rigorous bounds on solving the generator estimation problem. As the matrix exponential time-series can be obtained from linearly independent vector time-series by concatenation, this work opens up a new direction in spectral estimation, which circumvents the problem of crowded spectra, under the additional assumption of linear independence.

title: Action Intent as a Bridge: Transferring Manipulation Knowledge from Human-Centric Videos to Robots
abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have achieved promising performance for generalized robotic manipulation, yet their reliance on expensive real-robot data remains a fundamental bottleneck. A scalable alternative is to transfer knowledge from off-the-shelf human-centric videos. However, existing methods extract latent action representations that are entangled with scene-specific noise, diluting the transferred knowledge. Motivated by this limitation, we propose Action-Intent Transfer (AIT), a two-stage method that transfers knowledge through a clean action representation shared across humans and robots. In the first stage, AIT extracts explicit action intents and disentangles the implicit action intent from manipulation videos. In the second stage, AIT aligns the human and robot domains within this shared intent space and decodes the intent into executable robot actions. Extensive experiments in both simulation and real-world environments demonstrate that AIT transfers human knowledge more effectively and consistently outperforms prior baselines.

title: Binary Codes with a Forbidden Distance
abstract: The maximum size of a t-intersecting code in the set of words of length n over an alphabet of size m, a problem posed by Frankl and Füredi, was determined independently by Ahlswede and Khachatrian and by Frankl and Tokushige. Extending this result to the forbidden-intersection setting, Keevash, Lifshitz, Long and Minzer proved that, for m greater than two and n sufficiently large in terms of t, (t minus one)-avoiding codes have the same maximum size and the same extremal ball constructions as t-intersecting codes. They also raised the binary case. Here, t-intersecting requires every two distinct words to agree in at least t coordinates, while (t minus one)-avoiding forbids agreement in exactly t minus one coordinates. We solve the binary case for all t at least three and n at least the square of the sum of t and one. If the forbidden Hamming distance n minus t plus one is odd, the maximum size of a (t minus one)-avoiding code strictly exceeds the maximum t-intersecting size. If it is even, the two maxima coincide, but their extremal families differ: some maximum (t minus one)-avoiding codes are not t-intersecting. We also determine all maximum avoiding codes in the even case. For odd forbidden distances, weight parity and a fixed-point-free pairing determine the maximum, while the diameter theorem gives the comparison with t-intersecting codes. For even forbidden distances, parity splitting and coordinate deletion reduce the problem to avoiding two consecutive distances. Connected components, disjoint neighbourhoods, and Harper's vertex-isoperimetric theorem yield the upper bound, which is attained by a t-intersecting construction. The diameter theorem then determines the extremal structure, and elementary binomial estimates give the stated parameter range.

title: E2I-Flow: EEG-to-Image Reconstruction via Wavelet-Temporal Cross-Attention and Conditional Flow Matching
abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG)-based visual decoding and reconstruction aims to recover visual information from non-invasive brain signals. But there are challenges due to the complex temporal-frequency characteristics of EEG signals and the difficulty of discrete denoising framework in mapping neural activity to meaningful visual representations. Here, we propose E2I-Flow, an EEG-to-image decoding and reconstruction framework that combines a novel EEG encoder for time-frequency representation learning from EEG features, and conditional flow matching for visual decoding. A stationary-wavelet frequency branch and a temporal-mixing branch are integrated through bidirectional cross-attention and adaptive fusion, with the resulting EEG representations aligned to ground-truth image embeddings using contrastive and mean-squared-error loss supervisions. The aligned EEG representation is then used as a condition for a Transformer-based flow-matching model to predict the corresponding visual embedding for image synthesis. Experimental results show strong zero-shot EEG-to-image retrieval and improved visual reconstruction performance, outperforming several state-of-the-art baselines.

title: Late-time echoes from planar wave-packet scattering by an ultracompact star
abstract: We simulate the propagation and scattering of an incident plane scalar wave in the spacetime of an ultracompact, horizonless constant-density star using a time-domain multipole mode-sum method. By reconstructing the coherently superposed time-domain waveforms, we compare the star's dynamical response with that of a Schwarzschild black hole. We find that the early-time response closely mimics a black-hole ringdown due to wave scattering near the exterior unstable photon sphere. Conversely, the late-time signal develops a sequence of delayed echoes originating from wave trapping near the interior stable light ring and subsequent leakage through the exterior potential barrier. While individual multipoles exhibit regular echoes, their coherent superposition induces interference, producing complex waveforms with irregular profiles that nonetheless retain an underlying temporal organization with alternating peak separations. Finally, as a proof of concept, we perform a signal-to-noise ratio analysis using an assumed strain normalization, demonstrating that these weak, late-time signatures can be resolved by third-generation gravitational-wave detectors.

title: Long-lived quantum memories with rare-earth ions doped in crystals
abstract: Quantum memory is a core enabling device for large-scale quantum networks, serving as the fundamental building block for quantum repeaters and transportable quantum memories. Among various physical platforms, rare-earth-ion-doped crystals stand out as one of the most promising solid-state candidates for long-lived photonic quantum memories, owing to their exceptionally long spin coherence time and their compatibility with integration. In this review, we first introduce the physical mechanisms underlying long-lived spin coherence in rare-earth systems, with particular emphasis on the zero-first-order-Zeeman transition and dynamical decoupling techniques. We then review the experimental progress in this field, highlighting three distinct lifetimes--the spin coherence time, the light storage time, and the quantum storage time--and covering experiments that have achieved hour-scale spin coherence, minute- to hour-scale light storage, and minute-scale single-photon-level quantum storage. Finally, we discuss the remaining challenges that hinder the realization of practical long-lived quantum memories, explore potential strategies to overcome these obstacles, and outline the prospects for their future applications in quantum networks.

title: Future Representation Distillation for Imagination-free World Action Models
abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) use the predictive knowledge of pretrained video diffusion models for robot control through future video prediction. However, iterative video denoising is costly, and inaccurate visual predictions can compromise action prediction. Our key idea is to make this predictive knowledge available through visual representations computed from the current observation, enabling action prediction without generating future videos. We introduce DreamFree, a WAM that repurposes a pretrained video diffusion model as a predictive visual encoder through representation distillation. The visual encoder learns to predict a frozen video diffusion model's representation using only the current observation. An action module is then trained to predict actions by extracting action-relevant information from the visual encoder. Across real-world and simulated tasks, DreamFree achieves higher success rates than state-of-the-art VLAs and WAMs, while performing real-time closed-loop control at 11Hz with a 14B video diffusion backbone. Experiments show that DreamFree can translate stronger video priors and additional video data into better robot control and enable learning new robot tasks from video demonstrations, including videos from a different embodiment, without action annotation for the new tasks.

title: Unstable Stokes waves in constant vorticity flows of infinite depth
abstract: We study the spectral stability of small-amplitude Stokes waves with constant vorticity in infinite depth. We describe the spectrum near the origin and near the first nonzero double eigenvalue. For nonzero vorticity $ω<2\sqrt{g/3}$, where $g$ is the gravitational constant, the eigenvalues near the origin form a figure eight, whereas for $ω>2\sqrt{g/3}$ the local spectrum remains purely imaginary. Away from the origin, the interaction of two Fourier modes whose indices differ by two produces an unstable isola when $ω>-\sqrt{g/6}$, $ω\ne0$, and the resonant wave numbers are noninteger. This curve is a real analytic oval with an explicit leading ellipse and maximal growth of quadratic order in the amplitude. We also prove instability at the integer resonances needed to cover the remaining vorticities. Together with the classical irrotational result, these two mechanisms show that sufficiently small nonzero Stokes waves are spectrally unstable for every fixed constant vorticity. The proof uses finite-dimensional spectral reductions of the full Euler linearization. Near the origin, the finite-dimensional linearized operator has a one-sided limit as the Floquet exponent vanishes, which differs from the periodic linearization. We use the Kato transformation to construct a three-dimensional reduction with biorthogonal bases and use all three eigenvectors of the reference operator to calculate the Benjamin--Feir coefficient. At the nonzero collision, a real two-dimensional reduction and an explicit second-order calculation determine the unstable curve.

title: Learning to Falsify: Hierarchical Multiple Instance Learning for High Resolution AI-Generated Image Detection
abstract: Recent advances in generative models have made synthetic images increasingly photorealistic, posing growing challenges to reliable and generalizable detection of AI-generated images. Existing methods typically rely on holistic image-level classification, which may overlook local artifacts, especially in high-resolution images. To address this limitation, we formulate this task as a falsification-driven multiple instance learning problem, where a single fake patch can falsify the whole image, while a real image requires all patches to be authentic. Based on this formulation, we propose \textit{Learning to Falsify (LTF)}, a hierarchical multiple instance learning framework that models an image as multiple bags of instances across different spatial levels and aggregates their predictions under the falsification-inspired principle. We further introduce Cross-Shuffle during training to encourage the model to learn local artifact evidence rather than image-level shortcuts. Furthermore, we propose the \textit{Falsification-driven Test-time Aggregation Strategy (FATAS)}, a plug-and-play module that extends the same falsification-inspired principle to existing detectors by aggregating patch-level predictions. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LTF achieves strong generalization and robustness across multiple benchmarks, while FATAS substantially improves representative detectors in high-resolution scenarios without retraining. Code is available at https://github.com/HuiGuanLab/LTF.git

title: Star-shaped periodic solutions of a system of delay differential equations: A computer-assisted proof
abstract: In this paper, we consider a planar system of nonlinear delay differential equations and prove the existence of the star-shaped periodic solutions conjectured by Hara (Nonlinear Analysis: Theory, Methods \& Applications, 30:4555--4563 (1997)) for seven parameter values. These solutions cannot be obtained by a direct application of the standard Fourier spectral method, since the corresponding linearized operator is degenerate. From numerical observations of the Fourier coefficients, we derive an ansatz that writes a star-shaped periodic solution as a periodic profile in a rotating frame. Restricting the profile to real Fourier coefficients, we show that the resonance between the delay and the period of the profile fixes the rotation frequency exactly. We then validate a zero of the resulting real system with the radii polynomial approach and interval arithmetic, with bounds that cover all Fourier modes. For each parameter value, we also determine the fundamental period and the winding number of the solution.

title: A New Bound on Light-by-Light Scattering in the Low-Energy Regime
abstract: The superposition principle at the heart of optics states that electromagnetic fields do not interact in vacuum. This principle is not universal, instead electromagnetic fields couple weakly via quantum vacuum fluctuations. Striking consequences are light-by-light scattering and vacuum birefringence. Experimental results from colliding X-ray free-electron and optical high-intensity lasers combined with dark-field detection and polarimetry for background suppression are reported. This approach yields the most stringent bound for light-by-light scattering in the low-energy regime achieved to date -- improving upon previous experimental limits by ten orders of magnitude -- and paves the way for precision measurements.

title: The Price of List Replicability: Tight Bounds for Bias Estimation
abstract: We study the sample complexity of list replicable algorithms for estimating the biases of $d$ coins. An algorithm is $(k,\varepsilon,δ)$-list replicable if for every bias vector $\mathbf{p}\in[0,1]^d$, there is a set of outputs $L_{\mathbf{p}}\subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ of at most $k$ elements such that every $\mathbf{y}\in L_{\mathbf{p}}$ satisfies $\lVert\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{p}\rVert_\infty\leq\varepsilon$, and the algorithm output is in $L_{\mathbf{p}}$ with probability at least $1-δ$. Prior work gave a $(d+1,\varepsilon,δ)$-list replicable algorithm with sample complexity $\widetilde{O}\left(\frac{d^3}{\varepsilon^2}\right)$, but no nontrivial sample complexity lower bound was known. We establish the first non-trivial sample complexity lower bound for this problem and give an improved algorithm that matches it up to polylogarithmic factors. Together, these results determine the optimal sample complexity for list size $d+1$ to be $\widetildeΘ\left(\frac{d^2}{\varepsilon^2}\right)$, showing that the quadratic dependence on dimension is inherent up to polylogarithmic factors. More generally, for every $k\in[d+1,2^d]$, we establish matching upper and lower bounds of $\widetildeΘ\left(\frac{d^2}{\varepsilon^2\log k}\right)$ on the total sample complexity.

title: How market volatility responds to a preceding price trend: a lag-resolved measurement in cryptocurrencies and equities
abstract: We quantify the response of market volatility to a preceding price trend as a function of lag at minute resolution. The asymmetry of the response is investigated. The sample consists of trades in three of the largest cryptocurrencies on a single exchange and in three large US stocks and the S&P 500 exchange-traded fund between 2020 and 2026. For the cryptocurrencies the asymmetry is positive, matching the sign of the leverage effect. It follows the trend: it is greatest at the first measurable lag, 20 minutes, and weak at negative lags, where the trend follows the volatility. At those lags a scan over window lengths resolves a small component of opposite sign that has not yet been disentangled from what the statistic itself generates. For Bitcoin and Ether the asymmetry decays to one half by a lag of roughly an hour and a half. Decomposition under time reversal divides the asymmetry into a T-even part and a T-odd part. Only the latter carries an arrow of time. For Bitcoin and Ether the T-odd part is detected. At the first lag it is between 0.4 and 0.9 of the T-even part at windows of 10 and 20 minutes. At 20 minutes this is the ratio produced by a purely one-sided response in this statistic: at that window the response is consistent with being wholly one-sided in time. None of the equities exhibits a detectable T-odd part at 20 minutes in the straight-line fit over 2.5 trend scales. This fit is the shared instrument of comparison. The fund's return-variance correlation displays an arrow of time; the cryptocurrencies' asymmetry is independent of the shapes of the fits, and Bitcoin's and Ether's of their ranges. On simulated and shuffled data without coupling, the analysis yields zero with errors of the correct size. It also recovers the time scale of a one-sided response embedded in a simulated market.

title: A Universal Raw-IQ Radar Encoder for Cross-Sensor Human Sensing
abstract: Radar-based human sensing typically relies on end-to-end task-specific models trained on hand-chosen signal projections, which generalize poorly across unseen users, tasks, and hardware. We argue that the dominant signal processing choice, the micro-Doppler spectrogram, is a poor starting point for transfer because it keeps the Doppler axis, which carrier frequency rescales, and discards the angular axis, which carrier frequency leaves unchanged. We instead pretrain a convolutional beta-VAE without labels on clutter-removed raw radar measurements from four platforms spanning 60 and 77 GHz and 4 to 12 virtual antennas, aligned by a unified spectral interpolation grid. For every downstream benchmark the encoder stays frozen, and only a small supervised temporal classifier is trained on its embeddings. We compare against supervised models trained end to end on each benchmark and a pretrained radar foundation model across ten settings covering activity, gesture, sign-language, and gait recognition. When the test users and the radar are seen during training, our encoder is best on all five benchmarks. For users never seen in training, it leads on three of four benchmarks, by 4.8 to 23.2 points. On subject-disjoint gait recognition, it is best for each of the four held-out subjects and 8.3 points above the strongest baseline on average, even though its pretraining excluded every recording of this radar. Excluding the test radar from pretraining costs at most 5.3 points on any benchmark. Code is available at https://github.com/jonasmueler/UniversalRadarEncoder_WACV.

title: The Extension groups of one $\rm K$-type representations of graded Hecke algebra
abstract: We study the extension groups between one $\rm K$-type representations of the graded Hecke algebra $\mathbb H$. A one $\rm K$-type representation is a Hermitian representation of $\mbb H$ whose restriction to the Weyl group is irreducible. Using a Koszul-type resolution of $\mathbb H$-modules, we reduce the computation of $\operatorname{Ext}_{\mathbb H}^j(X,Y)$ to a combinatorial count, yielding explicit formulas for the classical types and a computer computation for the exceptional types.

title: Machine learning emulators of dynamic global vegetation models for fast gridded carbon budget predictions
abstract: The land carbon sink explains most of the variability of the atmospheric CO2 growth rate, but the Global Carbon Budget estimates it with dynamic global vegetation models (DGVMs) run once a year. Emulators could provide it sooner if they reproduce each model outside its training period. Here we show that convolutional neural network emulators of 19 of these models, driven by ERA5 climate and their own past predictions, reproduce the global land sink of these models and its spread over two years not used in training. Global monthly net biome production (NBP) anomalies were reproduced with a median R^2 of 0.81. The error of the multi-model mean annual NBP was at most 0.23 GtC yr^-1. At the grid-cell level, the median R^2 of monthly anomalies was 0.30, partly because of errors that accumulate in the emulated NBP history.

title: BtsPruner: Role-Aware Visual Token Pruning for Large Vision-Language Models
abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) often process hundreds or thousands of visual tokens, resulting in substantial computational and memory overhead during inference. Existing training-free pruning methods typically estimate token importance using language-model attention, visual attention, or feature similarity. However, these methods treat visual tokens with uniform criteria and overlook that tokens may serve different roles during visual encoding. In this work, we investigate the evolution of visual token roles in LVLMs and observe that tokens progressively transition from local detail carriers to globally referenced representatives as encoding proceeds. Based on this observation, we propose BtsPruner, a training-free role-aware visual token pruning framework that preserves complementary token roles under a fixed budget. Specifically, BtsPruner first identifies the token-role transition point based on the evolution of attention concentration. It then discovers globally referenced representatives from later encoding stages and recursively retrieves local detail tokens from earlier stages to recover complementary fine-grained evidence. Extensive experiments across LLaVA-1.5, LLaVA-NeXT, Qwen-VL, InternVL, and CogVLM demonstrate that BtsPruner achieves superior performance retention under aggressive token reduction. On LLaVA-1.5-7B, BtsPruner preserves 91.6% of the dense model's performance using only 32 of 576 visual tokens (5.6%). In the high-resolution LLaVA-NeXT-7B setting, it achieves up to a 5.95x CUDA-latency speedup.

title: Wavefront engineering with atomic Huygens' surfaces made simple
abstract: Atomic arrays provide a cooperative platform for light-mediated interactions in nonlocal metasurfaces which can operate in the quantum regime without nanofabricated optical elements or intrinsic material absorption. We present a minimal atomic implementation to harness wavefront engineering and create a near-ideal intrinsic atomic Huygens' surface. A simple bilayer square lattice with a two-atom unit cell, not limited to small lattice spacings, provides near-unity reflectionless transmission and a full $2π$ phase control of transmitted light without the localized site-dependent level shifts of previous proposals. This simplification is achieved through nonlocal radiative excitations that provide the familiar electric-dipole response with even radiation parity as well as an odd-parity radiation channel whose leading multipolar interpretation combines magnetic-dipole and electric-quadrupole contributions in atoms exhibiting only electric dipole transitions. This eliminates the need to simultaneously excite pure electric-dipole and magnetic-dipole responses with exactly matched radiation. We derive a two-mode model for this response and show that it accurately captures full coupled-dipole simulations near the optimal lattice spacings. Because of the wide applicability of coupled-dipole models, the relevance of our microscopic analysis extends beyond atomic physics to nanostructured metasurfaces. Moreover, the same platform also connects directly to established subradiance-protected single-photon storage protocols, suggesting a route toward combining wavefront engineering, storage, and retrieval in a simple atomic bilayer.

title: Decoy-state quantum key distribution with a leaky Mach-Zehnder receiver
abstract: We prove the security of phase-encoded decoy-state BB84 quantum key distribution for a Mach-Zehnder receiver with imbalanced beam splitters and two threshold detectors that leak fine-grained information about the detection patterns. For this, we derive a lower bound on Bob's single-photon contributions and combine it with the decoy-state method and a recent phase-error framework for leaky receivers. The leakage-induced correction to the phase-error rate is independent of channel loss, providing a loss-tolerant treatment of receiver leakage even in the presence of beam-splitter imbalance. Our results provide a practical route toward loss-tolerant security proofs for imperfect QKD receivers in the presence of receiver leakage.

title: A sharp Mittag-Leffler bound for series with separated exponents
abstract: Let $η\geq 0$ and $δ>0$, and let $(r_j)_{j\geq 0}$ be a sequence of real numbers satisfying $η\leq r_0 < r_1 < r_2 < \cdots$ and $r_{j+1}-r_j \geq δ$ for every $j\geq 0$. We prove that, for $δ\leq 1$ and every $x>0$, \[ \sum_{j=0}^\infty \frac{x^{r_j}}{\G(1+r_j)} \leq \sum_{j=0}^\infty \frac{x^{η+jδ}}{\G(1+η+jδ)} = x^ηE_{δ,1+η}(x^δ), \] where $E_{δ,1+η}$ denotes the two-parameter Mittag-Leffler function. Moreover, equality holds for some $x>0$ if and only if $r_j = η+ jδ$ for every $j$. The proof combines a finite compression argument for unimodal functions with a shift inequality for the Mittag-Leffler function. The upper bound $δ\leq 1$ is sharp, since counterexamples exist for every $1 < δ< 2$.

title: Exotic Dehn twists on sums of 4-manifolds, nuclei, and exotic structures
abstract: For closed 4-manifolds $X_1, X_2$, we give a sufficient condition, in terms of the Seiberg-Witten invariants of $X_i$, for the Dehn twist on $X_1\#X_2$ along the neck to be smoothly nontrivial. This provides a broad generalization of the result of Kronheimer-Mrowka for $K3\#K3$. We also show that the boundary Dehn twists on the punctured connected sums of many pairs of elliptic surfaces are smoothly nontrivial. We also detect new examples of exotic Dehn twists along Seifert fibered 3-manifolds in elliptic surfaces. As a consequence, we exhibit a new phenomenon in which "exotic diffeomorphisms detect exotic smooth structures on 4-manifolds": the triviality of the boundary Dehn twist characterizes the standard nucleus $N(n)$ among the nuclei $N(n)_{p,q}$ homeomorphic to it, provided that $n\equiv0 \bmod 4$. These results are proved by computing the families Bauer-Furuta invariant for a new framing of the families Dirac index.

title: Non-uniqueness of the amplitude reconstruction in the inverse scattering problem and a refinement of Hoehler's resonance clustering
abstract: Reaction-amplitude reconstruction in the inverse scattering problem is limited by the bilinear form of all reaction observables. At fixed kinematics, N complex amplitudes contain 2N real quantities, whereas complete measurements determine at most 2N-1 parameters. Uniqueness therefore depends on whether additional physical constraints, such as unitarity, supply the missing information. We examine the consequences for resonance identification, focusing on angular-momentum assignments. Building on published results showing how truncation redistributes pole-bearing contributions among effective partial waves, we examine exact and practical ambiguities associated with imposing coupled-channel unitarity. A 4 x 4 counterexample shows that different on-shell unitary amplitudes can produce identical measurable bilinears. Practical unitary descriptions can also yield different pole content while remaining compatible with experimental uncertainties. We update Hoehler's clustering using the thirteen four-star N* resonances in PDG 2026 and Bonn-Gatchina results published in 2025. Nearby poles with different partial-wave assignments occur both in the PDG compilation and within Bonn-Gatchina, so their proximity is not solely a consequence of PDG averaging. Some groupings persist, while others change appreciably. We discuss a conditional interpretation in which truncation redistributes a common pole-bearing contribution among effective partial waves, with additional reconstruction uncertainties potentially accounting for departures from coincident pole positions. These considerations allow, but do not establish, a common origin for cluster members. The necessity of separate states and the stability of their angular-momentum assignments remain questions for further investigation.

title: CANDO: Conservative Action-Noise Directional Optimization for Residual Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Pretrained generative policies provide strong behavior priors for robot control, but adapting them efficiently with online reinforcement learning remains difficult. A central challenge is how to improve a frozen generative policy without destroying the structure learned from offline demonstrations. Noise-space residual methods address this by modifying the policy's input noise, but existing noise-space methods typically regulate adaptation through fixed latent feasible regions, which may exclude valuable noise edits. In contrast, action-space residual methods are more sample-efficient, but their efficiency can still be further improved. We propose Conservative Noise Directional Optimization (CNDO), a noise-space residual RL method that improves a frozen generative policy by learning state- and noise-conditioned directions around Gaussian latent samples. CNDO removes predefined latent feasible regions and instead regulates noise-space adaptation through the soft conservative constraint, which consists of conservative value estimation and gated execution. We further introduce Conservative Action-Noise Directional Optimization (CANDO), which adds an action-space residual, combining structured latent-space improvement with local action correction. Experiments show that, once CNDO narrows the gap between noise-space and action-space residual learning, CANDO further improves over single-space optimization, achieving 76.1 NAUC and a 91.4% final success rate, surpassing the best single-space results by 6.6 NAUC and 4.1% success rate. More demos and info are available on https://cando-rl.github.io/.

title: The Survival Paradox of Close-In Planets Orbiting Red Clump Giants
abstract: Close-in planets orbiting core-helium-burning red-clump (RC) giants directly challenge tidal-engulfment theory, which predicts that planets within about 1 au of Sun-like stars should be engulfed during red-giant-branch (RGB) expansion. The existence of such survivors would imply missing physical processes in the late stages of stellar and planetary evolution. Yet only one such "forbidden" planet had been identified to date. Here we report three systems-24 Boo b, HD 12648 b, and TYC 4282-605-1 b-whose host stars are confirmed red-clump giants through asteroseismology, showing that each has already undergone dramatic expansion and contraction following helium ignition. Their planets now reside at orbital separations smaller than the maximum stellar radii attained during the RGB phase, implying that they should not have survived. Among them, 24 Boo b orbits at only 0.183 au with a 30-day period, making it the closest planet known around a red-clump giant. These discoveries demonstrate that this paradox is not an isolated anomaly but signals the emergence of a new class of evolved planetary systems. Their survival defies current models of stellar-planetary coevolution and points to unexplored physics shaping planetary architectures around post-RGB stars.

title: Coercive at the equilibrium, monotone nowhere: exact convergence certificates for learning in first-price auctions
abstract: The Bayes-Nash equilibria of an auction are the solutions of a variational inequality, and for standard auctions its operator fails every monotonicity notion, so the theory of monotone operators is unavailable to learning in auctions. We show what replaces monotonicity for the first-price auction: a certificate that is strong but local. For uniform values the single-population operator has an exact closed form and an exact Minty identity at the equilibrium; for two bidders its Gateaux derivative there is $L^2$-coercive with best constant exactly one in every piecewise-linear bid space with $m$ pieces, while the Minty inequality holds only on a ball whose radius decays like $m^{-5/2}$. The decay is exact: $m^{5/2}$ times the radius converges to $1/(8 \cdot 3^{1/4})$, and the worst perturbations converge to an alternating geometric profile with ratio $-(2-\sqrt{3})$. Refinement shrinks the ball, not the constant; independent learners see the same constant. For a general prior and bidder count there are two certificates, at the true equilibrium and at the equilibrium of the finite-dimensional bid space a learning algorithm runs in. The first is an explicit weight $w_F$, positive for every log-concave prior, equal to the second exactly for the value distributions $F(v)=v^a$. Otherwise the learners' certificate differs by knot masses, because the discretized equilibrium's slopes oscillate with a law proved for two and three bidders, and for four under a computer-verified bottom layer. The limit of the learners' certificate is proved in closed form, a function of the prior alone, and characterizes positivity: positive uniformly in $m$ in the limit exactly when that minimum is positive, with a known rate; for one prior at every $m$ by interval arithmetic. For more bidders the limit is conjectured. The exact identities and leading-order inequalities are machine-checked in Lean.

title: Are LLM Assistants Regulatory Ready? Answers from regenold's 2026 EU AI Act Q&A Challenge
abstract: Large language model (LLM) assistants are increasingly proposed for regulatory affairs, yet their reliability in regulatory tasks remains unclear. We introduce the EU AI Act Q&A Benchmark, an expert-curated benchmark of 110 open-ended questions about the EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689). Each question comes with an exemplary answer, question-specific correctness criteria, and expected references. Evaluation measures answer correctness, reference quality, conciseness, tone, and latency, with a multi-turn ``hard mode'' testing responses to simulated user pushback. We also present the results of the 2026 EU AI Act Q&A Challenge, based on the benchmark, where three off-the-shelf baselines and five purpose-built assistants (from four commercial developers and one academic entrant) were tested. Only two of the five submitted assistants consistently outperformed the baselines; one achieved high scores across all evaluated metrics. These results show that specialist development alone does not guarantee better performance and highlight the critical importance of LLM assistant evaluation in regulatory affairs. The benchmark code is openly available at https://github.com/regenold-GmbH/eu-ai-act-benchmark-2026/.

title: Strain-Glass Dynamics in the Superionic Conductor Na$_3$PS$_4$
abstract: Ionic conduction in solid-state electrolytes is conventionally described by mobile cations migrating through a static host lattice. Yet the fastest conductors are often the most disordered, and how disorder enhances transport remains unresolved at the mesoscale, inaccessible to ensemble-averaged probes. We use Bragg X-ray photon correlation spectroscopy to measure nanoscale structural dynamics of a single ball-milled Na$_3$PS$_4$ particle. We find that the cubic phase behaves as a strain glass: a frustrated configuration of three degenerate tetragonal variants with short-range order. Its domain-wall motion is stress-driven, crossing over irreversibly to thermally activated dynamics on annealing as residual milling stress is depleted. Rearrangements follow scale-free avalanche statistics, matching ferroelastic martensites but without external driving. The tetragonal polymorph shows none of these features and relaxes fifty times more slowly. These dynamics occur on timescales comparable to estimated ionic diffusion across the particle, indicating the host structure cannot be assumed static on transport-relevant timescales.

title: Predicting Void Points in Self-Occluding Forest Volumes
abstract: Synthetic Aperture Imaging (SAI) enables drones to observe forest canopies by warping and averaging multiple displaced views at a common depth. However, occlusion is suppressed rather than eliminated, causing poorly observed regions to appear occupied and leading to systematic biomass overestimation. The Deep Forest project cannot distinguish reconstruction artifacts from real vegetation because its training data relies on measured reflectance points, excluding empty space and preventing the network from learning explicit occupancy boundaries. This thesis addresses the problem by modifying training labels rather than the imaging process. Each simulated scene is rendered twice: as a 9x9 grid of top-down captures for focal-stack generation and as 550 depth-clipped slabs derived from scene geometry to provide occupancy labels, explicitly representing void space as a negative class. A Gazebo pipeline generates procedural forest stands containing 80-200 trees across three species. A pretrained Pix2Pix model translates rendered RGB images into a synthetic near-infrared band, and Light Field Rendering produces aligned focal stacks of 550 planes across three channels. Four architectures were evaluated on a held-out scene. The plain 2D U-Net achieved an IoU of 0.6290, outperforming the volumetric 3D U-Net (0.5707). Established reconstruction methods performed substantially worse: COLMAP achieved 0.3446 and DepthAnything3 0.2959, both after their respective optimal dilation sweeps. An RGB-input variant of the volumetric architecture achieved the highest IoU of 0.6514 without dilation or per-scene calibration. These results highlight the limitations of conventional reconstruction methods, which recover visible surfaces but struggle to infer occupancy within closed canopies.

title: Bilinear Korányi spherical maximal function on the Heisenberg group
abstract: We introduce the bilinear Korányi spherical means on the Heisenberg group $\mathbb{H}^n,$ and derive $L^{p_1}(\mathbb{H}^n) \times L^{p_2}(\mathbb{H}^n) \to L^{p}(\mathbb{H}^n)$ estimates for the associated bilinear Korányi spherical maximal function on $\mathbb{H}^n.$ We also address multilinear extensions of our results.

title: Eigenstates on $O^\ast$-algebras with an application to ladder operators
abstract: Following some recent results, we consider here a particular class of states on a $O^\ast$-algebra $\M$ which we call {\em eigenstates of an element} $A\in\M$, and we deduce some of their properties. Then, we apply our definition to a family of ladder elements, i.e. elements of $\M$ obeying certain algebraic (commutation) relations which are physically motivated, and we discuss several results for these states

title: Good slopes, congruence preservation, and gaps over residue rings
abstract: For $n\ge2$, a good slope of a permutation $f$ of $\mathbb{Z}_n=\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$ is an element $m\in\mathbb{Z}_n$ for which $x\mapsto f(x)+mx$ is a permutation. We call $f$ congruence-preserving if it preserves congruences modulo every divisor of $n$. For odd prime powers $n$, we classify all permutations with more than $n/2$ good slopes. Among permutations that are not congruence-preserving, we determine the maximum number of good slopes for $n=3^e$ with $e\ge2$, and for $n=25$, $125$ and $625$. Every permutation of $\mathbb{Z}_n$ has at most $φ(n)$ good slopes, where $φ$ is Euler's totient function. For several families of moduli with at least two distinct prime divisors, we prove a sharp upper bound for the number of good slopes of the permutations with fewer than $φ(n)$ good slopes. These families include $9q$ and $3q^e$ for every prime $q\ge5$ and every $e\ge1$. Together with a companion paper, this settles the bound for every odd composite modulus below $105$.

title: Mutual-Coupling-Aware Joint Precoding and Antenna Positioning for Movable-Antenna MU-MIMO Systems
abstract: Movable antennas (MAs) improve wireless communications by adapting antenna positions to the propagation environment. However, antenna movement also changes the mutual coupling (MC) among elements of the transmit and receive arrays, which affects the performance of MA-enabled systems. In this paper, we investigate MC-aware joint precoding and antenna positioning for a downlink multiuser multiple-input multiple-output (MU-MIMO) system with MAs at both the base station and users. We establish an MC-aware system model by combining field-response propagation with a circuit-based representation of the transmit and receive arrays. Based on this model, we formulate a weighted sum-rate (WSR) maximization problem that jointly optimizes multi-stream precoders and antenna positions. The problem is challenging because the precoders and positions are coupled through the propagation channels and position-dependent MC matrices. To address this challenge, we reformulate the problem in the antenna-current domain to to efficiently handle the MC matrices and develop a current-domain weighted minimum mean square error (WMMSE) framework for alternating optimization. Furthermore, we handle the nonconvex position updates within the framework by using majorization--minimization (MM) and solve the resulting convex subproblems with a dedicated conic alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) algorithm. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed design improves the WSR over both an MC-aware fixed array and a movable-array design that ignores MC during optimization.

title: Wigner-Function Fingerprints of Collective Excitations in Mirror-Terminated Waveguide QED
abstract: We investigate the emission profiles of singly excited collective states and propose a matched-mode witnessing protocol in a mirror-terminated waveguide quantum electrodynamics system. The amplitudes and relative phases of the initial collective excitation are encoded in the temporal mode of the emitted single-photon wavepacket, providing a route to state verification through the common waveguide output. We identify the emission mode associated with a chosen target state and employ an auxiliary virtual-cavity representation to evaluate the quantum state of this selected output mode. For a matched initial state, the selected mode contains the emitted single photon, whose Wigner function exhibits a pronounced non-classical negative dip, serving as a distinct fingerprint of the target many-body state. With the reference mode held fixed, different initial configurations yield different photon occupations and phase-space distributions, demonstrating the state selectivity of the protocol. These results connect collective-state verification with temporal-mode analysis of the emitted radiation, offering access to collective coherence with reduced reliance on qubit-resolved correlation measurements.

title: SEEK-VAU: Towards Evidence-Faithful Video Anomaly Understanding via Agentic Search
abstract: Most video anomaly understanding (VAU) systems still infer anomaly judgments from evidence collected in a feed-forward way under predefined rules, typically sampled frames, or events clustered from such frames. This protocol fails when the collected evidence is incomplete under imperfect predefined rules, because once reasoning begins the model can no longer search for the missing evidence. We address this limitation with SEEK-VAU, which reframes VAU as an agentic search-and-verify interaction protocol under a bounded search budget: instead of passively reasoning over pre-collected evidence, the policy actively gathers evidence across the three stages of an anomaly event chain (precursor, trigger, and aftermath) and verifies its sufficiency before finalization, turning event-chain completeness into an explicit design rather than an outcome of predefined rules. A bounded budget caps the cost of this search, but does not by itself teach the policy where to look or when to stop. To make this behavior learnable, we introduce evidence-faithful counterfactual verification (EFCV), which rewards selected evidence that remains supportive, compact, and necessary under counterfactual verification. We further introduce SEEK-Bench, featuring video-level episodes with temporal interval annotations, semantic QA and event-chain stage labels. Together, SEEK-VAU and SEEK-Bench establish a strong foundation for evidence-faithful and actively verifiable VAU.

title: CosmosAlpha: Multi-Relational Graph Search with Pareto-Guided Exploration for LLM-Driven Alpha Mining
abstract: Discovering predictive alpha factors from noisy financial data is a fundamental yet challenging problem in quantitative finance. LLM-driven formulaic alpha mining offers an attractive paradigm by combining interpretable symbolic expressions with iterative generation and refinement guided by quantitative feedback. However, existing generation-centric and tree-based search strategies primarily organize factors through generation lineage, leaving structural and statistical relationships across search branches underutilized. Consequently, information remains localized along parent--child trajectories, which can confine exploration to redundant regions. Moreover, effective factor discovery must account for multiple distinct objectives that cannot be adequately captured by a single search criterion. We introduce CosmosAlpha, a graph-based LLM factor-mining framework that represents discovered factors as a multi-relational graph encoding generation lineage, expression-structure similarity, and cross-sectional exposure correlation. A Graph Flow mechanism propagates search utilities across the graph, allowing each factor to be assessed using relational evidence from nearby factors rather than in isolation. Pareto-guided selection jointly considers quality, fertility and diversity, explicitly modeling their trade-offs within a multi-objective search framework. Across CSI 300 and CSI 500, CosmosAlpha-Graph achieves the best mean rank over seven predictive and portfolio metrics and outperforms its controlled CosmosAlpha-MCTS counterpart on every reported metric, showing a consistent advantage for relational graph search in LLM-driven factor mining. The source code is available at https://github.com/wzhmtldswz/CosmosAlpha

title: Inter-Agent Influence: Evaluating Persuasion, Deception, and Coercion in Multi-Agent Systems
abstract: The deployment of AI agents in multi-agent settings enables inter-agent influence, whereby agents can strategically steer each other's behaviour towards an intended outcome. Such capabilities pose novel risks, as malicious agents could direct others towards harmful actions. In this work we investigate three such capabilities - persuasion, deception, and coercion - across five realistic evaluation environments and a variety of agents instantiated with frontier language models. We observed significant inter-agent influence capabilities; in oversight environments, all tested models shifted overseer decisions from rejection to approval through persuasion, deception, or coercion. We also observed successful influence in non-hierarchical 'peer-to-peer' settings through redirection of a peer's safety research trajectory. As multi-agent deployments become increasingly commonplace, these results point to a pressing need for work on mitigating the risks from inter-agent influence. Code and data are available at https://github.com/Cooperative-AI-Foundation/inter-agent-influence.

title: Up in smoke: carbon-destruction in the terrestrial planet-forming region of a young Class I disk
abstract: Earth's surface and deep mantle are strongly depleted in carbon compared to the Sun. Sublimation of solid carbonaceous material in the inner midplanes of young disks could cause this depletion. We study such thermal processing in HOPS-68, a Class I protostar with a rich hydrocarbon spectrum. A companion paper has shown that it is recondensing refractory dust from a hot inner disk region, and that oxygen-bearing species are tracing a warm (300-500 K) molecular layer entrained in a disk-wind. In this work, we analyze the carbon species in the JWST spectrum of this source using local thermal equilibrium slab models. We detect warm (~400 K) HCN and C2H2 at the base of a disk wind, as well as colder (~40 K) C4H2, CH3, and CS in the outer disk or outflow cavity wall. Additionally, 13CCH2, CH4, and C6H2 are detected, while ALMA observations reveal C2H tracing the outflow cavity walls. We suggest that in a "refractory carbon destruction zone" in the inner disk, carbon-bearing species are released from the grains, possibly contributing to the observed carbon depletion of Earth. The disk wind then redistributes carbon carried by HCN and C2H2 from the inner disk to the colder outer disk, where UV-induced gas-phase reactions with C2H in the outflow cavity walls could produce the aliphatic carbon chains seen. This result implies that the Warm Carbon Chain Chemistry (WCCC, e.g. N. Sakai & S. Yamamoto 2013) might trace outflows rather than infall. The formation of aliphatic chains in the disk wind could promote the abundant aliphatic organics found in meteorites and asteroids.

title: Machine-Learning Molecular Dynamics Reveals Grotthuss Transport in Concentrated Electrolytes
abstract: Proton transfer is responsible for the anomalous high conductivity in acidic or basic aqueous solutions. Yet, the contribution of the proton transfer mechanism to the conductivity of concentrated aqueous solutions is unknown. In this work, we compute the transport properties of KOH(aq) systems with different concentrations, using Molecular Dynamics simulations with a Machine Learning Interatomic Potential (MLIP), which includes proton transfer. We quantify the contribution of the proton transfer mechanism to the diffusivities of hydroxide ions and water molecules, and the ionic conductivity and transport numbers of the electrolytes. The contribution is substantial at lower concentrations, but diminishes at very high concentrations.

title: Distributionally Robust Search: The Power of Information and the Limits of Moments
abstract: We study binary search for a target drawn from a distribution on $n$ ordered elements. The cost is the expected number of comparison queries. In our distributionally robust framework, the algorithm knows only an uncertainty set containing the distribution and minimizes its worst-case approximation ratio against an optimal strategy that knows the distribution. Collections of uncertainty sets capture different forms of information: quantiles, moments, general linear measurements, or approximate CDFs. This framework quantifies how much and what form of information is needed for near-optimal search. Our main result separates moments from general linear measurements. Although $n-1$ moments determine the distribution exactly, for every constant $δ\in(0,1)$, the first $n^{1-δ}$ exact moments can be as uninformative for search as no information: the worst-case approximation ratio remains $Ω(\log n)$. In contrast, for every constant $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$, $O(n^\varepsilon\log^4 n)$ suitably chosen linear measurements suffice for an $O(1/\varepsilon)$-approximation. The limitation lies in the measurements chosen, rather than linearity itself. Using LP duality and polynomial bounds of Rakhmanov and Bernstein, we construct distributions with identical moments and mass concentrated at different positions. For the upper bound, we combine dyadic sketches and Johnson--Lindenstrauss embeddings with a truncated median-search algorithm that converts uniform CDF approximation into search guarantees. Measuring information in bits, we prove a lower bound of $Ω(1/\varepsilon)$ on the approximation ratio for summaries of any form using at most $\frac12 n^\varepsilon\log n$ bits, for every sufficiently small constant $\varepsilon>0$. Quantiles match this within constant factors. For Kolmogorov balls of radius $n^{-\varepsilon}$ the optimal approximation ratio is $Θ(1/\varepsilon)$.

title: Morse homology of nonsingular Morse-Smale foliations and its duality theorem
abstract: We define a Morse homology of the foliation which is defined by a general nonsingular Morse-Smale flow, applying the framework of the Conley index theory. In fact, we define a chain and a boundary homomorphism, therefore, a cochain and a cohomology are obtained as well. Furthermore, we prove a duality theorem on the homology and the cohomology.

title: Distributed LTL Synthesis under Arbitrary Message Adversaries
abstract: Reactive synthesis is the problem of generating a program that produces outputs satisfying a logical specification for every input stream. We study distributed synthesis for two processes communicating in rounds over unreliable links, with at least one message delivered in every round. Despite this delivery guarantee, we show that synthesis from linear temporal logic specifications is undecidable, even when messages carry the processes' complete causal histories. More generally, we give a complete characterization of the communication restrictions that make synthesis decidable. Restrictions are described by a message adversary $A$, a set of allowed infinite graph histories: sequences of communication graphs, each specifying which messages are delivered in a round. Iterated chromatic subdivision associates these histories with points in the unit interval, yielding an image $π(A) \subseteq [0,1]$. For every $ω$-regular message adversary $A$, synthesis is decidable if and only if $π(A)$ is nowhere dense. In the decidable cases, our procedure takes a deterministic parity automaton for $A$ and a specification, decides realizability, and constructs a realizing distributed algorithm whenever one exists. Further, our topological arguments shed new light on the fundamental requirements of synthesis. They show that, for $ω$-regular message adversaries, synthesis is decidable if and only if consensus is repeatedly solvable in bounded time. This links two previously unrelated problems from formal verification and distributed computing through the processes' uncertainty about communication.

title: Tensor preduals, positive homogeneity and harmonicity in two-Lipschitz spaces
abstract: We study subspaces of two-Lipschitz mappings using group actions and tensor preduals. We first show that the ambient spaces contain large classical sequence spaces. We then use similarity actions to select smaller subspaces. Character-equivariant mappings form weak$^*$-closed fixed-point spaces and admit quotient tensor preduals. We give two applications. For mappings on Banach spaces, we describe positive homogeneity in each variable and construct bounded projections. For mappings on finitely generated groups, we characterize harmonicity in each variable. We show that the harmonic predual is the projective tensor product of the corresponding one-variable quotient preduals.

title: Optimized size, shape and orientation of rhombic transposition flaps and excisions by gradient-based methods
abstract: This work presents a new method for gradient-based optimization of the rhombic transposition flap and the excision it closes, which set the strain of the skin after closure. Previous studies swept at most three parameters. Here, using structural optimization methods, up to eight variables, two flap angles, two cut lengths and the size, shape and position of the rhombic excision, are optimized under up to 32 geometric and stress constraints. The skin is a pre-stretched, incompressible hyperelastic membrane that wrinkles instead of carrying compression. Smoothed level-sets on a fixed grid represent the cuts, and springs between interpolated points the sutures, so designs change without remeshing and the adjoint method gives the sensitivities. The energy the surgery adds to the skin is minimized, and the model reproduces the energies of a published 48-design sweep with a median deviation of 5%. The optimal flap angles, $(-23^\circ, 31^\circ)$, lie outside the swept range and add 63% less energy than the Limberg flap and 15% less than the best swept design. Under unequal in-vivo tension, the optimal flap turns with the direction of the tension. Fitting the excision to the lesion and its margin lowers the energy by a further 35%, and with all eight variables it is 78% below the Limberg flap. This optimum is the same for finer grids, narrower cuts and wider undermining, although wider undermining reduces its gain. Lowering its suture-line stress by 41% costs only 2.3% more energy.

title: Fat base schemes and unexpected hypersurfaces of type $(d+k,d)$
abstract: We study hypersurfaces of degree $d+k$ containing a prescribed zero-dimensional fat point scheme $Z\subset\mathbb{P}^n$ and having multiplicity at least $d$ along a general codimension-two linear subspace. We associate with this interpolation problem a vector bundle on $\mathbb{P}^1$ whose splitting type determines the dimensions of all linear systems of type $(d+k,d)$. For a fat point of multiplicity $m$, we determine the exact number of conditions detected by this bundle and introduce the corresponding effective length. This leads to an excess formula separating the contributions of the splitting type, the part of the fat structure invisible to degree-$k$ fibrewise sections, and the Hilbert-function defect of the fixed scheme. We also prove a truncation theorem showing that multiplicities larger than $k$ contribute only a uniform twist of the bundle and, geometrically, fixed hyperplane components. Finally, we exhibit explicit planar and three-dimensional examples showing that genuinely unexpected phenomena persist for nonreduced fixed base schemes, including geometrically irreducible unexpected hypersurfaces.

title: Curriculum unlearning in humans and neural networks
abstract: During learning, humans often benefit from curricula that teach simple rules before exceptions. However, we lack a computational explanation for this phenomenon. Here, using a canonical behavioural task and modelling with neural networks, we develop and test a theory for why simple-to-complex curricula succeed. We show that during learning, both humans and neural networks show simplicity biases, a tendency to learn simple rules that are underfit to the data. In neural networks this bias is accompanied by compression of neural representations. Simple-to-complex curricula help both types of learners overcome this compression, developing representations (and policy) with appropriate dimensionality for the task. We test and confirm a further prediction from this theory: learners that have been pre-exposed to simple tasks and with more compressed initial representations benefit more from curricula. These findings suggest that curricula help with ``unlearning'' of simple rules.

title: A research world model of power engineering learns its dynamics and reveals what-ifs
abstract: Decisions about the direction of research in power engineering determine which technologies mature and, through them, shape infrastructure that lasts decades, yet their consequences cannot be observed before they are taken, and existing forecasts of research fields extrapolate a single trajectory. Here we introduce research world models, which treat a research field as a dynamical system that can be acted upon, and establish one for power engineering from 1.1 million papers. A distilled language model reads each paper into role-typed concepts, two sophisticated, high-fidelity graph-temporal neural network cores learn how the resulting concept network evolves, and operators learned from natural experiments in the publication record estimate the effects of interventions. In temporally held-out tests, the model forecast years ahead which concepts would grow and which method-target pairs would be joined for the first time, outperforming tuned machine-learning baselines in most settings, and its estimated intervention effects tracked those realized in natural experiments it had not seen. Its training scheme and three of its operators replicated in two fields withheld from development. Questions posed in natural language are compiled by a domain-specialized 27-billion-parameter language model into executable actions and answered as paired simulations with and without the intervention. The answers were rated 4.1 of 5 for faithfulness by an independent language-model judge. By revealing the latent dynamics of a research field and its response to interventions, research world models offer a new way to simulate and test research decisions before they are made.

title: A Detailed Polarimetric Imaging Study of Type II Solar Radio Burst with the MWA: Detection of Linear Polarization
abstract: Type II radio bursts, produced by magnetohydrodynamic shocks propagating through the solar corona and interplanetary medium, serve as powerful diagnostics of shock properties and ambient coronal magnetic fields. While circular polarization in type II bursts has been extensively studied, most investigations rely on dynamic spectra (DS), providing only spatially integrated measurements. DS obscures spatial variations of the polarization sign and magnitude, potentially causing cancellation effects and misrepresenting true polarization levels. We present a full-polarimetric imaging study of a metric type II burst observed with the Murchison Widefield Array at 78--133 MHz. Remarkably, we report the first detection of linear polarization in a metric type II burst, reaching a polarization fraction of $\sim12\%$ with significant spectro-temporal variability across observing bands. The spectro-temporal, spatial, and morphological properties found in this study establish linear polarization as a new diagnostic of large-scale coronal and interplanetary magnetic field structure through full-Stokes imaging of metric solar radio bursts -- challenging conventional paradigms predicting negligible linear polarization from coherent plasma emission processes.

title: Time-invariant negativity and persistent bound entanglement in a cyclic two-qutrit family
abstract: We study the entanglement dynamics of two qutrits under collective dephasing for a family of states obtained by mixing a maximally entangled state that lives in the decoherence-free subspace with three nonstationary two-term states sharing a common amplitude ratio $r$. We obtain exact PPT and separability regions along the whole trajectory, a specialization of known results on cyclic sign invariant states, and we supply explicit certificates: a finite product decomposition, three fixed positive-map witnesses, and a closed realignment formula that detects every PPT-entangled state, so that no state is left undecided. The negativity is computed in closed form. It shows that the entanglement is time-invariant, positive and constant from the initial time although the state changes, exactly when the weight of the maximally entangled state exceeds the threshold $U_r=r/(1+r+r^2)$. To our knowledge, this is the first demonstration of time-invariant entanglement for qutrit--qutrit systems under collective dephasing. For smaller weights the entanglement decays and vanishes at a finite time: the state either becomes separable (entanglement sudden death) or, for $r\neq1$ in an intermediate range, loses distillability suddenly and remains bound entangled at all later times. Every state with negative partial transpose is one-copy distillable by a fixed local projection. The same trajectories arise from the global dephasing map and from a correlated local random-unitary semigroup, although the two channels differ on product inputs. Exact rational benchmarks and embeddings of the Horodecki and Ha--Kye--Park families are provided.

title: Abelian embeddings make useful promises: approximation of detrivialised equations
abstract: We study the following family of search problems: given a system of equations $x+y+z\equiv 0\pmod p$ promised to admit a solution that is nonconstant on every equation, find a $c$-colouring of the variables that makes no equation monochromatic. For $p\in\{2,3\}$, the problem recovers known tractable Promise Constraint Satisfaction Problems (PCSPs). For $p > 3$, we obtain a complete complexity classification: the problem is polynomial-time solvable for $c \geq 4$, yet even its decision version is NP-hard for $c = 3$, and it is not well-defined for $c = 2$. Our main conceptual contribution is a general tractability framework for PCSPs based on Abelian embeddings, a notion introduced by Bhangale, Khot, and Minzer [STOC 2022] in the study of quantitative approximation of satisfiable CSPs. We show that suitable Abelian embeddings yield polynomial-time PCSP reductions realised by singleton algorithms in the sense of Zhuk [FOCS 2026]. On the hardness side, the promise relation is far removed from the reconfigurable regime covered by the conditional hardness framework of Banakh, Barsukov, and Nakajima [LICS 2026]; our proof instead relies on a new additive-combinatorial rigidity theorem classifying special $3$-colourings of $\mathbb{Z}_p$.

title: Setting the Stage: Enhancing Music Recommendations with Spoken Introductions to Stimulate Serendipity
abstract: People like to keep their music listening fresh and interesting, but recommender systems often struggle to support this need. Even when a recommended song is potentially refreshing and enriching, listeners may not perceive it as such. Building on Silvia's appraisal theory of interest, this paper studies whether enhancing recommendations with spoken introductions, immersive or informative, can stimulate two distinct flavors of experienced serendipity: taste-broadening (sparking interest in music outside one's typical preferences) and taste-deepening (deepening interest in music within one's typical preferences). Results from a large-scale user study show that both introduction types stimulate taste-broadening and taste-deepening serendipity. Taste-broadening is most effectively stimulated through transportation (absorption in a narrative world), whereas taste-deepening is most effectively stimulated through cognitive elaboration (learning something new about the artist or the social context in which the music emerged). We discuss how these findings could be translated into practice through curated taste-broadening playlists, where both introduction types appear promising, and taste-deepening playlists, where informative introductions seem particularly effective.

title: Ground-Wing: A Parametric 3D Wing-in-Ground-Effect Dataset for Benchmarking Neural Surrogate Models
abstract: This paper presents a CFD dataset of a highly parametrized 3D wing operating in ground effect, designed for benchmarking neural surrogate models for aerodynamic prediction, using a wing shape and flow conditions typically encountered in motorsport applications. The dataset comprises 770 RANS simulations of 194 unique wing configurations, sampled across 27 airfoil profile variants and 4 distances from the ground, spanning variations in wing sweep, chord, taper, angle of attack, and tip twist. Six neural network architectures representing distinct paradigms --- convolutional (DoMINO), graph-based (X-MeshGraphNet), transformer-based (AB-UPT, GeoTransolver, GAOT), and JEPA-based (AeroJEPA) --- are evaluated on their ability to predict surface pressure coefficient and wall shear stress distributions, from which integral drag and lift coefficients are recovered. The dataset is intended to be used as a challenging benchmark for surrogate CFD models, due to the uniqueness of the ground effect being absent from other wing and airfoil datasets. The dataset is available for download at https://huggingface.co/datasets/andreacenzato/Ground-Wing

title: Identifying the determinants of soccer coach turnover by competing risks models: a case study on Italian League Serie A
abstract: This paper investigates the determinants of head coach turnover in the Italian Serie A over the period 2010-2019 by explicitly accounting for multiple exit mechanisms within a competing risks framework. Four mutually exclusive exit types are considered: end of contract, mutual consent, resignation, and sacking.
