Lastly, we introduce Contrastive Prototype Entropy Adaptation, which applies entropy minimization to csID samples and entropy maximization to csOOD samples, while prototype-level contrastive learning aligns csID features with their corresponding target prototypes and reduces the maximum similarity between csOOD features and known-class prototypes. Empirically, UAPA outperforms the strongest baselines on the CIFAR benchmarks and Tiny-ImageNet-C, improving average OSCR by 2.08 and 1.28 percentage points, respectively.

title: A Relative Telescope-Type Conjecture: Support and Generation in Half-Bounded Derived Categories
abstract: Let $R$ be a commutative noetherian ring. We ask whether complexes with finitely generated cohomology and a fixed support can be generated by relatively compact objects, using coproducts which exist in the half-bounded derived category. We prove that $\mathbf D^+_{\mathrm{fg},W}(R)=\operatorname{Loc}_{\mathrm{ex}}(\mathbf D^b_{\mathrm{fg},W}(R))$ whenever $W\subseteq\operatorname{Spec} R$ is specialization closed and has finite dimension. The same equality holds for every specialization-closed subset of $\operatorname{Spec} B$ when $B$ is a finite-type algebra over a noetherian domain $A$ of finite character and either $A$ or $B$ is regular. These equalities classify the thick Hom-submodules closed under existing coproducts. We also prove the corresponding bounded-above statement from the support results of Matsui--Takahashi. For an arbitrary noetherian ring, the bounded-below generation conjecture reduces to torsion complexes over quotient domains, with their support unchanged. Finally, over a regular noetherian domain of infinite dimension, we give a bounded-below object which is generated by bounded objects with the same support but has no bounded-below representative by finitely generated modules. The comparison functor from the bounded-below derived category of finite modules is therefore neither full nor essentially surjective.

title: Two-block paths in oriented graphs under the Ore-type condition
abstract: Stein conjectured that for every positive integer $k$, every oriented graph with minimum semi-degree greater than $k/2$ contains every oriented path of length $k$ [Springer Optim.Appl. 165 (2020), 459--486]. For directed paths this is a classical result of Jackson (1981). The two-block case of the conjecture was established by Chen, Hou and Zhou (2025). In this paper we prove the two-block analogue of Jackson's theorem. For all positive integers $s$ and $r$, let $P(s,r)$ be the oriented path consisting of two directed paths of lengths $s$ and $r$ with a common terminal vertex, and let $Q(s,r)$ be its reverse. We show that for all $K\ge3$ and all $s,r\ge1$ with $s+r\le K$, every oriented graph $D$ with $δ(D)\ge K$ and $d_D^+(u)+d_D^-(v)\ge K-1$ for every ordered pair of distinct vertices $(u,v)\notin A(D)$ contains both $P(s,r)$ and $Q(s,r)$. Our result is the two-block analogue of Jackson's theorem, and it extends the two-block result of Chen, Hou and Zhou. The proof iterates a shift of the terminal vertex of a longest path.

title: Just Between Us? Exploring a Wearable-Mediated Channel for Discreet Human-Agent Interaction in a Shared Game Setting
abstract: In shared settings, social robots may need to exchange information with an individual while limiting co-present others' access to or interpretation of that information. Publicly observable speech and gestures may not adequately support such exchanges. We investigate a wearable-mediated channel for discreet interaction that combines in-ear audio messages with deliberate rightward head tilts as responses. To examine its feasibility and participants' experiences, we studied 20 pairs (40 participants) playing a card game with a screen-based conversational agent representing a social robot, controlled by a researcher in a Wizard-of-Oz setup. Each pair played with and without the channel. One participant wore the device (the wearer), while the other (the non-wearer) was informed about the channel after gameplay. The channel conveyed information that could help the wearer or robot character select an opponent they could defeat. The information exchange and subsequent opponent selection occurred as intended in 39 of 40 channel-mediated turns. Wearers reported low perceived pressure/tension in both conditions, with no statistically significant difference between conditions, and favorable usability immediately after use. Retrospective interviews, however, revealed varied accounts of noticing the interaction among non-wearers and contrasting perceptions of teamwork and unfairness. These findings support the feasibility of wearable-mediated exchanges within this game and identify awareness and fairness as considerations for future designs.

title: Rate-Distortion-Perception Tradeoff for Vector Gaussian Sources with Limited Common Randomness: Exact Characterization and Approximate Universality
abstract: The distortion-rate-common randomness-perception (DRCP) theory characterizes how limited common randomness (CR) improves reconstruction fidelity under perceptual constraints, thereby providing an information-theoretic foundation for generative compression. In this paper, we characterize the DRCP tradeoff for vector Gaussian sources with limited CR under the squared-error distortion measure and the squared Wasserstein-2 perception measure. Specifically, we first establish a generalized reverse waterfilling characterization of globally optimal allocations. Second, we derive an analytical upper bound on the DRCP function through sequential greedy allocation of rate and CR. For fixed rate and CR budgets, the resulting representation is independent of the perception threshold. Finally, we establish its approximate universality through uniform performance guarantees: the achievable distortion exceeds the optimal distortion by at most $2ρ^*\approx0.2897$ times the total source variance, whereas the optimal-to-greedy distortion ratio is at least $η^*\approx0.7517$.

title: Quantum Simulation of Electronic Structure using Quantum Density Functional Theory on a Programmable Integrated Photonic Circuit
abstract: Quantum simulations of molecular electronic structure hold the potential for computational advantage but are inherently limited by the linear scaling of qubit requirements with respect to system size. Quantum Density Functional Theory (Q-DFT) addresses this constraint by reformulating the interacting many-body problem in terms of a non-interacting Kohn--Sham reference system. Here, we present and experimentally validate a Q-DFT algorithm that requires only $\mathcal{O}(\log_2(N))$ qubits to simulate a system of $N$ orbitals, thereby reducing resource overhead. More precisely, we solve the Kohn--Sham problem for the lithium hydride (LiH) molecule using the ensemble extension of the variational quantum eigensolver paradigm that minimizes the energy of the system in the subspace spanned by the ground and first excited states. To execute this task, we encode the problem with qubits on a quantum photonic platform, utilizing an architecture that combines a deterministic quantum dot single-photon source with a programmable integrated photonic circuit. By evaluating the molecular ground- and first excited-state properties, this work establishes a pathway for simulating larger molecular systems, demonstrating the viability of integrating qubit-efficient algorithms with advanced reconfigurable photonic hardware for near-term quantum chemistry applications.

title: Surrogate Models for Stochastic Al-Cu Phase-Field Solidification
abstract: Phase-field models resolve microstructural evolution during rapid alloy solidification, but their computational cost limits long trajectories, stochastic ensembles, and studies across process conditions. We present a variance-preserving denoising diffusion bridge model (VP-DDBM) for state-conditioned prediction of two-dimensional Al-Cu solidification. Given the current phase, concentration, and prescribed temperature fields, the model predicts the subsequent state and is applied autoregressively. Across two held-out thermal gradients, VP-DDBM produces lower long-horizon errors than deterministic U-Net and SI-ConvNeXt baselines in domain-mean phase, domain-mean Cu concentration, and leading-tip position. It also retains fine dendritic structure over long rollouts, whereas the deterministic U-Net progressively smooths the morphology. VP-DDBM predicts the phase and concentration evolution approximately $73\times$ faster than the phase-field solver, showing potential for faster process-condition screening and ensemble-based microstructure studies.

title: Precise and accurate nuclear electric quadrupole moment of $^{223}$Ra from molecular spectroscopy
abstract: Nuclear electric quadrupole moments of unstable isotopes are commonly extracted from laser spectroscopy of the atomic hyperfine structure, where the accuracy is limited to the several-percent level by the available electric-field-gradient (EFG) calculations. In this study, we determine the spectroscopic quadrupole moment of $^{223}$Ra (half-life $t_{1/2} = 11.4$ d) from hyperfine-resolved collinear resonance ionization spectroscopy of the radioactive molecule $^{223}$Ra$^{19}$F. The $X\,^2Σ^+$ electronic ground state of RaF provides a large axial EFG at the radium nucleus that can be calculated with relativistic coupled-cluster theory to sub-percent accuracy. Together with a three-fold improvement in spectral resolution over previous fast-beam measurements of radioactive molecules, this yields $Q_s = +1.211(7)_\mathrm{stat}(2)_\mathrm{syst}(5)_\mathrm{theo}\,e\mathrm{b}$ for $^{223}$Ra with a total uncertainty of 0.73%, approximately three times better than atomic and ionic determinations. This result demonstrates that molecular spectroscopy can provide access to the electromagnetic structure of unstable nuclei with a precision competitive with, and in favorable cases better than, atomic spectroscopy, and may thus be envisioned for studies beyond the limitations of current radioactive-atom experiments.

title: When Ground Truth Is Not Ground Truth: Automatic Labeling for Hallucination Detection
abstract: Hallucinations in Large Language Models (LLMs) remain a major challenge, as they can produce misleading, factually incorrect, or unverifiable information, thereby undermining their trustworthiness and reliability. However, reliable ground-truth labels remain a key challenge in evaluating hallucination detectors. Recent studies often construct labels automatically by comparing model generations with reference answers using similarity metrics such as BLEURT. This implicitly treats BLEURT similarity as a proxy for hallucination, despite its English-centric supervision, unbounded score range, and design as a similarity metric rather than a factuality measure, making threshold-based ground-truth construction potentially unreliable. Through comprehensive experiments using 15 automatic supervision judges, seven hallucination detection baselines, two generator models, two QA datasets, and five languages, we demonstrate that detector performance varies substantially with the choice of supervision judge. Human validation reveals substantial differences in labeling reliability, with QGen-9B achieving the lowest overall misclassification rate (12.86%), while BLEURT and BLEURT-n exhibit rates of 47.23% and 47.32%, respectively. Our findings highlight the limitations of automatic similarity-based labeling and the need for more reliable judging methods that better capture semantic and factual correctness.

title: Characterization of Integral Transforms for Hilbert Space-Valued Functions
abstract: The aim of this paper is to characterize the Fourier transform of functions taking values in a separable Hilbert space $\Hi$ and defined on locally compact abelian groups. Inspired by Krukowskis characterization of integral transforms on locally compact abelian groups, we establish characterizations of the Fourier, Laplace, and cosine transforms for separable Hilbert space-valued functions on locally compact abelian groups. Furthermore, we obtain a characterization of the group Fourier transform on the Heisenberg group.

title: Glauber Dynamics for Sampling Colorings: Rapid Mixing above $(1+1/\mathrm{e})Δ$ via Hidden Hard-Core Models
abstract: We show that for every $γ>0$ and every sufficiently large $Δ$, the Glauber dynamics for proper $q$-colorings of any $n$-vertex graph of maximum degree $Δ$ has spectral gap $Ω_γ(1/n)$, and hence mixing time $O_γ(n^2\log q)$, whenever $q\ge(1+1/\mathrm{e}+γ)Δ$. Our proof establishes a Bochner-type inequality by exploiting the spectral gaps of hard-core models hidden in the color classes. The constant $1+1/\mathrm{e}\approx1.368$ comes from the uniqueness threshold $\approx\mathrm{e}/Δ$ of the hard-core model on the infinite $Δ$-regular tree.

title: One-shot Distributed Learning via Weighted Averaging with Server-side Information
abstract: Distributed learning has drawn considerable attention due to its capability of learning from distributed data without aggregating raw observations. However, frequent exchange of model updates can become the main bottleneck of communication. Therefore, one-shot approaches where each worker fits a local model and sends it to the server to aggregate emerge. It is known that averaging can achieve the so-called pooled-data mean squared error (MSE) order of a hypothetical node that has access to data from the server and all the workers, and performs empirical risk minimization (ERM) on it. However, when the number of workers increases too fast compared to the local sample size, nonzero local estimation bias prevents averaging from achieving this order. In this paper, we study whether independent server data can overcome this limitation. We consider $m$ workers with $n$ observations each and a server with $p$ observations, all i.i.d., giving $N=mn+p$ observations in total. Under certain regularity conditions, a pooled-data ERM achieves MSE of order $\mathcal O(N^{-1})$. We analyze deterministic nonnegative averaging of convex-loss M-estimators, with equal worker weights and the server's own estimator included. Under our assumptions, including nonzero local bias of order $n^{-α}$, $α\geq1$, sample-size weighted averaging achieves the pooled-data MSE order whenever $m=\mathcal O(n^{2α-1})$. Above this worker scale, it does so if and only if $p=Ω(nm\cdot m/n^{2α-1})$. Hence, server-only estimation, whose MSE is of order $\mathcal{O}(p^{-1})$, can achieve pooled-data order while sample-size weighting fails. Analytical examples and synthetic experiments illustrate when averaging matches the pooled-data MSE order, complemented by CIFAR-10 experiments comparing aggregation strategies with linear and nonlinear classifiers.

title: Proving the Wrong Program: Miscompilations as a Threat to zkVM Guarantees
abstract: A zero-knowledge virtual machine (zkVM) lets an untrusted prover convince a verifier that a program, typically Rust compiled to RISC-V, ran correctly. The proof covers the compiled binary, so a miscompilation can make a correct zkVM produce a valid proof of a computation that differs from the developer's source. We present the first empirical study of miscompilation as a threat to zkVM guarantees, on the production zkVMs SP1 and Jolt. We assemble 88 known rustc and LLVM miscompilations with Rust reproducers, using an LLM agent to recover Rust triggers for 60 of 124 LLVM bugs reported only as LLVM IR. Many of the bugs carry over to zkVMs: 48 of the 88 make a guest commit a wrong output on SP1 and 46 on Jolt, including the same 15 rustc bugs on both. Most bugs that do not reproduce never reach the faulty code on the zkVM's target, e.g. because they need an instruction-set extension. Existing guest programs are rarely affected by accident. Across 13 guests of 10 popular SP1 projects, the buggy and the fixed compiler produce byte-identical binaries in 447 of the 552 guest-bug pairs that build, and the other 105 have the same code or agree on every input we ran. An attacker who contributes code to a guest, however, can trigger these bugs on purpose. For about $40 per project, an LLM agent found patches that look like ordinary optimisations, preserve the behaviour of the guest's source, and expose a known bug in 12 of 366 project-bug pairs, across 11 of 20 projects. In four cases the guest commits a wrong output, including an Ethereum client that rejects a valid block, and in the other eight it fails on a valid input. Reviewing or formally verifying the zkVM or the guest's source cannot catch such a patch, because both are correct. zkVM projects should treat their compiler as part of their trusted base and track the known bugs of their toolchain.

title: The Stringy Origin of Kerr Multipoles
abstract: We construct a new family of exact open and closed bosonic string solutions in flat spacetime that reproduce the root-Kerr and Kerr multipoles at every fixed multipole order in the large-mass and large-angular-momentum limit. These solutions provide explicit classical data for identifying associated quantum string states and testing their correspondence with rotating black holes.

title: Statistical approach of random packing of polydisperse similar hyperspheres: with application to binomial and lognormal size distributions
abstract: This paper addresses the packing fraction of polydisperse similar hyperspheres with a discrete binomial and continuous lognormal particle size distribution. First, a closed form expression is derived of a mix consisting of multiple discrete particles in D-dimensional Euclidean space R^D with small size differences. A recently developed analytical model for binary packings with small size ratio u is used, here applying it to the statistically probable particle pairs in the multi-sized mix. The new model is subsequently applied to discretely sized particles with a binomial number distribution and a constant size ratio u between each subsequent particle size. By taking the limit of u -> 1 and an infinite number of particles sizes, the binomial particle distribution is transformed into a continuous lognormal distribution. The resulting expression for the packing fraction can be solved in closed form, resulting in an original expression for the packing fraction of mixtures of hyperparticles with a lognormal distribution. This explicit expression is governed by the standard deviation, the Euclidean dimension D, and the monosized packing fraction of the considered particle shape. For a number of particle shapes and their packing modes (from looser to denser) the scaled expression is thoroughly compared with data reported in the literature. They concern packed particles with small standard deviations and in Euclidean dimensions D = 2 and 3, and good agreement is found. For large standard deviations the scaled packing fraction approaches a limiting value, which appears not to depend on the Euclidean dimension. Based on the insight, a closed form expression is put forward for the packing fraction that matches the small standard deviation solution, and the large standard deviation asymptote, so covering arbitrary standard deviations, Euclidean dimensions, particle types, and their mode of packing.

title: Closed- and open-system characterization of the Yukawa-SYK model in real time
abstract: Strongly correlated matter without quasiparticles is central to many-body physics, quantum chaos, and quantum gravity, motivating a considerable effort toward its realization in tabletop experiments. Two challenges remain: laboratory platforms are open systems, so conformal behavior must survive dissipation, and it must be identified through measurable quantities. We address both challenges in the Yukawa-Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev (YSYK) model, in which bosons and fermions interact as in, e.g., light-matter systems, but through random all-to-all couplings that drive the boson to criticality without fine tuning. Solving the model in real time using the Schwinger-Keldysh formalism, we treat closed and open systems within a unified framework and, in both cases, consider a thermal steady state to map their phase diagrams. In addition to the known conformal and impurity (or SYK$_2$) regimes, we identify novel high-temperature regimes in which the fermions are driven by an essentially bare boson and show that their dynamics is captured by a quadratic model with time-dependent random hopping. Across all regimes, the fermionic softening of the boson is bounded by a ``criticality budget'' determined only by the Yukawa coupling and the temperature. Coupling the boson with a thermal environment induces a mass shift that deforms the boundaries between different regimes and exhausts the criticality budget, thus imposing a bound on temperature and dissipation rate compatible with self-tuned criticality. We further introduce a set of markers built from the two-point functions that separate all identified regimes, are accessible in linear response, and require no fit of the conformal exponents. We complement them with the quantum Fisher information, deriving upper bounds with and without dissipation. These results may help characterize holographic quantum matter beyond the closed setting.

title: Approximating Distributions on Vertex Degrees in Random Hypergraphs via Stein's Method
abstract: Complex data are increasingly represented as hypergraphs. We establish bounds for approximating joint vertex-degree distributions by independent multivariate Poisson and correlated normal distributions in hypergraph models with independent hyperedges. We discuss the approximation of the distribution under different density regimes which are further supported by simulation studies.

title: Designing turbulence through hierarchies
abstract: Turbulence is defined by a set of emergent and singular phenomena: a constant-flux energy cascade, intermittency, a dissipation rate that survives the vanishing of viscosity, and the spontaneous loss of determinism of the inviscid limit. Which physical ingredients produce them remains unclear, because in fluids they always come together with incompressibility, spatial structure and vortex dynamics. Here we show that a hierarchy of inertia, coupled by the purely geometric nonlinearity of rigid constraints, is enough. A planar chain of rigid pendula whose lengths and masses decrease geometrically, coupled only through nearest-neighbor constraints, develops a far-from-equilibrium cascade that replaces thermal equipartition, with statistically local and time-irreversible energy transfer despite intrinsically nonlocal coupling. Its fluctuations are intermittent, yet self-similarity is restored by a hidden scale symmetry. As the viscosity vanishes, the dissipation rate saturates at a finite value, and thermal noise consistent with fluctuation-dissipation balance is amplified from the smallest to the largest scales within a fraction of a large-scale period. Because the hierarchy can be tuned and the same dynamics can be realized mechanically or electrically, turbulence becomes a property that can be designed and measured in the laboratory.

title: Methodological Assessment of Instrumented Indentation for Spatially Resolved Mesoscale Stiffness and Creep in Short Fiber-Reinforced Injection-Molded PBT Components
abstract: Instrumented indentation enables assessment of local mechanical properties in heterogeneous polymer systems, but specimen preparation and the selected indentation protocol significantly influence the quantitative interpretation of the measured response. This study develops and evaluates an experimental methodology for spatially resolved mesoscale characterization of both unreinforced and short fiber-reinforced composites. An unreinforced material system is used as a reference material to systematically examine the effects of indentation spacing, surface preparation, maximum indentation load, temporal loading parameters, and unloading evaluation. Indentation loads of 500, 1000, and 1750 mN are investigated in complementary experimental campaigns. The apparent indentation modulus exhibits moderate sensitivity to indentation load and loading time within the studied ranges. In contrast, indentation depth and the creep-related depth increment display greater sensitivity to the applied load history. Surface polishing minimizes topographical disturbances and enables reliable identification of residual indentation profiles and pile-up. Based on these methodological findings, a final load-hold-unload protocol with an indentation load of 1750 mN, a loading time of 6 s, a holding period of 300 s, and an unloading time of 4 s is applied to both unreinforced material and short fiber-reinforced composites. The mean apparent indentation modulus increases from 2.91 GPa for unreinforced material to 6.65 GPa for short fiber-reinforced composites, while the mean depth of indentation creep decreases from 2.36 to 1.91 microns. The coefficient of variation also increases for both quantities, indicating that short-fiber reinforcement enhances mean local stiffness and introduces pronounced spatial heterogeneity in both stiffness-related and time-dependent mesoscale indentation responses.

title: CLARA: A Cognitively-Driven Clarification Framework for Grounding Ambiguous Requests
abstract: Robotics and AI systems are increasingly deploying large vision-language models (LVLMs) to follow high-level instructions, from routine household chores to more complex organizational tasks. Yet, broad directives like "clean the room" or "organize the desk" frequently omit crucial details about user preferences and specific arrangement of objects that influence the desired outcome. Without any further guidance, such models tend to overestimate their grasp of ambiguous instructions and frequently assume they have sufficient understanding despite missing important details. In this paper, we propose CLARA (Conversational cLArification for Robotic Arrangement), a cognitively-driven clarification framework that proactively elicits key information from users, in a similar fashion as humans' clarification seeking behavior. Through targeted questioning, CLARA refines ambiguous requests into structured, detailed instructions describing precisely how objects should be organized or rearranged, according to the user's preferences. These clarifications then guide a diffusion-based image generation pipeline, producing realistic visual renderings of the final, desired scene. This final rendering also serves as a visual confirmation of the system's understanding from the user. Experimental results and user studies demonstrate that CLARA leads to more accurate and consistent outcomes compared to another State-of-the-Art LVLM system, highlighting the importance of interactive clarification for bridging the gap between vague directives and fully grounded task specifications.

title: Learning from Unlabeled Photographs for General Oral Image Analysis
abstract: Oral photographs contain rich clinical information and hold significant potential for artificial intelligence applications; however, most models are trained for individual tasks and rely on costly expert annotations. We hypothesized that self-supervised training on unlabeled oral photographs could produce transferable visual representations for heterogeneous vision tasks. To test this hypothesis, we developed DOVE (Dental Optical Visual Encoder) by domain-adaptive self-supervised pretraining on approximately 530,000 unlabeled oral photographs collected from publicly accessible sources. DOVE was benchmarked against 3 established baselines across 5 classification datasets and 4 segmentation datasets, covering both frozen backbone evaluation and end-to-end finetuning. DOVE achieved the strongest overall performance, ranking best in few-shot transfer and label efficiency on most benchmarks. Under the 20-shot frozen-backbone protocol, DOVE outperformed the second best DINOv3 by 4.37 percentage points in mean macro-F1 across classification datasets and by 4.49 percentage points in mean macro-Dice across segmentation tasks. Under end-to-end finetuning, DOVE achieved at least 80% of the strongest full-data baseline's performance across most evaluation datasets using only 10% of the labeled training data. Qualitative retrieval and feature analyses further indicated better organization of image-level and spatial representations. These findings support DOVE as a generalizable and label-efficient backbone for oral vision research.

title: DenseTwins: Dense Modality Decoupling for Multimodal Self-Supervision
abstract: Multimodal perception is central to many computer vision applications, including robotics and autonomous driving, where different sensing modalities provide complementary cues. Self-supervised learning offers a scalable solution for exploiting large amounts of unlabeled multimodal data. However, existing methods either neglect modality-specific information by enforcing feature-space alignment between modalities or learn only global representations without preserving spatial structure. We propose DenseTwins, a multimodal self-supervised framework that learns dense representations by explicitly decoupling the dense feature space into shared and modality-specific components. The proposed approach combines dense cross-modal correspondences with redundancy-reduction objectives, enabling the model to capture both shared semantics and modality-specific cues within a structured dense embedding space. DenseTwins jointly optimizes an intra-modal objective across augmented views and a cross-modal objective that aligns shared features while decorrelating modality-specific information. We evaluate DenseTwins across multiple multimodal benchmarks and sensing setups, achieving state-of-the-art or competitive performance across multimodal self-supervised baselines. Code available at: https://github.com/CarloSgaravatti/DenseTwins.

title: Cycle WAM: Coupling Action and Video through Cycle Consistency
abstract: Recent advances in video modeling have driven substantial progress in world action models (WAMs). Existing approaches exploit pretrained video priors by decoding actions from latent representations or inferring them from generated videos. The underlying link is causal: robot actions produce changes in the scene, and video observations of these changes provide evidence for inferring the actions that produced them. However, existing training formulations do not by themselves ensure that actions and their predicted visual consequences are consistent, potentially limiting the use of pretrained capabilities. We treat video and action as paired modalities linked by this causal relationship and learn their correspondence through a unified training framework designed to better exploit pretrained video priors. Cycle WAM first augments video-action co-training with bidirectional conversion to reinforce cross-modal correspondence and recover forward and inverse dynamics. It then introduces a differentiable cycle-reconstruction objective to further couple the two mappings. The resulting model supports both forward and inverse dynamics, with the potential to improve performance through more effective use of pretrained video priors. Cycle WAM achieves state-of-the-art performance among comparable methods on LIBERO-Pro and substantially improves DreamZero on DROID. Comparisons with UWM characterize its inverse-dynamics performance and show sharper visual detail in the displayed forward-dynamics predictions.

title: VISAGE: Vertex-based Intrinsic Surface Appearance GEneration via Dual-Stream Diffusion for Arbitrary 3D Heads
abstract: Recovering identity-faithful, physically based surface appearance for 3D human heads from sparse images remains challenging. Existing methods often rely on UV-based pipelines, introducing seam artefacts, or operate in image space, limiting surface consistency. We present VISAGE, Vertex-based Intrinsic Surface Appearance GEneration, a surface-based conditional diffusion framework that synthesises per-vertex albedo and roughness directly on arbitrary mesh topologies, without requiring consistent UV parameterisation at training time. VISAGE combines global spectral processing with local geodesic K-Nearest-Neighbour refinement, enforcing structural coherence while restoring detail beyond the truncated spectral basis. Multi-view RGB images condition the network via visibility-aware cross-attention, enabling occlusion-robust synthesis across the full head surface. Region-specific modules specialise in semantically demanding and distinct areas (eyes, mouth, skin and hair), while a tangent-space output projection recovers fine iris detail. We further introduce a scalable procedural augmentation pipeline that enriches raw geometry scans with physically plausible albedo, roughness and normal maps for training. The predicted attributes render directly as a single RGBA vertex-colour channel. VISAGE reduces FID by 42.7% on NPHM and 22.5% and 4.4% on zero-shot FaceVerse and i3DMM, respectively, relative to the strongest baseline, with a 7.2M-parameter core network.

title: A Unified AI Framework for Rapid and Accurate Waveform Generation of Compact Binary Coalescences
abstract: The astrophysical discovery potential of future gravitational wave detectors will hinge on accurate and rapid waveform generation. Third generation detectors are expected to observe many long duration compact binary coalescence signals that can probe binary formation and evolution as well as the nature of matter under extreme conditions. We develop a unified framework that combines physical modeling with deep learning. The framework uses an analytic residual spectral representation, shared learning, and decoders for each binary type. It generates waveforms for binary black holes, binary neutron stars, and neutron star black hole binaries, providing a single unified generator for all compact binary coalescences. The generated waveforms include the physical effects described by each reference model, such as spin precession, higher order modes, matter effects, and postmerger radiation for binary neutron stars. The waveforms span hundreds to thousands of cycles, with mean mismatches ranging from $5.89\times10^{-4}$ to $5.34\times10^{-2}$ relative to the reference waveforms. Batch generation achieves a maximum speedup of about 1800 over reference waveform generation.

title: Leakage-aware acoustic drone detection: fusing hand-crafted and pretrained audio features in a stacking ensemble
abstract: Small multirotor drones produce a characteristic acoustic signature, and microphones offer a low-cost way to detect them. High accuracies have been reported on public drone audio benchmarks, often with random clip-level splits of datasets built from a few long recordings and pieces of existing sound collections, so pieces of one source can appear in both training and test data. We study the binary task of the public DroneAudioDataset (11,704 one-second clips). Its 1,332 drone clips come from 257 five-second chunks of 7 recordings, and 96.4% of its non-drone clips are pieces of the 2,000 clips of the ESC-50 sound dataset. A grouped, source-disjoint protocol (five folds, three repeats) is compared with a random split. Each clip is described by 57 hand-crafted acoustic descriptors, reduced by a hybrid minimum-redundancy maximum-relevance and ReliefF selection or by NSGA-II multi-objective search, and by a 1024-dimensional embedding from the pretrained YAMNet network. Random Forest and XGBoost learners on both views form a stacking ensemble. Under the grouped protocol, the two-view stack reached a mean accuracy of 95.29% (SD 1.62 points over 15 test folds), a specificity of 98.29% and an area under the ROC curve of 0.990, and it correctly classified 98.78% of unseen ESC-50 source clips as non-drone. The random split overstated accuracy by 1.89 to 3.22 points for the four models. Adding YAMNet embeddings to the hand-crafted view raised accuracy by 1.11 points (higher in 12 of 15 folds). Hybrid selection matched the accuracy of all 44 baseline descriptors with 16 to 18 features, and NSGA-II retained 4 to 6 features at lower accuracy. The stack took 51.0 ms per clip on one CPU thread. Source-disjoint evaluation exposes the optimism of random splits and gives a reliable benchmark, and fusing hand-crafted with YAMNet features consistently improves detection in real time on one CPU thread.

title: ZeroGR: Filtering-First Constrained Decoding for Generative Recommendation
abstract: Generative recommendation is gaining traction in production, retrieving items by generating their identifiers one token at a time. The generated sequences must identify relevant catalog items, so constrained decoding couples relevance scoring with validity filtering. Because most possible sequences are invalid, scoring before filtering wastes computation on candidates that will be discarded. Our evaluation shows that filtering first can avoid this work with negligible impact on recommendation quality. We present ZeroGR, a filtering-first constrained decoding system for generative recommendation. ZeroGR uses a step-sliced filtering index to reduce GPU memory use by tailoring data representations to each decoding step. Its execution engine adopts shared-slot execution to accelerate data exchange across stages and hybrid projection to adapt computation to workload patterns, thereby reducing execution overhead. During index refreshes, ZeroGR applies layout-guided streaming construction to speed up updates and limit serving interference. Extensive evaluation shows that ZeroGR accelerates the filtering and scoring pipeline by up to $9.9\times$ over representative baselines while reducing GPU index memory use and accelerating index reconstruction.

title: Cross-Codec Robustness in Speech Watermarking
abstract: Generative speech models synthesize audio that is difficult to distinguish from human recordings. Synthetic speech can be watermarked as a proactive disclosure method, but watermarking models remain vulnerable to resynthesis attacks using neural audio codecs. This article investigates speech watermarking robustness across neural codec and digital signal processing attacks, when specific neural codecs are used for channel augmentation during training. We also present a novel zero-bit watermarking system that uses Descript Audio Codec as the generator. Our results demonstrate that the choice of augmentation codec significantly influences robustness generalization. Experiments show that augmentation with low-bitrate, high-quality neural codecs-Mimi and SNAC-results in promising robustness against unseen neural codecs and traditional attacks with limited quality impact.

title: BrainwashedLLM: Jailbreaking via Automated Adversarial Chain of Thoughts Discovery
abstract: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) achieve strong performance on complex tasks by generating explicit Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning, but the safety implications of this intermediate reasoning surface remain underexplored. We demonstrate that the reasoning trace itself is a powerful attack vector. Safety alignment in large models is substantially less robust to malicious reasoning embedded in the context than to direct imperative prompts. We introduce BrainwashedLLM, a weak-to-strong adversarial framework that automates the discovery of reasoning-based jailbreaks. First, we use Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), a Reinforcement Learning (RL) algorithm, with a multi-objective rule-based reward to fine-tune a small, white-box source model to generate adversarial reasoning traces. Crucially, the reward is computed entirely over the source's own reasoning trace. Second, we show that these traces transfer in a zero-shot manner. When traces are injected as input prefixes, they steer larger black-box LRMs to continue the adversarial reasoning and produce harmful outputs, without requiring prompt optimization, gradient access, or any form of output feedback from the target model. Across four state-of-the-art LRMs that span distinct architectures, BrainwashedLLM achieves ASR@5 between 0.74 and 0.98 across targets, within 16 points of query-based baselines, without querying the target during attack construction. To our knowledge, this is the first framework to use RL to directly optimize the CoT of LRMs as an attack surface without any target feedback, and the first to demonstrate zero-shot weak-to-strong transfer of reasoning traces. Our results suggest that exposed CoT is a vulnerability in LRMs and motivate architectural defenses that isolate the reasoning buffer. Warning: This paper contains potentially offensive and harmful text.

title: A Discontinuous Galerkin Framework for Efficient Simulation of Cyclic Voltammetry Models
abstract: We develop a numerical framework to efficiently simulate the cyclic voltammetry models based on discontinuous Galerkin (DG) spatial discretization combined with linearly implicit Euler time integration. The method is applied to two electrochemical mechanisms: a heterogeneous electron-transfer (ET) reaction and an electron-transfer reaction coupled with a catalytic chemical step (EC'). The governing time-dependent reaction-diffusion equations are expressed in dimensionless form and discretized in space using locally defined orthonormal Legendre polynomial basis functions. This discretization leads to a system of ordinary differential equations that is subsequently advanced in time using the linearly implicit Euler method. The resulting solver, denoted $\text{DG}_{\text{Impl}}$, is evaluated through numerical experiments and compared with MATLAB's $pdepe$ solver in terms of accuracy and computational efficiency. The numerical results demonstrate the convergence of $\text{DG}_{\text{Impl}}$ with respect to spatial and temporal discretizations and show that the method accurately reproduces the voltammetric responses of both ET and EC' mechanisms. For a prescribed relative error, $\text{DG}_{\text{Impl}}$ requires less computational time than $pdepe$ in the numerical experiments considered. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed DG formulation for the forward simulation of cyclic voltammetry models and provide a numerical foundation for subsequent adjoint-based parameter-estimation and inverse-problem formulations.

title: Bayesian-optimized magnetic-field-gradient sensing with a spin-orbit-coupled Bose-Einstein condensate
abstract: Building on our previous study of the expansion dynamics of a spin-orbit-coupled Bose-Einstein condensate, we propose a scheme for magnetic-field-gradient sensing that relates the maximum rotational deflection angle of the spin-density distribution to the magnetic-field gradient. We analyze the dependence of the sensing performance on key parameters and perform a systematic parameter optimization. A Bayesian optimization algorithm is introduced to efficiently identify the optimal parameter combination, thereby enhancing the sensitivity of magnetic-field-gradient sensing. Numerical simulations under the adopted noise model show that, compared with the parameter set used in our previous work, the optimized gradiometer improves the sensitivity by a factor of five. This work provides a new route for magnetic-field-gradient sensing and offers a reference for machine-learning-assisted quantum precision measurement.

title: OneTrans-GSR: A Generative Slate Ranking Paradigm Unifying Reranking and Mix-Ranking with One Autoregressive Transformer
abstract: Industrial recommender systems allocate substantial computation to pointwise candidate scoring, yet separate reranking and mix-ranking stages still assemble the final exposure slate using hand-crafted rules and specialized low-capacity models. Mix-ranking combines product cards, short videos, livestreams, and advertising cards supplied by distinct upstream business channels. Although these rules and models encode valuable domain knowledge, they are inherently limited in leveraging additional data and computation. They constrain the combinatorial space of candidate slates and determine objective trade-offs through manual tuning. To enable scalable and effective slate generation, we reformulate reranking and mix-ranking as a unified learning problem whose performance can improve with computation. Specifically, we instantiate this formulation across the reranking and mix-ranking stages and propose OneTrans-GSR, a single decoder-only policy that extends our deployed OneTrans backbone to generate the exposure slate end-to-end. During training, a reward model evaluates complete slates and guides reinforcement learning toward slate-level and long-term objectives. During decoding, business constraints are explicitly enforced. Offline evaluation shows that slate quality consistently improves as reward-model and policy compute increase. Deployed in a large-scale industrial recommendation system, OneTrans-GSR mixes heterogeneous content types within a unified slate. In online A/B tests, it improves GMV/u by 2.63%, advertiser value by 2.06%, and repurchase rate by 2.03%, while reducing end-to-end latency across the reranking and mix-ranking stages by 13%. These results mark a paradigm shift in slate generation: moving beyond human-engineered heuristics toward a general learned policy creates a scalable path for further algorithmic optimization and compute-driven improvement.

title: Pure Differentially Private Query Release via Laplace Input Smoothing
abstract: We study the offline release of a public family of $k$ statistical queries on a database of $N$ records from a public universe of size $d$, under pure $\varepsilon$-differential privacy. We give an efficient algorithm that, with probability at least $1-β$, answers all queries simultaneously to error $$O\left(\min\left\{1,\sqrt{\frac{\log(d/β)\log k}{N\varepsilon}}\right\}\right).$$ The output is a synthetic histogram on the data universe, and its running time depends polynomially on $N,d$ and $k$. This resolves a conjecture of Nikolov and Ullman (2021) with an efficient, polynomial-time construction. Fitzsimons (2026) recently established the same square-root error scale via an information-theoretic construction that relies on a computationally intractable Lipschitz envelope over the exponential space of possible outputs. In contrast, we introduce an input-side smoothing approach: we run a selection-only multiplicative-weights process after a single sparse Laplace perturbation of the input histogram. Departing from standard first-order stability analyses, we investigate the stability of stability by establishing a uniform lower bound on the second-order log-derivatives of the output transcript across $T$ rounds of multiplicative weight updates. We then develop an analytic smoothing principle showing that this curvature bound allows a sparse, coordinate-wise perturbation to guarantee pure differential privacy globally, attaining optimal utility through a conceptually simple, polynomial-time pure-DP mechanism.

title: Fortuitous BMN Operators from Multiple Cores
abstract: We develop a systematic construction of fortuitous cohomology classes in the BMN sector of $\mathcal N=4$ super Yang--Mills theory from multiple lower-rank building blocks. For arbitrary partitions of colour space, we construct corrected effective letters that obey the supersymmetry transformations of the corresponding lower-rank theories. These allow us to build gauge-invariant, $Q$-closed polynomial operators. A restriction map recovers the constituent cohomology classes, establishing non-exactness and fortuity without brute-force computations. As an explicit example, we combine two fortuitous $SU(2)$ cores to construct a fortuitous class in $SU(4)$. Our results provide a systematic approach to the structure of fortuitous cohomology at finite $N$.

title: Local resolution of the second log-Fitting ideal
abstract: Logarithmic Fitting ideals encode the complexity of the corresponding morphisms in a natural and intrinsic way, and their principalisation offers a new perspective on problems such as the resolution of cotangent sheaves and the monomialisation of morphisms. In this paper, we give a local resolution theorem for log-rank adapted morphisms: after finite sequences of smooth local blow-ups, the first two log-Fitting ideals \mathcal{F}\_{n--1}(σ) and \mathcal{F}\_{n--2}(σ) become principal monomial ideals.

title: Twist-three quark TMDs from back-to-back dijet production in next-to-eikonal DIS
abstract: We study back-to-back dijet production in deep inelastic scattering (DIS) at next-to-eikonal accuracy within the Color Glass Condensate framework, focusing on the quark-background contributions. We compute the quark-gluon and quark-antiquark production cross sections through next-to-leading power in the correlation limit for longitudinally and transversely polarized photons. In the quark-gluon channel, we derive both the kinematic corrections to the hard parts accompanying the twist-two quark distribution and the genuine twist-three contributions involving three-body quark-gluon-quark correlators. In the quark-antiquark channel, the interference of the eikonal amplitude with the double $t$-channel quark-exchange amplitudes probes three-body correlators with a different transverse arrangement of the fields. We express the results in terms of transverse momentum dependent (TMD) correlators and provide the corresponding hard coefficients. Our analysis extends the operator-level connection between the next-to-eikonal CGC framework and quark TMDs beyond leading power in the correlation limit.

title: Self-stabilising approximate clock synchronisation requires linear time
abstract: Synchronising the clocks of processes is a fundamental problem in distributed computing. We consider message-passing systems in which processes start in an arbitrary initial state (self-stabilisation) and up to $f$ processes may be non-transiently faulty. It is well known that synchronising clocks \emph{exactly} is at least as hard as consensus and requires $Θ(f)$ time. In contrast, without self-stabilisation, clocks can be synchronised \emph{approximately} much faster, in time independent of the number of non-transient faults [Srikanth and Toueg, JACM 1987; Welch and Lynch, Inf. Comput. 1988]. In this work, we show that deterministic self-stabilising approximate clock synchronisation tasks require $Ω(f)$ time to stabilise. This gives the first non-trivial time lower bound for these tasks, whose time complexity has remained open for over two decades [Dolev and Welch, JACM 2004; Dolev, Függer, Schmid and Lenzen, JACM 2014]. In particular, this answers the open question whether self-stabilising approximate clock synchronisation tasks are as hard as consensus or as easy as approximate agreement [Lenzen and Rybicki, JACM 2019]. The results show that guaranteeing \emph{both} transient and non-transient fault-tolerance simultaneously is expensive even for approximate synchronisation tasks. The lower bounds hold in a very strong model: the faulty processes can only crash, the local clocks of processes have no clock drift, and the message delay is bounded and known to all processes. The proof is based on a combinatorial topological argument showing that no fast finite-state protocol can ensure that the clocks behave consistently across all executions. To our knowledge, this is the first use of topological arguments to prove time lower bounds in the self-stabilising setting.

title: Crossover from Schwarzian dynamics to rotational soft modes in near-extremal Lovelock black holes
abstract: Near-extremal black holes are controlled by a small set of soft modes, and counting these modes fixes the coefficient of $\log T$ in the entropy. We ask whether genuine six-derivative interactions change that count, working in seven-dimensional third-order Lovelock gravity, the simplest setting where the cubic Lovelock term is dynamical. The multiplicities stay the same, but the naive count fails. At fixed charge the Maxwell mode is frozen out, and the fifteen rotational modes of the $S^5$ act as a quantum rotor that only switches on above the scale $K_J^{-1}$. As a result, the coefficient of $\log T$ runs from $3/2$ at the lowest temperatures to $9$ above that scale, and never reaches the naive Gaussian value $19/2$. We compute the moment of inertia $K_J$ from the charged slow-rotation solution and find that the Lovelock couplings move the crossover without changing the multiplicities. Only large AdS black holes have a wide window in which the full rotational contribution competes with the classical entropy. Adding a probe charged scalar, we derive an analytic near-horizon Schwinger threshold in the cubic coupling. Its large-AdS limit tells us when the broad rotational crossover window can coexist with the absence of a charged-scalar Breitenlohner--Freedman (BF) bound violation.

title: Limits to research in astrophysics
abstract: Fundamental physics faces several intrinsic limitations, such as the finite speed of light in vacuum, the absolute zero temperature, Heisenberg's uncertainty principle and so on. At the same time, the material resources necessary to conduct research in astrophysics, such as energy, fresh water, and rareearth elements, are also limited in both quantity and extraction capabilities, a concept often referred to as planetary boundaries. In the context of scientific research growing at a frenetic pace, following the greedy quenchless extractivist model of our era, and which is giving rise to an ever-increasing number of largescale, increasingly ambitious projects: what limits us, individually and collectively, in the practice of our occupation\,? In this conference proceeding, we discuss certain limiting factors we encounter in our daily work, which we need to reflect on collectively in order to move forward, toward a more sustainable and effective research that preserves the well-being of researchers, regardless of their career stage.

title: SPOD: Recovering Suppressed Temporal Evidence in Video-LLMs via Single-Pass Orthogonal Decomposition
abstract: Video Large Language Models (Video-LLMs) have achieved strong performance on many video understanding tasks, yet remain vulnerable to temporal hallucination in time-sensitive reasoning scenarios such as scene transition understanding and event ordering. Existing solutions either require costly retraining or introduce inefficient multi-pass inference and external supervision at test time. In this work, we show that temporal evidence is already encoded in Video-LLM hidden representations but is not fully exploited during standard inference. Motivated by this observation, we propose Single-Pass Orthogonal Decomposition (SPOD), a training-free framework that recovers suppressed temporal evidence through analytical hidden-state manipulation in a single forward pass. SPOD consists of two components: Frame Distinctiveness Analysis (FDA), which identifies salient frames from middle-layer hidden-state geometry, and Temporal Delta Subspace (TDS), which constructs orthogonal temporal and prior subspaces from weighted inter-frame hidden-state differences. By decomposing final hidden states into temporal, prior, and residual components and rescaling them independently, SPOD enhances dynamic information, suppresses static appearance bias, and preserves complementary information. Experiments on VidHalluc, EventHallusion, and VideoMMMU show that SPOD consistently outperforms strong inference-time baselines across temporal reasoning tasks and model architectures while retaining near-vanilla inference efficiency. These results suggest that improving temporal reasoning in Video-LLMs may depend not only on additional supervision, but also on recovering temporal evidence already present in their internal representations. Our code is available at https://github.com/VioAgnes/SPOD.

title: Effect of compensation on magnetic ordering in (Ga,Mn)As
abstract: The real mechanism of ferromagnetism in III-V diluted magnetic semiconductors such as Ga$_{1-x}$Mn$_x$As is still debated. The experimental results point out the realization of appreciable ferromagnetism at filling of the impurity band close to one-half that can be expressed in terms of compensation degree. Based on our recent results on the existence of two competing mechanisms of pair indirect exchange (with ferro- and antiferro alignment of Mn $d$ shells), a theory of magnetic ordering in (Ga,Mn)As is presented. The molecular-field-like equation is derived in which the effective exchange constant contains all necessary information about material, including the Mn content, the compensation degree, the crystal coordination, and the parameters of two competing pair exchange interactions. The Curie temperature depends crucially on the compensation degree. Depending on Mn content and compensation degree, three possible magnetic phases (paramagnetic, ferromagnetic, and spin-glass-like) are predicted. However, the spin-glass-like phase in (Ga,Mn)As is apparently not realized due to the additional inevitable compensation caused by As antisites. The phase transition into the ferromagnetic state occurs not only with Mn content variation but through the change of the compensation degree as well. The new mechanism of photoferromagnetic effect is predicted and discussed in the context of possible clarification of the magnetic ordering mechanism. It is assumed that the main obstacle to a possible increase in the Curie temperature is the increasing contribution of the antiferromagnetic superexchange between the nearest-neighbor Mn's, rather than compensatory (electric or magnetic) effects from Mn interstitials, as was previously stated. The comparison of our predictions with available experimental data is presented.

title: Finding Integer Roots of Polynomials in Nearly Optimal Time
abstract: Let $f\in\mathbb Z[x]$ be a polynomial of degree $n$ with integer coefficients of absolute value less than $2^b$. Using Pan's approximate factorization theorem, we give a deterministic algorithm that finds all distinct integer roots of $f$ in $\widetilde O(nb)$ bit operations. This matches the bit size of the input up to logarithmic factors and does not require $f$ to be square-free. Since we were unable to verify parts of the running time analysis of Pan's theorem, we also give a self-contained deterministic algorithm with running time $\widetilde O(nb+\min(n,b)^3b^2)$, which is $\widetilde O(nb)$ whenever $b\leq n^{1/4}$. This answers a question of Harvey and Hittmeir (2022), who asked whether integer roots can be found deterministically in quasilinear time, conditionally on Pan's theorem, and unconditionally for $b\leq n^{1/4}$. The fastest previous deterministic algorithm, due to Nir, takes $\widetilde O(n^{3/2}b)$ bit operations and works only for square-free polynomials. Instead of $p$-adic lifting, we combine approximate complex root finding with exact polynomial evaluation. We first approximate the complex roots of the polynomial formed by the top $\min(n,b)+1$ coefficients of $f$. Every integer root $r$ of $f$ with $|r|\geq 2$ lies within distance $2$ of some complex root of this truncated polynomial. Rounding the real parts of the approximate roots therefore gives a list of $O(\min(n,b))$ candidate integers that is guaranteed to contain all integer roots of $f$. Although a single candidate can have up to $b$ bits, a bound via the Mahler measure shows that the bit lengths of all candidates sum to $O(b)$. This allows us to test all candidates by exact multipoint evaluation in $\widetilde O(nb)$ bit operations.

title: Tree Covers for Directed Graphs: Distance Oracles, Routing Schemes and Spanners
abstract: In a seminal work [STOC'01; JACM'05], Thorup and Zwick showed that every weighted undirected graph admits a tree cover where each vertex belongs to $O(kn^{1/k})$ trees in expectation, and every pair has a path of stretch at most $2k-1$ in some tree. In this paper, we extend this structural property to directed graphs with nonnegative edge weights. Let $\mathrm{dist}_G(u \leftrightarrows v) = \mathrm{dist}_G(u \to v) + \mathrm{dist}_G(v \to u)$ denote the roundtrip distance. For every integer $k$, we construct a collection $\mathcal{T}$ of tree-pairs, each consisting of an in-tree and an out-tree rooted at the same vertex. Each vertex belongs to $O(kn^{1/k})$ tree-pairs in expectation, and for every ordered pair $(u, v)$ some tree-pair $T_{in}\cup T_{out} \in \mathcal{T}$ satisfies $\mathrm{dist}_{T_{in}\cup T_{out}}(u \to v) \le \mathrm{dist}_G(u \to v) + (k-1)\mathrm{dist}_G(u \leftrightarrows v).$ We call this a \emph{$k$-strong (roundtrip) tree cover}. While prior techniques partition distances into geometric scales and build separate structures for each scale, our construction handles all distances simultaneously within a single, unified hierarchy. This yields the first directed tree cover for general $k$ matching the classic Thorup-Zwick stretch-size trade-off. Our cover immediately implies improved constructions of roundtrip spanners, path-reporting distance oracles, and compact routing schemes, as well as their source-wise and prioritized variants. We also provide faster algorithms for these structures: for general $k \ge 4$, all the above objects can be constructed in $\widetilde{O}(\min\{mn, n^{2.5}\})$ expected time, breaking the $mn$ barrier in dense directed graphs.

title: dSIBP: a package for generating IBP seeds for QFT in de Sitter spacetime
abstract: Recent studies show that in addition to the flat spacetime, Integration-by-parts (IBP) relations and differential equations can also provide a systematic approach to Feynman integrals in de Sitter spacetime. dSIBP is a Mathematica package for the automated construction of IBP systems and differential equations. For dS integral families with massive and massless propagators, it generates a complete set of IBP seeds, assembles linear systems for external reduction, and constructs differential equations for the reduced master integrals. The implementation combines equations of motion, remaining terms and parity constraints, and provides reliable checks. We describe the conventions and public interface through worked examples.

title: Critical amplitudes of the Baxter-Wu model from MCPA and Wolff simulations: free-exponent and fixed-exponent fits
abstract: The two-dimensional Baxter-Wu model belongs to the universality class of the four-state Potts model. Exact expressions are available for its energy, specific heat, magnetization, and polarization amplitudes. We use these results as a benchmark for evaluating two simulation algorithms and two approaches to extracting critical amplitudes. Microcanonical population annealing (MCPA) and the sublattice-freezing Wolff algorithm yield highly consistent estimates for the energy and order parameters when applied to lattices of comparable size. According to the exact Joyce series, the local effective exponent does not stabilize at a constant value but instead undergoes a monotonic drift. This behaviour stems from corrections to scaling, which can be expressed as a series in the cube root of the reduced temperature. As a result, these corrections decay relatively slowly, with the leading term being of relative order $|t|^{2/3}$. When performing a fit with a free exponent on an automatically identified plateau, this drift gets incorporated into the estimated exponent, introducing a substantial bias in the derived amplitudes. In contrast, a fit that fixes the exponent to its exact value and explicitly accounts for the analytic correction series delivers a close match to the known exact amplitudes. Using this refined fitting approach, we obtain estimates for the susceptibility amplitudes and the universal amplitude ratios. These values are in good agreement with predictions from form-factor calculations. Additionally, we numerically determine the leading correction coefficient for the polarization.

title: TEXMET: A Deep Learning Benchmark for Archaeological Textile Reconstruction
abstract: The reconstruction of fragmented historical textiles presents a significant challenge in computational archaeology. The Oseberg ship burial, dating to 834 CE, yielded hundreds of degraded textile fragments that have resisted systematic computational analysis. While deep learning has revolutionized image-based puzzle solving, progress on archaeological textiles has been limited by the lack of domain-specific datasets and systematic evaluation of modern architectures. To address this gap, we present TEXMET, a curated dataset of 18,644 historical textile images from the Metropolitan Museum of Art's Open Access collection, representing the first textile-specific benchmark for puzzle-solving research. Using TEXMET, we conduct a systematic evaluation of three state-of-the-art puzzle-solving models: JPDVT, FCViT, and DiffAssemble. Our experiments reveal that the transformer-based models pre-trained on standard datasets fail to generalize to textiles, but domain-specific fine-tuning proves highly effective. The graph-based DiffAssemble model, when fine-tuned on TEXMET, achieves 85.89% puzzle accuracy on textile data. Most significantly, applying this fine-tuned model to 45 highly degraded Oseberg fragments yields a performance increase from 26.67% to 64.44% puzzle accuracy. These results establish TEXMET as a new benchmark for textile reconstruction and demonstrate that domain adaptation is essential for applying puzzle-solving methods to imagery of real archaeological materials.

title: Can multi-level Monte-Carlo address the sign problem in a finite-density Bose gas?
abstract: Numerical simulation of field theories with complex actions is frustrated by the sign problem, which causes an exponential growth in statistical sampling noise. A key example of such a theory is QCD at finite baryon chemical potential, which has important applications to the structure of atomic nuclei and neutron stars. Until now, the sign problem has precluded the possibility of first-principles numerical calculations that could provide key insight into these important physical systems. In this work, we propose an approach to avoiding this limitation by applying a reweighting procedure coupled with a multi-level Monte-Carlo sampling algorithm that offers an exponential enhancement of statistics to counteract the sign problem. We test the approach on a simpler model that displays the same sign problem at finite chemical potential. Our results demonstrate the promise of the proposed approach, significantly increasing the range over which precise calculations are possible, and providing improvements all the way up to the phase transition.

title: Smallest Multiplicative Stretch for an $α$-APASP Below $\widetilde O \left(n^ω\right)$ Runtime
abstract: Dor, Halperin and Zwick [FOCS'96; SICOMP'00] showed that $(2-\varepsilon)$-APASP is at least as hard as BMM for every fixed $0<\varepsilon<1$. Zwick [FOCS'98; JACM'02] gave a $2$-APASP algorithm in $\widetilde O(n^{ω+o(1)}\log W_{\max})$ runtime, where $W_{\max}$ is the maximum edge weight. Bringmann, K{ü}nnemann and W{ę}grzycki [STOC'19] removed this logarithmic factor. Using OpenAI's recent bound $ω\leq\frac{9}{4}$ gives $\widetilde O\left(n^{\frac{9}{4}+o(1)}\right)$ time. We present two weighted undirected $2$-APASP algorithms. The first uses $(\min,\max)$-products. Earlier rectangular FMM bounds of Vassilevska Williams, Yinzhan Xu, Zixuan Xu and Zhou [SODA'24] and Alman, Duan, Vassilevska Williams, Yinzhan Xu, Zixuan Xu and Zhou [SODA'25] give $\widetilde O(n^{2.36999465})$ runtime, below the previous $ω\leq2.371177$ of Dupont, Eisenberger, Kozlovskii, Mehrabian, Ruiz, See, Zhou, Alman, Vassilevska Williams and Balog [arXiv'26]. Current rectangular FMM bounds give $\widetilde O(n^{2.34549151})$, independent of $W_{\max}$. For integer weights, our second algorithm has $\widetilde O(n^{ω-\frac{(ω-2)^2}{ω-1}+o(1)}\log^{O(1)}W_{\max})$ runtime, with exponent below $ω$ whenever $ω>2$. The rectangular bounds of Uzna{ń}ski [arXiv'26] or of Amanov, van den Berg and Zuiddam [arXiv'26] give $\widetilde O(n^{2.17157288}\log^{O(1)}W_{\max})$.

title: Profinite approach to S-adic shift spaces II: Invertible directive sequences
abstract: This paper is the second in a series about (relatively) free profinite semigroups and S-adic representations of minimal shifts. The first installment introduced the key notions of profinite images and saturating properties. The present paper examines the relationship between relative invertibility conditions (on a directive sequence) and charging properties (of a shift). The main result shows that the two properties are equivalent under mild conditions. Moreover, charging properties are shown to be equivalent to density of subgroups generated by return words in relatively free profinite groups. The main result can then be used to deduce purely discrete statements about subgroups generated by return words in relatively free groups. We also highlight applications of the main result to the study of maximal bifix decoding, following earlier work by the second author. Finally, we establish some results on the effect of direct images on charging properties and explain how to apply these results to the case of episturmian shifts.

title: An oscillation result for slightly perturbed trigonometric series
abstract: We establish that any nontrivial anharmonic Fourier series with exponents quadratically close to the positive integers changes sign on each interval of length 2$π$.

title: Stochastic interpretation of the Water Waves equations
abstract: The aim of this article is to derive a stochastic interpretation of the Water Waves equations, based on the location uncertainty principle (LU). Next, these equations are used to infer simpler models from scaling limits, such as the Saint-Venant, Boussinesq and Serre-Green-Naghdi ones. Once adapted to the stochastic setting, these models have been successfully implemented numerically, and we show several experiments to assess their properties -- for example the breaking of the wave symmetry, and the influence of time correlated noises.

title: A RISC-V Simulator for the Tenstorrent Tensix Architecture
abstract: RISC-V based AI accelerators have become popular and not only for AI and ML, but also as vehicles for exploring HPC workloads more generally. Tenstorrent are one example, and whilst they document their Tensix architecture in detail and develop their software stack openly, running code has historically required a physical card, and their recently released simulator targets hardware equivalence rather than introspection. In this paper we present Wolfpine, a community developed RISC-V simulator for the Tensix architecture, supporting both the Wormhole and Blackhole generations and integrating seamlessly with the TT-Metal software stack. Constructed entirely from publicly available documentation, open source software and measurements on physical hardware, Wolfpine is written in pure Python for readability and ease of modification. An opt-in, provenance-tracked cost model adds timing fidelity incrementally, and typed event streams, per-component tracing and timeline export enable programmers to identify and diagnose performance bottlenecks that the hardware itself hides.

title: Analytical properties of the principal clamped transmission eigenpair for a planar region
abstract: This paper investigates the analytical properties of the principal eigenpair for the clamped transmission eigenvalue problem, which arises in the context of biharmonic (i.e. flexural wave) scattering by a clamped planar obstacle. By deriving a suitable Rayleigh quotient, we provide rigorous proofs for several fundamental properties that were previously only observed through numerical experiments. One of the results we have shown here is that the first eigenvalue is monotone decreasing with respect to the domain. Furthermore, we prove that the corresponding eigenfunction is of a single sign, a property analogous to the principal eigenfunction of the Dirichlet eigenvalues of the Laplacian. Another key result is a Faber--Krahn type inequality, establishing that the disk minimizes the principal eigenvalue among all domains of a given measure. The theoretical results are supported by a comprehensive numerical investigation.

title: Approximation Algorithms for Multi-Criteria Network Design Problems
abstract: Min-max multi-criteria optimization asks for a single feasible solution minimizing the maximum of its costs under $\ell$ nonnegative cost functions, a formulation that captures both fairness across groups and robustness across scenarios. It has proved hard to approximate even for basic problems: for robust shortest paths, polylogarithmic approximations are known only in quasi-polynomial time. For network design, the best known guarantee is an $\ell$-approximation, which is tight for the natural LP relaxation. We show that exponentially better and nearly optimal guarantees are achievable for two fundamental network design problems. For multi-criteria connectivity augmentation (MC-CAP), which asks to increase the edge connectivity of a given undirected graph by one, we give a randomized polynomial-time $O(\log \ell)$-approximation algorithm. Applying our augmentation procedure iteratively and analyzing its randomized choices jointly across iterations yields an $O(\log k \log \ell)$-approximation for the multi-criteria $k$-edge-connected spanning subgraph (MC-$k$-ECSS) problem, for every $k \geq 2$. We complement these algorithms with a nearly matching lower bound: for every fixed $\varepsilon > 0$, MC-CAP admits no polynomial-time $O(\log^{1-\varepsilon} \ell)$-approximation, even when the underlying graph is a star, unless $\mathsf{NP}\subseteq\mathsf{DTIME}\bigl(n^{\log^{O(1)}n}\bigr)$. The same hardness extends to the MC-$k$-ECSS problem.

title: The TNG50-SKIRT Atlas: Multi-wavelength properties of galaxy discs in the TNG50 simulation
abstract: We investigate the wavelength dependence of disc scale lengths in galaxies from the TNG50-SKIRT Atlas (TSA), and assess whether the simulated galaxies reproduce the structural properties and scaling relations observed in real galaxies. We measure disc scale lengths from 1D radial surface-brightness profiles of multi-wavelength synthetic images. The disc-dominated region is defined interactively per galaxy and applied consistently across bands. We restrict the analysis to nearly face-on, star-forming galaxies and retain only systems whose r-band profiles are well described by an exponential model. The resulting scale lengths are compared to observational samples and analysed using both dust-attenuated and dust-free images, as well as intrinsic stellar population maps. We find that the majority of TSA galaxies exhibit exponential discs in realistic mock observations. TSA galaxies reproduce the observed disc scale length-stellar mass (luminosity) relation, but are systematically larger at fixed mass or luminosity. The dependence of disc scale length on morphology is weak. Disc scale lengths correlate strongly across wavelengths, but decrease systematically with increasing wavelength. When normalised by the stellar-mass scale length, TSA galaxies exhibit a monotonic trend consistent with observations over the optical-to-NIR range. Comparing dust-free and dust-attenuated images and linking the results to intrinsic galaxy properties, we find that stellar population gradients are the primary driver of this wavelength dependence. In particular, radial gradients in stellar age dominate the effect, while metallicity gradients play a secondary role. Dust attenuation further enhances the wavelength dependence at short wavelengths but is not its main origin. Residual offsets in absolute scale length indicate the remaining differences between simulated and observed galaxy structure.

title: Optimal (Randomized) Compact Routing Schemes
abstract: Compact routing schemes route messages along short paths while every vertex stores little information. We study the trade-off between the stretch and the storage of compact routing schemes in undirected graphs, in four models: labeled and name-independent schemes, with average or worst-case local storage. We improve the best known stretch in all four models. Our main result is a labeled routing scheme with expected stretch $2k-1$ and $\widetilde O(n^{1/k})$ average local storage, in which only the routing is randomized. Under the Erdős girth conjecture, no scheme with this storage has stretch below $2k-1$, so our scheme is optimal, up to polylogarithmic factors in the storage. With deterministic routing, we obtain stretch $\approx2.47k$, the best known deterministic stretch with average storage. Worst-case local storage is the classical setting of compact routing. The leading coefficient $4$ in the stretch $4k-5$ of Thorup and Zwick~[SPAA'01] was improved only by Chechik~[PODC'13], to $\approx3.68$ in unweighted graphs. In unweighted graphs, we obtain expected stretch $(\frac83k+O(1),O(k))$, and deterministic stretch $\approx3.05k$. Name-independent routing is harder, since the source knows only the name of the destination. The best known stretch with $\widetilde O(n^{1/k})$ local storage in unweighted graphs was $96k$, by Abraham, Gavoille, and Malkhi~[DISC'04]. We improve it by more than a factor of $8$. With average storage, we obtain expected stretch $4k-5$, which matches the labeled scheme of Thorup and Zwick. With worst-case storage in unweighted graphs, we obtain expected stretch $(8k+O(1),O(k))$. All our schemes for unweighted graphs extend to weighted graphs with a small loss in the stretch, and still improve the previous unweighted bounds.

title: Controlling nitrogen incorporation in (Eu,Ba,Ca)TiO$_3$-derived perovskite-type oxynitrides through Fermi Level Engineering
abstract: Defect states directly influence not only functional properties, but also oxynitride formation during ammonolysis. Along with structural stability and charge balance, these defects can cause non-uniform nitrogen incorporation. To address this, the recently proposed Fermi Level Engineering concept provides a powerful alternative of rationalising oxynitride synthesis. By using the electron chemical potential, i.e., the Fermi level, as a unique descriptor, this approach can predict, understand, and manipulate defect formation enthalpies and charge transition levels, subsequently allowing to incorporate defect-property correlations to the concept. This work combines theoretical modelling and experimental characterisation of barium titanium oxynitrides to explain an intrinsic, self-limiting nitridation process. Progressive nitrogen incorporation causes a Fermi level downward shift, leaving further nitrogen substitution on oxygen sites energetically unfavourable, up to 0.03 N per unit formula. We demonstrate that A-site cation substitution in Eu$_{1-x}$Ba$_x$TiO$_3$- and Eu$_{1-x}$Ca$_x$TiO$_3$-derived oxynitrides can be applied to control compensation of the additional negative charge from N$^{3-}$ and keep the Fermi level high. The Eu$^{2+/3+}$ redox couple enables substitution of oxygen by nitrogen through pinning of the Fermi level at the europium charge transition level, at $\sim$ 2.9 eV above the VBM. This allows for higher nitrogen uptake of up to 0.65 per formula unit (taken from hot gas extraction) through a more controlled process. Further incorporation is then limited by an intra-Ti(O,N)$_6$ octahedra distortion due to internal bond-angle variance.
