To evaluate the proposed pipeline, we construct a synthetic evaluation dataset from 100 long-form videos across five genres by segmenting each video into short clips using a scene-change detection model and shuffling the resulting clips to remove their temporal order. Through objective evaluation and qualitative examples, we demonstrate that Clips2Story can effectively retrieve keyword-relevant clips and compose coherent storyboards based on user-specified keywords. Human evaluation further shows that Clips2Story outperforms a strong baseline in terms of narrative coherence, keyword alignment, and overall realism.

title: Decouple to Reuse: Fine-Grained Knowledge Augmentation for Time Series Foundation Models
abstract: Time series forecasting is critical for demand prediction and resource management in modern Web services, yet applying pretrained Time Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) to downstream tasks remains challenging due to domain shifts. Existing retrieval-augmented approaches typically retrieve coarse-grained window contexts and may introduce context-specific noise. To address this problem, we argue that temporal patterns should be reused at a decomposition level, as effective trend and seasonal dynamics may originate from different contexts. We propose \method, a two-stage \underline{F}ine-grained \underline{K}nowledge \underline{A}ugmentation framework that decouples and consolidates pre-training knowledge into compact, task-shared residual codebooks to enhance frozen TSFMs. Specifically, Stage I constructs dual-branch residual codebooks for decoupled trend and seasonal signals, while Stage II dynamically retrieves and merges these fine-grained patterns into target representations via task-adaptive aggregation and gate fusion. Extensive experiments across eight real-world benchmarks with four representative TSFM backbones demonstrate the superior effectiveness and computational efficiency of \method, while further validating the strong transferability of the residual codebooks across different backbones. The source code is available at the anonymous repository: https://github.com/yuppielqx/TSFM-Component-Token-Adapter

title: FedIA: Instance-Aware Cross-Modal Representations for Federated Prompt Learning
abstract: Federated Prompt Learning (FPL) enables parameter-efficient adaptation of pre-trained Vision-Language Models across decentralized clients without exchanging raw data. To cope with cross-client heterogeneity, existing FPL methods typically pair a globally shared prompt with a client-specific local prompt. However, this design personalizes only at the client level: the same local prompt is applied to all samples of a client, and the global and local prompts are combined in an input-agnostic, fixed manner. Consequently, it overlooks the substantial visual variations among samples within the same client and cannot adjust the balance between shared and personalized knowledge to each input. To address these limitations, we propose Federated Prompt Learning with Instance-Aware Cross-Modal Representations (FedIA), an FPL framework that learns instance-aware cross-modal representations. Specifically, FedIA first uses global text prompts as client-invariant semantic anchors to select image patches most relevant to each candidate class, suppressing distracting regions. The selected visual evidence then conditions the generation of instance-aware local text representations. Finally, an adaptive global-local fusion module calibrates the contributions of local and global text representations for each image-class pair. In this way, FedIA shifts personalization in FPL from the client level to the instance level while preserving the semantic knowledge shared across clients. Extensive experiments under domain shift, pathological label skew, and Dirichlet-based label skew show that FedIA outperforms FPL baselines, with maximum accuracy gains of 1.44\%-4.37\% over the latest baseline across the three settings. Ablation studies and analyses further verify the complementary contributions of instance-aware representation generation and adaptive global-local fusion.

title: Spectroscopic diagnostics of coronal fan loops using EIS/Hinode and AIA/SDO
abstract: We utilize spectroscopic and imaging data from the EIS/Hinode and the AIA/SDO to determine plasma and wave parameters along coronal fan loops. We determined the temperature along the loop lengths using the EM-loci method with EIS spectral lines and identified multi-thermal plasma components at temperatures ranging from 0.8-1.05, 1.2-1.4, and 1.6-1.8 MK. We further compared these temperature distributions along the loops with those derived from DEM analysis carried out using AIA coronal passbands. The multi-thermal nature of coronal fan loops can be well resolved using EIS spectroscopic data. We determined the density along the loop using the line-ratio method from the EIS Fe XII line pair. We found that density decreases slowly from the expected hydrostatic equilibrium. Our results demonstrate the multi-thermal nature of overdense loops, which can be well resolved with EIS spectroscopic data. We also determined the velocity amplitude of Alfvén waves from the non-thermal broadening of EIS Fe XII spectral line profiles. We further estimated the Alfvén wave energy flux in the corona by combining these parameters with the recently reported magnetic field strength of $\approx$200 G at the coronal footpoint of fan loops. The estimated Alfvén wave energy flux is $\approx$ 2$\times 10^7$ erg cm$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$, significantly higher than those reported in earlier studies, and can contribute to coronal losses due to radiation along the fan loops in the active region.

title: Spacetime Evolution Induced by a Massive Cosmic String in Numerical Relativity
abstract: Cosmic strings are one-dimensional topological defects formed during phase transitions in the early universe. ''Massive'' cosmic strings possess a sufficiently large tension to close their transverse space, forming a conical singularity outside the string, as a static gravitational effect. In a dynamical context, such strings are expected to drive topological inflation. In this work, we investigate the spacetime evolution induced by the formation of a massive cosmic string in a radiation-dominated cosmological background, imposing cylindrical symmetry. Using full numerical relativity simulations, we observe that the string core undergoes topological inflation and that its boundary moves inwards superluminally, which causally disconnects the core from the outer universe. Between the core and the asymptotic regions, a nearly matter-dominated decelerating region originates sourced by the oscillating string fields. This region is bounded by a local maximum (''belly'') and local minimum (''throat'') of the circumferential radius, while the throat recedes outwards at about 10% the speed of light. Furthermore, a gravitational wavefront is emitted from the string, characterizing the light cone of the string formation. Even behind the wavefront, the exterior region no longer exhibits a ''conical'' structure. Based on the simulation results, we construct a Penrose diagram, reflecting the causal structure of the entire spacetime.

title: From Waste to Discovery: Recycling High-Scored Unexposed Candidates in Taobao Feed Recommendation
abstract: Helping users discover new interests is vital to the long-term health of industrial recommender systems, yet the usual remedy, boosting exposure of under-explored (discovery) content, often backfires in production. We report URED (Unexposed Recycling for Efficient Discovery), a training-free recall-stage system serving Taobao feed recommendation at Alibaba for over six months to tens of millions of daily active users. It rests on a production-validated insight: naive boosting fails because it injects cold, information-poor candidates that rankers systematically over-estimate, buying no discovery gain while risking engagement. Items scored highly but never exposed (signals industrial pipelines routinely discard) form a pool that is both relevant and reliably predictable. Over a 30-day horizon URED aggregates them and re-injects at recall time through a lightweight pipeline spanning offline storage, distributed aggregation, and low-latency online serving, adding under 1% latency via a single O(1) lookup per request with no model retraining. Online A/B tests show +3.47% discovered categories and +8.47% content richness with engagement preserved: completion video views rise significantly (+2.62%) and total views move positive (+0.36%, not significant). Ablations confirm both design pillars are necessary: a one-day window collapses the discovery gain to +0.55% (not significant), and random injection without score filtering yields no gain while trending negative on engagement (-0.17%). Across production recall channels, URED reaches 13.9x the platform-average discovery rate (6.3x the strongest nearline baseline) at engagement quality on par with the platform average. We share deployment details and lessons for practitioners facing the exploration-exploitation dilemma under tight resource constraints.

title: Failure of superharmonicity near an isolated singularity of the critical biharmonic equation
abstract: Let $n\ge5$ and $u$ be a positive singular solution of $Δ^2u=u^{(n+4)/(n-4)}$ in a punctured ball. A long-standing question is where or not $ -Δu>0$ in the punctured ball. In this paper we show that the answer is negative. More precisely we construct a positive singular solution whose singularity at the origin is nonremovable, while its lower limit there is zero. On a normal subspace, $-Δu$ converges to a strictly negative constant. The spherical minimum has order $r^β$, where $2<β<4$, and the spherical Harnack ratio is unbounded. The proof uses balanced planar polygons, finitely many exterior parameters and a countable gluing construction.

title: SIM-Enabled Wave-Domain Processing in MIMO-OFDM Receivers: Architecture, Modeling, and Validation
abstract: This paper develops a wave-domain linear receiver for wideband MIMO-OFDM, where the main high-dimensional linear processing conventionally performed after sampling is physically shifted to propagation through stacked intelligent metasurfaces (SIMs). The proposed receiver transforms receive-port waveforms into OFDM-domain symbols through three cascaded SIM-enabled functional sections. The first section, SIM_1, performs channel-memory processing and channel shortening in an energy-concentration sense, suppressing the out-of-cyclic-prefix (CP) effective tail before OFDM analysis. SIM_2 realizes CP removal and discrete Fourier transform (DFT) analysis as cyclic-windowed OFDM matched filtering by exploiting useful-window memory and analytical Fourier phase coding. SIM_3 implements residual virtual-subcarrier MIMO linear detection, completing the wave-domain linear receive chain up to symbol slicing. Synchronization, control, slicing, and decoding remain digital, while the dominant linear receive operations are moved to the wave domain. A staged configuration framework is developed: the numerology-dependent OFDM analyzer is compiled offline, whereas the channel-dependent memory processor and detector are configured over the coherence time using architecture-aware learning-assisted control. Numerical results validate both functional replacement and link performance, confirming nearly lossless replacement under CP-sufficient MIMO-OFDM conditions, with robustness to residual timing offsets and effective channel-delay-profile perturbations. Substantial gains under CP-insufficient channels are also demonstrated by suppressing out-of-CP leakage before OFDM analysis.

title: Intra-Architecture Source Attribution for Stable Diffusion: A New Task with Benchmark Dataset and Baseline
abstract: Designing systems that attribute a generated image to its source model has lately become a major area of AI research. Most existing datasets and systems related to image source attribution are targeted towards the detection of architectural signatures of the source models. Distinct from this, focusing on stable diffusion, we introduce a novel task, IntrAA-SD, Intra-Architecture source Attribution for Stable Diffusion, where the source models to be differentiated share the same architectural backbone and differ only due to fine-tuning. The proposed task aligns with the emergence of fine-tuned generators having the same architecture, like Juggernaut XL and RealVis XL, which are fine-tuned versions of Stable Diffusion XL (SDXL). We provide a first-of-its-kind $140$K-image benchmark dataset containing images generated from different fine-tunes of SDXL, along with in-domain and out-of-distribution prompts. We also provide a baseline framework for IntrAA-SD, which leverages a style-conditioned Mixture-of-Experts network. It uses a frozen CLIP backbone to capture the image style and gate the MoE, which processes fine-tuned trace features from a high-resolution LoRA-adapted DINOv2 network. The fine-tuned models used, the prompting strategies considered, and the formation details employed in the novel dataset are elaborated. Our baseline intra-architecture source attribution method is evaluated in terms of attribution accuracy on our dataset, and ablation studies are also performed. Code and dataset is available at https://github.com/mallikagarg/IntrAA-SD.

title: How Far Can You Steer? Behavior-Capability Frontiers in Contrastive Activation Addition
abstract: Activation steering can modify language-model behavior without parameter updates, but behavioral efficacy alone does not determine whether an intervention is usable. Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) steers targeted behaviors using activation directions derived from contrasting examples, potentially degrading unrelated model capabilities in the process. We therefore study CAA through a behavior-capability frontier, selecting interventions that maximize behavioral gain subject to an explicit bound on capability degradation. We evaluate this framework across four instruction-tuned models, seven behaviors, and capability-loss budgets of 1%, 3%, and 5% (absolute percentage points). Validation-selected behavioral effects generalize strongly to held-out data ($ρ= 0.945$), while joint behavior-capability survival among nonzero operating points rises from 37.5% at the 1% budget to 72.7% at 3%, with limited additional improvement at 5%. Control experiments indicate that these effects depend on learned behavior directions rather than generic activation perturbations. Representational geometry is significantly but only modestly predictive of causal cross-behavior transfer. Finally, secondary capability, out-of-distribution, and open-ended evaluations show that interventions satisfying protected benchmarks can still degrade untested capabilities or transfer unevenly to free-form generation. These results characterize activation steering as a constrained intervention whose usable range depends on model, behavior, direction, layer, and evaluation budget, rather than a universal control knob.

title: The enhanced polylogarithm conjecture in weight two for imaginary quadratic fields
abstract: Zagier's polylogarithm conjecture predicts that special values of Dedekind zeta functions can be expressed in terms of polylogarithms at algebraic arguments. For imaginary quadratic fields, Zagier and Gangl refined it by lifting both sides to complex values modulo rational multiples of a power of $2πi$. In previous work, the author extended their enhanced zeta values from ideal classes to ray classes by means of the Shintani $L$-function of two variables and formulated the enhanced polylogarithm conjecture for ray classes. In this article, we prove this conjecture in weight two. More precisely, we establish a Galois-equivariant equality between the enhanced partial zeta values of ray classes and the enhanced dilogarithms of elements of the rational Bloch groups of the corresponding ray class fields. These elements are constructed explicitly, starting from the Eisenstein class of Doran and Kerr on the square of a CM elliptic curve and contracting it with the graphs of complex multiplication.

title: How Unbalanced Must a Latin Rectangle Be?
abstract: We view a $k\times n$ Latin rectangle as $n$ points in the grid $[n]^k$. Each symbol gives one point, whose coordinates are the columns it occupies. The rectangle is balanced when these points are pairwise equidistant in the $\ell_1$ metric. Its imbalance measures the distance from this ideal. We study the minimum imbalance from three sides. Constructively, we use a simulated annealing that moves symbols within rows and only penalises column clashes. Against the reference table of Voboril et al. (2025), it improves 33 of the 51 non-square values for $8\le n\le 13$, by up to 39.4%, and matches the rest. A cheap invariant, the row group, certifies that none of the 33 new rectangles is isotopic to rows of a group table, so the earlier column-swapping local search cannot reach any of them. Exactly, a computer-assisted branch and bound proves that the minimum imbalance of a $3\times 9$ rectangle is $56$. Díaz et al. found this value, but its optimality was open. A sharper pruning bound, derived from the identity $I=2\sum(d-t)^+$, reduces the search tree by a factor of $2.4$ to $3.3$ on the instances with $k\ge3$ that we solve. Asymptotically, the minimum imbalance is $Θ(n^3)$ for every fixed $k$. A pigeonhole argument gives a lower constant of order $k\,4^{-k}$, and random rectangles give an upper constant of order $\sqrt k$. For $k=2$, the limit of $\min I/n^3$ exists, a permuton attains it, and it lies between $4/375$ and $0.1196$. Perfect balance is an $\ell_1$-equilateral problem, so it forces $k=Ω(n/\log n)$ rows. For $2\times n$ rectangles, single two-minute annealing runs improve five of the seven six-hour MIP upper bounds for $14\le n\le 20$. Finally, the Lean 4 kernel checks every rectangle reported in this paper against a 74-line specification that imports only Lean's core library. We also prove the pigeonhole lower bound in Lean with Mathlib.

title: The quantized Hall effect knows which way the current flows: mirror covariance and rectification in a laterally asymmetric Hall bar
abstract: The quantized Hall effect is the textbook emblem of universality: a resistance fixed by $h/e^2$, apparently indifferent to the shape of the sample, to its edges and to the direction of the current. That indifference is only half true. The plateau value is universal; the plateau is not. In a gate-defined Hall bar with one hard and one soft edge, reversing the current moves the plateau edge, and exchanging the edges reverses the move. We identify the symmetry that forces this. Because a perpendicular field breaks time reversal, the relevant operation is the in-plane $C_2$ rotation; within the self-consistent screening model it gives the covariance relation $R_α[B,V_{\mathrm{conf}}(x),I]=R_α[B,V_{\mathrm{conf}}(-x),-I]$, exact deep in the nonlinear regime and independent of linear response or microscopic reversibility. It predicts a rectification that is odd under exchange of the gate voltages and reverses with the magnetic field. The field-reversal test leaves the frozen lateral disorder untouched, so it holds for a single sample; it has not yet been performed. A further measurement, collapsing one incompressible strip, discriminates between co-directed and chiral pictures of the current. Self-consistent calculations show the soft-edge strip widening from 69 to 106\,nm on current reversal, moving the Hall resistance from 0.940 to $0.999994\,h/2e^2$ within a bounded window in magnetic field. The effect is a gate-tunable vector-product nonreciprocity, not magnetochiral anisotropy.

title: Time-Varying Tails: Estimation, Inference, and Risk Measurement
abstract: Motivated by evidence that the tails of economic and financial time series need not be stable over time, we develop a framework for studying time-varying tails. We model the extreme value index as a smooth function of time in the locally stationary framework of Zhou and Wu (2009). We estimate it by a ratio-form kernel Hill estimator in which a single intermediate quantile thresholds the whole local window. We establish consistency and asymptotic normality, and we construct uniform confi- dence bands. We also propose a consistent test of tail stability under extremal clustering. Combined with the Weissman extrapolation method, the estimator of the extreme value index yields time- varying extreme Value-at-Risk and Expected Shortfall. In an empirical application, we find the tail of daily loss of S&P 500 is compatible with a constant shape, whereas that of volatility-filtered loss varies significantly.

title: Familiar letters, not related languages, let unseen languages into a shared space of meaning
abstract: Hundreds of languages have written text but almost no translations, and whether a model learning one from untranslated text builds on a related language or familiar letters is unclear: they usually coincide. Here we show that familiar letters, not a related language, let an unseen language into a shared space of meaning. GlyphMind, a tokenizer-free vision transformer that reads text as pixels and lets any sentence be shown in any script, was pretrained to align translations across 27 writing systems. Adapted on untranslated Lao, a language and script it had never seen, it retrieved English translations seven times as often as the strongest simple baseline. Rewritten in unfamiliar letters, Lao did not enter although its close relative Thai was in pretraining; Santali, which had none, entered in Devanagari, familiar from Hindi, but not in its own script. Transliteration into familiar scripts may thus open multilingual models to languages without translations.

title: MotoVerse: A Benchmark for Predictive Perception of Motorized Two-Wheelers in Dense Unstructured Traffic
abstract: Motorized Two-Wheelers (MTWs) dominate personal transport across much of the Global South, yet remain largely overlooked in predictive perception research for autonomous driving and ADAS. We introduce MotoVerse, a benchmark for predictive perception from an MTW's ego-centric perspective. MotoVerse comprises 949 maneuver clips collected in dense, unstructured traffic and trajectory annotations for over 31,000 surrounding road agents, including over 16,000 MTWs, enabling two complementary tasks: Ego-Rider Maneuver Anticipation (ERMA) and Traffic Agent Trajectory Prediction (TATP). Each clip is further annotated with an MTW-specific challenge taxonomy comprising dynamic ego-motion, weak traffic structure and contextual occlusion, enabling challenge-aware evaluation. We benchmark established conventional prediction models, general-purpose Vision-Language Models (VLMs), driving-specific VLMs and vision-language-action models. Our experiments reveal three key insights: (i) video backbones reach most of their full-observation accuracy from the first fifth of a maneuver, whereas zero-shot VLMs need most of the maneuver to be observed; (ii) zero-shot VLMs, whether general-purpose or driving-specific, largely remain close to simple baselines on both tasks; a preliminary LoRA study shows that adaptation lifts anticipation sharply but leaves trajectory prediction behind conventional models; and (iii) the rider's own motion drives forecasting difficulty: for every model, including a static baseline, errors are highest during left turns and rise under dynamic ego-motion. We believe MotoVerse will serve as a challenging benchmark for safer and more robust predictive AI for intelligent two-wheelers. The dataset and evaluation code are publicly available at https://github.com/VarunIIITH/MotoVerse.

title: Faster Cluster Decomposition with Stronger Bi-Criteria Guarantee
abstract: Partitioning the vertex set of a graph $G=(V,E)$ into clusters is a classical problem in computer science. As vertices within clusters should be well connected and cuts between clusters sparse, Oveis Gharan and Trevisan (SODA 2014, [OGT14]) proposed to measure the partition quality using inner and outer conductance, i.e., the bi-criteria guarantee. Specifically, when partitioning $V$ into vertex-disjoint subsets $P_1,\ldots, P_k$, every subgraph induced by $P_i$ should have high conductance, while the conductance of $P_i$ in $G$ should be low. They studied the existence of such a partition and designed a polynomial-time algorithm achieving this guarantee. For more than a decade, their algorithm remained the only one achieving this guarantee on its output clusters. In this paper, we study faster cluster decomposition algorithms under the same setup as [OGT14] and prove three results: 1. We make their existential result algorithmic: Our algorithms run in nearly-linear time, and achieve the same bi-criteria guarantee as the one in [OGT14] up to constant factors, including the asymptotically tight dependence on $k$. 2. We prove that their existential result holds algorithmically under a much weaker condition on the initial disjoint subsets. To achieve this, we develop a general algorithm framework that boosts the approximation guarantee of a solution: given an $α$-approximate solution to the $k$-way conductance problem, if $ρ_G(k+1)/ρ_G(k)=Ω\left(α/\varepsilon\right)$, then a $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximate solution can be obtained using only $O(k(1+\logα))$ minimum $s$-$t$ cut computations. 3. We present a nearly-linear time algorithm that finds clusters with the bi-criteria guarantee. Our algorithm has the same guarantee as the one in [OGT14], which, for any unweighted graph of $n$ vertices and $m$ edges, runs in $\widetilde{O}(knm^2)$ time.

title: Core Reactivity in Cs-Ba-O ternary system under pressure
abstract: High pressure can activate Cs $5p$ core electrons for covalent bonding. In this study, we investigate the Cs-Ba-O system at 150 and 250 GPa using first-principles structure searches. CsBa$_3$O$_8$ and CsBaO$_4$ both lie on the static-lattice convex hull at 250~GPa and exhibit mild Cs $5p$-O $2p$ bonding while retaining O$_2$ units with intermediate superoxide-peroxide character. Cs$_2$BaO$_3$ shows substantially stronger bonding but remains metastable with respect to CsO and BaO. A 1:1 Cs$_2$O-BaO$_2$ mixture provides a solid starting composition for investigating this chemistry, with core-reactive CsO among the predicted products at 250~GPa. Calculated Cs $L_3$-edge x-ray absorption near-edge spectra and powder diffraction patterns provide electronic and structural signatures to guide identification of the predicted phases in diamond anvil cell experiments.

title: Holistic Parallel Supervision for Expressive Speech to Speech Translation
abstract: Expressiveness is central to speech-to-speech translation (S2ST), yet existing datasets rarely align source and target speech jointly in content, prosody, timing, and speaker identity. Consequently, current systems often rely on indirect conditioning or transfer mechanisms. To obtain this supervision, we introduce a training-data construction strategy that combines professional dubbing, which provides human-performed correspondence in content, prosody, and timing, with multilingual voice conversion to reduce speaker mismatch. We evaluate this supervision using existing expressive S2ST systems and DirectS2ST, an end-to-end method developed in this work that predicts the complete target-speech representation directly from source speech. Experiments on English-German and English-Spanish show that holistic parallel supervision improves expressive realization across all evaluated systems. DirectS2ST exhibits the largest gains in content, prosody, timing, speaker similarity, and human-rated expressiveness. To our knowledge, this work provides the first systematic investigation of holistic parallel supervision for expressive S2ST.

title: Long-memory Hermite functional processes in functional time series spectral asymptotics
abstract: Functional Non-Central Limit Theorems (NCLTs) are derived, in the functional spectral domain (see RuizMedina, 2022), for square integrable transformations, mapping an H_{1}-valued Gaussian stationary functional sequence into a nonlinear H_{2}-valued sequence, where H_{1} and H_{2} are separable Hilbert spaces. Linear and nonlinear operator-based scalings are considered, leading to different limit LRD Hermite functional processes. Under bounded linear operator scalings, an infinite-dimensional version of Theorem 5.3.1 in Pipiras and Taqqu (2017) is obtained, involving a functional reduction theorem, extending Theorem 5.3.3 in Pipiras and Taqqu (2017). Alternatively, when an operator-valued exponent based nonlinear scaling is applied, we pay attention to the LRD dominant set at each active output direction, in the leading chaos. Both scaling scenarios allow the derivation of NCLTs under similar settings of conditions.

title: Geometric Multigrid Preconditioners for conforming Finite Element Methods on Arbitrarily Agglomerated Meshes
abstract: Geometric multigrid methods for conforming finite element discretisations classically require a nested mesh hierarchy, forcing coarse meshes to be conforming, which is unsuitable for general domains. In order to eliminate this geometric constraint, we introduce and analyse a family of multilevel auxiliary space preconditioners. At the first level, a conforming Lagrangian discretisation on a fine simplicial mesh is preconditioned by a non-conforming polytopal discretisation posed on an arbitrarily agglomerated coarse mesh. At the subsequent levels, the coarse problem is solved by a geometric multigrid method for that polytopal discretisation on further agglomerated meshes, so that the whole hierarchy is generated from the fine mesh by agglomeration alone. We consider two polytopal discretisations, a symmetric interior penalty discontinuous Galerkin method and a hybrid high-order method. The prolongation operator at the first level is an element-wise interpolation onto the fine mesh followed by nodal averaging, preceded in the hybrid high-order case by a local potential reconstruction. For point-Jacobi and vertex-star patch additive Schwarz smoothers, we prove that the condition number of the preconditioned system is bounded by $O((H/h)^3)$, where $H/h$ is the coarsening ratio, and by $O((H/h)^2)$ for the DG variant with penalty proportional to $H/h$. Numerical experiments in two and three dimensions, on structured and unstructured meshes with agglomerates generated by automatic clustering algorithms, confirm the robustness of the preconditioners.

title: When Does a Cross-Device Run Justify PASS? Obligation-Level Evidence Qualification under Partial Observability
abstract: A cross-device test can complete every command yet judge a business claim from evidence belonging to another device or attempt. We introduce an executable evidence contract that makes support qualification an explicit stage before predicate evaluation. It binds each obligation to admissible subjects, episodes, objects and observation scopes, and records unresolved support rather than treating an apparently successful observation as proof. We evaluate two implemented parts of the contract. A prospectively specified, 12-seed controlled study isolates association under reused identifiers across 2,304 claims. Given identical records and business policy, Atomic-Facts Flat produces 160 false PASS and 76.30% PASS recall; supplying computed associations reduces false PASS to five and increases PASS recall to 99.09%. Deterministic Closure produces zero false PASS and 100.00% PASS recall, improving on Atomic Flat in 11 seeds with one tie (two-sided sign p=0.00098). Most of the benefit comes from explicit association rather than graph notation. A separate prospective field characterization spans four workflows, 40 physical episodes and 80 claims. Against frozen reference labels, the physical-evidence verifier attains 95.00% accuracy and 100.00% PASS recall (27/27), with three false PASS judgments. The field results are descriptive: a policy-input mismatch prevents the planned matched-policy comparison, and post-hoc sensitivity does not establish superiority over a policy-informed textual baseline. Together, the studies characterize qualification on physical evidence and isolate the value of explicit association under a controlled matching contract.

title: The integral Chow rings of $\mathcal A_3$ and $\mathcal M_3$
abstract: Over $\mathbb C$, we compute the integral Chow ring of $\mathcal A_3$, the moduli stack of principally polarized abelian threefolds. Along the way, we compute the integral Chow ring of $\mathcal M_3$, the moduli stack of smooth genus-three curves. The ring $\CH(\mathcal A_3)$ is generated by the Chern classes of the Hodge bundle, along with three classes supported on the locus of decomposable abelian varieties, subject to 16 relations. The ring $\CH(\mathcal M_3)$ is generated by the Chern classes of the Hodge bundle, with five relations. In particular, we find that the top Chern class of the Hodge bundle, $λ_3$, has order 504 on $\mathcal A_3$ and 252 on $\mathcal M_3$. For $\mathcal A_3$, this removes the factor of 4 from the bound $252\mid\operatorname{ord}(λ_3)\mid 1008$ of Ekedahl and van der Geer.

title: ChanSFormer: A Channel Agnostic Vision Transformer for Multi-Channel Cell Painting Images
abstract: High-content multi-channel imaging, from Cell Painting assays to remote sensing, is central to modern scientific pipelines. Because these channels are highly heterogeneous and experimental configurations frequently evolve, a practical vision backbone must be fundamentally channel-agnostic. Current channel-adaptive vision transformers rely on global self-attention with learnable channel embeddings, which can be computed only for previously known channels. Attempts to overcome this limitation of new channels either discard the embeddings, losing channel identity, or process each channel independently, thereby eliminating critical cross-channel interactions. To address this, we introduce ChanSFormer, an efficient Vision Transformer that replaces rigid embeddings with disentangled spatial-channel attention and individual channel CLS tokens. This architecture natively preserves both distinct channel identities and cross-channel information flow. Furthermore, the individual channel class token design unlocks more informative feature representations for self-supervised learning and enables representation-based channel sampling while remaining channel-agnostic. We evaluate ChanSFormer on two biology multi-channel datasets, CHAMMI, JUMP-CP and a satellite dataset, So2Sat. Experimental results show that ChanSFormer outperforms state-of-the-art methods by 3.93%-4.27% on JUMP-CP in classification accuracy. It also demonstrates exceptional cross-dataset transferability under a self-supervised setting, outperforming previous methods by up to 2.72% in accuracy in the same classification tasks. Furthermore, the disentangled attention reduces the quadratic complexity of channel-by-spatial sequence length of the global attention baseline, thus improving throughput by 55%-313%. Code is available at https://github.com/cvlab-stonybrook/ChanSFormer.

title: The Maximum Principle and Optimal Gradient Estimates of Solutions to the Insulated Conductivity Problem
abstract: We study the insulated conductivity problem with two unit spherical inclusions embedded in a bounded domain in $\mathbb{R}^n$ with $n\ge3$. The gradient of solutions may blow up as the distance between the two inclusions goes to zero. We introduce bispherical coordinates and expand the solution in spherical harmonics. Then we use the maximum principle to give a new proof of the optimal gradient estimate obtained by Dong-Li-Yang.

title: Finiteness of Non-decomposable Critically Frustrated Signed Graphs
abstract: A signed graph $(G,σ)$ is a graph $G$ with a signature $σ$ labeling each edge with a positive or negative sign. Two signatures of $G$ are switching equivalent if one is obtained from the other by sequentially changing the signs of all edges in an edge-cut. The frustration index of a signed graph $(G, σ)$ is the minimum number of negative edges among all signatures switching equivalent to $σ$. A signed graph is critically $k$-frustrated if it has frustration index $k$, and the removal of any edge decreases its frustration index. A critically $k$-frustrated signed graph is prime if it is irreducible and contains no two edge-disjoint negative cycles. Steffen and Naserasr et al. asked if there are only finitely many prime critically $k$-frustrated signed graphs for any positive integer $k$. The cases $k\leq 3$ were proved to be true by Cappello et al., and later, the cases $k=4$ and $5$ were verified by Z. Wang. In this paper, the author proves the conjecture by a topological argument.

title: Research on gravitational waves from extreme mass ratio inspirals in an axisymmetric Finslerian extension of Schwarzschild spacetime
abstract: We investigate gravitational waves from extreme mass ratio inspirals in an axisymmetric Finslerian extension of the Schwarzschild spacetime. Its angular component is described by a two-dimensional Randers space, with the Schwarzschild limit recovered at Finslerian parameter $ε= 0$. This structure breaks spherical symmetry, causing generic orbits to undergo orbital plane precession. Using multipolar radiation reaction and adiabatic orbital averaging, we derive the leading order Finslerian corrections to the energy, axial angular momentum, and total angular momentum fluxes. These corrections enter at Newtonian order and take different forms. We then incorporate these corrections into a higher-order Schwarzschild hybrid flux model to evolve the orbital elements and construct waveforms at mass quadrupole order using the numerical kludge method. The Finslerian corrections affect both the conservative orbital dynamics and the dissipative inspiral, producing cumulative phase shifts relative to the Schwarzschild waveform. For the representative source observed by LISA over one year with signal-to-noise ratio of 20, the noise weighted mismatch analysis shows that Finslerian waveforms with $|ε| \gtrsim 2 \times 10^{-6}$ are distinguishable from their Schwarzschild counterparts, with higher initial eccentricities further lowering the distinguishable value of $|ε|$. For a Schwarzschild injection, the Fisher matrix analysis yields a marginalized $1σ$ uncertainty of $σ_ε\simeq 1.26 \times 10^{-6}$. These results show the potential of space-based gravitational wave detectors to probe the axisymmetric Finslerian extension of the Schwarzschild spacetime.

title: Phantom: Temporal Caching for Diffusion Models
abstract: Diffusion models have become the dominant paradigm for high-quality image generation, but their iterative inference across tens of timesteps incurs substantial computational overhead. Prior accelerators exploit temporal similarity in diffusion models via differential quantization or output sparsity, yet suffer from increased memory footprint, design complexity, and image degradation. In this work, we present Phantom, an algorithm-architecture co-designed accelerator built on temporal caching. We view temporal similarity as differential sparsity: between adjacent timesteps, only a small fraction of tokens (outliers) change significantly. Phantom recomputes only these outlier tokens and reuses the rest from a temporal cache. Phantom runs on standard systolic arrays with lightweight additions: a Phantom Engine at the global buffer that detects outliers and updates the cache as activations stream through, and a condensed pipeline that maps the resulting sparse updates onto dense systolic computation for FC, convolution, and attention layers. Evaluations on modern diffusion models show that Phantom achieves an average 4.0x speedup and 5.5x energy saving over GPUs and prior accelerators while preserving generation quality.

title: METRIC-GS: Selective Metric-Scale Estimation for 3D Gaussian Splatting
abstract: A 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) reconstruction inherits arbitrary units from structure-from-motion, so it cannot be measured or used to place AR content until someone supplies a scale. Both standard recipes are fragile on real captures: on five indoor scenes with tape-measured ceilings, a quantile floor-to-ceiling heuristic errs by 27% and metric-depth alignment by 35-71% across three networks. We present METRIC-GS, a selective scale estimator for real indoor photographs: it reads the scale off the reconstruction's own semantic content and, just as importantly, refuses when the evidence is thin. A frozen 2D teacher labels Gaussians by visibility-aware voting; instance-level size priors for architectural and furniture classes (doors, tables, the floor-to-ceiling gap) are fused by a robust maximum-likelihood step; and an inlier-mass test turns thin evidence into an explicit abstention that doubles as a router to a heavyweight metric model. On 47 ScanNet++ scenes with laser ground truth, with a configuration frozen before public evaluation, the estimator alone cuts the heuristic's mean error from 21.1% to 16.6% (9.3% on the 28 scenes it acts on) at ~11 s per scene. MASt3R remains the more accurate standalone estimator (9.9%), but routing only our refusals to it matches running it everywhere with 60% fewer invocations; this selective hybrid is the configuration we advocate. Visibility-aware voting raises the scenes the estimator can act on from 16 to 28 at unchanged deployed accuracy. Applied unchanged to 13 phone and drone captures of our own, on which MASt3R fails its own registration gate 12 times, the system improves all five captures it acts on and degrades none. We also report that a current feed-forward metric model scores 2.3% on a benchmark inside its training mixture and 28-35% on captures it has never seen: a published metric-scale number is a best case, not a deployment estimate.

title: Attraction-Ranking Mismatch in Out-of-Distribution Detection: Theory and Evidence from Hamiltonian Feature Dynamics
abstract: Attracting features toward learned in-distribution (ID) regions is an intuitive strategy for out-of-distribution (OOD) detection, but does such attraction improve detection? We investigate this question using class-conditioned Hamiltonian dynamics as a controlled testbed and identify an attraction-ranking mismatch: improving individual class-affinity scores need not improve the relative ordering of ID and OOD samples. Our analysis separates misalignment between the driving field and the detection score from ranking failure that persists even when they are aligned. An exact AUROC decomposition and a local boundary analysis identify relative score changes at the ID-OOD ranking boundary as the source of first-order AUROC change under regularity conditions. Experiments demonstrate that a score-aligned rule can improve performance on a held-out source validation split yet consistently degrade it after transfer, even without a single winning-class change. A separate perturbation study finds that near-boundary relative score changes track the direction of small AUROC changes in the tested settings. Finally, centroid approximation and shared scales connect the zero-step score to a static centroid family that includes the existing CTM detector. Together, these results explain why class attraction is insufficient to justify feature refinement and motivate evaluating its effect on the ranking boundary.

title: Who Pays for the Knowledge Models Copy? Model Collapse as Rogers' Paradox
abstract: Generative models trained on the output of earlier models lose knowledge across generations, rare knowledge first. The remedies that work all bring in information from outside the loop, and the theory of model collapse treats that supply as given: a fixed archive, drawn from a fixed distribution. We argue that the supply is the problem, and that cultural evolution has the theory of it. We read model collapse as Rogers' paradox: a population that comes to rely on copying ends up no better off than one that never copied, because copies go stale unless someone keeps learning for themselves. We test the identification in three steps. First, Rogers' model, fitted only to fully synthetic training, predicts to within a few percentage points how much rare knowledge language models, from word trigrams to a pretrained transformer, retain under other mixtures of fresh data. Second, when the world itself changes, a lineage that copies its own past needs more fresh data to keep up the faster the world changes, as Rogers' model says it must and as analyses that assume a fixed target cannot; a lineage that restarts every generation from fixed pretrained weights is largely insulated, because those weights are knowledge that is never copied. Third, we close the loop: when the people who write a model's training data can ask the model instead of finding things out, the supply of fresh data becomes endogenous. At equilibrium, the model is exactly as reliable as it is costly for people to find out for themselves, the population is no better off than without the model, and every increase in the share of model-written text must be paid for by more people learning for themselves. Users who check what they are told and relearn when it is wrong break the paradox. Filters that select plausible text are conformist and accelerate collapse; only checks that carry new information act as critical learning.

title: Vertical Segmented Waveguide-Enabled Pinching Antenna (V-SWAN)-Assisted EDMA-NOMA Integrated Sensing and Communication Systems
abstract: This paper proposes a vertical segmented waveguide-enabled pinching antenna (V-SWAN)-assisted downlink non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA)-integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) environmental division multiple access (EDMA) framework for simultaneously supporting multi-user communication and target sensing. In the proposed framework, multiple pinching antennas (PAs) are deployed along a segmented vertical dielectric waveguide to serve communication users (CUs), aerial users (AUs), and sensing target (ST). CUs are distributed on the ground, whereas AUs and ST are above the ground, where line-of-sight (LoS) and non-line-of-sight (NLoS) propagation conditions coexist. In particular, SWAN provides an effective platform for realizing EDMA by reducing the effective propagation distance and in-waveguide attenuation, thereby suppressing co-channel interference and enabling efficient multi-user transmission. The communication and sensing model are formulated, followed by the corresponding SINR expressions. We formulate the statistical characterizations for the combination of LoS and NLoS propagation for CUs, and LoS propagation for AUs and sensing channels for generalized multi-user, multi-PA scenarios. Based on these statistical characterizations, the segment outage and sensing outage probabilities are derived and evaluated for the generalized framework. The asymptotic evaluation is also done at a high transmit signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) to gain further insights. The results show that the proposed framework outperforms the conventional H-SWAN and single vertical pinching antenna system (V-PASS) in terms of segment outage probability, sensing outage probability, and segment sum rate. Monte Carlo simulation results closely match the analytical results, validating the accuracy of the derived expressions.

title: Optimal LCA and Sublinear Estimation for Bipartite Matching in $Δ^{O(1/\varepsilon)}$ Queries
abstract: A local computation algorithm (LCA) for matching answers ``who is the mate of $v$?'' by inspecting only a small part of the graph, with all answers consistent with one matching. For $n$-vertex graphs of maximum degree $Δ\ge2$, Levi et al. [Algorithmica'17] give a $(1-\varepsilon)$-approximate matching LCA using $(Δ/\varepsilon)^{O(1/\varepsilon^2)} \operatorname{polylog}(n)$ queries per invocation, while Yoshida et al. [SIAM J. Comput.'12] estimate the maximum matching size within additive error $\varepsilon n$ using $Δ^{O(1/\varepsilon^2)}$ queries. Behnezhad, Roghani, and Rubinstein [FOCS'23] proved a $Δ^{Ω(1/\varepsilon)}$ lower bound for both tasks, even on bipartite graphs and even when the LCA's matching guarantee is relaxed to additive $\varepsilon n$ error. This leaves a gap between linear and quadratic dependence on $1/\varepsilon$ in the exponent. We close this gap on bipartite graphs. We give an LCA that answers each mate query with $Δ^{O(1/\varepsilon)}$ queries for a $(1-\varepsilon)$-approximate matching, and an estimator for the maximum matching size within $\varepsilon n$ using $Δ^{O(1/\varepsilon)}$ queries. On general graphs, the same algorithm gives a half-integral fractional matching and estimates the maximum fractional matching size. Our approach runs $O(\varepsilon^{-1}\logΔ)$ rounds of a deterministic local optimization method in which vertices propose to neighbors and update prices according to incoming loads. We design its updates to admit exact recursive sampling with constant expected branching, obtaining the improved randomized bound without exploring full dependency neighborhoods. To our knowledge, this is the first LCA construction based on exact recursive sampling of the iterates of a deterministic continuous optimization method. We expect this approach to have applications beyond matching.

title: When Every Choice Is Correct: A Causal Study of Numerical Preference in Language Models
abstract: When a language model chooses a number between 1 and 30, every integer in the range is valid, yet the model can favor particular answers. We use numerical choice to study how preference is processed across layers and tokens. Perturbation probing and gradient attribution nominate neurons for activation interventions. In a selected Qwen3-4B case, a pre-answer edit changes 17 to 15 while both runs first emit 1. After the edit ends, selective cache and attention-output replacements trace part of its continuing influence on the second digit. Replacing one attention head's output or the other heads' outputs jointly produces similar immediate readout contributions; both interventions restore 17 but have different final log-odds effects on 7 versus 5. Holding later multilayer perceptron (MLP) outputs at their values from the edited run without either replacement reduces this effect gap from 0.119 to 0.0025 nat. Later computation therefore changes how similar local contributions affect the continuation. Retrospective estimates across eighteen contexts capture much of the probability movement but miss the selected answer switch. Prompt tests also separate influence from answer changes: one held-out prompt retains influence without switching, and only one of twelve fresh wordings qualifies for the reader/MLP test; there, joint MLP clamping again reduces the gap between the two reader effects while the answer remains 17. These results use numerical choice as a controlled case for studying persistent state and conditional downstream processing; they do not establish the origin or a complete circuit of natural numerical preference.

title: Spectroscopy-informed Deep Learning Searches for Photometric Little Red Dots in JWST Surveys
abstract: Little Red Dots (LRDs) are a population of compact, red sources discovered at high redshift with JWST that exhibit distinctive V-shaped spectral energy distributions (SEDs). Existing LRD samples are typically identified using a variety of color-based selection criteria, which can lead to differences in the populations recovered by different studies. We develop a cross-modal machine-learning framework that combines matched NIRCam imaging and NIRSpec/PRISM spectroscopy to transfer spectroscopic information into imaging-based representations, enabling LRD identification from JWST/NIRCam imaging alone. Applied to spectroscopically observed high-redshift galaxies previously classified as non-LRDs, our model identifies 35 new LRD candidates. The majority satisfy at least one independent LRD color selection criterion, and among the 13 candidates with medium- or high-resolution NIRSpec grating spectra, 10 exhibit broad H$α$ emission - a hallmark of LRDs. We further apply the classifier to public NIRCam imaging from the Dawn JWST Archive and two independent JWST surveys, yielding 357 and 23 additional LRD candidates, respectively. The candidates recovered by our method span a broader range of observed SED properties than those in existing samples, suggesting that current color-selected samples may not fully capture the diversity of LRD-like systems present in JWST surveys. Our findings highlight the value of spectroscopy-informed photometric classification as a powerful strategy for systematically mining large-area JWST imaging datasets and provide a practical framework for future studies of this emerging population.

title: Practical Estimation of the Bayes Optimal Fairness-Accuracy Tradeoff with Soft Labels
abstract: There is a fundamental limit to the best prediction error of any model for a given data distribution. In classification, the Bayes error quantifies this limit and serves as both a benchmark for trained models and a criterion to detect overfitting. The state-of-the-art Bayes error estimation techniques for binary classification use only soft labels (positive class probabilities) and require no input features or auxiliary training. We extend such notions to constrained classification problems, such as fairness. Fair classification is an important case of constrained or multi-objective classification. It requires a model not only to be accurate but also to yield fair outcomes (equal or near-equal true positive rates) across different demographic groups (e.g., race and gender). This leads to an inherent fairness-accuracy tradeoff or a Pareto frontier that is used to compare fair classifiers against each other. The focus of our work is to estimate the fundamental limit for this fairness-accuracy tradeoff. We derive an explicit expression for the fair Bayes error rate (i.e., best achievable error rate subject to given fairness constraints), and construct consistent, instance-free estimators for it using only soft labels and group information. We provably bound the bias and the sample complexity of our estimators. Empirically, our method produces a robust, low-variance estimate of the optimal fairness-accuracy tradeoff curve, even when the soft labels are noisy and derived from a classification model on hard labels.

title: The Effectiveness of Sliding Mode Control for Robust Vision Stabilization under the Plant-Binding Condition
abstract: Boundary-layer Sliding Mode Control (SMC) has been applied to vision-based stabilization, but identifying its activation condition against simpler causal baselines (LPF, PID) has been elusive. The operational condition is plant binding: the disturbance velocity approaches or exceeds the actuator slew limit, so the bounded per-step actuation budget binds. We validate this in two independent vision domains: handheld translation stabilization (12 1080p clips; LPF, PID, SMC, L1) and angular re-framing against a virtual slew-rate-limited pan-tilt-zoom (PTZ) plant. Outside binding, leave-one-out cross-validation makes SMC and LPF on translation statistically indistinguishable, and PID beats SMC on the angular 99th-percentile pointing offset by 5.85 degrees (95% CI clear of zero); inside binding -- reached only by sweeping the simulated slew limit, as both captured datasets land outside it -- the translation gap stays a tie and SMC beats PID on the angular worst case (Cohen's d up to +0.83). The PTZ plant's 100 degrees/s default sits on the cross-over, which explains a small-margin PID result previously reported in the angular setting. A complementary ablation shows raising the SMC reaching gain k costs mean tracking outside a narrow window.

title: Quantum Adiabatic Theorem under Wiener Noise: Maximal Mean-Square Estimates
authors: K. K. W. A. S. Kumara
abstract: We derive maximal mean-square adiabatic estimates for finite-dimensional stochastic Schrödinger equations with Hamiltonian-proportional Wiener noise. For deterministic $C^2$ Hamiltonians whose eigenvalues have constant multiplicities and do not cross on $[0,1]$, we construct a unitary stochastic adiabatic intertwiner driven by the same Wiener process as the exact propagator. A commutator argument, Itô calculus, and Doob's maximal inequality yield an explicit bound for the expected supremum of their squared operator-norm difference on a selected initial eigenspace. Under uniform coefficient bounds, the physical noise scaling $α=σT^{-γ}$, where $T$ is the total evolution time and $σ\geq0$ and $γ\geq0$ are fixed, gives maximal mean-square error $O(T^{-2}+σ^4T^{-4γ}+σ^2T^{-(2γ+1)})$. Consequently, adiabatic convergence holds for every $γ>0$ as $T\to\infty$, while $γ\geq1/2$ recovers the deterministic $O(T^{-1})$ bound for the root-mean-square maximal error. For fixed nonzero physical noise amplitude, the estimate leaves convergence unresolved.

title: Capelli Operators and the Bernstein-Sato polynomials of Minors
abstract: For every ideal of minors of a generic complex matrix, we determine all roots and their multiplicities in the Bernstein-Sato polynomial. These roots lie in explicit rational intervals indexed by the rank strata. Every nonintegral root is simple, whereas the multiplicity of each integral root equals the number of labels producing that root. We deduce the strong motivic monodromy conjecture, including the inequality relating pole orders to root multiplicities; for minors of size $r$, the largest possible root multiplicity over all matrix dimensions is $\lfloor\sqrt{4r-1}\rfloor$. Keywords. Bernstein-Sato polynomial, determinantal ideal, root multiplicities, strong monodromy conjecture.

title: Toward Shifted symplectic Chiralization: Deformation of Courant Algebroids
abstract: We study the chiralization of Poisson--Lie theory through graded symplectic geometry. We compare Courant deformations and classical $r$- and $R$-matrix constructions, obtaining integrable hierarchies and free field realizations. We give a variational description of the obstruction to Lie conformal bialgebra compatibility and recover Liberati's obstruction in the Virasoro case. We also introduce a vertex bialgebra analogue of quantized universal enveloping algebras and construct explicit quantizations to all orders of Cartan type Lie conformal bialgebra structures on $\operatorname{Cur}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$. These results contribute to the first author's broader programme of developing shifted symplectic chiralization as a geometric method for constructing chiral analogues of Poisson-Lie structures via $n$-shifted symplectic geometry, and exploring its connections with AKSZ theory and quantization.

title: The Cone Fixing the Reals of $\mathrm{HOD}^{M_{2n}(x)}$
abstract: For a cone of reals $x$, the reals of $\mathrm{HOD}^{L[x]}$ are precisely the reals in $Q_3$, or equivalently, the set of reals in $M_1$, the minimal proper class mouse with a Woodin cardinal. We show that if $z$ is any real coding $M_1|δ^{+M_1}$, then $z$ is the base of such a cone (so $M_1^{\#}$ is such a base). We also establish a kind of optimality for this result, by identifying a real $x$ such that $M_1\subseteq L[x]$ but $\mathbb{R}\cap\mathrm{HOD}^{L[x]}\not\subseteq M_1$, although there is a base for the cone in a generic extension of $L[x]$. We prove an analogous result for the reals of $\mathrm{HOD}^{M_{n}(x)}$ for even $n$, as well as an analogous optimality result which holds for all $n$.

title: Can a self-sustaining chemical network emerge due to just a few catalysts?
abstract: Understanding how self-sustaining chemical reaction networks can emerge from simple molecules is an important question in chemical approaches to the origin of life. Reflexively autocatalytic and food-generated (RAF) sets provide a mathematical framework for investigating this question. This line of research goes back to the early work of Kauffman on autocatalytic reaction networks and was subsequently developed through the probabilistic framework of Mossel and Steel. Further contributions by Hordijk, Steel, and collaborators extended the theory to more heterogeneous forms of catalysis, including reaction-dependent probabilities or power-law distributions of catalytic activity. We introduce a stochastic model that combines heterogeneous molecular catalytic activity with reaction-dependent molecule-reaction compatibility. By assigning random catalytic weights to molecules and incorporating compatibility through an explicit formulation of catalysis probabilities, our model provides a concrete and flexible setting that captures both sources of heterogeneity while remaining mathematically tractable. We establish novel and general criteria for RAF formation and nonformation. We further demonstrate that classical phase-transition criteria need not remain valid in the presence of reaction-dependent catalysis. For heavy-tailed catalytic weights, we identify and rigorously quantify an additional phase transition. In models with finite-mean catalytic weights, RAF formation and nonformation are governed by a catalytic intensity parameter. For infinite-mean weights, however, we show that RAFs may emerge with probability tending to one even when the catalytic intensity parameter tends to zero.

title: CoordX Protocol: Peer to Peer Cryptographically Verified Shared Records
abstract: People, companies and software agents often must work on shared records even when they do not trust each other. Today they usually give those records to a central server. The server keeps the canonical copy, authenticates users, and decides who has permissions to act on the record. The CoordX Protocol removes the need for that central server. In the CoordX protocol the author of a record holds full permission over it. Permission for any other party to create, read or update the record is assigned by explicit grants and keys. An invitation only starts contact between two parties. It gives no permission. Each record is a causal tree of signed entries, and each entry is immutable. Each entry names the permission that allowed it. Any party can get the proof of that permission and check it without help from anyone. Two honest parties that check the same bytes, with the same keys and local settings, always get the same answer. The content is encrypted, so the relays that may carry it in transit see only sealed bytes. To exclude a party from future content, the other parties move to new keys. The protocol does not choose a winning version, does not put entries in time order, and does not need global agreement. Applications decide what the entries mean above the level of the protocol.

title: TRACK: Multiple Instance Learning for Anti-Money Laundering in Transaction Networks
abstract: Anti-money laundering (AML) investigations are organized around accounts, while the suspicious evidence for an account may reside in only a few of its transactions. Yet many account-level detectors summarize transactions before learning, and message-passing models may aggregate once more over neighboring accounts. We name this discrepancy the aggregation mismatch and study it under an account-window benchmark label defined by the presence of at least one flagged transaction. We recast account-level AML detection as multiple instance learning, in which an account-window is a bag and its transactions are instances. We propose TRACK, which encodes every transaction with a shared encoder and selectively pools the encodings into an account decision. To emulate coarse supervision, we withhold the transaction labels of five AML datasets from TRACK throughout training. Under a time-ordered protocol, TRACK achieves the highest average precision among the tabular and graph baselines trained from account labels on every dataset. Despite using only account-window supervision, it remains competitive with edge classifiers trained directly from transaction labels. Its instance scores also rank flagged transactions well above chance and approach or exceed directly supervised ranking performance across datasets.

title: PIMROP: A Feasibility Study of Return-Oriented Programming on Commercial Processing-in-Memory Architectures
abstract: Processing-in-Memory places small programmable cores on the memory device, where they execute beside the DRAM banks and beyond the control-flow defenses that protect host programs. The security of this in-memory code is an attack surface that remains largely unstudied. We present PIMROP, to our knowledge the first demonstrated code-reuse attack on a commercial Processing in-Memory ISA. We show that return-oriented programming is feasible on a real, commercially shipped PIM instruction set, the UPMEM DPU, whose DRAM Processing Units run C compiled by a dedicated LLVM toolchain. We build Galileo-for-DPU, a gadget scanner adapted to the DPU's fixed-width, 8-byte-aligned RISC encoding, and run it entirely on the UPMEM functional simulator in a reproducible Docker and VM environment. We find the runtime library that every kernel links already yields 517 non-trivial gadgets covering all five canonical ROP primitive classes, and all 13 PrIM benchmarks we scanned carry gadgets as well. We then demonstrate two verified end-to-end attacks, each reproducible on 10 of 10 runs. In the first, a stack buffer overflow in a DPU kernel overwrites the saved return address and diverts control into a routine that copies a secret into host-readable memory. In the second, we leak the same secret using a chain of reused gadgets alone, without diverting control into any such routine. We further show that two standard defenses--stack canaries and _FORTIFY_SOURCE-style bounds-check fortification--fail on the DPU in ways specific to the platform (misplaced canary, silently inactive wrapper), and we verify a bounds-checked DMA that stops the attack on 10 of 10 runs with no effect on benign requests. To enable further research on PIM security, we open-source Galileo-for-DPU and our testing harness at https://github.com/wtegge2/ROP-in-PIM.

title: Thermodynamic signatures of the period-doubling route to chemical chaos
abstract: Chemical reaction networks can evolve from stable oscillations to chaos through successive period doublings. We investigate general properties of entropy-production fluctuations near the onset of chaos and within the chaotic regime in reversible, well-mixed reaction networks. Near an isolated supercritical period-doubling bifurcation, we find a one-sided divergence of the diffusion constant with exponent one. For chaotic attractors satisfying the stated conditions, the entropy variance per unit volume grows exponentially when the macroscopic limit is taken first. Its exponential growth rate is $2λ_{\max}$, where $λ_{\max}$ is the largest Lyapunov exponent, implying a divergent diffusion constant. We also discuss the volume dependence of the fluctuations and the underlying physical mechanisms.

title: Act-HiMotif: Hierarchical Daily Activity Schedule Generation via Learned Activity-Structure Motifs
abstract: Generating daily activity schedules from individual attributes (e.g., age and income) is valuable for activity-based travel modeling and human behavior simulation. The task is challenging because exact activity structures follow a highly imbalanced, long-tailed distribution, while the same structure can admit multiple duration allocations under a fixed full-day budget. Direct generation must therefore learn many exact activity structures from highly uneven observations while modeling their possible temporal realizations. However, many exact structures share recurring activity organization. Based on this observation, we propose Act-HiMotif, a hierarchical motif-based generative model that introduces learned, reusable activity-structure motifs as an intermediate representation between individual profiles and specific activity structures. Act-HiMotif first distinguishes home-only days from active days, then samples a motif from a profile-conditioned prior to guide activity-structure generation, and finally applies a budget-constrained duration allocator to generate activity durations that sum exactly to the full-day horizon. This hierarchy models home-only routing, activity-structure generation, and duration allocation at their corresponding levels, while motifs allow related structures to share statistical support without losing their distinct sequences. Experiments on large-scale travel survey data show that Act-HiMotif outperforms strong baselines in both in-distribution and spatial generalization settings, demonstrating the effectiveness of hierarchical generation and reusable activity-structure motifs for producing realistic profile-conditioned daily activity schedules.

title: Securing Web Agents with the Compile-Then-Execute Paradigm
abstract: Web agents commonly follow the ReAct paradigm, selecting each action from runtime observations that inherently mix trusted and untrusted content. This design makes their control flow vulnerable to prompt injections embedded in webpages. We introduce Baya, a compile-then-execute web agent designed to prevent prompt-injection-driven control-flow hijacking by design. Before accessing the live website, Baya compiles the user's request into an executable Python program that calls a Trusted Website API. The planning model does not observe live website content; only the compiled program processes it. Untrusted data may determine program values or select among branches defined during compilation, but it cannot redefine the user task or cause the model to synthesize new website operations at runtime. The Trusted Website API gives the compiler a unified view of the website's action space, enabling ahead-of-time planning without the stepwise action discovery required by reactive agents. Our evaluation across 581 valid WebArena Verified tasks shows that Baya achieves 77.8% aggregate utility, outperforming browser-only ReAct (55.1%) and API-enabled ReAct (66.7%). On WASP, a security benchmark for web agents, Baya achieves 0% attack success rate, compared with 16.2% for API-enabled ReAct and 25.5% for browser-only ReAct.

title: USI-Brain: Enhancing Underwater Spatial Intelligence via Spatial Data-Driven Vision-Language Modeling
abstract: Underwater spatial reasoning depends on object boundaries and geometric cues that are obscured by scattering, color distortion, and low visibility. Existing underwater resources capture these cues through images, annotations, and depth maps, but provide fragmented supervision for vision-language models. We present a spatial data engine that connects visual appearance with object-level geometry through enhancement, 2D and geometry-assisted question generation, and expert filtering. It produces 4.27M QA pairs across five capability groups. We use this corpus to train USI-Brain and introduce an Underwater Prior-guided Rectifier (UPR) that applies gated corrections to visual features. USI-Bench evaluates the resulting capabilities with 6,525 held-out QA pairs. On its 15 task metrics, USI-Brain and USI-Brain + UPR improve over Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct by 5.76 and 7.63 points on average, respectively, using signed differences on 100-point scales. Ablations show that geometry-assisted supervision improves depth and ordering by 4.8 and 6.1 points with UPR disabled, while UPR adds 18.0 points in scene description under matched training data. Both variants use raw images at evaluation. Across NautData, UWBench, and MarineEval, USI-Brain achieves the best or joint-best score on 28 of 32 metrics. Model weights and USI-Bench will be released at https://github.com/SKY-Zhu-91/USI-Brain.

title: Poissonian Pair Correlation and Discrepancy Rates
abstract: We prove the existence of a sequence in $[0,1)$ with Poissonian pair correlation (PPC) and optimal-order star discrepancy $D_N^*=O((\log N)/N)$, and further give a deterministic construction by applying a conditional-expectation rule to a nested dyadic random model. We also show that PPC imposes no universal discrepancy decay rate: for every positive sequence $ρ_N\to0$, there exists a PPC sequence with $D_N^*/ρ_N\to\infty$. Under suitable regularity and growth assumptions, we realize prescribed discrepancy asymptotics, including $D_N^*\sim c_βN^{-β}$ for every $0<β<1$, with $c_β>0$. We further construct a PPC sequence satisfying $D_N^*\asymp(\log N)/N$ for all sufficiently large $N$.

title: UniRestorer++: Scalable Universal Image Restoration with Multi-Granularity Degradation Modeling
abstract: Universal image restoration aims to handle diverse degradations within a single model, but a reliable scaling strategy remains underexplored. Increasing backbone depth and width can lead to performance saturation, while degradation-aware specialization depends on accurate degradation estimation and is vulnerable to errors on out-of-distribution and real-world inputs. We propose UniRestorer++, a scalable framework based on multi-granularity degradation modeling. It progressively refines degradation groups and introduces group-specific experts, coupling capacity growth with specialization. Degradation-estimation-based routing selects a root-to-leaf path, while granularity-estimation-based routing chooses a level along that path to balance specialization and robustness. Spatially dense degradation representation maps further enable region-aware routing for spatially non-uniform corruptions. We develop CDD-50, a benchmark covering 50 degradation categories from single to penta-degradation. Experiments show approximately log-linear PSNR trends over the evaluated model-size range and stronger scaling gains on out-of-distribution and real-world data than vanilla MoE scaling. UniRestorer++ achieves state-of-the-art performance across benchmarks and demonstrates zero-shot generalization and few-shot transfer on real-world images. Code: https://github.com/mrluin/UniRestorer_plusplus

title: Confucius4-R2T2: A Stable-Prefix Streaming ASR Model for Real Real-Time Transcription
abstract: Streaming speech recognition is increasingly consumed by machines, such as translators and voice agents, that act on each token as it appears. A token that is later revised costs wasted work or a wrong action. In this work, we present Confucius4-R2T2 (short for Real Real-Time Transcription), a stable-prefix streaming ASR model that never modifies its earlier output while maintaining high accuracy and low latency. R2T2 is obtained by post-training Qwen3-ASR-1.7B on 1,500 hours of Chinese and English audio while freezing its pre-trained audio encoder and projector. The adaptation is based on the concept of Longest Stable Prefix (LSP), a new notion that we introduce in this work. We prove that LSP is monotone under the prefix order, consistent with the full-audio output, and maximal among labels that equal a whole earlier output. Learning from LSP labels converts a full-context model into a stable-prefix streaming one without any architectural change. Extensive evaluations show that R2T2 brings streaming recognition close to the base model's full-context quality while delivering stable text with low emission lag. Its gains extend beyond the post-training languages, demonstrating a practical path from full-context ASR to stable streaming. We open-source the model weights and code at https://huggingface.co/netease-youdao/Confucius4-R2T2 and https://github.com/netease-youdao/Confucius4-R2T2.

title: Do Search-Augmented Recommenders Use the Latest Search Episode?
abstract: Search-augmented recommenders can use the latest search episode and earlier searches. We introduce FocalSwap to test how these inputs contribute to the next recommendation. For each recommendation, it changes the latest search slot or all search inputs while holding the target, candidates, pre-search history, and scorer fixed. It compares neutral masks with matched observed-search replacements, recording rank changes, RR gains relative to each control, and preference for the true focal search. A planted signal and GenSAR's current-query task confirm that the audit detects known input dependence. We evaluate behavioral and lexical evidence on KuaiSAR and Qilin, and recommendation checkpoints trained using the released SESRec and UniSAR implementations. Across three independently trained UniSAR checkpoints, the estimated all-source benefit depends on the control. On the same 66,139 rows, replacing all search inputs with a neutral ID yields a positive signed contribution, whereas replacing them with category/profile-matched observed search sequences gives smaller estimates, with an interval below zero for one checkpoint. The paired RR gaps range from $+2.770 \times 10^{-3}$ to $+6.604 \times 10^{-3}$, and every adjusted interval is above zero. Neutral masks change 59.7-61.7% of target ranks, while matched replacements change 44.1-44.8%. The control contrast persists across five alternative donor assignments per checkpoint. Under the primary neutral-mask and category-matched controls, positive latest-slot contribution is not established in SESRec or UniSAR. These results show why masking evidence should be compared with observed-search replacements when attributing a benefit to broader search state or the latest episode.

title: Single-crystal X-ray diffraction of BC8 carbon near terapascal pressures
abstract: Whether carbon forms crystalline structures beyond diamond at terapascal pressures remains unresolved. Predicted for nearly four decades, the denser BC8 phase has lacked direct crystallographic evidence. Here we report the first direct crystallographic identification of BC8 carbon, formed as a single crystal from molten carbon during laser-driven decaying-shock compression of [100]-oriented diamond following loading above 1.1 TPa. Using in situ orientation-resolved single-crystal X-ray diffraction, we observe discrete Bragg spots whose spacings and angular relationships are reproduced by a common orientation matrix within each indexed BC8 reflection group, providing constraints beyond powder peak matching. Our single-crystal formation strategy and direct diffraction evidence resolve the decades-long quest for a post-diamond carbon structure, demonstrating how dynamic loading pathways can make predicted high-pressure phases experimentally accessible.

title: DeepfakeGenome: Toward Next-Generation Deepfake Attribution
abstract: In recent years, AIGC technologies are capable of generating hyper-realistic forged facial images, posing severe threats to facial security safety. To tackle these challenges, early Deepfake research primarily centered on real-fake classification. Recently, growing efforts have been devoted to the Deepfake Attribution (DFA) of generated content. Nevertheless, existing research on Deepfake detection and attribution faces saturated performance in binary classification, limited diversity in datasets and algorithms, and imperfect evaluation protocols, which severely impede practical application. To address these limitations, we propose a comprehensive deepfake detection and attribution benchmark named DeepfakeGenome (DFG). It contains 100 facial forgery algorithms and 2M images in total, achieving 4x to 100x larger than prior DFA benchmarks. We further design 4 protocols for practical evaluation, including a novel retrieval-based attribution paradigm.
