Ultimately, our characterization demonstrates that these new concepts can help identify an ideal that is maximal and effectively represent any closed $τ$-neighborhood of $θ$ within these spaces.

title: Random waves on sub-Riemannian $SU(2)$
abstract: Random spherical eigenfunctions for the Lalplace-Beltrami operator are well understood and their local behavior, after renormalization, is described by Berry's random wave model. In this paper we construct a family of random fields on the sphere $\mathbb{S}^{3}$, identified with the group $SU(2)$, endowed with a sub-Riemannian structure. These fields are random eigenfunctions for the sub-Laplacian and they are constructed from matrix elements of unitary irreducible representations of $SU(2)$. We prove that the local behavior of such fields is the same as the Berry-Heisenberg random field on the Heisenberg group introduced in [10].

title: A Definition of Catastrophic Performance
abstract: A central challenge in AI is specifying objectives that align with human preferences. While existing theoretical results elucidate how misspecification impacts performance, they typically do not distinguish between merely suboptimal and catastrophic outcomes. To enable rigorous analysis of catastrophic risk from AI misalignment, we introduce a formal definition of catastrophic performance. Our definition is based on two reference values. The first, baseline value, captures the value attained if no agent is deployed. The second, orthogonal value, captures the value of a trajectory that is unrelated to human preferences, in a sense we describe. Orthogonal value is typically far worse than baseline value. We interpret these reference values through examples in which past human activity has altered the state of the environment to human benefit. Starting at the resulting state, an AI agent is deployed with the goal of accelerating further progress. Catastrophic performance represents this agent's undoing of benefits afforded by human activity.

title: ST-CGMDiff: Sparse-Conditioned Cross-Frequency Spatio-Temporal Latent Diffusion for Dynamic 3D Channel Gain Map Reconstruction
abstract: Accurate and efficient reconstruction of channel gain maps (CGMs) is essential for environment-aware wireless communications. Unlike prior works that focus on static CGMs at a single frequency band, this paper studies the construction of dynamic three-dimensional (3D) CGMs across multiple frequency bands over consecutive time slots, using limited channel measurements. Specifically, for a given transmitter (Tx) location, we represent the CGM at any given receiver (Rx) height as a two-dimensional (2D) grayscale image, where each pixel indicates the average channel gain over the corresponding Rx spatial grid cell. Accordingly, we propose ST-CGMDiff, a spatio-temporal latent diffusion framework that integrates sparse-observation conditioning and cross-frequency modeling to reconstruct dynamic 3D CGMs across multiple carrier frequencies and varying Rx heights within a unified model. In this framework, we jointly encode the input parameters, including the current sparse observations, observation masks, physical Tx and Rx z-coordinates, and carrier frequencies as spatial conditions. A frequency-conditioned convolutional gated recurrent unit (ConvGRU) then extracts causal information from previously constructed CGMs, while a spatially adaptive fusion mechanism balances historical information and current observations. Furthermore, bidirectional convolutional long short-term memory (BiConvLSTM) modules are introduced to capture the ordered dependencies among the selected Rx z-layers. Finally, we perform few-step latent diffusion followed by high-resolution residual refinement to generate the final CGM with improved spatial fidelity.

title: FedXCrop: Privacy-Preserving Crop Disease Detection via Federated Learning with Post-Aggregation Explainability under Non-IID Farm Distributions
abstract: Deep learning can classify crop diseases accurately from benchmark leaf images, but centralized training requires farms to share raw data, and predictions without explanations offer limited support for treatment decisions. We present FedXCrop, a federated crop disease classification pipeline that quantitatively evaluates explanations of the aggregated global model. A MobileNetV2 model trained centrally on PlantVillage achieved 99.38% test accuracy (standard deviation 0.05 over three seeds) on a fixed test set of 5,428 images across 38 classes. Federated models initialized with ImageNet weights were trained for 30 rounds across five clients. FedAvg achieved 98.81% accuracy with identically distributed clients and 98.81%, 98.59%, and 97.78% under Dirichlet label skew (alpha = 1, 0.5, and 0.1, respectively). FedProx was not significantly different from FedAvg at any heterogeneity level (McNemar p > 0.3). Grad-CAM and SmoothGrad explanations were evaluated on 380 test images. Both attributed more energy to the leaf than chance (0.70-0.78 versus 0.60), while Grad-CAM maps from federated and centralized models showed Spearman correlations of 0.74-0.76. Agreement decreased as heterogeneity increased, lesion localization was only modestly above chance, and a model-randomization test indicated that SmoothGrad maps depended substantially on image structure rather than learned parameters. In this setting, label skew reduced federated accuracy by 0.6-1.6 percentage points relative to centralized training. FedAvg largely preserved Grad-CAM behavior, while FedProx provided no measurable benefit.

title: Spatial structure of surface plasmon resonance under narrow-beam illumination and its implications for sensing
abstract: The reflection of light on a surface plasmon resonance structure can be understood as the interference between the direct Fresnel reflection and the light radiated back by the plasmon as it propagates along the metal film. When the beam waist is only an order of magnitude larger than the surface plasmon propagation length, these two contributions separate spatially, and their destructive interference localizes into a dark fringe within the reflected beam. We develop an analytical model of this effect, design a realistic setup based on off-the-shelf components to observe it, and simulate the complete experiment, from illumination to detection, with an open-source framework. In the regime where the interference is maximized, the spatial structure of the reflected beam becomes extremely sensitive to the outer medium. This allows us to define an observable more than an order of magnitude more sensitive than amplitude-based measurements, and we expect a comparable improvement in resolution.

title: Consistent Submodular Maximization with Full Foresight
abstract: Online algorithms with bounded recourse face three intertwined obstacles: uncertainty about the future, computational limits, and a limited budget for changes. We ask a fundamental question that separates consistency from the other two: what does solution stability cost when the entire future is known and computation is unlimited? We answer this question for monotone submodular maximization, where an algorithm must maintain a solution of at most $k$ arrived elements, with a constant number of changes per step. We determine the optimal approximation thresholds: $3/4$ for deterministic algorithms and $ξ^\star \approx 0.7942$ for randomized algorithms. For every $\varepsilon>0$, we get within $\varepsilon$ of these thresholds with worst-case recourse polynomial in $1/\varepsilon$, independent of $k$ and the stream length. We prove matching impossibility results even for coverage functions. We attain the sharp bounds by optimally balancing two opposing forces: preparing for future arrivals and protecting the current solution. For randomized algorithms, we use addition robustness against prefixes of the known future, which we analyze tightly via an interval-selection problem. For deterministic algorithms, we introduce certificates, paths in a fractional relaxation that maintain high value, which we round into an update schedule.

title: Calmness Modulus of Parameterized Convex Constraint Systems: Exact Closed-Form Formulas via Second-Order Admissibility
abstract: We resolve the open problem of deriving an exact, closed-form algebraic formula for the calmness modulus of $\mathcal{C}^2$ convex constrained feasible set mappings $\mathcal{F}(b) := \{ x \in \mathbb{R}^n \colon f_t(x) \le b_t, \, \forall t \in T \}$ under right-hand side perturbations at a given pair of the graph $(\bar{b}, \bar{x})$. First, under the condition $0_n \in \mathrm{int}\left(\mathrm{conv}\left\{ \nabla f_t(\bar{x}) ,\; t \in T(\bar{x}) \right\}\right)$, we prove that the calmness modulus coincides with the inverse distance from the origin to the boundary of the nominal subdifferential. Second, for general $\mathcal{C}^2$ convex systems where the previously mentioned interior condition does not hold, we introduce a second-order admissibility filtering over the active indexes. We show that this filtered family, $\mathcal{D}^0_2(\bar{x})$, yields an exact characterization of the calmness modulus relying solely on nominal data.

title: Explainable Anomaly Detection in 5G Networks through Continuous Time Graphs
abstract: 5G networks increasingly resemble distributed systems in their design. It then becomes crucial to move beyond traditional network-based detection methods and to explore alternative approaches. In this work, we propose a formalization of 5G network exchanges as a dynamic graph, on which we apply techniques from the field of graph-based learning to detect anomalies effectively. This representation allows for fine-grained analysis of packet-level semantic content, while simultaneously capturing sequential and topological contexts, both of which are essential for identifying sophisticated and multi-stage attacks. To assess the effectiveness of this formalism, we evaluate it with the most popular dynamic graph models, demonstrating its potential for 5G anomaly detection.

title: Understanding the Perception of Transliterated Offensive Social Media Posts Among Banglish and Hinglish Users
abstract: Effective content moderation depends on understanding not just what harmful content looks like, but how users perceive and respond to it. When offensive language is written in transliterated forms such as Banglish or Hinglish (Bangla or Hindi in Latin script), it may be interpreted very differently than in native scripts, with direct consequences for whether users report, ignore, or recognize it as harmful. Yet little is known about how script choice relates to user perception, or how these perceptions vary across demographic groups. To investigate these perceptions, we conducted a user study with $310$ participants ($193$ Hindi, $60$ Bangla, $57$ Bangla-Hindi bilingual speakers) who evaluated offensive posts in native scripts and transliterations. Participants provided offensiveness scores ($4.03$ for Banglish, $3.86$ for Hinglish) to transliterated posts, yet reporting fell from $20.9\%$ (native - Bangla, Hindi) to $18.2\%$ (transliterated - Banglish, Hinglish). Ignoring remained the dominant response (range $25.38\%-44\%$ overall). Women reported at higher probability than men for native-script ($23.6\%$ vs. $17.7\%$) and showed almost identical reporting probability in comparison to men for transliterated posts ($17.5\%$ vs. $17.9\%$), and younger participants ($<40$) rated Banglish content as more offensive than older participants ($\geq 40$), (Overall offensive score: $3.99$ vs. $3.78$). These findings identify transliteration as critical blind spot for moderation, underscoring the need for linguistically sensitive approaches to online safety.

title: Ambiguity Elimination via Successive Estimation in ISAC Systems with Reference Signals
abstract: Integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) systems can efficiently reuse 5G New Radio (NR) reference signals to enable joint communication and passive target detection. Among these, the Positioning Reference Signal (PRS) is widely adopted for high-performance sensing activities. However, the PRS configuration, given by the comb structure, introduces periodic ambiguities, resulting in ghost targets. Existing approaches mitigate this issue by combining PRS with additional reference signals, such as the DeModulation Reference Signal (DMRS), effectively removing ghosts but at the cost of higher complexity and sensing overhead. This paper proposes a low-complexity successive estimation strategy that initially allows ghost targets but progressively eliminates them using historical ambiguity-free estimations. The method comprises a matching process to associate current detections with historical real targets, and a pattern deviation detection mechanism to trigger a fallback to ambiguity-free estimation when the target set changes. We derive a sufficient condition that guarantees the correct matching as a function of target velocity, PRS comb size, subcarrier spacing, and sensing refresh rate. Using this condition, a parameter selection strategy is proposed to jointly improve sensing and communication performance. Numerical results demonstrate that our method achieves unambiguous detection while significantly reducing sensing resources, thus releasing more resources for communication compared to State-of-the-Art (SotA) approaches.

title: Separation Is a Riesz Energy: How Many Environments Does ICA Need?
abstract: How many environments and samples does it take to separate $d$ Gaussian sources whose variances change across environments? Each source has a signature, its vector of variances. The Riesz $2$-energy $E_j$ of source $j$ sums the inverse Fisher informations for rotating it towards other sources. With known whitening, we prove a worst-case squared-angle risk lower bound of order $E_j/(n+E_j)$ for orthogonal estimators at every $n$ and $d$. A quadratic pencil given the signatures attains $E_j/n$ up to a constant above a separation-dependent sample threshold, even with estimated whitening. For well-spread signatures at fixed $K$, the energy grows as $d^2$, $d\log d$ and $d$ for $K=2$, $3$ and $K\ge4$, respectively. A design with $K\asymp\log d$ and pairwise Fisher information bounded below by a constant makes $d\log d$ samples sufficient. The eigenvectors of a single fixed linear combination have an average first-order error coefficient of at least order $d^2$. Simulations up to $d=1000$ support the first-order predictions, and on task fMRI the energy helps rank split-half instability.

title: Bug2Scenario: Root-Cause-Preserving Test Scenario Amplification for Autonomous Driving Software
abstract: Simulation-based fuzzing exposes autonomous driving system (ADS) failures by repeatedly mutating and executing scenarios, but converting one failure into reusable regression scenarios remains difficult. Such variants test whether the mechanism persists after software changes, for example by varying weather or actor placement while retaining a collision's actor-route conflict. We present Bug2Scenario, a root-cause-guided post-fuzzing framework. From scenario data, traces, and oracle evidence, it extracts a root-cause pattern. An LLM proposes semantic variations over actors, missions, routes, and weather. Deterministic rules construct DriveFuzz-compatible scenarios. Execution evidence and manual review assess preservation. Separating these responsibilities prevents fluency, syntax, or recurring labels from masquerading as causal evidence. Under matched seeds, six LLM backbones, candidate budget, and execution pipeline, Bug2Scenario improves strict preservation by 6.7 percentage points (p=0.104; not significant) and boundary-inclusive preservation by 10.6 points (p=0.011). Feedback helps some initially unsuccessful seeds yield a strictly preserved candidate. Seed-level stopping then avoids further API calls and simulator runs. Remaining failures reflect actor-placement constraints, simulator instability, and incomplete or conflicting causal evidence. Bug2Scenario thus produces reliable ADS regression assets. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/YgcCoder/Bug2Sce.

title: Homology Features for X-Ray Hyperspectral Images Segmentation
abstract: Characterizing Multi-Energy X-ray Transmission (XRT) hyperspectral images presents significant challenges for traditional classification frameworks due to high-dimensional redundancy and non-linear spectral overlaps. Although manifold learning techniques such as UMAP enhance spectral representation by preserving non-linear correlations, they do not explicitly utilize the geometric structure of the embedded manifold for segmentation. This study introduces a hybrid architecture that integrates topological features derived from persistent homology with convolutional and graph neural networks. The approach computes Vietoris-Rips persistent homology on UMAP-projected superpixel point clouds to capture H 1 cyclic structures that encode spectral heterogeneity. These topological descriptors are combined with pixel-level CNN features through a broadcasting mechanism that propagates superpixel-level graph representations to full spatial resolution. Experimental results on XRT multi-energy imagery demonstrate that the proposed hybrid model significantly outperforms both CNN-only and superpixel-pooling fusion baselines, suggesting that topological features provide complementary discriminative information to local spectralspatial descriptors.

title: Exhaustive Search Is Hard to Beat in Constant Depth for Hyperclique and Orthogonal Vectors
abstract: A hyperclique in an $r$-uniform hypergraph is a set of vertices in which every $r$-subset is an edge. A simple exhaustive search algorithm detects a hyperclique on $\ell$ vertices in an $r$-uniform hypergraph on $m$ vertices by checking all $\binom{m}{\ell}$ sets of $\ell$ vertices. This algorithm can be expressed as a depth-two circuit with at most $m^\ell$ gates and wires. For hypercliques of *constant* size, Amano (2010) showed that this circuit is almost optimal: for large $r$, constant-depth circuits need $m^{\ell(1-O(\log r/r))}$ wires. We prove that this circuit remains hard to beat even for hypercliques of *polynomial* size. More precisely, circuits of depth $h$ need $m^{Ω(\ell)}$ gates for $\ell\leq m^{1/h-\varepsilon}$, and $m^{\ell(1-O(\log r/r))}$ gates for $\ell=m^{o(1)}$ that tends to infinity. Our hyperclique bound and the method behind it also lead to lower bounds for two central problems of fine-grained complexity. First, we extend the bound $n^{k/4}$ of Rossman (2008) for $k$-Clique from cliques of *constant* size to cliques of *polynomial* size: circuits of depth $h$ detecting a clique on $k$ vertices in an $n$-vertex graph need $n^{Ω(k)}$ gates for $k\leq n^{1/(h-1)-\varepsilon}$. Second, a reduction of Choudhury, Limaye, Sreenivasaiah, and Srinivasan (2026) turns our hyperclique bound into a lower bound of $n^{k-\varepsilon}$ gates for $k$-Orthogonal Vectors ($k$-OV) at every fixed depth for vectors of dimension $\log^{O(1)} n$; this proves the $k$-OV Conjecture for constant-depth circuits in polylogarithmic dimension. Finally, for $2$-OV in logarithmic dimension, we give a simple proof that depth-three circuits need $Ω(n^2)$ wires, which answers a question of Kane and Williams (2019).

title: Orientation of the spin axes of large Kuiper belt bodies as an indicator of the mechanism of their origin
abstract: The paper analyses the orientation of the spin axes of Kuiper Belt (KB) bodies that have satellites. For most of these bodies, the axes orientations were estimated under the assumption that the orbital planes of the satellites lie close to the bodies' equatorial planes. It was found that the spin axes of large scattered disks and plutinos' bodies, including four dwarf planets, are inclined at relatively small angles to the planes of their heliocentric orbits. This feature points to a possibility that all the scattered disk bodies, together with the bodies in the 3:2 resonance with Neptune, originated from the disruption of a single large body. The origin of the bodies of the so-called cold component of the KB is believed to differ from that of the scattered disk. The orientation of the spin axes of these bodies may also provide further evidence supporting this distinction.

title: Variational Splines and Generalized Gaussian Processes
abstract: Tikhonov regularization, kriging, and Gaussian-process regression share the same algorithm because, for a linear inverse problem with a Gaussian prior and Gaussian noise, the minimum-mean-square-error (MMSE) estimator is the solution of a regularized least-squares problem. We show that this equivalence survives the passage from vectors to generalized functions: the regularized least-squares estimators become generalized splines, and the Gaussian random vectors become generalized Gaussian processes (GGPs) on the dual of a nuclear space. A whitening operator $\mathrm{L}: \mathcal{S} \to L_2$ specifies both the native Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}_\mathrm{L} \subset \mathcal{S}'$ of the splines and a family of GGPs, which solve a stochastic differential equation subject to boundary conditions. We prove that the Gaussian spaces of these processes are congruent to the core $\mathrm{L}^\ast(L_2)$ of the native space, and that their MMSE estimators from finitely many linear measurements are generalized splines. Our framework extends the classical correspondences of Kimeldorf-Wahba, Parzen and Kailath in two respects: our estimators form a broader class that includes generalized functions, and we give a proper Bayesian treatment of the case where the null space of $\mathrm{L}$ is non-trivial. The framework gives a precise meaning to statements such as ``fractional splines are the optimal estimators of fractional Brownian motion,'' and it provides a rigorous Bayesian formulation of infinite-dimensional linear inverse problems.

title: A Dichotomy for Terminal Cyclability
abstract: Given an undirected graph $G$ and a set $R \subseteq V(G)$ of terminals, Terminal Cyclability asks whether $G$ contains a simple cycle visiting every vertex of $R$. We establish a complexity dichotomy for this problem on red-minor-closed classes of annotated graphs. In particular, we show that Terminal Cyclability is polynomial-time solvable on every such class excluding any annotated planar graph. The problem is NP-complete whenever the class contains all annotated planar graphs. More precisely, we give an $|G|^{2^{\mathbf{poly}(b)}}$-time algorithm, where $b$ is the bidimensionality of $(G,R)$. Our main technical contribution is the introduction of a weak irrelevant vertex rule. Rather than removing irrelevant vertices until the treewidth becomes constant, we only remove irrelevant vertices until the treewidth is logarithmic in the graph size. Such a weakening is necessary as a parameter-only treewidth threshold for an irrelevant vertex rule in this setting is known to be impossible to realise. Combined with a single-exponential algorithm for Terminal Cyclability parameterized by treewidth, this yields the polynomial-time algorithm for our dichotomy.

title: One ISAC Array, Two Worst Cases: Hardware Impairments in Beamforming and AoA Estimation
abstract: In integrated sensing and communication (ISAC), the same base-station array beamforms toward users and estimates their angle of arrival (AoA). In this paper, we study how element-level gain, phase, and position errors affect both functions of a beam-scanning uniform linear array. Any array produces a correlation peak at the true angle, of finite height and width, surrounded by sidelobes. Impairments shift this peak, make it lower and wider, and raise the sidelobes relative to it. A single decomposition explains these three effects: the gain-weighted least-squares fit of the per-antenna phase errors splits them into a tilt, which shifts the peak, and a residual, whose power is taken from the peak and redistributed over the sidelobes according to its spatial spectrum. A beam steered toward the strongest direction suffers from the lower peak only, whereas the AoA estimate suffers from its shift even without noise, and also from the lowering and sidelobes with noise. The worst cases for the two ISAC functions are thus nearly disjoint, and we characterize both: the worst case for beamforming leaves the AoA estimate unbiased, and the worst case for localization loses little beamforming gain. The worst case for localization is a single defect at the junction between two subarrays, and its error, relative to the main-lobe width, does not decrease with the number of antennas. We also characterize random impairments and the effect of noise. In practical terms, our analysis shows that the calibration of a dual-function array must be assessed with respect to both functions.

title: Ghost Target Elimination in 5G Reference Signals ISAC via Multi-static Multilateration
abstract: Integrated Sensing and Communication (ISAC) systems can reuse 5G New Radio (NR) reference signals to enable joint communication and environmental sensing. Among these signals, the Positioning Reference Signal (PRS) is particularly suitable for range and Doppler estimation. However, its comb structure introduces periodic ambiguities that generate ghost targets. Existing solutions resolve these ambiguities by combining PRS with additional signals such as the DeModulation Reference Signal (DMRS), which increases sensing overhead. This paper proposes a PRS-only sensing framework that resolves ambiguities using multi-static observations. Instead of removing ghosts locally at each receiver, the proposed method exploits spatial diversity and performs ambiguity resolution at a fusion anchor. The anchor jointly estimates target locations and ambiguity indices via multilateration across multiple sensing nodes. This approach eliminates the need for additional reference signals while maintaining low receiver complexity. Simulation results show that the proposed method reliably resolves ghost targets and achieves superior detection performance compared to benchmark methods across various scenarios, while significantly enhancing resource efficiency by enabling sensing using PRS-only transmissions.

title: SO3LR Tauri: Generally Applicable Force Fields for Reactive (Bio)Molecular Simulations Covering the Periodic Table
abstract: Machine-learned force fields (MLFFs) aim to create a unified model that describes all major classes of (bio)molecules at quantum-mechanical accuracy. We present SO3LR Tauri, a family of MLFFs developed toward this goal, coupling a fast SO3krates network to explicit, physics-based interaction modules: pair-specific short-range repulsion, environment-dependent dispersion, and electrostatics, each improved beyond its original formulation. The models are trained on 148 million structures spanning 85 elements, drawn from several quantum-chemical datasets. Against coupled-cluster references, the models accurately reproduce nucleobase-pair and charged protein-ligand interactions, carbohydrate conformer ordering, and molecular dipoles. They also resolve the transition pathways of organic and enzymatic reactions. Dynamical simulations recover experimental densities of water and organic solvents, the hydration structure of mono- and divalent ions, the pKa values of amino-acid side chains, and the structure and dynamics of proteins, membranes, nucleic acids, glycoproteins, and metal-containing biomolecules, all without system-specific fitting. Released in three sizes, the models reach 0.7-3.2 $μ$s/atom and scale to 27-84 million atoms on a single GPU. Much work remains to be done: achieving predictive accuracy for static and dynamic liquid properties, reaction barriers, coverage of chemical and conformational space, and the sampling and inference speed needed to describe biomolecular processes.

title: Zuse: A Decision Model for European Languages
abstract: Decision models read a document and return a probability for each of a fixed set of options instead of generating text. Several appeared in 2026, but none has published results outside English. We describe Zuse, three decision models (4B, 9B and 27B) that train a low-rank adapter and a pointer head on frozen open-weight bases, targeting 27 European languages, and use them to study how this design behaves across languages and tasks. On a broad European suite of 11 sources excluded from training, covering 9 task groups and 27 languages, a development set that also guided model selection, the 27B model reaches 87.5% accuracy with a pooled expected calibration error of 0.016, and 0.035 when weighted per source. Post-hoc analyses of these single-seed results give three findings. First, miscalibration is structured by task rather than language: on parallel reading and topic items in 26 languages the confidence gap varies about as much as sampling noise, while across sources it spans -0.07 to +0.09, with knowledge tasks overconfident and acceptability judgements underconfident at all three sizes, so one fitted temperature cannot correct both. Second, the share of decisions that can be automated at a 5% error budget follows chance-corrected skill (Spearman 0.97 over 33 source and model pairs) more closely than raw accuracy (0.91). Third, reach beyond the training languages is set by the base model: across 210 languages, changing the training run moved scores by at most about 2 points within a size, while languages outside the base's documented list trail by 23 to 28 points at every size. On English public suites Zuse is behind Jev and Kev, including Kev models on the same bases. We also report two pitfalls in building multi-source training data: label-word collision between topic schemes, and an injection augmentation that taught a shortcut. Zuse can be tried at https://bineric.com/zuse.

title: Finite-time mixing and reaction in packed bed reactors
abstract: We investigate mixing dynamics in porous media at finite times, using pore-scale lattice-Boltzmann simulations combined with Lagrangian particle tracking. We compute fluid deformation in randomly packed beds based on the moving Protean frame approach introduced by Lester 2018. From the extracted Lagrangian kinematics, we construct a mixing model based on lamellar aggregation that well predicts the Eulerian scalar fields obtained from simulations. Our results reveal an early time mixing regime dominated by shear-driven fluid deformation, where solute mixing arises from the random overlap of diffusive concentration elements. In this regime, mixing proceeds slowly and follows a temporal decay of concentration variance, $σ_c^2 \sim Pe^{-α/(2α+1)} t^{-1/2}$, where Pe is the Peclet number and $α$ the exponent characterizing shear deformation. This dynamic arises when the Peclet number is small relative to the ratio between the exponential-mixing and shear-deformation timescales. This analysis also demonstrates that shear-induced mixing govern the homogenization of early-stage reactions at the fluid-solid interface in finite-size random packed beds, typically operating at moderate Peclet numbers $Pe =O(10^2)$.

title: Hyperbolic Nanocavities for Single-Molecule Vibrational Strong Coupling
abstract: Hyperbolic phonon polaritons (HPhPs) in low-loss anisotropic materials such as hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) provide extreme sub-diffractional field confinement in the mid-infrared, making them attractive for enhancing the interaction of light with molecular vibrations. Collective vibrational strong coupling between molecular ensembles and HPhPs has already been demonstrated in extended slabs. Reaching this regime with a single molecule, however, remains a major challenge, and would provide a platform for investigating how vacuum electromagnetic fields influence molecular dynamics and chemical reactivity. Here, we show theoretically that single-molecule vibrational strong coupling can be reached in hBN nanocavities that laterally confine HPhPs within a finite volume. Combining full-wave electromagnetic simulations with the few-mode quantization approach, we find that these nanocavities support a rich set of asymmetric resonances that strongly enhance the local spectral density, with frequencies that follow from simple HPhP ray trajectories and can be tuned through the cavity aspect ratio. We identify resonances with quality factors of about $600$ and effective mode volumes of $|V_{\mathrm{eff}}| \sim 10^{-7}λ^{3}$, sufficient for single-molecule strong coupling with vibrational transitions with dipole moments on the order of $1\,\mathrm{D}$. These results establish hyperbolic nanocavities as a promising platform for single-molecule vibrational strong coupling and open new routes toward the local control of vibrational dynamics and molecular energy flow.

title: Sharp asymptotic stability of the IPM equation in $\mathbb{R}^2$ via isopycnal coordinates
abstract: We study the incompressible porous media (IPM) equation, a model describing the motion of a fluid with variable density through a porous medium under the action of gravity. We prove that the stably stratified state, in which heavier fluid lies below lighter fluid, is nonlinearly stable: small perturbations decay over time and the fluid returns to equilibrium. Our result holds in the sharp Sobolev setting $H^s(\mathbb R^2)$ for every $s>2$: this threshold cannot be improved, since the equation is ill-posed in $H^2(\mathbb R^2)$. This result follows from a proof of global well-posedness at critical Besov regularity, with smallness required only in a norm invariant under the natural scaling of the equation. We also prove optimal decay rates for suitably localized initial data. The main difficulty is that the stabilizing effect of stratification acts only in some directions, while the nonlinear transport acts in all of them. Reaching the sharp regularity threshold requires two main novelties. First, we rewrite the equation in \emph{isopycnal coordinates}, which follow the level sets of the density: in these coordinates the transport becomes one-dimensional, and the anisotropic stabilizing mechanism can be exploited at minimal regularity. Second, we establish new \emph{anisotropic commutator estimates} which allow us to control the remaining nonlinear terms. Finally, we show that the estimates obtained in isopycnal coordinates can be transferred back to the original variables.

title: From Continuum-Kinematics-Inspired Peridynamics to Simplicial Hyperelasticity
abstract: We develop a variational and functional-analytic framework for continuum-kinematics-inspired peridynamics with simultaneous nonlocal interactions among multiple points. We encode the finite-difference data of each interacting simplex in a simplicial deformation gradient. For nondegenerate simplices in three dimensions, the gradient, its cofactor, and its determinant encode the associated continuum-kinematics-inspired peridynamic line, area, and volume changes, respectively. This unified representation leads to a class of simplicial hyperelastic energies with general, possibly nonadditive, constitutive dependence on the affine deformation of an interacting simplex, thereby extending the original continuum-kinematics-inspired peridynamic framework. To describe interactions occurring at different scales and over different simplex geometries, we introduce radial- and shape-weighted nonlocal spaces. Their multipoint seminorms control two-point energies induced by the edge marginals of the interaction measure. This comparison yields nonlocal Poincaré inequalities and fractional Sobolev embeddings. We establish existence of equilibrium configurations by two complementary mechanisms. Particle-wise averaged convexity yields weak lower semicontinuity of the associated energy functionals. Under stronger assumptions on the edge marginals, fractional compactness gives existence for nonconvex energy densities. These results provide a mathematical foundation for simplicial and continuum-kinematics-inspired peridynamic models.

title: Three Homogenization Models for a Nonlinear Heterogeneous Rod with Microscale Dead Loading
abstract: A discrete chain of one-dimensional elements with concentrated elastic stiffness is analyzed to investigate the effect of self-equilibrated dead loads acting at the microscale. Three homogenization models are formulated for a finite chain whose total length is much larger than the unit-cell length. Model (i) homogenizes the elastic properties and the microscopic loading simultaneously, yielding an equivalent rod with homogeneous axial and flexural stiffnesses, an effective prestress state, and a distribution of nonlinear rotational springs. In Models (ii) and (iii), the microforces remain periodically distributed as external loads. Model (ii) has homogeneous axial and flexural stiffnesses, whereas Model (iii) retains piecewise-constant axial stiffness. Model (i) is shown to recover the continuum limit of the fully loaded discrete system and to provide the most accurate, fully homogenized description. Incorporating the microforces into the nonlinear homogenization procedure produces an unconventional prestress and a distributed rotational constraint, including rotational springs with negative tangent stiffness. The nonlinear equilibrium equation of Model (i) admits a closed-form solution in terms of elliptic functions, enabling analysis of large deflections and initial post-buckling behavior of a cantilever. The model predicts tensile and compressive buckling, as well as restabilization of the straight configuration. Finally, combined control of the end load and microforces is explored for soft-robotic actuation. Suitable loading paths allow switching between straight and bent configurations and changing the bifurcation character from supercritical to subcritical.

title: Rubric Curriculum RL: Exploiting the Generation-Verification Gap in Non-Verifiable Domains
abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has led to significant gains in math and code generation. Extending these gains to open-ended domains remains challenging: ground-truth verification is unavailable, human annotation is expensive, and learned reward models are prone to reward hacking. The generation-verification gap, where judging good outputs is easier than producing them, offers a potential path to improvement. However, rubric-based judges are often imprecise and stationary, so policies can overfit or reward hack them. We introduce Rubric Curriculum RL (RcRL), which exploits this gap without new data, human annotations, or stronger teacher models. We combine pairwise preferences over rollouts with a curriculum over rubric criteria, yielding a more discriminative signal than absolute scoring and a non-stationary objective. Whereas baselines plateau within a few hundred steps, RcRL preserves output entropy and keeps improving past 1000 steps. On creative writing, RcRL achieves a 70.5% human win rate against the base model, with gains across benchmarks and judges. On HealthBench, RcRL improves over the base model by 14.6% (full set) and 25.4% (consensus subset), outperforming all training baselines, including instance-specific rubrics.

title: Certified Collision Exclusion and an Unconditional Upper Bound $Λ<0.156821$ for the de Bruijn--Newman Constant
abstract: The de Bruijn--Newman constant $Λ$ is the transition time beyond which all zeros of the heat-deformed Riemann $ξ$-function are real. We develop a computer-assisted collision-exclusion method and obtain the bound $Λ<156821/10^6=0.156821$, in the normalisation of Polymath. The proof combines the published finite-height verification and the starting inequality $Λ\leq1/5$ with a compact-interior continuation theorem, five stable prime-polynomial Gram sources, certified moving-index recovery, a balanced real-jet transfer and a uniform Euler-product barrier at infinity. The resulting closed time-band exclusion, together with uniform remote reality, forces strictness at the proposed endpoint. The finite certificate uses 664,505 structural Fourier coefficients, 44,182 closed torus boxes, 184 separator moments and 17,385 separator rectangles. We isolate a Cauchy--Schwarz obstruction intrinsic to the four-prime source family, explaining the narrow feasibility margin of the certified endpoint. We state the proof-to-certificate interface and distinguish the present unconditional logical claim from other recent, as yet unrefereed, computational bounds.

title: Missing solutions in scalar-Gauss-Bonnet gravity
abstract: We discover novel neutron star solutions under scalar-Gauss-Bonnet (sGB) gravity which have been missed altogether in the existing literature. The complete solution space also reveals a new regularity condition that has to be satisfied by all scalarized stars. Certain scalarized branches of neutron star solutions under sGB gravity have long been known to abruptly terminate on stellar mass-radius diagrams at lower stellar radii, a phenomenon that has no counterpart in classical scalar-tensor theories. Such termination has been strongly suspected to be physical rather than a numerical artifact nevertheless, since sGB theories feature a regularity condition at the center of the star, which can prevent the existence of certain configurations. Motivated by the recently re-emerging phase-transition view of scalarization, we first predict that these terminated branches can reappear after a "gap." We confirm this by finding such reappearing branches, and also determine which parts of the theory parameter space are more amenable to such occurrences. We then show that the previously known central regularity condition cannot explain all the non-existing solutions in the gaps, which leads us to the discovery of a new, non-central, condition for the existence of scalarized neutron stars under sGB gravity.

title: CAPE-JEPA - Cross-modal Adversarial Probabilistic Embedding JEPA
abstract: Cross-modal remote sensing image retrieval (RS-CMIR) requires representations that are simultaneously modality-invariant and semantically discriminative, despite the profound physical gap between heterogeneous sensors such as Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) and multispectral imagery. Recent JEPA-based Predictive self-supervised approaches such as X-JEPA formulate cross-modal alignment as a deterministic latent forecasting task, implicitly assuming uniform patch predictability and leaving cross-modal distributional alignment unaddressed. We propose CAPE-JEPA, a probabilistic cross-modal Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture with three contributions: (i) a cross-attentional Gaussian predictor outputting per-patch parameters (mu, sigma^2) conditioned on opposite-modality context, trained via negative log-likelihood to model inherent cross-sensor prediction uncertainty; (ii) adversarial distributional regularization combining unimodal isotropic Gaussian regularization with a novel cross-modal adversarial variant that aligns modality distributions via worst-case Epps-Pulley characteristic function tests without explicit sample pairing; and (iii) in-training contrastive learning with attention-pooled heads for scene-level discriminative grounding. Evaluated on BigEarthNet-14K (BEN-14K) and fMoW across SAR, multispectral, and RGB modalities, CAPE-JEPA surpasses X-JEPA by up to 13.74 points on BEN-14K and 15.59 points on fMoW, outperforming all baselines including SkySense and CROMA across both unimodal and cross-modal directions while using fewer parameters (407.30M vs. 432.72M).

title: Existence of Lagrangian Mean Curvature Flow Singularities with Bounded Mean Curvature
abstract: In every dimension $n \ge 3$, we show there exist Lagrangian mean curvature flows that develop neck pinch singularities such that the mean curvature remains uniformly bounded. This follows from a related result that, under a structural assumption on the singularity formation, the mean curvature at small scales near the singularity can be bounded by the Lagrangian angle at outer scales with suitable weights. Applying this result to a subset of the finite-time Lagrangian mean curvature flow singularities constructed in the companion paper [arXiv:2607.03152] and the infinite-time Lagrangian mean curvature flow singularities constructed by Tsai, Wood, and the second-named author [arXiv:2401.02228] then gives examples of both finite-time and infinite-time singularity formation with uniformly bounded mean curvature.

title: Optical linear polarization of the Be--X-ray pulsar binary LS V +44 17
abstract: We present the optical $BVR$ polarization measurements for the Be--X-ray pulsar binary LS V +44 17 from its giant outburst in early 2023 and subsequently over three years. We detect a significant polarization of about $\approx1.1$--$2.1\%$, which includes the interstellar contribution. Polarization evolves significantly with time since the outburst. The interstellar polarization was found to be $\approx2.5$--$2.9\%$. The obtained intrinsic optical polarization of LS V +44 17 after correction is between $0.5$--$1.7\%$, perpendicular to the interstellar polarization direction. We consider various plausible sources of optical polarization and infer scattering in the Be decretion disk to be the most dominant source based on time and spectral evolution. Changing intrinsic PA with time hints at a plausible precession of the Be disk.

title: A Polynomial Erdős-Pósa bound for Eulerian digraphs
abstract: In [Combinatorica 1996], Reed, Robertson, Seymour and Thomas proved Younger's conjecture dating back to 1973 that states that directed cycles have the Erdős-Pósa property. Specifically, they showed that every directed graph $D$ contains either $k$ arc-disjoint cycles or a set of at most $f(k)$ arcs that intersect every directed cycle. The function $f$, depending only on $k$, is however notoriously large--in fact, not even elementary. The first improvement on this function was only very recently provided by Hatzel, Kreutzer, Milani, and Muzi [FOCS 2024] who showed that $f$ can be taken to be an exponential tower of height $8$. In this work, we improve this function to $O(k^4)$ in the case where the digraph is Eulerian. This also answers an open question by Wahlström [Springer Monographs in Mathematics 2018] who asked explicitly when Eulerian digraphs have a polynomial Erdős-Pósa property. The only other known result about Erdős-Pósa on Eulerian digraphs is a result from Seymour [Combinatorica 1996] who showed that $f(k)=k$ when the Eulerian digraph admits a linkless embedding in 3-space, and such an equality is not possible for general Eulerian digraphs. We also complement our positive result, by showing that the result of Seymour cannot be extended to give a linear bound ($O(k)$) on general Eulerian digraphs, by showing that even on Eulerian digraphs the lower bound for the Erdős-Pósa property is $Ω(k \log k)$.

title: Transversal Passivity: Dissipation Relative to Input and Output Manifolds
abstract: This paper introduces transversal passivity, a local dissipation property for regulating input and output signals to prescribed manifolds. Its supply rate is built from the transverse port errors induced by nearest-point projections, so that motion along the manifolds is not penalized. We give a necessary condition and a constructive sufficient condition for the property and relate it to existing passivity notions. For feedback interconnections through negative-adjoint linear channels, power conservation no longer cancels the transverse supply. The residual is governed by compatibility defects that depend only on the channels and the prescribed manifolds, so it can be assessed before any closed-loop analysis, and it falls into a hierarchy of exact compatibility, quadratic cancellation, and nonzero quadratic residuals. Since transversal storages are only positive semidefinite, port convergence is obtained by combining compact confinement, for instance by conserved quantities, with a dissipation margin, and we identify a geometric obstruction under which no quadratic margin is available near the feasible states. A federated learning case study with heterogeneous data shows that port convergence can be certified even though no server target is compatible with the interconnection, and that the obstruction arises for a natural choice of target.

title: Law-Dependent Poisson-Refresh Randomised Feedback Control for Stochastic Systems
abstract: This paper studies a continuous-time probabilistic control problem for stochastic systems in which the feedback law assigns a probability distribution over control inputs. The control is modelled as a law-dependent Poisson-refresh process: it is held constant between refresh times and resampled at Poisson times from a feedback rule depending on the current state and state law. The closed-loop system is therefore formulated as a jump--diffusion for the joint state--control process. The objective is to design the sampling rule by comparing the realised closed-loop system with a prescribed reference description. The cost separates two local terms: a relative-entropy penalty for the instantaneous refresh kernel and a state-side drift-mismatch cost. The state-side term is evaluated at the realised control value and is motivated by a frozen-control Girsanov identity. Under global Lipschitz, moment, and uniform ellipticity assumptions, we prove well-posedness of the closed loop and a dynamic programming principle on the joint state--control law space. For linear data and admissible mean-dependent affine-Gaussian refresh rules, the full joint law need not remain Gaussian, but the first and second moments of the joint state--control process close exactly. This yields a deterministic reduced control problem on moment space, with an explicit running cost, a reduced Hamiltonian, and a verification theorem.

title: Hopf-Galois Structures on Extensions Arising from Division Points on Elliptic Curves
abstract: We provide a general construction of infinite Hopf-Galois extensions from a direct system of finite Hopf-Galois extensions. We then apply this framework to extensions generated by division points on elliptic curves. Specifically, for a number field $K$ and an elliptic curve $E/K$ of rank at least $1$ with $P\in E(K)$ of infinite order, we consider for each integer $n\geq 2$ the extension $L_n=K(Q_n)$, where $Q_n\in E(\overline{K})$ is such that $nQ_n=P$. We show that the finite-level extensions $L_n/K$ need not be Hopf-Galois, and we give sufficient conditions for them to be so. We then prove that the infinite extension $L_\infty=\bigcup_{n\geq 2}L_n$ of $K$ is potentially Hopf-Galois, meaning it becomes Hopf-Galois after a finite extension of the base field.

title: HarnessFlow: MCTS-Guided Harness Optimization for LLM Agents
abstract: The performance of large language model (LLM) agents depends on both the underlying model and the harness that governs interaction with tools and the environment. Yet harness design remains largely manual, and automating it requires navigating an open-ended search space through costly end-to-end evaluations. We introduce HarnessFlow, a framework for optimizing complete executable harnesses under a limited candidate-evaluation budget, with the model and task environment held fixed. HarnessFlow organizes candidates and their evaluation histories in a refinement tree, using a Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS)-based policy to balance exploitation and exploration. A coding agent refines selected harnesses using archived code, execution feedback, and a library of reusable harness mechanisms. With 15 refinement attempts per benchmark, HarnessFlow achieves the highest mean test scores among the compared methods on six benchmarks spanning agentic tasks, coding, and web interaction. The optimized harnesses achieve an average score of 69.48%, outperforming the initial harnesses and Meta-Harness by 10.89 and 3.95 percentage points, respectively, while incurring lower average per-task execution costs than hand-engineered baselines. These results suggest that structured harness search offers a promising route toward automating the design of capable and efficient LLM agents.

title: Learning Noise Optimization for Reward Alignment in Few-Step Generative Models
abstract: Reward alignment for diffusion- and flow-based generative models is often formulated over stochastic trajectories, making it less suitable for few-step deterministic generators. Initial noise optimization provides a trajectory-free alternative, but existing gradient-free methods require costly per-sample search at inference. We introduce LeNO (Learning Noise Optimization), which amortizes reward-guided initial noise optimization into a learned residual transport while keeping the pretrained generator frozen. LeNO learns an anchor-conditioned distribution over noise corrections using Local GRPO and scalar rewards, eliminating iterative test-time optimization. For Gaussian initial noise with norm-preserving projection, we derive a tractable upper bound on the KL divergence between the corrected noise distribution and the original prior, providing a principled regularization objective. We evaluate LeNO on few-step text-to-image and protein structure generation, including expensive black-box designability rewards. Across both domains, LeNO improves target rewards with a single noise correction at inference while largely preserving generation quality and diversity.

title: From the quantum group $U_{q^{1/2}}( {\widehat {\mathfrak{sl}}}_2 )$ to the Kronecker quantum cluster algebra
abstract: Let $\mathcal A_q$ be the Kronecker quantum cluster algebra with principal coefficients. We construct an explicit algebra homomorphism from the whole quantum group ${U_{q^{1/2}}}( {\widehat {\mathfrak{sl}_2}} )$ to $\mathcal A_q$, whose images together with either of the two frozen variables generate $\mathcal A_q$. As an application, we obtain algebra homomorphisms from the split $\imath$quantum groups of affine $\widehat {\mathfrak{sl}}_2$ to $\mathcal A_q$. Moreover, we explicitly determine the images of the positive and negative real and imaginary root vectors of ${U_{q^{1/2}}}( {\widehat {\mathfrak{sl}_2}} )$ in terms of quantum cluster variables.

title: Analysis of Local Open-Weight LLM Agents on Vulnerability-Reproduction Tasks
abstract: Open-weight language models that fit on a single consumer GPU are becoming capable on a growing range of tasks, and they matter because they can run locally without sending the code to a hosted service. Vulnerability reproduction, turning a vulnerability description into an input that crashes the vulnerable build, is a natural target for them, since it is an automated analysis task closer to test generation than to code comprehension and it runs against a build that must be executed rather than read. In order to assess whether current models can perform it, we evaluate twelve configurations of local models, spanning three generations, two architectures and three quantization levels, on ten CyberGym vulnerability-reproduction tasks, three runs each under one harness, and release the full artefact. We show that every configuration, down to the 4B model, solves most of the six easier tasks, and configurations separate only on the remaining four. For the harder tasks, the 27B model is required. Quantization did not change what the models solved in any matched pair, but it changed how fast they got there, and the mixture of experts reached the same scores in less wall clock. We also examine the agent trajectories. Almost every run we examined, including those that fail, names the vulnerable function and states the correct hypothesis, and what separates a solved task from an unsolved one is whether that hypothesis becomes a working input.

title: CrossPressor: Scalable Cross-View Fusion for Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting
abstract: Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting (3D-GS) becomes increasingly difficult to scale to long multi-view sequences. Anchor-based compression methods such as ZPressor alleviate representation growth by decoding Gaussians only from a compact set of anchor feature maps, but keeping these anchors fixed forces each one to aggregate an increasing number of support views. We identify this representation--fusion mismatch and introduce \textbf{CrossPressor}, a training-free method for scalable anchor-based fusion. CrossPressor preserves all decoder-facing anchor queries while constraining the view-growing support sequence through coverage-cycled evidence routing, distributing retained spatial evidence across support views and fusion layers while keeping all support views represented. Routing before K/V projection, together with joint context packing, further reduces support-side fusion cost without retraining. CrossPressor maintains reconstruction quality close to dense fusion while achieving up to $26.12\times$ faster cross-view fusion and $1.43\times$ end-to-end acceleration on long input sequences. Our project page is at: https://yuhsihu.github.io/CrossPressor.

title: A Systematic Benchmark for Evaluating Multimodal Personalized Reasoning of Vision-Language Models
abstract: People often make decisions by holistically reasoning over heterogeneous forms of personal information. In this paper, we study the relatively underexplored capability of multimodal personalized reasoning in multimodal large language models (MLLMs). To this end, we introduce \texttt{MPRBench}, a novel and comprehensive benchmark specifically designed to evaluate personalized reasoning across a wide range of tasks and real-world challenges. \texttt{MPRBench} consists of 12 sub-tasks and additionally supports interpretable analysis of representative error cases. Through extensive experiments, we find that current personalized MLLMs still struggle with personalized reasoning due to several key challenges, including inaccurate recognition of personalized concepts and sensitivity to irrelevant personal information. We hope that MPRBench will stimulate further research on personalized reasoning in MLLMs. Code and data are available at https://github.com/kkdh15/MPRBench

title: Connection of surface code patches based on entanglement distillation without postselection
abstract: Distributed quantum computing is a promising approach for overcoming the scalability limitations of fault-tolerant quantum computing. Entanglement distillation, a process that extracts higher-fidelity entangled states from noisy ones, plays a key role in distributed quantum computing. However, simple distillation protocols typically rely on postselection, which poses practical challenges for implementation. Here, we propose a scheme for distributed surface-code quantum computing that benefits from entanglement distillation even without postselection. Numerical simulations show that the logical error rates in the proposed scheme are lower than those in the setting without distillation. Additionally, we demonstrate that the logical error rates can be suppressed further by exploiting the asymmetry between spacelike and timelike errors in the surface code. The proposed scheme offers a practical and simple approach to distributed quantum computing with surface codes.

title: Homology and Topology of Partially Ordered Fields
abstract: We develop a unified homology theory for directed partial orders (DPOs) and lattice-ordered positive cones on fields of characteristic zero. With the underlying field and its operations fixed, we define order?carrying spaces independently by topological conditions, establish a bijection with DPO positive cones, and characterize lattice orders by intersections of minimal open neighborhoods. A unified comparison theorem identifies graded Ext for region ideals with sheaf cohomology and multiplicative Tor with the reduced singular homology of truncated regions, giving a topological interpretation of the existence and preservation of reduced decompositions. We obtain canonical cohomological obstructions to lattice ordering, prove that a coefficient module for positive multiplication is flat if and only if the multiplier has a positive inverse, and show that every strict extension of positive cones on the same field produces a nonzero first Tor obstruction. Finally, we place the concrete lattice recently constructed by Bao-Zhang within this framework.

title: SonoDyno: A Sonic Dynamometer for Engine Speed and Load Estimation from Audio
abstract: Controllable engine sound synthesis, Active Sound Design and engine order analysis all build on the relationship between the sound of an engine and its momentary operating state: its speed and its load. Recordings of engine sound are abundant in archives, sample packs and online video, yet they rarely carry time-aligned annotations of that state, which limits their applicability to controllable engine sound generation. We present SonoDyno, which estimates the engine speed, the cylinder count and an engine-normalized load intensity from a microphone signal alone, with no tachometer, no bus access and no prior knowledge of the engine configuration. A convolutional scorer of 124,302 parameters reads the harmonic order energy of each frame at three time-frequency resolutions to jointly score cylinder count and speed, and a decoder imposes the rotational dynamics of the engine on the speed trajectory. A second head estimates the load intensity, the position of the torque between the engine's drag floor at 0 and its full-load ceiling at 1, from the order levels at the decoded speed. On recordings of engines it has never heard, with microphone position, engine type and cylinder count unknown, SonoDyno places 93 to 97% of the frames within 2% of the true speed, identifies the cylinder count with 80% accuracy and confuses the octave on fewer than 2% of the frames. On an unseen engine of a known type, the load intensity has a mean absolute error of 0.12, and the sign of the torque, driving or braking, is right on 91% of the frames. General pitch trackers fall behind even when the harmonic order of each engine is supplied: on our validation recordings and at a tolerance of 5%, the best of them places 62% of the frames within the tolerance, against 96% for SonoDyno.

title: CLEAR: Structured Specifications for Controllable Long-Horizon ML Research Engineering
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly being used to automate machine learning (ML) research workflows, ranging from code development and experiment execution to research reproduction and scientific discovery. Recent systems demonstrate that LLMs can perform substantial portions of ML research engineering with limited human intervention. These advances suggest a shift from automating individual research tasks toward automating long-horizon workflows that transform research artifacts into executable ML systems. However, ML research engineering remains substantially more difficult than isolated code generation. A research artifact typically specifies a system only implicitly through a mixture of natural-language descriptions, equations, pseudo-code, implementation details, datasets, and evaluation protocols. An agent must first infer the intended computational structure, translate it into executable components, coordinate their dependencies, and repeatedly diagnose and repair failures during execution. Consequently, the quality of the final system depends not only on code generation, but also on whether the agent can maintain a consistent representation of what should be implemented throughout this long-horizon process.

title: A brief overview of the baryon cycle in galaxies
abstract: Galaxy formation and evolution is governed by the continuous exchange of gas between the cosmic web, the circumgalactic medium (CGM), and the interstellar medium (ISM) of galaxies. This brief review summarises our current understanding of this baryon cycle, from the accretion of gas onto galaxies to its conversion into stars, and the feedback processes that regulate the growth of galaxies. Several open questions will be highlighted, that will encourage progresses in cosmological simulations, multiwavelength observations, and theory to resolve.

title: Learning Pseudo-Riemannian Manifolds for Heterophilic Graphs via Graph Signature
abstract: Several widely used families of Graph Neural Networks carry a positive-definite geometric prior. Graph convolution read as heat diffusion needs a positive semi-definite operator, hyperbolic models place features on positive-definite Riemannian manifolds, and dot-product and GAT-style attention scores use positive-definite inner products. On heterophilic graphs, where edges often signify dissimilarity or structural repulsion, that prior is a mismatch: no positive-definite form can assign a negative squared distance to a direction the labels separate. To measure the mismatch, we introduce the Graph Signature Index ($s_{\mathcal{G}}$), the inertia of a class-compatibility matrix built from label topology alone, and we prove that no value of the edge or node homophily index in $(0,1)$ rules out a negative eigenvalue. We then propose the Pseudo-Riemannian Attention Network (PRAT), whose attention logit is a signed squared pseudo-distance under a learnable diagonal metric initialized from $s_{\mathcal{G}}$. The design is diagnose-then-learn: the signature supplies a sign structure that unconstrained training keeps outside near-zero directions, and the projection learns the rest of the metric around it. Across fifteen node-classification benchmarks PRAT outperforms or matches the strongest heterophily-adapted models. A controlled ablation ties that performance to the sign structure itself: with architecture and protocol fixed, forbidding the metric to be indefinite costs accuracy on the graphs $s_{\mathcal{G}}$ marks as indefinite and leaves the others unchanged.

title: Online Bayesian Inference for a Dirichlet Process Mixture of Binary Logit Models
abstract: Flexible travel behaviour models for preference heterogeneity have largely remained within the batch-estimation paradigm. The growing availability of continuously collected behavioural data, for example from smartphone applications, highlights the need for methods that update posterior inference on such heterogeneity as new observations arrive. This study proposes an online Bayesian inference method for a Dirichlet process mixture of binary logit models. The main challenge is to update the posterior as observations arrive while allowing the latent cluster structure to expand and historical cluster assignments to be revised. We develop a sequential Monte Carlo sampler using a sequence of Pólya--Gamma-augmented partial-data posteriors, local particle-weight corrections, and recursively maintained sufficient statistics. Each observation's contribution can be added, removed, or replaced in these summaries, supporting both sequential coefficient updating and rejuvenation that revisits historical cluster assignments. The simulation study shows that observation-by-observation sequential updating yields final posterior summaries close to those obtained by batch Markov chain Monte Carlo. Sensitivity analyses further demonstrate trade-offs between posterior approximation accuracy and computational cost as the number of particles and rejuvenation settings are varied. An illustrative empirical application shows how the method tracks posterior evolution and produces observation-specific provisional posterior summaries with low latency as real-world trip records are processed sequentially. The proposed approach provides a methodological foundation for online inference in travel behaviour models with parameter heterogeneity and for future extensions to richer choice structures, low-latency decision support, and online anomaly screening.

title: Retrials in Loss Systems: Mean-Field Analysis, Erlang Bounds, and Power-of-$d$ Comparison
abstract: We consider a system of $N$ parallel, homogeneous servers, each with finite capacity $C$. Jobs requiring one unit of capacity arrive according to a Poisson process with total rate $Nλ$ and have exponential service times with rate $μ$. We study a decentralized random--retrial policy with $d$ attempts: upon arrival, a job is assigned to a uniformly chosen server; if the server is full, the job is reassigned to another uniformly chosen server, for at most $d$ attempts; if all $d$ attempts fail, the job is rejected. In the mean-field limit, we prove that the stationary blocking probability is characterized by the unique solution of a fixed-point equation involving the Erlang-B loss function, and we establish global convergence of the fluid model to this equilibrium. We also compare the mean-field stationary blocking probability with the analogous quantity in the power-of-$d$ model under the same parameters $(C,λ,μ)$. For the same $d$, we show, via coupling techniques, that the blocking probability under power-of-$d$ is always less than or equal to the blocking under retrial-of-$d$; but if we consider $d$ and $\tilde d$ with $\tilde d>d$, then the retrial-of-$\tilde d$ policy achieves a strictly lower blocking than the power-of-$d$ policy when $ρ=λ/μ$ is sufficiently large. Moreover we show that for some specific cases, like $C=2$, $d=2$ and $\tilde d=3$, it occurs for all $ρ>0$, not only for $ρ$ sufficiently large. We complement the analysis with simulations that estimate the load level above which retrial-of-$\tilde d$ outperforms power-of-$d$ in terms of blocking.

title: Beyond Identity Creation: Bilinear Sybil Cost in Identities and Time
abstract: Sybil defenses price the creation of an identity, yet influence goes, again and again, to active identities. We study the cost of maintaining influence. A defense has a bilinear Sybil cost with ratio $A$ if keeping $s$ identities active for $T$ periods costs at least $sT/A$ honest units: the average cost per identity-window is at least $1/A$ times an honest participant's cost. Recurrence alone does not guarantee this cost. The cost can be carried over from earlier periods, shared among many identities, or be negligible when fast hardware does the work of thousands of honest devices. We give four sufficient conditions for a defense that checks every identity each period to achieve bilinear Sybil cost: identity binding, freshness, a shared deadline, and sequential, non-batchable work. They yield two guarantees: a bilinear total cost, with $A$ the speed advantage of the adversary's fastest hardware, and, because the work must be fresh and finished by a common deadline, a bound on the identities active in a period by the processors running at that time. We prove that none of the four follows from the other three. A verifiable delay function on an identity-bound input meets all four without payments, with $A$ of 2 to 8 for CPUs and about 28 for a hypothetical ASIC, against $10^3$ to $10^7$ for hash puzzles. We measure one active identity per core per period against about 80,000 under a signed heartbeat, no gain from batching up to 1,000 identities, and rejection of all tested attacks.

title: Small 5-chromatic unit-distance graphs in disks of radius 3/2, 5/4 and 23/20
abstract: We give three explicit unit-distance graphs in the plane with chromatic number 5 whose vertices lie in small disks: a graph with 773 vertices inside an open disk of radius 3/2, one with 5713 vertices inside an open disk of radius 5/4, and one with 8168 vertices inside an open disk of radius 23/20. The smallest examples previously reported for these radii have 11725, 11725 and 31171 vertices. All coordinates are exact elements of Q(sqrt3, sqrt5, sqrt11). In each case 5-chromaticity is certified by an explicit 5-colouring and a DRAT proof that no 4-colouring exists. The 773-vertex graph is vertex-critical.

title: NextGAN: Towards Simple and Scalable GAN Training for Image and Video Generation
abstract: Adversarial training enables one- and few-step image and video generation, but conventional adversarial losses supervise critic values without directly specifying the gradients used to update the generator. We present NEXTGAN, which trains a scalar critic by regressing its input gradient onto displacements between independently paired reference and generated features at interpolated locations in frozen representation spaces. For a fixed generator, this regression is equivalent to an adversarial objective with a gradient-energy penalty, while the generator retains the standard potential-based GAN update. The same objective adapts pre-trained image and video generators with up to 14B parameters, without auxiliary losses, online teacher scores, or trajectories. On ImageNet $256 \times 256$, NEXTGAN achieves one-step FIDs of 2.87 with pixel-space JiT-B and 1.54 with latent-space DiT-XL/1; its adversarial form further reaches 1.36. For text-to-video generation, a single trained Wan2.1-1.3B model supports one-, two-, and four-step sampling, achieving the highest VBench total scores among the compared 1.3B methods at one and two steps. At two steps, NEXTGAN scores 83.13, exceeding rCM and AnyFlow by 1.25 and 0.47 points, respectively. Code is available at https://github.com/LINs-lab/NextGAN.git.

title: Consistency Learning and Distillation for One-Step MIMO-OFDM Channel Estimation
abstract: Iterative neural channel estimators can improve recovery under pilot contamination, but repeated network evaluations increase inference cost. This paper develops observation-anchored consistency and Consistency Mid-Training (CMT) estimators for one-step channel estimation in multiple-input multiple-output orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (MIMO-OFDM) systems. Both estimators refine pilot-derived least-squares channel estimates in the delay-beam domain. Consistency learning couples endpoint predictions along noisy-to-clean paths. CMT then refines a compact consistency-trained student to predict a flow-matching teacher's endpoint from intermediate trajectory states. Across the evaluated SNR range, the compact CMT student reduces uncoded symbol error rate (SER) by 9.6-20.2% relative to the one-step flow-matching baseline (0.44-0.98 dB in logarithmic SER reduction), while using 74.5% fewer parameters and 73.0% fewer network multiply-accumulates.

title: Evaluating Human-LLM Alignment on Visualization Preference
abstract: There are often multiple valid visualizations, spanning different chart types, visual encodings, and aesthetic choices, that can all support a user's goal of analyzing a dataset. Determining which of these candidate visualizations is most appropriate, however, remains challenging. Prior work has leveraged expert-curated taxonomies to guide visualization design and subsequent quality evaluation, a practical evaluation model must also account for human-centric factors. Latest visualization tools integrate Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate and refine visualizations, using LLM-as-a-judge to provide design feedback. Without a deeper understanding of whether, and in what ways, human and LLM perceptions of visualizations align, there is a real risk of deploying low-quality agents that do not reflect human judgment. We study this question through a pilot experiment - we formulate the problem as a preference task over curated chart pairs and compare the judgments of state-of-the-art vision models with those of a panel of human annotators. We establish a cautionary tale: such judges risk filtering out informative, compelling displays. We find that frontier models collapse human subjectivity, a rich signal that reveals contrasting design choices, into near-deterministic verdicts.

title: Quo Vadis, Driving Scene Reconstruction? Occlusion-Aware Gaussian Densification
abstract: While recent feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting methods enable efficient driving-scene reconstruction from surround-view images, their reliance on a single observation fundamentally hinders novel-view synthesis. Regions occluded in the input can become visible from novel viewpoints, leaving the reconstructed Gaussians under-constrained and incomplete. Moving beyond image-space inpainting for rendered views, we introduce OccSplat, a feed-forward framework whose core contribution is Occlusion-Aware Gaussian Densification, explicitly targeting missing scene geometry rather than missing pixels. By predicting new Gaussian primitives for unsupported regions, OccSplat completes the scene directly in the 3D representation. Specifically, OccSplat first identifies occluded regions that lack Gaussian support through Gaussian Occlusion Mapping. Gaussian Occlusion Completion then generates new primitives for these regions. The predicted primitives are integrated into the original representation to improve novel-view synthesis while retaining feed-forward inference without per-scene optimization. Experiments on the nuScenes benchmark demonstrate that OccSplat improves on the compared methods and yields particularly large gains in occluded regions, leading to more accurate and visually coherent driving-scene reconstruction.

title: Quantitatively Probing the Tilt Angle Failures in 4D-STEM Polarisation Analysis
abstract: Four-dimensional scanning transmission electron microscopy (4D-STEM) is increasingly used to map polarisation in ferroic textures such as domain walls, vortices, merons and skyrmions. These textures are accompanied by local strain, lattice rotation and misorientation, which also modulate the diffraction features used to infer polar order. Even small deviations from the zone axis can therefore produce contrast that is indistinguishable from a polarisation signal. Here we quantify the tilt sensitivity of two polarisation-sensitive signals, diffraction disc intensity and Kikuchi band intensity, in three ferroelectrics with distinct polar distortions: PbTiO3, BaTiO3 and Cu3B7O13Cl boracite. We find that tilts of only 0.01-0.05 degrees reverse most Friedel-pair disc asymmetries, and even the most robust disc pairs reverse by 0.04 degrees in BaTiO3, 0.14 degrees in PbTiO3 and 0.18 degrees in boracite, producing contrast equal and opposite to that of the polarisation. Kikuchi band contrast is the only signal that reports absolute polarity without knowledge of the specimen thickness, but it does so only up to 0.09 degrees in PbTiO3, 0.015 degrees in BaTiO3 and 0.02 degrees in boracite. From these results we define tilt tolerances for each signal and material, and propose practical criteria for distinguishing polarisation contrast from misorientation. The analysis also applies to scanning electron microscopy-based diffraction, including electron backscatter diffraction.

title: On generalized $k$-token graphs with distinguishable tokens and a maximum capacity of $s$ tokens per vertex
abstract: Supertoken graphs \(F^s_{k\times1}(G)\), also known as generalized token graphs, model configurations of \(k\) distinguishable tokens on a graph \(G\), with at most \(s\) tokens at each vertex. We study structural and metric properties of these graphs in terms of the base graph. For regular \(G\), we characterize when \(F^s_{k\times1}(G)\) is regular. We show that bipartiteness is inherited from \(G\) and characterize it for complete base graphs. For \(s\ge2\), we characterize connectedness and show that \(t\)-vertex-connectivity of \(G\) implies \(t\)-vertex-connectivity of the supertoken graph. We obtain exact diameter formulas in several regimes, including complete graphs and stars, and derive lower bounds and a conjectured formula for odd cycles. We also determine the clique number, give bounds and equality conditions for the chromatic number, and characterize planarity for complete base graphs.
