Considering neutral massless scalar perturbations for charged de Sitter black hole, we not only shed light on the quasinormal mode spectrum, but also clarify whether the modifications from conformal Killing gravity and nonlinear electrodynamics can rescue the strong cosmic censorship conjecture, and further investigate how characteristic parameters affect its validity. As the first instance for investigating the conjecture in the framework of conformal Killing gravity, this paper reports some unexpected findings.

title: Small inertia limit of the distribution-dependent stochastic Cucker--Smale equation
abstract: This paper investigates the small inertia limit of the distribution-dependent stochastic Cucker--Smale equation with the full velocity alignment source term, which serves as the mean-field equation for the stochastic Cucker--Smale model. Inspired by the idea of Hottovy et al. \cite{Hottovy2015} to rearrange SDEs via integration by parts, we repeatedly perform integration by parts on independent copies of our equation. Then we define a global position correction and a quadratic remainder, both with uniformly bounded tails. Applying the Aldous criterion, we obtain tightness of the position correction, which in turn yields tightness of the position process. Subsequently, using the averaging method on the fast time scale, the quadratic functional can be decomposed into the equilibrium average, local quadratic fluctuations, and exponential transients. Then, the Poisson--Lyapunov equation is employed to prove the convergence of the time integral. Finally, under various suitable assumptions, we obtain the weak convergence of the laws of the approximating processes to the law of the solution of the small-inertia limit equation, along with the identification of the limiting process, and also the convergence rate of strong $L^1$-convergence. The extra noise-induced drift term can be expressed as the solution of a contraction-type Fredholm equation. This paper is complementary to the deterministic particle limit work of \cite{Carrillo2021,Choi2021} .

title: Nowcasting Future Performance for Population Pruning in Survival-of-the-Fittest Training
abstract: Training high-performing neural networks often involves evaluating populations of candidate models with varying hyperparameters, architectures, or random seeds. Training every candidate to completion is computationally expensive, yet stopping seemingly weaker runs early risks discarding models that would ultimately perform better, as learning curves can cross. To address this challenge, we investigate whether intermediate training checkpoints can predict future model accuracy and enable more informed pruning decisions. Our nowcasters predict test accuracy five epochs ahead or at the end of training. They are trained with accuracy and loss histories, weight statistics, and SANE representations as inputs. SANE is a transformer autoencoder that encodes a checkpoint as a sequence of latent tokens. We then use the nowcasters in Survival-of-the-Fittest (SOTF) training. SOTF repeatedly ranks runs during training by predicted accuracy and stops the lowest-ranked ones. Our results show that weight statistics work best for five-epoch forecasts, and SANE representations work best for final accuracy prediction. For evaluation, we compare SOTF with pruning the population by current accuracy. In homogeneous model zoos such as the CNN zoos, pruning by current accuracy already retains a final model only slightly worse than the best. Model zoos with a larger spread in performance, such as the ResNet-18 and ViT zoos, are more difficult to prune by current accuracy alone. In these zoos, SOTF with nowcasted final accuracy almost closes the gap to the best model.

title: HELIX: HEterogeneous LLM Inference with FleXible and Fine-Grained Partitioning
abstract: LLM inference is inherently heterogeneous, with performance bottlenecks shifting throughout inference phases down to individual operators. This has motivated heterogeneous serving systems that disaggregate execution across specialized accelerators, typically through fixed partitions such as prefill/decode or attention/FFN. However, these approaches commit to a partitioning strategy in advance, limiting their ability to adapt to different workloads and model architectures while forcing emerging accelerators into predefined roles. We present HELIX, a vLLM-based software stack that discovers, compiles and dispatches workload-aware partitions across heterogeneous accelerators at the operator granularity. At engine initialization, HELIX automatically determines hardware-specific operator placements that minimize execution latency, accounting for profiled execution costs, communication overheads, device capabilities, and memory constraints. It combines dynamic programming, piecewise compilation, and heterogeneous subgraph dispatch, enabling accelerators with partial operator coverage to participate in LLM inference without predefined model partitions. HELIX provides an open-source unified framework for exploring, evaluating, and integrating heterogeneous accelerators for LLM inference, lowering the barrier to emerging hardware by exposing them as subgraph executors. In systems combining H100 and B200 GPUs with emerging accelerators, HELIX resolves LLM partitions that multi-query decoding latency by up to 3$\times$ for dense and sparse transformer models and up to 3.5$\times$ for hybrid state-space models, relative to standard attention-FFN disaggregation.

title: An Interaction-Aware Decision Framework for FDIC-Assisted Distressed Bank Acquisitions: Empirical Evidence from the FDIC Failed-Bank Panel and the SVB-First Citizens Case
abstract: Acquirers of failed banks weigh acquisition value, regulatory protection, risk, buyer strength, and execution difficulty jointly, because each signal's meaning depends on the others: high non-performing loans matter less when government loss sharing absorbs the losses. The proposed Spider Network Filtering Framework encodes such dependencies as four interpretable interaction rules among five dimensions, yielding graph-inspired features for a logistic model and a Pursue/Caution/Avoid decision rule. We evaluate it on 55 acquisitions assisted by the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation in 2008-2024 by acquirers with a parent listed in the United States. Six financial inputs come from regulatory reports published before each failure; two deal terms, which the winning bidder knows when it bids but investors learn at the announcement, come from the regulator's press releases. The outcome, a positive three-day abnormal return around the announcement, records the market's initial reception, not realized success. Under grouped, nested cross-validation, the Spider-enhanced model reaches a mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.594, against 0.615 for logistic regression on the same inputs and 0.632 for ridge regression; permutation tests that repeat the full model selection give at most weak evidence that any of them ranks better than chance. The Spider score used directly does not rank better than chance, and an apparent link between target distress and higher returns disappears against a bank-sector benchmark. Thresholds tuned for the F1 score approve most acquisitions with negative returns and realize negative utility when each costs three times what a positively received acquisition gains.

title: Scythe: Semantic-Aware Rewriting for Fast,Effective Program Reduction
abstract: Automated program reduction shrinks a program into a smaller one that preserves a property of interest. Language-agnostic grammar-based reducers are easy to retarget across languages, but because they reason only about syntax, they cannot perform the coupled edits needed to remove whole declarations, e.g., a method cannot be deleted while it is still called. As a result, they waste oracle calls on edits that cannot succeed and often leave irrelevant declarations behind. We present SCYTHE, a fast, semantic-aware pre-processing step that runs in front of any grammar-based reducer without modifying it. SCYTHE encodes the program as a typed declaration dependency graph and applies a set of semantic-aware operators that decouple declarations from their use sites, making them removable while keeping the program well-typed. Fine-grained token-level minimization is then left to the downstream reducer. On 73 benchmarks across C, Java, and Solidity, combining SCYTHE with PERSES never yields a larger result than PERSES alone, and a strictly smaller one on 70 of 73 cases. On average, the combination produces programs 55.6% smaller (up to 95.5%) and is 2.3$\times$ faster (up to 7.4$\times$). SCYTHE also boosts LATRA, a reducer that, unlike the purely syntactic PERSES, also applies language-specific transformations: the combination produces programs 10.6% smaller (up to 61.8%) and is 2.4$\times$ faster on average. Video: https://youtu.be/uEq_YYU0zZw

title: Primary and Secondary Star Formation in the Spiral Waves of NGC 628
abstract: To determine the role of spiral arms and stellar feedback on the formation of stars, we examine the positions of optically identified and emerging star clusters in NGC 628. We find that the youngest clusters extend further into the spiral arms at small radii than at large radii, as expected when the angular flow rate through a wave-like arm increases with greater distance from corotation. The embedded or emerging star clusters (eYSCs) are identified relative to four distinct morphological features in the 7.7 micron image: spiral arm filaments, spiral arm spurs, spiral interarm feathers, and bubbles. Spiral arm-related eYSCs are presumably first-generation stars made from interstellar gas that was directly compressed by the density wave, while clusters along the rims of bubbles are secondary generations produced by feedback compression. The mass functions of the first and second generations differ: eYSCs in spiral arm filaments extend to significantly higher masses than eYSCs in bubbles. Secondary star formation continues downstream from primary star formation, removing the expected age gradient through the arms. Bubble eYSCs account for approximately one-third of all the emerging cluster mass. The outer arms have a more mixed distribution of spiral- and bubble-related eYSCs than the inner arms, potentially providing a way to distinguish wave and material arms and to find corotation in wave-like arms. Among the 17 most massive clusters with log M(Msun)>4, eight of them are in four tight pairs; in at least one case, the dynamical time for the pair is comparable to the cluster ages.

title: Dialect Matters: A Dialect-Aware Baseline for Igala-English Machine Translation
abstract: The massive permeability of intelligent systems in every sphere of human activities have greatly enhanced clarity, ease of work, and increased general global understanding which has significantly awaken the use of intelligent systems by all users. Intelligent systems greatly rely on precise dataset/corpus for the correctness of their output. Despite efforts by researchers to address Low-resource language in the Natural Language Processing (NLP), Igala still has zero parallel corpora despite efforts by researchers. We present a dialect-aware baseline for Igala-English machine translation, among first open systems and first with dialectal variation analysis. Our dataset of 1137 sentences (899 training) is first with dialect tags: Idah 459 (40.4%), Ankpa 297 (26.1%), Ibaji 160 (14.1%), Other 187 (16.4%), Ogugu 32 (2.8%). Same English yields 20-60 Igala forms. Mixed-dialect training achieves balanced BLEU 11.66 versus Idah-only model which drops 4.7 BLEU on Ibaji (13.2 on Idah, 8.5 on Ibaji), proving dialect fairness requires mixing. Fine-tuned from Helsinki-NLP/opus-mt-en-mul (78M), epoch ablation shows convergence at 8 epochs and overfitting at 15. BLEU 11.66, chrF 46.69. Analysis shows 899 sentences on log-linear trend consistent with African low-resource literature. This work provides first dialectal impact analysis for Igala and establishes baseline for future work.

title: EmoReward: Self-Evolving Reward Calibration for Emotional Video Generation RL
abstract: Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) has advanced generative model post-training in verifiable domains such as code and mathematics, but evaluating video quality, especially emotional expression, often depends on subjective aesthetics and has no uniquely correct target. Existing approaches typically rely on fixed rewards for visual quality, motion quality, and text alignment that poorly capture emotional intent and can invite reward hacking, while RLHF is difficult to scale and subject to individual aesthetic differences that complicate the calibration of facial, body motion, and chromatic cues across narrative contexts. We introduce EmoReward, a new self-evolving training mechanism that distills evidence reliability from reward traces collected during an actual training run to adaptively guide multi-reward weight allocation in subsequent training by determining which emotional evidence to trust and how much to weight it. EmoReward first plans specific grounding cues from the emotional prompt to guide evaluation, then uses heterogeneous signal primitives to score the generated video during the act stage. Reflective Reward Gating calibrates their contributions through instance-level gates for phase, face confidence, conflict, and subtlety, then renormalizes weights over the active set to produce the sample's fused reward. RewardMemory then estimates each primitive's reliability from rollout scores and outcomes within each emotional regime in the finished training run, then fixes bounded multipliers that calibrate fusion weights in the next training run without updating reward models. Experiments on HunyuanVideo 1.5 show improvements across multiple RL algorithms and compare EmoReward with other agentic reward methods under SAGE-GRPO. Ablations and transfer experiments on SD 3.5 and FLUX further support adaptive reward calibration for visual generation.

title: IDSISA: Influence-Distilled Sharded Training for Efficient Machine Unlearning
abstract: Machine unlearning removes the influence of specific training examples to comply with privacy regulations. Full retraining gives strong guarantees but is computationally prohibitive at scale; approximate methods are efficient but lack formal guarantees. SISA (Sharded, Isolated, Sliced, and Aggregated training) achieves certified deletion through data sharding and independent retraining, but random partitioning scatters forget requests across most shards, and isolated retraining degrades utility. We introduce IDSISA (Influence-Distilled SISA), which uses influence functions to concentrate forget-prone samples into few shards and distillation from unaffected shards to recover utility lost to isolation. The deletion guarantee inherited from SISA's retraining step remains exact and requires no probabilistic qualification; the distillation-based utility recovery is a separately quantified, empirically bounded approximation ($ε_{\text{cert}} \leq 0.015$ in expectation). We further formalize certification under sequences of repeated deletion requests, where cross-shard distillation can create dependencies between shards; we prove that a closure-based cascading retraining procedure restores the deletion guarantee to the full aggregated model under any deletion sequence. Experiments on ResNet-18/CIFAR-10, ResNet-18/CIFAR-100, BiLSTM/IMDB, TCN/IMDB, and a fully connected network on Fashion-MNIST show $14-91\%$ better selective forgetting, up to $50\%$ better utility retention in relative terms (with consistent percentage-point gains on the other architectures, where a relative baseline is undefined), and unlearning-time changes ranging from $-6.7\%$ to $+6.4\%$ depending on architecture, relative to SISA.

title: The group of strong automorphisms of the differential field of transseries
abstract: We describe the group of strongly additive automorphisms of the differential field $\mathbb T$ of transseries as a non-trivial semidirect product. We show that this group is torsion-free and has trivial center, and that many naturally arising differential subfields of $\mathbb T$ are definably closed in $\mathbb T$.

title: Deliberate Latent Reasoning for Sequential Recommendation
abstract: Sequential recommenders are widely applied in real-world scenarios to model user preferences and behavior patterns based on user interactions. Recent advances in sequential recommendation enhance transformer-based models with latent reasoning to refine user representations by autoregressively generating intermediate reasoning vectors. However, exploring the optimal reasoning depth for diverse user histories remains challenging: existing methods typically employ a fixed number of reasoning steps for all users. This ``one-size-fits-all'' strategy often leads to suboptimal representation learning due to over-thinking in simple histories or under-thinking in complex ones. To address this issue, we propose DESRec, a deliberate latent reasoning framework that performs personalized latent reasoning to learn more informative reasoning states and enhance user modeling for sequential recommendation. Specifically, it designs a reasoning step selection module that identifies the optimal reasoning step for each user sequence during the training phase. Through a self-distillation mechanism, it compresses this most informative state into the final reasoning step, which serves as the final user representation for item ranking during inference. Moreover, it introduces a progressive preference extraction mechanism for personalized reasoning, which dynamically segments a user's history into a variable number of periods and summarizes each into a latent milestone representing the user's preference for that period. It will be used as the input of the subsequent reasoning. The number of milestones varies with the users' history, enabling a personalized reasoning over users' evolving interests. Extensive experimental results on six public datasets and four backbone recommenders demonstrate the superiority of DESRec over eight baseline models.

title: From Admission to Retention: Predicting Durable Offspring in Quality-Diversity Search
abstract: Automated failure discovery can be framed as a diversity problem: the objective is to expose distinct ways a system fails rather than a single critical adversarial case. Yet uniform parent sampling provides no way to allocate search effort toward individuals likely to produce durable archive contributions. We study this credit assignment problem in an unstructured Quality-Diversity (QD) archive, testing whether signals available before an individual has reproduced distinguish offspring that merely enter the archive from those still retained generations later. Across a planar-arm benchmark and two robotic-locomotion tasks, the same signals are often associated with entry and persistence in opposite directions. In particular, lineage depth is the clearest such signal, and its persistence discrimination grows with population capacity, which is associated with lower turnover. Biasing parent selection toward the signals with the strongest measured association to survival nevertheless does not improve search: moderate bias matches uniform sampling, and strong bias reduces QD-score.

title: H^2MARL: Hierarchical Heterogeneous Multi-agent Reinforcement Learning for Humanoid Robot Control
abstract: Coordinated whole-body control of humanoid robots remains challenging due to high-dimensional coupled dynamics and substantial physical heterogeneity across joint degrees of freedom (JDoFs). Existing multi-agent reinforcement learning methods either employ coarse agent partitions or directly apply generic heterogeneous-agent algorithms, while hierarchical controllers commonly optimize high-level planning and low-level execution independently, leading to uncoordinated motion. In this paper, we propose H^2MARL, a hierarchical heterogeneous multi-agent reinforcement learning framework with two key mechanisms. We first formulate humanoid whole-body control using a JDoF-level physical-heterogeneity-aware policy factorization, where each torque-actuated JDoF is conditioned on an explicit descriptor of its actuation, kinematic, and dynamic properties. Moreover, we develop a closed-loop policy-executor co-optimization mechanism that jointly adapts the high-level pose planner and the low-level joint executor using shared interaction trajectories, thereby reducing the distribution mismatch between planning and execution. Extensive experiments in MuJoCo and Isaac Gym demonstrate that H^2MARL consistently improves locomotion stability, gait coordination, and motion quality over homogeneous, coarse-grained, and independently optimized alternatives.

title: Distributed Consensus, Optimization, and Learning under Communication Constraints
abstract: Many modern engineering applications require distributed problem-solving in which multiple nodes in a network cooperate to achieve a common optimization objective. Numerous distributed optimization and learning algorithms rely on consensus-based distributed coordination to ensure network-wide agreement via iterative local interactions. In these algorithms, the accuracy, frequency, and reliability of information exchange among network nodes directly influence system performance, including convergence behavior, training delay, and model accuracy. This tutorial article adopts a bottom-up approach to present the fundamentals of consensus averaging and distributed optimization methods, and highlights the impact of network connectivity, information flow, and communication uncertainty on network cooperation and optimization performance. Building on these theoretical insights, we discuss key design principles for communication-constrained distributed learning across diverse network topologies and review common approaches to communication-efficient learning, particularly in wireless networks. Despite substantial progress, further efforts are needed to bridge the gap between theory and practice and fully realize the potential of cooperative and networked intelligence.

title: Construction Contracts for Generated Embedded Domain-Specific Language Programs: A Measurement Protocol and a Conditional Effect
abstract: A generated domain-specific program can be accepted by its host and still miss the reference construction. We measure the two events separately and test a short construction contract. The vehicle is Open Quantum Assembly Language (OpenQASM) 3. One 3-billion-parameter generator is run under seven conditions on 100 quantum approximate optimization (QAOA) and 100 variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) instances. Eighty of 100 QAOA signatures appear in some training split. Exact McNemar tests and 95% paired bootstrap intervals are used. The contract, a card, lists structural decisions, enters the prompt, and is checked without a simulator. Parse rates are 0.55 to 0.97 and full structural match is 0.02 to 0.87. On QAOA, at fixed weights, the card moves full match by +32.0 percentage points on card-trained weights (interval +22 to +42) and by -13.0 (-23 to -3) without that training. The +45.0-point difference is not a deployment contrast. The same-step plan-free gain is +23.0 (+13 to +33); the primary distributional score does not separate it. Against the earlier checkpoint the gain is +27.0 (+17 to +37), and the checkpoint also changes. A rule card is not separated from the learned planner, nor is a predicted-card compiler (0.760 vs. 0.780). On 20 QAOA rows outside every training split, the interval includes zero. Under this card, VQE adherence is 0.020 and full match stays near 0.03. Report the two checks separately. Insert a card only into a generator trained to read it, and only where a pilot shows adherence.

title: Field evolution of the multi-$k$ magnetic states in NdB$_4$ revealed by neutron diffraction
abstract: We investigate the magnetic states of the Shastry-Sutherland-lattice magnet NdB$_4$ using single-crystal neutron diffraction. We focus on magnetic fields applied along the tetragonal $c$ axis, which stabilise the fractional 1/5~magnetisation plateau. In the low-temperature phase below 4.9 K, the transition into the plateau state at approximately 12 kOe is marked by a change in the propagation vectors from $(1/5,0,-2/5)$ and its double $(2/5,0,1/5)$ to $(0,0,1/5)$ and $(0,0,2/5)$. At the transition from the plateau to a nominally `field-polarised' state near 33 kOe, all magnetic reflections associated with non-integer propagation vectors disappear, whereas reflections corresponding to the $\mathbf{k}=0$ component persist throughout the entire field range. We conclude that that the in-plane components survive even in the high-field phase and that the polarisation is, in fact, incomplete. The observed field dependence provides direct support for a description of NdB$_4$ in terms of two coupled magnetic instabilities: all-in-all-out order of the in-plane moments and a spin-density wave of the out-of-plane components.

title: Probing black bounce spacetime through mass accretion rate
abstract: We study steady, spherically symmetric accretion of a collisionless kinetic gas onto a compact object described by the Simpson--Visser (SV) metric, a one-parameter regularization of the Schwarzschild spacetime. Using the standard relativistic Vlasov formalism, we adopt boundary conditions at a finite injection radius $R$ and compute the mass accretion rate $\dot{M}$ for Vlasov gas with both monoenergetic and Maxwell--Jüttner distribution functions. Throughout the computation, we also take into account the influence of particle's angular momentum. We carefully investigate the influence of the black bounce parameter on the mass accretion rate $\dot{M}$. By expanding accretion rate in terms of bounce parameter $a$, we found that the leading-order correction appears at quadratic order in $a$. This work extends the Vlasov accretion framework to a broader class of spherically symmetric spacetimes and quantifies the impact of the geometric modification on the accretion flow. In particular, since the shadows of the SV and Schwarzschild black holes are degenerate, comparing their mass accretion rates may offer a complementary probe for distinguishing these geometries in future astrophysical observations.

title: Stability of energy gap of macroscopic quantum matter
abstract: In quantum many-body physics and quantum field theory, it is often assumed that gapped systems remain gapped under sufficiently weak local perturbations. However, to what extent this assumption holds is elusive, except for some special systems. In this work, we examine the stability of energy gap of macroscopic quantum matter that is only subject to two physically natural conditions, locality and translation invariance. We first show that in any spatial dimension, there are gapped local Hamiltonians with a unique ground state and an unstable gap, i.e., they become gapless under certain arbitrarily weak local perturbation in the thermodynamic limit. We then prove that for both spin and fermionic systems in one dimension, such Hamiltonians with an unstable gap must not only break translation invariance but also be fine-tuned. We further show that in any dimension greater than one, there are fine-tuned local translation invariant Hamiltonians with a unique ground state and an unstable gap. These results greatly sharpen our understanding of the fundamental problem of the stability of quantum phases of matter. We also discuss implications of our results on, for example, anyon superconductivity and higher-form symmetries.

title: Emergent regularity of walking patterns: evidence from Swiss cities
abstract: Human travel behaviour is characterised by high temporal and spatial regularity, as demonstrated by the Exploration and Preferential Return (EPR) mechanism, whereby individuals alternate between exploring new locations and preferentially returning to previously visited places. Yet, existing evidence is based on aggregated mobility data that cannot distinguish short trips or separate active mobility (i.e., walking and biking) from other mobility modes. This limits our ability to assess the benefits of walking activities and proximity-based policies such as the 15-minute city. Here, we analyse the spatial distribution and duration of walking habits of 1,318 participants, tracked during a 4-week time use survey in major Swiss cities - which are very close to the 15-minute city model. We find that walking activity is highly concentrated around individuals' home and work locations. These two attractors create walking patterns that are fundamentally different from other transport modes, which are instead used for longer trips and to connect home-workplace. We then introduce a dual-center EPR model, with empirically derived parameters, to simulate the decaying probability of walking away from the centers. Combining empirical data and the EPR framework, we find that groups with higher walking times show a stronger tendency to take long-distance walks and explore more destinations. In general, walking behavior reflects both individual circumstances and residential context: walking durations are shorter among people without a public transport pass, car owners, and residents of low-density rural areas. These findings provide a basis for more targeted assessments of walkability and active-mobility-oriented urban design.

title: Online Control of the Family-wise Error Rate (FWER) for Multi-stage Platform Trials
abstract: In platform trials, multiple intervention arms can enter or leave the study at any time, which brings the challenge of how to control the type I error rate. Online testing procedures, where a stream of hypotheses are tested over time and the total number of hypotheses is unknown, might be a viable choice for error rate control in platform trials. Interim analyses in a multi-stage design offer the opportunity of early stopping for success or futility in clinical trials by testing the same hypothesis at different time points. Some methods targeting false-discovery rate (FDR) or family-wise error rate (FWER) control for multi-stage platform trials have been proposed. However, a method which controls the FWER and allows new arms to be added at any time without prior information is yet to be established. The ADDIS-Spending (ADaptive DIScarding Alpha-spending) procedure controls the FWER in an online setting. We propose the group sequential ADDIS-Spending algorithm to enable interim analyses for each hypothesis in platform trials. The developed method can update the error level of an individual hypothesis at all (interim) analyses whenever new decisions on other hypotheses are made. We compare alternative approaches with our method in a simulation study. The proposed method yields competitive results in the conducted simulations.

title: Dipolar boson stars as static two-body systems: an effective-one-body description
abstract: Dipolar boson stars consist of two scalar-field lumps held in static equilibrium by the balance between gravitational attraction and scalar repulsion. The repulsion stems from a $π$ phase difference between the harmonically varying complex scalar field sourcing each lump. We construct sequences of these configurations numerically and describe them analytically as bound states of two boson stars within the effective-one-body (EOB) formalism. We map the EOB potential previously derived for the scattering of two boson stars onto an energy-dependent Schwarzschild-like radial potential. We find that the EOB-based analytical prediction for the binding energy of the system agrees remarkably well with the numerical values. The analytical prediction for the critical gravitational coupling beyond which no static equilibrium exists is also consistent with the numerical results.

title: Real alternative Daugavet property without Daugavet property in a separable complex Banach space
abstract: We construct a separable complex Banach space whose underlying real space has the alternative Daugavet property, although the complex space fails the Daugavet property, thereby answering an open question posed by Kadets, Martin, and Paya in 2006.

title: Exploiting floating point emulation in tensor contractions in relativistic coupled cluster theory
abstract: In this manuscript we outline a computational strategy to leverage a vendor-optimized implementation of the Ozaki scheme I for floating point emulation as part of an implementation of the Transpose-Transpose-GEMM-Transpose (TTGT) pattern for tensor contractions, and assess its potential to accelerate two of the most expensive tensor contractions appearing in relativistic coupled cluster theory in high-end accelerators such as the NVIDIA Blackwell B200 system in which there is a strong differential in the performance of computations for double and lower precision datatypes. Our results indicate that this emulation-based TTGT strategy can provide significant speedups compared to runs without emulation, and can be competitive with state-of-the-art, vendor-optimized tensor contraction libraries using native double precision as compute datatype. More importantly, our scheme provides a path towards easily allowing users to tune the desired accuracy in the tensor contraction steps, including cases where precision between single and double is sufficient for the application.

title: Vertex-subgraph eigenvector centrality for connected induced subgraphs
abstract: Eigenvector centrality evaluates the importance of vertices through adjacency relations, while higher-order subgraph structures provide additional information for centrality analysis. This motivates the simultaneous evaluation of vertices and subgraphs within a unified spectral framework. In this paper, we propose vertex-subgraph eigenvector centrality (VSC), which jointly determines the centralities of vertices and connected induced subgraphs of order three. The vertex centrality depends on the centralities of the subgraphs containing it and those of the other vertices in these subgraphs, whereas the subgraph centrality depends on the centralities of its constituent vertices. To distinguish induced paths P3 from triangles K3, the capacity of each subgraph is defined as its number of edges. The resulting coupled nonlinear eigenvalue equations are represented by a fourth-order symmetric nonnegative tensor. We prove that this tensor is weakly irreducible for every connected graph with at least three vertices, which guarantees the existence and uniqueness, up to scaling, of a positive Perron eigenvector. Numerical experiments on four real-world networks compare VSC with classical centrality measures and show that capacity weighting has a greater effect on subgraph rankings than on vertex rankings.

title: Rigidity of Ricci solitons for $φ$-related metallic semi-Riemannian structures on para-Kenmotsu manifolds
abstract: In this paper, we investigate Ricci solitons in the para-Kenmotsu setting with respect to a $φ$-related metallic semi-Riemannian metric arising from the underlying almost paracontact metric structure, under the assumption that the potential vector field is pointwise collinear with the Reeb vector field. We first establish the relation $\tS=S+2nβ\bigl(g-η\otimesη\bigr)$ between the Ricci tensors of the original metric $g$ and the $φ$-related metallic metric $\tg$. We then show that the Ricci soliton equation implies that the original metric $g$ is of $η$-Einstein type. By combining this condition with the contracted Bianchi identity, we obtain a rigidity result implying $f=0$, $λ=\frac{2n}{C}$, $S=-2ng$, and consequently $\tS=-\frac{2n}{C}\tg$. Thus, every Ricci soliton in this setting whose potential vector field is pointwise collinear with the Reeb vector field is necessarily trivial, and both $g$ and $\tg$ are Einstein. Finally, we provide two five-dimensional para-Kenmotsu examples: one realizing the resulting trivial Einstein Ricci soliton and another showing that failure of the required Einstein condition prevents the existence of such a soliton.

title: Positive coexistence solutions for systems of multi-kernel Hammerstein type equations
abstract: We investigate positive solutions with both components nontrivial for systems of Hammerstein integral equations associated with a general $2\times2$ matrix of Green's kernels, thereby extending the decoupled (diagonal) case to systems with cross-coupling. Such systems arise from boundary value problems in which the unknowns may be coupled both in the differential equations and in the boundary conditions, a setting that has received considerably less attention than the decoupled case. Using a component-wise Krasnosel'ski\uı compression--expansion fixed point theorem in product cones, we derive existence and non-existence criteria. A multiplicity result guaranteeing at least two positive solutions is also obtained, by means of the fixed point index in cones. As an application, we consider radially symmetric solutions for an elliptic system on an annulus with coupled Robin boundary conditions.

title: Modeling Gene Expression Noise: From Transcriptional Dynamics to Cell Growth and Division
abstract: Gene expression is inherently noisy, leading to substantial cell-to-cell variation in mRNA and protein levels. The telegraph model and the simpler bursty model provide good fits to single-cell count distributions and have been used extensively to understand transcriptional kinetics and estimate the kinetic parameters. However, these models all describe a static cell. Here, we review models of stochastic gene expression in growing and dividing cells which aim to understand how a cell's own life history, from its birth, through copying its genome, to its division, leaves a distinct fluctuation signature on molecule numbers. We discuss the biochemical and biophysical processes captured by these models, their analytical tractability, the concept of cyclo-stationary behavior, when this is well approximated by the steady-state of static models and how the distributions of molecular numbers measured under these conditions sensitively depend on the experimental setup. This is followed by a discussion of how these models are fitted to single-cell measurements, how biological variability can be separated from measurement noise, and which computational advances make this feasible for thousands of genes. We finish by highlighting the open problems in the field.

title: Constrained Mean Variance Portfolio Selection under Reflected Factor Dynamics: Stochastic Riccati Equations, Neumann Problems,and a Deep Solver
abstract: We study extended stochastic Riccati equations (ESREs) arising in constrained continuous time mean variance portfolio selection with random market coefficients. Reflected Markovian diffusions are introduced to model factor dynamics in a bounded state space, naturally leading to homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions. A logarithmic transformation converts the extended stochastic Riccati equations into quadratic backward stochastic differential equations (BSDEs) driven by the reflected factors. We establish their probabilistic representation through semilinear parabolic Neumann problems and prove existence and uniqueness of bounded continuous viscosity solutions. Existence is obtained through stability and comparison arguments for quadratic BSDEs, whereas uniqueness is established by combining a Kobylanski-type transformation with a viscosity comparison principle adapted to the Neumann boundary setting. We further develop a Deep BSDE method combining reflected-path simulation, geometry-aware boundary treatment, and efficient evaluation of the constrained Hamiltonian. Numerical experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the method, providing a mesh-free framework for high-dimensional constrained portfolio problems with Neumann boundary.

title: Evaluating the prediction of subgrid eddy kinetic energy from a machine learning model
abstract: Global climate model resolution is still too coarse to fully resolve mesoscale processes, therefore subgrid closures are required to approximate the feedback of eddies onto the resolved flow. With high-resolution datasets now readily available, there has been a rapid growth in the use of machine learning to develop new eddy closures that could help reduce model biases and uncertainty. In this work we employ an offline learning approach with a convolutional neural network to predict subgrid eddy kinetic energy ($KE_e$), laying the initial groundwork for a machine-learned scale-aware GEOMETRIC eddy closure for the UK's Earth System Model. We address the question of whether global parameterizations are needed or if regional closures are sufficient by evaluating a number of neural network models through region and feature ablation experiments. ML parameterization models generalize to unseen regions when their training data share similar feature and target distributions with those regions. Models that fail to generalize incur distributional shift, or employ different filtering scales for the true eddy kinetic energy field. When holding out features, there is improvement among the generalizable ML models, with some feature spaces leading to improvements in some regions but degrading performance in others. Generally, power spectral density of $KE_e$ tend to diverge at small scales, though some feature spaces are able to minimize this divergence. Overall, the best performing model trained on all regions achieves time-mean and anomaly R2 scores of R2$\approx 0.95$ and R2$\approx 0.8 - 0.9$, respectively.

title: Spatially and Compositionally Controlled Multimodal Glioblastoma MRI Synthesis with Latent Diffusion
abstract: Glioblastoma exhibits substantial heterogeneity in tumour morphology and composition across MRI modalities, often making available clinical datasets highly unbalanced in terms of patient pathologies. We propose a two-stage latent diffusion model (LDM) framework for the generation of explicitly controllable 2D glioblastoma MRI scans. First, a segmentation LDM generates tumour maps conditioned on location, spatial extent, axial position, and subregion composition. Second, a modality-conditioned LDM with ControlNet generates T1, T1Gd, T2, and FLAIR images adhering to the requested segmentation. On a held-out test set, generated segmentations achieved a mean centroid error of 0.842 pixels and a subregion proportion error of 0.795 percentage points. ControlNet improved Fréchet inception distance (FID) across all four modalities, reducing pooled FID from 42.59 to 36.12. An expert reader study yielded mean quality ratings of 6.60 for real images, 6.83 for ControlNet-generated images, and 6.77 for fully synthetic images.

title: Dynamically Reentrant Skyrmion Phase in Oscillating Magnetic Fields
abstract: We address a central open question in driven topological matter by investigating the nonequilibrium response of a two-dimensional magnet with Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interactions subjected to a periodically oscillating magnetic field. Using extensive Monte Carlo simulations, we uncover a dynamically reentrant skyrmion phase that emerges within a finite window of field amplitudes and bias fields, sandwiched between the conventional skyrmion and polarized ferromagnetic phases. This phase has no equilibrium counterpart and originates from an imbalance between skyrmion creation and annihilation over a single field cycle, leading to a reversal of the period-averaged topological charge. We show that the re-entrant phase exists only in the dynamic response regime where the system can follow the drive, and is suppressed at higher driving frequencies. Our results establish periodic driving as a nonequilibrium control parameter for stabilizing and reversing skyrmion topology.

title: EvoOPD: Evolving Privileged Information Strategies for Black-Box On-Policy Distillation
abstract: Proprietary language models exhibit strong reasoning and coding capabilities, but their output distributions are inaccessible, making fine-grained distillation methods that rely on teacher logits difficult to apply directly to black-box models. We observe that rich textual feedback from a black-box teacher can be treated as privileged information (PI) and converted, through a PI-conditioned privileged teacher, into dense supervision signals on the student's own trajectories. However, what PI should be acquired from the teacher to most effectively support student learning remains unclear. PI strategies that differ in where they focus, what information they request, and how much detail they provide can have substantially different effects on the current student, and their relative effectiveness can further change as training progresses. Based on this observation, we propose Evolving Privileged Information Strategies for Black-Box On-Policy Distillation (EvoOPD), which treats PI acquisition itself as an optimization problem and maintains a PI Strategy Bank that evolves with the student state. EvoOPD uses the measured repair utility of PI on the current student to adapt the focus, information type, and granularity of teacher feedback, allowing the acquired information to continually match the student's learning needs. We systematically evaluate EvoOPD on mathematical reasoning and code generation with Qwen3-1.7B, 4B, and 8B students. EvoOPD achieves the best overall performance in all six model-task settings, improving over the strongest baseline in each setting by an average of 2.14 percentage points in mathematics and 1.30 points in code. Further analysis shows that the relative effectiveness of PI acquisition strategies changes with student state, making a fixed strategy difficult to sustain as the best choice throughout distillation.

title: Using Experience Twice: Dynamic Process Rubrics for Privileged Token-Level Credit Assignment
abstract: Agent trajectories often contain both successful decisions and failed attempts, yet optimization with sparse trajectory-level rewards struggles to identify which critical decisions should be reinforced or suppressed. We observe that meaningful distinctions among on-policy trajectories can be distilled into natural-language process rubrics and used as process supervision signals. Based on this insight, we propose Online Rubric Self-Distillation (ORSD), which leverages self-derived process rubrics for dense token-level supervision, thereby augmenting outcome-centric reinforcement learning. Specifically, the current policy independently generates multiple rubric bundles at each step according to the same group of trajectories, extracting candidate process rubrics from cross-trajectory behavioral differences. A frozen verifier then evaluates all rubric items against each trajectory in the group, and selects one candidate bundle based on bundle-level alignment between rubric satisfaction and task success. ORSD treats the selected rubric bundle as privileged information during training, then compares the log-likelihoods of the original tokens with and without the rubric. The resulting likelihood gap provides token-specific process credit, which is added to the original trajectory-level GRPO advantage through additive advantage shaping. ORSD thus bridges trajectory-level outcome supervision and fine-grained process supervision, enabling token-level credit assignment using process signals. Extensive experiments on ALFWorld and WebShop show that ORSD accelerates policy improvement and boosts final task performance for both Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-4B under the same environment-interaction budget. Our code is available at https://github.com/AnnaXChun/ORSD.

title: MKD2World: A Typed Spatial MarkDown World Model For Web Agents
abstract: Graphical user interface (GUI) agents can improve decision-making with world-model foresight, provided that predicted states accurately reflect post-action interfaces. Existing state representations fail to jointly capture interface layout, UI semantics, and explicit locations. We introduce Typed Spatial Markdown (TSM), a Markdown-style textual state representation for desktop web interfaces. TSM serializes block-level and atomic-level UI elements according to their spatial relationships, jointly encoding their types, visual semantics, explicit locations, optional control states, and hierarchical membership. To train a screenshot-to-TSM renderer, we construct AtomBlock-WebUI, a dataset with precise annotations at both granularities. By injecting element-type labels into HTML and directly extracting bounding boxes after rendering, we avoid annotation errors caused by post-hoc inference from webpage structures. Building on TSM, we propose MKD2World, a desktop web world model trained in two stages for current-state description and action-conditioned next-state prediction. During inference, the web agent queries MKD2World as needed and performs a ``digest'' step, in which it interprets each predicted state and extracts task-relevant evidence for selecting the best action. Experiments show that MKD2World-9B achieves an EleF1 score of 26.50 on the out-of-domain test set, outperforming GPT-5.6-Sol(14.98) by 11.52 points. Across Online-Mind2Web tasks, MKD2World-9B improves the success rate of the Qwen3.5-35B web agent from 22.94% to 37.61%, achieving competitive performance among leading open-source GUI world models. Code is available at https://github.com/OmniAI-Lab-CUHKSZ/MKD2World.

title: When Do Summaries Become Instructions? Unsupported Policy in LLM Agents' Self-Written Handoff Summaries
abstract: Long-running LLM agents compact their context, replacing most history with a summary. We ask whether handoff summaries state permissions or requirements the record does not support, whether such sentences change what the next instance (the successor) does, and where they come from. Synthetic tool-use tasks carry a ground-truth permission ledger; same-snapshot replay reruns the successor with those whole sentences replaced by neutral filler. Two AI readers, reading only rule-flagged held-out summaries, confirmed unsupported restrictions in 1.2% and 2.4% of all readable summaries from two open-weight models, and unsupported authorizations in 0.1% and 1.3%. For restrictions, a pre-specified replay test was not significant (p = 0.58); a follow-up, planned after it, found a fragile effect (p = 0.027). Neutralizing false approvals cut unauthorized actions from 24 to 7 of 120 held-out runs (post hoc; later set: 17 to 11 of 48). Most development restrictions followed the agent's earlier reasoning that an action needs approval (post hoc). In pre-specified tests, replacing the system prompt's "Some actions need approval." with one saying where requirements come from cut unsupported restrictions from 5.0% to 1.8% of development summaries and, on held-out templates, from 1.8% to 0.3% (both p < 10^-9), while requests for approvals the ledger requires barely changed. Code and data: https://github.com/Chuw1/handoff-audit

title: Adapting Sleep Foundation Models for Dense Sleep Spindle Localization
abstract: Adapting sleep foundation models to dense electroencephalography (EEG) event localization is challenging because multi-second representations may not preserve sufficient temporal detail for precise boundary recovery. We address sleep spindle localization by adapting a frozen SleepFM encoder with a local time-frequency pathway that preserves spindle-relevant spectral content and intra-token position. The local representation drives localization, while residual cross-attention incorporates SleepFM temporal context. Dense predictions are obtained through localized token-to-sample reconstruction and temporal refinement. Tested on the Massive Online Data Annotation (MODA), the proposed model achieves an event-level $F_1$ of $0.8080 \pm 0.0040$ at IoU 0.2 across six folds. Ablations show that localization primarily depends on local spectral and sub-token temporal information, while the pretrained representation provides complementary context. These results indicate that dense adaptation benefits from preserving information below the pretrained token scale. Code will be released upon acceptance.

title: The dwarf galaxy NGC 185: the flagship of Andromeda's dwarf galaxies for the study of evolved multiple stellar populations
abstract: Reaching galaxies at 10-15 Mpc with HST and JWST requires star formation history (SFH) diagnostics that do not rely on the faint main sequence turn-off. We investigate whether horizontal branch (HB), red clump (RC), and red and asymptotic giant branch (RGB, AGB) stars can fill this role for dwarf elliptical galaxies, using NGC 185 as a test case. We use stellar evolution models of low- and intermediate-mass stars as inputs to population synthesis simulations that reproduce the colour distribution and luminosity function of stars in the (mF606W-mF814W, mF814W) diagram. The study of the stars populating the HB is used to derive the distance modulus and reddening, the average mass loss suffered by the stars during the ascending on the RGB and the SFH occurred during the ancient epochs, before 7 Gyr ago. The luminosity function of the RC gives us constraints on the recent SFH (<8 Gyr). The distribution of HB stars yields a reddening E(B-V)=0.20 mag and a distance modulus DM=24.10 mag for NGC 185. The average mass lost by low-mass stars during the RGB phase is 0.22 +- 0.01 Msun. Star formation was concentrated at early epochs, with half of the stars formed more than 11 Gyr ago. The morphology of the HB indicates essentially no metallicity spread among stars older than 8 Gyr, whereas the slope of the RGB suggests that part of the stars younger than 5-6 Gyr are slightly enriched in metals. Once RGB mass loss is adequately constrained, evolved stars can provide a reliable SFH for dwarf elliptical galaxies well beyond the reach of MSTO-based methods. We discuss the implications for more distant systems and the remaining uncertainties in the underlying stellar models.

title: Magnetism among the oldest white dwarfs in the solar neighbourhood
abstract: We present a new circular polarisation survey of approximately 100 white dwarfs selected as featureless DC stars and combine our measurements with previous observations. Our compilation contains 205 objects, of which 24 show firm circular polarisation detections, while another four show marginal signals that require confirmation. Four magnetic white dwarfs originally classified as DC show polarisation spectra with significant contributions from spectral lines. Depending on the treatment of these objects and of the marginal detections, the inferred fraction of magnetic objects in the DC selected sample lies between approximately 10 and 14%. Among objects without identifiable line contributions, the circular polarisation never exceeds approximately 2%, substantially below the levels observed in some hotter magnetic white dwarfs with prominent spectral features. This is unlikely a symptom of field decay, since in our sample we find no significant evidence for a dependence of magnetic incidence on cooling age, and magnetic fields are detected in stars with cooling ages exceeding 9 Gyr. Instead, strong spectral line opacity provides a natural mechanism for producing much larger polarisation amplitudes than the continuum. In the full sample considered here, the incidence of detectable magnetism increases with stellar mass. Most average-mass magnetic stars for which repeated observations are available show no clear polarimetric variability, whereas variability appears more common among the most massive objects.

title: Population synthesis of substellar companions surviving common-envelope evolution
abstract: Predicting the population of substellar companions around white dwarfs (WDs) requires accounting for both companions that avoid engulfment during stellar evolution and those that survive common-envelope (CE) evolution. While the former population was investigated in our previous population-synthesis study, a comprehensive population synthesis of the latter remains lacking. We investigated the fate of engulfed substellar companions within the same population-synthesis framework. We aim to predict the occurrence rates and properties of companions surviving CE evolution, identify the conditions permitting survival, and assess their detectability. We determined the stellar structure at the onset of CE evolution and calculated CE outcomes for different ejection efficiencies considering gravitational and thermal energy or the full internal energy of the envelope. Survival is rare and strongly depends on the evolutionary stage at engulfment. No companions entering CE evolution during the red-giant branch or early asymptotic-giant branch survive. Survivors originate exclusively from the thermally pulsing asymptotic-giant branch, when stellar envelopes can become weakly bound, allowing even relatively low-mass companions to survive. The resulting systems typically have orbital periods of a few hours. We predict occurrence rates of up to 0.16% among WDs, corresponding to an upper limit of 2.53 companions to WDs within 50 pc. Transit detection is primarily limited by orbital geometry, whereas all predicted survivors would produce detectable infrared excess with JWST out to 50pc. We predict that CE evolution produces a small but observable population of close substellar companions to WDs. Survival is governed not only by companion mass but critically by the envelope structure at engulfment, particularly during thermal pulses, and by the contribution of recombination energy to envelope ejection.

title: Who Gets Counted? Large Language Models, Informative Refusal, and Downstream Bias in Name-Based Demographic Classification
abstract: Researchers routinely infer gender, race, and ethnicity from names, yet the standard tools used for this task misclassify the groups that diversity research most needs to measure. Large language models (LLMs) have been proposed as a remedy because they label diverse names accurately. We ask whether that accuracy carries over to the estimates researchers report. Across 10,000 Chinese names, 19,998 North Carolina voters with self-reported race, and 300 political science authors with human reference codes, we compare three LLMs with seven traditional tools and link the voter sample to party registration and age. Selective labeling explains part of the LLMs' accuracy advantage. Claude Haiku labels half of the voters, and a traditional tool limited to its most confident half is more accurate. Hard labels from every tool understate the White--Black gap in Democratic registration by 36% to 65%, while BIRDiE estimation on BISG posteriors comes within 0.03 of it. Haiku's missing labels select on age, inflating the age gap by six years. Combined with BISG, LLM answers sharpen individual labels without a demonstrated gain in BIRDiE accuracy. Classifiers should be judged by the estimates they produce, including the consequences of missing labels

title: An ambient metric framework for sharp compactness of the constant $Q_{2N}$-curvature problem
abstract: We develop a geometric method for studying $C^{2N}$-compactness of positive solutions to the constant $Q_{2N}$-curvature equation on closed Riemannian $n$-manifolds, for every integer $N\ge1$ and every dimension $n>2N$. Assuming the GJMS operator is invertible, its Green function is positive, and the positive mass condition holds, we establish sharp dimension ranges for the compactness of the set of all positive solutions with prescribed positive constant $Q_{2N}$-curvature. The largest dimension for compactness is $24$ for $N=1$ ([21]), $2N+20$ for $N=2,3$ ([11]), $2N+19$ for $N=4,5$, $2N+18$ for $N=6,7,8$, $2N+17$ for $9\le N\le17$, and $2N+16$ for all $N\ge18$. The constructions in [4,5,33,11] for $N=1,2,3$ and in the companion paper [12] for $N\ge4$ give noncompact examples in every dimension exceeding the corresponding compactness bound. We show that these $L^{\infty}$-unbounded examples can be chosen to satisfy the same operator and mass hypotheses, proving sharpness within this class. Our method relates the Pohozaev quadratic forms to the Hessian $D^2\mathscr{F}(g_c)$, where $\mathscr{F}$ is the volume-normalized total $Q_{2N}$-curvature functional and $g_c$ is the standard round metric on $\mathbb{S}^n$. The ambient metric argument of [12] supplies an explicit formula for $D^2\mathscr{F}(g_c)$ on transverse-traceless tensors. The York decomposition projects metric perturbations onto this space. The scalar--vector--tensor decomposition represents the Pohozaev quadratic forms by explicit finite-dimensional matrices. We prove that these matrices are positive definite throughout the stated dimension range, a crucial step in establishing compactness.

title: A Tensor-Network Chebyshev-Galerkin Method for Boundary-Value Problems in Computational Mechanics
abstract: Quantum-inspired numerical methods for partial differential equations represent discretized fields and operators as quantics tensor trains (QTT), so that their cost depends on how compressible the problem is rather than on the number of unknowns. Global spectral formulations in this setting have so far relied on Fourier bases, restricted to periodic problems, or on collocation, which does not preserve the variational structure exploited by tensor-network solvers. We introduce a QTT Chebyshev-Galerkin method that assembles and solves global spectral systems directly in compressed form, without forming the underlying arrays. Starting from the weak formulation, the method handles coupled elliptic systems with variable coefficients, smoothly mapped geometries, and mixed Dirichlet-Robin boundary conditions, and yields symmetric positive-definite systems suited to variational tensor-network solvers. Parameters and random inputs enter as additional coordinates, so the same construction returns the solution over an entire parameter space in a single solve. In linear elasticity, the method retains spectral convergence and reaches errors below $10^{-8}$ on a three-dimensional benchmark, beyond those attained by QTT finite differences and Q2/Q4 FEniCSx finite elements over the tested range. A six-parameter cantilever design study covering $1.7\times10^{7}$ designs is solved in a single 92s run, and a stochastic problem with ten random coordinates is represented with $2.4\times10^{6}$ times less memory than its full coefficient array.

title: Addition by Subtraction: Toward Mitigating Fragile Safety Alignment in Large Language Models
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) undergo safety alignment to prevent harmful generations, yet they remain vulnerable to jailbreak attacks. Recent work reveals a deeper structural weakness: safety alignment can be highly sparse, such that pruning a small number of safety-critical neurons or ablating a single refusal direction can substantially undermine aligned behavior. In this work, we take the first steps toward strengthening safety alignment such that it is less dependent on sparse model components. We propose Addition by Subtraction, which gradually removes identified safety-critical neurons during finetuning and uses preference optimization to re-establish safety-aligned behavior through other parts of the model. Our results show that the resulting models are substantially more robust to pruning-based attacks. Remarkably, these benefits generalize beyond the white-box attacks motivating our design: Addition by Subtraction improves robustness against other sparsity-based interventions, including refusal-direction ablation, as well as a broad range of black-box jailbreak attacks. The finetuned models also exhibit improved truthfulness while largely preserving general capabilities. Comprehensive experiments across four models from three vendors demonstrate consistent improvements in safety robustness, reducing attack success rates by up to 90% for some attacks.

title: RAGAM-AI: A Hybrid Reinforcement Learning based Agentic approach powered by Generative AI for Edge Resource Management
abstract: Resource management for distributed edge networks hosting different services has been handled efficiently using Reinforcement learning (RL). Reward generalization in complex workflows is still an open issue within the RL realm. Therefore, this work proposes RAGAM-AI, a hybrid framework that combines the capabilities of RL algorithms and Generative-AI (Gen-AI) for powering an Agentic AI workflow that optimizes resource allocation at the Multi-access Edge Computing (MEC) units. This framework further resolves the reward generalization issue by utilizing Large Language Model (LLM) for feedback. A Multi- Agent Soft-Actor Critic (MASAC) using MathΣtral as a reward oracle is implemented for managing resource allocations at the MEC. RAGAM-AI interprets system state information and evaluates multi-objective trade-offs guiding the resource orchestration loop over distributed edge server agents. The complexity of the framework is further brought down by incorporating surrogate reward model. The overall performance is evaluated against the single agent SAC, REINFORCE and random policies for benchmarking. On using RAGAM-AI, lower allocation deviations for CPU, memory and bandwidth resources are reported while minimizing the latency and data rate costs. A scalable AI as a feedback (AIAF) solution optimizing network resources with significant performance improvement is thus presented.

title: FA-Agent: An extensible multimodal agent framework for first-arrival picking in mountainous seismic data
abstract: First-arrival traveltimes underpin near-surface velocity modeling and static corrections, but in low signal-to-noise mountainous land data the first arrival is often weak, intermittent, and masked by strong direct waves and noise. Energy-based pickers then pick later arrivals or noise, and deep-learning pickers usually require retraining for a new survey. Because erroneous picks bias first-arrival tomography, many difficult zones are still inspected and corrected manually. We present FA-Agent, an agent framework for first-arrival picking built on a multimodal large language model. It combines a model that performs visual recognition and makes decisions, tools that process the data, and skills that carry experience of processing mountainous data. The framework is open and extensible: new pickers, denoising methods, and quality-control tools can be added, and new experience can be written into the skills. It is restricted neither to mountainous data nor to a particular model. Emulating a seismic data processor, the agent first surveys the whole gather to find zones needing attention, then examines them in enlarged views, and finally keeps, corrects, or removes the initial picks. On semi-synthetic gathers with known first arrivals and real mountainous noise, the agent picked the first arrival with high accuracy where it was clearly visible and removed the picks where it was invisible and could not be judged. Applied to randomly sampled gathers from a mountainous survey, it corrected picks onto weak first-arrival branches and removed picks where no first arrival could be confirmed, and it performed well on the most difficult data. Cases reviewed by experts are added to the skills automatically, so the agent improves with use, and a locally deployed model keeps confidential data on site. FA-Agent can thus become an essential component of future automated seismic data processing workflows.

title: LungMend: A Healthy-Only Latent Diffusion Shape Prior for Lung Mask Correction in Severe Tuberculosis CT
abstract: Lung segmentation models such as R231 are widely used, but they fail on severe tuberculosis (TB) CT: cavities and consolidations look like non-lung tissue and are left out of the mask. We present LungMend, a post-processing model that corrects such masks using only healthy anatomy. A latent diffusion model, trained on healthy lungs with synthetically corrupted masks, learns to recover the complete lung from the faulty mask and the bone anatomy, without any pathological data or CT intensities. LungMend recovers cavities and consolidations that R231 misses and improves accuracy on expert-annotated slices. Code: https://github.com/noureddinekhiati/LungMend

title: Approximate minimax regret for conditionally similar tests
abstract: We construct approximately minimax regret optimal tests in a scalar Gaussian instrumental variables experiment. This example shows how conditionally similar tests allow a novel approximation approach, allowing us to optimize weights over alternatives to minimize worst-case power regret. Stochastic mirror descent and averaging yield finite-iteration guarantees with exact conditional similarity. We establish bounds for exact and simulated powers and illustrate the procedure numerically. This initial algorithm shows how existing nearly-optimal test computation methods can be extended to include composite alternative hypothesis sets without the computational cost associated with maintaining size control.

title: Spectral properties of twisted soft waveguides
abstract: We discuss a model of a soft waveguide described by Schrödinger operator whose potential is a twisted straight channel of non-circular profile. We show that a compactly supported twist makes the operator subcritical, the property being expressed in terms of a Hardy-type inequality. On the other hand, a periodic twist raises the essential spectrum and its local slowdown may give rise to isolated eigenvalues below the essential spectrum threshold.

title: From Fixed Defaults to Calibrated Activation Policies for Long-Term Time-Series Forecasting
abstract: Long-term time-series forecasting supports decisions in energy, transportation, and other applications where reliable predictions are needed beyond the observed data. Although forecasting research has advanced model architectures, fixed activation configurations provide limited guidance on how activation choices should vary across datasets and prediction horizons. This study aims to establish when task-specific activation choices improve forecasting accuracy and how previous experiments can guide the selection of suitable configurations for new tasks. We develop a calibrated selection policy that learns a reliable default from prior experiments, adapts the activation function and its location to each task, and retains the default when evidence for a change is insufficient. In an evaluation supported by 1,225 Informer training runs across 17 dataset variants and 51 forecasting tasks, the policy reduces mean squared error by 7.86% on average relative to the conventional fixed-activation baseline and improves 72.55% of tasks. These findings establish activation choice and placement as practical opportunities for improving existing forecasting models and show how accumulated experimental evidence can guide configuration decisions without repeating an exhaustive search for every task.

title: Asymptotic behavior of generic Riemann solutions to one-dimensional full compressible Navier-Stokes-Poisson equations
abstract: This paper investigates the time-asymptotic stability of the one-dimensional full compressible Navier-Stokes-Poisson equations, assuming that the corresponding quasi-neutral Euler equations admit a generic Riemann solution consisting of a shock, a contact discontinuity, and a rarefaction wave. It is proved that there exists a unique global-in-time solution, which converges in $L^\infty$ norm, as time goes to infinity, to the ansatz composed of a viscous shock with a time-dependent shift, a viscous contact wave, and an inviscid rarefaction wave. The main difficulty arises from the non-conservative lower-order source terms induced by the electric potential in the momentum and energy equations, which significantly complicates the proof of the existence of individual waves (especially the viscous shock) and the derivation of the relative entropy estimates. To overcome this, we make full use of the Poisson equation satisfied by the electric potential, and combine the weighted relative entropy method with the $a$-contraction method with shifts to close the estimates within the $H^2$-perturbation framework.

title: Two-sided estimates for two-point local time tails of branching random walks: a Green function criterion
abstract: This paper is devoted to the study of the joint tails of local times at two distinct sites for branching random walks (BRWs). Our principle results establish a general Green-function criterion for two-sided exponential tail bounds with a common spatial factor given by a three-point Green function convolution, and further identify a strict inequality that must be satisfied by the corresponding exponential constants. In particular, we verify this criterion for subcritical BRWs on finitely generated groups, for critical BRWs on non-elementary hyperbolic groups, and for critical BRWs on $\mathbb{Z}^d$ with $d\geq 5$. As applications, we revisit the growth rate of visited sites on spheres in hyperbolic groups obtained by Sidoravicius et al. [Commun. Pure Appl. Math. 2023], and also establish lower bounds for the probabilities of visiting finite sets in Euclidean lattices.

title: Mortality Is Undecidable for $2 \times 2$ Integer Matrices
abstract: The matrix mortality problem asks whether a given finite family of matrices can be multiplied, in any order and with possible repetition, to get the zero matrix. It is one of the most basic decision problems about matrix products, and it arises naturally in the study of switched linear systems and of finite automata. Mortality is trivially decidable in dimension one and has been known to be undecidable for integer matrices in dimensions three and higher since 1970; only the problem in dimension $2$ is left open. We resolve this problem by proving that mortality is undecidable for families of 5,799 distinct $2\times2$ integer matrices. All but one of the matrices are fixed and nonsingular, with determinants $\pm p$ for a single fixed prime $p$. The input affects only the remaining rank-one matrix, which encodes this input into its kernel. Our proof encodes the computation of a fixed universal machine into products of $2\times2$ matrices. We represent each configuration of the computation by a single rational number, which we identify with a line through the origin in $\mathbb{Q}^2$, and each nonsingular matrix carries out a small piece of one computation step. The main difficulty is that the matrices may be multiplied in any order, so we design them to check their own work: a "wrong'' step puts a factor of a prime number $p$ into the denominator of the rational number corresponding to the current computation step, where no later matrix can remove it. As a result, products of these matrices can go from one encoded configuration to another only by following a valid computation. The rank-one matrix then turns the question of whether the machine halts into the question of whether some product equals zero. A companion formalization in the Lean proof assistant verifies the complete reduction.

title: EPISTEME: Trustworthy Coding Agents Through Tool Call Intent
abstract: Coding agents change software through tool calls. Tool calls mutate the local state. For good? For bad? Nobody knows. Agents never say why a tool call is made. We propose the epistemic agent design, in which the harness guarantees that the model declares why a tool call is made. The harness then records what the command actually did and checks the self-reported declaration against these effects. The result is a journal 1) that can guard calls before they run and 2) that supports audits and forensics. For evaluation, we use ImpossibleBench, whose tasks can be passed only by cheating, and demonstrate that forcing the agents to say why results in exposed cheating. Across 49 reward-hacking runs of two open-weight models, the journal exposed 90%.

title: Playing Soccer Like Humans Do: Learning Versatile and Agile Humanoid Soccer via Latent Motion Priors
abstract: Humanoid soccer requires a robot to seamlessly combine agile locomotion, ball manipulation, and impact-rich contact dynamics across a continuous, dynamic behavioral spectrum. Yet existing approaches either cover only a limited set of skills, or forego motion priors entirely and produce unnatural behaviors, leaving the combination of a unified skill set and human-like motion quality unaddressed. We present soccerbot, a hierarchical reinforcement learning framework that resolves both limitations through a structured latent motion prior distilled from large-scale human soccer motion capture data. By constraining policy learning within this dynamically plausible motion manifold, a single skill-conditioned policy naturally learns to perform moving, dribbling, trapping, and kicking in a unified formulation, while inherently producing human-like motion and fluid transitions during commanded skill switching. Augmented by robustness-oriented simulation design, soccerbot transfers zero-shot to the Unitree G1 humanoid robot, demonstrating agile, natural, and robust execution of the full soccer skill repertoire under real-world conditions.

title: Natural Expansiveness and Equilibrium States for Semiflows
abstract: We introduce natural expansiveness, a notion of expansiveness for non-invertible dynamical systems which is defined by using the natural extension. We show that every expansive homeomorphism or flow, every positive expansive endomorphism and every positive expansive semiflow without end points is naturally expansive. Moreover, we prove that the suspension of a naturally expansive endomorphism is naturally expansive. This gives examples of naturally expansive semiflows which are neither positive expansive nor restrictions of expansive flows. Then we extend natural expansiveness and the topological pressure to semiflows which are not necessarily continuous, by using a pseudosemimetric $d_ρ$. We introduce the notion of $d_ρ$-conjugacy, and we prove that every regular impulsive semiflow is $d_ρ$-conjugate to a continuous semiflow. As an application, we obtain the existence and uniqueness of equilibrium states for regular impulsive semiflows.

title: Box-Shift: Fixed-Complexity Counter-Hypothesis Generation for Soft-Output MIMO Box Decoding
abstract: Box Decoding is a sort-free tree-search multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) detector with a fixed per-layer cost independent of the quadrature amplitude modulation (QAM) order. Its regular datapath is well suited to hardware implementation, but the detector has so far been limited to hard-output operation in uncoded systems. Its fixed four-point box spans two adjacent Gray-coded QAM levels per axis, leaving most bits without counter-hypotheses for higher-order QAM. This missing counter-hypothesis (MCH) problem prevents the direct computation of finite max-log log-likelihood ratios (LLRs). We propose the \emph{Box-Shift} algorithm, which shifts the existing box to the nearest node carrying the complementary value of each Gray-coded bit at each detection layer. Unlike Bit-Flip, Box-Shift analytically identifies the partially optimal counter-hypothesis using one inverter per bit and updates the path metric through an index-domain increment. The proposed method preserves the sort-free, QAM-order-independent structure of Box Decoding.
