We further show that the gradient of $\mathcal{L}_{SC}$ depends on predicate scores rather than ground-truth labels: for two-predicate rules it amplifies the ordering the model already holds, and when all scores in a group are equal it suppresses predicates in more exclusion rules more strongly, explaining why the penalty can lower recall while improving consistency. On Action Genome, activating $\mathcal{L}_{SC}$ after two warm-up epochs reduces R@20 from 42.21% to 35.18% while lowering the No-Constraint contradiction rate from 45.92% to 4.07% (matched-budget R@20: 40.48% CoupledSGA vs. 44.78% SceneSayerODE). CoupledSGA is a testbed, not a state-of-the-art claim: With-Constraint recall captures the cost of enforcing structural consistency but not the improvement. We recommend reporting No-Constraint results alongside a contradiction rate for methods that constrain predicate co-activation.

title: Deterministic Oracle Complexity for Goldstein Stationarity in Nonsmooth Nonconvex Optimization with Constraints
abstract: We consider the deterministic oracle complexity of finding a $(δ,ε)$-Goldstein stationary point of a Lipschitz function under constraints. The problem is posed in $\mathbb{R}^d$, where $d$ denotes the dimension; constraints are specified either by a closed feasible set or by a single explicit inequality. For closed feasible sets that are star-shaped with respect to an interior ball, including all convex bodies, we use a resisting-oracle construction to show that every deterministic algorithm needs $Ω(ε^{-2})$ objective-oracle calls in the worst case when $d\gtrsimε^{-2}$ and $δ\lesssimε$. For explicit inequalities satisfying uniform Goldstein constraint qualification and strict feasibility, finding Goldstein KKT stationary points requires exponentially many oracle calls in $d$ in the worst case, even at fixed stationarity accuracy. This exponential dependence holds under dimension-independent constraint regularity and strict-feasibility bounds, with a sufficiently small neighborhood radius and complementary slackness error. The result covers common constraints such as ball and box constraints and also allows nonconvex feasible regions. For convex coercive constraints with a Slater point, the resisting-oracle argument also gives an $Ω(ε^{-2})$ oracle-call bound in the same dimension and radius regime while allowing a larger complementary slackness error. These results hold for all deterministic algorithms using a local oracle, whether or not the returned point was queried. Each constructed objective has a strictly feasible global minimizer; the lower bounds therefore concern the information required to find stationary points, not their existence.

title: Photonic and Electronic Interaction of TMD-Hybridized ZnO Nanowire Lasers
abstract: Semiconductor nanowire lasers are promising on-chip coherent light sources for photonic integrated circuits, but integration inevitably places them in contact with other materials, thereby changing their properties upon hybridization. In this study, we examine the photonic and electronic coupling between single ZnO nanowire lasers and TMDs. Using deterministic nanomanipulation, we first hybridized the same nanowire first with a WS$_2$ monolayer and then with a MoS$_2$ monolayer. The respective lasing threshold rises, the emission is strongly quenched at high pump power densities, and the mode envelope blueshifts. Upon hybridization with bilayer, trilayer, and bulk MoS$_2$, lasing is fully suppressed. Finite-Difference Eigenmode simulations show that the TMD absorbs part of the evanescent field. Because this absorption is wavelength dependent, it also removes modes from the low-energy flank of the envelope, which accounts for small difference between the two monolayers, while the blueshift itself follows the increase of the carrier density at threshold. Density functional theory calculations that include the interface dipole predict a type-I alignment at the ideal ZnO(10$\bar{1}$0)/TMD interface, which turns into type~II for a moderately reduced dipole, as expected for hydroxylated facets in air. In both cases, holes are transferred from the nanowire into the TMD and removed from the gain medium. Evanescent absorption and hole transfer thus jointly suppress lasing, and both must be accounted for when integrating nanowire lasers with 2D materials.

title: TailSteer: Trajectory-Tail Steering for Drift-Resistant Multi-turn Image Editing
abstract: Strong single-turn editing performance does not guarantee reliable multi-turn interaction: as edited outputs are repeatedly reused, small unintended changes can accumulate into severe visual drift. This long-term drift is often mitigated through training on multi-turn data or cross-turn rollouts, potentially altering pretrained priors, or through specialized inference-time mechanisms that are difficult to scale to foundation models. We introduce TailSteer, a final-stage training framework that improves multi-turn robustness while retaining the generative and editing capabilities acquired through earlier training. TailSteer follows a simple principle: keep early denoising dynamics close to those of the base model and concentrate preservation corrections near the trajectory tail, where fine-grained deviations can be suppressed. These corrections are learned from the editor's own on-policy denoising rollouts, using unchanged source content as a preservation reference without requiring curated ground-truth editing pairs. Experiments across the FLUX, SenseNova, and Qwen families show that TailSteer substantially reduces cumulative drift over 15-20 editing turns while largely preserving base-model performance on extensive text-to-image and single-image editing benchmarks. These results demonstrate that long-horizon editing robustness can be unlocked in foundation models after TailSteer, rather than by relearning their existing capabilities.

title: Arthur packets for $\mathrm{G}_2$ over $p$-adic fields
abstract: We describe Arthur packets for the split reductive group $\mathrm{G}_2$ over a $p$-adic field and compute their stable and endoscopic character distributions. The construction uses the twisted Aubert duality recently studied by Cheng--Kaletha. We identify the corresponding Xu packets on $\mathrm{PGSO}_8$ and their triality-twisted characters. We also extend the result to long-root and short-root Arthur packets corresponding to unitary generic representations of $\mathrm{PGL}_2$.

title: Using AI Predictions to Augment Rather Than Replace Surveys
abstract: LLMs can predict human survey responses with nontrivial accuracy. What this means for the future of social surveys remains hotly contested. Optimists anticipate a coming era of synthetic respondents; skeptics see a fragile and overhyped substitute. This article advocates a position: AI predictions cannot replace surveys, but they can augment them. Using prediction-powered inference (PPI), a statistical framework rooted in survey methodology and known in sociology as "mixed subjects design", the study tests whether AI predictions can improve the statistical efficiency of social surveys when combined with census-scale auxiliary information. Applying the framework to 83 social outcomes in the General Social Survey (GSS) and National Health Interview Survey (NHIS), with American Community Survey (ACS) being the auxiliary file, we find that supervised predictors yield effective-sample-size gains of about 7-12 percent when estimating the mean, while LLM gains are smaller but positive.

title: A family of symmetric counterexamples to the bent sum decomposition conjecture
abstract: In this paper, we provide an infinite family of counterexamples to Tokareva's conjecture on sums of two bent functions. The conjecture states that every Boolean function in an even number of variables $n$ of algebraic degree at most $n/2$ can be written as the sum of two bent functions. We show that for every $n=2^k\geq 8$, the symmetric function $F_n=1+σ_2+σ_4+σ_6+\cdots+σ_{n/2}$ has degree $n/2$ and cannot be written as a sum of at most two bent functions. Here $σ_j$ is the elementary symmetric Boolean polynomial of degree $j$. Furthermore, we show that the eight-variable member of this family can be represented as the sum of exactly three bent functions. Using the connection between bent-sum decompositions and derivatives of bent functions, we also obtain an infinite family of balanced Boolean functions that cannot be derivatives of bent functions.

title: Generalized Sorting via Four-Cycles
abstract: We study the generalized sorting problem where only a subset of the pairs can be compared. Equivalently, we are given an $n$-vertex $m$-edge graph $G=(V, E)$ where the vertex set $V$ is to be sorted, and the edge set $E$ indicates possible comparisons. The goal is to sort $V$ with as few (adaptive) queries to $E$ as possible. When $G$ is the complete graph, the problem is equivalent to standard sorting for which $Θ(n \log n)$ queries are sufficient and necessary. All classical sorting algorithms crucially rely on the ability to compare any pair and do not imply an $o(n^2)$-query algorithm in the general case. This was improved 15 years ago by Huang, Kannan, and Khanna [FOCS'11] who achieved a bound of $\widetilde{O}(n\sqrt{n})$. Kuszmaul and Narayanan [FOCS'21] later gave a bound of $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{m n})$, which is more efficient for sparse graphs, but matches the $\widetilde{O}(n\sqrt{n})$ barrier for dense graphs. In this paper, we present an algorithm for generalized sorting that makes at most $\widetilde{O}(n^{4/3})$ queries, therefore breaking the longstanding $\widetilde{O}(n\sqrt{n})$ barrier for all graphs. The key to our result is to query edges that belong to many (specific types of) four-cycles. We show that querying such edges allows the algorithm to verify the direction of many other edges (specifically, their opposing edges in the four-cycles) and thus achieve a much better amortized query cost.

title: CMS ECAL VFE Production Qualification
abstract: Upgrading the CMS ECAL barrel for the HL-LHC requires replacement of all on-detector electronics, including 12240 Very-Front-End (VFE) cards employing CATIA and LiTE-DTU ASICs for amplification and digitisation of signals from ECAL's 61200 lead-tungstate crystals. All production VFEs undergo the same qualification procedure: functional testing, environmental stress screening, and calibration. We have received and functionally tested 13596 unique VFEs; two never passed our test criteria. Results for other VFEs are uniform and within expectations, demonstrating the excellent quality of the cards. Key metrics, such as a gain ratio of $10.21 \pm 0.07$ and power consumption of $1.805 \pm 0.013~\mathrm{W}$, demonstrate high consistency across the batch.

title: Fixed-Radius Neighbourhoods in Three-Dimensional Unit-Cube Graphs
abstract: We prove Conjecture 4 of Chan, Chang, Gao, Kisfaludi-Bak, Le, and Zheng (SoCG 2026): for every fixed integer $r\ge0$, the radius-$r$ neighbourhoods of a unit-cube graph in $\mathbb{R}^3$ have bounded VC-dimension. Our bound is $2^{2^{O(r)}}$, independent of the number of vertices. The main ingredient is a VC-dimension bound for reachability through arbitrary fixed-length sequences of three-dimensional generalized dominance relations. Its proof uses groups ordered in two coordinates, with neighbouring groups acting as barriers that preserve this invariant when one layer is removed. Combining these bounds with the existing interval-representation framework, we obtain a Las Vegas algorithm that, for every fixed integer $Δ\ge1$, decides whether a graph given by $n$ cube centres has diameter at most $Δ$ in expected $O_Δ(n^{2-\varepsilon_Δ})$ time, for an explicit constant $\varepsilon_Δ>0$. Finally, for every integer $r\ge7$, we construct unit-cube graphs with rational centres whose radius-$r$ neighbourhoods have VC-dimension $Ω(r^3)$.

title: EvoWorld: Towards Out-of-Sight World Evolution in Generative Video Models
abstract: Generative video models are increasingly used as visual world simulators, yet their primary strength lies in rendering plausible pixels rather than reasoning about how a world should evolve. Coherent world evolution requires more than visual fidelity: when an event occurs, a model must infer its consequences for the entities in the world and then render the resulting state. For example, after a wild beast appears, the model should not only depict the wild beast, but also infer whether a nearby person should flee, take cover, or fight back based on the realized scene. Existing diffusion-based video models lack an explicit mechanism for maintaining world state and reasoning over such event-conditioned consequences, often producing visually plausible but behaviorally static or causally inconsistent outputs. To make this reasoning gap concrete and measurable, we propose a new problem, Out-of-Sight Causal Evolution, which requires a model to render an event, reason about its consequences for the evolving world state, and reveal a causally plausible outcome as the world continues to evolve, even out of sight. As a baseline reference solution, we introduce EvoWorld, a brain-renderer collaboration framework in which a vision-language model serves as the world brain: it observes generated segments, maintains an evolving account of the world, and reasons about plausible state transitions, while a segment-autoregressive video renderer realizes them visually. We further introduce EvoWorld-Data and EvoWorld-Bench for training and evaluating event realization, causal reactions, and revisit consistency. Experiments show that EvoWorld substantially improves event-conditioned causal evolution over recent models while preserving visual quality and consistency, establishing a reference point for reasoning-guided, autonomous world evolution beyond the current field of view.

title: A Drift-Diffusion Approach for Pearson Type IV Heavy-Tail Distributions
abstract: Non-Gaussian stationary fluctuations with heavy tails and finite-order moment cutoffs are ubiquitous in non-equilibrium systems. Here, we derive the Pearson type IV distribution as the stationary solution of a standardized Fokker-Planck equation with linear drift and quadratic diffusion. We establish necessary and sufficient conditions for its emergence and show that the linear-quadratic structure, although sufficient, is not necessary. We also give explicit closed expressions for the cumulative distribution function, a moment recurrence relation, skewness, kurtosis, and mode. From a physical perspective, our results reveal that heavy tails and asymmetry originate from distinct features of state-dependent diffusion: its local nonlinear curvature and gradient, respectively. In particular, asymmetric stationary fluctuations can emerge even in the presence of a symmetric linear restoring drift. This framework provides a general stochastic description of asymmetric heavy-tailed fluctuations in non-equilibrium systems, including space plasma turbulence.

title: Inflationary attractors in metric-affine gravity
abstract: We study single-field slow-roll inflation in metric-affine gravity (MAG). We consider the most general action up to operators linear in curvature and quadratic in the distortion, without propagating torsion and non-metricity. We first impose projective invariance and promote every coefficient to a function of the scalar field. After integrating out the non-dynamical distortion, the net contribution is a correction $k(ϕ)$ to the scalar kinetic term. We then consider the class of $ξ$-attractors for which the non-minimal couplings and the scalar potential are fixed by a single function $f(ϕ)$. It is well-known that in the metric formulation the strong-coupling regime is universally the Starobinsky attractor. In the Palatini framework, instead, this attractor is lost and the predictions become model-dependent. Here, we show that the MAG framework restores universality: in the strong coupling limit with finite ratios of the distortion couplings to $ξ$ we have an $α$-attractor, $n_s=1-2/N_*$ and $r=12α/N_*^2$, with $α=1+ζ/(6ξ)$. The ratio $ζ/ξ$ encodes the distortion contribution. Starobinsky and Palatini inflation are recovered as specific limits. Through a numerical parameter scan we show that almost all the healthy points lie on one of the two attractors : either Nieh-Yan-like inflation (studied in a previous work and extended here) or the new MAG $α$-attractor found here. Finally, we explicitly drop projective invariance and analyse the general MAG theory. The same large-field asymptotic structure survives. We conclude that no extra inflationary phenomenology is reached by the non-projectively invariant operators: the $α$-attractor is a general prediction of MAG.

title: A Quantum Lower Bound for Triangle Finding
abstract: Triangle finding is a fundamental problem in graph theory that has played a central role in the development of quantum algorithmic techniques. For $N$-vertex graphs given by their adjacency matrices, a long line of work has improved the quantum query upper bound from $O(N^{3/2})$ to $O(N^{5/4})$. However, the best known lower bound has remained the elementary $Ω(N)$ bound obtained from unstructured search. We prove the first superlinear quantum query lower bound for triangle finding, showing that $Ω(N^{13/12})$ queries are necessary. Our result also implies the same lower bound for triangle detection and for detecting every fixed connected non-bipartite graph. The proof builds on the compressed oracle approach of Zhandry and the transfer approaches of Belovs. It compares the computation on graphs with a planted triangle to the computation on random graphs conditioned to be triangle-free, through a map on the input registers that almost commutes with every query. We average over local changes to the input while preserving its distribution, through a procedure known as conditional resampling. Our main technical contribution is a set of estimates that let us control the query error under this averaging, despite the dependence introduced by conditioning a dense graph to be triangle-free.

title: Light (anti)nuclei production via coalescence in electron-proton collisions: from HERA to EIC
abstract: Light (anti)nuclei production provides a sensitive probe of the particle-emitting source and of the coalescence mechanism in high-energy collisions. In this work, a coalescence model implemented as an afterburner to PYTHIA 8 is validated against pp data from ALICE and ep data from ZEUS. The validated framework is then applied to ep collisions at EIC energies to predict deuteron and antideuteron production within the ePIC acceptance. The results indicate sizeable yields and a clear matter-antimatter asymmetry in the proton-going direction, making this measurement a promising observable for studying coalescence and proton structure at the EIC.

title: The Exact Number of Pentagons in Book-Free Graphs
abstract: Let $B_k$ denote the book consisting of $k$ triangles sharing a common edge. We prove that there exist absolute constants $ρ>0$ and $N$ such that, for every pair of integers $n,k$ with $n\ge N$ and $2\le k\le ρn$, writing $n=5q+r$ with $0\le r<5$, \[ \operatorname{ex}(n,C_5,B_k)=q^{\,5-r}(q+1)^r, \] with the balanced complete $C_5$-blow-ups as the only extremal graphs. The linear order of this range is best possible since for all sufficiently large $n$, the formula fails whenever $k\ge0.14n$.

title: A Unified Framework for Extending Centrality Measures to Groups
abstract: We propose a unified framework for extending centrality measures from individual nodes to groups. For each centrality measure, we introduce four group variants---maximum, minimum, sum, and proportional---which differ in how individual contributions are aggregated at the group level. The framework builds on a new unified perspective on major classes of centrality measures, according to which the score of a node can be expressed as a sum of assessments made by individual nodes, pairs of nodes, or groups of nodes. Each of the four variants then corresponds to a different rule for aggregating the assessments of the members of a group.

title: Earthquake Forecast via Neutrino Tomography at the DUNE Baseline
abstract: We investigate the sensitivity of accelerator-based neutrino oscillations to localized electron-density enhancements associated with seismic fault zones along the Fermilab SURF baseline of the Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (DUNE). Motivated by the reactor antineutrino proposal of Wang, Chen, and Li, we model the anomaly as a uniform-density slab embedded in the surrounding crust and calculate exact three flavour oscillation probabilities using layer by layer evolution. Our results show that localized density enhancements can produce measurable variations in muon-to-electron appearance probabilities for both neutrinos and antineutrinos, with potentially significant relative effects. The predicted variations exhibit weak dependence on the leptonic CP violating phase, suggesting that time-differential measurements may help reduce uncertainties associated with the unknown CP phase. However, the event statistics required for a statistically significant detection substantially exceed those expected during a short-duration precursor interval. Consequently, detecting sufficiently persistent density anomalies may be possible under favourable conditions, whereas short-term earthquake forecasting is not feasible with the nominal DUNE configuration. Our findings establish a theoretical framework for exploring localized Earth-density perturbations through long-baseline neutrino oscillations.

title: How Rich is the Rich-Club? Super Rich-Club Organization in Complex Networks
abstract: The rich-club coefficient is used in complex networks to quantify the tendency of progressively higher-degree nodes to be more densely connected than expected by chance. However, it does not capture whether high degree nodes towards the core are actually more interconnected than the original network. Here, we jointly analyze the rich-club coefficient and an enrichment coefficient, which quantifies whether the internal average degree of progressively higher-degree subgraphs is greater than that of the original network, despite the decreasing number of nodes. We apply this framework to real and synthetic networks. Our results reveal three distinct regimes of core organization: rich-club organization without enrichment, enrichment without rich-club organization, and a combination of both, which we call Super Rich-Club organization. In the latter regime, high-degree nodes form cohesive and unusually dense cores that support efficient communication. Our results show that characterizing core organization across structural scales requires considering both relative density and internal connectivity, revealing a stronger form of core organization in real systems with implications for network structure, spectral properties that govern dynamical processes, and communicability.

title: Proof of two conjectures on the log-concavity of partition ranks and cranks
abstract: Let $M(m,n)$ and $N(m,n)$ denote the numbers of partitions of $n$ with crank $m$ and rank $m$, respectively. Ji and Zang proved that the crank sequence $(M(m,n))_{|m|\le n-1}$ is unimodal for every $n\ge44$. Bringmann, Man, and Rolen subsequently established the unimodality of the rank sequence $(N(m,n))_{|m|\le n-2}$ for every $n\ge39$. Ji and Zang also conjectured that $(M(m,n))_{|m|\le n-71}$ is log-concave for every $n\ge72$, and that $(N(m,n))_{|m|\le n-72}$ is log-concave for every $n\ge73$. In this paper, we prove both conjectures.

title: Bass martingales need not stretch
abstract: In classical optimal transport, the equivalence of optimality, convex gradient structure, and cyclical monotonicity is a central paradigm. Known counterexamples to this equivalence rely on carefully constructed costs. In contrast, we show that this equivalence can fail in martingale transport in dimension ${d \ge 2}$: already for the canonical martingale Benamou-Brenier problem and irreducible marginals we have the strict inclusions \[ \text{optimality} \;\subsetneq \; \text{(Bass) convex gradient structure} \;\subsetneq\; \text{martingale cyclical monotonicity}\, . \] However, under the stronger assumption of strict irreducibility, we establish that these three notions coincide. Understanding when the gradient structure guarantees optimality is also of practical relevance, since algorithms based on the Bass gradient representation are used in financial model calibration. All our counterexamples are based on the following phenomenon: for $d\ge2$, there exist two one-step martingales $X,Y$ with the same initial and terminal laws, and a convex function $ψ$ such that \[ 0=\mathbb E\big[\mathbb E[ψ(Y_1)\mid Y_0]-ψ(Y_0)\big] < \mathbb E\big[\mathbb E[ψ(X_1)\mid X_0]-ψ(X_0)\big] <\infty. \]

title: Continual Classification Beyond the Kernel Regime: Harnessing the Sparsity Bias of L2 Regularization in Diagonal Linear Networks
abstract: We study logistic regression for continual learning with linear predictors in a high-dimensional statistical setting. Existing theoretical work has largely focused on continual linear regression with variants of L2 regularization, motivated by their analytical simplicity and connection to the kernel regime of neural networks. We first derive the optimal L2 regularization strength for continual linear classification and characterize its generalization performance, recovering behavior analogous to prior results for continual linear regression. Next, we examine the effect of L2 regularization in deeper models using a minimal two-layer diagonal linear network. In the single-task setting, L2 regularization on the weights of such models is known to promote sparsity in the resulting predictor, yielding a rich, sparse feature-learning regime beyond the kernel regime (a similar effect arises in two-layer ReLU networks). However, in continual learning, where L2 regularization is typically centered on previous-task weights, this sparsity bias is no longer preserved. We therefore propose a weighted variant of L2 regularization that extends this beneficial sparsity bias to continual learning. We show theoretically and empirically that, for a sufficiently sparse teacher, our variant converges substantially faster than directly learning a linear predictor with conventional continual L2 or L1 regularization, trading some long-horizon bias for markedly improved performance over moderate task horizons.

title: Route First, See Later: Enabling Vision Agents to Reason Scientifically by Separating Routing Policy from Action Spaces
abstract: Scientific image-analysis workflows require agents to select among diverse capabilities like description, detection, counting, and segmentation. Current multi-tool architectures conflate intent interpretation with visual execution, masking whether a failure arises from flawed reasoning (misrouting) or failed perception (invalid tool execution). This lack of auditability renders agents unreliable for high-stakes scientific automation. We introduce ZETA, an extensible architecture that operationalizes the decoupling of routing policy from action execution. ZETA resolves scientific intent before invoking specialized visual tools, treating measurement as a deterministic operation grounded in explicit geometry rather than generative output. This architecture exposes the "black box" of agent decision-making, allowing routing correctness and downstream execution to be evaluated as independent failure modes. To our knowledge, we provide the first controlled study in scientific vision-agent routing that isolates explicit routing-policy specification while holding the legal action interface fixed. Evaluation on a zero-shot benchmark of 51 scientific-intent queries shows that explicit routing semantics can substantially improve routing accuracy, particularly at semantically adjacent action boundaries, although improvements vary across models. For Qwen 3.8, explicit routing-policy specification improves segmentation routing accuracy from 6.2% to 75.0% and detection routing accuracy from 60.0% to 100%. ZETA's execution traces make routing decisions and downstream artifacts separately observable, providing a basis for distinguishing intent-selection errors from visual execution failures. ZETA establishes the necessary infrastructure to isolate execution errors from interpretive ones, a critical requirement for deploying reliable scientific vision agents.

title: Near-Quantum-Limited Readout for the Princeton Axion Search using a sub-GHz Kinetic Inductance Traveling Wave Parametric Amplifier
abstract: Parametric amplifiers are a workhorse for near-quantum-limited measurements above 1 GHz. However, amplifier development has been more limited below 1 GHz. We present a kinetic inductance traveling-wave parametric amplifier (KI-TWPA) operating over 300-700 MHz, with gain exceeding 30 dB and pump powers of a few hundred nanowatts. The system noise performance, as measured by a variable-temperature noise source, is 2.5-3.5 quanta. This device is a versatile new tool for precision measurements of sub-GHz signals, with applications including readout of semiconductor spin qubits, superconducting detector arrays, and searches for new physics beyond the Standard Model. We characterize aspects of the amplifier performance relevant to axion searches, including gain drift, compression point, amplifier noise at various operating temperatures, readout with an input circulator, and magnetic field insensitivity.

title: U.S. State Guidance on AI in K-12 Education: A Comparative Content and Citation Analysis
abstract: In the years following the public release of ChatGPT in late 2022, more than half of U.S. states have published formal guidelines around AI usage in K-12 education, creating a record of largely independent state education departments responding to a shared technological disruption. In this work, we analyze publicly available AI usage guidance documents from 35 states in the U.S. and Puerto Rico. We compare the guidance in these documents across various dimensions, including pedagogy and instruction, audience, actionability, workforce and career readiness, responsible use and equity, and alignment with state-level demographics and administrative capacity. Finally, we investigate who authored these documents and their cited sources, identifying epistemic foundations underlying their claims. We find that guidance priorities converge on topics anchored in laws such as data privacy and academic integrity, each addressed in 97% of documents. While most documents mention equity of access (86%) and algorithmic bias (97%), fewer discuss specific marginalized populations. Across documents, there is a common framing of urgency around AI integration to prepare students for workforce readiness (86%) and promote loosely-defined personalized learning (86%), which is not matched by specific guidance for capacity-building, actionability, or accountability. State priorities show no relationship to state demographics, capacity, or partisanship. Instead, we identify notable interdependencies between states with shared citations to non-profit organizations like TeachAI and Code.org, with some states reproducing TeachAI's model guidance near-verbatim, and peer citations concentrating on a few early states such as Oregon and Washington. No state includes parents as contributors on these documents, and only five include students.

title: Energetic Nonthermal Electrons within the Above-the-looptop Regions in Solar Flares: Acceleration, Feedback, and Quasi-Periodic Pulsations
abstract: Solar flares are among the most dramatic events in the solar system, releasing substantial magnetic energy and accelerating a large number of electrons to high energies. Notably, in certain events, the above-the-looptop region may contain a significant population of nonthermal electrons, both in number and energy. For the first time, we adopt a novel numerical method that combines magnetohydrodynamics with energetic particles incorporating feedback from nonthermal electrons to investigate electron acceleration and transport in solar flares. We find that a large fraction of energetic electrons are accelerated via the current sheet and termination shock regions. Most energetic electrons are concentrated in the above-the-looptop region, carrying a sizable amount of the released energy. We observe that greater feedback of nonthermal electrons leads to steeper energy spectra. The energy density of the nonthermal electrons oscillates due to the periodic impact of magnetic islands into the above-the-looptop, which may help explain the observed quasi-periodic pulsations (QPPs). Our simulations provide new insights into the origin of nonthermal electrons and associated emissions in the above-the-looptop region.

title: Rethinking Access Control for AI Agents: Recent Advances and Open Challenges
abstract: Large language model agents access data, invoke tools, and act on users' behalf. Keeping these actions within authorized bounds is challenging because agents choose their own execution paths while permissions and operating conditions may change. This paper surveys recent advances in agent access control across four areas: policy specification and derivation, identity and delegation, action and resource enforcement, and information flow control. We compare their control objects, enforcement boundaries, and assumptions to examine what individual mechanisms achieve and how they can work together. Building on this analysis, we rethink four aspects of authorization: plan selection shapes permission requirements; contextual information can inform decisions without itself granting authority; restrictions must retain their meaning across system interfaces; and authorization must be reassessed as workflows evolve. These insights motivate open challenges and future directions, together with concrete research questions and evaluation criteria. In particular, evaluation should examine both observed agent behavior and the unauthorized effects that remain enabled. Our analysis connects existing mechanisms to the requirements for preserving authorization throughout an agent workflow.

title: Migration and eccentricity damping timescales in overstable resonant planetary systems: hydrodynamic and N-body simulations
abstract: Tidal interactions between planets and discs modify semimajor axes and eccentricities. These effects are represented by migration and eccentricity damping timescales in analytical and Nbody models, although they are assumed constant. This approximation is uncertain in resonant multiplanet systems, where coupled planet disc evolution can produce non-linear torque feedback. We investigate migration and eccentricity damping in two planet systems undergoing resonant and overstable evolution near the 2:1 mean motion resonance. Using hydrodynamic simulations with varying disc surface densities, viscosities, and aspect ratios, we measure both timescales from energy and angular momentum exchange between the planets and disc. We find that both timescales are time dependent and vary throughout the evolution. In resonant systems, sign reversals occur owing to eccentricity oscillations and disc torque variations. Moreover, migration timescales normalised by their expected dependence on planetary mass, disc surface density, and aspect ratio deviate between models. Likewise, the common relation between migration and eccentricity damping timescales is not recovered. We compare the hydrodynamic evolution with several Nbody approaches. Models with constant migration and damping timescales fail to reproduce the hydrodynamic evolution, whereas torque-based approaches provide better agreement. In particular, approaches including corotation torque saturation and planetary eccentricity reproduce the hydrodynamic evolution in the type I migration regime, whereas additional corrections are required when planets partially open gaps. These results show that time-dependent torque-based prescriptions provide a consistent physical link between hydrodynamic simulations and simplified Nbody models of resonant planetary systems.

title: Generalised Killing Spinors and Euclidean Hypersurfaces
abstract: We study when the number of spinors satisfying the same generalised Killing equation for a symmetric endomorphism field $W$ forces local realisation as a Euclidean hypersurface. Let $N=2^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}$ be the rank of the complex spinor bundle. We show that in dimension $n\geq4$, if the complex dimension of the solution space exceeds $N/2$, then the metric and $W$ satisfy the Gauss--Codazzi equations. This is proved in the smooth category by combining the curvature defects into a single bivector and bounding the dimension of its kernel on spinors, using algebraic curvature symmetries to handle exceptional cases. Examples obtained from non-flat four-dimensional hyperkähler manifolds show that this threshold is sharp for every $n\geq4$. In dimension three, the Heisenberg group carries the maximal number of common solutions while failing the Euclidean Gauss equation. Further, in the real analytic category, we use existing extension theorems for Einstein metrics and parallel spinors to extend all common solutions to parallel spinors on a single local Ricci-flat ambient manifold. Using Wang's counts of parallel spinors, we obtain an independent proof of the sharp threshold for real analytic data.

title: An Explicit Construction of Commuting Quantum KdV Hamiltonians in the Universal Virasoro Vertex Algebra
abstract: We give an explicit formula for elements $H_{2k}$ of conformal weight $2k$, $k\ge1$, in the universal Virasoro vertex operator algebra $V$ at every central charge, such that $H_{2k}(0)H_{2l}\in TV$ for all $k,l\ge1$. Modulo translation, the kernel of $H_4(0)$ is generated by $[H_{2k}]$ in each positive even weight and is zero in positive odd weights. The formula uses a realization on differential polynomials by possibly infinite-order differential operators in a completion of the Weyl algebra, together with the inverse of the identity plus a nilpotent operator on each weight space. A Koszul-type exactness argument for the classical KdV flows proves conservation; uniqueness and the Jacobi identity give commutativity. The classical limit recovers the normalized Gelfand--Dickey densities. Explicit low-weight elements and exact symbolic verifications illustrate the construction.

title: PyRUA-REAL: Robot Exploration and Adaptive Learning through RSI in the Real World
abstract: Coding agents powered by models such as GPT-6-Astra connect spatial reasoning with executable robot behavior, raising the question of how such agents can produce lasting improvements in robot capabilities from physical interaction. In this work, we study embodied recursive self-improvement (RSI) through real-world exploration, code refinement, and deployment using PyRUA-REAL, a framework in which coding agents retain interaction experience as persistent memory and reusable executable skills that inform subsequent exploration and improvement. Our empirical study places physical manipulation at the center of the improvement process, examining how agents collaborate, what kinds of execution feedback support effective code refinement, and how task specifications and previously acquired skills influence robustness and task transfer. We further investigate the efficiency and capability of the resulting programs when deployed without involving an online agent for decision-making. Across eight real-world tasks, PyRUA-REAL achieves an average success rate of 91.1%. In complementary evaluation on 42 tasks from the RoboDojo benchmark, it achieves an average success rate of 84.4%. This study provides empirical guidance for turning physical exploration into reusable robot skills that support continued improvement and robust, efficient deployment.

title: Born spreading with consistent shower starting scales in MC@NLO and FxFx merging
abstract: Negative weights are a major cost in NLO event generation matched to parton showers at the LHC, as they increase the number of events needed for a given statistical precision. Born spreading reduces the fraction of negative-weight $\mathbb S$ events in MC@NLO by redistributing the Born contribution over the radiation variables. It introduces no bias only if everything that is passed to the parton shower together with $\mathbb S$ events depends on Born-level quantities alone. We show that the same condition is needed for the MC counterterms to reproduce the first shower emission, independently of how the radiation phase space is integrated. In MadGraph5_aMC@NLO, the $\mathbb S$-event starting scales did not fully satisfy this condition, which so far prevented the public release of Born spreading. We present a new and consistent construction of the starting scales for ordinary MC@NLO, FxFx merging and MC@NLO-$Δ$, with which Born spreading is now publicly available, including for merged samples. We also study modified formulations of the MC counterterms, and FxFx-merged $W$+jets production with up to two jets at NLO, for which Born spreading reduces the fraction of negative weights after merging without affecting the predictions, and the event samples are generated six times faster than with the former implementation.

title: Benchmarking Fine-Grained Visual Reasoning for Remote Sensing in Urban Management
abstract: Fine-grained visual reasoning is essential for remote sensing in urban management, yet remains underexplored in the evaluation of multimodal large language models (MLLMs). We introduce UMBench, a fine-grained urban remote sensing benchmark built from unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) images for multiple urban management tasks such as traffic monitoring, urban construction, environmental quality, and disaster warning. Evaluations on UMBench reveal that current MLLMs often rely on scene-level priors and overlook fine-grained visual evidence. To address this issue, we further propose a novel evidence-first chain-of-thought method that directs models to inspect fine-grained visual evidence in a training-free manner. Experiments show that our method can improve the performance of both open-source and commercial MLLMs on UMBench.

title: Non-compact Kogut-Susskind gauge theories: 1D lattice models with exact ${\rm SL}(2,\mathbb{R})$ gauge invariance
abstract: The Kogut-Susskind (KS) formulation of gauge theories constructs quantum many-body Hamiltonians with gauge invariance under a compact Lie group exactly implemented on a spatial lattice. Here, we revisit this construction for a non-compact gauge group. Although motivated in part by theories like general relativity whose first-order formulation involves the non-compact Lorentz group as a local symmetry, we focus on simpler cases in one spatial dimension akin to the Schwinger model. In a bottom-up approach, we show how exact gauge invariance under the simplest non-compact Lie group ${\rm SL}(2,\mathbb{R})$ can be retained exactly on a 1D lattice, and highlight the differences that arise with respect to compact gauge groups, including a continuous spectrum of the Casimir operators of the gauge fields and the emergence of infinite-dimensional representations of the matter fields. For the pure gauge theory, we discuss how a consistent restriction to the positive semigroup ${\rm SL}^{+}(2,\mathbb{R})$ reproduces well-known results from the quantization of Jackiw-Teitelboim (JT) gravity. Motivated by the constraint structure of general dilaton gravity, we introduce static charges coupled to the non-compact gauge field, which can be realised by single-fermion degrees of freedom living in an additional, synthetic dimension. With static charges our lattice model remains exactly integrable, but when extending to dynamical fermionic matter, we arrive at an interacting 1D ${\rm SL}(2,\mathbb{R})$ KS gauge theory. We give an interpretation of this model as a chain of charges sequentially connected by strings whose tension pulls matter left or right depending on the sign of the relative continuous ${\rm SL}(2,\mathbb{R})$ fluxes. This picture becomes exact when the involved ${\rm SL}(2,\mathbb{R})$ charges are strongly self-interacting, where we solve the reduced two-body problem analytically.

title: Energy Efficient Near-Threshold Voltage Massive MIMO Computing
abstract: Near-Threshold Computing (NTC) offers a substan- tial energy savings, i.e., up to 10x, for digital circuits. However, due to Process, Voltage, and Temperature (PVT) variations, low voltage operating digital processors face increased susceptibility to timing errors. This work equips conventional massive MIMO algorithms with computational error detection mechanisms, en- abling reliable operation down to near-threshold voltages. While conventional hardware based Timing Error Detection (TED) systems introduce substantial overhead, this work modifies MIMO algorithms to seamlessly integrate low overhead Algorithm Based Fault Tolerance (ABFT). A co-simulation framework combining transistor level SPICE simulations and workload aware fault injection is developed to investigate reliability, Bit Error Rate (BER), energy savings, and overheads of modified algorithms operating at low voltages. The transistor-level characterization was performed in PSpice using generic Level-1 Shichman-Hodges CMOS transistor models with Monte Carlo parameter variations. No specific CMOS fabrication process node was assumed. Conse- quently, the reported energy savings are analytical estimates and are not specific to a particular CMOS fabrication technology. We evaluate Gauss Seidel (GS), ADMM based infinity norm detection (ADMIN), and Conjugate Gradient (CG) detectors using circuit derived fault models. Results demonstrate remarkable algorith- mic resilience. Although undetected computational errors in some trials near the Point of First Failure (PoFF) were observed, BER increases by only 0.7% to 1.4%, while beyond PoFF, ABFT reported nearly all erroneous cases. The proposed checksum based ABFT detects most arithmetic and memory errors, with an estimated overhead below 2% for a 64 x 16 MIMO system, decreasing further for larger configurations.

title: Approximation and Hardness for the Data Validation Problem
abstract: Finnah, Gönsch and Otto [Eur. J. Oper. Res. 2025] recently introduced the Data Validation Problem (DVP): Given a transitive directed acyclic graph $G$ on $n$ vertices (resp. tasks) and $m$ edges (resp. precedences) and a probing budget, a policy can successively pay a probing fee and probe an edge in $G$ as long as the total probing fees do not exceed the budget. If a probe succeeds, the targeted edge $e$ is removed from $G$ and we receive a reward; if the probe fails, the edge stays in $G$ and cannot be probed again. We seek a policy with maximum expected cumulative reward. Crucially, $G$ must stay transitive throughout the probing process, so a policy can only challenge the precedence between consecutive tasks, that is, only probe edges in the transitive reduction of the current precedence graph. We show that DVP is strongly NP-hard and W[1]-hard with the probing budget $T$ as a parameter, even in the deterministic case (when every probe has probability $0$ or $1$ to succeed) and with unit probing costs and rewards. For the same setting, we give an approximation-preserving reduction from the Densest $k$-Subgraph (D$k$S) Problem, with the consequence that there is no polynomial-time $2^{(\log n)^{1-δ}}$-approximation algorithm and no FPT $\sqrt{T}$-approximation algorithm for DVP, assuming the Almost-Exponential Time Hypothesis and the Strongish Planted Clique Hypothesis, respectively. We also present the first known policies with provable worst-case guarantees for DVP, namely an $m$-approximation algorithm for instances with uniform probabilities and probing costs, a $2T/p_{\min}^T$-approximation algorithm for general instances, where $p_{\min}$ is the minimum probing success probability, and an exact FPT algorithm on tournament graphs, in the deterministic setting.

title: Entanglement Entropy in Non Relativistic Collisions
abstract: We study numerically the build-up of entanglement entropy between two colliding, non relativistic particles, that are driven by the plain Schrödinger equation containing local, finite range potentials, and whose initial state is the product of two independent wave packets. Different situations are considered, ranging from a tunnel and mirror effect at low energy in front of a barrier, to higher energies, and also attraction rather than repulsion. While the calculated wave functions and density matrices significantly depend on the physical situations described by our models, the build-up trends and values in time of entanglement entropy look surprisingly alike one another.

title: Stability and Perfection in Constrained Weighted Network Games
abstract: We introduce a general framework of constrained weighted network formation in which agents allocate resources across coalitional interactions while facing feasibility constraints. More precisely, we allow arbitrary coalitions of agents to be assigned a continuous weight, and we incorporate both coalitional capacity constraints and individual budget constraints into the model. This framework extends the weighted network formation model of Bich and Morhaim by combining continuous interaction intensities with endogenous feasibility restrictions. Within this setting, we introduce a new notion of stability -- called coalitionwise stability -- extending pairwise stability to constrained network games. Under standard continuity and componentwise quasiconcavity assumptions on payoff functions, we establish the existence of coalitionwise stable networks. We then investigate refinements of stability inspired by the notion of perfect equilibrium introduced by Selten, and by the notion of perfect pairwise stability developed by Bich and Teteryatnikova for network games. The presence of feasibility constraints fundamentally alters the geometry of the feasible set, which no longer possesses a product structure. As a consequence, trembling-hand type refinements become substantially more delicate, since perturbations of some interactions may render other interactions infeasible. Nevertheless, we introduce constrained analogues of both the trembling-hand and perturbative notions of perfect stability considered by Bich and Teteryatnikova, and study their existence and their relationship. In particular, we show the equivalence between these trembling-hand and perturbative formulations under some componentwise monotonicity assumption.

title: Finding full immersions is fixed-parameter tractable in labeled tour graphs
abstract: We give an $O_H(n^5)$-time algorithm to test whether an $n$-vertex labeled tour graph has a full immersion isomorphic to a labeled tour graph $H$. A labeled tour graph is a connected $4$-regular graph whose edges are labeled by binary vectors of fixed length. To obtain a full immersion, a vertex may be removed only by pairing up its four incident edges and "splitting off" both pairs, summing the labels within each pair. Even for one-bit labels, no polynomial-time algorithm was previously known for arbitrary fixed $H$. Our main tool is of independent interest: we give an algorithmic min-max theorem that, in particular, characterizes the maximum number of odd-length circuits in a rooted circuit decomposition of an Eulerian graph. Our results have implications for vertex-minors, whose study is motivated by applications in quantum networking, connections with graph minor theory, and the goal of developing an irrelevant vertex technique for dense graphs. For vertex-minors, circle graphs play the same role as planar graphs do for graph minors. As a corollary of our main theorem, we obtain a fixed-parameter tractable algorithm for apex-vertex-minor testing in $k$-apex circle graphs. We also prove an irrelevant vertex theorem for such graphs of large rank-width. More broadly, our results are essential to forthcoming work of three of the authors proving a structure theorem for graphs with a forbidden vertex-minor. There, our min-max theorem plays the role of both the algorithmic $A$-paths and Two Paths Theorems.

title: WISE: An Agentic Framework for Whole-page Multimodal Search Experience Attribution
abstract: Algorithm-driven services, including search, recommendation, and advertising, rely on multi-stage model pipelines. While research prioritizes model optimization, post-deployment monitoring focuses on operational reliability. Yet operationally healthy systems may still produce poor-quality results, exposing a gap in existing evaluation and monitoring practices. However, a systematic problem formulation and benchmark for this task remain lacking. To bridge this gap, we formulate System Quality Diagnosis (SQD) for algorithm-driven services, a new task that extends quality evaluation beyond identifying poor outcomes to attributing their causes across system components. Focusing on industrial search, we propose WISE, an agentic framework for end-to-end quality diagnosis that discovers user-facing issues and traces their origins to underlying algorithmic components. To improve diagnostic reliability, we introduce ReTrace for constructing evidence-consistent trajectory supervision and Adaptive Harness-Policy Optimization (AHPO) for failure-guided optimization of the agent harness and model policy. To enable systematic evaluation, we construct WISE-BENCH, a real-world multimodal search benchmark that combines user-facing evidence, internal pipeline traces, and expert diagnosis annotations. Extensive experiments show consistent gains across model scales, with WISE achieving 75.20% end-to-end accuracy on Qwen3.5-35B-A3B. In production, WISE supports quality auditing, online quality assurance, and model optimization, reducing diagnosis costs and improving downstream relevance models.

title: Regularization vs. Convolution in Kernel-Based Hypothesis Testing
abstract: The maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) test is a popular nonparametric test on general domains. Two lines of work have studied its optimality through structurally different approaches. The first, a convolution approach on $\mathbb{R}^d$, uses translation-invariant kernels with a shrinking bandwidth and is minimax optimal over Sobolev balls under $L^2$-separation; the second, a regularization approach on general measurable spaces, uses spectral regularization of the kernel covariance operator and is minimax optimal over Hellinger- and $χ^2$-separated alternatives. In this paper, we study the regularization approach over Sobolev balls under $L^2$-separation, which reveals the connection between the two approaches. We show that, with a translation-invariant kernel on $\mathbb{R}^d$, both are ways of meeting a single condition on the kernel's spectral density: the spectral regularized discrepancy captures the $L^2$-separation $Δ$ of a Sobolev alternative of smoothness $s$ as soon as the regularization parameter $λ$ is below the spectral density on frequencies up to $Δ^{-1/(2s)}$. A kernel with a shrinking bandwidth $h$ meets this condition with $λ\asymp h^d$, and under this coupling the constant regularizer, which gives the MMD test itself, attains the Sobolev minimax rate. This explains, from a spectral perspective, the need for a shrinking bandwidth in the convolution approach. With a non-constant spectral regularizer, our analysis requires the bandwidth to shrink only when the spectral density decays faster than any polynomial, as for the Gaussian kernel. Thus, for Matérn and Laplace kernels, a fixed bandwidth with $λ\to 0$ attains the Sobolev minimax rate. Finally, an adaptive test over a grid of bandwidths and regularization parameters is minimax optimal, up to a $\log\log$ factor, over both classes without prior knowledge of the smoothness.

title: Machine Learning the Complete Active-Space Wavefunction Reconstruction
abstract: Machine-learned interatomic potentials enable multireference-quality reaction dynamics but do not retain the electronic structure underlying the predicted energies and forces. Recovering this information by independently performing complete active space self-consistent field (CASSCF) calculations is both expensive and potentially inconsistent. We introduce the Complete Active-Space Wave Function Reconstruction (CAS-WR) model, which learns the geometry-dependent electronic structure from CASSCF data and reconstructs the CAS wave function without repeated orbital optimization. Combined with uncertainty-based active learning, CAS-WR is demonstrated for the Diels--Alder reaction and \ce{TiC+}-catalyzed C--H activation. The approach enables trajectory-resolved analysis of multiconfigurational electronic structure across reactive ensembles. Preliminary applications to excited-state proton transfer and transition-metal photocatalysis suggest that CAS-WR can provide a general route toward recovering electronic structure along complex ground- and excited-state reactive dynamics.

title: A local Yang-Baxter obstruction for the hard-square model
abstract: Many exact solutions of two-dimensional lattice models rest on an analytic family of weights satisfying the Yang-Baxter equation. The hard-hexagon model was solved in this way, while the neighbouring hard-square model has no known closed form. We determine the height alphabets that encode hard squares without hidden heights, and there are exactly two connected ones, the occupation variables themselves and the four heights of Andrews, Baxter and Forrester. Hard hexagons is integrable on both, but no analytic Yang-Baxter family of face weights passes through hard squares at nonzero activity on either. The difference lies in the exclusion rule, which for hard squares turns a few Yang-Baxter equations into polynomial identities that force auxiliary weights to vanish. A closed form for hard squares is not excluded, but a solution by this route would have to leave these encodings or go beyond a single analytic family through the model. Encodings with hidden heights remain open.

title: Semantic Residual Vector Quantization for Sign Language Generation
abstract: Sign language generation (SLG) maps written sentences into signing motion while preserving both lexical content and fine-grained articulation. This requires a model to decide what signs should be expressed and to realize them through precise handshape, trajectory, facial expression and body coordination. Existing pose-based systems and reconstruction-only motion tokenizers often entangle these two decisions, leaving the generator without an explicit text-aligned intermediate target for what to sign before refining how to sign it. To address this issue, we introduce Semantic Residual Vector Quantization (SRVQ), a framework for SLG that frames generation as a two-level process moving from semantics to kinematics. The newly introduced SRV Quantizer learns a hierarchy in which the first residual level encodes sign content and subsequent levels refine pose, handshape, trajectory, and body coordination, all within a single quantizer and without separate semantic representations or external planning stages. Through word-aware conditioning for hierarchical code generation, a masked semantic generator predicts semantic codes and a kinematic generator completes the residual codes for full SMPL-X motion synthesis. We evaluate using retrieval and FID in a shared text-motion embedding space, alongside standard geometric metrics. On CSL-Daily and Phoenix-2014T, SRVQ achieves R@1 of 82.3 and 70.3, outperforming the previous SOTA by 30 and 46 points, respectively.

title: Target PageRank: Matching Prescribed PageRank Scores via Budgeted Edge Additions
abstract: PageRank is widely used to quantify the importance of nodes in directed networks. In applications such as recommendation systems, it is increasingly important that the PageRank distribution provides a fair representation of node exposure. This motivates the problem of making minimal changes to a graph so that the PageRank values of a given set of target nodes $T$ match a desired vector $\boldsymbol{t}$. In this paper, we study this problem under an edge-addition budget $B$, where exactly $B$ edges may be added to the graph. We show that deciding whether a multiset of exactly $B$ added edges can make the target nodes attain their desired absolute PageRank scores is NP-complete. After this, we define the $\ell_1$ Target PageRank problem in which we seek to minimize the $\ell_1$ distance between the target vector and resultant vector. We show that this optimization problem admits no polynomial-time multiplicative constant-factor approximation unless $P=NP$. Motivated by these hardness results, we propose two greedy heuristics for approaching the target PageRank vector. We additionally propose a Random Walk Hungarian (RWH) heuristic that addresses the addition of edges between dissimilar nodes by incorporating a penalty for such edges. Finally, we evaluate the proposed heuristics on several real-world and synthetic datasets and compare their performance in terms of PageRank accuracy, computational efficiency, and the relevance of the added edges.

title: FedFiOT: Fisher-Weighted Optimal Transport for Model Merging in One-Shot and Few-Round Federated Learning
abstract: One-shot and few-round federated learning (FL) reduce communication burden by constructing a global model within one or a few communication rounds, but often achieve lower performance than conventional multi-round FL. Without frequent synchronization, client models may drift apart, causing neurons that learn similar features to occupy different positions across clients. At the same time, local data heterogeneity can cause corresponding parameters to differ in their importance to each client's predictions. Together, these challenges cause direct averaging to combine mismatched neurons and assign equal weight to parameters despite differences in their importance. We propose FedFiOT, a Fisher-weighted optimal transport framework for one-shot and few-round FL that leverages Fisher information to quantify parameter importance and guide neuron alignment and model aggregation. FedFiOT jointly optimizes neuron correspondences and global model parameters through alternating minimization of a shared Fisher-weighted objective. Theoretically, we show that FedFiOT's optimization procedure monotonically decreases the layer-wise merging objective and establish a stationarity bound that quantifies the effects of client heterogeneity and nonuniform Fisher weighting.Experiments across multiple datasets demonstrate consistent improvements over competing baselines in both one-shot and few-round federated learning settings.

title: Fundamental Limits of Coherent Imaging in The Presence of Atmospheric Turbulence
abstract: We study the fundamental limits of jointly estimating the signal amplitude and the atmospheric phase distortion in complex-valued multi-look coherent imaging, where the measurements are corrupted by multiplicative speckle and additive Gaussian noise, all looks share a known Gaussian sensing matrix, and both parameters belong to structured classes. By analyzing a constrained maximum likelihood estimator, we establish an upper bound on the joint minimax risk that holds uniformly over the admissible parameter classes, while oracle reductions and Fano-type arguments yield worst-case lower bounds over the admissible parameter classes. These results quantify the effects of structural complexity, signal and measurement dimensions, the number of looks, and the noise level, and establish matching minimax rates in several settings, with a remaining gap for phase estimation at low noise when the measurement dimension exceeds the signal dimension. We also construct a two-stage estimator for signal recovery under arbitrary diagonal sign distortions in the real-valued analogue. Under additional conditions, it recovers the signs up to a global sign with high probability and yields a uniform signal risk bound without a distortion-complexity term. Numerical experiments illustrate the dependence of the joint, signal, and phase errors on the model parameters and provide further support for the theoretical analysis.

title: Constraining the white-dwarf mass in the intermediate polar IGR J17014-4306 using X-ray and optical spectroscopy
abstract: Intermediate polars (IPs), a subclass of magnetic cataclysmic variables, often show discrepancies between white-dwarf (WD) mass measurements from X-ray spectral modeling and optical dynamical studies. We investigate the IP IGR J17014-4306. We performed a joint spectral analysis of NuSTAR observations combined with archival XMM-Newton and Swift data, modeling the broad-band X-ray spectrum with a multi-temperature cooling-flow model. Additionally, we obtained time-resolved optical spectroscopy with the SOAR telescope to measure the radial velocity of the donor star and constrain the system's orbital parameters. The X-ray spectral analysis reveals a very high post-shock plasma temperature of $kT_{\max}=50_{-8}^{+11}\,\mathrm{keV}$, corresponding to a WD mass of $M_{\mathrm{WD}}=0.94_{-0.07}^{+0.09}\,M_\odot$. We also fitted the NuSTAR spectrum above 10 keV with the ipolar30KK model, obtaining $M_{\mathrm{WD}}=0.88_{-0.12}^{+0.14}\,M_\odot$. Our optical spectroscopy yields a radial-velocity semi-amplitude for the companion star of $K_2=165\pm4\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$ and an optical mass function of $f(M)=0.249\pm0.018\,M_\odot$. Combined with the eclipse geometry and the WD mass estimate from the X-ray models, these results favor a high mass ratio, $0.76\lesssim q\lesssim0.95$, and a donor-star mass of approximately $0.67\lesssim M_2/M_\odot\lesssim0.89$. In the limiting case of $q=1$, the WD mass has an upper limit of $1.14\,M_\odot$. Together with the X-ray measurements, this indicates a relatively massive WD. The lack of an independent measurement of the WD dynamical mass leaves it unclear whether the dynamical mass is consistent with the X-ray measurements or whether the X-ray mass is underestimated, as has been found for other IPs. Thus, our constraints make IGR J17014-4306 an important system for improving our understanding of IPs.

title: Go-Go-Go: the game of Go without turns
abstract: The study of variants of classic games has a long history, with chess alone inspiring countless variants that have been proposed, analyzed, and studied. The game of Go, despite rivaling chess in age, cultural relevance, popularity, and strategic depth, has seen drastically fewer variants. We introduce Go-Go-Go, a variant of the classic game of Go where there are no turns, and players play stones simultaneously and asynchronously on the board. The variant (which is to be played through a computer) includes a basic mechanism to avoid excessive spamming of moves, by imposing a minimal delay between moves that depends on their relative spatial distance. Apart from the lack of time discretization, most of the ruleset of the original game is either directly maintained or adapted in a natural way that preserves the original spirit. The first playtesting indicates that this results in the preservation of much of the emerging strategies and "flavor" of Go, while replacing the long strategic reasoning with fast paced, instinctive action fueled by quick reflexes. Play testers also report the need to balance immediate but suboptimal reactions with more reasoned but slower plays. We offer a publicly available, playable, OpenSource, and online reference implementation of Go-Go-Go at http://gogogo.di.unimi.it

title: Cosmological Backreaction and the Separate Universe Conjecture: Dynamical volume partitioning of Newtonian cosmologies
abstract: We provide a description of general Newtonian cosmologies for collisionless matter in terms of an exact and dynamical volume partitioning of global realizations of Newtonian models. Employing the formalism for the description of cosmological backreaction, an interaction between the inhomogeneities of the formation of structures in the Universe and their average properties can be analyzed. Our results can be regarded as a tool for many potential applications in the context of Newtonian simulations, but they also provide an exact way to assume analytical properties of the universe models on regional scales in conformity with global integral constraints on their average properties. We discuss approaches in relation to `separate Universe conjectures' in the literature and examine their consistency with the exact partitioning framework. In particular, using the Average Expansion Rate Approximation (AvERA) as an example, we show that identifying locally assigned Friedmannian rates with physical regional expansion rates is constrained by the global Newtonian 3-torus condition. Alternatively, when the simulation cells are interpreted as non-material control volumes, Reynolds transport introduces mass flux and flux-backreaction terms, so that their dynamics is not in general that of independent Friedmann domains. We also discuss the corresponding consistency conditions for stable clustering prescriptions.

title: Integrated Identity Protection for Semantic Communications in Embodied IoT Systems
abstract: Embodied Internet of Things (IoT) systems are promoting the adoption of task-oriented semantic communication (SemCom), in which the trustworthy task decisions require both semantic information reliability and source legitimacy. However, existing trustworthy designs in SemCom mainly focus on semantic content recovery and protection, with limited attention to source legitimacy. Motivated by this limitation, this paper establishes a new information exploitation paradigm for integrated SemCom-identity protection to address active source impersonation and passive identity inference by treating each SemCom signal as an inherent carrier of both task-relevant semantic information and transmitter physical identity information. We first examine these two information resources and then analyze their integration feasibility at the observation, processing, and decision levels. To exploit these resources for trustworthy decision making, we further develop a dual-branch identity protection mechanism under different operating modes. In the authentication mode, semantic recovery and physical-layer source verification are performed in parallel using the same received observation. In the concealment mode, identity exposure is suppressed while semantic recovery quality is maintained to support anonymous sensing reports. The resulting outputs are jointly interpreted to support task decisions under mode-specific identity protection requirements. Finally, two representative case studies on active source impersonation and passive identity inference are presented to evaluate the proposed framework.

title: Ranking Agreement Does Not Reveal Paragraph-Edit Agreement in Two Released Paper Acceptance Predictors
abstract: A fast acceptance classifier could select revisions for a slower evaluator. We ask whether agreement on existing papers supports that use. We compare a classifier of word and document features with two released text-only acceptance predictors fine-tuned from the same language model with three billion parameters. For 198 papers from the International Conference on Learning Representations, we compare model rankings of the original papers and of paragraph rewrites screened automatically for unchanged facts, claim strength, and attribution. The classifier ranks original papers closely with one predictor and moderately with the other, but shows no detectable agreement with either on which rewrites raise scores. The tests specified in advance used reduced numerical precision. Rounding error dominated the small score responses. We therefore rescored the released weights in full 32-bit precision as a post hoc check; edit agreement remained near zero. At this precision, when each predictor chooses among five rewrites per paper, its average raw score is under two points out of 100 higher than with random choice. The evidence covers presentation rewrites and two open predictors from one family; transfer to costly evaluators remains untested. Revision selectors should therefore be checked against the intended evaluator on the revisions they rank.

title: Open-shell Configuration State Functions as trial states for phaseless auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo
abstract: The accurate description of open-shell states in molecular systems poses challenges for approximate electronic structure methods. One emerging approach is to variationally optimize the orbitals of a single user-selected Configuration State Function (CSF), i.e., a linear combination of Slater determinants that is constructed as an eigenstate of the total spin operator. In this work we explore the use of these orbital-optimized single CSFs as trial wavefunctions in phaseless auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo (ph-AFQMC), a stochastic method that recovers electron correlation by evolving an initial state in imaginary time, subject to a constraint imposed by the trial state. We investigate the symmetric stretch of H-He-H, a series of small $p$-block compounds with diradicaloid singlet states, twisted ethene conformers, and a bimetallic iron-sulfur complex. We find that accurate energetics are obtained for states dominated by open-shell character, and that for certain atoms and diatomics the accuracy can be significantly improved when the trial is made to also preserve the relevant angular momentum symmetries. Furthermore, our study reveals that the open-shell CSF trial is suboptimal when the target electronic state reflects a significant mixture of ionic and covalent character, e.g., at shorter bond lengths in H-He-H and for the superexchange-stabilized ground state of [2Fe-2S]$^{2+}$. Our findings suggest that ph-AFQMC using CSF trial states is a promising method for many (but not all) strongly correlated molecular states, especially given its relatively low computational cost, and that it provides a reasonable non-perturbative way to recover some of the dynamic correlation that is otherwise missing in the CSF.

title: A Frame-Level View and Image-Quality Annotation Tool for Fetal Echocardiography: Comparison with Spreadsheet Annotation
abstract: Objective: To develop the Cardiologist Annotation Tool (CAT) for frame-level cardiac view and image-quality annotation in fetal echocardiography and compare it with spreadsheet-based annotation. Methods: CAT provides cine playback, frame navigation, and keyboard-based labeling without manual frame-range entry. Experts annotated 25 studies using both methods, and spreadsheet annotations were audited for predefined data-entry errors. In a randomized crossover study, six medical students annotated two normal studies, one with each method, against an expert reference. Results: Among 1,746 spreadsheet-annotated files, 6.2% contained major or critical data-entry errors, more frequently in congenital heart disease than normal studies (10.9% vs 3.4%). CAT yielded more annotated view segments per clip (3.6 vs 1.5). Rates of labeled and correctly labeled frames per minute were 1.77 and 1.68 times those with spreadsheets, respectively (both P = 0.031), with gains in all six students. No detectable difference in view-label accuracy was observed. Conclusion: CAT eliminates manual frame-range entry and enables finer-grained, structured annotation of fetal echocardiography, providing a practical approach to preparing datasets for AI research.

title: Magnetic Properties of Galactic Molecular Clouds
abstract: The earliest studies of molecular clouds (MCs) showed scaling relations between mass and radius M$\sim$R^s with exponent s $\approx$ 2, known as the third Larson relation. More recent CO surveys indicate 2 < s < 3 in the inner Milky Way (MW) and nearby galaxies. These observations appear consistent with the virial equilibrium (VE) of magnetically subcritical clouds, bound by the pressure Pe of the midplane ISM. The VE equations for such clouds are consistent with 2 < s < 3 for magnetically subcritical clouds, but not for magnetically critical, supercritical, or nonmagnetic clouds. We fit the subcritical VE equations to M-R trends observed in CO surveys of $\sim$1500 clouds, with correlation coefficients 0.8 - 1. The fits indicate median mass-to-flux ratio lambda $\approx$ 0.7, magnetic field strength Btot $\approx$ 60$\mathrm{μG}$, and Pe/k $\approx$ 5 x 10^5 cm^-3 K in the inner MW, with lesser values in M33 and M31. For 18 MW "bones," VE analysis assuming likely values of Pe also indicates subcritical values of lambda, as found from polarization observations. These results indicate that many giant molecular clouds (GMCs) are consistent with pressure-bound magnetically subcritical virial equilibrium. If so, GMCs may have low star formation efficiency (SFE) because their relatively strong fields cause filaments, clumps and cores to form slowly, while feedback and turbulence disperse them rapidly. The fields in their clumps and cores are likely weak enough to allow star-forming collapse, according to Zeeman and DCF observations, and according to MHD simulations which predict SFE $\approx$ 0.5-2%.

title: Transforming Integer Grids to Spatial Intuition: Perception, Not Planning, Governs ARC-AGI-3
abstract: Sample-efficient fluid intelligence requires agents that rapidly form working models of unfamiliar interactive environments. ARC-AGI-3 tests this across uninstructed visual games scored by Relative Human Action Efficiency, which penalizes exploratory waste quadratically. When frontier models read raw integer grids, serialization destroys spatial topology, and they spend hundreds of actions rediscovering basic boundaries and symmetries. We introduce SARBLOH, an open-weight agent built on the premise that spatial perception, not planning capacity, governs interactive reasoning on ARC-AGI-3. A zero-parameter O(HW) perception engine turns each frame, in 35 ms, into an object inventory with bipartite temporal tracking, a geometric briefing that separates proven invariants from affordance hypotheses, and an annotated canvas. Paired with a code-as-action runtime, the agent writes algorithmic hypotheses instead of low-level moves. Across eight presentations, grounded perception raises the rubric score from 3/28 to 25/28 points while cutting token use by 89.4%. On 23 held-out games, geometric invariants generalize with 100% accuracy, while single-frame affordance guesses fall to 6-50%, so active verification probes remain necessary. On the public set, Run A (briefing off) solved 143 of 183 levels in 8.2 hours at 59.4% single-pass efficiency; Run B (briefing on) reached 63.5%. Within the nine-hour budget on one Kaggle RTX PRO 6000 GPU, SARBLOH scored 16.53 on the hidden Kaggle evaluation, 13.7x the first Milestone winner.

title: 5-brane webs and generalised symmetries
abstract: 5-brane webs provide a powerful geometric description of five-dimensional quantum field theories, encoding data such as symmetries and dualities. Although the extraction of continuous 0-form symmetries from these systems is well understood, their higher-form symmetries have received less attention. We develop a microscopic prescription for determining 1-form symmetries directly from 5-brane webs.
