Here we experimentally observe ITI through coherent microwave reflection spectroscopy of a superconducting artificial atom realized by a Kerr parametric oscillator. Using strong parametric driving, we access a regime in which two transitions become nearly degenerate and simultaneously contribute to the reflected response. The observed spectral lineshapes are not adequately captured by a model of independent transitions. By contrast, theoretical calculations that incorporate dissipative coupling between the corresponding transition coherences reproduce the essential features of the measured spectra. These results provide experimental evidence for ITI and demonstrate that dissipative coupling between transition coherences can qualitatively modify spectroscopic responses. More broadly, our work identifies transition coherences as a new arena for quantum interference in open quantum systems.

title: Detecting Nonbilocal Correlations via Parameterized Elegant Joint Measurement
abstract: Quantum networks constitute a defining resource for quantum information processing; however, their nonclassical behavior is jointly governed by the choice of measurement basis and the independence of the distributed sources. We study a bilocal entanglement-swapping network in which the central node performs a three-parameter elegant joint measurement (EJM). For two independent Bell-state sources, we construct two binary edge observables and then derive a quantum prediction involving three parameters, which surpasses the classical constraints. In particular, the parameter θ controls both the degree of entanglement of the EJM basis states and the maximum value of the quantum prediction. These results provide an analytic and directly reproducible route for tuning nonbilocal correlations in an experimentally relevant two-source network.

title: Development of time-resolved fluorescence spectroscopy using heralded emission spectroscopy for organic light-emitting materials
abstract: Organic light-emitting materials are widely used in optoelectronics and bioimaging, but sometimes conventional fluorescence spectroscopy techniques can be limited by scattering, background fluorescence, photon pile-up and photobleaching. We report a quantum-spectroscopic approach using frequency-entangled, nondegenerate photon pairs generated via spontaneous parametric down-conversion with heralded detection, to perform photoluminescence lifetime measurements at low excitation intensities. We demonstrate this approach across three organic light-emitting material classes: the fluorescent dye Rhodamine 6G, an organic semiconducting conjugated polymer poly[2-methoxy-5-(2-ethylhexyloxy)-1,4-phenylenevinylene] (MEH-PPV), and a fluorescent protein mOrange. The intrinsic timing correlation between signal and idler photons enables coincidence gating that suppresses uncorrelated background counts. Across all materials and integration times of 500, 1000 and 3600 seconds, heralded detection yields signal-to-noise ratios 1.6-3.0 times higher than classical pulsed-laser excitation attenuated to match heralded photon counts in the fitting range. For MEH-PPV, this roughly halves the noise amplitude. Our measured lifetimes closely match long-integration classical pulsed-laser reference values.

title: Emergent Symmetry in Constant-Density Flocks
abstract: In two dimensions, the ordered phase of constant-density flocks is described by a single angle field, which makes them arguably the simplest systems with a scale-free ordered phase of collective motion. We show that the equation governing the corresponding Nambu-Goldstone mode, completed with terms previously discarded, possesses on large scales an invariance combining a shear and a Galilean boost. Broken at the bare level, this symmetry is restored at the unique attractive fixed point, and the associated Ward identities fix the scaling exponents exactly, as confirmed numerically.

title: Adapt the Object to the Subject: Representative Study Material for Empirical Software Engineering
abstract: External validity is a central concern in empirical software engineering, yet the debate has largely focused on whether study participants are representative. How well the study objects they reason about - code, models, or requirements - are representative of each participant's own work is often overlooked. Practitioners' own artifacts would be ideal, but are often out of reach, so researchers sample from public datasets or construct objects artificially. Whether this lack of subject-object fit affects participants' ability to act on the material remains unknown. We take a first step toward answering this question for requirements. We propose an approach that uses an LLM to generate context-adapted synthetic requirements just-in-time during an online survey from a short, participant-supplied context description, optionally injecting requirements smells as controlled stimuli. To validate the approach, we conducted a controlled experiment with 31 industry practitioners in a 2x2 design that crosses stimulus generation (static vs. synthetic) with quality (clean vs. smelly). Each participant rated the perceived representativeness and assessability of 20 requirements. Using Bayesian data analysis within a statistical causal-inference framework, we find that perceived representativeness has a strong positive effect on assessability. Synthetic requirements are rated as more representative and, primarily due to this gain, more assessable than static ones sourced from public datasets; smell injection leaves both perceptions unchanged. Our results support treating a lack of study-object representativeness as a first-class validity threat and position context-adapted synthetic study objects as a practical addition to the empirical methodology toolbox.

title: Optimal Learning in Games with Arbitrary Delays: Best-of-Both-Worlds for Self-Play and Adversarial Opponents
abstract: We study learning in zero-sum games with delayed feedback. We introduce Multi-Anchor Optimistic Online Mirror Descent (MAO-OMD), a single algorithm which obtains optimal fast rates in self-play on smooth games, while simultaneously maintaining minimax optimal guarantees against arbitrary opponents. In particular, in smooth zero-sum games with arbitrary and unknown feedback delays, MAO-OMD obtains $O(σ_{\max}+1)$ social and individual regrets when used by both players, where $σ_{\max}$ denotes the maximum number of outstanding gradients, while also guaranteeing minimax optimal $O(\sqrt{T+d_{\mathrm{tot}}})$ individual regret against arbitrary opponents, where $d_{\mathrm{tot}}$ is the total delay. Moreover, we show that these optimal rates cannot be obtained simultaneously using the standard black-box reduction to the undelayed setting. We also extend our results to multi-player games, and to games with player-dependent delay sequences.

title: Unobserved Consideration and Consumer Welfare
abstract: Can welfare effects of price change be identified when consumers' consideration sets are heterogeneous and unobserved? We establish that the welfare distribution is the same functional of structural choice probabilities under stable but limited consideration as under full consideration. The result permits unrestricted income-effects, preference heterogeneity, and dependence between preferences and consideration. Within this class, limited consideration admits a full-consideration representation preserving choice-probabilities and money-metric compensation: consideration/preferences can remain unidentified while demand and welfare are identified. When consideration sets contract as prices rise, the welfare distribution can be bounded using demand and a bound on choice-set attrition.

title: Adapters as Data: The Latent Space of LoRAs
abstract: LoRA adapters are usually treated as finished artifacts rather than as a data modality. Prior work has shown that LoRA adapters populate a low-dimensional manifold that a linear PCA basis already organizes well enough to support different operations such as sampling, editing, and inversion. We ask what a learned, nonlinear latent adds beyond this. We train a transformer autoencoder on the same population of LoRA identity adapters, mapping each into a latent space and compare every operation against the identical operation applied directly to the raw adapter weights. The latent preserves the capabilities already available in weight space, sampling diverse identities and editing individual attributes. Beyond preservation, we show that the latent is far more robust to displacement than weight space, degrading into distorted but still valid faces rather than texture. Fixed-dimensional weight-space representations cannot natively host adapters of more than one rank, so we extend our sequential autoencoder to hold mixed-rank adapters within one shared latent. This gives a path toward treating adapter weights of varying architecture as a single, general modality rather than one tied to a fixed rank, and points to a learned, nonlinear latent as the mechanism that could carry this generalization further, toward heterogeneous populations of adapters.

title: Discrete quadrature spectrum of composite bosons: Weyl relation, intensity correlations, and binned homodyne detection
abstract: A composite boson made of two fermions can look elementary under one measurement and composite under another. In an exactly solvable paired-mode model we compare three probes: classical drives, periodically binned quadrature statistics, and intensity correlations $g^{(2)}$. The Weyl defect has an exact product formula and a controlled dilute expansion in the Schmidt moments. The binned observables are instead piecewise constant in the Schmidt weights and sensitive to single eigenvalues crossing bin edges; on the flat-spectrum ladder they converge slowly and nonmonotonically over the computed range. A spectral filter and a polar correction recover an exact Pauli algebra; a heralded joint projection then extracts a logical singlet from the vacua of two independent copies of the composite, with probability set by the accepted weight and the mixedness of the filtered reduced qubit. Finite-mode examples with Schmidt number about three succeed at the percent level despite order-one Weyl defects; near-unit $g^{(2)}$ does not control the binned algebra. For flat spectra the construction converges strongly to its oscillator counterpart, whose vacuum overlap is strictly positive at every scale; for infinite spectra with summable Schmidt amplitudes it converges at all but countably many filter cutoffs, positivity at the cutoffs studied remaining open.

title: Online Optimization for Controlling HVAC Systems
abstract: Heating, ventilation, and air-conditioning (HVAC) systems account for a significant portion of buildings' energy consumption, motivating the design of energy- and cost-efficient control strategies. However, conventional strategies employ simple, reactive control, without incorporating a model. Therefore, in this paper we adopt an economic model predictive control framework and focus on designing online algorithms to solve the control input design problems with a limited computational budget. In particular, we propose two tailored online algorithms based on projected gradient descent, with a custom projection routine, and the projected primal-dual method. We discuss the pros and cons of both algorithm designs, focusing in particular on computational efficiency. We further compare them through numerical experiments simulating the control of an HVAC system over the course of a day. The results show that computationally efficient online solvers for HVAC systems control are indeed possible. Moreover, the performance closely matches that of a baseline algorithm with unlimited computational budget, in terms of reference temperature tracking and comfort temperature range enforcement.

title: The Intrusion Pathway: How Non-Evidential Context Degrades Language Model Performance
abstract: Language models lose accuracy when a prompt contains non-evidential context: irrelevant statements from unrelated domains, or random off-distribution tokens, with no competing answer and no semantic overlap with the query. Such noise pervades retrieval-augmented, tool-using, and long-context deployments, yet the failure has lacked a mechanistic account. We trace the corruption to the Intrusion Pathway, which starts with MLPs enriching both query-subject and irrelevant-token representations, parroting heads carry prefix-token content to the prediction position, and relational readers largely avoid unrelated sources. Nevertheless, preserved subject enrichment and selective reading do not prevent intrusion in the broader computation. We then localize part of this interference to a sparse set of attention heads, which we call intrusion heads. Their prefix-derived writes promote distractor-related content, while their reduced support for the correct answer arises primarily from weaker non-prefix contributions rather than direct suppression by the prefix. The same heads transfer across tasks and distractor types and are largely weight-disjoint from the heads that integrate relevant contextual evidence, enabling a class-conditional intervention. Replacing the corrupted last-token residual with its clean counterpart, an oracle probe that requires a matched clean forward pass, recovers 97.6% on average of the distractor-induced drop across four downstream tasks. A deployable mask level knockout of about ten heads, roughly 1% of the model's attention heads, recovers 57% at bounded cost to helpful context.

title: Flexible Piezoelectric Tactile Sensing System for Intelligent Object Recognition
abstract: Tactile sensing provides information about object properties that can improve robotic grasping and manipulation. However, accurate object recognition during the early stages of grasping remains challenging, particularly under strict real-time constraints. This study presents a flexible, distributed piezoelectric tactile sensing system for early-stage object recognition. The system was experimentally evaluated using six everyday objects and three recognition approaches: feature-based classification using support vector machines (SVMs), raw-signal classification using 1D convolutional neural networks (1D-CNNs) and convolutional recurrent neural networks (C-RNNs), and spatiotemporal heatmap classification using a 2D-CNN. The effects of sensor count and temporal window size on recognition accuracy and real-time feasibility were systematically investigated. Increasing the number of sensing elements improved recognition performance across all approaches. The best-performing method, based on spatiotemporal heatmaps and a 2D-CNN, achieved F1-scores of 0.9796, 0.9846, and 0.9903 using 16, 24, and 32 sensors, respectively. The optimal configuration, comprising 32 sensors and a 100-ms temporal window (50 samples), was deployed on an embedded edge platform, achieving an end-to-end recognition latency of approximately 101 ms from contact onset and an energy consumption of 63.8 microjoules per inference. These results demonstrate the potential of distributed piezoelectric tactile sensing for accurate, energy-efficient, and real-time object recognition during robotic grasping.

title: Bridging Structure and Semantics: Knowledge Graph Verification via Triple-to-Text Alignment
abstract: Semantic accuracy is an important dimension of knowledge graph quality. Graph-based scoring methods exploit relational structure, while textual representations allow classifiers to draw on knowledge encoded by pre-trained language models (PLMs). We present GenVer, a generative verifier that scores triples using both their serialized form and generated natural language representations (NLRs). A triple-text alignment procedure selects training pairs for a sequence-to-sequence generator; a BERT-based classifier then combines features from each triple and its generated NLR. On four FactFB variants, constructed from FB15k using perturbed negative triples, GenVer obtains the highest classification accuracy among the evaluated baselines, ranging from 88.56% to 91.52%. The experiments suggest that generated representations can help triple classification, while the case analysis also exposes semantic drift and high-confidence errors.

title: Reliability-Aware Z-Grammars and Z-Automata over a Credible-Grade Semiring
abstract: Fuzzy grammars and weighted automata usually attach to each word a single grade, which records how strongly the word is generated but not how far that record can be trusted. We study weighted grammars and finite automata whose weights are scalar grade-reliability pairs inspired by Z-numbers. Sequential composition multiplies both components, while aggregation selects a derivation by its credible grade, the product of grade and reliability, with ties resolved by grade. On the canonical carrier, in which the weights of zero grade or zero reliability are identified with zero, the resulting structure is a commutative selective semiring, isomorphic to a subsemiring of a lexicographically ordered product, and its credible-grade projection is a homomorphism onto the Viterbi semiring. We compare several alternative combination rules and identify the carriers on which the relevant algebraic laws hold. Standard results on weighted automata then yield a rational characterization and closure properties. We prove that positive credible-grade cuts and selected-run reliability filters of finite automata are regular and effectively constructible for rational weights and thresholds, and we exhibit distinctions that the scalar projection cannot see: a reliability filter that no scalar reweighting of the same one-state automaton implements, nonmonotonicity under the addition of runs, and an unambiguous automaton with no deterministic equivalent although its scalar projection is deterministic. A count-based example illustrates an attestation penalty for grammar rules. The construction concerns scalar pairs, and its extension to arbitrary fuzzy-valued Z-numbers remains open.

title: Multi-epoch monitoring of the faint northern component in 3C 84 during 2016-2021
abstract: We present the results of multi-epoch very long baseline interferometry (VLBI) observations of the sub-parsec-scale northern jet component of 3C 84 (known as the N1 component) at 7 mm from 2016 to 2021. The peak position of the N1 component exhibits positional variations of approximately 0.2 mas at a distance of about 2.5 mas from the central radio core (C1) throughout the observation period. Although a linear fit yields a small proper motion of $μ_{\rm{Dec}}=0.054\pm0.019~\rm{mas}~\rm{yr}^{-1}$, corresponding to an apparent velocity of $β_{\rm{app}}=0.062\pm0.021$, this displacement is comparable to the observed positional scatter, and the hypothesis that N1 exhibits systematic motion is not statistically supported. In contrast, the peak flux density varies by approximately a factor of two on timescales of several months. We propose two possible explanations for the observed behavior of N1. One is that N1 is the counterpart of the southern hotspot C3, but its motion has been halted by a collision with a compact and dense cloud along its path; in this case, the flux variability may be caused by changes in the free-free absorption opacity of the non-uniform cloud. The other possibility is that N1 is part of the northern jet that is heavily obscured by foreground free-free absorption and is observed through a gap in the absorbing medium; in this case, the variability may reflect intrinsic changes in the jet and its interaction with a non-uniform ambient medium. These results provide new constraints on the physical origin of N1 and on the circumnuclear environment of 3C 84.

title: PBPO: Prefix-Block Policy Optimization for Diffusion Language Models
abstract: Diffusion Large Language Models (dLLMs) commonly decode responses by proceeding autoregressively across blocks while iteratively denoising multiple tokens within each block. This structure makes block-level policy optimization a natural adaptation of autoregressive policy optimization. However, the exact likelihood of a completed block is intractable because it marginalizes over the intermediate states and reveal orders of the denoising process. To realize the block-level formulation, we construct a prefix-block state and use a single model evaluation to define a factorized one-step surrogate for the block likelihood. The resulting block surrogate ratio is a product of its token surrogate ratios, allowing variation at individual positions to propagate across the entire block before clipping. We therefore introduce Prefix-Block Policy Optimization (PBPO), which preserves block-level conditioning but applies surrogate importance weighting and clipping separately to each token. PBPO further diversifies repeated updates by resampling corrupted views of the prompt and revealed prefix, a design motivated by masked-dLLM pre-training. Under our analysis assumptions, block-product weighting amplifies the variance of gradient contributions relative to token-local weighting. Across two LLaDA-family initializations, six benchmarks, and three generation lengths, PBPO achieves competitive performance against existing dLLM RL methods.

title: EnergyBench: a live, gate-aligned benchmark of day-ahead forecasts for European power markets
abstract: Energy forecasting models are usually compared on backtests and fixed public datasets. Backtests can use data that did not yet exist when the forecast would have been made, and a fixed test set, reused across studies and possibly contained in the pretraining data of foundation models, invites overfitting to the benchmark. EnergyBench evaluates every entry live instead. Each day at 11:30 CET/CEST, thirty minutes before the day-ahead (SDAC) gate closes, every model forecasts the next day's price, wind and solar generation and load on the 15-minute grid for six bidding zones (BE, NL, FR, DE-LU, DK1, DK2). Unlike existing live benchmarks, EnergyBench runs the models itself, on one information set that it freezes at the cut-off and publishes, including three numerical weather prediction models, so that foundation models can be compared with and without the same weather covariates under the actual market deadline. Errors are pooled per series against a seasonal-naive baseline, and models are ranked by a Bradley-Terry rating on the Elo scale with a day-bootstrap interval. The field spans baselines, linear and gradient-boosted models on the frozen weather, eighteen time-series foundation models from eleven families, ensembles, and the grid operators' own forecasts. Over the first thirty-two live days, the covariates reduced the error of each of the ten foundation models run with and without them by 37-51% on matched races (64-73% on wind, 48-61% on solar). Used zero-shot, these models match or outperform a LightGBM model trained on the same covariates. Model size, from 3M to 331M parameters, has a much smaller effect, and median ensembles of the covariate models rank highest. The grid operators' pre-gate forecasts remain ahead on wind and solar, where the best single foundation models have 16-22% more error; on load the gap is 4-6%, within the intervals.

title: Geometric Functional Inequalities for Markov Processes: An Invitation via the Langevin Diffusion
abstract: Functional inequalities provide a language for reasoning about the long-time properties of ergodic Markov processes in terms of their macroscopic geometry. This article offers an informal introduction to functional inequalities for readers who are more familiar with probabilistic tools based around couplings, Lyapunov techniques, and similar. The main ideas are developed through the overdamped Langevin diffusion, where various functionals related to this convergence admit particularly transparent expressions, and for which the key associated inequalities -- namely, the Poincaré and logarithmic Sobolev inequalities -- are especially well-studied. We explain the qualitative content of these inequalities, what they imply about convergence to equilibrium, how they transform and compose under natural operations, and how they interface with classical probabilistic approaches. Related inequalities are discussed more briefly, and an annotated guide is provided for readers wishing to enter the wider literature.

title: On computing the determinant over a ring
abstract: An algorithm is presented for computing the determinant and the characteristic polynomial of a matrix $A$ over an arbitrary commutative ring R. The algorithm uses $O(n^ω)$ ring additions, subtractions and multiplications, where $ω>2$ is a feasible exponent for matrix multiplication, that is, such that two $n\times n$ matrices over R can be multiplied using $O(n^ω)$ ring operations. The algorithm involves no division and no zero test, and its control depends only on $n$: for each $n$ it is a straight-line program. The approach combines a polynomial matrix point of view and a block Krylov point of view on the characteristic polynomial, which makes Strassen's elimination of divisions efficient. A bivariate matrix $λI-L(t)$, obtained from $A$ by a homotopy, is compressed in $\log n$ steps, each of which halves the dimension while only doubling the degree in $λ$. The cost of the homotopy is controlled by truncating the power series in $t$ at an order that only grows with the compression steps, from a constant to $n$.

title: Discrete Choice under Congestion: Equilibrium and Welfare
abstract: In many choice settings, a rise in aggregate demand for an option lowers an individual's payoff from choosing it. Driving becomes less attractive than taking a train when more commuters drive, clogging the highway. In such cases, a targeted intervention that mitigates the externality at the congested option can divert it elsewhere and also undermine preference based sorting, making overall welfare effects theoretically ambiguous. We develop an empirical framework to analyze such scenarios of endogenous congestion. We show that in these settings, equilibrium exists and is unique without restrictions on functional-form of utilities or dimension/distribution of preference heterogeneity, and even when congestion at one option affects payoffs from other choices. Under a linear-index structure, micro-data on choice enables semiparametric identification of utility contrasts and welfare effects of some, but not all, interventions. We apply the framework to Cambridge undergraduate admissions, where candidates apply through one constituent college, and admission probability depends on application numbers relative to capacity in that college. Using administrative micro-data on 25,325 applicants, we calculate welfare under two counterfactuals: (i) centralized random allocation and (ii) higher rent at popular colleges. Random allocation reduces welfare for everyone: it removes individual choice without improving admission chances since, by design, lower congestion at a college exactly counterbalances the lower probability of being allocated there. Targeted rent increase produces both gains and losses, with median loss for men and median gain for women. This exercise shows how identified preferences and equilibrium feedback jointly determine welfare when choices entail externalities.

title: Geometry-Evolving Barrier Functions for Safety Evaluation in Dynamic Environments
abstract: Autonomous systems operating in dynamic environments often involve multiple interacting agents, giving rise to high-dimensional safety evaluation problems. Hamilton--Jacobi (HJ) reachability provides rigorous finite-horizon safety guarantees, but solving a global HJ partial differential equation (PDE) over the entire state space leads to prohibitive computational complexity. In this paper, we introduce Geometry-Evolving Barrier Functions (GEBFs), a novel representation for dynamic safety evaluation that propagates local safety geometry of the solution to a terminal-value HJ PDE. By evolving the value, gradient, and curvature information along a Hamiltonian-induced reference trajectory, GEBFs provide a compact representation of the local HJ safety landscape. Under suitable local regularity assumptions, we establish consistency between the GEBF and the value, gradient, and Hessian of the HJ solution along an HJ-optimal characteristic. Building on these theoretical results, we develop an iterative algorithm that couples local geometric propagation with trajectory refinement. We further establish a trajectory-wise one-sided relationship between the GEBF and HJ value function, together with a fixed-point consistency result for the iterative scheme. Experiments on widely adopted agent--obstacle collision-avoidance benchmarks, across low- and high-dimensional systems, demonstrate that GEBFs accurately capture the evolution of dynamic safety boundaries, while achieving substantially lower computational cost than conventional HJ reachability.

title: The Zhukovskiy-Volterra gyroscope: geometry and reduction
abstract: We describe a symplectic reduction of the Zhukovskiy integrable case of motion of a rigid body about a fixed point with a gyroscope in $\mathbb R^n$ to an integrable magnetic flow on a sphere $S^{n-1}$. We also present Zhukovskiy's geometric interpretation of motion of the Euler top with a gyroscope, aka the Zhukovskiy--Volterra gyroscope, and perform a symplectic reduction of this system to an integrable magnetic flow on a $2$-dimensional sphere.

title: Singular viscosity-exponent limit for one-dimensional compressible Navier-Stokes equations with far field vacuum
abstract: We consider the limit $δ\to1^+$ for the one-dimensional compressible Navier-Stokes equations with viscosity $μ(ρ)=ρ^δ$ and far field vacuum. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first result on the viscosity-exponent limit $δ\to1^+$ for strong solutions with far field vacuum. With far field vacuum, the diffusion coefficient $ρ^{δ-1}$ does not converge uniformly to $1$ on $\mathbb R$ as $δ\to1^+$. The main difficulty is to obtain uniform estimates for this limit. By introducing some new weighted density variables, we establish local well-posedness and uniform estimates without requiring $ρ_0^{(δ-1)/2}\in L^2(\mathbb R)$. We prove strong convergence to the known global $δ=1$ solution obtained in \cite{WenZhangDCDS2025} on a local time interval independent of $δ$. With one additional order of regularity of the initial data and the limit solution, the convergence holds on every fixed finite time interval, and the maximal life-spans of the $δ>1$ solutions tend to $+\infty$ as $δ\to1^+$.

title: On the anisotropic mean curvature flow in the Gaussian space
abstract: In this paper, we study the anisotropic mean curvature flow in the Gaussian space endowed with a Finsler metric obtained from a Minkowski metric by a conformal deformation. We first derive the conformal transformation formulas for the fundamental tensor, the Cartan tensor, and the Chern connection of the conformally related Finsler metrics. Based on these formulas, we express the anisotropic mean curvature in the Gaussian space in terms of the corresponding anisotropic mean curvature with respect to the original Minkowski metric, and derive the associated evolution equation. Finally, we establish the short-time existence and uniqueness of smooth solutions by reformulating the geometric evolution equation as a strictly parabolic quasilinear partial differential equation.

title: Thinking Is Not Writing: Designing AI Chatbots to Connect Reasoning and Revision
abstract: Supporting students' argumentative writing with AI requires connecting reflection to their revision processes. We present Maike, a Socratic chatbot supporting writing through argument diagnosis, targeted questioning, and a student model across Think and Write modes. In a classroom study, 65 secondary-school students used Maike or a control chatbot sharing the interface, language model, and Think/Write modes. Approximately 40% of students improved their essay scores. However, Maike users engaged more in idea-level dialogue (56% vs. 44%) and moved iteratively between discussion and editing. Transitions from ideas discussed in dialogue to revisions were positively associated with score gains. These findings suggest a design target for AI writing support: coordinating reflection with revision. We contribute an architecture for supporting argumentative reasoning without generating essay text and an approach linking interaction patterns to writing processes and outcomes. As AI becomes embedded in classrooms, understanding these connections is essential to assessing (and designing for) its educational value.

title: Rain Beyond Streaks: Cascaded Realistic Rain and Wet Surface Synthesis via Scene Priors
abstract: Realistic rain synthesis is a persistent challenge for vision systems operating in adverse weather. Existing methods primarily focus on generating rain streaks, often neglecting consequent surface effects such as reflections and puddles, which are critical for perceptual realism and robustness of downstream vision tasks. We introduce CascadeRS, a rain synthesis framework that leverages depth and segmentation priors to render scene-consistent rain and surface effects. In addition to rain streaks, CascadeRS produces reflections and puddles aligned with scene semantics through a physics-inspired zero-shot, controllable generative pipeline. It produces photorealistic rainy urban scenes, with high perceptual realism, which we validate qualitatively with an extensive user study and quantitatively. We produce the Cityscapes-CascadeRS dataset, to study downstream task performance under real rainy conditions. Our results establish CascadeRS as a scalable and realistic rain-generation framework for evaluating and enhancing the robustness of vision in adverse rainy weather. Code and dataset are available via https://github.com/nis-research/CascadeRainSynthesis

title: Comment on the recent claims of H0 measurements with the ZTF DR2 SN Ia sample (arXiv:2610.36051)
abstract: Karchev et al. (2026) derived a value of H0 by combining the ZTF SN Ia DR2 sample with SH0ES calibrator Type Ia supernovae (SNe Ia; Riess et al. 2022), used to anchor the SN Ia absolute luminosity. The ZTF SN Ia DR2 dataset (Rigault et al., 2025) is the largest (O(3000)) SN Ia sample to date obtained with a single telescope. However, as emphasized in the data release, the absolute photometric calibration of the survey has not yet been established to the precision required for cosmological inference. The relative photometric zeropoint offset between the SH0ES and ZTF SN Ia DR2 samples, which is fully degenerate with H0, is therefore unknown and cannot be determined from publicly available data. The photometric corrections introduced in Karchev et al. (2026) do not address this global calibration offset. Consequently, their reported H0 determination is not supported by the available calibration information. We nonetheless share the excitement of pursuing state-of-the-art cosmology with ZTF and are actively working toward the release of a fully calibrated dataset

title: A Murnaghan--Nakayama rule for dual stable Grothendieck functions
abstract: We give a closed boundary formula for multiplication by power sums in the dual stable Grothendieck basis. The off-diagonal coefficients are signed binomial coefficients supported on corner-connected broken ribbons, which are skew diagrams connected through edges or vertices and containing no square of four boxes. For such a diagram, the smallest power-sum index with a nonzero coefficient is the number of boxes plus the number of edge-connected components minus one. All larger indices give nonzero coefficients when the boundary statistic is positive and zero coefficients when it vanishes. The diagonal coefficient is minus the number of removable corners of the indexing partition. The formula evaluates the stable specialization of Nguyen's Murnaghan--Nakayama rule for K-k-Schur functions. We give two independent proofs, one using Newton's identity and the dual Pieri rules and the other using determinantal formulas and Schur complements.

title: Power-Swing Blocking Scheme Based on Continuous and Higher-Order Incremental Quantities for Systems with Inverter-Based Resources
abstract: Conventional power-swing blocking (PSB) schemes for distance protection face new and emerging challenges as the penetration levels of inverter-based resources (IBRs) increase. Several papers highlight interoperability issues concerning faster power swings and unconventional impedance trajectories. Revised relay settings are proposed in attempts to deal with the problems. However, the blinder-based PSB methodology suffers from being dependent on the speed of the apparent impedance trajectory over the tiny region between the blinders, making it difficult to distinguish between fast swings and faults. Moreover, blinders have the inherent limitation that they cannot operate if the measured impedance is inside the blinders when the fault is cleared and immediately enters the distance zones during the first swing cycle - an issue often overlooked in the current literature. This paper proposes a novel PSB scheme based on higher-order incremental quantities (IQs) for difficult swing scenarios with IBRs and synchronous generators (SGs). PSCAD/EMTDC simulations of an SG and an implemented grid-forming (GFM) inverter validate its superior performance compared to conventional dual-blinder PSB schemes. The impacts of GFM inverters on the impedance measured by distance relays during the fault-to-swing transition and first power swing cycle are also discussed.

title: Dataset Collection and Fine-Tuning of NLLB for German--English Translation
abstract: This paper describes the curation of a high-quality parallel corpus from OPUS Books and the fine-tuning of Meta's NLLB-200 models for German--English translation. We detail a dataset extraction pipeline that filters 45k raw OPUS sentence pairs to 25k high-quality examples through encoding validation, length filtering, language identification, deduplication, and quality scoring. We present a reproducible fine-tuning methodology optimized for consumer GPUs using mixed precision, gradient accumulation, and gradient checkpointing. Our fine-tuned NLLB-600M model achieves statistically significant improvements (+3.4 BLEU, +2.6 chrF++, -3.2 TER) over the base model on literary and technical German-English translation. We demonstrate practical deployment by integrating the fine-tuned model into LinguaHaru, an existing open-source document translation system, achieving format-preserving translation across PDF and Office documents. All dataset preparation scripts, training code, and evaluation tools are provided for reproducibility. The fine-tuned model is available at HuggingFace.

title: VocabulARy 2.0: A Generative AR System Enabling Personalised 3D Mnemonics for Vocabulary Learning in Context
abstract: Mnemonics support vocabulary learning by linking unfamiliar words to familiar concepts through memorable verbal and visual associations. We present a generative AR system that enables learners to create personalised 3D mnemonics by transforming familiar objects in their surroundings into situated mnemonic anchors. The system scans the environment, detects visible objects, and generates bilingual flashcards. After selecting a word, the learner describes a personal association. The system combines this description with an image of the selected object to generate a textured 3D model using generative AI. Learners can then place the model relative to the real object, transforming it into a situated mnemonic anchor.

title: Holomorphic planes in $M\times \mathbb{T}^2$ from weakly exact Lagrangians in $M$
abstract: Let $(M,ω_M)$ be closed symplectic manifold containing a closed Lagrangian submanifold $L$ with $ω_M$ vanishing on $π_2(M,L)$. We prove that there is a nonconstant $J$-holomorphic plane $u:\mathbb{C}\rightarrow M\times \mathbb{T}^2$ for any almost complex structure $ J$ on $M\times \mathbb{T}^2$ tamed by $ω_M\oplusω_{\text{std}}$.

title: Constrained Quantum Imaginary Time in Krylov Space
abstract: We introduce constrained quantum imaginary time evolution (CQITE), extending quantum imaginary time evolution (QITE) to constrained-search dynamics for ground-state preparation with prescribed expectation-value constraints. A central challenge in practical QITE is constructing a compact unitary representation of the imaginary-time evolution while maintaining accuracy and controlling the approximation error. We resolve this challenge by deriving an exact characterization of the imaginary-time evolution from the Krylov space generated by repeated applications of the Hamiltonian to the initial state. This characterization induces a hierarchy of operator directions expressed through nested anti-commutators. Truncating the hierarchy produces a systematic static operator pool, with polynomial size in the system size at any fixed truncation order. The resulting construction provides a principled route to compact unitary approximations of imaginary-time dynamics. Numerical tests on spin models show close agreement with exact constrained imaginary-time evolution and small constraint deviations, while a fermionic example yields energies close to the analytic constrained-search reference.

title: Interlacing of the Volume and Half-Volume Spectra
abstract: We give a direct proof of the weak interlacing inequalities \[ω_p\leq\widetildeω_p\leqω_{p+1}\] between the volume and half-volume spectra of a closed connected Riemannian manifold $M^{n+1}$, $n+1\geq3$. We also prove that, for a residual set of smooth metrics, the area of every smooth embedded half-volume CMC boundary lies outside the rational span of the areas of smooth closed embedded minimal hypersurfaces. For dimensions $3\le n+1\le 5$, these results yield strict interlacing for generic metrics and a lower bound of order $A^{n+1}$ for the number of distinct half-volume CMC boundaries with area at most $A$.

title: Multirobust Control Pulses Designed by Iterative Quantum Kolmogorov-Arnold-Moser Algorithm
abstract: We introduce a multi-robust quantum control strategy designed to suppress multilevel leakage outside the computational qubit space while simultaneously ensuring robustness against unknown inhomogeneities in control parameters. It is based on a reformulation of the Derivative Removal by Adiabatic Gate (DRAG) technique which allows for the full incorporation of control pulses originally designed for two-level models by using the iterative quantum Kolmogorov-Arnold-Moser (KAM) algorithm. We apply it for optimal robust control designed by inverse optimization (RIO), referred to as RDK pulses. We analyze the performance of RDK pulses on various durations, iterations, and robustness types. We show that the two-level robustness is restored after only a few iterations with an asymptotic exponential approximation (i.e. as a superasymptotic series), even for relatively short pulse durations and that the resulting pulses are near optimal in terms of energy compared to the optimal RIO pulses defined in the qubit subspace. Such pulses are well suited for superconducting transmons as well as other forms of qubits embedded in a multi-level structure. By effectively reproducing a two-level dynamics within a multi-level system, this approach is versatile thanks to its compatibility with two-level control strategies under conditions (smoothness, duration) that are analyzed.

title: Reliable Bistatic Ranging With Unreliable Communication Payloads
abstract: This paper addresses a key challenge in bistatic integrated sensing and communications (ISAC): \textit{How to achieve reliable ranging using communication data signals that cannot be reliably recovered?} In modern communication systems, data payloads typically occupy far more time-frequency resources than pilots, offering substantially more observations to improve sensing accuracy. Exploiting them requires recovering the transmitted symbols to form sensing references. However, propagation and reflection losses can severely weaken target echoes. The sensing receiver may therefore be unable to recover data transmitted at a high rate selected for communication users. We first show that, at low signal-to-noise ratios (SNRs), using hard symbol decisions as sensing references can introduce a persistent bias in the estimated channel impulse response (CIR). This bias produces an error floor and spurious peaks in the power delay profile (PDP) that persist even after coherent accumulation over a large number of observations. To address this limitation, we develop a pilot-initialized expectation-maximization (EM) estimator that iteratively refines the CIR using posterior symbol moments. Under local regularity conditions and successful initialization, we establish that the EM method converges to the local maximum-likelihood (ML) solution for a sufficiently large number of OFDM data symbols. The converged estimator is asymptotically unbiased, where the CIR estimation mean-square error (MSE) at each delay bin decays as $O(1/M)$ by accumulating $M$ data symbols. Thus, estimation error can vanish through sufficient accumulation even while symbol recovery remains highly unreliable. Numerical results validate the proposed method, demonstrating substantially higher target detection probabilities than pilot-only and hard-decision-based bistatic ranging under the same low-SNR conditions.

title: Cepheid Metallicity in the Leavitt Law (C-MetaLL) survey: X First spectroscopic characterization of Galactic Type II Cepheids and calibration of the Period-Wesenheit-Metallicity relations
abstract: Type II Cepheids (T2Cs) are Population II pulsating stars that serve as distance indicators through their period--luminosity relation. Along with RR Lyrae stars and the tip of the red giant branch, they offer an independent route to the Hubble constant, helping assess systematic uncertainties in its determination. We aim to investigate the impact of chemical composition on T2Cs' period--luminosity relations by building a homogeneous spectroscopic sample of Galactic T2Cs with iron and oxygen abundances. We observed 80 Galactic T2Cs with UVES at the ESO Very Large Telescope. For 74 stars, we derived stellar parameters and iron and oxygen abundances through a self-consistent spectroscopic analysis based on equivalent widths of absorption lines. This sample nearly doubles the number of T2Cs with spectroscopic metallicity measurements available in the literature. We used these abundances to test theoretical predictions for the instability strip and, together with $Gaia$ parallaxes, to derive Period--Wesenheit--metallicity (PWZ) relations. In agreement with theoretical predictions, the metallicity coefficient ($γ$) is small and statistically consistent with zero in all relations, ranging from approximately $-0.02$ to $+0.17$ mag dex$^{-1}$. We also estimated distances to 22 Galactic Globular Clusters hosting T2Cs, finding agreement within uncertainties with independent literature estimates. Our results show that metallicity has, at most, a minor impact on T2Cs' pulsation properties and distance scale, supporting their reliability as Population II distance indicators.

title: Decodability Is Not Validity: Evaluating Nuisance Sensitivity in Language Model Concept Probes
abstract: Two concept probes can be equally accurate at predicting a concept from a language model's hidden states while their scores contain different mixtures of the target concept and a correlated nuisance attribute. In four target--nuisance settings (two aspect sentiments in CEBaB; occupation and gender in BiasBios; Amazon review sentiment with negation, and with first-person framing), two LLMs, and a population of concept extractors, we compare decodability with discriminant evidence: the score's dependence on the nuisance at fixed target, and its response to input edits intended to change only the nuisance, filtered by two LLM judges and compared against placebo edits. Under correlated training data, extractors that are statistically equivalent in held-out AUROC differ up to several-fold in nuisance sensitivity in three of the four settings, and decodability is not a reliable proxy for it: their rank correlation changes sign across settings. The effect follows the probe's training data, not the nuisance's natural association with the target: first-person framing, unrelated to sentiment in natural reviews, is absorbed at least as much as negation, which co-occurs with negative sentiment, and decorrelated training removes the systematic effect. Selecting extractors with nuisance-aware development diagnostics, which need nuisance labels but no counterfactuals, lowers counterfactual nuisance sensitivity wherever the default choice is sensitive, at a small accuracy cost. Concept measurements should be validated, not just decoded.

title: Search for dark matter axions at 1-2 micro-eV with a RADES-DarkQuantum haloscope at CERN
abstract: The QCD axion remains one of the most compelling candidates for the dark matter of the Universe, yet the mass range around $1$\text{--}\SI{2}{\micro\electronvolt} remains essentially unexplored. In this paper, we describe a proposal to employ CERN's M1 superconducting magnet to deploy a haloscope to perform a search for galactic axion and axion-like particle dark matter providing continuous coverage from approximately 1.2 to 1.8 \SI{}{\micro\electronvolt}. Under conservative assumptions, the experiment can reach the QCD axion band over a significant fraction of the scanned range, while optimistic detector performance would allow sensitivity to benchmark models such as KSVZ and DFSZ over a large part of the explored mass interval. With the current long shut-down of CERN's accelerators providing a unique and timely window, such an experiment will deliver high-impact results even in conservative scenarios and potentially delivering a definitive test of the axion dark matter paradigm in the unexplored $1$\text{--}\SI{2}{\micro\electronvolt} mass range.

title: Nonlinear Interaction and Topological Selection Rules in two Skyrmion Merging: Emergence of Skyrmionium Textures
abstract: The nonlinear interaction of closely spaced magnetic skyrmions remains poorly understood, particularly the conditions governing their merger into a single skyrmion or a stable skyrmionium. Here, we investigate the merging dynamics of two Néel skyrmions using analytical modelling and micromagnetic simulations based on Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert dynamics. We examine the effects of exchange, Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction, anisotropy, and magnetostatic energies by varying the initial separation, polarity, winding number, and skyrmion size. Our results reveal a topological selection rule: skyrmions with identical polarity and opposite winding numbers form a stable skyrmionium at intermediate overlap, while all other configurations relax into a single skyrmion. We also identify a critical radius below which the skyrmionium collapses, showing that its formation requires both the appropriate topology and a minimum size. Energy analysis reveals that the transition involves cooperative relaxation of exchange frustration and redistribution of Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya and magnetostatic energies, leading to a double-domain-wall structure. The resulting skyrmionium exhibits persistent breathing oscillations around an equilibrium radius, confirming its dynamical stability as a metastable state. These findings establish a predictive framework for controlling skyrmion merging and provide design guidelines for engineering skyrmionium textures in chiral magnetic nanostructures.

title: A Sequential Framework for Urban Drone Delivery: Network Design, Vehicle Sizing, and Energy and Cost Assessment
abstract: A sequential engineering framework is presented for urban drone delivery, linking hub location, route planning, mission-specific vehicle sizing, and energy and operating cost assessment. Aggregate origin-destination demand is assumed known a priori. For each hub configuration, the maximum required link distance is minimized, and feasible routes that return to their departure hubs are generated. Route frequencies are determined using mixed-integer linear programming to satisfy delivery demand. The resulting range requirement guides motor-propeller selection and battery sizing to minimize vehicle takeoff mass. Flight distances and frequencies, cruise performance, and vehicle dimensions are combined to estimate monthly energy consumption, fleet size, hub area, staffing, and operating cost. The framework is applied to district-level Seoul delivery data. Increasing the number of hubs from one to four reduces the required range from 30.6 to 21.9 km and vehicle takeoff mass from 8.12 to 6.12 kg. Despite a 21.5% increase in total flight distance, monthly flight energy consumption decreases by 13.1%, from 15.2 to 13.2 MWh. Battery replacement is the largest vehicle-related operating expense, while operating cost per delivery increases from USD 1.18 to USD 2.20 because of higher rent and labor costs at the hubs. Among the designs evaluated, range-matched vehicles achieve the lowest operating cost in the two- and four-hub networks; a longer-range vehicle is least costly in the three-hub network. Sensitivity analyses further examine the effects of delivery demand and operating assumptions. The results demonstrate that reductions in vehicle mass and energy consumption do not necessarily lead to lower system operating cost.

title: Self-Supervised Learning of Local Predictive Directions as a Neural Computation
abstract: Natural sensory dynamics are globally nonlinear but often exhibit simple local geometry, with nearby trajectories evolving preferentially along a small number of predictive directions. We ask how neural circuits could discover this geometry directly from temporal experience. We introduce Local Predictive Directions (LPD), a self-supervised framework that learns local directions whose projections maximally predict near-future trajectory evolution. LPD applies past-future canonical correlation analysis to temporal differences, making the learned representation invariant to translations of the underlying state while avoiding estimation of equilibria or a global dynamical model. To represent systems with multiple predictive regimes, we introduce a non-negative similarity-matching objective, with offline and online algorithms, that partitions trajectory segments into predictive domains, each associated with a distinct local predictive direction. The online algorithm admits a natural neural-network interpretation: the resulting activities provide soft domain assignments, while synaptic weights encode the corresponding local predictive filters. On stochastic nonlinear dynamical systems, LPD recovers the local predictive geometry and partitions trajectories into distinct dynamical regimes. On naturalistic sensory streams, the online algorithm produces center-surround spatial receptive fields and ON/OFF sustained and transient temporal filters resembling those of early visual neurons. Our results suggest that predictive learning can provide a self-supervised mechanism by which neural circuits discover the local geometry of environmental dynamics and represent it in receptive fields.

title: Self-Supervised Diffusion Models for Handwritten Signature Verification via Ruin Reconstruction
abstract: Handwritten signature verification (HSV) is a critical biometric technique in legal and forensic authentication, whose efficacy hinges on the discriminability of signature representations. Current HSV methods predominantly adopt supervised learning to enhance representation quality, leaving self-supervised learning largely unexplored. We propose \emph{SigDiffuser}, a diffusion-based self-supervised framework for signature representation and verification. At its core, \emph{SigDiffuser} introduces a novel pretext task termed \emph{Reconstruction from Ruins (RFR)}, which deliberately ``ruins'' signatures through severe crumpling, obliterating their structural integrity and writing styles. A visual encoder is employed to capture crucial handwriting patterns from intact signature regions, guiding the denoiser to reconstruct the ``ruined'' portions and learning meaningful representations. Additionally, we introduce a \emph{pyramidal feature aggregation module (PFAM)} to bridge the visual encoder and denoiser, enhancing representation quality via hierarchical aggregation and modulation. Extensive experiments on multilingual signature datasets demonstrate that \emph{SigDiffuser} significantly outperforms both state-of-the-art SSL methods and HSV models. We further show that increasing the crumpling severity on signatures effectively improves representation quality. Notably, our work demonstrates that extreme destruction, coupled with self-supervised diffusion models, can yield superior signature representation compared to traditional mild deformations, paving new avenues for HSV and other biometric domains. Code will be publicly available.

title: MV-Sign: Multi-View 3D Motion Integration and Enhanced Text-to-Motion Conditioning for Sign Language Production
abstract: Sign language production (SLP) aims to generate appropriate sign language motion from spoken language text. However, current 3D SLP methods suffer from noisy supervision and weak text conditioning. Specifically, these methods typically rely on pseudo-3D motion data fitted from single-view frontal videos, which introduces severe self-occlusion and loses fine-grained hand details, ultimately degrading downstream production. To overcome these limitations, we propose a comprehensive framework that jointly integrates multi-view 3D motion data and optimizes the text-conditioning pathway. First, we introduce How2Sign-MV3D, a high-fidelity dataset constructed via a novel cross-view curation pipeline that fuses multi-view estimates to resolve occlusions and filter non-signing segments. Second, we design a robust SLP model incorporating a sign-aware spatio-temporal VQ-VAE (ST-VQVAE) for joint body-hand tokenization, a pseudo-gloss adapter, and keyframe-aware retrieval to enhance text-to-motion alignment. Evaluated on the How2Sign benchmark, our framework reduces body and hand DTW-PA-JPE by 32.8% and 20.9% respectively compared to the state-of-the-art. Finally, we release two new high-quality 3D datasets, ASLCitizen-3D and MM-WAuslan-MV3D, alongside SGNify-MV as a multi-view video benchmark to support broader community research.

title: Different Corpora, Different Skills? A Paired Study of Small Language Models
abstract: Small language models are often trained under tight data budgets, where the choice of pretraining corpus may matter as much as model size or training recipe. We compare two contrasting corpora at matched 10-million- and 37-million-word budgets: the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica and the BabyLM 2026 strict pretraining corpus. For each corpus, we train teacher models, distilled 58-million-parameter Baby-Llama students, and no-distillation student ablations, using the same model families, training recipes, and evaluation protocol across corpora. Across BLiMP, BLiMP Supplement, EWoK, Entity Tracking, and COMPS, the corpora produce different skill profiles rather than a single quality ranking. BabyLM 2026 is consistently stronger on linguistic acceptability benchmarks, while Britannica is often stronger on Entity Tracking, a synthetic state-tracking task. The contrast appears across teacher and student models and at both budgets, with the cleanest cross-seed replication in the distilled student comparison. Targeted controls show that the central contrast persists after matching training exposure and at a longer diagnostic context; direct teacher ensembling also does not reproduce the 10M Britannica student's Entity Tracking behavior. Entity Tracking magnitudes nevertheless remain sensitive to training dynamics. For this corpus pair, corpus choice can therefore produce different relative skill profiles at small scale, motivating multi-benchmark evaluation when comparing pretraining data.

title: On bordism classes of symmetric products of surfaces
abstract: We explicitly determine the complex bordism class of the $n$-th symmetric product of a complex curve of genus $g$. In particular, we provide an explicit formula expressing this class as an integral linear combination of bordism classes of products of complex projective spaces. Similarly, we determine the unoriented bordism class of the $n$-th symmetric product of a non-orientable surface of genus $g$ (i.e., $\#_{i=1}^{g+1}\mathbb R P^2$). It turns out that these classes are also expressed as a $\mathbb Z_2$-linear combination of bordism classes of products of even-dimensional real projective spaces. We also give an affirmative answer to a non-orientable version of the Blagojević--Grujić--Živaljević conjecture stating that the topological type of any symmetric product of a noncompact surface of finite type determines the topological type of the surface itself.

title: CMDiff: Left Atrial Scar Segmentation from 3D LGE MRI Using Conditional Mask Diffusion Model: A Feasibility Study
abstract: Late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) cardiac MRI enables non-invasive assessment of left atrial (LA) scar, an imaging marker associated with atrial fibrillation ablation outcome. However, automatic scar segmentation is hindered by low contrast, the thin atrial wall, scarce labels, and extreme class imbalance. Conditional diffusion offers iterative mask generation, but its suitability for sparse 3D LA scar segmentation remains unclear. To address this gap, we propose Conditional Mask Diffusion (CMDiff), which predicts clean masks using a dynamic-encoder-conditioned 3D sinusoidal UNet. We compared CMDiff with a deterministic baseline on identical cases in five-fold cross-validation of 60 scar-labelled public LASCARQS subjects, with 48 training and 12 held-out cases per fold. CMDiff achieved a scar DSC of 0.47 $\pm$ 0.08, HD95 of 12.89 $\pm$ 6.39 mm, and ASD of 1.91 $\pm$ 0.96 mm, compared with deterministic baseline values of 0.51 $\pm$ 0.08, 10.86 $\pm$ 5.39 mm, and 1.58 $\pm$ 1.03 mm, respectively. Under the same implementation, clean-mask prediction performed substantially better than the noise-prediction configuration evaluated in this study. Thus, CMDiff was technically feasible but did not improve segmentation performance: DSC was lower, and both HD95 and ASD were higher. Direct mask diffusion therefore provides an analytical alternative, but not a competitive performance advance for this task. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/jizhang02/CMDiff.

title: Newton Steps are Faster for Linear Complementarity Problems
abstract: Linear Complementarity Problems (LCPs) with sufficient matrices form a well-studied class of problems, dating back from the foundational works of Cottle and Dantzig (1968). LCPs capture convex quadratic programs, and admit reductions from problems such as discounted stochastic games or mean-payoff games. While the original approach for solving these problems was based on pivoting methods, in their 1991 book, Kojima, Megiddo, Noma, and Yoshise introduced an interior point method (IPM) with running time that is polynomial in the input size, but which depends linearly on a certain parameter called the handicap number of the matrix. Despite the ensuing rich literature on sufficient LCP IPMs, the linear dependence on the handicap number has not been improved since then. We present an IPM whose running time depends on the square root of the handicap number. The algorithm can decrease the duality gap by a constant factor in $O\left(\min\left\{\sqrt{n} (1+κ),n^{9/8}\sqrt{1+κ}\right\}\right)$ iterations. Curiously, this can already be achieved using standard Newton updates. We analyze the IPM in a norm defined by a local weighting, where centralizing Newton steps quadratically converge to the central path, without any dependence on the handicap number. The weights arise from a characterization by Rump (Linear Algebra and Its Applications, 1997, 1998, 2003) of the sign-real spectral radius and its relation to sufficiency; another ingredient of our proof is a new operator norm characterization of the handicap number. Moreover, the connection to Rump's work also enables us to show coNP-completeness of testing sufficiency, and approximation hardness of the handicap number.

title: The fixed-point proportion of Lattès maps
abstract: How often does an element of the geometric iterated Galois group of a Lattès map fix a vertex of the tree? Let A/K be an abelian variety over a separably closed field of characteristic 0, G <= Aut(A,0) finite, and alpha an isogeny of degree at least 2 normalising G. The Lattès map on X=A/G has a preimage tree governed by alpha-power torsion; we determine the fixed-point proportion in every dimension. For zeta in G the weight is the reciprocal of the number of fixed points of zeta in alpha-power torsion (zero if infinite); equivalently, it is a product of p-adic absolute values of determinants on the alpha-active subspaces; for scalar alpha=m the proportion is (1/|G|) times the sum over 1 != zeta in G of the product over p dividing m of the p-adic absolute value of det(1 - zeta | H_1(A,Z)). We deduce positivity and vanishing criteria, prove the groups G_infinity are martingale groups, determine the limit law, and reduce groups with translations to the fixed-origin case. In dimension one we determine ten values for scalar multipliers and nontrivial G <= Aut(E,0), and for the eight quadratic Lattès classes the proportions are 1/8, 1/4 and 5/16. Bridy-Jones-Kelsey-Lodge exclude the Lattès case from their main theorem; their Theorem 2.5 periodic-point bound is attained, via reductions modulo split primes p = 1 (mod 4), for the map (x^2+a)/(x^2-a), a^2 = -1, and we settle the exceptional case of the Fariña-Asategui-Radi conjecture.

title: Wigner distribution modeling of nuclear state in NuWro Monte Carlo event generator
abstract: We develop a method to use the Wigner distribution (WD) description of the nuclear initial state of $^{12}$C, $^{16}$O, $^{40}$Ar, and $^{56}$Fe for quasielastic scattering in the NuWro Monte Carlo event generator. We propose two different algorithms to deal with the problem of negative values of the WDs. In our treatment, finite-nucleus WDs provide a correlation between the position and the momentum of bound nucleons that is very different from what is assumed in the standard approaches based on the Fermi gas model and spectral functions. We show that the use of WDs leads to effects that can be measured experimentally and may be relevant for future neutrino oscillation experiments.

title: Thurston algorithm for real entire maps: existence and uniqueness
abstract: This paper deals with the real Thurston pullback algorithm for entire maps with finitely many finite singular values, all real. Given a finite forward-invariant marking containing the singular values and satisfying an interval no-Levy-cycle condition, the pullback is shown to have a unique fixed point and it is shown that every orbit converges to it. The resulting entire map uniquely realises the marked dynamics up to positive affine conjugacy. Thus this paper established Thurston realisation and uniqueness in the setting of real entire maps with a finite postsingular set. As usual, the realisation problem reduces to the existence of a fixed point of the Thurston map $T$ which in the real setting acts on a simplex $W$ of dimension $s-2$ if the required postsingular set consists of $s$ points. The key estimate concerns a finite real preimage interval: when its critical multiplicity is bounded and its endpoint values stay separated from the singular values unless they equal to one, its hyperbolic diameter grows at most double-logarithmically as the separation tends to zero. An expansive marking (absence of Levy cycles) then rules out configurations near the boundary of the simplex whose displacement under the Thurston map is at most a fixed multiple of their distance to the boundary. Using a version of the Brouwer fixed point theorem, this immediately implies that the Thurston map $T$ has a fixed point. The argument permits infinitely many real and non-real critical points and different behaviours as the real variable tends to $+\infty$ and $-\infty$. Additional estimates for fixed labelled inverse branches, which are not strictly necessary for the proof of the Main Theorem, are given in the appendices.

title: Data-quality monitoring of luminosity blocks with ATLAS Open Data: an open benchmark and a learned within-run detector
abstract: Data-quality monitoring at the LHC decides, luminosity block by luminosity block, which collision data enter physics analyses, yet its methods cannot be compared openly because the experiments' monitoring data are not public. We construct a public benchmark from the ATLAS Open Data release of the 2015--2016 proton--proton collisions at $\sqrt{s}=13$~TeV: 1289-bin histograms of reconstructed jets, electrons, photons, muons and the missing transverse momentum computed from them, for 39\,828 luminosity blocks of all 217 runs in the Good Run Lists; eight types of detector defects injected at event level at three strengths; real-data labels from the Good Run Lists and the liquid-argon calorimeter error flag; and a time-ordered protocol in which every detector is trained and calibrated on earlier runs only. Histogram shapes differ far more between runs than within a run (median $χ^2/n_\mathrm{dof}$ of 5.9 against 1.1), so references and autoencoders built across runs fail, and all competitive detectors use residuals with respect to a robust reference of each run. A gradient-boosted classifier on position-invariant features of these residuals, trained on synthetic defects and calibrated by split-conformal prediction, detects 43\% of the luminosity blocks with injected defects at a false-positive rate of 1.0\%, against 25\% for a matched-filter scan and 63\% for a single-histogram test that knows the defect pattern. For defect types excluded from its training, its efficiency falls to 18\%; adding pattern-agnostic synthetic detector failures to the training raises it to 34\%, above the scan, at a cost of three percentage points on the known types.

title: Axis-LoRA: Probing and Adapting Embedding Models for Personal-Memory Retrieval
abstract: As LLMs are increasingly asked questions about a user's personal experiences, retrieval must distinguish memories by time, place, person, and event. Current personal-memory pipelines rely on frozen dense embedding models to embed memories for retrieval, but we find that these models do not capture the four axes well. Swapping a memory's date or place barely shifts its embedding, and a trained projection on top of the frozen embedding does not recover the missing signal. The problem lives inside the model, where each axis is encoded by a distinct attention-head pattern. Guided by these findings, we propose Axis-LoRA, a per-axis adapter that places four LoRA branches inside the embedding model and combines them via a per-query gate. Across three standard embedding models evaluated on LongMemEval, ATM-Bench, and LoCoMo, Axis-LoRA improves 4-benchmark mean R@10 by $+1.28$ to $+1.56$~pp while training only a small fraction of the base parameters on a small axis-counterfactual training set. Code is available at https://github.com/dohoonkim-ai/axis-lora.

title: Recurrence and Uniqueness Criteria for Markov Processes from Moments of Integral-Type Functionals
abstract: We investigate recurrence and uniqueness of continuous-time Markov chains using moments of integral-type functionals. Unlike the classical criteria from Chen (2004) and the Feller-Reuter criterion, we develop general unified conditions for recurrence and uniqueness of Markov processes based on moments of integral-type functionals. The associated criteria follow directly from these conditions whenever the mean functionals can be expressed explicitly. As applications, explicit recurrence and uniqueness criteria are derived for single-birth, single-death, and birth-death processes on trees.

title: Continuous Space-Time Finite Element Simulations for Biomedical Flows with Large Boundary Motion and Time-Periodicity
abstract: We present an axisymmetric continuous simplex space-time finite element method for incompressible fluid flow. Compared to conventional time-stepping methods, the space-time approach has several advantages. First, the motion of the domain is incorporated into the space-time geometry, allowing for large boundary motion without remeshing or projection of the solution. Second, the method allows for time-periodic solutions to be computed directly, without the need to simulate multiple cycles. Third, the space-time mesh can be partitioned in time as well as in space, which enables parallelism in time. The method is demonstrated on an intra-aortic balloon pump (IABP) in a rigid tube. The balloon inflation is modelled based on measured data, and includes a travelling wave along the balloon. The method is able to resolve complex flow features such as jets and recirculation zones. A refinement study shows convergence under temporal, spatial and combined space-time refinement. In weak scaling tests up to 960 ranks, the cost per solver iteration remains approximately constant, and partitioning the mesh into time slabs improves the convergence of the linear solver compared to partitions that cut through both space and time.

title: Sparse Bayesian Sensing for Antenna Arrays with Per-Element Gain, Phase, and Position Errors
abstract: The sensing capabilities of 6G wireless communication systems rely on accurate models of phased-array antennas. However, hardware imperfections can introduce a mismatch between the assumed and the actual array response, leading to performance degradations. To prevent these, we propose a parametric, model-based sparse Bayesian learning (SBL) channel estimation algorithm with integrated self-calibration, which accounts for antenna-position deviations as well as gain and phase offsets. The algorithm learns channel parameters such as delay and direction-of-arrival (DoA), together with per-antenna complex weights and position deviations based on fast variational SBL with dictionary refinement. We derive a marginal-likelihood-based cost function for the antenna position update. The sensing performance is evaluated in terms of the optimal subpattern-assignment (OSPA) metric of the delay and DoA. The proposed method approaches a benchmark based on the derived hybrid Cramér--Rao lower bound (HCRLB) in the considered single-snapshot sensing scenarios. Finally, we investigate the influence of the detection threshold using synthetic and measurement data. On single-snapshot measurements, our algorithm reduces the position OSPA from about 6 m to 0.2 m for an appropriately chosen threshold.

title: GradFlex: a Gradient-Based Method for Weak Lensing Flexion Measurement
abstract: Flexion, the second-order gravitational lensing distortion, probes small-scale mass distribution and complement the cosmic shear measurement. However, its detection is highly challenging due to the faint signal and the contamination arising from the intrinsic galaxy morphology. In this Letter, we present GradFlex, a new method that extracts flexion from the gradient field of galaxy surface brightness distributions without assuming a specific point-spread function model or galaxy morphology. Using surface-brightness conservation, we relate the pre- and post-lensing gradient fields and derive flexion estimators from ensemble-averaged statistics of the corresponding spins. Tests on numerical simulations across diverse galaxy morphologies and multiple noise realizations demonstrate its reliability under realistic observing conditions. Combined with shear measurements, it could tighten constraints on cluster density profiles and enable more detailed studies of substructure than shear alone.

title: Generate-then-Rank: Learning Symbolic Goal Interpretation for Embodied Agents
abstract: Goal interpretation is to translate a natural language instruction into a formal symbolic goal that a planner can execute. It is critical for embodied agents because any error here propagates to every downstream planning and action step. Doing it well requires both generating suitable candidates and reliably selecting among them. We present a two-stage generate-then-rank approach to Goal Interpretation in the Embodied Agent Interface (EAI). First, supervised fine-tuning adapts a Large Language Model (LLM) to EAI's output convention. Second, Candidate-Output Ranking from Errors (CORE) learns preferences over complete outputs from the model's own generated alternatives. We conducted experiments on the household scenes of the Embodied Agent Interface Benchmark. Multiple open source LLMs including DeepSeek-V3 chat, DeepSeek-Reasoner, and Qwen2.5-7B and Qwen2.5-72B were evaluated. The proposed method outperformed the baseline models including LLMs with simple prompting, chain-of-thought, and knowledge graph based approaches.

title: Estimating Spectrum-Free Information Bounds for Generative Surrogates Beyond Conditional Collapse
abstract: Conditional generative surrogates in high-energy physics, such as models that predict reconstructed jets from partons, are often evaluated on $1\text{D}$ marginal divergences among other metrics. Taken alone these metrics can reward conditional collapse. On a CMS simulation benchmark, a sampler that ignores the conditioner beats a trained Mixture Density Network (MDN) on all four target marginals under both KL and Wasserstein-1, and cannot be stably separated from a Conditional Flow Matching (CFM) model on two of the four. We instead score the models with the Continuous Ranked Probability Skill Score (CRPSS) from forecast verification, taking the exact marginal as the reference. We show how global skill depends on the evaluation spectrum, and we also report it within bins of a conditioning variable, where that dependence largely goes away. We then introduce a data-driven $k$-Nearest-Neighbor ($k$-NN) extrapolation that estimates the best CRPS the conditioning information allows. Both models agree with this estimate on all four targets, which suggests that current architectures have reached the information available in the conditioner, at least as far as these per-target scores can tell.

title: Instantiating the Knowledge Plane
abstract: In 2003, Clark et al. proposed the "Knowledge Plane", a layer of intelligent agents that share rich information about network state in order to collaboratively manage the Internet across administrative boundaries. The technology of the day lacked the two capabilities it demanded most: reasoning and unstructured communication. Thus, automated network management has remained largely confined to single domains, while interdomain problems are still resolved by human operators on the phone. We argue that agentic large language models can finally unlock the potential of the Knowledge Plane, but that doing so will require solving new research problems that arise particularly in this decentralized, multi-agent, coopetitive setting that have received limited attention in the literature thus far.

title: STAG-Net: Structure-Aware Attention over Landmark Groups for Lightweight Head Pose Estimation
