WAM-Sim structures persistent context across three temporal and semantic scales: pose-aligned structural tokens encoding persistent road topology, read-only scene tokens supplying geolocated background appearance, and write-once instance tokens preserving individual traffic participant identities across occlusions and chunk boundaries. To restore visual sharpness and physical plausibility degraded by multi-scale conditioning, we introduce an online post-training framework that optimizes self-generated rollouts via flow-matching RL guided by hierarchy-aligned visual rewards and a vision-language model physical judge. The invariant memory empirically confines policy optimization within the anchored context, helping suppress semantic collapse and reward hacking, while online RL systematically enforces physical commonsense and fine-grained visual fidelity. On the nuScenes benchmark, WAM-Sim achieves a superior generation fidelity (FID=3.47, FVD=25.72) and strong downstream perception performance (24.16 mAP, 71.23 road mIoU). On minute-scale rollouts of self-collected data, WAM-Sim substantially mitigates structural and identity drift, preserving high scene similarity and subject identity coherence across extended horizons. Project page: https://fudan-generative-vision.github.io/WAM-Sim.

title: CardioLM: A multilingual suite of small language models for the cardiology domain
abstract: Background: Cardiovascular care generates large volumes of clinical free-text documentation in local languages. However, clinical natural language processing (NLP) resources remain concentrated in English, and no existing benchmark is cardiology-specific, multilingual, and broad in entity coverage. Methods: We present two contributions. The first is CardioCCC, a corpus of 508 cardiology case reports originally published in Spanish and extended to Czech, Dutch, English, Italian, Romanian, and Swedish through machine translation, annotation projection, and clinician review, with annotations covering diseases, symptoms, procedures, and medications. The second is CardioLM, comprising CardioBERTa, a set of language-specific encoders obtained by continued pretraining on cardiology and biomedical corpora, and CardioNER, a set of named entity recognition (NER) models fine-tuned on CardioCCC. Results: Cardiology-specific pretraining reduced pseudo-perplexity by up to a factor of eight, yet changed strict span-level F1 by at most 0.04, with benefits concentrated in languages whose backbones lacked biomedical coverage. The jointly trained multilingual XLM-RoBERTa-large models achieved the best strict F1 in nearly every language and entity type, exceeding the strongest monolingual system by up to 0.13 F1. A large share of residual errors concerned boundary detection: relaxed matching recovered 0.10-0.23 F1 for disease, procedure, and symptom, but only 0.01-0.07 for medication. Clinicians rated CardioNER well above a rule- and dictionary-based baseline, with the mean rating across entity types rising from 26% to 73%. Conclusions: Specialty-specific pretraining is not the decisive factor for downstream entity recognition, whereas multilingual joint training yields the strongest results in nearly all settings and a simpler deployment path for multi-country clinical information extraction.

title: IDPrior: Decoupling Identity Generation from Facial Image Synthesis
abstract: Large-scale identity-labeled face datasets are essential for training modern face recognition models, yet collecting and annotating such data is costly and raises privacy and ethical concerns. Existing synthetic face generation methods typically derive identities from predefined class labels, unconditional image generation, or predefined latent sampling strategies, without explicitly modeling the underlying distribution of facial identities. In this paper, we propose IDPrior, a two-stage framework that decouples identity generation from image synthesis. We first learn a diffusion prior in the embedding space of a pretrained face recognition model to model the distribution of facial identities and generate novel identity embeddings. These embeddings are then used to condition a pretrained identity-conditioned diffusion model (DM), enabling the synthesis of multiple images of the same identity. This modular design provides a scalable approach to identity generation while remaining compatible with existing and future identity-conditioned DMs. Experiments indicate that IDPrior generates diverse and well-separated identities while maintaining a closer correspondence to the distribution of authentic identities. Face recognition models trained on datasets generated using IDPrior-generated identities achieve competitive or improved performance compared with existing synthetic-data-based methods across multiple face verification benchmarks. Code and generated datasets are publicly available at https://github.com/fdbtrs/IDperturb.

title: Bouncing or Merging in Drop-Bath Impacts
abstract: When a liquid drop impacts a liquid surface, it deforms the surface, trapping a thin layer of air between drop and bath. The drop then either bounces off the bath or, if the gas film ruptures, merges with it. We present a model for drop-bath impacts that can accurately predict whether a drop will bounce or merge, and compare it to theory-driven experiments. The model incorporates a lubrication description of the deforming trapped gas film, which accounts for its significant curvature, within a finite-element framework. Capturing this outcome requires micro- and nano-scale physics: van der Waals-driven disjoining pressure and gas-kinetic effects that depend on the mean free path of the gas. Using only independently measured material parameters, we obtain the first quantitative agreement with experiment for the critical impact speed separating bounce from merge. We explore the behaviour of drop-bath impacts at low ambient air pressure, and then investigate the bounce-merge threshold for impacts onto shallow baths and thin films, finding a bounce-merge-bounce-merge transition as the bath depth decreases.

title: P-curvature from a TQFT viewpoint
abstract: This paper is motivated by the recent discovery, in symplectic topology, of a relation (partly proved, partly conjectural) between quantum connection and quantum Steenrod operations. We introduce an abstract TQFT framework, based on certain features of the definition of deformed symplectic cohomology, in which such a relation holds generally.

title: Constructive Probability, Foundations and Numerical Analysis for mathematical finance and machine learning
abstract: This monograph sets out a constructive theory of stochastic processes in the continuum, in the sense of constructive field theory: the continuum is not postulated but reached as the limit of a sequence of lattice approximations, with the renormalisation the limit requires exhibited rather than assumed, and the limit controlled by estimates that can be checked. The primitive object is not a sigma-algebra but de Finetti's prevision, the price of finitely many gambles at a fixed resolution, which coherence turns into a conditional expectation. The theorem at the centre of the book, called plainly the fundamental theorem, is at once de Finetti's fundamental theorem of probability, the fundamental theorem of Bayesian statistics, and the one-period fundamental theorem of asset pricing; the financial vocabulary is a convenience only. The applications are two, mathematical finance and machine learning, and they are one mathematics read in opposite directions: an assessment is a price in the one and a prediction in the other, and both are computed by one adjoint recursion, the adjoint of a propagation in the first case and backpropagation in the second. Carried through, the two directions give sharp rates of convergence rather than asymptotic orders: for the moments of Ito diffusions, for the value function of Feynman-Kac semigroups, and for the measure changes of the fundamental theorem, the last as a limit theorem for reweighted generators, under a condition keeping the reweighting well behaved. A measure change is thus calculated, not postulated: a lattice approximation with Farkas' lemma computes it, completeness makes it unique, and the passage to the continuum is earned by the regularity of what is computed. Sixty-seven Python scripts regenerate every numerical table, and much of the finite-dimensional core of the argument has been verified in Lean 4.

title: tok: a textual concrete syntax of BPMN and DMN for humans and AI agents
abstract: tok is a plain-text notation for Business Process Model and Notation (BPMN) 2.0.2 process models and Decision Model and Notation (DMN) 1.5 decisions. One engine checks a tok document against both standards, compiles the document to XML with an automatic diagram, and serves language-model applications through the Model Context Protocol. The paper classifies the notation as an alternative concrete syntax of the BPMN and DMN metamodels and reports one study. A tok model takes 2.2 times fewer tokens than the smallest BPMN XML of 893 files exported by 37 tools and 7.7 times fewer than the files as exported. The checker signals 98.2% of 1,411 injected faults, against 85.8% for the XML Schema with bpmnlint. Four language models new to tok write valid tok from a one-page reference for 85.7 to 100% of 87 process descriptions from two datasets and valid BPMN XML for every description, and the strongest model writes tok with 25% and 19% fewer tokens than BPMN XML. As agents with a lean skill and one checker tool, the models write valid tok for 97.6 to 100% of the descriptions, the strongest model spends 21% and 14% fewer tokens on tok than on BPMN XML, and a skill which sends the model to read the reference through a tool costs 1.7 to 2.8 times the tokens of the lean skill. Of 47 event logs simulated from public models, 44 fit their source models, and tok imports every model discovered from the logs.

title: Operational Indirect Rate-Distortion Functions for Classification Tasks
abstract: In goal-oriented communications, indirect source coding involves two sources: a semantic source $X$ and an observation $Z$, which is the only source available at the encoder. In this paper, we consider this framework for classification, where the decoder only needs to reconstruct $X$. We argue that the gap between the indirect rate-distortion function and the performance of practical learned coding schemes, such as variational information bottleneck (VIB) and variational autoencoder (VAE) architectures, comes from three effects: the latent representation, the choice of the deep neural network (DNN) architecture and training loss, and whether the encoder is aware of the task. To quantify these effects, we introduce four operational rate-distortion functions that account for the DNN architecture and the training loss, and we establish a hierarchy among them. We then derive these functions for a Gaussian mixture source, where $X$ is the mixture state. Numerical results, both for the Gaussian mixture and for practical coding schemes on the CIFAR-100 dataset, quantify the rate loss incurred by each effect.

title: ChemE-as-Code: An Open-Source Platform for Agentic AI in Chemical Engineering
abstract: ChemE-as-Code provides an open-source environment in which AI agents built on large language models (LLMs) can carry out chemical engineering work and engineers can check it. Its calculation tools range from catalysis through process simulation to plant layout, HAZOP and life cycle assessment, and skills tell a general-purpose agent how to use them. Engineering files are linked, machine-readable and versioned in Git; calculations run outside the LLM, each value records its origin, and automated checks report inconsistencies and out-of-date results by file and line. In an illustrative ammonia case, agents developed a written task into a preliminary basic-engineering package (simulation files, P&IDs, layout, HAZOP, datasheets, relief) for USD 224 of API cost in the design sessions. Planted faults and engineering changes show that the checks find what their rules cover and miss the rest, so they guide human review rather than replace it. No independent engineer has reviewed the design.

title: Circe: Training-Free LLM Self-Evaluation via Component Interaction Consistency
abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in real-world applications, evaluating the correctness of their responses is crucial for reliable use. However, such evaluation is challenging because reference answers are rarely available in practice. Existing reference-free methods mainly rely on output signals, which may assign high scores to incorrect responses and thus do not necessarily reflect correctness. This motivates exploring the model's internal computation for complementary correctness signals. Recent studies exploit internal states, but they mainly analyze hidden-state trajectories across layers, which record only the combined updates of attention and feed-forward networks (FFNs) and overlook how these components interact. We therefore propose Circe, a training-free self-evaluation method that assesses a response using both internal and external signals, without reference answers or repeated sampling. For internal signals, we first introduce component interaction consistency (CIC), which measures the directional alignment between attention updates in earlier layers and attention-induced FFN output changes in later layers. We further incorporate representation geometry (RG) to characterize normalized displacement and angular changes along layerwise hidden-state trajectories. For the external signal, we convert the mean negative log-likelihood of generated tokens into a bounded likelihood confidence (LC) score. Finally, we fuse CIC, RG, and LC into a unified correctness score. Experiments on five LLMs and six benchmarks across four domains show that our method distinguishes correct from incorrect responses more effectively than existing baselines, and generalizes to multilingual, multimodal, and open-world settings.

title: Beyond the Keyword: A Human-Annotated Benchmark for Arabic Anxiety-Related Discourse
abstract: Keyword retrieval returns expressions of personal anxiety together with many other uses of anxiety-related language. We present a benchmark of 1,000 Arabic Twitter/X posts retrieved with the keyword qalaq ("anxiety/worry") and annotated for six discourse functions. Two native Arabic-speaking annotators labeled every post independently, reaching 51.1% raw agreement (Cohen's $κ= 0.378$). We then reviewed all 489 disagreements and all 511 agreements under the same guidelines. The review changed 120 of the agreed labels (23.5%), which shows that agreements need auditing as well as disagreements. The final labels form a consensus reference; on a random sample of 200 posts, an additional annotator agreed with it on 60.5% of posts ($κ= 0.517$). Against this reference, Fanar-C-2-27B reaches 79.8% accuracy and macro-F1 0.784 ($κ= 0.749$). Its errors concentrate in the residual category (41.1% of errors; precision 0.905, recall 0.447), whose definition is internally inconsistent in the executed prompt, so the low recall cannot be attributed to the model alone. Sociopolitical Anxiety (27.1%) outnumbers Personal Emotional Expression (22.0%); these are assignment proportions in the sample, not estimates of prevalence or retrieval precision. We release the guidelines, a residual-subtype scheme, a fixed data split, label provenance, and evaluation code.

title: Leakage- and Label-Aware Benchmarking of Class-Imbalance Strategies for Multimodal Chest X-Ray and EHR Classification
abstract: Benchmarks of class-imbalance strategies for multimodal chest X-ray (CXR) and electronic health record (EHR) prediction are often evaluated on record-level splits of cohorts in which one patient contributes several radiographs. We audit such a benchmark on 29,083 MIMIC-CXR radiographs of 10,479 patients with eight diagnosis targets. First, the record-split benchmark was misleading: a lookup table that copies the label of a development-set radiograph with the same EHR vector nearly matched the best model, and on unseen patients every model fell to the level of predicting every case positive. Second, tracing the labels back to MIMIC-IV explained why: each patient's labels are keyword matches on the diagnosis codes of a single admission, copied, with one EHR vector per patient, to all of the patient's radiographs, so about a third of the radiographs carry labels that differ from the codes of their own admission. Third, under patient-separated evaluation with admission-aligned and rule-refined labels, the initial conclusions do not hold: in the evaluated configurations no imbalance strategy raised the observed mean macro F2 over no augmentation by more than 0.01, tuned tree ensembles showed no consistent advantage over tuned logistic regression, and the released EHR variables stayed at the level of the all-positive baseline, whereas the diagnostic history available at imaging time and image embeddings exceeded it, including, with rule-refined labels, a CheXpert-trained encoder that never saw these radiographs; RAD-DINO had seen 96.6% of them during self-supervised pretraining. Adding either encoder to the diagnostic history gave no statistically significant F2 gain; exploratory AUROC gains were significant with RAD-DINO but not with DenseNet. We provide reusable diagnostics, a leakage-aware protocol and a checklist.

title: Requirements Nobody Wrote Down: Emergence in a Public-Sector ML Pipeline
abstract: Governments increasingly use machine learning (ML) to handle data volumes beyond their analytical capacity, yet little is known about how requirements arise and evolve as an ML experiment moves toward operational use. Requirements Engineering (RE) for ML often assumes that requirements can be elicited upfront; in the public sector, however, demands arrive vague, stakeholders speak different professional languages, and what counts as a ``good'' result is unknown in advance. We report a 15-month case study of a thematic classification pipeline for Brazil's national digital participation platform, which holds over 60,000 citizen proposals, triangulating 43 project artifacts with interviews of six project participants. Institutional demands arrived as broad goals, endorsed but not sponsored, and only 40\% of the 95 reconstructed requirements and criteria were ever formalized. The pipeline's key requirements emerged largely from experiments, model outputs, and integration work, shaped by technical decisions and institutional constraints; the central one, the classification categories, was settled by a government taxonomy chosen for its institutional legitimacy. Acceptance relied on technical metrics, domain judgment, and political assessment, without shared thresholds or validation of usefulness in practice. In public-sector ML, technical and institutional artifacts thus act as elicitation instruments, and experimentation and integration belong to the requirements process.

title: Invariance before structure: two modes of emergent compression in representation learning
abstract: Learned representations show striking invariance across biological and artificial neural networks, with different substrates and variations driven by drift, heterogeneity and initialisation. To understand this invariance, we propose Emergent Adaptive Representation Learning (EARL), a framework that distinguishes two modes of emergence in learned representations: state-space compression, where a learned representation gains predictive power over its own future beyond what the network's units can predict individually, and parameter-space compression, where networks with different micro-level parameters converge to the same representation. We formalise both as Fisher sensitivities and introduce ensemble-level information-theoretic measures for each. In a recurrent reservoir with a trained bottleneck, parameter-space compression rises within the first few epochs of training and partly independently of the task, whereas state-space compression rises about 30 epochs later and only when the network begins to learn the temporal structure of the task. These results suggest that invariance to the substrate and task-specific emergent structure are acquired in distinct phases of learning.

title: A Behavioural Framework for Predicting and Understanding Loss of Control in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Systems
abstract: Frontier artificial intelligence (AI) systems are increasingly operating over longer horizons with diminishing human oversight, raising the risk of loss of control: systems acting beyond effective human control with potentially irreversible consequences. Because such failures may become observable only after containment is difficult, they must be assessed prospectively. We introduce a behavioural framework that decomposes loss-of-control risk into three factors: misaligned motive, harm-enabling capability, and monitoring evasion. We operationalise these factors through 13 measurable aspects and 29 evaluation tasks, whose scores are combined into a single loss-of-control (LoC) score. Across 13 frontier models, the LoC score shows strong prospective validity, correlating with failure rates in contained long-horizon risk scenarios (Pearson r = 0.84). Risk varies systematically across models and cannot be explained by capability alone. We further show that the framework can guide targeted mitigations: fine-tuning and monitoring directed at diagnosed vulnerabilities reduce failure rates while largely preserving general performance. These results provide a practical basis for predicting, understanding, and mitigating loss-of-control risk before it materialises.

title: Phase-Matched Design of Pinching-Antenna Elements on a 60-GHz Dielectric Rod Waveguide
abstract: The radiation of pinching antennas, dielectric elements placed on a dielectric waveguide, depends on the element shape. We explain it with a phase-matching, or prism-coupler, picture: the guided rod mode couples into the denser antenna plate at an angle set by the plate-mode effective index, about 31 degrees at 60 GHz, and radiates through the face it reaches first. This yields a simple sizing rule linking element height to contact length. Rectangular, isosceles and right-triangular elements of equal contact length and height are compared from 53 to 67 GHz in full-wave openEMS simulations including the waveguide-to-rod transitions. The rectangle peaks sharply at the rule, reaching 15.9 dBi. The right triangle keeps its gain within 0.7 dB and its side lobes at least 10 dB down over a two-to-one height range. At the rule, both outperform the isosceles element by 1.2 to 2.1 dB, and all remain matched.

title: Rotation Is Token-Blind: A Structural Criterion for Post-Training Quantization of Feed-Forward Geometry Transformers
abstract: Feed-forward 3D models use Transformers to predict camera poses, depth, and structure in one pass, avoiding iterative multi-view optimization. Long sequences and deep attention incur high compute and memory costs, motivating Post-Training Quantization (PTQ) for deployment. Existing PTQ methods mainly suppress channel-wise outliers by smoothing or orthogonal rotation. Geometry Transformers introduce a different challenge: heterogeneous token types share one activation quantization grid. A few special tokens may exert high leverage over global outputs and be updated by only a subset of blocks. Token-blind transforms, which apply the same transformation to every token, reduce overall quantization error but cannot remove differentiated degradation across token types. We propose QMapAnything, a structure-aware PTQ framework. We cast floating-point-preserving rotation and smoothing as a token-blind reparameterization group, and prove that they yield common-mode gains while leaving relative token SNR unchanged. We introduce a statistic $Γ$ that combines a special token's quantization disadvantage and output leverage to predict whether differentiated bias correction is needed beyond rotation. Experiments on geometric benchmarks show that W4A8 closely matches full-precision performance. Under W8A8, peak memory falls by $2.2$--$3.1\times$ versus FP32, with up to $3.1\times$ speedup on real hardware. These results provide a principled and efficient approach to deploying feed-forward 3D reconstruction models in resource-constrained edges.

title: A Note on the Cut-Locus-Corrected Fréchet Mean Central Limit Theorem
abstract: We record two observations concerning \cite{HLW24}. First, the proof of its Theorem~1 yields the population linearization (13)--(14) at \textit{any critical point} of the Fréchet function $F_μ$, under its remaining geometric and measure-theoretic assumptions; neither \textit{isolation} nor a \textit{nonsingular} Hessian of $F_μ$ is needed. Second, its Theorem~2 is given a shorter proof by applying the M-estimator theorem \cite[Theorem~5.23, pp.~53--54]{vdV98} to negative squared distance in normal coordinates, as opposed to the Donsker argument used there. We verify the pointwise differentiability, local square-integrable Lipschitz bound, second order expansion of population loss, consistency, and empirical maximization hypotheses. The resulting covariance retains the cut-locus correction. The same argument applies to a measurable selection of \textit{local} sample Fréchet minima when the population Hessian is positive definite.

title: Can $n_s$ hint at a parity-odd sector of gravity?
abstract: We study slow-roll inflation in the context of metric-affine gravity. We consider the most general projectively invariant metric-affine theory at most quadratic in the distortion and linear in curvature with no propagating torsion and non-metricity and couple it non-minimally to a scalar field. We focus on the class of $ξ$-attractors, in which a single function $f(ϕ)$ fixes the whole scalar sector. Integrating out the non-dynamical distortion generates a correction to the kinetic term $k(ϕ)$ which is $f'(ϕ)^2$ times a ratio of polynomials in $f(ϕ)$. The new kinetic term can develop poles at finite field values, where the distortion field equations degenerate. We classify the poles and derive the conditions on the effective couplings for poles of order $p=2$ and $p=3$, the maximal order allowed in this setting. We then proceed to study inflation. Second-order poles realize $α$-attractors with $α$ fixed by the residue and are already available in the parity-even sector of the theory. Third-order poles instead require the parity-odd sector: whenever the parity-odd quadratic couplings vanish, the kinetic function splits into two independent terms with poles of order at most $p=2$. Third-order pole-inflation, as we confirm numerically for $f(ϕ)\proptoϕ^2$, yields $r\propto N_*^{-3/2}$ with a tunable amplitude and $n_s\simeq 1-\tfrac{3}{2N_*}$, a spectral index mildly larger than the $α$-attractor prediction and well centered in the region preferred by the current combination of ACT, SPT and DESI data. Moreover, when inflation happens far away from the pole we also find a further universal attractor, an inverse-linear plateau, with $n_s \simeq 1-\frac{4}{3N_*}$ and $r\propto N_*^{-4/3}$, testable with the forthcoming BICEP/Keck observations.

title: On the Spectral Dependence of Decentralized Stochastic Gradient Tracking
abstract: We study how the spectral geometry of the mixing matrix enters the convergence of decentralized stochastic gradient tracking (GT) for smooth strongly convex problems. General bounds contain the factor $Δ_λ^{-3}$ in the higher-order stochastic term, where $Δ_λ$ is the absolute spectral gap. We show that, even for two agents with identical quadratic objectives, the exact steady-state mean-square disagreement scales as $α^2σ^2Δ_λ^{-3}$ as the nontrivial eigenvalue approaches $-1$, provided the stepsize $α$ is sufficiently small relative to the gap. Here $σ^2$ is the gradient-noise variance. By unrolling the disagreement recursion, we establish a stochastic bound that averages all nontrivial eigenvalue contributions for diagonalizable mixing matrices, up to an eigenvector conditioning factor. As a real or complex eigenvalue approaches the unit circle away from $1$, its contribution grows as the inverse cube of its distance to the circle; growth can be slower near $1$. For symmetric mixing with gaps $p$ at $1$ and $ν$ at $-1$, the weighted sum $θ_1/p+θ_2/ν^3$ replaces the prior factor $(Δ_λν^2)^{-1}$. For $N$ agents, $Nθ_1$ and $Nθ_2$ count the nonnegative and negative nontrivial eigenvalues, respectively. On a symmetric family, a finite-horizon lower bound for the average iterate matches the worst-case factor $p^{-1}+ν^{-3}$ up to universal constants. Numerical experiments confirm the predicted scaling.

title: CoRD: Coupled Rollouts Fill the Blind Spot of On-Policy Distillation
abstract: On-policy distillation trains a student on its own rollouts, so states the teacher would reach but the student does not are seldom supervised. We introduce CoRD (coupled-rollout distillation), which keeps the on-policy loss and moves only the distribution of training states toward the teacher, drawing rollouts from a geometric interpolation of student and teacher through the maximal coupling of speculative decoding. The coupling keeps the student's token wherever the two distributions agree and otherwise substitutes a token from the part of the target the student underweights, so interventions are as rare as any exact sampler allows and recede as the student learns. Across six base students from two model families (Qwen3 and Qwen3.5, 0.6B to 4B), CoRD raises average pass@1 over on-policy distillation by 0.9 to 2.0 points and pass@8 by 1.2 to 3.4 points on five public math benchmarks at equal steps and data. On frozen teacher-reached states, a 4B student trained with CoRD reaches in 16 steps a gap closure that on-policy distillation does not reach in 80, and substitution rules intervening at least as often in other directions fall short of CoRD.

title: Monopoles, Scattering and Generalized Symmetries on a Quantum Computer
abstract: Quantum computers have advanced to the stage that interesting many-body quantum phenomena can be observed. A striking example is the magnetic monopole paradox, a problem that was only solved recently using the language of generalized symmetries. Here we demonstrate a quantum spin chain analogue of magnetic monopole scattering on Quantinuum System Model H2. We implement a novel protocol for preparing a localized quasiparticle wavepacket on top of the ground state. By combining this protocol with time evolution across a duality defect, we efficiently convert local particles into non-local string-like excitations. We demonstrate this particle-to-string conversion in the transverse-field Ising model and a symmetry-protected topological (SPT) phase of the cluster model. Our results establish duality defects and generalized symmetries as practical resources for preparing and probing non-local excitations on quantum hardware.

title: Bri3D: Bridging the Object-Scene Gap in Single-Image 3D Generation via Scene-Anchor
abstract: Generating compositional 3D scenes from a single image requires recovering detailed object geometry and coherent spatial arrangements. Existing object-to-scene methods, including SAM3D and MIDI, extend object generation through image-context reasoning or inter-instance modeling. Coordinating objects remains challenging with limited scene-level supervision. Directly extending object-centric generators to entire scenes can degrade geometry and fail to preserve instance scale, orientation, and pose. We propose Bri3D, a framework bridging scene-level structural reasoning and object-level generative priors through instance-aware voxel scene anchors. Bri3D predicts a color-coded scene scaffold encoding coarse object geometry and spatial arrangements. Each instance is extracted as a scene anchor and refined into a pose-preserving, prior-compatible voxel support, enabling a frozen object generator to synthesize detailed textured geometry in the anchor-defined spatial reference. This coarse-to-fine design separates scene organization from object-scale detail synthesis, focusing scene-level training on spatial organization and anchor refinement while reusing pretrained object priors. Experiments demonstrate improvements in scene layout, object geometry, visual quality, and generalization. Bri3D predicts scene layouts efficiently; full scene generation is faster than SceneGen and SAM3D.

title: TCSExam: Evaluating Frontier LLMs on the Full Range of TCS Research
abstract: Can large language models (LLMs) advance theoretical computer science and resolve its long-standing open conjectures? To study progress toward this goal, we introduce TCSExam, a unified framework and benchmark covering the full range of TCS research. It evaluates theorem proving, solver engineering, and constructions alongside direct attempts to resolve open conjectures, capturing both concrete research accomplishments and progress toward long-standing research goals. TCSExam-Full contains 100 expert-reviewed tasks, with submissions checked by the Lean kernel or an executable task checker. TCSExam-Lite selects 20 tasks, five per track, reducing the number of task attempts by 80% at the same per-attempt budget. We evaluate eight agents on Full and nine on Lite. The TCSExam Index combines all four tracks: GPT-6 Astra leads Full (71.9), and Opus 5.5 leads Lite (72.3). Full and Lite rankings are strongly aligned across eight shared agents (Spearman's $ρ=0.93$), supporting Lite as a compact, discriminative benchmark. The evaluations yield improved solver outputs and mathematical constructions, together with independently verified special cases and bounds from open-conjecture attempts. TCSExam provides an extensible framework with task sources, Docker build recipes, and evaluation tools for reproducible use.

title: Multiplicity via symmetry for the Minkowski mean curvature equation: Dirichlet and Neumann problems
abstract: We consider the Minkowski mean curvature equation $$ -\operatorname{div}\left(\frac{\nabla u}{\sqrt{1-|\nabla u|^2}}\right) =λu+μh(x,u) \quad \text{in } Ω, \quad \mathcal B u = 0 \quad \text{on } \partial Ω, $$ where $\mathcal B \in \{ \mathcal D, \mathcal N \}$ is a Dirichlet or Neumann boundary condition and $Ω$ is a smooth bounded domain, required to be convex in the Neumann case. Moreover, $λ, μ\geq0$ are parameters, and $h(x,u)$ is odd with respect to $u$ and positive for $u > 0$. Using minmax methods in nonsmooth critical point theory, we prove that $λ>λ^\mathcal B_k$ yields at least $k$ pairs of nontrivial solutions with negative energy for every $μ\geq0$, where $λ_k^\mathcal B$ are the corresponding Laplacian eigenvalues, indexed by $λ^\mathcal B_0=0$. Moreover, if $H(x,u):=\int_0^u h(x,t)\,dt=o(u^2)$ as $u\to0$, we prove that for $λ\in[λ^\mathcal B_k,λ^\mathcal B_{k+1})$ and every $j\geq\max\{1,k\}$, sufficiently large $μ$ yields at least $2j-k$ distinct pairs of solutions: $j$ with negative energy and $j-k$ with positive energy.

title: Time-Indexed Skill Success Models for Latency-Aware Skill Selection and Timing in Dynamic Manipulation
abstract: Robots that manipulate moving objects act on observations that are outdated when the chosen skill starts, and the best skill can change within a few hundred milliseconds. Skill competence models, however, predict success for a launch at the moment of observation. We propose time-indexed skill success models, which predict whole-task success when a skill is launched after a given delay. Trained on rollouts branched at a grid of launch delays, they let a receding-horizon planner select both the skill and its launch time under fixed or random latency. In a MuJoCo study in which a UR5e captures a sliding puck with three skills, the planner exceeded a static competence model by 2.8 to 6.2 percentage points at 100 to 300 ms of latency, including when that model was evaluated on point or sampled forecasts of the launch state. Across five complete runs (three training seeds and two distribution shifts), all 80 paired 95% intervals against four baselines excluded zero. On delayed launches, the time-indexed model was calibrated (expected calibration error 0.009 against 0.239), and pausing the world during latency overstated success by up to 23 points. On a real UR5e that captures a rolling ball after 0.2 s of injected latency, a static model trained in a hardware-matched simulator predicted 99% success on a prespecified subset of 35 delayed launches that it rated at least 0.8. Of these, 63% succeeded (95% interval 46 to 77%), and the time-indexed model predicted 56%. In this single-skill, predictable regime, a matched physics-based forecast was also well calibrated.

title: Reversible Dynamics, Asymmetric Actions: Parking as a Trajectory-Level Affordance
abstract: Drivers are often told to back into a tight parking space, not drive in nose first. The advice looks paradoxical, because a slow car is dynamically reversible: reverse its speed and replay the steering backward, and it retraces a feasible path. Played backward, though, reverse-in shows a car driving forward out of the space. Reverse-in and forward-in are different tasks: they share a start position but end facing opposite ways. We separate three clearances between car and obstacles. Static fit $F$ is the clearance the parked car keeps at its best acceptable destination pose. Eventual access $A_\infty$ is the clearance it can keep all the way there with unlimited corrections. Resource-bounded access $A_K$ is the clearance that survives a budget of $K$ reversals, switches between forward and reverse. They satisfy $F\ge A_\infty\ge A_K$. In one fully specified scene (one car, bay, aisle and start), a certified argument proves $A_\infty=F=0.5000$ m for both tasks. In this scene, all certified forward/reverse asymmetry therefore arises at finite $K$: it lies in how many corrections each task needs, not in the clearance either can eventually keep. With one reversal, an explicit path gives reverse-in at least $0.4410$ m clearance. A certified reachability argument caps forward-in's one-reversal clearance at $d_0<0.1720002$ m. With two reversals, forward-in gets at least $0.2833$ m. To keep a clearance strictly above any $d$ with $d_0\le d<0.2833$ m, reverse-in thus needs exactly one reversal and forward-in exactly two when both tasks move forward first. If both move in reverse first, the counts are two and three. The contrast depends on the start position (Section 4.15). Proposed experiments test whether observers distinguish fit, eventual access and budgeted access. They compare these with simpler cues, such as how the turning body sweeps, and learned manoeuvre labels.

title: High resolution 3D localization of ultrasound sparse sources using a SAGE algorithm
abstract: Reliable localization and characterization of cavitation activity are central to many ultrasound imaging and therapy monitoring applications. Passive acoustic mapping (PAM) can estimate cavitation distributions without prior assumptions but remains limited by the system point spread function. While advanced PAM methods improve spatial resolution, their performance may degrade for transient emissions with uncertain emission times. In this work, we propose a parametric source localization framework based on the Space-Alternating Generalized Expectation-Maximization (SAGE) algorithm to estimate source positions and emitted waveforms directly from array channel data. A greedy source extraction and localization procedure is first used to initialize the model order and source parameters, after which SAGE iteratively refines each source estimate. The proposed method was validated on 49 simulated acquisitions containing up to seven simultaneously emitting sources with emission time uncertainties of 12 microseconds, achieving a source localization precision of 0.24 mm (standard deviation of the total localization error). Experimental evaluation on proton-induced nanodroplet vaporization data acquired with an ultrasound matrix array demonstrated improved spatial resolution compared to a beamforming-based approach and sub-millimeter agreement between vaporization maps and the proton distribution in all three spatial dimensions. These results highlight the potential of parametric source localization for high-resolution proton therapy monitoring and provide a general framework for the localization of simultaneously emitting sparse ultrasound sources.

title: Autler-townes energy-level engineering for high-quality all-microwave qubit gate
abstract: High-fidelity entangling gates are essential for realizing large-scale fault-tolerant superconducting quantum computing, yet existing approaches are limited: frequency-tuning techniques induce decoherence, while all-microwave-driven schemes suffer the trade-off between gate speed and leakage rate. Here, we introduce an energy-level engineering technique that employs the Autler-Townes effect to manipulate the nonlinearity of qubits without perturbing the computational subspace or degrading coherence time. This approach enables an experimentally validated, fast (97 ns) and high-fidelity (99.40(9)%) CZ gate, where error analysis reveals that gate errors arise mainly from static decoherence. The scheme facilitates fast, high-quality all-microwave gate operations with a simple topology and can be applied across various quantum platforms.

title: Quantifying the remaining search space in analogue optimisation
abstract: Benchmarking analogue optimisers requires certifying not only how close a returned energy is to the optimum, but also how many better configurations may remain. Semidefinite relaxations provide rigorous bounds on the ground-state energy and selected observables, yet reveal little about the size of this residual search space. We introduce a deterministic, instance-specific upper bound on the number of binary configurations whose energies improve upon a returned state by a prescribed margin. Combined with a semidefinite energy interval, this yields a complementary certificate of both the magnitude and multiplicity of any possible improvement. To judge an analogue optimiser's native performance, we provide a generalisation of the framework to obtain bounds on the Haar volume of the remaining continuous phase-space. To further characterise the remaining search space, we extend our bounds to resolve regions in configuration space in both the binary and continuous setting. Our approach couples a variational-Chernoff reduction with an elimination bound of the resulting partition function. Comparisons with exact enumeration and independent Haar sampling are consistent with the bounds on small instances. In numerical experiments at $N=1000$, even the largest family-median bound restricts the potentially improving binary configurations to less than $10^{-144}$ of the full configuration space, while the largest upper bound on the corresponding Haar volume is of order $10^{-499}$.

title: Estimating Vertical Ocean Velocity from Horizontal Currents: Linear and Depth-Conditional Neural-Network Approaches on a High-Resolution Regional Ocean Model
abstract: The vertical component of the ocean velocity, w, is several orders of magnitude smaller than the horizontal components u and v, yet it controls vertical tracer transport, upwelling, and mixed-layer ventilation. Because w is extremely difficult to measure directly and is normally obtained only diagnostically from the continuity equation, predicting it from the horizontal velocity field is a problem of both practical and physical interest. We address this problem with two data-driven methods, a physically-motivated linear baseline and a convolutional neural network conditioned on depth through Feature-wise Linear Modulation (FiLM). Both methods are applied to a high-resolution regional simulation of the Coastal and Regional Ocean Community model over the Western Mediterranean, using a sub-region of the south-west Mediterranean Sea as a training region and two independent, out-of-sample regions for validation: the Alboran Sea, with a distinct dynamical regime driven by Atlantic inflow through the Strait of Gibraltar, and a transition region between Almería and Cartagena, between the Alboran Sea and the open western Mediterranean. Once the FiLM network is regularized enough to avoid overfitting to a single training domain, we find that its comparison with the physically interpretable linear baseline is domain- and depth-dependent rather than uniform: near the reference depth, essentially all of the achievable out-of-sample performance on both validation domains is already captured by the linear model, but at the deepest levels tested the FiLM network outperforms the linear baseline on the transition domain, whereas on Alboran it does not.

title: A positive answer to Barsotti and Carman's question on unit groups of Burnside rings of fusion systems
abstract: Let F be a saturated fusion system on a finite 2-group S, and let B(F) be the Burnside ring of F. Barsotti and Carman proved that when S is abelian, B(F)^*=B(S)^* if and only if F=F_S(S). Barsotti and Carman asked on page 728 of their paper whether there exists a counterexample to Corollary 9.3 for a nonabelian 2-group. We have given a positive answer. Our main conclusion is that the following are equivalent for all finite 2-groups: (1)F=F_S(S); (2)B(F)^*=B(S)^*; (3)For every maximal subgroup M of S, 1-[S/M] is in B(F)^*.

title: ArcadeDB in Python: An In-Process Multi-Model Database
abstract: Some Python workflows need transactional reads and writes over documents, traversals over a graph, and similarity search over vector embeddings. In practice these are split across separate systems (a document store, a graph engine, and a vector index), and the data is copied between them and kept consistent by application code. ArcadeDB is an open-source multi-model database engine, written in Java, that supports all three access patterns and can be embedded in a host process. We present arcadedb-embedded, a Python package that runs ArcadeDB inside the Python process via JPype, using a Java Runtime Environment bundled in the wheel. One pip install gives a database with documents, a property graph, and vector search, and needs no Java installation. Query results can be returned as Python lists, NumPy arrays, pandas DataFrames, or Arrow tables. We demonstrate a hybrid retrieval workflow that chains vector search, SQL filtering, and graph traversal over one dataset. We benchmark arcadedb-embedded against SQLite, DuckDB, LadybugDB, and Chroma, and report its costs.

title: A Little Derandomization Goes a Long Way: Unconditional Circuit Lower Bounds using Low-Degree PIT
Tight Asymptotic Bounds on the Maximum Number of Linear Regions of Piecewise-Linear Kolmogorov--Arnold networks
abstract: Schoots et al.~\citep{schoots2025relating} (AISTATS 2025) established a generally loose upper bound on the number of linear regions of continuous piecewise-linear (CPWL) Kolmogorov--Arnold networks (KANs), without providing a lower bound. We consider a $T$-layer network with width vector $\mathbf n=(n_0,\ldots,n_T)$, input dimension $n_0=d$, output width $n_T=1$, and at most $k\geq2$ affine segments per edge. Our matching upper and lower bounds determine the tight growth order $Θ_{\mathbf n}(k^{\sum_{\ell=1}^{T}ρ_{\ell-1}})$ in $k$, where $ρ_{\ell-1}:=\min_{0\leq s\leq\ell-1}n_s$. When every hidden width is at least $d$, the tight order simplifies to $Θ_{\mathbf n}(k^{dT})$. The upper bound of \citep{schoots2025relating} is $k^{\sum_{\ell=1}^{T}n_{\ell-1}n_\ell}$. Our upper bound improves it by a factor of $Θ_{\mathbf n}\!\left(k^{\sum_{\ell=1}^{T}n_{\ell-1}n_\ell-\sum_{\ell=1}^{T}ρ_{\ell-1}} \right)$, with strict asymptotic improvement whenever a hidden layer has width greater than one. We further compare CPWL KANs with rectified linear unit (ReLU) networks using dense parameterizations with at most $Λ$ parameters per model and the same fixed nonlinear depth $T$. Counting trainable knot locations and optimizing the widths and $k$, we prove that the maximum region count of CPWL KANs divided by that of ReLU networks is $Θ_{d,T}(Λ^{d\lfloor T/2\rfloor})$ as $Λ\to\infty$, yielding a polynomial advantage for KANs when $T\geq2$. These tight bounds characterize the attainable geometric complexity of CPWL KANs, providing a foundation for understanding their expressive power and guiding architectural design.

title: Darboux transformations of linear birth-death processes
abstract: In a previous paper we characterized the lower-upper (LU) and upper-lower (UL) factorizations of the infinitesimal generator of a possibly nonconservative birth-death process whose Darboux transformations are again generators of birth-death processes. Here we apply these results to several classical models with linear rates and explicitly known spectral measures: the $M/M/\infty$ queue (Charlier polynomials), the linear birth-death processes (Meixner and Laguerre polynomials), and the linear models of Ismail, Letessier and Valent (associated Laguerre polynomials). For each of them we compute the factors in closed form, determine the admissible ranges of the parameters, and describe the rates, spectral measures and orthogonal polynomials of the Darboux-transformed processes.

title: Joint Higher-Order Low-Rank Tensor Decompositions for Multichannel Acoustic System Compression
abstract: Multichannel room impulse responses (RIRs) in acoustics are often long and therefore the sample count becomes large if seen as finite impulse response (FIR) filters, making storage and real-time convolution costly. Pole-zero (PZ) models are an established way to represent RIRs compactly as infinite impulse response (IIR) transfer functions. We show that a PZ model implies a low-rank canonical polyadic decomposition (CPD) of tensorized RIRs: the early reflections form a sparse rank-1 sum, while the late reverberation admits a CPD with factors determined by the poles. This motivates higher-order-tensor-based compression of RIRs via the block term decomposition (BTD), a generalization of the CPD. We propose two multichannel compression schemes: (i) a stacked multichannel block term decomposition (SMCBTD) applied to a (D+1)-mode tensor of RIRs, and (ii) a joint multichannel block term decomposition (JMCBTD) that shares subsets of factors across channels discovered by spectral clustering on factor-subspace affinity graphs. Both are optimized by an alternating higher-order orthogonal iteration (HOOI) procedure. On simulated rooms as well as measured datasets, the proposed methods achieve consistently lower reconstruction error at equal compression ratios compared to separate single-channel decompositions and a generalized low-rank approximation of matrices (GLRAM) baseline. The largest gains occur with scalar cores (i.e., CPD), supporting the PZ-to-CPD modelling link. We also find D = 3 to be a practical sweet spot, offering most of the achievable gain at moderate compute/memory cost. The compressed models enable efficient downstream multichannel convolution.

title: QRAE: Query-Relevant Attention Entropy for Context Compression in DeepSearch Agents
abstract: DeepSearch LLM agents repeatedly search and carry retrieved sources into subsequent reasoning steps. This expanding context increases token consumption and latency, although many results do not contribute to later reasoning. We propose Query-Relevant Attention Entropy (QRAE), an online context compression method that uses sparse evidence-assessment heads to decide which intact retrieved chunks should persist across reasoning steps. It scores bounded candidate batches through paired prefills: a query-free control suppresses shared attention responses, while normalized entropy measures the breadth of the positive response within each chunk. High-scoring chunks enter a persistent evidence whitelist and are included in the reasoning context. Uncertain chunks remain outside the reasoning context but are retained in a candidate cache, where they can be retrieved for later reevaluation. QRAE requires neither an additional generative compression pass nor modification of the attention operator. Across multiple DeepSearch benchmarks and reasoning models, QRAE improves task success by an average of 2.35 percentage points and reduces end-to-end latency and reported token usage by an average of 30% and 45%, respectively. These benefits generalize to a model with nearly 100B parameters.

title: Stealthy Malicious Interference Detection in UAV Formations: A Power-Domain Signaling Game Approach
abstract: Reliable intra-swarm communication is fundamental to cooperative sensing, control, and mission execution in unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) swarms. In open low-altitude shared-spectrum environments, coexisting UAVs may cause benign interference through spectrum reuse and signal leakage, while jamming UAVs may deliberately degrade critical intra-swarm links. Since a jamming UAV can adjust its transmit power to disguise signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio (SINR) degradation as link fluctuation in benign interference, stealthy jammer UAV detection remains a challenge. In this paper, we propose a novel belief-driven stealthy jammer UAV detection scheme from the perspective of Bayesian security game. To capture stealthy interference in shared-spectrum UAV swarms, the interfering UAV is modeled as a hidden benign or jamming type, whose transmit power strategy induces the SINR observed by the defender. The defender updates its posterior belief from the observed SINR and decides whether to maintain normal operation or trigger defensive power boosting. We characterize pure-strategy perfect Bayesian equilibrium (PBE) conditions under separating structures with distinguishable type and pooling structures with indistinguishable observations. Numerical results show that the proposed scheme improves the defender's expected utility compared to the conventional schemes.

title: A characterization of purely atomic von Neumann algebras
abstract: Let $M$ be a semifinite von Neumann algebra with a faithful normal semifinite trace $τ$, and let $Φ$ be an Orlicz function. We prove that the noncommutative Orlicz space $L^Φ(M,τ)$ is contained in $M$ if and only if $M$ is purely atomic and there is $δ>0$ such that $τ(e)\geqδ$ for every nonzero projection $e\in M$. We also prove that every left $M$-module map on $L^Φ(M,τ)$ is bounded. As a consequence, a left ideal of $M$ contained in $L^Φ(M,τ)$ and dense in it admits an $M$-invariant algebraic complement if and only if it is equal to $L^Φ(M,τ)$. These results extend a theorem of Fidaleo and Zsidó from $L^2$ to all noncommutative Orlicz spaces.

title: Perception Over Geometry: Rethinking Gaussian Allocation in Mesh-based Splatting
abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables photorealistic novel-view synthesis but lacks explicit topology for geometric editing. Existing mesh-based methods enable geometric manipulation by associating Gaussians with triangular mesh faces, typically assigning a fixed number of Gaussians to each face. However, the representation capacity required for appearance reconstruction depends on local appearance complexity rather than merely on mesh tessellation density. To address these limitations, we propose P-MGS, a framework that separates appearance modeling from geometric control to achieve high quality rendering, compact representation, and flexible mesh editing. P-MGS introduces a perceptual complexity guided allocation strategy that distributes Gaussians according to surface appearance demand estimated from multiview observations. To preserve reconstruction flexibility, Gaussians are optimized without mesh constraints and subsequently associated with the original mesh through post hoc binding, retaining adaptive refinement while preserving mesh topology. During mesh editing, local affine deformation transfer updates Gaussian centers and covariances under mesh deformation, reducing misalignment and floating artifacts. Experiments demonstrate superior average novel view synthesis quality with fewer Gaussians and coherent mesh editing.

title: Solving Linear Programs in the Matrix Multiplication Time
abstract: We give a randomized algorithm for feasible bounded-box linear programs with $n$ variables and $d\le n=O(d)$ linearly independent equality constraints. For additive accuracy $ε$, its expected running time is $O((n^ω+n^2\log n)\log(1/ε))$, where $ω$ is the matrix multiplication exponent. This answers the matrix-multiplication-time open question posted in Song's Ph.D. thesis [Son19] in this setting.

title: A stability order barrier and SSP bound for Runge--Kutta methods with non-negative coefficients: AI-assisted proofs
abstract: We prove three results about Runge--Kutta methods with non-negative coefficients. First, every $s$-stage implicit Runge--Kutta method of order at least two has SSP coefficient at most $2s$; the bound is sharp and is attained by a known diagonally implicit method, so full implicitness gives no advantage over DIRK at second order. This extends the second-order DIRK result of Kocsis \& Németh to full coefficient matrices and settles a conjecture of Ketcheson, Macdonald & Gottlieb. These proofs were found with the assistance of AI tools, which uncovered an interesting relationship between the Butcher matrices for SSP methods and phase-type distributions, and led to the proof of the second result: a bound on the SSP coefficient of $s$-stage implicit Runge--Kutta method of order at least three. The third result in this work is a proof that a third-order Runge--Kutta method with entrywise non-negative $A$ and $b$ cannot be algebraically stable. This algebraically intensive proof was also AI-assisted. This paper describes the iterative process of AI-assisted results, and presents an approach that centers human understanding and creativity in the AI-assisted mathematical endeavor.

title: How Far Can Lightweight LLMs Go in Intent-to-SLO Translation?
abstract: Intent-based networking (IBN) promises QoS provisioning in which the network derives the configuration from operator-stated goals. Its first step, translating a natural-language intent into enforceable service-level objectives (SLOs) grounded in a live snapshot of the network state, increasingly relies on large language models (LLMs). These large models add cost and energy to the management loop and typically require multi-GPU, cloud-hosted infrastructure. Can lightweight open LLMs take over this step dependably? We answer this question with a five-dimensional evaluation of ten LLMs with <10B parameters from five families, under four prompting setups, on 716 placement intents. We evaluate translation performance, intent validation, hallucination, energy impact, and robustness to diverse phrasing. The best configurations translate intents with a strict F1 of 0.943 and reject up to 191 of 195 invalid intents. With few-shot reasoning, the strongest models hallucinate unsupported QoS requirements in only about one response in a hundred, whereas the zero-shot setup struggles. A translated intent costs 0.044-0.148 Wh of GPU energy without reasoning, and added energy cost for reasoning pays off for the weaker models. Furthermore, we show that realistic rephrasing lowers the rejection of invalid intents in 15 of 16 configurations for the best-performing models, leaving robust intent validation as a key open challenge for reliable IBN. Our code and data are available: https://github.com/ggck43/intent2slo.

title: Crosstalk-Induced Row Hammer Attacks on Quantum Random Access Codes
abstract: Quantum processors remain susceptible to crosstalk-induced effects despite the continuous evolution of their underlying hardware architectures. In this work, we experimentally investigate the effectiveness of crosstalk-induced attacks across six IBM superconducting quantum processors and one IQM processor. Our results demonstrate that such attacks can be launched across all the platforms, due to persistance of crosstalk, although their effectiveness varies significantly between devices. The probability of a measurement outcome flip in the victim qubits reaches a maximum value of $60\%$. Also, it is seen that processors sharing identical coupling graphs exhibit different vulnerability profiles, indicating that connectivity alone is insufficient to predict attack efficiency. Finally, to demonstrate the practical relevance of these attacks, we study their impact on quantum random access codes (QRACs), observing a degradation in their average success probabilities.

title: Technohybridism: Recursive Semantic Normalization in AI-Mediated Societies
abstract: Language-generating AI systems are no longer only objects of linguistic interaction: their outputs increasingly re-enter the communicative and institutional practices from which their training material was drawn. Drawing on social theory, social epistemology, and the philosophy of language, this article develops a sociotechnical account of that re-entry. We introduce recursive semantic normalization: the process through which machine-generated formulations, once recurrently taken up, evaluated, reused, and institutionally retained, participate in the reproduction and transformation of semantic regularities. Under the heading of technohybridism, we argue that the relevant unit of analysis is the hybrid semantic system, a recursively coupled configuration of human practices, computational generation, and institutional uptake. First, we distinguish the concept from neighbouring accounts, including model collapse, looping effects, machine habitus, machine culture, and the epistemology of AI testimony. Second, we develop an analytical model that separates generation, selection, uptake, and persistence and distinguishes machine-attributable change from change that would have occurred anyway. Third, we analyse uptake as routinized, institutionally diffused, and socially stratified practice and state conditions under which machine-derived regularities become norms. Fourth, we identify social-epistemic consequences: the laundering of provenance that weakens epistemic vigilance, the erosion of the cognitive diversity on which collective inquiry depends, and the narrowing of shared hermeneutical resources. An evidential ladder for empirical research follows. The account attributes no normative authority to machine outputs; what changes is the field within which human and institutional uptake operates.

title: Boundary-preserving randomized neural network methods for Poisson equations on general two- and three-dimensional domains
abstract: In this paper, we propose a boundary-preserving randomized neural network method for Poisson equations with Dirichlet boundary conditions in two and three dimensions. A linear lifting imposes the boundary conditions exactly, without balancing penalty weights between interior and boundary residuals. We construct the liftings by generalized barycentric coordinates and transfinite interpolation on convex and nonconvex polygons and polyhedra, and by radial parameterization on star-shaped curved domains. Numerical experiments on different domains show that the proposed method substantially reduces errors compared with the standard randomized neural network method.

title: Mass loss in AF supergiants: At the verge of the Eddington limit and still with weak line-driven winds
abstract: We study global atmosphere models of AF supergiants. In agreement with previous studies, we found super-Eddington layers in the photospheres of these stars, which lead to density inversions. Our tests showed that the super-Eddington layers are caused by hydrogen ionization. The analysis of radial perturbations has not revealed any instability of such layers, but we show that super-Eddington layers in an optically thick environment are prone to instabilities due to nonradial perturbations. We predict the wind parameters of AF supergiants from our global wind code with a comoving-frame radiative force. Despite the existence of density inversions, the predicted mass-loss rates are significantly lower than those estimated from observations. Theoretical values approach the observational estimates only for the most luminous supergiants, which are close to the Eddington limit due to light scattering on free electrons. Part of the discrepancy between the mass-loss rates could be attributed to the influence of the clumping on the observational properties. Low mass-loss rates imply that the winds of AF supergiants may be strongly influenced by the magnetic fields, suggesting an explanation for the observed spectral variability of these stars.

title: Tilting bundles and modifying modules in relative dimension one
abstract: For projective morphisms $π:Y\to X=\operatorname{Spec}R$ over noetherian complete local rings, with fibres of dimension at most one and $\mathbf{R}π_*\mathcal{O}_Y\cong\mathcal{O}_X$, we construct a tilting fan from cones of pretilting bundles. Maximal cones parametrize tilting bundles, and facet adjacency encodes irreducible mutation. Completeness in positive rank is equivalent to finiteness of tilting bundles modulo line-bundle twists. For closed fibres that are split ADE highest-root cycles or their Stein contractions, we identify tilting bundles with chambers of restricted affine Tits cones and determine the fan. Over normal Gorenstein complete local domains, reflexive pushforward takes pretilting bundles on normal projective birational models with fibres of dimension at most one and $π^!\mathcal{O}_X\cong\mathcal{O}_Y$ to modifying modules. Pushforwards of canonical tilting bundles recover models as module blowups and detect contractions by additive containment, yielding an Auslander--McKay embedding. The hypersurfaces $R=S[[u,v]]/(uv-f)$, with $S$ a regular complete local ring and $f\in S$ a nonzero nonunit, generalize type $A$ Du Val surfaces and $cA_n$ threefolds to arbitrary dimension. We classify modifying modules by divisor flags and rank-one reflexive twists; flag blowups turn the embedding into an equivalence. If $f$ has $r\ge2$ prime factors counted with multiplicity, reflexive pushforward on any maximal-flag model gives a mutation-preserving surjection from tilting bundles, parametrized by chambers of affine type $\widetilde{A}_{r-1}$, to maximal modifying modules. Its fibres are affine Weyl group orbits determined by repeated factors. All maximal-flag models and maximal modification algebras are derived equivalent. These algebras are noncommutative crepant resolutions exactly when $S/(p)$ is regular for every prime factor $p$ of $f$.

title: Compression Through a Context Lens: Evaluating Adaptation, Quantization, and Distillation in Arabic Legal LLMs
abstract: Model compression can facilitate the deployment of large language models in resource-constrained legal settings, but its effects on domain-specific performance may depend on the evaluation protocol. We investigate this issue using ArabLegalEval, a Saudi Arabic legal benchmark, under both with-context and no-context evaluation. The former provides supporting legal passages, while the latter assesses performance without external context. Removing the context produces accuracy gaps of up to 27 percentage points for the base model. We examine three stages: domain adaptation, quantization, and knowledge distillation across FANAR-9B, JAIS-8B, and Qwen2.5-7B. Four-bit quantization reduces model memory by 64-71%, with changes in no-context MCQ accuracy ranging from -3.2 to +1.6 percentage points. Distillation produces more variable results, with accuracy generally declining as student size decreases. A Qwen2.5-7B student distilled from FANAR achieves 76.6% no-context accuracy, compared with 77.2% for its teacher. Our findings suggest that no-context evaluation provides a useful complement to context-supported testing when assessing the effects of adaptation and compression on Arabic legal language models.

title: Pressure-Induced Phase Transition and Superconducting Properties of LiPdH$_2$: A First-Principles Study
abstract: We present a detailed first-principles investigation of the superconducting hydride LiPdH$_2$, focusing on the competition between its tetragonal $P4/mmm$ and rhombohedral $R\bar{3}m$ phases. Our results reveal a pressure-induced phase transition near 220 GPa, where $R\bar{3}m$ overtakes $P4/mmm$ in thermodynamic stability. The $R\bar{3}m$ phase is predicted to be superconducting, with $T_{\rm c}$ values of up to 46 K in the harmonic approximation and 28 K at the anharmonic level. In contrast, although the $P4/mmm$ phase is stable up to 200 GPa, it maintains a more rigid electronic character with weaker hydrogen involvement, resulting in lower superconducting performance. Ionic quantum and anharmonic effects play a decisive role in stabilizing $P4/mmm$ and shaping its superconducting properties, whereas these effects diminish rapidly with pressure. These findings highlight the interplay between structural stability, hydrogen orbital activity, and quantum effect in optimizing the superconductivity of hydrogen-based superconductors.

title: Orientation and slip statistics of spheroids settling in turbulence
abstract: Small spheroids settling through turbulence are turned broadside-on by fluid inertia and tilted away by velocity gradients. We describe their orientation and slip statistics through the crossover from random orientation to alignment, in the overdamped limit. With quasi-static Stokes drag the leading inertial torque is an exact gradient flow on the orientation sphere, its potential quadratic in the cosine of the tilt and only rescaled by mobility anisotropy. The orientation performs an overdamped random walk in a quadratic well, and isotropic Gaussian white noise gives exactly a Boltzmann distribution. For forcing of finite correlation time, a closure keeps this form with its width set by linear response; it recovers the uniform density as settling vanishes and, for fixed-orientation forcing statistics, the aligned coefficient of rapid-settling theory, and errs most in the crossover. The root-mean-square lateral slip peaks where the alignment rate approaches the Kolmogorov rate, as faster settling strengthens the sideways drift at a given tilt but suppresses the tilt; the nearly shape-independent ratio, which tensor-forced simulations reproduce, lets a measured peak constrain the torque coefficient or dissipation rate for given forcing statistics. Dissipation intermittency enters as a lognormal superposition of Boltzmann distributions, which fattens the tails but leaves the leading aligned mean-square tilt unchanged. The superposition reproduces the shape of plate orientation distributions from direct numerical simulations, where a single Boltzmann distribution fails; published moments confirm the predicted spread beyond the weakest torques, and at strong alignment the measured fourth-order tilt moment lies between the two predictions.

title: Parameter-dependent inhomogeneous boundary-value problems in spaces of continuously differentiable functions
abstract: We investigate a broad class of linear inhomogeneous boundary-value problems of order $r$ for systems of ordinary differential equations depending on a parameter $μ$ belonging to an abstract metric space $\mathcal M$. The solutions belong to the spaces of continuously differentiable vector-valued functions $(C^{(n+r)})^m$, $n\in\mathbb{N}\cup\{0\}$, $m, r \in \mathbb{N}$. The boundary conditions have the most general form $By=c$, where $B$ is an arbitrary continuous linear operator from $(C^{(n+r)})^m$ to $\mathbb{C}^{rm}$. Thus, they may contain derivatives of the unknown vector-valued function of integer and/or fractional orders up to $n+r$ inclusive. We establish necessary and sufficient conditions for the continuous dependence of solutions on the parameter $μ$. Furthermore, we prove that the solutions of the original problems can be approximated in the space $(C^{(n+r)})^m$ by solutions of systems of ordinary differential equations with polynomial coefficients, polynomial right-hand sides, and multipoint boundary conditions, where the approximating problems are constructed independently of the right-hand sides of the original problem.

title: Isomorphisms and automorphisms of minimal comaximal hypergraphs of commutative rings
abstract: Let $R$ be a commutative ring with exactly $n\ge 2$ maximal ideals and let $k\ge 2$. We study the minimal $k$-uniform comaximal hypergraph $\mathcal{H}_k(R)$, whose vertices are the nonunits outside the Jacobson radical and whose edges are the irredundant $k$-element comaximal families. For $2\le k\le n$ we show that $\mathcal{H}_k(R)$ is a blow-up of the hypergraph of irredundant $k$-coverings of $\{1,\dots,n\}$, and that its reduced form reconstructs the maximal ideals up to permutation; for $k>n$ there are no edges. We obtain a general description of $\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{H}_k(R))$ and characterize isomorphisms of such hypergraphs. For $3\le k\le n$ its automorphism group properly contains that of the comaximal graph, and for finite rings with $n\ge 3$ and every $2\le k\le n$, $\mathcal{H}_k(R)$ has the same isomorphism invariants as the comaximal graph, namely $|J(R)|$ and $R/J(R)$. The case $k=2$ recovers and extends the automorphism results for comaximal graphs obtained previously. We also compare the minimal and non-minimal comaximal hypergraphs and identify a condition under which the latter has the same automorphism group and isomorphism invariants as the comaximal graph. The same method determines the vertex set and the automorphism group of the $k$-zero-divisor hypergraph of a product of integral domains, and shows that for finite products of finite fields this hypergraph determines the ring.

title: Direct calculation of dipole moment surfaces through second-order symmetry-adapted perturbation theory for properties
abstract: Interaction-induced dipole moment surfaces are vital for calculating line intensities and collision-induced absorption coefficients for van der Waals complexes. We introduce the perturbative corrections, of second order with respect to the interaction operator, to the dipole moment (or, in general, any one-electron property) change due to noncovalent interactions. These are obtained in the spirit of the symmetry-adapted perturbation theory for properties (propSAPT) method, developed recently by some of us [B. Tyrcha et al., JCTC 21(9), 4562--4578 (2025)]. When orbital relaxation effects due to the external property field are properly introduced, these can be understood as analytical derivatives of the second-order SAPT interaction energies. We apply the newly introduced formalism to calculations of dipole moment surfaces for three light van der Waals complexes: He...Ar, He...H$_2$ and the H$_2$ dimer. The propSAPT method is compared against finite-field SAPT calculations and finite-field supermolecular CCSD(T) as the reference.

title: Reviving the Discarded High-Resolution Feature for Transformer-Based Tiny Object Detection
abstract: Tiny object detection remains challenging because tiny instances occupy only a few pixels, and their fine-grained details are easily lost during feature downsampling. Although the highest-resolution feature preserves rich local details for tiny objects, DETR-like detectors often discard it due to its large computational cost, while directly reintroducing this feature also brings dense background noise. To address this problem, we propose ReDHF, a novel framework that Revives the Discarded High-resolution Feature for tiny object detection. ReDHF has three cooperative components. Cross-Scale Deformable Fusion (CSDF) first constructs a semantically enhanced highest-resolution feature and injects its fine-grained details into the shallow feature under a moderate cost. Ellipse-Guided Shallow Supervision (EGSS) then guides the enhanced feature to learn more reliable classification and localization priors by applying geometry-adaptive auxiliary supervision. Full-Scale Query Interaction (FSQI) further enables decoder queries to access both low-level details and high-level semantic information, allowing them to aggregate richer cues for tiny objects. Extensive experiments show that ReDHF consistently improves multiple baselines across different DETR variants and achieves state-of-the-art performance on the evaluated benchmarks. The best ReDHF variants surpass their baselines by +1.4 AP on AI-TOD-v2, +1.6 AP on VisDrone, and +1.5 AP on SODA-D, with especially notable gains on tiny and small objects.

title: Leveraging deep generative modelling at the agent level in discrete-event simulations
abstract: Emulators are often invoked to facilitate parameter inference in computationally intensive agent-based simulations (ABSs). Most approaches, however, require a large sample of pre-existing outputs on which such emulators can be trained. For computationally intensive simulations, this sample can be prohibitively expensive to generate. We propose a new approach to leverage emulators at the agent level in event-based ABSs to reduce the computational requirements of the simulation itself. We demonstrate this in a computationally intensive ``multi-disease'' ABS, Thanzi La Onse, which self-consistently simulates a wide range of medical conditions in a population. By applying conditional tabular generative adversarial networks to replace the modelling of one of the simulated causes of ill health, road traffic injuries (RTIs), we are able to improve its simulation run-time by 86.6% (95% bootstrap confidence interval [85.2, 88.1]), while recovering the evolution of cause-specific mean disability adjusted life years with a 13% error, despite the low assumed incidence of fatal RTIs (~2%). Crucially, we do so while retaining the full ABS framework, and correctly recovering multi-disease dynamics. This represents a crucial step towards enabling full-model emulators for very computationally intensive simulations, and making large ABS amenable to rigorous parameter inference and a full understanding of parameter sensitivity.

title: SEER: A Scalable Event-Driven Runtime for Parallel Execution of Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Environments
abstract: Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) is increasingly used in systems where many entities interact in a shared environment. In these workloads, policy inference can be batched on GPUs, but the CPU-side environment path still updates entity states, resolves local interactions, and builds observations inside each $\mathrm{env.step}$. This path can dominate latency in interaction-intensive workloads after policy batching. Existing vectorized environment interfaces and general event-driven runtimes do not directly address the fine-grained cross-entity work inside one bounded MARL step while preserving the step-level semantics expected by learning systems. We present SEER (Scalable Event-Driven Environment Runtime), a runtime for MARL environment execution under an explicit event-locality contract. SEER models each environment step as a bounded stream of timestamped events. If direct state updates are entity-local and cross-entity effects are represented as ordered future events, SEER can run independent events in parallel while preserving serial-equivalent boundary outputs.
