NegWAM constructs negative trajectories that are geometrically close to the expert trajectory yet carry safety risks, uses them as repulsive anchors to steer predictions away from dangerous behavior, and encodes them as scene-conditioned rider tokens to learn scene--trajectory compatibility. During training, NegWAM jointly optimizes the flow-matching and near-expert negative objectives, while the auxiliary rider branch is discarded at inference, incurring no additional overhead. On NAVSIM v2, NegWAM achieves 40.4 EPDMS on navhard, a 4.1% relative improvement over the strongest compared scorer-free WAM baseline, and achieves 93.3 EPDMS on navtest. These results demonstrate that NegWAM achieves strong performance in safety-critical scenarios while preserving routine-driving performance. Zero-shot closed-loop evaluation on HUGSIM further demonstrates cross-benchmark generalization. The code is available at https://github.com/Zizizi-hao/NegWAM.

title: Photometric eclipse-center variations over the long cycles of Magellanic double-periodic variables
abstract: Double-periodic variables (DPVs) are interacting binaries with an orbital modulation and a longer cycle of uncertain origin. I searched for long-cycle-dependent eclipse-center variations in Magellanic DPVs and tested whether changing disk brightness can produce analogous shifts with fixed conjunctions. I analyzed Optical Gravitational Lensing Experiment (OGLE) photometry for 109 eclipsing-DPV candidates. In separate long-phase intervals, I measured centers of eclipses by profile fitting to local flux minima ($Q$) and by shifting a fixed eclipse template ($T$). A single synthetic semidetached DPV provided a separate numerical experiment. Of 49 curated systems with sufficient timing data, 27 show at least one $Q$ or $T$ modulation under the adopted procedure. Some selections depend on the fitting choice, but ten systems retain a selected $Q$ curve with all tested local functions and windows. Three have both estimators selected in both eclipses, without establishing whether conjunction times change. Using local color interpolation, 14 of 16 systems measured in both eclipses are redder at the deeper, phase-0 eclipse. In the artificial system, fixed conjunctions coexist with large photometric shifts and quadrature-brightness changes, although the large tilted-disk cases do not reproduce the selected observed crossing phases. Long-cycle-dependent photometric eclipse-center variations occur in a substantial fraction of the evaluable, curated sample, not necessarily of all DPVs. Circumstellar brightness changes can produce such shifts, but the single artificial system neither fits an observed DPV nor establishes disk tilt as the cause. Genuine conjunction-time changes remain possible in individual objects.

title: Identifying Neural Dynamics Using Nonlinear Interventional State Space Models
abstract: State-space models (SSMs) recover low-dimensional latent dynamics from high-dimensional observations, but latents are generally not identifiable from observational data alone. Interventional state-space models (iSSMs) use perturbations to break observational symmetries and identify parameters up to permutation, scaling, and shift. However, prior work restricts identifiability to linear latent dynamics and piecewise-linear emissions, excluding many behaviors characteristic of neural circuits. We extend iSSMs to a substantially broader model class: we prove that (i) affine identifiability holds under general injective emission functions and Gaussian latent transitions, and (ii) with interventions, identifiability up to permutation, scaling, and shift is preserved under general nonlinear latent dynamics. We validate our theory on simulated FitzHugh-Nagumo dynamics, and then demonstrate two applications: adjudicating between competing models of decision-making; and predicting responses to unseen micro-stimulation in macaque and human neural recordings, with proof-of-concept generalization to a held-out stimulation site in the latter. Finally, simulations yield practical guidance for designing stimulation protocols that improve identifiability.

title: Sum-of-Squares Refutation Implies Planted Recovery for Semirandom CSPs
abstract: We give a $n^{O(\ell)}$-time algorithm for solving semirandom planted instances of a $k$-ary Boolean constraint satisfaction problem (CSP) with $m \gtrsim \left(\frac{n}{\ell}\right)^{k/2} \ell \, \mathrm{polylog}(n)$ constraints, for any choice of the runtime parameter $\ell$. Up to $\mathrm{polylog}(n)$ factors, this matches the known runtime vs.\ number of constraints trade-off for refuting semirandom CSPs, as well as the trade-off for solving fully random planted CSPs. Prior work on designing algorithms for semirandom CSPs follows a high-level blueprint of decomposing the constraint hypergraph $\mathcal{H}$ of the instance into pieces, each with an explicit pseudorandom property that allows the standard algorithm for random CSPs to succeed on every piece. We depart considerably from this framework and instead implicitly \emph{learn} such a decomposition, without appealing directly to explicit properties such as expansion. More generally, we construct such a learning algorithm from the assumption that semirandom $k$-XOR has Sum-of-Squares certificates of refutation. This yields the broader implication that any Sum-of-Squares refutation algorithm for semirandom $k$-XOR gives a corresponding algorithm for solving semirandom planted CSPs, and instantiating this reduction with known Sum-of-Squares algorithms for refuting semirandom $k$-XOR gives our main algorithm. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first reduction from search to refutation for (semi)random CSPs.

title: Octavius: A High-Performance Analysis Toolkit for Galaxy Simulations
abstract: Increased computing power and more efficient codes have allowed cosmological simulations of galaxy formation to grow massively in scale: the analysis of their outputs has consequently become a big data computational challenge. We present Octavius, a high-performance, hybrid-parallel simulation analysis toolkit. Octavius ingests a simulation snapshot with associated halo catalogue, locates galaxies with a 6D friends-of-friends algorithm, then produces an HDF5 catalogue of properties for haloes, subhaloes, and galaxies. The analysis is fast and memory efficient: we compare the performance against the widely used predecessor toolkit, Caesar, and show Octavius delivers order-of-magnitude improvements in speed with a factor of >5 reduction in peak memory. We demonstrate near-linear strong scaling of compute and linear peak memory scaling with the number of halo-assigned particles. Compute times scale with the superlinear computational load of larger haloes; we note the pipeline is presently I/O-limited. The code is written in Python and uses a declarative, plugin-based architecture so as to be easily extensible. Octavius can currently analyse SIMBA, SWIFT-KIARA, SWIFT-EAGLE, SWIFT-COLIBRE, and TNG snapshots; AHF, HBT-HERONS, and SUBFIND halo catalogues are supported. Properties computed include masses, galaxy photometry with dust attenuation, and kinematic, radial, morphological, and virial quantities. Output catalogues are easily accessed through a provided user API. The code is open sourced at https://github.com/jp-duminy/octavius

title: Create Your Own Work Stack: Deploying Self-hosted AI and Tooling in a Tech Startup
abstract: Self-hosting AI is often presented as a way to reduce inference costs and increase control, but deployment introduces its own costs. We report our experience deploying a hybrid AI stack at Grayhat Developers, a small software company with an AI-intensive development workflow. Our initial motivation was to counter the growing cost of commercial AI usage: Claude/Codex incurred approximately \$325 per month, with more than 25.93 billion recorded tokens. We experimented with local open-source models as replacements for commercial coding agents, but after learning that their performance and inference speed were insufficient, we adopted a hybrid approach in which commercial agents remained responsible for complex tasks while local models handled lower-complexity tasks, organizational information retrieval, and synchronization with self-hosted tools including Outline, Plane, and ERPNext. We estimated that approximately 30--40\% of our commercial AI workload was associated with context transfer, documentation synchronization, task management, and related operational coordination. By moving this work to local models, we estimate that approximately 90\% of this coordination workload could be handled without commercial inference, corresponding to an estimated 27--36\% reduction in overall commercial-AI workload or cost-equivalent usage. Our first internal deployment nevertheless failed to achieve adoption because it introduced UX friction. Replacing it with a centrally configured deployment substantially improved feedback and adoption. We conclude that local inference is most useful not as a wholesale replacement for commercial AI, but as part of a hybrid architecture that assigns tasks according to their capability requirements, cost, context demands, and operational sensitivity.

title: A Hybrid UKF with Explicit Drivetrain Modeling for Low-Velocity State Estimation of Electric Vehicles
abstract: Longitudinal velocity is a core input for vehicle control, driver-assistance, and automated driving functions. Production wheel-speed sensors deliver only a few pulses per revolution, so they lose resolution below 1 km/h, the regime in which automated parking and traffic-jam assistance operate. The motor speed from the electric machine's resolver stays finely resolved down to standstill but reaches the wheels only through a compliant drivetrain. We therefore estimate the longitudinal velocity with an unscented Kalman filter (UKF) on a double-track model adapted to low velocities and incorporate the motor speed along two routes, one purely physical and one hybrid. The first augments the model with an explicit torsional spring-damper drivetrain, making the motor speed a state of the estimator. The second feeds the output of a neural network-based virtual wheel-speed sensor into the UKF as a pseudo-measurement. Both routes are compared against two baselines, a wheel-speed-only configuration and one that adds the motor-speed sensor but treats the driveline as rigid. Because the model is numerically stiff near standstill, the comparison rests on a systematic study of explicit and semi-implicit discretization schemes. All four configurations are evaluated against an inertial reference in real-world test drives with two distinct series-production electric vehicles, anonymized as Vehicle A and Vehicle B for confidentiality. Below 1 km/h, both proposed estimators lower the velocity root-mean-square error by at least 54% and 45% against both baselines on Vehicle A. Carried over zero-shot to Vehicle B without re-tuning on target-vehicle data, they lower it by at least 41% and 51%. Both estimators therefore carry across vehicles without a new identification campaign.

title: Cloudy Skies: Early Detection of Jamming Against Iridium LEO Satellite-IoT Links
abstract: Low Earth Orbit (LEO) satellite-IoT systems increasingly provide connectivity to mobile assets in remote areas, which makes their resilience to radio-frequency jamming a growing concern. Timely jamming detection, i.e., before complete link failure, has been studied for terrestrial networks and Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS), but it remains unclear whether these approaches are effective on LEO links, where propagation varies rapidly, the received signal is weak, and jamming should be detected from the messages that are still correctly received. This paper investigates the extent to which jamming of Iridium LEO satellite-IoT links can be detected from the physical layer of correctly decoded messages. To this aim, we collect and publicly release a real-world dataset of Iridium messages under 47 jamming conditions, spanning two propagation environments, static and mobile receivers, and different jammer distances, powers, and signal types. We use this dataset to analyze three one-class autoencoder-based anomaly detectors operating on physical-layer information and compare them against two signal-quality estimators commonly used as jamming indicators in GNSS-based applications. Our results show that detectability is governed by the rise of the receiver noise floor, through which jammer power, distance, and receiver mobility act. With 1000-sample chunks, i.e., 40 ms of received signal at 25,000 samples per second (about four correctly decoded messages), the autoencoders reach an AUC of at least 0.84 whenever a noise jammer raises the noise floor by at least 9 dB, whereas the $C/N_0$ and SNR estimators fail, since received messages, although correctly decoded, retain a high SNR under jamming. Therefore, timely jamming detection for LEO satellite-IoT links like Iridium should rely on physical-layer information beyond the signal-quality metrics adopted in the GNSS domain.

title: H-BRICK: Hierarchical Boundary Reachability Index with Compressed Kleene Closure for Directed Grid Graphs
abstract: Repeated directed reachability queries arise in online path planning, task-agent allocation, and swarm control on static grid maps, where reachability is asymmetric and full transitive closure is storage-prohibitive. We introduce H-BRICK, a Hierarchical Boundary Reachability Index with Compressed Kleene closure for exact cell-to-cell queries on directed grid graphs. H-BRICK partitions the graph into tiles, computes a local Boolean Kleene closure within each tile, and projects it onto the tile's boundary ports. The resulting directed port-to-port summaries are then composed recursively across shared interfaces up to a single root covering the graph. We prove algebraically that the construction is exact: in the Boolean Kleene algebra of binary relations, every composed summary equals the boundary projection of the regional reflexive transitive closure, and every cell-to-cell query agrees with reachability in the original graph. Experiments on directed grid graphs across diverse map topologies compare H-BRICK against directed search and component-based baselines, and compare its storage requirements against full transitive closure. A batched reachability evaluation further demonstrates that sharing endpoint lifts across many-source/many-target queries amortizes hierarchical traversal and, at k=64, yields a 5.0x-22.9x throughput improvement over the scalar query loop. The results show that hierarchical boundary compression is most advantageous in query-intensive spatial graphs where online search traverses large reachable regions and the hierarchy maintains compact boundary interfaces.

title: Goos-Hänchen Shifts at 458 nm from DUV Dichroic Laser Mirrors
abstract: We report polarization- and angle-dependent lateral beam shifts observed at 458~nm upon reflection from a deep-ultraviolet (DUV) dichroic multilayer mirror. These Goos--Hänchen (GH) shifts originate from the phase of the complex Fresnel reflection coefficient and are quantitatively reproduced using a transfer-matrix model. Simultaneous reflectance (R), transmittance (T), and GH shift measurements provide complementary constraints on the coating's amplitude and phase response. The analysis is extended to transmission, predicting analogous phase-induced lateral shifts. In frequency-doubling cavities using dichroic mirrors, these phase effects can accumulate over multiple reflections, leading to deviations from ray-optics predictions that may affect cavity mode structure and resonance conditions. Our results show a GH shift of as much as 2~\textmu m (\bm{$\approx 4.4λ$}), which, combined with RT data, enables improved characterization of the phase response of the multilayer coating. The p-polarized reflectance is minimized at a pseudo-Brewster angle of \bm{$θ_B \approx 46^\circ$} at 458~nm, providing a natural reference point around which the GH shift is enhanced.

title: Overcoming Fundamental Control Limitations in Powered Descent Flight through Robust Incremental Nonlinear Dynamic Inversion
abstract: This work identifies a fundamental, controller-independent limitation in reusable launch vehicle powered descent: a sudden $180^\circ$ phase transition in the open-loop transfer functions from the control inputs to the lateral drift and drift rate. The transition occurs inside the flight envelope, reverses the effective control direction, and can destabilize the closed loop system under uncertainty. An analytical condition governing this transition is derived, its physical mechanism is established, and its dependence on vehicle mass, aerodynamic properties, and geometry is characterized. An Incremental Nonlinear Dynamic Inversion (INDI)-based control architecture is then developed to inherently address this limitation and is tuned via $\mathcal{H}_\infty$ Closed Loop Shaping to provide local robustness and performance guarantees. The internal dynamics introduced by the INDI inversion are analytically derived and proven to be stable throughout the flight envelope. The proposed controller is compared against a robust gain-scheduled baseline controller through linear stability analysis and an extensive nonlinear Monte Carlo campaign. Both controllers achieve 100% success across the considered Monte Carlo campaign, though the INDI-based controller provides improved tracking performance, superior nominal and dispersed stability margins, requires fewer controller design points, and reduces controller tuning complexity.

title: Linking chiral nuclear forces to light-ion collisions: a global sensitivity analysis
abstract: Ultrarelativistic $^{16}$O+$^{16}$O and $^{20}$Ne+$^{20}$Ne collisions recently performed at the Large Hadron Collider have imaged quadrupole and octupole correlations between nucleons through the collective flow of emitted hadrons. We establish a quantitative link between these correlations and the low-energy constants (LECs) that enter chiral inter-nucleon interactions. Emulators built using the subspace-projected coupled-cluster method enable a global sensitivity analysis of the ground-state quadrupole mean-square eccentricity, revealing that quadrupole correlations respond linearly and additively to all 16 LECs at next-to-next-to-leading order in the chiral expansion. The sensitivities differ markedly in $^{16}$O and $^{20}$Ne, and are complementary to those of the binding energy and charge radius, the bulk observables to which nuclear interactions are typically calibrated. In particular, $^{20}$Ne collisions dominantly probe the spin-orbit part of two-nucleon interactions. Soft-particle correlations in light-ion collisions thus constitute a new type of data to study nuclear forces and their emergence from quantum chromodynamics.

title: Adaptive pairwise preference elicitation for decision support: identifying the best alternative with fewer judgments
abstract: Interactive decision support systems often require repeated preference judgments, although identifying the best alternative may not justify eliciting all \(n(n-1)/2\) pairwise comparisons. We propose ALEC (Adaptive Lexicographic Elicitation of Comparisons), which re-ranks the alternatives after each judgment and asks the first unobserved pair in the lexicographic order of the current ranking, using the Analytic Hierarchy Process as the concrete setting. Under a log-normal error model, directly comparing a contrast maximises the one-step reduction in its effective resistance. Posterior bounds on the probability of a wrong choice or of exceeding a relative-loss tolerance provide stopping rules valid under adaptive questioning, while a consistency-and-margin condition gives a deterministic certificate of agreement with the full-matrix winner. Simulations show that re-ranking is most useful in larger problems with limited budgets; ALEC outperforms Harker's original rule in most scenarios with \(n\ge11\), while under a common stopping rule it achieves higher hit-rate point estimates than the stronger Harker-log variant at a modest additional questioning cost. With a 5\% loss tolerance and a cap of \(2n\) additional comparisons, the stopping rule saves \res{prot-s06-saveadd-min}--\res{prot-s06-saveadd-max}\% of them, while among runs stopped by the bound the observed rate of losses above tolerance remains at most \res{s06-errearly-max}\%, against a nominal 10\%. ALEC therefore provides an adaptive elicitation module for decision support systems that balances decision precision against user effort.

title: Categorified convergence: dropping the 'ultra' from 'virtual ultracategories'
abstract: Virtual ultracategories are a recent categorification of topological spaces seen as sets of points together with a convergence relation between points and ultrafilters. However, a topology can also be described in terms of convergence of filters: in this paper, we thus introduce an analogue of virtual ultracategories based on filters rather than ultrafilters. At the topological level, convergence of filters is completely determined by its restriction to ultrafilters. Our main result shows that, under the assumption of tautness, the same phenomenon holds at the categorified level, thereby offering a non-ultra-biased perspective on virtual ultracategories.

title: ProtoGestalt: Interpretable Prototypes for Facial Phenotyping and Diagnosis of Rare Genetic Disorders
abstract: Rare genetic disorders are difficult to diagnose due to their diversity and overlapping clinical features. Facial morphology can provide diagnostic clues, yet most diagnostic models offer limited interpretability and are not designed to support broad screening for undiagnosed disease. We present ProtoGestalt, an interpretable prototype-based framework for facial phenotyping, rare-disease screening, and syndrome identification. The method extends prototype learning by constraining learned visual features to select facial regions, allowing predictions to be explained through localized and additive evidence. We assess ProtoGestalt's ability to distinguish syndromic from unaffected faces on multiple control datasets and class prevalence values. We further evaluate it's diagnostic performance on syndromes observed during training. The learned prototype-based representations provide significant separation between syndromic and case-matched control images and retain useful performance as the proportion of controls increases. The framework also demonstrates the ability to differentiate among syndromes. Although reasonably accurate specialized models for facial classification of rare disorders already exist, ProtoGestalt offers an interpretable alternative that links predictions to anatomically meaningful facial regions, potentially supporting clinical decision-making and the discovery of phenotype-gene associations.

title: The first gap for minimal submanifolds in spheres
abstract: Let $f:M^n\to\Sn^{n+q}(1)$ be a minimal immersion of a closed connected manifold with $n\ge3$ and $q\ge2$, and let $S$ be the squared length of its second fundamental form. We prove an integral inequality that gives $\max_M S\ge n$ if the immersion is not totally geodesic. If $n\ne4$ or $q=2$, equality $\max_M S=n$ holds if and only if the immersion is a Clifford minimal hypersurface; if $n=4$ and $q\ge3$, equality holds if and only if the immersion is a Clifford minimal hypersurface or the standard minimal embedding of $\mathbb{CP}^2$ in $\Sn^7(1)$. Both classifications are understood up to an ambient isometry, a totally geodesic inclusion, and a finite covering. We construct the integral inequalities using polynomial weights and divergence identities. The required algebraic estimates are proved by sums of squared tensor norms.

title: An Agent-Driven, Cross-Validated Inverse-Design Pipeline for Dielectric Metasurfaces
abstract: Inverse design of dielectric metasurfaces is powerful but labour-intensive: each new target requires choosing a parameterization and a figure of merit, managing compute resources, and critically assessing results that may be numerically unconverged, sensitive to fabrication errors or trapped in local optima. Here we present an open-source pipeline in which an artificial intelligence (AI) coding agent turns a plain-language specification into metasurface optimization runs, executes them, analyses every run with a fixed checklist and proposes the next iteration. Designs are optimized with differentiable three-dimensional rigorous coupled-wave analysis (RCWA), including robustness to fabrication tolerances, and every reported design is independently verified with finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) simulations. We demonstrate the workflow at 1550 nm on a freeform silicon metagrating, on a polarization-independent meta-atom library assembled into beam-deflecting supercells, and on metalenses built from the same library. In the metagrating case, the independent FDTD verification revealed a 5\% overestimate of the efficiency by the optimization model that a conventional convergence test had not detected, and the robust design retained most of its efficiency under $\pm$10~nm fabrication errors. In the other cases, instead, the obtained RCWA results are confirmed by full-wave simulations.

title: FreeOcc: Decoupling Ego-Motion for Efficient 4D Occupancy Forecasting via Continuous Flow Matching
abstract: Current 4D occupancy world models use heavy cross-attention or deep recurrence to disentangle ego-motion from scene dynamics. This requires significant computational capacity. However, this effort is largely redundant since the ego-vehicle's intended future motion is provided by the downstream motion planner. We present FreeOcc, a lightweight continuous-time world model that introduces explicit $SE(2)$ geometric decoupling into a conditional flow-matching framework. By mathematically factoring out self-motion, we create a purely dynamic feature space. This space supports attention-free temporal fusion and allows physics-constrained ODEs to operate strictly on residual agent kinematics. To maximize deployment efficiency, FreeOcc introduces an uncertainty-aware blending mechanism. This routes well-observed voxels to a single-pass decoder, reserving the ODE solver exclusively for ambiguous, high-uncertainty regions. Requiring only 28.3M parameters-roughly 40% of comparable models-our optimal ensemble mode (FreeOcc-E) runs at 27 FPS. On nuScenes, FreeOcc achieves state-of-the-art forecasting performance with a 0.47 m Near Field Chamfer Distance (NFCD) and 32.1% mIoU. Furthermore, the model transfers zero-shot to SemanticKITTI. It also proves highly robust, retaining 92.8% of its ideal mIoU under significant sensor packet loss and timestamp jitter.

title: Accelerating Quantum-Classical Auxiliary-Field Quantum Monte Carlo with Shadow-Trained Neural Quantum States
abstract: Quantum-classical auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo (QC-AFQMC) uses a trial state prepared on a quantum computer to improve the accuracy of the classical AFQMC algorithm. State-of-the-art QC-AFQMC represents this state with matchgate shadows, so every trial-walker overlap and local energy must be averaged over many snapshots, making this classical computation a bottleneck. Here we distill the matchgate shadow data into a symmetry-constrained, noise-aware, autoregressive transformer neural quantum state (NQS). Used as the AFQMC trial state, the NQS evaluates overlaps, force biases, and local energies without repeatedly summing over the matchgate shadows. For a nickel-catalyzed oxidative-addition reaction, the noise-awareness of our NQS design successfully recovers the ideal-upCCD AFQMC barrier and reaction energy within statistical uncertainty, while standard QC-AFQMC execution with the same shadow data yields qualitatively inaccurate results as a result of hardware noise. Since the shadow data are needed only for training, the estimated classical cost for the nickel system falls by approximately 99% relative to our previous QC-AFQMC implementation.

title: SubRoformer: Subband Time-Domain Representation for Music Source Separation
abstract: Music source separation extracts vocals and instruments from a mixed recording, enabling remixing, content production, and music analysis. Existing systems commonly operate on waveforms or full-band spectrograms. Waveform inputs contain many samples even in short segments, whereas a single spectrogram resolution imposes a shared time-frequency resolution trade-off across frequency ranges. We propose SubRoFormer, a Transformer-based system comprising a subband module and a residual RoFormer module. The subband module decomposes the mixture into frequency-localized, lower-rate signals for separation. It then reconstructs the target waveforms from the estimated subbands. The residual RoFormer module models temporal and cross-band relationships on temporally compressed features. It combines this context with fine-rate features through gated residual fusion to estimate source-specific complex masks. On the MUSDB18-HQ test set, training only on MUSDB18-HQ yields an average signal-to-distortion ratio (SDR) of 10.63 dB across four stems using target-specific models, achieving state-of-the-art performance among the compared systems without extra training data. With 500 additional training songs, a single model jointly separating all four stems achieves an average SDR of 11.59 dB, establishing state-of-the-art performance among the compared single-model multi-stem systems trained with extra data. Code and checkpoints are released at https://github.com/ArchiMickey/SubRoformer.

title: Between Hi-Fi and MMI: the overlap of redundancy and synergy in partial information decomposition
abstract: Partial information decomposition (PID) splits the information that two sources carry about a target into redundant, unique and synergistic parts, with nonnegative decompositions lying on a segment where redundancy measures are bounded by the positive part of the co-information and the smaller source-target information. We parameterize this segment by the overlap, the common excess of redundancy and synergy over their net balance, and show that for many of the named PID measures, their redundancy can be written as the largest positive part of the co-information over a set of reference distributions. This common form induces an ordering of those PIDs on the segment. With the smallest redundancy and synergy and the largest unique atoms of any nonnegative PID, the information-theoretic version of Hi-Fi, a feature-importance method, is the zero-overlap end of the segment for two sources, with the maximum overlap bound given by the minimum mutual information (MMI) PID. We introduce, by splitting the co-information into a pairwise maximum- entropy part and the third-order connected information, a PID that sits at zero overlap except when pairwise redundancy and triadic synergy coexist. For three or more sources the bivariate results hold on every pair of merged source groups, and among all nonnegative solutions of the lattice equations MMI and Hi-Fi still give the smallest and largest unique atoms but zero overlap on all pairs at once is often unattainable. Two inequalities across pairs are necessary in general and sufficient for three sources. For identity targets zero overlap is possible exactly when the sources' information diagram is nonnegative. In random three- and four-source distributions zero overlap on all pairs fails in 21-100% of the cases.

title: Drift-Resilient Predictive Interference Management: Online Adaptation of an Extreme-Value Predictor
abstract: Predictive interference management supports ultra-reliable low-latency communication (URLLC) by allocating finite-blocklength resources against a high conditional quantile of next-slot interference. Building on an extreme-value-theory/kernel-density-estimation (EVT/KDE) predictor with quantile-defined interference states, this paper makes the predictor resilient to unannounced shifts in the interference distribution. Its cumulative refitting on all past observations does not specify how the state partition and retained samples should evolve after a regime change. We show that drift first makes the quantile partition inefficient: cumulative refitting preserves tail support and coverage but cannot recover conditional resolution, and pays for it in channel use, whereas discarding history starves the tail estimator. We therefore propose event-triggered quantile-space adaptation. A nonparametric cumulative sum (CUSUM) on the predictor's level stream detects change. At each confirmed event, the quantile partition is re-derived from post-change observations, retained history is re-binned under it, and each state is refit from a bounded per-state memory, capped to balance stale-regime bias against tail-estimation variance, with a closed-form L-moment tail estimator. At a nominal coverage target $η\!=\!0.99$, relative to matched cumulative refitting with fixed states, the proposed method reduces channel use by $5.7$--$13.2\%$ and quantile pinball loss by $25$--$50\%$ across abrupt, incremental, compound, downward, and reversal drift, with coverage changing by $-0.5$ to $+1.0$ percentage points. At matched achieved coverage, it saves $4$--$18\%$ of channel uses, while resource use in load-only and stationary cases changes by less than $0.5\%$. With $K$ samples per state and $L$ states, predictor memory is bounded at $O(KL)$ rather than growing as $O(t)$.

title: Beyond K/V Caches: Cross-Model State Handoff in Hybrid Linear-Attention LLMs
abstract: Production deployments often use different models to balance cost and quality through cascading, routing, and switching models during long conversations. Context accumulates across turns. Each switch requires the target to repeat prefill over this context. Existing methods transfer full-attention (FA) K/V caches across models. Hybrid linear-attention models also retain recurrent states (REC) and convolution histories (Conv). The interaction between Conv and REC complicates cross-model state transfer. Conv perturbations can change keys and values in recurrent layers and alter REC updates. Conv histories are overwritten, but changes in REC can still affect later outputs. More accurate REC reconstruction need not improve continuation. Building on this, we propose Hybrid State Transfer (HST) for all three state types. It uses structured REC maps and preserves history order during Conv alignment. We calibrate the adapters using the frozen target's outputs during continuation. FA cache map updates are merged offline. Across five benchmarks, Qwen3.5 4B$\rightarrow$27B and 9B$\rightarrow$27B achieve mean task retentions of 89.88% and 94.11%, respectively. With source caches already available, separate timing on synthetic 16K inputs yields handoff body speedups of $21.66\times$ and $21.91\times$.

title: Who Can Evaluate AI Independently? A Framework for Analysing Evaluation Infrastructure
abstract: AI evaluation is increasingly central to AI safety and governance, yet taking part in an evaluation does not by itself confer authority over its design, its execution or the resources it depends on. This paper examines how infrastructure arrangements distribute that authority, and so shape who can evaluate AI systems independently. Drawing on Science and Technology Studies, political economy and applied evaluation standards, we introduce PAAI (Power, Access, Adequacy, Independence), a framework for examining who controls evaluation infrastructure, the terms on which it is available, whether it is adequate to the evaluation's purpose and what autonomy it supports. We apply PAAI to twelve African AI evaluation projects (2022-2025) and to the documented roles of all ten member institutes in the three published joint testing exercises of the international network of AI Safety Institutes. We identify three recurring configurations: extractive collaboration, dependent innovation and constrained independence. African actors often contribute data, language expertise and task design while external institutions retain authority over infrastructure and evaluation frameworks; design authority without infrastructure authority never yielded more than partial independence. The joint testing exercises show a similar division among mostly high-income members: the institutes that led each exercise also ran the models, while Kenya, the network's only African member, moved from annotation to task design with no documented model execution. Participation in evaluation does not by itself produce evaluative authority. For evaluation to serve as a credible governance mechanism, access must come with control over priorities, methods, publication and continuity.

title: Linear bounds and sharp exponential growth for commuting matrix algebra
abstract: For any $m$ pairwise commuting matrices $\{A_i\}_{i=1}^{m}\subset \M_n(\F)$, we prove $\dim_\F \F[A_1,\cdots, A_m]\leq (2^m-1)(n-1)+1$, answering Bergman's question on the existence of a linear bound for a fixed number $m$.

title: How Far Can Untrained Neural Networks Go in Anomaly Detection? From Tables to Pixels
abstract: Anomaly detection (AD) is often framed as a representation-learning problem, where strong performance is expected to require learned features or AD-specific optimization. However, this view can overlook the intrinsic separability of anomalies from normal references, even in the absence of learned representations. We therefore investigate how far untrained neural networks can go in anomaly detection. To this end, we propose PRISM, a framework combining fixed random nonlinear features with normal-reference Mahalanobis scoring for tabular detection and dense visual localization. Across 47 tabular datasets in ADBench, PRISM-T achieves the highest mean AUROC (86.4%) and the second-highest mean AUPRC (65.9%) among the compared methods. On MVTec AD and VisA, covering 27 visual categories, PRISM-V achieves mean image-level and pixel-level AUROCs of 90.4% and 96.4%, respectively. Notably, both models achieve these results without neural weight optimization or pretrained representations. A theoretical analysis further characterizes how nonlinear transformations affect the mean and covariance contributions to the Mahalanobis score gap, while empirical analyses examine the resulting score separability. These findings establish PRISM as both a competitive anomaly detector and a prior-to-learning baseline for assessing the added value of learned representations in anomaly detection.

title: Necessary and sufficient conditions for the self-normalized central limit theorem for independent triangular arrays
abstract: For a rowwise independent triangular array $\{X_{n,i}:1\le i\le n\}$, put $S_n=\sum_{i=1}^nX_{n,i}$ and $V_n^2=\sum_{i=1}^nX_{n,i}^2$. We prove that $S_n/V_n\xrightarrow{\mathrm d}{\mathrm N}(0,1)$ implies $\max_{i\le n}|X_{n,i}|/V_n\xrightarrow{\mathbb P}0$. The same assumption gives $V_n^2/b_n^2\xrightarrow{\mathbb P}1$ for any choice of medians $b_n^2$ of $V_n^2$. Combined with the results of Shao (2018), this yields necessary and sufficient conditions for the self-normalized central limit theorem and resolves his conjecture for independent sequences. The proof identifies the joint limits of the sum and its sum of squares, then uses the standard normal ratio to remove every non-Gaussian component.

title: Describe Your Facial Expressions by Linking Image Encoders and Large Language Models
abstract: This paper presents a novel task of describing human facial expressions of a facial image in natural language, which captures the nuances of facial actions and emotional states beyond traditional emotion categories or facial action units (AUs). To achieve the facial expression captioning model, we propose a three-stage training framework that trains a vision-to-language model using synthesized image-text pairs and the BLIP-2 pre-training techniques. To overcome the challenge of missing training image-text pairs for facial expression captioning, we propose a strategy that involves synthesizing and combining captions using GPT-3.5 and existing annotations on either emotion categories or AUs. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in generating captions that describe details of facial actions and emotions, as well as the inferential relationship between them, even when those emotions are not present in the training data. It is also demonstrated that the vision-to-language task enhances the performance of the intermediate visual features on both AU detection and emotion classification tasks.

title: H-TRIP: Exact Many-to-Many Distance Index for Multi-Robot Exploration
abstract: Frontier-based exploration systems repeatedly evaluate geodesic travel costs between robot poses and candidate viewpoints, and tour-based planners consume the full pairwise distance matrix built from them. Recomputing these matrices with one graph search per source scales with the explored map size, whereas distance caches that refresh only locally affected or newly created frontiers can retain stale costs between surviving pairs when newly discovered free space creates a global shortcut. We present H-TRIP (Hierarchical Tropical Rank-one Incremental Propagation), an exact distance index grounded in Kleene algebra over the min-plus semiring for monotonically growing occupancy grids. H-TRIP partitions the known map into a spatial hierarchy with fixed boundary ports. Each unknown-to-free revelation is decomposed into efficient rank-one min-plus edge insertions at the affected leaf, and only decreased port-to-port summaries are propagated along its ancestor chain. A shared hierarchical lift evaluates the dense many-to-many matrix of shortest distances for all active query points on the occupancy map. We prove that sequential insertions preserve exact shortest-path distances on the grid. Benchmark experiments confirm exact agreement with reference searches on fully built maps and show that dense many-to-many queries at a few dozen viewpoints are up to two orders of magnitude faster than sequential k x BFS. On exploration runs with sixteen robots, in-loop queries on the growing occupancy graph are 2.21x-8.59x faster than co-scheduled k x BFS on maps with side 256, 512, and 1024 cells.

title: FATE: Fault-Aware Transfer Error for Unsupervised Anomaly Detection
abstract: We study unsupervised industrial anomaly detection in the single-class setting, where a detector learns only from normal images of one product category. Reconstruction-based detectors model normal features from a frozen encoder, but their target layers are usually chosen by architectural convention. We instead ask what information one block can pass to another. Treating depth as a sequence of discrete transitions, we train eight directed, token-wise predictors from block 1 and blocks 21-23 to blocks 7 and 14. Adjacent-layer cosine similarity drops at four repeatable fault lines in DINOv2 ViT-L, separating stable depth segments. The deepest blocks retain semantic context but lose local detail, so the residual of a source-to-sensitive prediction measures information that cannot be transported. The fault structure constrains the source and target roles, and the same rule transfers to ViT-B and RADIO-B. A bounded foreground prior, calibrated only on normal training images, suppresses background residuals while retaining a positive floor for evidence outside the estimated foreground. With the same eight channels and a common training-only calibration procedure in every single-category model, category-averaged image AUROC reaches 99.75 on MVTec-AD, 99.42 on VisA and 94.27 on Real-IAD; object-level AUROC on Real-IAD is 96.26. For the 448x448 runs, category-averaged P-AUROC/P-AUPRO on a common 256x256 evaluation grid is 98.46/95.97 on MVTec-AD, 99.21/96.12 on VisA and 99.26/96.59 on Real-IAD.

title: Structured Agentic Learning for Persistent Spatial Acquisition in RDT-TAIS-Assisted Communications
abstract: Persistent TAIS operation can reduce repeated radio-information acquisition by reusing environmental knowledge across control intervals. This knowledge changes with radio-environment evolution and current communication task. This paper studies persistent spatial knowledge maintenance for TAIS control and formulates it as a sequential information-acquisition problem that maximizes effective communication performance while accounting for physical-acquisition overhead under an outage-reliability constraint. We develop structured agentic spatial intelligence (ASI), which realizes a communication-oriented agent that maintains persistent spatial knowledge, forms beliefs from radio and context observations, and adapts physical information acquisition through closed-loop interaction with the radio environment. By jointly exploiting radio-consistent context inference, temporal knowledge-sufficiency assessment, graph-structured regional reasoning, and predictive outage-risk feedback, structured ASI determines when additional acquisition is needed, where it is directed, and how much physical information is sufficient before stopping or escalating to full radio-environment reacquisition. Numerical results show that structured ASI improves the effective rate by 2.59% while reducing acquisition overhead by 25.0% at six structural changes per 100 control intervals, and achieves a 2.82% effective-rate gain with a 41.8% overhead reduction over a heterogeneous 400-interval mission.

title: Educational robotics beyond ROS: a custom library for direct transfer of Webots controllers in the Turtlebot3
abstract: Robot Operating System (ROS) is becoming a standard in robotics courses at higher education, but its installation, configuration and distributed programming model can introduce a significant entry barrier in the new landscape of AI-based master and degree studies, where many students do not have a strong informatics background. This paper presents an educational experience that enables students to program a TurtleBot3 Burger directly in Python, while preserving a direct transfer path from simulation to the physical robot. The approach is based on a custom library that mirrors the Webots API, allowing the same controller code to be executed in the simulator and on the real TurtleBot3 with minimal modification. The library provides access to the robot motors, wheel encoders, inertial sensors and LiDAR, and is complemented by scripts that automate deployment and execution on the physical platform. It was used in a master-level course on introductory autonomous vehicles, and initial student feedback suggests that the approach reduces the perceived complexity of ROS-related infrastructure and helps learners focus on algorithmic logic and real-world behaviour.

title: First-Order Model Checking on Monadically Dependent Graph Classes
abstract: Monadically dependent graph classes are those in which first-order logic cannot encode all graphs. They include all nowhere dense classes and all classes of bounded twin-width. We show that first-order model checking is fixed-parameter tractable on every monadically dependent graph class. Together with the known hardness result for hereditary classes that are not monadically dependent, this gives a complete characterization of the hereditary graph classes with fixed-parameter tractable first-order model checking. This resolves a central open problem in algorithmic model theory. Our proof combines ideas from structural graph theory (graph decompositions), finite model theory (locality of first-order logic), and model theory (counting types). In particular, we show that in monadically dependent classes, tuples of fixed length have only $|U|^{O(1)}$ types of fixed quantifier rank over any set of parameters $U$.

title: Detecting Silent Faults at the Environment-Trainer Boundary in Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Robot reinforcement learning increasingly runs environments outside the trainer: in another process, on another machine, in another language. Many faults at this boundary raise no error. We make the boundary a wire protocol and ask what notices a fault in it. On Pendulum, HalfCheetah, Hopper and a 7-joint arm (Pusher), we injected up to 23 faults into what crosses the wire and 2 into the trainer's log, from one value to every value. Unless every value was wrong, a learning-curve threshold caught at most one run in ten, and a comparison with ten fault-free seeds at most 21%. A clean evaluation of all 1,060 final policies agreed with the curves: of the 728 boundary-fault runs both curve checks passed, 723 scored no more than three standard deviations below fault-free seeds, though nearly all ended on other weights and, for reward faults, logged other returns. Checks of the run itself, not of its outcome, saw every fault. A step ledger kept on both sides and compared step by step caught and located every fault that crossed, on Pendulum, Hopper and Pusher on one machine and on Pendulum across two, with no fault-free run and, on Pendulum, a median 3% more training time. An episode record kept at the environment caught the faults in the trainer's log. We list such faults found in practice, in Gymnasium 1.3 and our own code and, reported by others, in five multi-agent libraries, and recommend a step ledger and episode counts kept at the environment.

title: A Smoothly Truncated Dark Matter Spike around a Black Hole in an Einstein-Cluster Model
abstract: We introduce a finite dark matter spike around a static, spherically symmetric black hole, with a general power-law index and an Einstein-cluster stress tensor. Smooth inner depletion and outer truncation ensure that the density and its first radial derivative vanish at both boundaries, while a single normalization preserves the prescribed exterior mass. The resulting spacetime contains an inner vacuum gap, a matter region with vanishing radial pressure, and an outer Schwarzschild vacuum. We derive the enclosed mass, density maximum, local logarithmic slope, and matched metric without surface layers, including exact polynomial-root representations of the matter-region metric for spike indices $7/3$ and $3/2$. Energy conditions and radial stability of the constituent circular orbits constrain the admissible configurations. A sufficient bound guarantees these properties for an inner edge at or beyond the Schwarzschild marginal-stability radius and also ensures positivity of the massless-scalar potential. Comparisons at a common mass budget examine how boundary regularity and radial concentration jointly affect the gravitational response. Shadows and light deflection also depend on the global redshift and mass calibration. Scalar waves matched across the three regions with one infinity-normalized time coordinate distinguish local gap-redshift effects from propagation through the complete geometry. The smoothly truncated profile provides a controlled equilibrium model for investigating how finite support and mass redistribution affect black hole observables; its taper scales, formation, and collective stability require additional physical input.

title: Uniqueness and nondegeneracy for a critical Choquard equation with Hardy potential
abstract: We study the critical Choquard equation \[ -Δu-μ|x|^{-2}u =\bigl(|\cdot|^{2-N}*|u|^p\bigr)|u|^{p-2}u \qquad\text{in }\mathbb R^N, \] where $|\cdot|^{2-N}$ is the Newton kernel, $p=\frac{N+2}{N-2}$, and $0<μ<\frac{(N-2)^2}{4}$. For every $N\ge3$, we prove that positive solutions in $D^{1,2}(\mathbb R^N)$ are radially symmetric about the origin, unique up to dilation, and nondegenerate. Our proof uses normalized logarithmic derivatives to obtain a cooperative system. The resulting monotonicity principle underlies both the uniqueness and nondegeneracy arguments, and remains effective in the subquadratic range $1<p<2$, corresponding to $N\ge7$. Consequently, the linearized quadratic form has Morse index one and the sharp inequality admits a global quadratic remainder estimate. The best constant is strictly concave in the Hardy parameter on $\bigl[0,\frac{(N-2)^2}{4}\bigr)$, is of class $C^2$ with strictly negative second derivative in the interior, and satisfies two-sided bounds that agree to first order at $μ=0$.

title: MCUFlowNet: Hardware-Aware Neural Architecture Search for Optical Flow on Microcontrollers
abstract: Dense optical flow allows small drones to avoid obstacles. However, few dense optical flow networks are designed for microcontrollers (MCUs) with neural accelerators, whose on-chip SRAM limits the input resolution. We present PACE-NAS, a macro-to-micro neural architecture search framework that decouples memory from latency: a macro design fixes the backbone and its peak SRAM, and a micro design searches operators and depths to trade accuracy against compiler-estimated latency. We apply it to EdgeFlowNet on a Grove Vision AI V2 board (Ethos-U55), where profiling locates the peak SRAM at the full-resolution output head. Replacing transposed convolutions with bilinear upsampling and convolutions lowers the peak SRAM by 18%, and two lightweight context modules lower the endpoint error (EPE) without raising the peak. All searched subnets share this peak, so the search needs no memory constraint. We name the Pareto-optimal models MCUFlowNet; the fastest variant, MCUFlowNet-S, runs 1.76x faster than a retrained EdgeFlowNet at a 1.6% higher EPE and, in simulated forest flights at 2 m/s, reaches the goal without collision in 51.5% of trials, against 41.8%. PACE-NAS also applies to semantic segmentation, where a searched PIDNet-S variant runs 1.17x faster at similar accuracy. Code is available at https://gitlab.kuleuven.be/emedia-research-lab/esat-stadius/mcuflownet/mcuflownet.

title: Detecting Weather Fronts from Satellite Observations: What Does Reanalysis Add?
abstract: Weather fronts are transition regions between air masses with contrasting thermodynamic properties and are associated with mid-latitude precipitation and severe weather. We investigate machine learning (ML) methods for detecting weather fronts and quantify the contribution of reanalysis data to performance. We compare two configurations of the same ML model for pixel-wise frontal classification over the North Atlantic and Europe: (1) using only geostationary infrared satellite observations, and (2) additionally using 28 ERA5 reanalysis fields. The satellite-only model achieves a neighbourhood critical success index at a 150 km tolerance (CSI@150) of $0.402$, which lies within the range of agreement between analyses from different meteorological services. The satellite$+$ERA5 model achieves $0.575$, an improvement of $0.173$. Our analysis shows that low-level winds are the least predictable from the satellite representation ($R^2 = 0.23$, compared with $0.88$ for temperature), while removing winds or moisture causes the largest decreases in detection performance.

title: Classification of analytic $\text{SO}^o(p,q)$-actions on closed $(p+q-1)$-dimensional manifolds II : $p \geq 3$, $q=1,2$
abstract: This paper provides a classification of analytic actions of the semi-orthogonal groups $\text{SO}^\circ(p,1)$ and $\text{SO}^\circ(p,2)$, for $p \geq 3$, on closed, connected manifolds of dimension $p$ and $p+1$ respectively. It is a sequel to a previous paper, which treats the case $p,q \geq 3$. Adapting Uchida's methods, we explicitly construct analytic actions of $\text{SO}^\circ(p,1)$ on $\text{S}^{p}$ and $\text{S}^{p-1} \times \text{S}^{1}$, and analytic actions of $\text{SO}^\circ(p,2)$ on $\text{S}^{p+1}$, $\text{S}^{p} \times \text{S}^{1}$ and $\text{S}^{p-1} \times \text{S}^{2}$, and we classify them up to analytic isomorphism, using a result of Hitchin and Schneider's classification of analytic $\text{SL}_2(\mathbb{R})$ actions on surfaces. The main result demonstrates that any analytic $\text{SO}^\circ(p,q)$ action, $q=1,2$, on a closed, connected $(p+q-1)$-dimensional manifold is covered by one of the constructed actions or by an action on $\text{SO}^\circ(p,q) \times_P \text{S}^1$, where $P$ is a maximal parabolic subgroup of $\text{SO}^\circ(p,q)$.

title: Commissioning and Performance of the LHCb Upstream Tracker
abstract: The Upstream Tracker is a new, high-precision silicon strip detector installed in the LHCb experiment as part of the overall LHCb Upgrade I project. The detector is an integral part of the tracking system, and plays a crucial role in the reconstruction of charged particles in the new fully software-based trigger. An overview of the Upstream Tracker detector design, its commissioning, and performance are presented.

title: Machine learning quantum data to accelerate quantum Monte Carlo
abstract: Simulating strongly correlated electrons in molecules and materials remains a central goal for quantum computing. A promising strategy uses quantum processors to prepare trial wavefunctions that guide classical quantum Monte Carlo (QMC). However, the enormous computational cost of repeatedly processing quantum measurements has severely limited the practical scalability of this approach. Here, we overcome this bottleneck by compressing quantum measurement data into machine-learning models that efficiently provide the wavefunction overlaps needed by QMC. This accelerates quantum-classical QMC by orders of magnitude, enabling chemically accurate simulations on up to 40 qubits, more than doubling the scale of previous hardware demonstrations with comparable accuracy. We demonstrate our approach on hydrogen chains and strongly correlated iron-sulfur clusters using measurements from Google's Willow processor. By enabling efficient reuse of quantum-state information on the classical coprocessor, our framework addresses a fundamental bottleneck in hybrid quantum algorithms that will persist even into the fault-tolerant era.

title: Non-Unitary Quantum Butterfly Effect: Theory and Experiment
abstract: We present a generalization of the out of time order correlator (OTOC) for non-unitary systems. For a Haar-random brickwork qudit-circuit, peppered with local, projective measurement, we calculate the infinite-temperature, ensemble-average OTOC. Utilizing transfer matrix machinery, we find that the OTOC asymptotically decays exponentially and that the decay depends on the rate of measurement. In the thermodynamic limit, with sparse measurement, the OTOC approximately exhibits a Gaussian shape. Phenomenologically, this corresponds to the development of a causal scrambling front where unlike the unitary case, the signal decays in the bulk of the causal cone. We develop a Monte Carlo framework to compute the OTOC. We then estimate the OTOC directly via quantum simulation and on Quantinuum's trapped-ion quantum computer. We resolve the unitary and non-unitary OTOC phenomenology despite the presence of hardware noise. Our analytic results characterize how local nonunitary channels affect OTOC decay, providing a quantitative benchmark for the cumulative effects of a broad class of hardware noise on many-body dynamics.

title: A Generative Foundation Model for Multimodal Tokamak Tasks
abstract: Tokamak experiments record diverse measurements, including waveforms, profiles, fields, and scalars, which are used to reconstruct the plasma, forecast its evolution, recover associated control signals, and estimate disruption risk. Most models are built separately for one task and a fixed set of inputs and outputs, and each relies on a prescribed subset of diagnostics rather than structuring the full multimodal observation set to extract global, cross-signal information about the discharge. These limitations motivate a reusable foundation model that adapts to each task's input-output schema and models heterogeneous target signals jointly, rather than retraining a separate model for every configuration. In this work, we extend the TokaMark benchmark with two groups of tasks for actuator action inversion and disruption prediction, yielding 20 MAST tasks in six groups with explicit schemas and evaluation protocols. Then, we introduce GenToka, a generative tokamak foundation model that jointly generates schema-selected targets through a shared conditional diffusion Transformer, with signal-specific codecs preserving native time series, profiles, fields, and scalars; foundation pretraining and task-specific adaptation transfer cross-signal structure across all six groups. Evaluation on MAST measurements shows that GenToka reduces macro-average normalized root mean squared error relative to TokaMind by 4.7% on Groups 1-4 and by 17.7% on Group 5, and improves macro-average window-level F1 on Group 6 by 8.4% at a common validation-selected threshold. GenToka provides a reusable, generative, and multimodal pathway for experimental tokamaks, linking plasma-state reconstruction, actuator inference, and disruption warning from shared measurements to support more integrated, data-driven fusion plasma prediction and control research.

title: Interpretable Multimodal MRI-Clinical Fusion for Functional Outcome Prediction After Acute Ischemic Stroke
abstract: This study evaluates the added prognostic value of day-1 multimodal MRI for predicting three-month functional outcome after acute ischemic stroke (AIS). Sixty-six AIS patients with ADC, DWI, FLAIR, and clinical data were analyzed. Three-dimensional pretrained ResNet embeddings were extracted from each MRI modality, reduced using fold-isolated principal component analysis, and combined with structured clinical variables and ADC-derived lesion biomarkers. Linear support vector machines were evaluated using eight-fold stratified group cross-validation across MRI modality combinations. Clinical-only modeling achieved strong performance (AUC = $0.899 \pm 0.151$), while MRI-only models showed limited discrimination (AUC $\approx$ $0.67$-$0.73$). Among multimodal configurations, FLAIR-clinical fusion achieved the highest mean cross-validated performance (AUC = $0.948 \pm 0.061$), followed by ADC-clinical fusion (AUC = $0.941 \pm 0.094$). Full ADC-DWI-FLAIR fusion did not consistently outperform single-modality clinical fusion. Feature-importance analysis identified age, NIHSS subscores, ADC lesion burden, and learned FLAIR representations as key contributors, while qualitative FLAIR activation maps showed responses over lesion-like regions. These findings suggest that compact day-1 FLAIR and ADC representations provide complementary prognostic information beyond clinical variables and support interpretable, data-efficient outcome prediction in AIS.

title: AI-Native Task-Oriented Semantic Communications over a Relay: Benefits and Vulnerabilities
abstract: Semantic communication (SemCom) using a relay node is considered, where the relay assists in conveying task-relevant information from a source to a destination, with meaning defined by classification labels. A joint end-to-end design of the source encoder, relay transformation, and destination decoders is developed to optimize both semantic inference accuracy and perceptual reconstruction quality for image data. Relay-assisted schemes are shown to outperform direct transmission, with gains that become more pronounced in low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) regimes across different relaying strategies. Alongside these performance benefits, however, a key security vulnerability introduced by the relay is identified, and a Byzantine attack is formulated in which the relay injects structured, learned perturbations into its transmitted signal. The attack operates on intermediate communication representations subject to channel effects, with perturbations generated through a learned mapping applied at test time. It is shown to significantly degrade semantic inference accuracy at the destination. These results reveal a clear trade-off between SemCom gains and security risks in relay-assisted systems, motivating the need for secure relay designs that account for insider threats.

title: La-JEPA: Compact Robot Policies with Latent World Modeling
abstract: World-action models adapt pretrained video generators, and vision-language-action models build on pretrained vision-language backbones; both tie policy architecture and inference cost to large transformers designed for generation rather than control. It remains unclear how much these generation-oriented choices affect control. In this work, we introduce Latent Action JEPA (La-JEPA), a compact world-action model whose policy transformer is trained from scratch in the feature space of a pretrained V-JEPA 2.1 encoder. Following Fast-WAM, La-JEPA learns to predict future features jointly with actions during training and generates only actions at inference. Among policies without embodied pretraining, La-JEPA achieves state-of-the-art performance in clean and randomized RoboTwin 2.0 scenes and on LIBERO-Plus with correct instructions, while using far fewer parameters than the strongest competing policies. It runs substantially faster than Fast-WAM at comparable performance and outperforms the closest JEPA-based methods, LeapBot-WA and JEPA-WAM, on LIBERO-Plus and RoboTwin 2.0 without their pretrained policy backbones. On four real-robot tasks, its average success is comparable to pi0.5 and above non-embodied-pretrained baselines. Through a design study of the choices behind La-JEPA, we show that JEPA features outperform video VAE latents, most clearly out of distribution, and that training-time future prediction choices significantly impact the policy even when future prediction is skipped at inference. We correct the LIBERO-Plus instructions, as the officially released evaluator corrupts them for most variants, and re-evaluate several strong open baselines. Without a generative pretrained policy backbone, La-JEPA is better and faster than far larger policies, suggesting that robot foundation models may benefit from architectures designed for control rather than inherited from generation.

title: Improving Context-Shift Robustness of Convolutional Networks via Context-Regularized Cross-Entropy
abstract: Image classification models often encounter objects in diverse and unpredictable contexts at test time, which may differ substantially from those seen during training. This phenomenon, termed context shift, exposes a key fragility in neural networks: when models rely on non-causal contextual cues for prediction, shifts in context can lead to significant performance degradation. In this paper, we propose a novel training framework to improve the robustness of convolutional neural networks under context shift. Our approach leverages spatial feature attribution to guide models toward making predictions that rely less on contextual regions and more on object-relevant features. As a first step, recognizing a theoretical limitation of existing feature attribution methods we introduce a new variant, ContrastiveCAMs, which produces more faithful attribution maps of model predictions. Building on ContrastiveCAMs, we further propose Context-Regularized Cross-Entropy (CR-CE), a modification of the standard cross-entropy loss that regularizes the model's attention by suppressing the influence of contextual regions, thereby improving robustness to context shift. We evaluate the effectiveness of our approach on several medium-to-large scale datasets (Waterbirds, Spawrious, ImageNet/ImageNet-BG, Hard-ImageNet), and report consistent improvements in context-shift robustness.

title: Bounded GARCH Processes
abstract: We propose a novel class of Bounded GARCH (B-GARCH) processes designed to characterise the conditional heteroskedasticity of continuous time series constrained within a compact interval. While standard GARCH specifications are tailored for R-valued data, many empirical series, such as realised correlation, unemployment rates, expenditure shares, and relative humidity, are bounded. Fitting a traditional GARCH model to such data creates a severe support mismatch, frequently generating predictions and density forecasts that breach the natural boundaries of the data (boundary violation). Furthermore, conventional approaches utilising non-linear link transformations onto the real line might induce interpretability issues and estimation biases. To address these limitations, our proposed B-GARCH framework ensures a proper predictive distribution and an equation for the dynamic conditional variance with a parameter constraint that strictly preserves the bounded support of the entire process almost surely. We establish the fundamental probabilistic properties of the process, proving strict stationarity and ergodicity, and address parameter estimation via conditional maximum likelihood. The asymptotic consistency and normality of the estimators are rigorously derived, and their finite-sample performance is validated through Monte Carlo simulations. An empirical application to the monthly realised correlation between the Vanguard Real Estate ETF (VNQ) and the iShares 20+ Year Treasury Bond ETF (TLT) demonstrates that B-GARCH models effectively capture volatility clustering while completely eliminating boundary violation issue that plagues traditional GARCH models.

title: Non-Isothermal Plane Couette Flow for the Boltzmann Equation in Three Dimensions
abstract: We study the Boltzmann equation for a non-isothermal plane Couette flow in the three-dimensional channel $\mathbb T_x\times(-1,1)_y\times\mathbb T_z$ for Maxwell molecules. For sufficiently small shear rate and wall temperature perturbations, we construct a unique steady solution near the global Maxwellian. For the corresponding unsteady boundary value problem, we establish the global existence and uniqueness of solutions arising from small perturbations of the steady state, together with their exponential convergence to the steady state as $t\to\infty$. A major difficulty in both the steady and unsteady problems is to close the outgoing mass fluxes generated by diffuse reflection. To overcome this difficulty, we develop a new boundary flux transmission framework which, in the slab geometry, yields steady and time-dependent wall flux estimates through the boundary-to-boundary transmission between the two walls. We further extend this framework to damped transport equations with diffuse reflection in general bounded $C^1$ domains, even when the damping coefficient degenerates at large velocities.

title: Patch Attention Wisely: Understanding Patch Length in Attention-Based Forecasting
abstract: Attention-based time series forecasters commonly group consecutive observations into patches. Patch length is known to have a substantial impact on forecasting performance, yet its selection remains largely empirical. We develop a theoretical framework that explains why patch length matters for forecasting accuracy and provides a principled basis for its selection. For linear state-space models, we derive an exact factorization of the forecasting coefficient matrix that separates forecast dynamics from filtering dynamics. We show that dominance of a single forecast component at long horizons does not generally imply a rank-one representation. This explains why longer horizons alone need not reduce representational complexity. We combine the factorization with estimation bounds to develop a patch-selection criterion that balances representation and estimation errors under temporal dependence. Our analysis establishes conditions under which balanced patching is justified and clarifies how predictive structure, head count, training sample size, and long-run dependence enter the selection criterion.

title: Primitive Quantum Gates for an $SU(3)$ Discrete Subgroup: $Σ(216\times3)$
abstract: We construct a primitive gate set for the digital quantum simulation of the $648$-element discrete subgroup of $SU(3)$, $\dsb$. The five algorithmic primitives are the inversion, group multiplication, trace, group Fourier transform, and kinetic-phase gates, for which we provide qubit and qutrit--qubit decompositions. For a fiducial shear-viscosity calculation on a $10^3$ spatial lattice with $50$ time steps and a total synthesis-error budget of $10^{-8}$, the estimated fault-tolerant costs are $2.3$--$6.8\times10^{10}$ $T$ gates in the qubit architecture and $1.3$--$5.9\times10^{12}$ $R$ gates in the qutrit--qubit architecture.

title: RouteAlign: Aligning Task Requirements with Model Profiles for LLM Service Selection
abstract: LLM service selection requires performance evidence that reflects the demands of the current task. Aggregate scores obscure differences in capability and difficulty, while semantically related examples can involve different combinations of skills. We present RouteAlign, which uses task requirements to structure both the measurement of model performance and the selection of services. Task requirements describe capability demand and difficulty, enabling alignment with corresponding model performance measurements. Historical requirements determine how outcomes contribute to global profiles and local capability estimates; incoming requirements determine how those measurements inform the current decision. A shared scorer integrates the evidence, and a generation-cost preference controls selection among eligible services. Evaluation across diverse tasks and heterogeneous LLM services shows that RouteAlign extends the empirical quality-cost frontier toward higher task quality. Comparisons with open Jev-style decision backends show consistent quality gains, with lower generation cost than their strongest tested configuration. Ablations support the contribution of local performance evidence, while catalog-update experiments demonstrate effective reuse of the fitted scorer with refreshed model measurements.

title: Chiral invariant mass and scale symmetry in dense matter from a dilaton compensated parity doublet model
abstract: In the parity doublet model the nucleon mass includes a chiral invariant part $m_0$, which is conventionally assumed to be medium independent. We promote this assumption to a dynamical question by making the model scale invariant using a dilaton compensator $χ$, so that the effective chiral invariant mass $m_{\rm inv}^\ast = m_0\tildeχ$, with $\tildeχ= χ/f_χ$, responds to the partial restoration of scale symmetry in the medium. We fit the model parameters by using vacuum spectra, nuclear matter properties, and NICER mass--radius posteriors---with the hadronic equation of state connected to 2+1-flavor Nambu--Jona-Lasinio quark matter by an interpolation. The best fit gives $m_0 = 657$ MeV, a maximum neutron-star mass of $2.30\,M_\odot$ and $R_{1.4} = 12.22$ km, with the mass--radius sequence passing through all three NICER credible regions. The resulting tidal deformabilities, $Λ_{1.4} = 387$ and $\tildeΛ= 463$, are consistent with GW170817 measurements. The in-medium analysis separates the two restorations: at the hadron--quark matching density the chiral condensate falls to $56\%$ of its vacuum value, while the dilaton decreases only to $94\%$, so the nucleon arrives at the matching density with $90\%$ of its mass carried by the invariant part. The order parameters of chiral and scale symmetries organize the in-medium probes, making the $ω$ an almost pure probe of scale symmetry and the $ρ$ of chiral restoration, which gives us a clue on the origin of hadron mass.

title: Pohlmeyer reduction of Newton-Cartan strings
abstract: We develop a Pohlmeyer-type reduction for classical non-relativistic strings on string Newton-Cartan backgrounds. For strings on a two-sphere, we identify the invariant reduced field, show that its dynamics is integrable, and construct a Lax representation. We relate this intrinsic formulation to the non-relativistic expansion of relativistic strings and obtain a dictionary between non-relativistic string solutions and their reduced counterparts. The construction explicitly determines which relativistic solitonic configurations survive the non-relativistic limit and which decouple. Moreover, it provides a framework for applying integrability methods to Newton-Cartan string dynamics.

title: Counting multigeodesics and the Selberg-Delange method
abstract: We study the counting function $\mathcal{P}^m(X,x)$ for $m$-multigeodesics of length at most $x$ on a compact hyperbolic surface $X$ where $m$ is a positive integer. Building on the Selberg-Delange method, originally developed for counting integers with exactly $m$ prime factors in the interval $[1,x]$, we prove a large $x$ asymptotic for $\mathcal{P}^m(X,x)$. We show that for fixed $m$ as $x\to\infty$ the asymptotic is independent of the surface, whereas for $\frac{m}{\log x}$ bounded away from zero, the asymptotic depends on an infinite Euler product over the lengths of primitive closed geodesics. We also study the distribution of the function $ω_1$, defined on multigeodesics $Γ$ as $ω_1(Γ)=k-1$ for $Γ=(γ_1,...,γ_k)$ a $k$-multigeodesic. We show that as $x\to\infty$, the distribution of $ω_1$ in the set of multigeodesics of length $\leq x$ is close to that of a Poisson random variable with parameter $\log x$. Both of these theorems rely on studying the generating function of the random variable $ω_1$ which we relate to the Selberg zeta function.

title: Analytical Modeling of the Admittance Tensor of Periodic Elliptical Meta-Atoms
abstract: A metasurface is an electrically thin interface that controls the phase, amplitude and polarization of a wave, upon reflection or transmission. Printed on a grounded dielectric substrate and spatially modulated across the aperture, it converts a guided surface wave into a radiated leaky wave, a mechanism used in holographic metasurface antennas. Controlling this conversion requires synthesizing a prescribed distribution of admittance tensors, each derived from the homogenization of a subwavelength unit cell. Many numerical and semi-analytical methods have been proposed to relate the geometry of a meta-atom to the tensor it produces. This paper presents, to the author's knowledge, the first analytical model, restricted to elliptical meta-atoms on a uniform lattice. The Galerkin method is applied directly to the geometry of the patches, without spatial meshing. An affine transformation maps any rotated ellipse onto the unit disk, so that a single formulation covers every configuration. A wideband response takes from minutes to tens of minutes with a periodic full-wave solver, while the proposed model evaluates it in a few tens of milliseconds on the same workstation, roughly three orders of magnitude faster. The predicted admittance agrees with a method-of-moments reference up to the fundamental resonance and captures the guided-mode anomaly of the substrate. Beyond the physical insight it brings, the model is a differentiable function of the geometry, which makes the quasi-real-time design of optimized metasurfaces possible.

title: Reflective Nature Experiences in Virtual Reality
abstract: This paper presents the design and evaluation of an accessible virtual reality (VR) nature experience developed to promote mindfulness, reduce stress, and support emotional well-being. The system immerses users in a calming natural environment through realistic landscapes, ambient soundscapes, guided breathing exercises, and interactive checkpoints that encourage reflection. Accessibility was a central design consideration, particularly for users with diverse physical and sensory abilities or limited access to natural environments and traditional mindfulness resources.
