Finally, we also report additional proper motion measurements for eight of the other nine known JADES Y-dwarf candidates, highlighting JWST extragalactic surveys as a powerful route to building a statistically useful, parallax-calibrated sample of Y dwarfs.

title: Estimating Distribution Grid Upgrade Costs based on County-level Building Electrification Projections
abstract: Building electrification projections are typically developed at aggregated geographic levels to support bulk power system analysis, even though a significant portion of the infrastructure investments required to accommodate electrification occurs within distribution systems. Existing methodologies to disaggregate load growth projections onto distribution networks are based on context-specific analyses that require detailed data on building electricity consumption, distribution feeders, and geographic parcels, which are often proprietary and unavailable for policy and economic impact studies. This paper presents a methodology to disaggregate county-level building electrification projections onto representative distribution feeders and evaluate their impact on distribution upgrade costs. The proposed approach combines bulk system end-use electrification projections with representative feeder sets to generate building-level electrification measures. These measures are then used to create load profiles that are consistent with county-level projections while preserving the spatial diversity of electrification demand required for distribution infrastructure analysis. Using a case study of Genesee County, in Michigan, the results show that the proposed methodology is able to capture a diversity of feeder-level responses to electrification and represent the different realities that building electrification produces within the distribution system. This allows to represent localized load variations and capture more realistic distribution system upgrade costs driven by electrification.

title: Atomic Static Electric Quadrupole Polarizability from Relativistic Many-Body Theory With Application To Thulium $\left(6s^2\, 4f^{13}\right)$\, $^2F_{7/2}$ and $^2F_{5/2}$
abstract: In the present work a method for calculating atomic static electric rank-$n$ tensor quadrupole polarizabilities $α_Q^{(n)}(J)$ for arbitrary atomic electronic structure is presented. It is based on a linear-symmetry representation of atomic states using large-scale relativistic configuration interaction wavefunctions, and the quadrupole polarizabilities are obtained by a sum-over-states approach. The major result from applying this method to atomic thulium is $α_Q^{(0)}(\frac{7}{2}) = 2496^{+0}_{-231}$ \au for the electronic ground term $^2F_{7/2}$ static electric scalar quadrupole polarizability which is roughly a factor of four smaller than same property in the electronic ground state of the cesium atom. This finding adds to the favorable properties of thulium atoms in atomic-clock research.

title: Multimagnon bound states in the polarized phase of anisotropic antiferromagnets
abstract: We investigate single-ion bound magnon states in the high-field polarized phase of uniaxial antiferromagnets. By solving the two-particle problem exactly, we determine the dispersion of bound magnon pairs both below and above the continuum. We also obtain rigorous bounds on their binding energies by using the Gershgorin circle theorem. For spin-1 easy-axis systems, two-magnon bound states with zero total momentum emerge as low-energy excitations once the ratio of single-ion anisotropy to exchange exceeds a threshold value. As the field decreases, magnon pairs condense, driving a transition into a spin-nematic phase. Beyond the two-magnon problem, we develop a general strong-coupling approach that describes $n$-magnon single-ion bound states ($n\leq 2S$) in large-$S$ easy-axis antiferromagnets. The Bose-Einstein condensation of these multi-magnon excitations yields a rich hierarchy of field-induced multipolar phases stabilized by single-ion anisotropy. Comparisons with recent experiments on Na$_2$BaNi(PO$_4$)$_2$ and Sr$_2$CoGe$_2$O$_7$ illustrate the quantitative power of our theory.

title: Asymptotic analysis of the dynamical field-field correlation function of the impenetrable Bose gas
abstract: We study the long-time, large-distance asymptotic behaviour of the two-point correlation function of fields of the impenetrable Bose gas in equilibrium states characterized by a quasi-momentum distribution (or filling fraction). This includes, in particular, the cases of Gibbs and generalized Gibbs ensembles. The overall structure of the asymptotic expansion depends on the number of Fermi points, those points for which the quasi-momentum distribution takes the value $1/2$. The leading asymptotic behaviour is determined by a relaxation rate, a logarithmic correction term and an amplitude for which we provide simple and explicit expressions. In the case of two Fermi points the first sub-leading correction is calculated as well.

title: Connectivity in a New Bounded-Space Dynamic Model
abstract: We introduce a new model for dynamic algorithms in which the algorithm has read-only oracle access to a dynamically changing input and random access to its own bounded workspace. It is a dynamic analogue of the time-space tradeoffs for static inputs studied in complexity theory, where only writable memory counts as space. We study dynamic undirected $s$-$t$ connectivity: after every edge update to an $n$-vertex graph, an algorithm with $S$ words of workspace must report whether $s$ and $t$ are connected. The graph is accessed via adjacency list queries (degree, $j$-th neighbor) or adjacency matrix queries. Our algorithms are randomized; our lower bounds hold for randomized algorithms with $cn$ bits of workspace, $c>0$ a small constant ($cn/\log n$ for the worst-case matrix bound). We prove: (1) With adjacency lists, worst-case time $\tildeΘ(n^2/S^2)$ per insertion is necessary and sufficient for incremental algorithms. (2) With an adjacency matrix, worst-case time $\tildeΩ(n^2/S)$ per insertion is necessary for incremental algorithms, and sufficient for $S\ge\sqrt{n}$. (3) With amortization, incremental algorithms achieve $\tilde O(n/S)$ time per insertion with adjacency lists and $\tilde O(n^2/S)$ with an adjacency matrix, while $\tildeΩ(\sqrt{n/S})$ and $\tildeΩ(n\sqrt{n/S})$, respectively, are necessary. (4) Fully dynamic algorithms need amortized time $\tildeΩ(n/S)$ per update with adjacency lists and $\tildeΩ(n^2/S)$ with an adjacency matrix, even on forests, where both bounds are tight (lists: under bounded degree). Conventional dynamic connectivity admits polylogarithmic update time with $Ω(n)$ words of space. In contrast, our lower bounds show that polynomial update time is necessary whenever $S\le n^{1-\varepsilon}$, even for a single pair of vertices and even for incremental algorithms with amortized guarantees.

title: USB Gym: A Gymnasium Testbed for Closed-Loop Ultrasound View Matching
abstract: Background and Objective: Our main goal is ultrasound guidance: moving a probe until its image matches a target view. Published methods for each part of a guide are evaluated in separate simulators. We asked whether these methods, combined into one guide, are good enough. Methods: We built USB Gym, a testbed whose standard engine simulates ultrasound from public patient CT, with a network drawing organ textures from CT labels. Its guide has three replaceable parts (slots), an organ segmenter, a controller and a reward, which received 20 published methods, each run on the same 60 episodes of six held-out patients. In each slot, a published method replaced ours only if detectably better on these patients. The better of this combination and our original guide on 20 new CTs is the benchmark baseline. A pose oracle, reading the exact probe pose available only in simulation, set the reference. The results below are exploratory. Results: On these CTs, the probe started on average 16.0 mm from the target view; the pose oracle brought it to 1.5 mm. Of the results known when the combination was fixed, only an image-similarity reward (SSIM) was slightly but detectably better, so the combination was our guide with that reward. This combination was the benchmark baseline, ending at 13.7 mm (16% of the oracle's progress). Conclusions: Combining untuned published methods with ours did not guide the probe near the target view; the task remains under-explored. The testbed accepts new methods; no guide was tested on hardware.

title: From elementary processes to chaos: a discrete-time two-stage contagion model and its continuous limit
abstract: Two-stage contagion, in which adoption requires two contacts with adopters, combined with population turnover produces bistability and relaxation oscillations, but no chaos, in Katriel's differential equations. From the elementary reactions, without reference to the differential equations, we derive a discrete-time model in which the population is updated in rounds of length $τ$, as in elections, meetings or turns of a game: each individual makes at most one transition per round, events compete as exponential risks, and adoptions take effect from the next round. The model is a Markov chain whose large-population limit is a map $F_τ$; Katriel's equations are recovered as $τ\to0$. Taking the probability $p$ of adoption after a single contact as bifurcation parameter, with rates and round length fixed, $F_τ$ goes from extinction through a window of chaos to a stable equilibrium; for $β/γ=46$, $μ/γ=0.002$, $γτ=5.5$ the computed window is $0.023\le p\le0.056$, bounded by the invasion threshold and by a boundary crisis beyond a subcritical Neimark--Sacker point. One-stage contagion ($p=1$), $p=0$ and permanent adoption showed no chaos in our scans. In all tests the chaotic attractor was unique up to coexistence with simpler attractors, with one positive Lyapunov exponent. In the same window Katriel's equations have a periodic relaxation cycle with troughs of $10^{-44}$--$10^{-164}$: the round structure does not create the oscillation but turns it into chaos and shrinks the oscillatory range in $p$ from $(0.022,0.41)$ to $(0.022,0.056)$. The chaos is thus not an artefact of discretising a stable state, but a property of two-stage contagion with synchronous updating.

title: Kinetic models of a K channel with 2 stage voltage sensor activation and an opening step
abstract: The activation of a K channel with 2 voltage sensors and a separate opening step may be described by a 4 state kinetic equation. If $k_{o}$ and $k_{c}$ are the opening and closing rates, and $α$ and $β$ are the voltage sensor rates such that $k_{o}$ $\ggα,k_{c}\ggβ$ and $k_{o}$ $\gg k_{c}$, the kinetic equation may be reduced to a 3 state model where the effective backward rate from the activated-open state is $2βk_{c}/(k_{o}+k_{c})$. However, if a K channel voltage sensor activates in 2 stages, and there is a separate opening step, the occupation probabilities of the states of the channel satisfy a 10 state kinetic equation. When the time constants of the characteristic equation for each voltage sensor differ by an order of magnitude, and $k_{o}$ $\gg k_{c}$, the open state probability is proportional to $n^{2}$, where $n$ satisfies a rate equation, and the derived rates have a similar voltage dependence to the rates $α_{n}$ and $β_{n}$ from voltage clamp data.

title: Global solutions for continuous-time Burgers equations and infinite-volume polymer measures
abstract: We study the stochastic Burgers equation on the whole space, driven by space-homogeneous Gaussian noises that are white in time and colored in space, for both positive and zero viscosity. We show that in dimension one, for any fixed average velocity, there is a unique ergodic global solution to the Burgers equation for all nonnegative viscosities, and that the One Force---One Solution principle holds. We also describe the basin of attraction and show that these global solutions are one-point pullback attractors. Moreover, the viscous global solution converges to the inviscid global solution as the viscosity tends to zero. Our technique relies on the study of polymer measures; accordingly, we establish the existence and uniqueness of infinite-volume polymer measures in a given asymptotic direction, as well as their convergence to semi-infinite minimizers in the zero-temperature limit. We also establish the existence part of all these results in arbitrary dimension larger than one.

title: Pointless K3 surfaces over finite fields
abstract: We prove that K3 surfaces with no rational points over the finite field with $q$ elements exist if and only if $q \leq 11$. Our approach applies linear programming techniques to improve on generic sphere packing bounds for the discriminants of even rootless definite lattices. These bounds are applied to constrain the possible zeta functions of K3 surfaces with no rational points via the Artin--Tate formula. The remaining cases are ruled out by direct analysis of primitive embeddings of particular lattices into Niemeier lattices.

title: Twisted Yangians of quasi-split type DI and Drinfeld type current relations
abstract: We study the twisted Yangian associated with the quasi-split symmetric pair $(\mathfrak{o}_{2n}, \mathfrak{o}_{n-1}\oplus \mathfrak{o}_{n+1})$ of type DI. Working in the transposed $R$-matrix presentation of arXiv:2607.14692, we show that the generating matrix $S(u)$ admits no Gaussian decomposition. We decompose instead the matrix $\widehat{S}(u) = G\,S(u)$, where $G$ is the constant term of $S(u)$. A chain of quasi-determinantal embeddings lowers the rank within this family of pairs and ends at $(\mathfrak{o}_4,\mathfrak{o}_3)$. Together with a direct study of a degenerate block of type AI, this gives a presentation of the special twisted Yangian $SY^{\mathrm{tw}}(\mathfrak{o}_{2n},\mathfrak{o}_{n-1}\oplus \mathfrak{o}_{n+1})$ by Drinfeld type current relations. The two fork nodes of the Dynkin diagram carry Drinfeld's presentation of $Y(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$. All other relations are those of split type DI, except that the Serre relation with a doubled fork node has zero right hand side. For $n\ge3$ we obtain an explicit isomorphism between the $R$-matrix presentation of Guay and Regelskis and the Drinfeld presentation of Lu and Zhang. The Drinfeld generators are expressed through the Gaussian series of $\widehat{S}(u)$. With quasi-split type AIII (Lu and Zhang), this completes the explicit comparison for the classical quasi-split types with a nontrivial diagram involution.

title: Unifying Central Flow, Rod Flow, and the Edge Coupling
abstract: At the edge of stability, the iterates of gradient descent oscillate along the sharp directions of the Hessian. This poses a significant challenge for continuous-time models as the usual continuous-time approximation -- the gradient flow -- admits no oscillations. Several continuous-time models have been proposed to capture the behavior at the edge of stability, among them central flow and rod flow. Although both models can be interpreted as performing a coarse-graining in time, the connection between them remains poorly understood. Here we show that both flows can be derived from a third object, the edge coupling: a functional on consecutive iterates whose critical points are the fixed points and period-two orbits of gradient descent. It is revealed that the two flows correspond to coarse-grainings at different time scales. Rod flow coarse-grains over only the fastest time scale, while central flow coarse-grains over both the fast and intermediate time scales. Furthermore, using the edge coupling, we derive rod flows and central flows for momentum methods such as heavy ball and Adam. We verify the derived flows experimentally on representative neural network architectures, where they track the discrete iterates throughout all phases of training -- including the transition from the stable regime to the edge of stability.

title: A Theoretical Analysis of a Bilevel Optimization Formulation for Combined Local-Global Optical Flow Models
abstract: This paper analyzes a bilevel formulation for learning the regularization parameter of combined local-global (CLG) optical flow models. The lower-level problem computes the flow from a Lucas--Kanade data term and a quadratic or total variation (TV) regularizer, and the upper-level problem selects the parameter that minimizes the squared distance to a ground-truth flow. The setting is finite-dimensional, and a full-rank assumption makes the lower-level solution unique. For the quadratic model we derive sufficient conditions for the existence of an optimal parameter, for every optimal parameter to be positive, and for strict local optimality. For TV regularization an optimal parameter always exists, because the lower-level solution vanishes for large parameters, and we give a sufficient condition for positivity that accounts for the coupling of the two flow components through the local structure tensors. Synthetic examples illustrate the conditions, including cases in which they fail.

title: OraRefer: Segmentation-Guided Multi-Photograph Fusion for Oral Cancer Screening with Guaranteed Patient-Level Sensitivity
abstract: Oral cancer and the oral potentially malignant disorders (OPMD) that can precede it are visible on the oral mucosa, which makes smartphone photographs a promising tool for screening. Deep learning models for this task classify individual photographs. However, screening refers patients, not photographs: a patient is usually photographed several times, and the referral decision must miss no more than a set share of patients with disease. We propose OraRefer, a patient-level screening model that reads each photograph with a segmentation-guided foundation model that conditions its class decision on the predicted lesion, combines all photographs of a patient with risk factors, and refers through a threshold with a finite-sample sensitivity guarantee. The model localizes the mouth itself, so inference needs no annotation. On 3000 photographs of 714 patients, patient-level fusion reaches an AUROC of 0.919 and outperforms attention-based multiple-instance learning. At a 90% sensitivity target, OraRefer detects 95% of patients with OPMD or cancer and misses 3 of 61 patients with cancer, at a specificity of 0.610. Because the threshold is calibrated without retraining, each clinic can set its own guaranteed operating point on a local calibration sample.

title: Radio-to-Pose Information for Gauge-Drift Correction in Cooperative Localization
abstract: Cooperative localization uses odometry and inter-robot measurements to estimate the motion of a robot team. These measurements describe only relative geometry, but the team's estimated position and orientation can drift together over time, i.e., gauge drift. In this work, we study correction of this gauge drift using a radio attenuation map registered in the same world coordinate frame used for robot poses. Specifically, we propose Radio-to-Pose Information (RPI), an interface that converts power residuals and their pose derivatives into a Gaussian information matrix and vector pair. RPI builds on the insight that received power is sensitive to shared displacement in the world map. The pose estimator uses the interface together with odometry and inter-robot measurements to update poses and minimize uncertainty. We characterize the shared motions detectable from the map and observed links. For an uncertain shared map, RPI keeps correlations across robots and time and reproduces joint Gaussian pose estimates and covariances. Across $1000$ simulated Gaussian trials, RPI matches the results of joint estimation. Across 32 paired trials with a registered map, RPI reduces common-position RMSE from $0.542$m to $0.140$m in a $50\times50$m arena compared with a baseline that uses radio only to weight relative measurements.

title: SpecCTMC: Exact Speculative Simulation of Diffusion Language Model Continuous-Time Markov Chains
abstract: Masked diffusion language models offer parallel text generation, but independently sampling multiple tokens can disrupt their dependencies and change the output distribution. Exact continuous-time sampling avoids this approximation, yet typically requires one sequential model evaluation per token. We introduce SpecCTMC, a training-free speculative sampler that reduces this sequential bottleneck without a separate draft model. SpecCTMC proposes successive token updates using previously computed model predictions, evaluates their intermediate states in parallel, and applies an exact acceptance-and-correction procedure. We prove that SpecCTMC preserves the joint distribution of event times, generation order, and token values of the underlying continuous-time Markov chain. It therefore introduces neither time-discretization error nor additional factorization error from parallel decoding. Experiments on LLaDA-8B-Instruct and Dream-v0-Instruct-7B across five benchmarks demonstrate 1.73-4.38x fewer sequential model evaluations than direct continuous-time sampling, while preserving the reference sampling distribution. Our code is available at: https://github.com/kasakh/specctmc

title: StrataFlux: Memory-Hierarchy-Native Low-Bit LLM Inference
abstract: Quantization reduces the memory and bandwidth demands of large language model (LLM) inference but can degrade accuracy; offloading higher-precision data can instead stall generation. We introduce StrataFlux, a framework that challenges this tradeoff by recovering accuracy lost to low-bit weight and key-value (KV) cache quantization while retaining quantization's memory and speed advantages. StrataFlux co-designs refinement representation, selection, and delivery to make host RAM and solid-state drives useful sources of additional precision. Its selective precision streaming reduces transfer volume, overlaps delivery with computation, and reuses fetched precision across decoding steps so generation need not wait for every transfer. We evaluate 2-4-bit weights and 2-3-bit KV-cache on dedicated GPUs and unified-memory platforms. For 2-bit Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct weights, StrataFlux reduces WikiText-2 perplexity from 9.46 to 8.40 while maintaining 95.4% of the quantized base's throughput on RTX 5090. With 2-bit weights and KV, StrataFlux raises Qwen3-8B's AIME 2024/2025 accuracy from 11.0% to 47.1% at unchanged GPU memory use. At 128K context, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with 3-bit weights and 2-bit KV achieves comparable perplexity and speed to vLLM's 4-bit AWQ weights and 8-bit KV on RTX 5090, using approximately half the GPU memory. These results show that GPU-resident precision need not set the accuracy ceiling, nor offloading-tier latency dictate decoding speed.

title: SHORE: Stability-Hybrid On-Policy Reinforcement Learning for Online Bin Packing
abstract: Online 3D bin packing with a processing buffer requires choosing which box to pack, its orientation, and its placement while keeping the stack stable under unknown future arrivals. A collapse ends the episode and forfeits the remaining volume. Existing methods use geometric rules or hard stability masks, limiting how risk can influence the joint choice of box, orientation, and placement. We propose Stability-Hybrid On-Policy Reinforcement Learning (SHORE), which combines a learned stability probability of a placement with an on-policy estimate of its return conditional on stability. A 3D U-Net learns stability from executed outcomes and simulated alternatives, revealing outcomes of actions underrepresented in early rollouts. A discrete on-policy actor--critic uses stability predictions in both its action values and policy prior, with gates that limit the effect of an untrained or changing model. In deployment, SHORE does not require additional search or simulation overhead. In Isaac Gym, SHORE reaches 73\% space utilization by 0.4M environment steps, while the same learner without stability modeling reaches that level at about 1M. On the expanded 60-box set, SHORE achieves 0.734 space utilization versus 0.588 for the GOPT state-of-the-art baseline, with a higher placement-failure frequency (1.03\% vs. 0.63\%), trading more risk for greater packed volume. The results show faster learning and higher utilization on the more demanding realistic box arrival set. Ablations suggest that simulated alternatives provide useful early supervision, while executed outcomes alone sustain later performance. We also demonstrate the method on a real robot to verify the simplicity of integrating the method to real bin packing pipelines.

title: The singular Gaussian scaling limit for a tagged particle in the infinite-dimensional Dyson model at $β=2$
abstract: We prove a logarithmic central limit theorem for a tagged particle in infinite-dimensional Dyson Brownian motion at inverse temperature $β=2$, starting from the sine$_2$ point process. The fluctuation is of order $\sqrt{\log t}$, which is subdiffusive and substantially slower than the polynomial fluctuations of classical short-range interacting particle systems, reflecting the rigidity induced by long-range logarithmic repulsion. We further identify the scaling limit as the singular Gaussian field corresponding to the zero-Hurst parameter, which provides a realisation of the singular Gaussian field as a scaling limit of a tagged particle raised by Dürr, Goldstein and Lebowitz (Comm. Pure Appl. Math. 38 (1985)).

title: Information Elicitation by Ordinal Agreement
abstract: Ordinal information is central to tasks ranging from conference peer review to Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback for large language models. In many such settings, there is no objective ground truth against which reports can be directly verified, making incentive-compatible elicitation challenging. Peer-prediction mechanisms have been designed to achieve truthful elicitation despite the lack of ground-truth verification. However, existing peer-prediction methods do not provide incentives for agents to truthfully compress rich private information (e.g. reviews) into coarser ordinal reports (e.g. rankings) requested by the mechanisms. We propose a simple ordinal peer-prediction mechanism that rewards agents based on pairwise agreement, measured by Kendall tau. Under a broad class of Bayesian Stochastically Order Consistent models---which includes classical models such as Mallows and Thurstone---we prove that truthful reporting is stochastically dominant, and strongly truthful under index-equivariant strategies. This provides robust incentives even for agents with non-linear utility functions, such as risk aversion. Our mechanism further accommodates heterogeneous agents, top-K reports, and subset assignments, where each agent is scored against one randomly drawn peer. Experiments on synthetic Mallows and Thurstone data, together with a real-data stress test on the SUSHI preference dataset, show right-shifted truthful-payment distributions and the highest normalized sensitivity among tested baselines.

title: CascadeFilter: Cost-Efficient Semantic Filtering with Joint Threshold Selection
abstract: Semantic filtering selects records that satisfy a natural-language predicate and is an important operation in data analytics based on large language models (LLMs). Executing an expensive model on every document incurs substantial inference cost. Existing approaches reduce this cost by accepting predictions from cheaper models and forwarding uncertain records to an oracle. Task Cascades further varies document portions and operations, and provides an accuracy-guaranteed extension. However, its threshold calibration follows a prescribed adjustment sequence after cascade assembly, rather than minimizing cost over alternative combinations of stage thresholds. Motivated by this, we propose CascadeFilter, a three-stage semantic filtering method that jointly searches the thresholds for a small language model operating on extracted evidence and full documents, with unresolved records forwarded to the oracle. For a fixed cascade, we formulate threshold selection as minimizing token-aware cost subject to an oracle-relative error constraint, and select the least-cost certified configuration in a pre-specified grid. A finite-population calibration procedure bounds oracle-relative error after selection, using fixed-sequence tests on threshold tracks to allocate the multiple-testing budget. We further combine lexical and dense retrieval, reranking, and neighborhood-supported confidence to improve evidence extraction and routing. These components enhance the cascade while leaving its certification interface unchanged. Across six datasets and 13 evaluation settings, the reported results have the highest benchmark accuracy and macro-averaged F1 score in 12 settings each. These comparisons describe the reported operating points; the accuracy guarantee concerns agreement with the oracle.

title: VisionSIM: Beyond Idealized Sensors - A Multi-Modal Simulator for Robot Perception
abstract: Robotic perception increasingly relies on heterogeneous sensor suites combining cameras with emerging modalities (event, SPAD, iToF/dToF, and thermal). Yet existing simulators idealize these sensors, hiding critical modality-specific failure modes that limit real-world deployment. We present VisionSIM, a unified, physically grounded simulation platform that elevates sensor realism to a first-class concern by modeling the raw physical measurement process for diverse conventional and emerging modalities. We expose fine-grained control over physical sensor parameters, reproducing failure modes overlooked by general-purpose simulators: pileup and glare for LiDAR; phase wrapping, saturation, and motion artifacts for iToF; refractory drops for event cameras; and history-dependent emission for thermal cameras. This enables principled cross-modality comparison on identical scenes and trajectories. We release the platform and a large indoor dataset with synchronized raw measurements and rich ground-truth annotations.

title: NPCBench: A Clinical Apprenticeship Benchmark for Multimodal Care-Pathway Reasoning in Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma
abstract: Current medical benchmarks typically break down clinical competence into isolated factual questions, single-image tasks, or static case vignettes. These tests score individual answers, but reveal less about whether a model can integrate subspecialty knowledge with multimodal evidence and track a patient's condition throughout a course of care. To close this gap, we introduce NPCBench, a clinical apprenticeship benchmark for nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC). NPCBench mirrors specialist training, from guideline and foundational knowledge to case planning, longitudinal review, CarePath integration, and open-ended consultation. It contains 4,777 component and consultation items and a 100-patient CarePath cohort with 417 scored diagnostic and care tasks. The episode-level evaluation tests whether diagnostic and care answers are jointly correct within a care pathway. By linking stepwise tasks to patient-level care trajectories, NPCBench evaluates whether models ground decisions in visual evidence, interpret changes in patient state, and meet clinical requirements in consultation. Across 30 evaluated models, we observe a composition gap: strong performance on individual tasks does not ensure jointly correct diagnostic and care answers for the same patient. Among 21 multimodal models, strict CarePath success reaches at most 23%. Paired controls and physician calibration further examine evidence grounding, longitudinal revision, and consultation judging. Overall, NPCBench broadens the evaluation of medical artificial intelligence beyond static question-answering paradigms to an apprenticeship-oriented assessment of clinical workflows, thereby offering a testbed for evidence-based and temporally coherent reasoning in oncology care.

title: Modelling and analysis of a cocktail phage therapy with coinfection
abstract: We analyze a delay differential model for phage therapy in which a cocktail of $n$ different types of bacteriophages, each with its own latency period, is administered and coinfection is allowed. We prove the global existence, uniqueness and nonnegativity of solutions, and the existence of an invariant region, under suitable conditions, in which the bacteria are eradicated exponentially fast. We determine the stability of the bacteria-free equilibrium in terms of the administered doses and give sufficient conditions for the nonexistence of coexistence equilibria, showing that coinfection may allow bacteria and phages to coexist even when the doses are large. For a cocktail of two phage types with the same latency period, we obtain a complete description of the biologically feasible coexistence equilibria, which may be zero, one or two. Numerical simulations illustrate the theoretical results.

title: Lord of the Precision, the Two Floats: Double-Word Arithmetic for Complex Numbers
abstract: Datacenter GPUs increasingly favour low-precision floating-point formats, offering higher throughput than FP64. Double-word (DW) arithmetic represents numbers as unevaluated sums of two floating-point values, providing higher accuracy. We present the first error analysis of complex DW multiplication and division. Both operations reduce to sums of two DW products, combined using one of three DW addition algorithms: accurate, sloppy, or Madd. Normalising DW products ensures nonoverlapping components, but omitting this step reduces the number of arithmetic operations. We bound the resulting overlap and prove that Madd retains a relative error bound of $3u^2+O(u^3)$ for overlapping inputs, where $u$ is the unit roundoff. For all variants, we establish relative error bounds of the form $(ακ+β)u^2+O(u^3)$, where $κ$ is the condition number of the sum of products. Our analysis shows that the less expensive sloppy addition suffices. We implement these variants in CompleXDW, an open-source C++ library for CPUs and GPUs. In the high-energy physics code MadGraph7, FP32-based DW arithmetic achieves up to 2.9x and 2.1x higher throughput than FP64 on NVIDIA L40S and AMD Radeon Pro W7900 GPUs, respectively, while losing approximately 1.4 correct significant digits.

title: MOMASPLAT: Dynamic Novel-View Demonstration Augmentation for Mobile Manipulation
abstract: Visuomotor policies trained through imitation learning are highly sensitive to changes in camera viewpoint. This is particularly problematic for mobile manipulation (MoMa), where robots rarely execute manipulation from the exact same base pose used during demonstration collection due to navigation uncertainty, localization drift, and environmental constraints. Recent approaches use novel-view synthesis (NVS) to augment demonstrations with unseen viewpoints, but they assume static scenes and therefore fail to re-render the manipulated object during the post-contact interaction phase, leaving the most critical parts of the demonstration unaugmented. We present MOMASPLAT, a novel-view demonstration augmentation framework for mobile manipulation that synthesizes full manipulation trajectories from unseen robot base poses, including dynamic object interactions. Our key insight is that standard MoMa data collection naturally provides the multiview observations needed to reconstruct both the static scene and the manipulated object in 3D. MOMASPLAT combines 3D Gaussian Splatting, feed-forward 3D foundation models, and kinematics-based action retargeting to separately reconstruct the scene and manipulated object, render them from novel viewpoints, and generate geometrically consistent synthetic demonstrations paired with transformed actions. We evaluate MOMASPLAT on five real-world mobile manipulation tasks involving both rigid and articulated objects across three scenes, and validate the fidelity of its synthesized demonstrations against ground truth in simulation. MOMASPLAT substantially improves robustness to unseen base poses, more than doubling the average success rate of the strongest baseline and maintaining non-trivial success at large base displacements where all baselines fail, while reducing the need for largescale real-world data collection.

title: SLA: Scaling Spatial-Language-Action Model via Continual Pre-training
abstract: Reliable robotic manipulation requires both semantic understanding and precise control in three-dimensional space. However, vision-language-action (VLA) foundations largely inherit visual representations from 2D vision-language pre-training, while spatial supervision is often introduced only during task-specific adaptation. Developing spatial understanding as a transferable foundation-model capability therefore calls for learning from broader robot experience. We present SLA, a Spatial-Language-Action Model that scales implicit spatial alignment to continual pre-training and maintains it during downstream post-training. Initialized from a pretrained pi05 policy, SLA jointly optimizes action prediction and alignment between intermediate visual embeddings and spatial representations from a frozen 3D perception model. We curate and unify heterogeneous robot datasets to support spatial learning across diverse embodiments, tasks, and scenes. To accommodate this diversity, we introduce feature-dependent gates that adaptively aggregate visual embeddings from multiple VLA layers for spatial supervision. The teacher further exploits partially available depth and camera calibration alongside RGB observations, enabling effective use of heterogeneous geometric annotations. Probabilistic state dropout encourages reliance on visual cues and mitigates overfitting to demonstration trajectories. All auxiliary components are used only during training, allowing direct reuse of pretrained VLA weights and preserving the original inference architecture.

title: A Simple Approach to the Complexity of Mean Field Ising Spin Glasses
abstract: The geometry of spherical spin glasses is relatively well understood, thanks in large part to the Kac-Rice formula. However, this formula does not directly apply to discrete spin systems, and much less is known mathematically about the geometry of Ising spin glasses. In this paper, we present a simple method for counting local optima and gapped states in a broad class of discrete spin glasses. To illustrate its scope, we compute the annealed complexities ("configurational entropies," in the physics language) of mixed Ising spin glasses with potentials, such as external fields, and of the Ghatak-Sherrington model. These computations recover several existing results in the mathematics and physics literature as special cases. We can also compute energy-constrained complexity, finding a critical energy threshold analogous to the spherical case, but for gapped states of pure Ising spin glasses. Finally, we use our method to establish a form of disorder persistence for gapped states, identifying a transition between $3$-spin and $4$-spin glasses.

title: New results on cyclic and ordered Ramsey numbers
abstract: Inspired by the work of Poljak, Bašić, Damnjanović, Stevanović, and Stošić used the Kissat SAT solver in a recent paper to systematically determine the small cyclic and ordered Ramsey numbers of several families of graphs. By studying the patterns in their data, Bašić et al. formulated 15 conjectures on cyclic and ordered Ramsey numbers. In this paper, we confirm 9 of their conjectures, trace confirmations of 2 more to existing literature, and, perhaps surprisingly, disprove another one.

title: Muir: Linear Attention with Sensitivity-Allocated Gating and Matched-Filter Readout
abstract: Linear attention compresses context into a fixed-size key-value state for linear-time training and constant-memory inference. Gated delta-rule models decay this state and erase its prediction for an incoming key before writing a new value; Gated DeltaNet-2 (GDN-2) generalizes this with channel-wise decay and decoupled, full-rank erase and write gates. However, we show that state updates are far less sensitive to erasure than to writes: key activation and unit normalization concentrate key energy onto a sparse subset of channels, whereas value writes scale all channels, so the erase gate can be parameterized at lower rank. Furthermore, slow-decaying state rows accumulate much larger norms than fast rows, dominating unweighted readout and forcing stronger write-time erasure to suppress interference. Guided by this analysis, we introduce Muir, which fuses all gates into a sensitivity-allocated low-rank projection, re-weights state rows with a matched-filter readout gate, and reinvests the saved parameters in a wider feed-forward network. Because standard chunkwise algorithms become numerically unstable at the large chunk sizes needed to saturate wide matrix units, we design a parallel update for stable, efficient training. Across 166M-1.34B parameters, Muir lowers perplexity by 1.8-2.0% over GDN-2 and 2.5-3.6% over Transformer, raises commonsense accuracy by up to 1.9 points, and improves extractive recall over GDN-2. At 1.34B, Muir outperforms both baselines on multi-hop and multi-needle recall, extrapolates 2,560x from its 4K training length to 10M-token streams without perplexity drift, and maintains near-100% passkey retrieval to 1M tokens with static readout. Muir achieves these gains while matching GDN-2 throughput, reaching its 100B-token validation loss 1.2x faster, and training 2.7x faster than Transformer at 32K.

title: On the elliptic regularization of maximal slope curves
abstract: We consider the so-called Weighted Energy-Dissipation approximation of gradient flows in metric spaces. We prove the convergence of minimizers to maximal slope curves under assumptions that are close to those of the original existence theory for metric gradient flows. The proof relies on an energy-dissipation identity for the approximating curves and on an adaptation of a general stability result for maximal slope curves.

title: An Improved Minimization Method: Eliminating Shift and Variance Inflation While Maintaining Marginal Balance
abstract: Pocock and Simon's minimization method is a widely used approach for covariate-adaptive randomization in clinical trials. However, it can exhibit the shift problem under unequal allocation and variance inflation of the imbalances in additional covariates. In this paper, we propose a new minimization method that preserves the conventional biased-coin allocation probability while ensuring marginal imbalances bounded in probability. Meanwhile, the proposed procedure guarantees that neither the shift problem nor variance inflation occurs. Simulation and empirical studies demonstrate the excellent performance of the proposed procedure.

title: Module-Aware Optimization for Graph Neural Networks
abstract: Different optimizers impose different geometries on parameter updates. Adaptive methods such as Adam and AdamW use coordinate-wise updates, while matrix-aware optimizers such as Muon utilize weight-matrix structure through orthogonalized updates. For Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), however, the effective geometry of its weight matrices is shaped not only by its learned channel-mixing weights, but also by the graph-propagated representations it acts on. Thus, even if an update is well normalized as a matrix, its effect on the layer output can be amplified when applied to graph-propagated features. To address this gap, we introduce GraphMuon, a graph-aware optimizer that adapts Muon's matrix updates to the covariance structure of graph-propagated layer inputs. GraphMuon performs orthogonalization in a metric defined by these propagated representations and normalizes step sizes according to the update's induced effect on the layer representation. We show that theoretically, vanilla Muon can suffer from graph-induced update amplification, while our GraphMuon can mitigate this effect. As such, our GraphMuon yields a graph-metric analogue of Muon's polar update step. Empirically, GraphMuon achieves $1.32\times$-$2.42\times$ validation-loss time-to-target speedups over AdamW on three large-scale OGB benchmarks. Across 15 dataset-architecture configurations spanning node classification, inductive graph classification, and graph regression, it achieves lower time-to-target in 13 cases, while maintaining competitive or superior predictive performance. Code is available at https://github.com/guy-hadad/GraphMuon.

title: SensorGuard-RV: Sensor-to-Register Data Protection for Resource-Constrained RISC-V Devices
abstract: Embedded systems rely on sensor measurements that traverse a complex hardware-firmware stack (e.g. peripheral interfaces, communication buses, memory, and drivers) before reaching the applications that use them. At worst, an attacker with access to this path may successfully intercept, overwrite, fabricate, or replay readings. This may cause systems that act on such data, such as flight controllers and industrial processes, to behave incorrectly or unsafely. Existing defences, such as trusted execution environments and trusted I/O paths, still depend on trusted driver software and correctly configured access control, which remain fragile in practice. In response, we present SensorGuard-RV, a hardware-first approach that delivers sensor samples into processor registers without trusting intermediate software, buses, or memory. After configuration, a write-once ownership switch hands the sensor to a fixed-function controller that performs hardware-level authenticated encryption on sensor samples under a key inaccessible to software. We develop a new RISC-V instruction then instructs the CPU to decrypt the sample and writes it to a register only after verifying its tag and rejecting replays, including across resets. We implement SensorGuard-RV on the NEORV32 core with an ADXL362 SPI accelerometer on an Artix-7 FPGA. At 100 MHz, a protected sample reaches a register in 5,191 cycles (51.9 $μ$s), of which the two Ascon authenticated encryption engines account for 30. Because fixed-function acquisition removes per-byte software polling, the protected loop sustains 19,015 transactions/s, 5.3% above a software-driven SPI baseline. The added logic (3,155 LUTs and 2,215 registers; 5.0% and 1.7% of the device) is dominated by the Ascon engine and preserves the 100 MHz clock, while estimated power rises from 118 to 368 mW.

title: Steinberg module and top-dimensional cohomology for arithmetic Chevalley groups
abstract: We prove that for a Chevalley--Demazure group scheme $\mathcal{G}$ of type $G_2$, $F_4$ or $E_8$ and a Euclidean ring $\mathcal{O}$ with field of fractions $K$, the Steinberg module of $\mathcal{G}(K)$ is generated by integral apartment classes. As a consequence, the top-dimensional rational cohomology of $\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{O})$ vanishes if $\mathcal{O}$ is a ring of integers, extending results of Tóth and of Brück--Santos Rego--Sroka.

title: When Can Pulsar Timing Distinguish a Propagation Mass from a Weak Longitudinal Background?
abstract: A weak longitudinal background can imitate the angular response of a gravitational-wave propagation mass. We quantify this ambiguity in a compressed Gaussian experiment constructed from the NANOGrav 15-year timing data. At a false-alarm probability of $10^{-3}$, allowing a weak longitudinal component in a massless background costs at least 16.29 percentage points of optimal rejection power for a specified source in a 20-pulsar subarray. Expanding the array to 40 pulsars at the same background level recovers at least 7.62 points. In a separate low-background experiment, we allow the same continuous range of longitudinal amplitudes at zero and positive mass. Across that range and three injected background levels, one test rejects zero mass with at least 97.38\% power at either of two masses separated by 1.08\%. With false assignment limited to $10^{-3}$ at the other mass, the power to identify either mass is at most 1.584\%. A cutoff can thus be identifiable before its position within a frequency cell can be resolved.

title: FedReason: Large Language Models as Weight-Space Meta-Aggregators for Heterogeneous Federated Learning
abstract: Federated learning servers combine client models with a fixed aggregation rule, and each rule in common use is designed for one kind of heterogeneity. We study whether a large language model (LLM) that inspects the client models can choose the rule itself, without any training on the server. In FedReason, the LLM is called every ten rounds. It analyses the weights by running code in a restricted server-side sandbox, sees only the printed results, may score a few candidates on a 500-image proxy set, and submits a short Python aggregation program. The server applies the program until the next call and falls back to FedAvg whenever its output is invalid. Full weight tensors never leave the server. We evaluated FedReason with Claude Opus 5.5 on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 with ResNet-18 under Dirichlet label skew, width-heterogeneous sub-models and Byzantine clients, in 168 runs against 14 baselines. Across 12 paired label-skew runs it beat FedAvg by 1.26 percentage points on average (10 wins), and a control that spends the same per-round proxy budget on choosing among standard rules by 1.08 points. It was the strongest server-side rule on CIFAR-100 but did not beat SCAFFOLD, which changes client training. With three of ten clients malicious, it excluded all sign-flipping clients from the first round and stayed about one point below FLTrust without training a root model. Without proxy feedback, accuracy fell from 73.8% to 38.8% in one seed. A 60-round run cost 0.79 USD in API fees on average.

title: Space of Geometric Gibbs Measures: Uniqueness, Ergodicity, and Teichmüller Complex Manifold Structure
abstract: Building on our previous work, in which geometric Gibbs measures were introduced to complete the space of classical Gibbs measures under the Teichmüller metric, we establish the uniqueness of geometric Gibbs measures in this paper. This result completes the construction of a Teichmüller complex manifold structure on the space of all geometric Gibbs measures. Using the welding technique, we uncover a connection between geometric Gibbs measures and harmonic measures on dynamical quasicircles. This connection allows us to establish asymptotic conformal rigidity for these dynamical quasicircles. Finally, we establish a foundation for the systematic study of the ergodic properties of geometric Gibbs measures.

title: Anisotropy lifts topological protection of transport in pumped spin chains
abstract: We investigate the prospect of topological spin pumping and transport in a dimerized spin-$\frac{1}{2}$ anisotropic XY chain with tunable in-plane anisotropy. Through a Jordan-Wigner transformation, the system maps onto an extended Rice-Mele-type fermionic model whose momentum-space band structure exhibits gapped regions characterized by nonzero Chern numbers ($\pm 1$) as well as trivial and gapless regimes. Conventional momentum-space analysis therefore predicts quantized Thouless-type spin pumping in parts of the Chern number diagram. However, real-space time evolution under open boundary conditions reveals that the spin transport is generally not quantized away from the isotropic limit. In the anisotropic regime, eigen-energy states within the transporting subspace hybridize during the driving cycle, leading to a transport that depends on details of the driving protocol. Quantized pumping and transport survive only in the isotropic limit, where the Hamiltonian reduces to decoupled Rice-Mele sectors and the transported spin component is conserved. Our results demonstrate that momentum-space topological invariants alone do not guarantee quantized spin transport in anisotropic spin chains. More broadly, they show that the conventional Thouless-pumping framework does not straightforwardly extend to situations where the transported quantity is not conserved, highlighting the importance of real-space diagnostics in topological transport phenomena.

title: Hybrid Machine Learning for Imbalanced Landing-Phase Safety Event Prediction from Flight Data
abstract: Landing-phase safety-event prediction requires the detection of rare abnormal approaches within strongly imbalanced multivariate flight data. Capturing coupled temporal behavior while distinguishing event-specific signatures across airport operating contexts remains a central modeling challenge. This study proposes an interpretable hybrid feature-fusion framework for multiclass landing-phase safety-event prediction. A long short-term memory (LSTM) autoencoder trained on nominal flight windows characterizes deviations from routine approach behavior. Its continuous reconstruction-error descriptor is fused with parameter-specific statistical flight-history features and supplied to a class-weighted XGBoost classifier to distinguish Normal, Speed High, Path High, and Flaps Late windows. The framework is evaluated using 53,750 NASA DASHlink approach windows from three arrival airports. Pooled and airport-specific learning strategies are compared alongside component-level benchmarks, repeated pipeline retraining, and feature-attribution analysis. The results demonstrate strong class-balanced detection, with mean macro recall above 0.90 across all airports under repeated partitioning and retraining. Component comparisons establish the importance of class weighting and show that continuous feature fusion outperforms reconstruction-error-only and hard-gate alternatives. Airport-level comparisons reveal benefits from local specialization at the two airports with larger datasets and from pooled training at the airport with the smallest dataset. Feature attributions associate predictions with operationally relevant vertical-path, configuration, speed, and approach-context variables. The framework provides an interpretable approach to rare-event detection and practical guidance for adapting flight-data monitoring models to airport-level data availability.

title: Algorithmic Construction of Vector-Valued Modular Forms and Application to an $A_4\times\mathbb{Z}_4$-invariant Model of Leptons
abstract: We present an algorithmic procedure that constructs the Vector-Valued Modular Forms (VVMFs) of finite modular groups, as well as its implementation in a companion code. The usual method consists in building the first few VVMFs, whose tensor products then generate the others. We address the difficulty of systematically finding the minimal set of VVMFs that suffices to produce all higher-weight ones, and we propose a method to identify it that makes use of the Burnside-Brauer theorem. For any given group, whose basic group-theoretic and representation-theoretic description is provided by the user, the code determines the minimal set of VVMFs, explicitly builds it using general results of the theory of such functions, then performs the tensor products that generate any other VVMF. Importantly, it automatically takes into account all caveats that might arise during the study of new groups. Our approach reproduces the known results for the finite modular groups explored in the recent phenomenological literature on modular flavor symmetries, and works for additional groups which we tested. We illustrate our algorithm and the working of our code by studying a model of leptons based on the unexplored finite modular group $A_4\times\mathbb{Z}_4$.

title: Top-Quark Pair Production and Decay in Extended Higgs Sectors
abstract: Extensions of the Higgs sector in the Standard Model address outstanding questions like the first-order electroweak phase transition and also present a rich collider phenomenology. The two-Higgs-doublet model is a minimal extension of the Standard Model with an extra complex $SU(2)_L$ doublet, and consists of an extra scalar, a pseudoscalar and a pair of charged Higgs bosons along with a Standard-Model-like Higgs boson. We present a modified version of the hvq library of the POWHEG-BOX-V2 event generator interfaced with the OpenLoops 2 amplitude generator to obtain predictions for top-quark pair production at NLO accuracy, including top-quark decays with full spin correlations in a framework that extends the SM Higgs sector with an extra heavy scalar and a pseudoscalar. The interference effects between the scalar and pseudoscalar signals, and the Standard Model QCD background are implemented. We include parton showers and hadronisation, and take detector effects into consideration. The status of our work and plans to extend it to future collider projects are discussed.

title: When Less is More: Emerging Network-Wide Use Cases for Hollow-Core Fibers in Optical Networks [Invited]
abstract: Hollow-Core Fiber (HCF) is emerging as a disruptive technology for next-generation optical networks, offering 30\% lower propagation latency than standard Single-Mode Fiber (SMF), record-low attenuation (0.05-0.1 dB/km), and nonlinearities reduced by three to four orders of magnitude. While the physical-layer benefits of HCF have been extensively demonstrated, recent industrial commitments by hyperscalers (e.g., Microsoft, Amazon) and the rapid maturation of nested antiresonant nodeless fibers (NANF) call for a systematic assessment of the impact of HCF at the network level. Building on a series of prior contributions, we overview four emerging network-wide use cases for the selective deployment of HCF in hybrid SMF/HCF networks: (i) latency-constrained Edge Data Center (edgeDC) consolidation; (ii) energy-efficient high-power amplification; (iii) capacity scaling via single-fiber bidirectional (BiDi) transmission; and (iv) coexistence of classical and quantum (QKD) channels. Consolidated results across realistic metro, national, and continental topologies convey a unifying message: in each use case, a selective HCF upgrade captures a significant share of the achievable benefit compared to a network overhaul. The required HCF budget is use-case-specific, i.e., 6-24\% of the total network fiber length for edgeDC consolidation (up to 50\% fewer edgeDCs), 40\% of the network links for QKD/classical coexistence (up to 38\% fewer quantum modules), and 40-60\% of the network links for energy-efficient capacity scaling via BiDi-HCF (up to 28\% lower network power per Tbps and 70\% more served traffic, at half the HCF strand count of a unidirectional HCF upgrade), whereas for energy-efficient high-power amplification the gain keeps growing with the HCF budget (up to 60\% lower network power per Tbps at the national scale) and what saturates is the benefit of increasing the EDFA output power.

title: SCALE: Real-Time Latent Communication for Cyber-Physical Agents
abstract: Latent communication enables agents to collaborate efficiently by directly exchanging intermediate model representations rather than raw sensor data or text messages. Existing approaches, however, are primarily designed for LLM agents and do not consider the bandwidth constraints and heterogeneous task deadlines faced by cyber-physical agents. In this work, we propose SCALE, a real-time latent communication method tailored for cyber-physical agents. Motivated by the spatio-temporal continuity of the physical world, SCALE matches tokens across consecutive latent messages using similarity scores to identify reusable information and avoid redundant transmission. It then profiles the semantic gain and communication cost of transmitting different amounts of latent information. Based on these profiles, SCALE employs a real-time scheduler that jointly determines which pending messages to transmit and how many latent tokens to send, subject to available bandwidth and task deadlines. We evaluate SCALE across three cyber-physical benchmarks and a physical spider robot case study under diverse network conditions and heterogeneous task deadlines. Our results show that SCALE significantly improves both task performance and on-time delivery in bandwidth-constrained networks. Our code is available at: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/SCALE-4E80/.

title: On supersoluble like groups of automorphisms of compact Riemann surfaces
abstract: Let $G$ be a not necessary full automorphism group of a compact Riemann surface of genus $g$. We found sharp bounds for $|G|$ in the terms of $g$ when $G$ belongs to one of the following classes of finite groups sharing similar properties with supersoluble groups: 2-nilpotent, with the Sylow tower of supersoluble type, with $\mathbb{P}$-subnormal cyclic primary subgroups, widely supersoluble, with submodular Sylow subgroups, with submodular cyclic primary subgroups and strongly supersoluble.

title: Learning a patient world model for health system simulation in intensive care
abstract: Designing healthcare strategies requires anticipating their clinical and operational consequences before implementation, a task that often relies on health system simulation. Such a simulation necessitates modeling how patient states evolve and generate care demands. However, conventional approaches typically tailor compact state transitions to a single policy question and omit history-dependent dynamics, thus requiring the redefinition of states and transitions when there is a new question that entails different clinical information. We propose to learn a patient world model from longitudinal EHRs using a neural network to provide a shared clinical representation of patient trajectories that can serve simulation questions across scenarios. Taking ICU operations as an example, we train the model on MIMIC-IV, freeze it, and couple its time-queryable predictions to shared ICU calendars, resources, and queues via scenario-specific mappings, so that one model renders admission demand, care tasks, and discharge proposals across simulations evaluating ICU bed capacity, care dispatch, and post-ICU transfer capacity. Experiments show that our model matches Markov and semi-Markov comparators in aggregate occupancy and directional responses to capacity and dispatch policies. It also reproduces policy gains from replayed observed trajectories. For patients entering the same support state from different prior trajectories, the learned representation captures a 24-h recovery difference (-6.4 predicted versus -6.7 observed percentage points), a contrast missed by compact state models, which propagates into distinct simulated care demand, queue burden, and bed use. These results indicate that a learned world model of patient dynamics has the potential to replace question-specific state models, allowing new care policies to be evaluated by reconfiguring the scenario without model rebuilding.

title: Adaptive Low-Light Enhancement for Road Anomaly Detection: A Multi-Architecture Benchmark and Edge Deployment Study
abstract: Road anomaly detection systems on autonomous vehicles must function reliably under degraded visual conditions including darkness, rain, and Harmattan dust haze. This paper benchmarks four object detection architectures, YOLOv8n, YOLOv12n, RT-DETR, and Faster R-CNN, under physically grounded lighting and weather degradation, and shows that uniform application of the SCI low-light enhancement network is actively harmful at dusk-level lighting (-16.1% to -30.7% mAP@50). We propose a lightweight, training-free luminance-adaptive router that selects between no enhancement, moderate SCI, and denoising plus strong SCI based on per-frame Rec. 601 luminance, recovering most of the dusk penalty while preserving low-light gains, and we validate the full pipeline on NVIDIA Jetson Nano edge hardware.

title: Synthesis of Ovarian Cancer Multi-Omics Datasets: A Biology-Informed Evaluation Framework
abstract: Paired multi-omic cancer cohorts are costly to assemble and difficult to share, motivating synthetic cohorts as a complementary resource. As generative model development accelerates, we shift the focus from proposing yet another architecture to defining evaluation criteria that determine whether synthetic data preserve biologically relevant structure. We introduce a biology-informed and patient-disjoint framework for evaluating the generation of paired RNA expression and copy-number variation (CNV) profiles, and apply it to the longitudinal DECIDER high-grade serous ovarian cancer cohort. The framework assesses modality-specific fidelity and coherence between RNA and CNV pairs using agreement between real training and held-out data as a reference, alongside complementary training-data proximity diagnostics. We adapt three multi-omic integration architectures based on variational autoencoders to generate paired profiles. The model leading several fidelity and coherence measures also shows the strongest training-data proximity. The protocol and case study offer the community a reference for comparing future multi-omic generators.

title: Extensions to the Navier-Stokes-Fourier Equations for Rarefied Transport: Entropy Variable Formulation, Heat Transfer and Dispersion of a Non-Linear Entropy Stable Closure
abstract: We assess the non-linear version of the Entropy Stable Extension to the Navier-Stokes-Fourier equations which were originally derived in arXiv:2407.17334. Using an identity for the derivative of the inverse of linearized collision operator, we show that the Entropy Stable Extension takes the form of a fourth-order quasi-cubic system of equations when written in entropy variables. Furthermore, we find that the quasi-linear contributions to the extension retain the highest order derivative contributions and the entropy stability of the full extension. This quasi-linear approximation is applied to the stationary heat transfer between parallel plates where we find that a specification of the boundary conditions that interpolates between the continuum and collisions limits can yield temperature profiles that better agree with DSMC predictions than Navier-Stokes-Fourier equations with Smoluchowski boundary conditions, while also giving a heat flux prediction that better agrees with the Sherman-Lees heat flux than the Navier-Stokes-Fourier prediction. We conclude with a brief study of dispersion of plane waves according to the linearized equations in one dimension where we show that all frequency modes are stable and relate this to entropy stability.

title: Recalibration-Aware Optimization of ZEFOZ Operating Points in $^{167}\mathrm{Er}^{3+}:\mathrm{Y}_2\mathrm{SiO}_5$ for Quantum Memories
abstract: Erbium-doped solids like $^{167}\mathrm{Er}^{3+}:\mathrm{Y}_2\mathrm{SiO}_5$ have properties that make them suitable for quantum-network memories, however, their unquenched effective electronic spin causes rapid magnetic decoherence. Operating at Zero First-Order Zeeman (ZEFOZ) points allows us to mitigate this, where we evaluate the ZEFOZ landscape for Site-2 $^{167}\mathrm{Er}^{3+}$ by incorporating a full-Hessian spin-Hamiltonian treatment with the anisotropic magnetic-field covariance derived from the native $^{89}\mathrm{Y}$ crystal lattice directly. Operating-point screening criteria were adopted to devise a Pareto-optimal frontier of four transition pairs to balance modeled Y-only magnetic pure-dephasing lifetimes ($T_{ϕ,Y}^{(2)}$) against microwave control authority. The $ε_{14}\leftrightarrowε_{15}$ transition exhibits the longest modeled Y-bath-induced quadratic pure-dephasing time, $T_{ϕ,Y}^{(2)}>2.2\times10^5~\mathrm{s}$, while the $ε_{12}\leftrightarrowε_{13}$ transition stood out, achieving a Rabi frequency coefficient of $1.248 \times 10^5~\mathrm{Hz/mT}$. An assumption-based Hamiltonian-uncertainty analysis demonstrates that while uncompensated deviations shift the ZEFOZ condition away from its nominal magnetic-field coordinate, the shifted operating points can be recovered via numerical vector-field recalibration. The Pareto-optimal coordinates were mathematically recovered for all sampled Hamiltonian perturbations, and the $84.1^{\mathrm{st}}$-percentile field relocations ranged from $10.95$ to $27.97~\mathrm{mT}$. The intended operation near $10~\mathrm{mK}$ must be taken into account for the suppression of Er-induced spectral diffusion through electronic-spin polarization, while the extended Y-bath pure-dephasing timescales also remain conditional on the adopted temporal-correlation model.

title: A Near-Optimal Generalized Sorting Algorithm
abstract: We continue the study of the classic \emph{generalized sorting problem}, a basic variant of ordinary sorting. There are $n$ elements and an (initially hidden) total ordering $π$ over them. Unlike in ordinary sorting, however, only \emph{some} comparisons are allowed: those given by the edges of an undirected graph $G = (V, E)$ on the elements. How many comparisons are needed to find the total ordering? In ordinary sorting, $Θ(n \log n)$ comparisons are necessary and sufficient. For generalized sorting, however, the best known upper bound has been $\tilde{O}(n^{3/2})$ since the work of Huang, Kannan, and Khanna (FOCS 2011), who even asked whether the problem might in fact require $n^{1+Ω(1)}$ comparisons. We show that it does not: we give a randomized algorithm that uses $O(n \log^4 n)$ comparisons in expectation. Thus, up to logarithmic factors, generalized sorting is no harder than ordinary sorting.

title: A Multimodal Haptic Interface for Simultaneous Softness and Thermal Modulation
abstract: Haptic interactions, such as touching an object in virtual reality, involve detecting a plethora of sensations through the skin. Whilst tactile displays exist to simulate and manipulate all of these cues individually, little progress has been made constructing devices that can control multiple cues simultaneously. This paper presents a tactile display technology that offers both softness and temperature change. A prototype display, based on particle jamming and the thermal transfer of heated and cooled water, is evaluated in terms of its ability to change both stiffness and temperature. Mechanical evaluations demonstrate controllable stiffness increase of 300%, whilst thermal characterisation showed strong surface uniformity and a range of achievable temperatures from 10°C up to 50°C, with closed-loop control maintaining a 0.2°C error from a setpoint. This work advances the design of multimodal tactile displays with applications to perceptual research, medical simulation, and affective haptics.

title: Scaling Up Analog CIM: A Simulation Framework for Topology-Aware Mapping
abstract: Analog compute-in-memory (CIM) enables energy-efficient AI inference by performing in-situ matrix multiplication. The growing demand for deploying larger models motivates chiplet integration to expand CIM capacity. However, simulation abstractions based on local operator costs and aggregate communication metrics obscure the impact of weight-mapping topology when CIM system scales up. We develop a phase analysis that quantifies how strongly mapping topology affects system performance across hardware configurations and how mapping optimization translates into latency gains. To evaluate and exploit this design space, we present Isobar, a simulation platform integrating CIM decompositions, heterogeneous execution, and resource modeling. Validated against silicon measurements and cycle-accurate simulation, Isobar provides reliable cost estimates that enable effective mapping search across model and hardware configurations. For Gemma-7B prefill, Isobar-guided mapping reduces communication time by 23.3% and end-to-end latency by 18.6% relative to the strongest baseline. Isobar's system-level modeling show that analog CIM retains energy-efficiency potential relative to GPU when scaled to thousands of dies, and identify topology-aware mapping as a key design dimension for efficient execution.

title: Core-Lock Scheduling for 5G NR LDPC Decoders
abstract: Accelerating iterative LDPC decoding while preserving error-correction reliability is a critical challenge in latency-constrained 5G New Radio (NR) and non-terrestrial networks. This paper proposes a hardware-efficient core-lock scheduling mechanism that evaluates the core syndrome weight after each layer update to selectively bypass extension layers. With the selected threshold $θ{=}0.20$, the mechanism reduces decoding latency by up to 31.3\% when integrated with static schedules, and by up to 45.5\% compared to alternative dynamic schemes utilizing the full parity-check matrix, without block error rate (BLER) degradation. Compared with an estimated fully parallel full-matrix checker, the core-only approach yields a 76\% reduction in shifter network area and a 73\% reduction in XOR gate count. For decoders with existing early termination, the proposed mechanism requires only a compact adder tree and a comparator.

title: Spectral Regimes of Truncated sinc-Power and Pulse-Train Kernels: Edge Exponents, Per-Edge Plunges, and the Landau-Widom Limit
abstract: A signal band-limited to one rectangular band and observed through a finite window is the classical concentration problem of Slepian, Landau, Pollak, and Widom. The eigenvalues of the operator cluster near one and near zero, separated by a transition called the plunge. The plunge width grows like the logarithm of the window length, with a universal coefficient of one over pi squared set by the band-edge jump. This paper follows the clusters and the plunge as the band is deformed. An elementwise power of the kernel smooths the band edge, and the plunge gives way to a power-law edge with exponent one less than the power. Disjoint copies of the band widen the plunge in proportion to the number of band edges, as the multiple-interval theorem of Landau and Widom implies, so the coefficient is a per-edge constant. Shrinking each band to a line gives the classical finite-rank operator. Overlapping bands give a multilevel staircase, and a self-similar band gives a cluster hierarchy governed by the Cantor dimension. At the smooth edge, rescaled eigenvalues do not collapse onto one curve. The edge descriptor passes from a constant to an exponent to an integer to a fractal dimension. For the single band, classical results place all eigenfilter zeros on the unit circle, with more of them inside the band as the order rises, so the dominant eigenvectors act as lowpass filters.

title: A physics-based-preconditioned quasi-Newton solver for energy- and momentum-conserving implicit hybrid particle-in-cell simulations
abstract: Explicit hybrid particle-in-cell (PIC) schemes, with kinetic ions and fluid electrons, accumulate numerical heating over long simulations and are unstable to finite-grid instabilities. Energy-conserving implicit integration removes heating and instabilities, but may be inefficient due to the need of nonlinear iteration. We present a fast quasi-Newton solver for an implicit hybrid-PIC formulation. The nonlinear residual employs the electric field and electron pressure as nonlinear unknowns, and nonlinearly eliminates particles. The formulation is strictly energy conserving and, on Cartesian meshes, also momentum conserving. The nonlinear iteration is efficiently performed with a quasi-Newton solver that replaces the true Jacobian with an approximate one without spoiling conservation properties upon convergence. The approximate Jacobian replaces the particle ion linear response with an analytical mass matrix that is local and requires minimal storage. This approximate Jacobian is efficiently inverted with a physics-based multigrid preconditioner, adapted from Hall MHD. We verify the scheme linearly with whistler, kinetic Alfvén, and cylindrical normal modes, and nonlinearly with the GEM reconnection challenge. On GEM, explicit integration needs a forty-times-smaller time step, and nine times the wall-clock time, to reach an energy conservation comparable to that of the implicit solver. We apply the method to the simulation of a three-dimensional field-reversed configuration formation by external coils.

title: StepBack: Step-Level Error-Localized Resampling for Efficient Test-Time Reasoning
abstract: Self-consistency (SC) is a widely used decoding strategy for improving chain-of-thought reasoning, but it requires sampling many complete reasoning trajectories with a preset budget. Its efficient variants reduce the cost mainly by stopping full-trajectory sampling early or distributing the number of samples across questions. In this paper, we propose StepBack, a step-level error-localized resampling method for efficient test-time reasoning. Given a small set of draft trajectories, StepBack localizes likely first error positions using lightweight signals and then resamples the detected error step and its suffix, followed by majority answer voting. Empirically, StepBack matches the accuracy of SC on average across seven mathematical reasoning and multi-hop QA benchmarks, while reducing token usage by up to 41.26%. In addition, by nature, StepBack can be combined with adaptive inference methods such as Adaptive Consistency, further improving their inference-time efficiency.

title: Augmented Lagrangian methods with telescopic subproblems for MPCCs and cardinality constraints with general constraints: constraint-preserving swaps and B-stationarity
abstract: We consider optimization problems with general equality and inequality constraints and partitioned cardinality constraints, which include complementarity constraints. In the augmented Lagrangian method that we consider, the bounds and the cardinality constraints are kept in the subproblems, which are solved by the Telescopic Method. The limit points of this method are B-stationary, without constraint qualifications, if the penalty parameters remain bounded, but not in general. The reason is that the swaps of the Telescopic Method pass through points at which the constraints have different values, and the corresponding variation of the penalty term grows with the penalty parameter. With unbounded penalty parameters and a derivative test outside the current face, the feasible limit points at which a linear independence constraint qualification holds are M-stationary for MPCCs. We modify the swaps, by means of a scaled Newton restoration, so that they preserve the values of the constraints, and we prove that every feasible limit point at which this constraint qualification holds is then B-stationary (S-stationary for MPCCs), whatever the behavior of the penalty parameters. Counterexamples show that the modification is necessary, even with exact solutions of the subproblems, and that the constraint qualification cannot be weakened to one of Mangasarian-Fromovitz type. In the MacMPEC collection, the method found certified S- or B-stationary points in 185 of the 193 instances, more than Algencan and the regularization method of Scholtes. In experiments with cardinality-constrained portfolios and sparse principal component analysis, the constraint-preserving swaps improved the original swaps and the methods applied to complementarity reformulations.

title: Synaptic Multi-Weight Wafer-Scale Domain Wall Magnetic Tunnel Junctions Driven by Spin Orbit Torque
abstract: Spintronic synaptic devices based on magnetic random access memory (MRAM) are a rapidly evolving class within the analog neuromorphic architecture. However, obtaining the multi-weight or analog behavior desired for improved neural network inference accuracy in scaled MRAM remains a challenge. In this study, we demonstrate and tune up to eight distinct resistance levels in 300 mm wafer-scale magnetic tunnel junction artificial synapses driven by spin orbit torque.
