abstract: Large language models have achieved remarkable performance across a wide range of tasks, yet they remain susceptible to jailbreak attacks that circumvent safety mechanisms and elicit harmful or unintended outputs. Although safety can be improved through model fine-tuning, such approaches can be computationally expensive and may degrade previously acquired capabilities through catastrophic forgetting. Recent jailbreak defenses have therefore explored targeted interventions on specific model components associated with unsafe behavior. However, existing approaches typically decouple two inherently related decisions: where to intervene and how to modify the selected components. Such sequential optimization may be suboptimal because the optimal intervention location can depend on the intervention applied there, and vice versa. In this work, we introduce AttentionSwitch, the first jailbreak defense to jointly optimize intervention sites and strengths within a frozen LLM. Specifically, AttentionSwitch learns a sparse set of attention heads together with query-conditioned multiplicative scaling factors, allowing the outputs of the selected heads to be either attenuated or amplified without altering the directions of their representations. Across popular language models and jailbreak attacks, AttentionSwitch outperforms existing defenses, with particularly strong results when training data is scarce.

title: Random Symbolic Boosting: A Geometric Approach to Symbolic Regression
abstract: Symbolic models offer interpretability, but their construction through generational evolution can be computationally expensive. This article presents Random Symbolic Boosting (RSB), a method that constructs explicit additive symbolic models via boosting over populations of randomly generated syntax trees, eliminating the need for generational evolution. The idea combines two observations: high-dimensional spaces can be spanned by enough linearly independent vectors, and the semantics of syntax trees can be directly manipulated as such vectors. It is shown that, for Ordinary Least Squares, the boosting process guarantees a monotonic reduction of the training error for both regression and classification. Furthermore, an adaptive geometric early stopping mechanism is introduced. It is based on the angle between the prediction and target vectors, is independent of the problems scale, and requires no adjustments across tasks. Evaluated on a standard benchmark for symbolic regression, the method is located at the Pareto-optimal point between predictive accuracy and training time, ranking first on the real-world datasets. Additionally, it was tested on a large tabular classification benchmark with 200 problems, achieving competitive results.

title: Measurement-Aware Multimodal LLM for No-Reference Low-Dose CT Quality Assessment
abstract: No-reference image quality assessment (IQA) of low-dose CT predicts the score that radiologists would assign to a slice without a full-dose reference, as needed to compare dose protocols and denoisers. Trained CT IQA networks agree well with radiologists but output only a score, whereas multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can explain a score but perform poorly on CT when only prompted. We propose a measurement-aware MLLM, built on Qwen3.8-27B, that rates a slice from its image together with six image-domain measurements of noise, sharpness, high-frequency content and streaks, given to the language model as percentiles in text. On the LDCT-IQA 2023 test set, it reaches an Overall score of 2.735, on par with the retrained challenge winner (2.735) and MedSigLIP-FiLM (2.713), and substantially above its base MLLM used as a zero-shot agent. Shuffling the measurements at test time reduces the score by 0.048, mostly through noise, but the same measurements also lead the model to assign higher scores to over-smoothed denoised images.

title: AtariBench: Evaluating Spatiotemporal Reasoning of Vision-Language Models in Atari Gameplay
abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have achieved strong performance on static visual understanding benchmarks, yet their ability to act in dynamic environments remains less well understood. We introduce AtariBench, a controlled benchmark that evaluates VLMs across 20 Atari 2600 games, requiring models to make sequential decisions from high-temporal-resolution gameplay streams. By decoupling fast in-game dynamics from wall-clock inference speed, AtariBench focuses on whether models can perceive rapid visual state changes, reason over spatiotemporal dynamics, and ground actions in the current observation. Our experiments reveal substantial limitations in state-of-the-art VLMs: models often fail to infer object motion and direction, exhibit brittle sequential decision-making, and over-rely on textual interaction history despite newly appended visual feedback. We further introduce a separability analysis to identify which in-game scores provide reliable signals of model competence, and use the benchmark to study how memory design and prompting strategies affect performance. Overall, AtariBench exposes a persistent gap between passive visual perception and active decision-making, providing a lightweight and rigorous testbed for developing VLMs that can reason and act in dynamic environments.

title: Debate to Deceive: Poisoning LLM's Fact-Checking via Game-Theoretic Multi-Agent Debate
abstract: Knowledge attacks on Large Language Models, such as manipulating fact-checking judgments, pose significant risks to AI reliability. Existing approaches -- adversarial suffix/template injection and single-agent self-reflection -- lack robustness across diverse defenses and are prone to confirmation bias and costly trial-and-error, respectively. We propose Debate-to-Deceive (D2D), a multi-agent debate framework grounded in human debate structure and rhetorical style, enabling agents to generate adversarial passages that are semantically coherent, rhetorically effective, and resistant to early confirmation bias. D2D formalizes the adversarial process as an evolutionary game in which agents adaptively evolve their rhetorical strategies (Logos, Pathos, Ethos) through competition. To manage the intractably large LLM output space, we decouple agent behavior into a strategic layer, which selects a rhetorical action from a compact strategy space via evolutionary-inspired learning dynamics, and a generation layer, where the LLM produces a concrete passage conditioned on that strategy and the debate context. On four fact-checking benchmarks (FEVER, HealthVer, CLIMATE-FEVER, and SciFact), D2D substantially outperforms existing attacks and evades most defenses.

title: Goals as a Representational Layer for Human-AI Collaboration
abstract: Goals are central to how people, teams, and organizations structure their work. Yet, while generative artificial intelligence (AI) systems increasingly operate across a worker's context, information about why a person is pursuing a task, beyond local prompts and interactions, is typically missing. We argue that goals should become an explicit representational layer mediating interactions among people, AI systems, and organizations. Because human goals are hierarchical, partially latent, and dynamically evolving, such a layer must be multidimensional, both grounded in human articulation and inferred from available evidence, and continuously updated. A goal layer could connect immediate requests to broader outcomes, improve the organization and retrieval of relevant context, support reflection and coordination, and provide a foundation for training, aligning, and evaluating AI systems in terms of human-centered outcomes. We highlight these opportunities while identifying open challenges involving goal inference, socio-cognitive frictions, alignment, privacy, and governance.

title: Conflict-Aware Meta-Learning for Generalizable Speech Deepfake Detection
abstract: Speech deepfake detectors built on large self-supervised learning front-ends achieve high in-domain accuracy, yet suffer degradation under domain shift caused by unseen synthesizers, transmission codecs, or unfamiliar acoustic conditions. Meta-learning, particularly model-agnostic meta-learning for domain generalization (MLDG), addresses this issue by simulating domain shifts. However, applying MLDG directly introduces a bi-level optimization challenge that remains unsolved. First, effective domain-shift emulation requires genuine distributional gaps between meta-splits, yet such gaps can frequently produce gradient conflicts, destabilizing the bi-level optimization. Second, the stochastic nature of mini-batch gradients causes the reference direction to fluctuate across iterations, resulting in an optimization trajectory that fails to achieve domain generalization. We propose a conflict-aware meta-learning (CAML) framework, which addresses both challenges through three complementary components. Firstly, base domain gradient surgery (base-DGS) introduces an asymmetric projection that treats the meta-train gradient as a primary anchor. Secondly, EMA-DGS replaces the unstable anchor with its exponential moving average (EMA), providing a stable optimization trajectory anchor that substantially reduces domain-shift-induced conflict detections. Thirdly, layer-wise DGS (LW-DGS) further extends the framework to individual parameter tensors, enabling fine-grained, layer-specific intervention that targets conflict-prone layers while leaving well-aligned parameters intact. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed CAML framework achieves lower EER than the compared baselines on most cross-dataset evaluations across multiple cross-dataset benchmarks and architectures, achieving a maximum relative improvement of 45.2% in terms of EER.

title: 13,000-Fold Frequency Down Conversion From 280 MHz to 21 kHz Using Mechanical Frequency Combs
abstract: Optical frequency combs bridge the microwave and terahertz regimes by down-converting terahertz optical energy into microwave signals. A photodetector converts the comb's equally spaced lines, generated through optical nonlinearities, into a low-frequency tone at their spacing. Here, we present the first mechanical version of this process, using mechanical frequency combs to downconvert energy over 4 orders of magnitude, from the MHz to kHz regime. Thin-film lithium niobate (LN) is used to design an acoustic resonator with a wide range of mode frequencies. We achieve phononic comb excitation from 250 MHz to 900 MHz and compare the electrical and laser Doppler vibrometer (LDV) measurements at 277 MHz. We then show the low-frequency spectrum of the devices, highlighting mechanical motion at the comb's spacing and demonstrating energy transfer from 277 MHz to 21 kHz.

title: Multi-monopoles and monodromy around the wobbly divisor
abstract: The multi-monopole equations are a generalisation of the Seiberg--Witten equations where the spinor is coupled to an auxiliary vector bundle. The signed count of multi-monopoles on a 3-manifold can vary according to a new type of wall-crossing phenomenon. For products $S^1\times C$, where $C$ is a closed Riemann surface, we relate the wall and chamber structure to loops in the complement of the wobbly divisor of $C$. Such a loop induces a monodromy map on the multi-vortex moduli space, and the count of its fixed points is expected to agree with the count of multi-monopoles on $S^1\times C$ in the given chamber. By studying singularities of framed multi-vortex moduli spaces, we are able to understand these monodromy maps for various loops. Counting fixed points suggests that product 3-manifolds display incredibly rich wall-crossing behaviour.

title: Bichromatic light-induced electronic torques on the Néel vector in Rashba magnetic multipoles from $p$-wave magnets to $i$-wave altermagnets
abstract: Light can control magnetic order on ultrafast timescales, but for a two-dimensional magnet with an out-of-plane order parameter $\boldsymbol N\parallel\hat z$, the inverse Faraday field is collinear with $\boldsymbol N$ and gives no transverse torque. Here we show that bichromatic $(ω,bω)$ light generates electronic torques perpendicular to $\boldsymbol N$ in Rashba-coupled magnetic multipoles, from $p$-wave ($n=1$) magnets to $i$-wave ($n=6$) altermagnets. Beyond high-frequency effective fields, we evaluate the exact Floquet response and the generalized torque per occupied electron, for prescribed occupations. The momentum-dependent exchange terms dominate this Fermi-sea torque and remove the leading-order zeros (amplitude-ratio blindspots) of the momentum-independent field in the channels tested. For out-of-plane $\boldsymbol N$, rotational symmetry permits a transverse torque only if $\gcd(n,b+1)=1$ for counter-rotating beams or $\gcd(n,b-1)=1$ for co-rotating beams. For in-plane $\boldsymbol N$, the Fermi sea also gives a torque component along $\hat z$ that the momentum-independent field cannot produce. We classify the active channels, with $n=1,\dots,6$ and $b=1,\dots,7$, by frequency scaling and origin (cycle-averaged versus oscillating exchange). As a control, a Rashba ferromagnet ($n=0$) has one symmetry-allowed out-of-plane channel and a weak in-plane response without a selection rule. Finite-momentum occupied-state physics is therefore essential for light-driven torques in unconventional magnets, and the exact Floquet calculation validates and extends the high-frequency description.

title: Robust Adaptive Lyapunov-Based MPC for Nonlinear Systems with Experimental Validation on Quadcopter Attitude Control
abstract: In this paper, a computationally efficient robust adaptive Lyapunov-based model predictive control (RALMPC) framework is proposed for a class of constrained nonlinear systems subject to uncertainties and external disturbances. A radial basis function neural network (RBFNN), introduced to approximate non-parametric uncertainties, is incorporated into a control Lyapunov function analysis, together with integral barrier Lyapunov functionals for state constraint enforcement. This analysis yields control and adaptation laws for parametric uncertainties, external disturbances, RBFNN weights, and worst-case approximation error, rendering the closed-loop system uniformly bounded while ensuring convergence of tracking errors to compact sets around the origin. The resulting guarantees are then embedded into the RALMPC optimal control problem through a contractive constraint, thus combining formal closed-loop stability with real-time performance optimization; at the same time, the adaptation laws allow the RALMPC prediction model to be updated online. Comparative hardware-in-the-loop simulations against state-of-the-art MPC schemes validate the efficacy and computational efficiency of the proposed framework. Ultimately, RALMPC is experimentally validated on a custom-built quadcopter platform for time-varying attitude tracking, demonstrating its practical feasibility; comparisons against alternative strategies confirm its superiority in achieving improved closed-loop performance.

title: CrowdDirector: Runtime Orchestration of Crowd Simulation through Natural-Language Directives
abstract: Natural language offers an intuitive way to direct a virtual crowd while a simulation is running. Handwritten rules execute efficiently but cannot respond flexibly to varied instructions, whereas asking a large language model (LLM) to control the crowd at every update introduces repeated latency, cost, and the risk of unsupported actions. We present CrowdDirector, a framework that uses an LLM only when the user adds or changes an instruction. The LLM translates the request into a structured instruction, and a scene validator checks whether the entities and actions it references exist in the current Unity scene. Accepted instructions are stored and remain continuously active as the simulation is running. At each simulation tick, a graph neural network uses the current scene state and active instruction to choose an available action and target for each agent, while Unity handles movement, interactions, and animation. The network is trained offline on simulated scenarios, with LLM guidance on how agents should respond to instructions. Our evaluations show the scene validator's feasibility decisions matched human judgements more often than the LLM's own assessment, and on a behavioural benchmark CrowdDirector follows user instructions more closely than handwritten rules while avoiding repeated LLM calls. It therefore provides a practical middle ground between fixed rules and continuous LLM control.

title: Pruning free resolutions over a complete intersection
abstract: Given a free resolution $F_\bullet$ over a polynomial ring $R$ and a system of higher homotopies on it for a regular sequence $a_1,\dots,a_c$, we can use the Eisenbud-Shamash construction to build a free resolution over $\overline{R}=R/(a_1,\dots,a_c)$. We provide a combinatorial formula for the new system of higher homotopies on a pruned free resolution $F_{\bullet}^{\mathcal{M}}$ that corresponds to a pruning of the Eisenbud-Shamash resolution.

title: Global regularity of the two-dimensional fractional Boussinesq equations with critical dissipation
abstract: In the present paper, our primary focus is on the Boussinesq equations with fractional velocity dissipation $Λ^αu$ and temperature diffusion $Λ^βθ$. On the critical balance line $α+β=1$, establishing global regularity for weak velocity dissipation has been obstructed by the quadratic convective-buoyancy feedback, and all available results below $α=\frac{10}{13}$ require a smallness assumption on the initial temperature. In this paper, we prove large-data global regularity across the extended regime $α>\frac{\sqrt{57}-5}{4} \approx 0.637$. This provides a step beyond the previous barrier $α=\frac{10}{13}$, unconditionally dismantling the temperature smallness assumption that has persisted in the literature for over a decade. The mathematical mechanism relies on a high-order Quadratic Normal Form transformation $H=ω-R_αθ-\Bop(θ,θ)$ tailored to eliminate non-resonant quadratic vorticity-temperature interactions. Crucially, by uncovering the exact physical scalings of the underlying multilinear commutators and maintaining sharp fractional conjugates in the $L^m$-energy framework, we ensure that the global energy closure is governed entirely by the quadratic thermal dissipation. Once an integrability threshold $m>\frac{2}α$ is attained, a fine Littlewood-Paley transport estimate drives a fractional regularity gain $H \in B_{r,\infty}^{3α-2}$, ensuring the velocity field achieves critical drift regularity $C^α$. By Silvestre-type drift regularization, this spontaneously generates positive Hölder continuity for the temperature, which in turn elevates the drift regularity strictly beyond the critical threshold, unlocking non-local Schauder estimates to prevent finite-time singularity formation.

title: The Complex Magnetic Anatomy of a White Dwarf Chromosphere
abstract: This study presents phase-resolved spectroscopy and spectropolarimetry of the DAHe white dwarf LP 705-64. Here, two apparently discrete chromospheric regions are observed to alternate in visibility and magnetic polarity with rotation, with field strengths of 9.5 and 22 MG based on the measured Zeeman splitting in Hα. As in the class prototype GD 356, emission line equivalent widths vary in antiphase with the broadband light curve. The 9.5 MG field is visible for 60 per cent of the stellar rotation and stays nearly constant, whereas the 22 MG field increases modestly during the remaining phases. Notably, the time-series transitions between magnetic regions are abrupt and transit-like in morphology, requiring at least one magnetic region to be highly localised and significantly smaller than the areas inferred for the dark surface spots. Both the intensity and the Stokes V/I spectra indicate a field configuration significantly more complex than an offset dipole, but higher-cadence data are necessary to distinguish between a global field and localised magnetic regions. All data are consistent with magnetic, chromospheric, and dark surface regions that are co-located and thus physically related. These findings support a model of chromospheric emission that is intrinsic and localised, consistent with predictions of dynamo-driven electrical currents that heat the upper atmosphere near magnetic poles.

title: MEDALLION: Manifold Embedding Distillation and Attributions for Low-dimensional Latent InterpretatiON
abstract: Dimensionality reduction is widely used to visualize high-dimensional data and guide scientific discovery, yet interpreting which original features contribute to low-dimensional representations remains challenging, particularly for black-box methods such as t-SNE and UMAP. We introduce \textbf{MEDALLION} (Manifold Embedding Distillation and Attributions for Low-dimensional Latent InterpretatiON), a novel framework for interpreting low-dimensional embeddings through knowledge distillation and neural feature attribution. MEDALLION distills any given embedding with a neural encoder which we explain via a broad range of existing neural feature attribution methods. Through experiments on MNIST and applications in single-cell transcriptomics, we show MEDALLION provides informative feature attributions that cast additional insights into the underlying embedding and compare its performance with existing interpretability approaches.

title: Conflux: Preventing Privilege Escalation with Principal Contexts and System-Level Evaluation
abstract: LLM agents combine information from multiple principals while acting externally. We formalise privilege escalation (PE) as the system-level security objective: an action may proceed only if every principal that influenced it would allow it. Model-level defences remain probabilistic, so enforcement must sit outside model judgement. We present Conflux, a principal-context defence. Its kernel, ITES, derives authority from provenance and the organisation's existing access-control system and intersects the permissions of every influencing principal. We prove a conditional authority-confinement theorem: under complete mediation, no-laundering provenance, a known non-empty decision context, fresh permission checks, and action binding, the kernel admits no action that escalates privilege with respect to any recorded influencing principal. The theorem covers the represented value-influence fragment; control influence from tool, branch, recipient, or plan-step selection remains a refinement obligation. Conflux extends the kernel with independent policy ports, argument-aware authorisation, disclosure, consent, delegation, restriction, and exposure planning. We describe two system- level evaluators. SLED is a black-box evaluator: it exhaustively explores a declared finite model of a defence up to a bound. SLED-V is a white-box evaluator: it checks a serialisable intermediate representation against security and provenance properties. The evidence is bounded and partial. The appendix reports retained AgentDojo, SLED, and SLED-V results, including the limits of those runs. No result in this paper is an unbounded deployment guarantee.

title: Bicoherence States from QPO-Accretion Flow Coupling in Black Hole X-ray Binaries
abstract: We calculate the bispectrum of a black hole X-ray binary light curve model where lognormal fluctuations associated with the inner flow are multiplicatively modulated by a quasi-periodic oscillation (QPO) and its harmonic. The bispectrum is a third-order Fourier statistic which measures the strength of nonlinear relationships between frequencies in a timeseries. When applied to black hole X-ray binaries, the bispectrum reveals nonlinear coupling between QPOs and the broadband noise. These couplings are sorted into a small set of states and X-ray binaries are observed to transition between these states as they undergo spectral transitions. We show that the model we consider is able to reproduce all of the canonical bispectral states analytically. We consider other sources of incoherent variability which dilute this model light curve and find that changes in this dilution, together with changes in the QPO amplitude, drive the transitions between the bispectral states. We also show that the larger QPO amplitudes of high-inclination sources favor the cross state and the weaker QPOs of low-inclination sources favor the hypotenuse state, which can explain the empirically observed correlation. Additionally, any dilution by equatorial winds, which are seen mainly at high inclination, would push high-inclination sources further toward the cross state.

title: ReKV: Overlapping Quantized KV Transfer and Suffix Recomputation
abstract: Prefill--decode disaggregation moves a prompt's key--value (KV) cache between workers before the first token can be generated. Reducing this handoff to either cache compression or recomputation misses a useful choice: which layers to transmit, at what precision, and which layers to execute again on the decode worker. ReKV transfers a quantized prefix KV cache and one BF16 boundary state, then reconstructs a contiguous suffix while the prefix is in flight. In a model-shaped synthetic benchmark on cross-node H100s, the Q8 configuration meeting separately evaluated quality criteria reduces 8K handoff latency by $2.36\times$, $2.84\times$, and $3.65\times$ over BF16 transfer for Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen2.5-3B, and Qwen3-8B. It is also faster than the best measured transfer-only or recompute-only action at those points. A separate real-weight BF16 recomputation experiment reduces prefill-to-token-return time by $1.16$--$1.63\times$. The preferred action changes with prompt length and link bandwidth.

title: Federated training performs as well as centralized for 3D Latent Diffusion for Diagnosis-Conditioned Brain MRI Synthesis
abstract: Generative models of brain MRI are useful to understand brain conditions, and to enrich scarce and imbalanced neuroimaging data. However, training these models requires large, multi-site training sets, which is challenging. Federated learning (FL) allows for training deep learning models without sharing data. We show that training a 3D conditional latent model federatedly (where data is kept private at each site) performs similarly to centralized training (where all the data have been copied to a single site). We evaluate three metrics: conditional fidelity (how well generated MRIs perform in classification), diversity (how the generated images match the real data distribution, using MultiScale-SSIM), and realism (how close generated images are to real images, using Fréchet Inception Distance). Our results show that federated training is a viable route to develop multi-site generative models of brain MRI.

title: StarLoc: A Practical Approach to Encoding Geographic Locators in IPv6 for Starlink
abstract: LEO satellite networks such as Starlink provide Internet connectivity across continents, oceans, and airspace. IP geolocation providers map Starlink's IPv6 prefixes to locations mainly through its self-published GeoFeed. However, users may be far away from their assigned Points of Presence (PoPs), one label covers an entire prefix, and labels and PoP mappings can change while addresses stay the same. We characterize Starlink's IPv6 addressing using 925 historical GeoFeed snapshots (2024--2026), one year of PoP mappings, and over 7.9 million observed IPv6 addresses. Our findings reveal that customer prefixes lack clear geographic structure, prefix labels lie a median of 540km from their PoPs, and relabeling a single /40 can affect the reported locations of up to 65,536 possible /56 delegations. To address these challenges, we propose StarLoc, a geographic Locator--Identifier separation scheme that embeds terminal location into IPv6 addresses using a resolution-adaptive H3 Locator while preserving existing Starlink prefixes, /56 delegations, and stable Endpoint Identifiers. To balance accuracy and privacy, StarLoc reveals only cells with at least a certain number of terminals, and operators can cap resolution in sensitive regions or withhold location entirely. Unlike topology-based schemes, StarLoc encodes physical location and lets Locators follow moving users.

title: Cantor's onion: a uniformly quasiregular map whose Julia set is a Cantor set of spheres
abstract: For integers $d,m\ge2$ with $1/d+1/m<1$, we construct a uniformly quasiregular map of $\mathbb{S}^3$ of degree $d^2+m^2$ whose Julia set is a Cantor set of concentric round spheres. To our knowledge, this is the first example of a uniformly quasiregular map in dimension three with infinitely many Fatou components. The map is a three-dimensional analogue of McMullen's maps $z^d+λ/z^m$, built from two Zorich-type power maps glued across a single shell by a slit construction. Its Julia set has Hausdorff dimension $2+s$, where $d^{-s}+m^{-s}=1$, and the restriction of the map to its Julia set is a skew product over the shift on two symbols and has topological entropy $\log(d^2+m^2)$. We also prove that uniformly quasiregular maps that expand uniformly near their Julia set, possibly with branching there, have no wandering domains and only finitely many periodic Fatou components, all of them attracting basins. The map constructed here belongs to this class.

title: Gain-Dependent Entropy Characterization of a Zener Avalanche Noise TRNG via Dual NIST Standards: Toward Low-Cost Hardware Entropy for ICS Deployments
abstract: True random number generators based on Zener avalanche noise offer a low-cost entropy source for industrial control system and IoT edge devices, yet the relationship between amplifier gain, coupling capacitance, and entropy quality remains uncharacterized under current NIST standards. This paper presents a comprehensive entropy assessment of an op-amp-based Zener avalanche noise generator across five gain configurations and two coupling capacitor values, evaluated against the NIST SP 800-22 statistical test suite and the SP~800-90B entropy source assessment using 1.44 billion raw bits per configuration. We identify a three-phase autocorrelation structure, attributed to comparator saturation-recovery dynamics, consistent across all gain settings. A direct-current substitution experiment, replacing the Zener diode with a stable voltage source at the same bias point, reduces switching activity by approximately 97%, confirming that Zener avalanche noise, rather than amplifier self-excitation, is the necessary entropy source. The coupling capacitor is further shown to govern comparator overdrive and entropy quality independent of this source mechanism, with the smaller capacitance improving entropy, throughput, and bias. The combined results identify an optimal gain configuration achieving a perfect statistical test score, NIST-compliant min-entropy, and peak entropy throughput at a bill-of-materials cost under five dollars, offering practical design guidance for low-cost entropy sources in industrial and embedded deployments.

title: On Lipschitz Explosion in Deep Neural Networks with Normalization: Consequences for Optimization and Adversarial Robustness
abstract: Can a network look stable at every layer and still be exponentially unstable as a whole? The Lipschitz constant of a neural network is a basic stability quantity appearing in optimization guarantees, generalization bounds, and robustness certificates. Deep networks naturally admit two such notions, input Lipschitzness, measuring sensitivity to data perturbations, and parameter Lipschitzness, measuring sensitivity to weight perturbations. We prove that, for deep networks with normalization layers, with batch normalization as the canonical example, both Lipschitz constants can grow exponentially with depth and hence with parameter dimension, even under strong per-layer norm control such as $\|W_\ell\|_2\le 1$, and already for linear activations. Thus, a mechanism widely used to stabilize training can create severe worst-case instabilities that are invisible locally, i.e., from layerwise norm bounds alone. Parameter-Lipschitz explosion turns Lipschitz-dependent nonsmooth optimization guarantees into exponential-in-dimension bounds for deep normalized networks, while input-Lipschitz explosion makes worst-case Lipschitz-based generalization and robustness certificates vacuous. The latter also yields a concrete rank-separation mechanism for adversarial vulnerability. The theory predicts that perturbations introducing new singular directions should be amplified much more strongly than perturbations at the same noise level that remain within the input's original singular subspace. Experiments on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and CIFAR-10 support this prediction, showing that rank-creating perturbations cause substantially sharper drops in accuracy, confidence, and margins than same-subspace perturbations.

title: Features of Non-Local Quantum Correlations in Nuclei
abstract: Classical simulation of quantum many-body systems is challenged by the combined effects of entanglement and non-stabilizerness (magic). Non-local magic, $M^{\mathrm{NL}}_α$, quantifies the component of non-stabilizerness that cannot be removed by local unitary transformations and provides a measure of quantum complexity beyond entanglement alone. It is bounded from below by the antiflatness of the entanglement spectrum, ${F}_A$. We calculate stabilizer Rényi entropies, non-local magic, entanglement-spectrum antiflatness, and entanglement entropy in shell-model ground states of more than 260 even-even, odd-even, and odd-odd nuclei, using a bipartition into proton and neutron sectors. We find that the previously established bound $4{F}_A\leq{M}^{\mathrm{NL}}_{\mathrm{lin}}$ holds for every nucleus studied and approaches saturation in the limit of separable states. Odd-odd nuclei exhibit markedly different patterns of entanglement and magic compared with even-even and odd-even systems, revealing distinctive signatures of proton-neutron quantum correlations and providing new insight into the complexity generated by nuclear interactions.

title: Reducing Data-Center Load Transfers with Ride-Through-Aware Voltage Control
abstract: Fault-induced transfers of large data centers to backup supply can cause abrupt reductions in grid-served demand. Coordinating reactive-power support to mitigate these transfers requires consideration of facility-specific voltage--duration ride-through characteristics, particularly when support capacity is limited. This paper develops a ride-through-aware extension of quadratic voltage control that assesses voltage deviations relative to the admissible margins specified by these characteristics. We establish four design requirements that jointly express envelope-based severity, duration dependence, and preventive voltage-restoration incentives. Within a multiplicatively gated quadratic class, we derive necessary and sufficient conditions for satisfying these requirements and construct an explicit family of envelope-normalized objectives. We apply the proposed objectives to reactive-power coordination and evaluate their performance on the IEEE 14-bus, New England 39-bus, and NPCC 140-bus systems. Comparisons with Volt/VAR control, conventional nominal-voltage tracking, and recent data-center voltage-control methods demonstrate improved data-center retention under matched reactive-power support constraints. In the IEEE 14-bus study, the proposed controller reduces the mean data-center disconnection rate by 44.8\% and grid-demand loss by 27.4\% compared with the best-performing baseline. These results highlight the benefit of incorporating data-center ride-through requirements into reactive-power allocation.

title: Semantic Conditional Similarity (SCS): A Formal Mathematical Framework
abstract: Semantic Textual Similarity (STS) operates on document pairs, returning a single scalar per comparison. In a multi-document setting where several sources may have contributed to one or more targets, pairwise STS cannot disentangle each source's marginal semantic contribution from their shared vocabulary. In this paper, Semantic Conditional Similarity (SCS) is introduced as a conditional form of STS that computes similarity between two documents after eliminating semantic elements shared with a third via set-theoretic operations. SCS makes four contributions: 1) it introduces directionality, partitioning pairwise relations into lateral (inter-source) and vertical (source-to-target) classes; 2) conditioning induces role-dependent asymmetry by extending the comparison domain from unordered pairs to ordered, conditioned triples of a target, a reference, and a conditioning document; 3) SCS introduces inter-document conditioning by subtracting shared content from a third document, complementing the intra-document conditioning in recent C-STS work; and 4) the set-theoretic decomposition achieves threshold-free partitioning of shared and residual content, requiring no arbitrary similarity cutoff. Although developed for the $n \to 1$ configuration, the framework extends to $1 \to n$ via vertical role reversal and to $m \to n$ via independent composition of source- and target-side conditioning. With the established $1 \to 1$ case, these span the full spectrum of document cardinality. SCS scores should be interpreted ordinally, as rankings of marginal contributions rather than absolute measurements. The broader implication is that metric space axioms commonly assumed in similarity formalizations constrain expressiveness in role-differentiated multi-document settings, and that extending the domain to conditioned triples can recover information that pairwise-symmetric comparisons suppress.

title: Jacobian-Causal Memory Control for Persistent Memory in Language Model Systems
abstract: Persistent-memory systems choose not only which records are retrieved but which prior information can alter current inference. We propose Jacobian-causal memory control (JCMC), which represents each authorized memory intervention by a predicted influence signature in a shared behavioral measurement space, selects interventions against a target effect and side-effect budget, and compares predicted with observed effects before retaining or rolling back the intervention. Under explicit smoothness and bounded-estimation assumptions, we prove a quadratic local-approximation bound, characterize the target effects reachable by a set of signatures, bound selection regret under signature error, and bound non-additive interactions between simultaneous memories. The paper reports no benchmark measurements; it defines a paired counterfactual estimator and an evaluation protocol comparing JCMC with relevance, graph, and policy-filtered retrieval baselines. The central claim is narrowed or falsified if those simpler baselines match effect targeting, side-effect control, and rollback utility under equal model, memory, policy, and cost budgets.

title: Guardrail Erosion in Domain Fine-Tuned Large Language Models: A Paired Audit of Knowledge-Centric Abstention in Biomedical LLMs
abstract: The number of domain fine-tuned models, particularly in the biomedical domain, is rapidly expanding. Fine-tuning promises high-performing models at a fraction of the cost of training a base model, but it can also produce unintended behavioral changes. Multiple studies have shown that safety guardrails can erode with fine-tuning, yet large-scale studies across model architectures, data mixtures, and fine-tuning methodologies remain limited. Where prior work in this space has studied value-centric refusal, this work focuses on knowledge-centric abstention. We audit 25 biomedical domain fine-tuned large language models against 11 paired base checkpoints on MedAbstain and ClinDet-Bench to evaluate the impact of fine-tuning on knowledge-centric abstention. We find that defined appropriate abstention measured by these benchmarks, already low in base models (median 8.3% on MedAbstain), falls further after fine-tuning (median 4.2%, decreasing in 21 of 25 pairs on MedAbstain), and that the magnitude and direction of change are heterogeneous across pairs. These results motivate fine-tuning methods that improve domain-specific capability while preserving appropriate caution.

title: Aligning, Fast and Slow: A Control-Theoretic Oversight Framework for Long-Horizon Trajectories and Maintained Deployments
abstract: AI agents can pass checks on individual tasks while retaining memory or code changes that alter their later behavior. We introduce a control-theoretic framework that couples a fast loop controlling proposed actions with a slow loop reviewing persistent changes and reassessing configurations after model or tool updates. When measurement errors and changes between checks are bounded and controllers can enforce their decisions, we derive a deployment-level bound and a rule for dividing review effort. In simulation, dividing a fixed review budget between both loops reduces mean maximum departure from intended behavior roughly twelvefold compared with review confined to individual runs. In coding stress tests with authored memories and five matched seeds, combined controls reduce mean severity on a 0-3 scale from 0.325 without gates to 0.117, resolving 33 of 120 issues versus 35 without gates; in trading stress tests, combined controls reduce mean shortfall in low-emission purchases from 0.892 without gates to 0.107. The overall framework helps developers and auditors compare and enforce oversight designs, while the agent studies test component controls rather than the full deployment-level guarantee.

title: Extrapolation Matters: Sparse-Only Depth Completion Beyond LiDAR Coverage
abstract: Extrapolation beyond LiDAR coverage is an important yet under-evaluated challenge of depth completion. In real camera--LiDAR systems, partial sensor overlap, occlusions, and limited field coverage often leave large image regions weakly observed or completely unobserved by LiDAR. Thus, we investigate depth completion in this beyond-coverage regime using only sparse supervision from raw single-sweep LiDAR, without dense depth labels, LiDAR accumulation, or pseudo-LiDAR generation. Our approach leverages a frozen monocular depth foundation model, lightweight per-frame alignment to sparse LiDAR geometry, and a refinement module that fuses the aligned prior with sparse LiDAR anchors to predict dense metric depth. To regularize learning under raw sparse supervision, we introduce a high-frequency normal-consistency loss defined as the image-space gradient of the per-pixel normal cosine discrepancy. This term penalizes spatial variation in scalar angular error; it does not directly match changes in neighboring normal vectors. We further introduce an evaluation protocol that explicitly separates LiDAR-supported and beyond-coverage regions, revealing extrapolative behavior that conventional depth-completion metrics can obscure. Our method achieves strong depth accuracy beyond LiDAR coverage while remaining competitive in LiDAR-covered regions, providing a practical way to deploy monocular foundation priors in multi-sensor systems.

title: Multi-Model Over-the-Air Federated Learning via Transceiver Beamforming and Device Grouping
abstract: This paper considers uplink communication design for training multiple independent machine learning models via wireless federated learning. To reduce communication delay, we utilize multi-antenna beamforming and propose a multi-model over-the-air (M-OTA) uplink transmission and aggregation method for simultaneous training of multiple models. Devices are formed into groups for local model training based on the model assignments per communication round and simultaneously perform OTA aggregation over a multi-access channel. Based on the M-OTA transmission and reception process, we formulate a joint optimization of transmit and receive beamforming and device grouping over $T$ communication rounds to maximize the training convergence rates of all models. We analyze the per-model optimality gap, which captures the impact of noisy aggregation and inter-model interference on the learning performance. We further show that the $T$-round joint optimization problem can be decomposed into per-round online optimization to devise solutions. Following this, we propose a device grouping strategy that explores channel correlation among devices to maximize OTA aggregation performance. Furthermore, we present a low-complexity iterative algorithm for joint transmit-receive beamforming with closed-form updates. Simulation shows that our proposed M-OTA approach substantially outperforms the conventional single-model sequential OTA approach and other commonly used beamforming schemes.

title: Blind Noise Equalization for Large Data Matrices under General Variance Profiles
abstract: Low-rank approximation is a basic tool for inference from large and noisy data matrices. However, when noise variances differ across entries, a setting known as heteroskedasticity, the noise can distort the observed spectrum, producing spurious components and obscuring weak signals. To address these challenges, we develop BRINE (Blind Resolvent-based Iterative Noise Equalizer), a data-driven procedure that iteratively rescales rows and columns to equalize the average noise variance across both dimensions. Under suitable conditions, this procedure restores the Marchenko-Pastur law for the noise spectrum and can amplify signal components without prior knowledge of the signal or noise structure. A key idea underlying our approach is to equalize the diagonal entries of the data resolvent as a proxy for equalizing the unknown noise variances. At the population level, we identify a potential function that characterizes this equalization and motivates an iterative minimization procedure. We prove convergence of the iterations to the true equalizer for arbitrary positive variance profiles, with a geometric rate under mild conditions. The updates can be estimated directly from noisy data, and we establish probabilistic error bounds for the scaling factors. Simulations and experiments across diverse biological data modalities and preprocessing pipelines illustrate the effectiveness of our approach.

title: Learning from How Users Interpret: Personalizing Recommendation Explanation Order
abstract: Personalized explanations typically adapt their content or presentation based on preferences, interaction histories, or other user characteristics. We examine whether regularities inferred from prior textual interpretations can support personalization of explanation organization. In a controlled within participant study with 122 participants, prior interpretations were represented along three dimensions: information selection, relative salience, and relational organization. The relational dimension was partially operationalized through co mobilization. These representations were aggregated into fixed historical profiles and used to organize otherwise identical explanation sentences. Participants encountered four organization procedures: the OWN historical profile, the DONOR historical profile, a population profile called POP, and a language model procedure using the historical profile called PROFILE LLM. Post exposure objective comprehension was the primary outcome. OWN achieved 86.5 percent correct responses, compared with 66.0 percent for DONOR, 63.9 percent for POP, and 73.0 percent for PROFILE LLM. Mixed effects analyses showed higher comprehension with OWN than with each alternative procedure. No reliable overall condition effect was detected for recommendation acceptance. These findings indicate that historical profiles derived from prior interpretations can provide an actionable signal for personalizing explanation order while keeping explanatory content and wording fixed.

title: Talanov dynamics and chirp-controlled rogue-wave formation for the vector nonlinear Schrödinger equation
abstract: We study the focusing vector nonlinear Schrödinger equation, or Manakov system, for a pair of coupled initial conditions with compactly supported, concave parabolic density profiles and phases depending quadratically on the spatial coordinate. We focus on the natural class of self-similar solutions generated by such profiles, whose dispersionless evolution we refer to as Talanov dynamics. We extend the criterion for blow-up in finite time, first established for a single field, to the Manakov case. For arbitrary initial chirps in the two fields, we provide closed-form expressions for their evolution, and an explicit expression for the time of the gradient catastrophe, if it occurs, and we classify the effect of the coupling on the catastrophe. Depending on the initial chirps, the two fields may catastrophise, or relax, as each would if decoupled. However, coupling can also force the catastrophe in fields that would otherwise relax if decoupled. For identical initial supports, and in the presence of dispersion, we numerically show that the same dispersionless criterion determines, in the semiclassical regime, whether the fully dispersive solution relaxes or develops a rogue wave in each field, whose onset time is accurately predicted by the corresponding dispersionless catastrophe time, in direct analogy with the scalar case. As chirp and amplitude are relatively easy to control experimentally, we expect these results to be relevant to experiments in nonlinear optics and Bose-Einstein condensates, extending to coupled systems observations made for the scalar equation.

title: Training Stability under Adaptive Curricula
abstract: Unsupervised Environment Design (UED) approaches train reinforcement learning (RL) agents on diverse curricula that may evolve with their capabilities. While prior work has largely focused on how these curricula are constructed, we study whether their students remain trainable under the resulting distributions. Across multiple UED mechanisms, environment complexities, and extended training horizons, we identify recurring learner-side pathologies, including parameter growth, degraded value--outcome ordering, and loss of representational diversity, that accompany stagnation and performance degradation. These findings connect limitations in UED to optimization failures previously identified in conventional deep RL, while showing how adaptive curricula couple the learner's optimization state to its future training distribution. Controlled interventions show that mitigating selected pathologies improves learning. Stabilizing the learner improves long-horizon performance and zero-shot generalization without changing the curriculum rule or increasing environment interaction. Our results establish learner trainability as a complementary design principle for UED. Effective curricula require students that remain capable of learning from the distributions they produce.

title: Not All Latents Are Equal: Importance-Weighted Latent Graph Generation
abstract: Graph generation has shown tremendous effectiveness in modeling complex scientific tasks ranging from molecule generation to optimized circuit design. Most recent advancements have developed models that learn to denoise noisy graphs using either discrete diffusion or flow matching. However, discrete graph diffusion scales quadratically with the number of nodes, making it difficult to use such models on larger graphs. On the other hand, latent graph generation instead seeks to denoise noisy graph latents, which scale better to more nodes due to their lower dimension. However, in practice, latent graph generation models lag behind their discrete counterparts in performance. We study this problem, finding that it is caused by the unequal distribution of that different latent dimensions have on graph reconstruction. the impact. We observe that the vast majority of impact is contained in only a smaller number of latent dimensions. Since equal emphasis is placed on reconstructing the entire latent in the loss function, existing models are optimized to reconstruct information irrelevant to the downstream task. To tackle this problem, we propose Latent Importance Reweighting ({\bf LIR)} which weights each latent dimensions via it's importance to final graph reconstruction. Importance is calculated as the relative influence of a single latent unit on graph reconstruction, which is represented via the Jacobian of the decoder relative to the latent. Our method is model-agnostic and requires no additional model parameters or hyperparameters. Experiments show that LIR can boost performance and lead to faster training convergence when applied to two different autoencoders on various benchmark datasets. Code: https://github.com/biraaj/GraphGenLatentReweight

title: TopoSHAP: Shapley for Explainable and Efficient Topological Deep Learning
abstract: Topological deep learning (TDL) extends learning on graphs, such as molecules or social networks, to higher-order structures, such as rings in a molecule or groups in a social network. Explaining which of these structures drive a model's predictions, and which architectural components matter most for its performance, remains challenging. We introduce TopoSHAP, an efficient and general explanation framework that addresses both questions across topological domains and model architectures. TopoSHAP-cell assigns Shapley values to topological data cells and extracts compact explanations. These explanations match or outperform graph-based counterparts on GraphXAI benchmark data while running up to 112$\times$ faster. They also reveal advantageous topological feature design, leading to measured improvements in explanation recovery and predictive accuracy. On the architecture side, TopoSHAP-neighbor explains how neighborhoods contribute to model performance, and turns these evaluations into a backward-elimination search that identifies smaller, competitive architectures early in training. This is up to $11.3\times$ cheaper than traditional TDL training sweeps.

title: SteerGR: Steering Generative Recommendation via Sparse Autoencoders for Controllable Game Discovery
abstract: Generative recommendation aims to predict item identifiers from user interaction histories, but explicit control over the properties of recommended items remains underexplored. A key challenge is to connect human-readable concepts to internal features whose interventions effectively change the recommended items. To address this, we propose Steerable Generative Recommender (SteerGR), a framework that uses sparse autoencoders for concept-level control in game discovery. SteerGR proceeds through three stages: (i) Concept Definition and Grounding for defining play concepts with an LLM; (ii) Feature Discovery and Selection for discovering candidate features by their concept associations and selecting one by its steering effect; and (iii) Sparse Feature Intervention for amplifying or suppressing selected features to steer recommendations without retraining the recommender. Extensive experiments with two industrial generative recommendation models on a real-world game dataset show that the selected features successfully steer recommendations toward or away from target concepts. We believe this work takes a first step to extend SAE-based steering from LLMs to industrial generative recommendation.

title: AircraftWitness: How Often Aircraft Can Locate Recordings
abstract: Aircraft overhead can reveal where an outdoor recording was made. Propellers and rotors leave Doppler curves in audio, and public ADS-B archives log equipped aircraft. We measure how often, blind and against chance. Our main test was registered and timestamped before any audio, and its two amendments came before any answer was read. It covers 24 new places, with the recorders' own clocks, a 300 s slack and a 20 km square. The best of three locators places clear-pass clips within 1 km at 4 places, where a uniform guess predicts 0.57 (p = 0.0065 after correcting for the pick). With the wrong time or swapped audio it places none. The other two hit 1 and 2. On 360 clips from 7 places of a GPS-timed network, two locators place 6% and 8% within 1 km. By place, a unit chosen after that run, they hit 4 and 5 of 7 where a uniform guess predicts 2.3. On 1,600 random public recordings, picked and cut without the truth in a time-bounded run, the three locators answer at most 20 times and place at most 2. We release AircraftWitness, a benchmark, and pass labels for 11.7 million recordings.

title: Online Bin Packing with Dispatch Deadlines
abstract: We study a generalization of online bin packing by introducing dispatch deadlines. Items arrive over time in an online fashion. Each item has an arrival time, a size in $(0,1]$, and a deadline, all of which are revealed only when the item arrives. The algorithm must immediately and irrevocably assign the item to a unit-capacity bin that has not yet been dispatched. Each bin must be dispatched no later than the earliest deadline of the items assigned to it, and once it is dispatched, it cannot be used for future items. The goal is to minimize the number of bins used. Applications arise naturally in logistics. Additionally, the offline version of this problem has appeared under several names, including the clique partition problem in weighted interval graphs and the BinSchedule problem. This problem is also a special case of online bin packing with conflicts and is closely related to online bin packing models with delay costs. We study the competitive ratios of several classical online bin packing algorithms when applied to this problem, and show that a similar hierarchy of competitive ratios carries over. Our main technical results are that the competitive ratio of First-Fit is exactly $16/7 \approx 2.28571$, and that no deterministic online algorithm has a competitive ratio less than $11/5 = 2.2$, showing that First-Fit is quite close to best possible. In addition, Next-Fit and Worst-Fit have competitive ratio exactly $3$, and every algorithm in the Any-Fit class has competitive ratio between $16/7$ and $3$.

title: Exact optimality of augmented order-of-addition designs
abstract: We prove that, for the pairwise-ordering model with at least three components, adding any run to an order-of-addition orthogonal array gives a $D$-optimal design among all exact designs of the enlarged size, allowing replication. We also establish the corresponding result for foldover designs: adding any reversal pair to a foldover order-of-addition orthogonal array gives a $D$-optimal design within the foldover class at the enlarged size. Both augmentations also minimise the average prediction variance and a covariance-scaled information discrepancy, and maximise the minimum relative efficiency. The key step represents the scaled discrepancy through signed comparisons of triples and derives a sharp integer lower bound; classical spectral inequalities then give the exact-size optima, and signed four-component relative-order counts characterise equality. Complete reversal pairs additionally protect the estimation of pairwise-ordering effects against arbitrary reversal-invariant nuisance means. At the smallest estimable five-component foldover size, exact enumeration identifies five determinant-optimal classes with different prediction and balance properties, and a seven-component example shows that deleting a reversal pair need not be optimal even when it minimises the discrepancy. Constructions through ten components illustrate the attained run sizes.

title: High-Dimensional Off-Policy Evaluation without Sample Splitting using an Onsager Correction
abstract: Reward models used for off-policy evaluation (OPE) are commonly selected using held-out data. When sample size and context dimension grow proportionally, the difference in test risk between models fitted on the full sample and on a fixed fraction of it need not vanish. Held-out evaluation can therefore consistently estimate the test risk of the model trained on the smaller sample, but because the relative ranking of candidate reward models can change after full-data refitting, held-out selection can be suboptimal. We develop an Onsager-corrected, target-policy-weighted criterion that estimates the full-data reward model's out-of-sample risk under the target policy using only its training observations. This enables early stopping along the full-data gradient-descent trajectory without sample splitting. For neural networks with fixed depth and hidden width under Gaussian contexts, single-index rewards, context-dependent multi-index target policies, and known context-independent logging, we prove uniform consistency of our criterion over a fixed finite set of gradient-descent iterates and a near-oracle guarantee for the selected reward model. The same correction yields a doubly robust estimator that consistently estimates the true policy value without sample splitting, even when reward-model prediction error does not vanish. Experiments show decreasing risk-estimation error as dimension grows at a fixed sample-to-dimension ratio, and improved reward-model selection relative to held-out baselines. Empirically, our correction also reduces the root mean squared error of doubly robust value estimates computed from the same data used to fit and select the reward models.

title: MotionDecipher: LLM-Assisted Clinical Interpretation of Human Motion Signals for Efficient Gait Analysis
abstract: Clinical gait and motion analysis is widely used to guide targeted interventions for patients with neurological disorders, the outcome of which is typically a report with descriptions of joint movements and forces. Current practices rely on experts' manual effort, which is labor-intensive and time-consuming. Recent advancements in Large Language Models (LLMs) provide opportunities to address this problem, but translating human motion into clinical gait descriptions remains challenging because the quality of the context directly affects LLMs' reasoning capability over continuous motion signals. To tackle this, we introduce MotionDecipher, a novel framework bridging the semantic gap between motion data and clinical interpretations. Specifically, we made 3 key advancements: 1) a Human Motion Tokenizer that converts motion signals into domain-specific tokens for time- and frequency-informed gait interpretation; 2) a Meta Feature Selector that transforms tokens into Structured Representations; and 3) a Hybrid Context Constructor to determine the optimal demonstration-based prompt for In-Context Learning. We evaluated MotionDecipher on data collected at an accredited gait lab from 122 patients and 46 controls. Results show that MotionDecipher achieves 0.91 BERTScore (13% over GPT-5), while expert evaluation ranks MotionDecipher highest in Correctness, Completeness, and Conciseness compared to baselines, highlighting its promise for efficient gait analysis.

title: Constructing Casimirs for the quantum reflection equation
abstract: We explore the quantum reflection equation in the case of a full-dimensional $n\times n$ matrix $\mathbb A$. Using the technique of $q$-determinants, we find closed expressions for the quantum Pfaffian (in the case of even $n$) and for new quantum Casimirs that are ratios of special quantum (Sklyanin) minors of $\mathbb A$. Special attention is paid to the self-adjointness property of the newly constructed Casimirs. We put forward a conjecture that, adopting a natural ansatz for a quantum deformation of a Casimir of a classical algebra, self-adjointness implies commutativity. We also explore the relationship to networks of quantum cluster variables.

title: MotionBench-XAI: Benchmarking What Shapes Shapley Explanations in Spatiotemporal Machine Learning
abstract: Predicting outcomes from spatiotemporal data, such as assessing Parkinson's severity from human motion, often requires explainability in addition to accuracy. Practitioners need to know what drove the prediction, whether it be spatial (a body joint), temporal (a specific window), or both. Shapley values are attributions computed by treating input features as players in a cooperative game and measuring how the model output changes as coalitions of players are removed. Computing them involves choosing what counts as players, how absent players are imputed, and how the game is evaluated. How these choices affect explanation quality is poorly understood for spatiotemporal data, and real data carries no ground-truth attributions to check against. We present MotionBench-XAI, a benchmark built on i) five synthetic spatiotemporal datasets with exact ground-truth Shapley values, ii) three real datasets across clinical gait, electrocardiogram, and audio, iii) ten attribution methods across three player sets, and iv) three trained architectures. We show that grouping features into players, across time, space, or both, matters more than the choice of imputer. Generative imputers improve explanations only when their conditional models are accurate. On real data, the standard proxy metrics select contradictory best methods. We distill these findings into practical insights and provide an open-source pipeline.

title: Driver Takeovers and Longitudinal Responses Analysis from Naturalistic Driving
abstract: As Level 2 advanced driver-assistance systems (ADAS) become more widely used, understanding driver-system interaction is increasingly important for traffic safety. However, limited real-world data make these interactions difficult to study. We present ADAS-TO, a naturalistic dataset of 16,446 takeover clips from 364 drivers across 2,585 different drives. It combines road video, vehicle kinematics, driver inputs, and ADAS status. To analyze takeover behavior, we retained 6,206 manually reviewed takeover events during continued lane keeping or car following. We excluded events in which the driver intentionally changed lanes, turned, or made a stop beyond the ADAS's capabilities (e.g., at a red light or stop sign) shortly after takeover. Drivers began intervening before ADAS disengaged in 65.6% of takeovers involving braking or steering. When the ego vehicle was still closing on a lead vehicle at disengagement, longitudinal safety margins often narrowed further after the transfer to manual control. Among 2,031 such events, 78.5% had a lower minimum time-to-collision (TTC) in the five seconds after disengagement than in the five seconds before it. For events involving braking, the mean TTC trajectory reached its minimum about 1.2 s after disengagement. We model the subsequent braking response using a Gazis-Herman-Rothery (GHR) car-following law. Its median five-second spacing root-mean-square error is 1.34 m with observed lead motion and 1.84 m with predicted lead motion. The fitted model expresses braking as a response to looming, with stronger responses at higher speeds and shorter gaps. Applied before takeover, it shows that greater looming than predicted by the human-response reference is associated with disengagement. These findings support continued assessment of longitudinal safety after ADAS disengagement, while the driver's braking response develops.

title: The Matthews Correlation Coefficient: Fifty years
abstract: Fifty years after its introduction, the Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC) remains central -and debated- in binary classification. This survey offers a comprehensive retrospective and an in-depth analysis of MCC, covering its historical development, mathematical foundations, and implications for practice. We clarify long-standing misconceptions, formalize its equivalences (to Pearson's correlation and to Chi2 in 2x2 tables), and examine its behavior under class imbalance. Beyond MCC, we develop analytical (derivatives) and graphical (contour plots) frameworks that generalize to any confusion-matrix-based metric. These frameworks expose structural properties -bias, robustness, sensitivity- that scalar summaries conceal, and they provide actionable guidance for selecting and interpreting performance measures in applications where reliability and fairness matter. Together, our results position MCC within a broader toolkit while clarifying when it is informative -and when alternatives may be preferable.

title: On the Few-Shot Adaptation of Vision-Language Models: A Few Gradient Signs Are All You Need
abstract: The limited supervision available for the few-shot adaptation of vision-language models makes gradient estimation particularly noisy. We find that the gradient magnitudes are severely miscalibrated, while the signs of a small top-magnitude subset remain informative. This motivates SignSparseSGD and DynSignSparseSGD, two state-free optimizers that use gradient magnitudes only to select where to update and fixed-magnitude signs to decide how to update. The static variant fixes the support after the first minibatch. The dynamic variant refreshes it at every step. Across 11 datasets, three CLIP backbones, and five shot levels, the proposed methods are competitive with or outperform parameter-efficient and optimization-based baselines on average, while exhibiting markedly lower sensitivity to long training schedules. They introduce no task-specific modules, maintain no first- or second-moment optimizer states, and use one shared configuration across datasets, backbones, and shot levels. Our code is included in the supplementary materials and will be released upon publication.

title: Proof of the Cordero-Torregrosa Conjecture and an Improved Order Bound for Paired Jacobian Evaluations
abstract: In solving systems of nonlinear equations, one of the main objectives is to construct iterative methods that attain high orders of convergence using as few evaluations as possible. However, the information a method obtains during each iteration imposes limitations on the order it can guarantee. The Cordero--Torregrosa conjecture proposes a bound on this order in terms of the number of evaluations of the function and its Jacobian. In this work, we prove this bound for the universal local order of one iteration, without requiring the number of Jacobian evaluations to be less than or equal to the number of function evaluations. In particular, our result also covers the case in which more evaluations of the Jacobian than of the function are performed. The proof encompasses deterministic, causal, memoryless methods whose rules may be arbitrary, without imposing rationality, continuity, or computability conditions. Moreover, we prove that when each Jacobian evaluation is performed at a point where the value of the function is already known, a more restrictive bound on the order of convergence can be obtained. Finally, we propose a new conjecture that establishes a refined bound through a product of factors determined by the distribution of evaluations, under additional dimensional conditions. These results provide a better understanding of the limitations imposed by the available information and raise new possibilities for studying high-order iterative methods.

title: Scale as a Modality: Multi-Scale Pixel-Space Diffusion Transformers
abstract: Latent diffusion models rely on pretrained autoencoders that introduce lossy compression and constrain spatial granularity. Pixel-space diffusion avoids this bottleneck and enables flexible tokenization at multiple spatial scales, yet existing approaches largely adopt two-level coarse-to-fine architectures with limited cross-scale interaction. We introduce MS-pDiT, a multi-scale pixel-space diffusion transformer that treats spatial scale as a modality. MS-pDiT tokenizes the same noisy image at multiple patch sizes, processes each scale in a dedicated transformer stream, and enables bidirectional information exchange through compacted MM-DiT-style joint attention, with attention cost independent of the finest patch size. This design establishes the number of scales as a new architectural scaling dimension. On ImageNet $256\times256$, increasing the number of scales from two to five consistently improves FID from 4.39 to 2.31, 2.26, and 2.19, while adding an intermediate scale substantially outperforms increasing depth under comparable parameter budgets. Further analysis highlights the importance of bidirectional cross-scale interaction and late introduction of fine-grained streams. MS-pDiT achieves FID scores of 1.43 and 1.44 on ImageNet $256\times256$ and $512\times512$, respectively, and naturally extends to text-to-image generation, achieving 0.86 on GenEval and 83.9 on DPG-Bench.

title: Tags Helping Tags: Coordination-Free Power Boosting for Battery-less Backscatter Networks
abstract: Battery-less backscatter sensor nodes powered by radio-frequency wireless power transfer are attractive for large or hard-to-reach deployments, but their range is typically limited by the forward power-transfer link rather than by communication sensitivity. We present a method for improving power delivery, and thus range, in dense tag deployments by having nearby tags act as helpers: each helper terminates its antenna in purely reactive impedances, reflecting the power beacon's signal toward a target tag so that it combines constructively with the direct line-of-sight path and increases the power the target harvests. On a hardware testbed, helpers using discrete impedance control are shown to increase the target tag's harvested power by over 50% above an all-absorbing baseline, while randomly set helper impedances give no reliable benefit, and are sometimes even detrimental. We further propose and implement a local algorithm that lets each helper tune its own impedance using only measurements of the target's packet rate, without channel estimation or coordination between helpers, and we show that it brings the target's packet rate close to that of an independently tuned configuration. These results suggest that independent, passive sensor nodes can cooperatively extend each other's power-transfer range with minimal added infrastructure.

title: Generative Search and Recommendation at Shopify
abstract: Search and recommendation at Shopify require retrieving relevant products from a changing catalog of billions of products under strict latency constraints. We present SID-LLM, which casts both tasks as generating semantic IDs: short sequences of content-derived tokens representing products. We jointly pre-train SID-LLM on catalog and behavioral data, giving search and recommendation a shared representation and training objective. We show that reinforcement learning further improves judged search relevance. Furthermore, distillation from task-specific experts improves recommendation quality over joint supervised fine-tuning without a statistically detected loss in search quality. Finally, for efficient serving, we pair multi-token prediction with a lightweight ranker, improving retrieval quality over our autoregressive baseline while reducing latency. We evaluate SID-LLM both as a standalone retriever and as a component of Shopify's production search and recommendation systems. As a standalone search system, SID-LLM achieves quality comparable to Shopify's existing multi-model search stack while meeting production latency requirements. Integrating SID-LLM into the search and recommendation stacks provides significant gains in both offline evaluations and online A/B tests. Together, these results demonstrate the practical value of semantic-ID generation as a unified approach to product discovery at scale.

title: Laser-Direct-Written polymer WGM microring laser integrated on a fiber tip for refractive index sensing
abstract: Whispering-gallery-mode (WGM) microlasers are promising for refractometric sensing, but their practical implementation can be limited by the need for stable resonator-coupler alignment. Here, we demonstrate a Rhodamine B-doped polymer WGM microring laser directly fabricated on an optical-fiber tip, eliminating the external resonator-fiber coupling interface at the sensing head. Micro-droplet coating and UV laser direct writing are combined for fabrication, while finite-difference time-domain simulations guide the microring laser design. The microlasers operate in air and water with thresholds of 0.224 uJ and 0.458 uJ, respectively. Refractometric measurements in aqueous glucose solutions yield a bulk refractive index sensitivity of 364.95 nm/RIU and a detection limit of 2.47 x 10^(-4) RIU. Water-induced polymer changes and photobleaching are also investigated. This fiber-tip architecture provides a basis for probe-based refractometric sensing in environmental and biochemical applications.

title: Local contraction of stochastic affine recursions of $\mathbb{R}^d$
abstract: We consider affine stochastic recursions $X^x_{n+1}=A_{n+1}X^x_n+B_{n+1}$ in $\mathbb{R}^d$, where $(B_n,A_n)$ are i.i.d. in $\operatorname{Aff}(\mathbb{R}^d)$ with strongly irreducible and proximal linear part. In the critical regime where the top Lyapunov exponent vanishes, we show that the recursion is locally contractive in every direction, yielding uniqueness, up to a positive multiplicative constant, of the $μ$-invariant non-zero Radon measure. This extends to every dimension $d\geq 2$ a result of Babillot-Bougerol-Élie (1997) in dimension one. The proof is based on the study of the asymptotic behaviour of the "joint process" $(X^x_n,X^y_n)$, using geometric and measure-theoretic properties of the diagonal affine action. A key ingredient is an abstract criterion for the total dissipativity of semigroup actions, which we apply to this process.

title: Electrohydrodynamic interactions of two Quincke rotors: asymptotic theory and boundary element simulations
abstract: Weakly conducting spheres suspended in a leaky dielectric fluid can undergo spontaneous Quincke rotation when the applied electric field exceeds a critical value. We investigate how electric and hydrodynamic interactions modify this instability and the subsequent rotation of two spheres at fixed separation and orientation. Starting from electric dipole and hydrodynamic rotlet interactions, we develop a systematic far-field asymptotic theory. Away from onset, slow drift of the rotation axes makes a regular expansion fail at long times. A multiple-scale expansion gives slow phase equations that select the axes according to pair orientation and field strength. Near onset, weak interactions produce corrections comparable to the isolated rotation magnitude. A detuned multiple-scale expansion gives coupled equations for the transverse dipole amplitudes. Their linearization identifies four collective rotation modes, whose critical fields and steady branches with one active mode are determined together with their stability. At leading order near onset, electric interaction shifts all four modal thresholds equally, whereas hydrodynamic interaction makes counter-rotation appear first for pair angles below $\cos^{-1}(1/\sqrt3)\simeq54.7^\circ$ and co-rotation above it. Away from onset, the angle separating stable counter-rotation from stable co-rotation increases with field strength. Boundary element method (BEM) simulations place onset within a field interval for each configuration and resolve the growth and relaxation of rotation. Steady-speed comparisons show how pair orientation changes the balance between electric and hydrodynamic effects. We compare the unexpanded dipole-rotlet model of Das and Saintillan [Phys. Rev. E 87, 043014 (2013)] with our asymptotic theory and BEM simulations.

title: Impact of color in computer and human-based object recognition under occlusion
