Our intention with this work is to improve ZK performance by introducing fundamental changes in the low-level architectural structure of proof generation. These changes affect performance curves for most current proof generation algorithms. In particular, this paper explores the trade-offs between increased parallelization on GPUs and the resultant memory management problems that occur due to this parallelization. We implement a parallelized PlonK in order to analyze these trade-offs and make arguments concerning the nature of data flows within the proving protocol. Our results lead us to consider multi-GPU environments to maximize performance for large circuit sizes. Such environments introduce issues of communication, efficient hardware management, data partition, and data transfers. This paper further discusses the use cases that motivate multi-GPU implementations, their cost models, and the use of remote direct memory access (RDMA) for data transfer among GPUs.

title: Video Stitching from Multiple Moving Cameras
abstract: We address geometric video alignment for the same scene captured by multiple freely moving cameras. Existing methods, which are based on image stitching or video stabilization, are typically limited to two cameras or must assume the restrictive setting of a fixed linear ordering of the cameras. We propose MViS, a lightweight test-time optimization framework for joint multi-view alignment with temporal consistency. MViS uses a spatial-transformer-inspired net to jointly process frames from all views within a short temporal window and predict per-view, per-time homographies. Optimization proceeds in two stages: geometry-guided alignment followed by appearance-based refinement, with both stages enforcing multi-view and temporal consistency across the sequence. The method requires no scene-specific hyperparameter tuning, handles arbitrary and time-varying view-intersection graphs, and remains robust under rapid camera motion. On a standard two-view video benchmark, MViS matches or surpasses the state of the art. To facilitate evaluation in more complex scenarios, we introduce an annotated dataset with more than two freely moving cameras and establish the first benchmark for this setting. Project page: https://bgu-cs-vil.github.io/MViS-project/ .

title: Symmetric Zassenhaus splittings for bounded and unbounded operators
abstract: We establish rigorous local-error bounds for the entire family of symmetric Zassenhaus splittings for possibly unbounded operators, under explicit assumptions on commutator bounds, regularity-preserving flows, and conjugation identities. Truncated symmetric Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff expansions yield an explicit coefficient formula for the Zassenhaus exponents and identify vanishing commutator expressions. In order to extend these cancellations to the realm of unbounded operators, we prove a general theorem on finite expansions of multiple operator conjugations with controlled integral remainders. For splittings of order 2n, our argument gives the sufficient commutator-length bound 4n-1, revealing regularity requirements that are not apparent from the formal order calculation. Using the Schrödinger equation with a quadratic potential as an example, we show that the order-dependent regularity requirements can reduce to one fixed weighted Sobolev space for all splitting orders.

title: Inverse design of superconductors and semiconductors with differentiable foundation models
abstract: Designing a crystal for a target property requires choosing its elements, stoichiometry, and atomic structure together, yet gradients exist only for the continuous structural variables. We introduce differentiable Equiformer fast effective-atom theory (DEFEAT), which lets a pretrained EquiformerV3 foundation model accept continuous species weights and site occupancies without retraining on fractional data, thereby enabling gradient-based materials optimization. Gradients from fine-tuned property models and a machine-learned energy penalty then guide updates to composition, atom count, atomic positions, and lattice vectors in a single optimization. In a search for phonon-mediated superconductors, density-functional perturbation theory on 45 structurally novel designs gives isotropic Allen-Dynes critical temperatures above 10 K for 39; the highest is 24.0 K for ZrTiNb2CN3, and H4LiPd3 (23.2 K) lies on the static DFT hull. In searches for photovoltaic absorbers, SCAN calculations confirm ten novel crystal structures with band gaps within 20% of a 1.34 eV target on their respective raw or empirically corrected scales, all within 70 meV/atom of the DFT hull, and show that the systematic gap error of the training functional propagates into the designs unless the objective corrects for it. Quasiharmonic free energies from machine-learned potentials further show that finite-temperature competition with solid phases can reorder candidates relative to the static hull.

title: Half-precision inference of AI weather prediction models: negligible loss of skill at a fraction of the cost
abstract: AI weather prediction models are released with 32-bit (fp32) weights and run in fp32 by default, although current GPUs compute much faster in 16-bit formats. We run five publicly available models -- Aurora, Pangu-Weather, FourCastNet, SFNO and FastNet -- on a single 16 GB GPU from 52 initial dates in 2024, in fp32 and with their networks in half precision (fp16), and verify the forecasts against ERA5. The physical state must stay in fp32: converting the whole model rounds it in physical units, which in fp16 overflows and in bf16 discards meaningful information. With the state, its normalisation and denormalisation in fp32, running the network in fp16 changes the global RMSE by at most 1.4%, and by about 0.5% or less for four of the five models, equivalent to less than one hour of lead time up to day 8 and at most two hours at day 10. The differences show no systematic pattern by region, scale or for tropical and extratropical storms, apart from a small tropical penalty in FourCastNet, and fp16 leaves the CRPS, spread and calibration of Aurora's ensemble almost unchanged. No value overflowed fp16's numeric range (+/-65,504); the largest stay 38 to 544 times below it. A 10-day forecast in fp16 is 1.3-3.5 times faster than in fp32 and uses 1.4-3.7 times less energy. Sensitivity experiments show that rules of thumb from other applications of reduced precision carry over only partly: the first and last layers dominate for some models but not for others, and no type of layer is sensitive on its own. For running AI weather models on a single GPU, fp16 with the state in fp32 is practically lossless at a fraction of the cost. bf16, often preferred for its wider range, is as fast but less accurate than fp16 for every model, and simple 8-bit quantisation costs far more skill.

title: Bayesian Inverse Problems for EUV reflectometry with regularized JKO scheme
abstract: We study a Bayesian inverse problem in EUV reflectometry, where optical constants and layer thicknesses are inferred from angle- and wavelength-resolved reflection measurements. The physical process is modeled and evaluated using an efficient forward model based on the transfer matrix method. As an alternative to computationally expensive sampling-based inference, we employ an Eulerian, entropically regularized Jordan-Kinderlehrer-Otto (JKO) scheme that minimizes the Kullback--Leibler divergence via proximal steps in the Wasserstein space. Using the Benamou--Brenier dynamic formulation and a Hopf-Cole transform, each JKO step is reformulated as a pair of heat equations coupled only through their initial and terminal conditions, enabling an efficient fixed-point solver. The resulting high-dimensional densities are discretized on tensor-product grids and represented in tensor-train format, exploiting Kronecker structure for scalable computation. Preconditioning based on estimated posterior moments further improves tractability. We test the method with numerical experiments on EUV reflectometry data for a ruthenium--silicon ($\ce{Ru}$ on $\ce{Si}$) specimen and compare the learned tensor-train posterior to ensemble Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) reference samples. We demonstrate a use case in which we are able to reuse the tensor-train posterior to obtain samples for shifted target distributions with less computational effort than a comparable MCMC method.

title: An Empirical Evaluation of a Weighted PALU Model for Internet Traffic Networks
abstract: The PALU model is a hybrid power law generative framework that decomposes Internet traffic graphs into three structural components: a preferential attachment core, degree one leaf nodes, and disconnected satellite clusters. Although the original PALU formulation provided a theoretical basis for this decomposition, it was never validated against real traffic data and was restricted to unweighted networks. This work presents the first empirical evaluation of PALU against real Internet traffic, using packet traces from the MAWI WIDE samplepoint F dataset. We introduce a weighted extension of the model incorporating strength degree scaling, and develop a packet-to-graph pipeline for parameter estimation across multiple observation window sizes. Results show that the power law degree exponent $α\approx 2.0$ remains stable across observation scales from $10^5$ to $3 \times 10^6$ packets, consistent with the PALU structural prediction. However, the satellite cluster parameter $λ$ and the weighted scaling parameter $θ$ exhibit systematic dependence on observation scale, and the Poisson star assumption for unattached components is formally rejected at all tested window sizes. These results indicate that PALU captures important aspects of Internet traffic structure but requires an explicit observation model to fully account for finite sampling effects.

title: Expert Spindles in the Wild: Enriched Supervision for a Dense Detector
abstract: Sleep spindles are a hallmark of healthy NREM sleep whose frequency, amplitude, density, duration and topography vary with brain maturation, age and disease. Their manual annotation is impractical and variable between scorers, yet the public references used to train automatic detectors cover these characteristics only partially: stage N2 only, a single central derivation, or short pre-selected segments. Measuring duration and density requires dense detectors that learn event boundaries from annotated onsets and offsets, and therefore inherit the protocol under which those boundaries were scored. We introduce Expert Spindles in the Wild (ESW), a stage-agnostic expert spindle annotation set covering 19 complete MASS-SS2 recordings ($\approx$150 h of continuous EEG, 29,819 events). A sleep neurophysiologist annotated the recordings using the full EEG montage, blinded to sleep-stage labels and prior spindle annotations. On the 15 nights shared with historical scorers, ESW recovers 92.7% of E1 and 73.7% of E2 events, while recovering 81.6% of the MODA expert-consensus events on the common excerpts. Despite stage-blind annotation, 99.0% of ESW events occur in N2/N3. Used to train a fixed dense detector on a frozen SleepFM encoder, ESW reaches an event-level $F_1$ of 0.680 on 166 unseen MODA subjects, compared with 0.635 for E2 ($ΔF_1$ = +0.045, paired-bootstrap 95% CI [0.024, 0.065]). ESW is thus useful supervision for cross-dataset detection, and closer annotation-level agreement with the MODA consensus did not translate into better transfer performance in this experiment. The annotations are released under the MASS data-use terms (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23894975).

title: Isometric Classification of Sobolev Spaces
abstract: We show that the norm obtained by summing the $L^1$ norms of all weak derivatives through order $k$, including the function itself, determines both $n$ and $k$ on the real Sobolev space $W^{k,1}(\R^n)$. Every surjective linear isometry for this norm is given by a translation, a signed permutation of the coordinates and multiplication by a fixed sign $c\in\{-1,1\}$.

title: Quantum Interference Control of Coupled Atomic Spins
abstract: We propose a protocol for the non-resonant electric control of quantum states in atomic-scale spin systems using Landau-Zener-Stückelberg-Majorana (LZSM) interferometry. We focus on a Ti-Ti-Fe trimer on a thin MgO layer, a platform that has recently emerged as a promising candidate for qubit realization using electron spin resonance combined with scanning tunneling microscopy (ESR-STM). We first analyze a Ti dimer in the absence of the Fe atom and show, through a detailed spectroscopic study, that avoided level crossings can be engineered by combining the in-plane component of the external magnetic field, the tip magnetic field, and the applied bias voltage, which allows the system to be tuned electrically through these crossings. Based on this, we develop LZSM protocols for coherent state control in the dimer using non-resonant LZSM-STM. We then consider the full trimer, where the Fe atom generates a local magnetic field at the remote Ti atom, enabling non-local spin control. We show that this remote and non-resonant manipulation reduces unwanted effects associated with tunneling electrons and enables quantum operations on short timescales. Our results show that quantum interference can be used as a resource for electrically driven, non-resonant, and non-local spin control in atomic-scale systems. This approach enables fast quantum operations while mitigating decoherence, offering a promising route toward scalable atom-based qubit architectures.

title: Locally Adaptive Conformal Prediction for Polynomial Chaos Expansions
abstract: This work develops a locally adaptive jackknife+ conformal prediction framework for polynomial chaos expansions. Therein, the non-conformity scores are normalized with an auxiliary polynomial chaos expansion trained on the log-transformed leave-one-out residuals of the base model. We show that the coverage guarantee of jackknife+ conformal prediction carries over to the adaptive intervals if the leave-one-out auxiliary models are trained on nested leave-one-out residuals. For fixed-basis polynomial chaos expansions fitted by ordinary least squares, all required quantities are derived in closed form and the guarantee-preserving adaptive intervals are obtained from a single model fit, without any model retraining. For sparse polynomial chaos expansions, where multiple model fits are necessary, we propose a heuristic simplification that limits the computational overhead of adaptivity at the cost of the formal coverage guarantee. Numerical experiments on an academic benchmark with known heteroscedastic noise and on an engineering simulation dataset show that the suggested method attains the target coverage while providing intervals that adapt to local prediction uncertainty, therefore being considerably more statistically efficient. These advantages are particularly prominent in high-uncertainty regions of the input space, where the performance of non-adaptive methods degrades substantially.

title: Hostages
abstract: Our house has been taken over. It is not completely destroyed, but many of its essential functions and facilities no longer work as they used to. Essentially, they are out of our control. Artificial intelligence, through its large language models (LLMs), has taken it. And we, the inhabitants of the house, without really noticing what was happening, and surprised by the effectiveness of LLMs, have handed over our most sacred belongings: the capacity to think about a problem, the joy of having an idea that solves it, the beautiful effort needed to consolidate an idea in our common language. And there is no turning back. We are mathematicians, and our whole world is in check. We wonder: is it checkmate? Can we take back control of our house, which will undoubtedly not work in the same way? Paradoxically, the weapons that attacked us are built on some of our own ideas. Of course, it is not entirely our work. The computer science knowledge needed to develop these large models evolved in both its theoretical and its material aspects. As technology evolved (infinitely small processors, infinitely large computing centers), turning quantity into quality, computer scientists encoded into software the ideas needed to produce these tools (let us not call them weapons). These notes look into the past and the future of the mathematical profession. What will inevitably happen? What will remain and what will disappear? And, in consequence, what is our line of action? To organize the ideas, after some introductory historical comments, we try to answer the questions: (1) Is mathematics necessary for the development of our society? (2) Will mathematicians be necessary in the near future? (3) How the profession will change, through a list of exercises: open questions and possible actions.

title: Scanning Probe Control, Quantum Dynamics, and Dispersive Readout of Suspended Carbon Nanotube Resonators
abstract: Suspended carbon nanotubes (CNTs) offer promising opportunities for quantum nanomechanics owing to their small effective mass, strong electrostatic tunability, and mechanical nonlinearity. We develop a unified theoretical framework for coherent control and readout of a suspended CNT driven by an atomic force microscope (AFM) tip and capacitively coupled to a Cooper-pair box (CPB). We first derive the linear and nonlinear Duffing response of the CNT and quantify the effects of AFM force gradients, tip-position fluctuations, and voltage noise on mechanical stability, dephasing, and heating. These results establish operating conditions for coherent actuation with limited backaction. We then quantize the Duffing oscillator, derive its Kerr anharmonicity, and identify the requirements for selective control of individual vibrational transitions. Estimates of thermal occupation and active cooling illustrate the constraints for CNT modes spanning frequencies from 54 MHz to 5.37 GHz. Finally, we derive the CNT--CPB interaction and its dispersive limit, showing how phonon number and parity can be mapped onto the CPB through Ramsey interferometry and detected using quantum-capacitance readout. The resulting framework identifies the conditions under which localized AFM actuation, nonlinear quantum dynamics, and superconducting state-resolved detection can operate within a single CNT device.

title: Mathematical foundations and numerical simulations of BDNK hydrodynamics: from heavy-ion collisions to astrophysics
abstract: We present new developments in the mathematical foundations and numerical simulations of the causal and stable first-order relativistic viscous hydrodynamic theory by Bemfica, Disconzi, Noronha, and Kovtun (BDNK) in general spacetimes. We develop two independent flux-conservative algorithms for arbitrary 3+1-dimensional spacetime metrics. Both are hyperbolic, causal, and well-posed, pass convergence tests, and reproduce known results. The first uses a new first-order reduction with mathematically preserved constraints, whose numerical violations can be handled with cleaning fields (the resulting coupled system is proven hyperbolic and well-posed). The second uses a new mixed-order formulation, whose solutions are proven strictly equivalent to the original BDNK system, without cleaning fields. Our proofs rely on a new general theorem providing sufficient conditions for transforming a mixed-order system with arbitrary-order equations into a strictly hyperbolic system, strengthening a classical result by Choquet Bruhat for weak hyperbolicity. We introduce a new practical prescription for selecting admissible hydrodynamic frames for a broad class of equations of state, including nonconformal ones relevant to heavy-ion collisions and astrophysics. Our simulations capture viscous shock broadening and suppression of Kelvin--Helmholtz vortices, reproduce Bjorken and Gubser flows, and study departures from stationary ideal-fluid configurations in Michel accretion and rotating tori on fixed Schwarzschild and Kerr backgrounds. For heavy-ion collisions, we perform boost invariant simulations with a lattice-QCD-based equation of state and fluctuating TRENTo initial conditions, comparing BDNK with a minimal Israel--Stewart theory. The descriptions agree at small shear viscosity but can differ substantially at larger viscosities, particularly for early initialization with rapid longitudinal expansion.

title: MSR-ABC: Complementary Feature Fusion for Clear Cell Renal Cell Carcinoma Classification
abstract: Clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) classification from computed tomography (CT) may benefit from representations that capture different aspects of tumour phenotype. However, simply concatenating reconstruction-derived features, image--text embeddings, and radiomic descriptors may not fully exploit their complementary information. We propose MSR-ABC, a global--local framework integrating MedVAE, MedSigLIP, and radiomics. Spatially matched local image descriptors interact through cross-representation attention, while radiomic auxiliary supervision encourages the pooled local representation to retain quantitative tumour attributes. A gated residual mechanism integrates local information with global summaries. Area-aware pooling and visual and soft-text prompting complete the framework. We evaluate discrimination using a patient-level split of 396 KiTS23 cases and an external cohort of 111 TCGA/TCIA cases, reporting mean AUROC over three training seeds with 95% patient-bootstrap confidence intervals. MSR-ABC achieves mean AUROCs of 0.806 internally and 0.879 externally. Internally, it exceeds global MedVAE--radiomics and three-source concatenation by 3.35 and 3.61 AUROC percentage points, respectively. Removing any source lowers mean AUROC in both cohorts, with the largest decreases following radiomics removal. Individual removal of cross-representation attention, auxiliary supervision, or gated fusion also lowers internal mean AUROC. These findings are consistent with complementary contributions within the integrated architecture and support further investigation of structured representation fusion for non-invasive renal tumour characterisation.

title: Extended Model-Based Learned Inertial Odometry
abstract: Inertial odometry is a compelling approach to state estimation for agile quadrotor flight due to its affordability, low weight, and robustness to perceptual degradation. However, relying only on integrated inertial measurements is impractical, as sensor errors and time-varying biases lead to significant pose drift. Although recent advances have enabled inertial odometry for drone racing, existing approaches show limited generalization to trajectories not seen during training. This work improves generalization by adopting a body-frame representation and incorporating body-frame torque dynamics into the learning pipeline. The learned model predicts short-horizon relative displacements, which are fused with IMU measurements in an Extended Kalman Filter. Experimental results show that the proposed method outperforms the previous state-of-the-art learned inertial odometry approach for quadrotor pose estimation on unseen trajectories. An additional evaluation on four public quadrotor datasets, with whole trajectory shapes held out of training, confirms a lower velocity error on every held-out set and shows that the torque input is most informative when it is derived from the rotor signals. Code, data pipeline and trained models are publicly available.

title: Scalable Full-Horizon SFC Deployment over Predictable SAGIN Topologies via Configurable Column Generation Framework
abstract: Space-air-ground integrated networks (SAGINs) integrate heterogeneous communication and computing resources to support ubiquitous services. Service function chains (SFCs) enable complex services to be composed of ordered functions and executed collaboratively across these resources. Mobility continuously reshapes connectivity throughout service execution, yet much of the resulting topology evolution is predictable. Decisions based only on isolated topology snapshots may therefore overlook valuable future connectivity. We formulate an admission-first, cost-aware model on a time-expanded graph for SFC deployment. Our key observation is that temporal feasibility is request-specific, whereas global coupling arises mainly from shared-resource competition. We therefore develop a configurable column-generation framework in which complete request deployments form columns and a restricted master problem coordinates admission and resources. SAGINFE, a fast constructive heuristic built on per-flow embedding (PFE), supplies a standalone feasible solution and initial columns. Configurable pricing schedules combine early-terminated and stricter searches, supplemented by selective PFE candidates. Candidates undergo feasibility and exact reduced-cost checks. Request-wise pricing can run in parallel, followed by finite-pool integer selection. The default configuration improves the admission-first objective over initialization on all 120 main instances. Four pricing workers achieve up to a 2.69-fold median pricing-stage speedup while preserving admitted request counts in the tested cases.

title: Absence of Excited Bound States for All Fibers of the Fröhlich Polaron at Weak Coupling
abstract: We study the discrete spectrum of the three-dimensional Fröhlich polaron at weak coupling and fixed total momentum. We prove that, for sufficiently small coupling and every total momentum $0<|ξ|\le 1/4$, the ground-state eigenvalue is the only eigenvalue below the essential spectrum. Our proof builds on the analogous zero-momentum result of Seiringer (2023). Combined with that result and the work of Dahlbaek (2017), this implies that, at sufficiently weak coupling, no fiber Hamiltonian has a discrete excited eigenvalue.

title: Finite-strain second-gradient elasticity with an energetic surface: existence of minimizers, incremental theory and elastocapillary beading
abstract: We develop a finite-strain theory of second-gradient elasticity for solids with a material surface endowed with its own constitutive energy. The bulk second gradient plays two complementary roles. First, under suitable coercivity assumptions and convexity with respect to the second gradient, we prove the existence of minimizers for nonnegative, lower semicontinuous surface energy densities, without requiring convexity, polyconvexity, positive one-homogeneity, or an upper growth bound on the surface energy. Second, it introduces an intrinsic bulk length scale that affects the onset of instability and wavelength selection. To investigate these effects, we derive an incremental small-on-large formulation in the finitely deformed configuration and apply it to the elastocapillary beading of an axially stretched soft cylinder. For an infinite cylinder and the parameters considered, increasing the second-gradient modulus delays bifurcation and shifts the critical mode towards longer wavelengths. Above a finite threshold of this modulus, the critical stretch saturates in the long-wave limit. The model is implemented in the open-source finite element code OOFEM using C1-continuous isogeometric analysis. Finite-cylinder simulations yield onset stretches in close agreement with the analytical predictions. Selected post-bifurcation branches traced by arc-length continuation exhibit beaded states and supercritical bifurcation at small second-gradient moduli, whereas larger moduli are associated with subcritical bifurcation and the formation of distinct thick and thin segments.

title: SQUALO II: Probing Accretion Through CO Molecular Outflows in Massive Star-forming Clumps
abstract: Molecular outflows probe protostellar accretion and mass transfer from clump scales to forming stars. We present an ALMA study of CO (J=2-1) outflows toward 13 massive clumps from the SQUALO sample, spanning a broad evolutionary range and exhibiting clump-scale infall. We identify 51 high-velocity CO lobes associated with 31 outflow systems and derive their physical and dynamical properties assuming local thermodynamic equilibrium. Outflow inferred accretion rates are typically 10^{-5}-10^{-3} Msun/yr, consistent with active massive star formation. The maximum outflow velocity shows little dependence on candidate driving-core mass, indicating that it is not a reliable tracer of protostellar mass in clustered environments. Outflow momentum flux correlates positively with clump surface density, whereas accretion rate shows a tentative, statistically nonsignificant decrease with increasing virial parameter. Total outflow inferred accretion rate shows a tentative positive relation with clump-scale infall rate but remains systematically lower, suggesting that the detected outflows represent only part of the large-scale mass flux. The clump L/M ratio moderately anticorrelates with projected outflow length, although projection, observational limitations, and the embedded source population prevent a unique evolutionary interpretation. Together with the continuum derived fragmentation properties, our results show that compact cores embedded within infalling clumps drive the outflows. The tentative relation between clump-scale infall and protostellar accretion suggests a possible connection across these scales, although our observations do not directly trace mass transfer from filaments to individual protostars.

title: Dual-Number Associative Arrays for One-Pass Provenance and Sensitivity
abstract: Associative arrays and GraphBLAS express sparse computations as matrix operations over a chosen semiring, but the result normally contains only the ordinary value. We define a dual-number extension $D_k(S)=S\ltimes S^k$ that carries this value together with $k$ independent auxiliary channels in the same computation. We prove that the construction is a split square-zero extension of any commutative semiring. Over min-plus, the auxiliary value is the weight of the shortest walk constrained to use the corresponding edge, excluding the weight of that edge. This gives an exact shortest-path membership test for that edge, although ties return the union of the edges on all optimal paths. We implement the min-plus construction using sparse \texttt{python-graphblas} operations, with a fixpoint test that checks the value and auxiliary components together. We validate the implementation across 18,692 checks, including 2,825 tied target pairs. On random graphs with 100,000 vertices and 32 seed edges, the dual method is $3.39\times$ faster than the sequential algorithm but $1.50\times$ slower than a min-plus-specific batched method. This difference is largely explained by the dual method requiring $1.55\times$ as many sweeps. Thus, the main contribution is a general algebraic approach with competitive sparse performance, rather than information that specialized min-plus algorithms cannot already compute.

title: Generalized and Classical Harnack Inequalities for semilinear equations on Carnot Groups
abstract: We prove generalized and classical Harnack inequalities for non-negative smooth solutions of divergence-form semilinear subelliptic equations on Carnot groups. The proof combines smooth horizontal Gauss--Green and coarea formulas, energy estimates for level sets, a Vitali covering argument, and a horizontal Keller--Osserman barrier. The companion paper, Reference [10], develops the geometric foundations and extends the estimates to weak solutions with nonsmooth data.

title: Multi-Mode Pinching-Antenna-Based OFDM Systems: A Robust Design Perspective
abstract: A robust transmission framework is proposed for a multi-mode pinching-antenna (MPA)-based orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM) system under both channel state information (CSI) errors and PA positioning errors. A physical model is first developed based on the multi-mode coupled-mode equations (CMEs), which characterizes the frequency-dependent guided-mode propagation and the coupling among guided modes and PAs over the OFDM band. Based on this model, a worst-case sum-rate maximization problem is formulated to jointly optimize the baseband beamformer and the intended PA positions under CSI and PA positioning errors, subject to user quality-of-service (QoS) and transmit-power constraints. To solve the resulting non convex problem, the worst-case CSI is exactly obtained for any given PA positions by solving trust-region subproblems, while the PA positioning errors are handled by grid-based and second-order approximation-based scenario constructions. Then, an alternating optimization (AO) algorithm is developed, where the baseband beamformer and the intended PA positions are updated via the weighted minimum mean-square error (WMMSE) method and successive convex approximation (SCA), respectively. Both subproblems are solved efficiently by exploiting the Karush--Kuhn--Tucker (KKT) conditions. Numerical results show that the proposed robust design outperforms the non-robust and conventional robust benchmarks with the same multi-mode architecture in terms of both worst-case sum rate and QoS satisfaction. They also demonstrate that the proposed robust design satisfies the QoS requirements of all users more reliably than the baselines that consider either CSI errors or PA positioning errors.

title: Discrete total variation under the multinomial, Part 4: variance under a general distribution
abstract: We study the variance of the reference-centered discrete total variation $d_{\mathbf p}=\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}|X_{j+1}-X_j-N(p_{j+1}-p_j)|$ of $X\sim\mathrm{Mult}(N;\mathbf p)$ for fixed $n\ge3$ and fixed $\mathbf p$ with all $p_i>0$, as $N\to\infty$. We prove $\mathrm{Var}(d_{\mathbf p})=N\,v(\mathbf p)+O(1)$, where $v(\mathbf p)$, the variance of the sum of absolute values of the limiting Gaussian edge vector, is expressed through the exact multinomial edge variances and correlations and Nabeya's covariance formula for folded bivariate normal variables. Unlike in the uniform case, non-adjacent edge pairs generally contribute to $v(\mathbf p)$. The $O(1)$ remainder is controlled by a lattice Edgeworth expansion and Poisson summation; it oscillates with the lattice phases $\{N(p_{j+1}-p_j)\}$, and for $n=3,4$, where a pair of edges exhausts the bins, the summation runs over a sublattice coset. The formula reduces to the known uniform result (the classical Hoel--Kamat variance), gives a closed form when the reference law is a symmetric comb, and has a shape-independent large-bin limit for positive $C^1$ profiles. For the statistic $d_{\mathbf r}$ centered at a reference law $\mathbf r\ne\mathbf p$ the absolute values linearize: when every edge is mismatched the variance is that of a linear form in the counts up to an exponentially small error, and in mixed (triangular-array) regimes it is given to $o(N)$ by bivariate folded-normal covariances. The two-bin formulas are recorded from the companion preprints, and exact finite-$N$ reductions for $n\le4$ are used for validation.

title: A Hybrid Quantum-Classical Coarse-to-Fine Finite Element Solver for Heterogeneous Darcy Flow
abstract: Quantum linear system algorithms offer theoretical potential for solving large sparse systems from PDE discretizations. However, applying them directly to fine-scale problems remains impractical on near-term hardware because of limited qubits, restricted circuit depth, and noise. They also prepare a quantum state rather than solution coefficients, whose recovery requires measurement and reconstruction. In this work, we develop a hybrid quantum-classical coarse-to-fine finite element framework for heterogeneous Darcy flow. We investigate whether a measured quantum coarse solution improves fine-grid initialization and reduces subsequent classical solver work. Rather than solve the full fine-scale system on a quantum device, we apply a method inspired by the Variational Quantum Linear Solver (VQLS) to the Galerkin coarse system. We reconstruct the approximate coarse solution from measurements, prolongate it to the fine grid, and use it to initialize a classical preconditioned iterative solve.} Numerical experiments on steady heterogeneous Darcy flow and a time-dependent SPE10-based problem show that measured quantum coarse solutions can improve fine-grid initialization, while classical correction recovers accurate pressure fields. The effect on classical solver iterations depends on the problem. All quantum computations were simulated using Qiskit Aer.

title: Magic Can Superactivate Quantum Capacity
abstract: Environmental magic can enable two channels with zero quantum capacity to transmit quantum information jointly. We establish this superactivation within a family of discrete quantum convolution channels with fixed Clifford interactions. For the couplings considered, stabilizer-mixture environments induce entanglement-breaking channels. We construct a mixed magic environment whose induced channel has positive private capacity and a Choi state with positive partial transpose, hence zero quantum capacity. A half-erasure auxiliary activates this channel through the Smith--Yard mechanism. Finite-block encoding and decoding over a self-complementary convolution auxiliary then realize a higher-dimensional erasure channel that still permits activation. We also bound the activated capacity by the modified relative entropy of magic of the main environment. Replacing either environment of the convolution pair by any stabilizer mixture makes the joint quantum capacity vanish, identifying environmental magic as a necessary resource on both sides for this realization.

title: Modular Hamiltonian and Typicality of Degenerate States
abstract: Free fermions exhibit Eigenstate Typicality (ET) meaning that the reduced density matrix, $ρ$, of a small spatial subsystem of a {\sl single}, typical, excited energy eigenstate is gaussian with a modular hamiltonian, $h \equiv -\log ρ$, asymptotically proportional to the free fermion hamiltonian. In effect, the ET may be thought of as providing an independent route to establishing the Fermi-Dirac (FD) distribution for free fermions. We revisit this argument for fermions belonging to a superposition of degenerate eigenstates. Specifically, we show that the modular hamiltonian corresponding to a superposition of degenerate eigenstates in a 1-d free fermion lattice system is interacting, and therefore the reduced density matrix for the subsystem is not gaussian. Measurements of the single particle distribution of a small subsystem would then exhibit non-thermal deviations from the FD distribution. These features may be traced to a violation of Wick's theorem for the chosen excited state. We develop a perturbation theory for the modular hamiltonian corresponding to a weak mixture of degenerate states and study the modular hamiltonian (exactly) computationally. Finally, we speculate that initial conditions in a realistic fermi system evolving towards equilibrium might be encoded in the interaction terms of the modular hamiltonian and consequent correlations of fermions.

title: Coordinatewise Epsilon for Adam under Heavy-Tailed Noise
abstract: Adam estimates second moments coordinatewise, but typically adds the same scalar $\varepsilon$ to every denominator. We study how this shared $\varepsilon$ affects convergence when noise and curvature vary across coordinates. Under coordinatewise finite-$p$ noise moments, $p\in(1,2]$, choosing $\varepsilon_i$ from the noise and curvature bounds for each coordinate attains the heavy-tailed $\ell_1$-stationarity benchmark $O(T^{-\frac{p-1}{3p-2}})$, matching the known optimal time exponent for smooth nonconvex stochastic optimization. For $1<p<2$, Adam with a shared $\varepsilon_t$ admits a lower bound of order $Ω(T^{-\frac{p-1}{2p}})$. This lower bound holds for every predictable scalar choice of $η_t$, $β_{1,t}$, $β_{2,t}$, and $\varepsilon_t$, precluding a dimension-uniform benchmark rate for this class.

title: RuACT: Recovering Inactive Rubrics as Adaptive Critics and Teachers
abstract: Rubric-based reinforcement learning (RL) extends RL with verifiable rewards to open-ended tasks by scoring each response against query-specific rubrics. Under group-relative optimization, however, a rubric that every sampled response fails (unreachable) or passes (saturated) gives all responses the same outcome and no learning signal; in Qwen3-4B medical training, 60.88% of query-rubric observations are inactive. We find that the two states lack different supervision: stating an unreachable rubric in the prompt raises its satisfaction from 1.13% to 91.25%, whereas responses that all pass a saturated rubric still differ in quality. We therefore propose RuACT (Rubrics as Adaptive Critics and Teachers), which assigns each inactive rubric the role that supplies what it lacks. Rubric as Teacher uses unreachable rubrics as privileged information for reward-gated on-policy self-distillation, and Rubric as Critic decomposes saturated rubrics into child rubrics that separate current responses while sharing the parent's weight. RuACT outperforms GRPO, rubric reweighting, and rubric-guided exploration on all four medical and scientific benchmarks with Qwen3-4B and achieves the best average with Qwen3-1.7B. On initially unreachable rubrics, unguided recovery rises from 35.02% to 42.86%, while child refinement improves reward-quality alignment on independent rollouts from 57.74% to 60.77%. Code is available at https://github.com/ZJU-REAL/RuACT.

title: Transformer-FSQ: Discrete Latents for Extreme KV-Cache Compression
abstract: Private, personalised language models must run on local consumer devices, where large, frontier models cannot fit, and retaining long contexts is non-trivial. Sequential memory---the key-value (KV) cache---grows linearly with context length, quickly dwarfing the model itself: for Qwen3-1.7B-Base, 200,000 retained entries require 21 GiB, 6.6 times more than the model weights. Yet the KV-cache compression methods we measured fail beyond moderate compression ratios. We introduce Transformer-FSQ, addressing extreme KV-cache compression by replacing standard key and value projections with a finite scalar quantisation bottleneck. Our cache stores a packed vector of discrete integer codes per token, with no per-token quantisation metadata. Converting a pretrained transformer trains only these projections on 0.25 tokens per original parameter. We evaluate Transformer-FSQ against five baseline families on models from 0.6B to 8B parameters. On long-context retrieval (RULER), from 12$\times$ to 97.5$\times$ Transformer-FSQ is the most accurate method we evaluate, across scales. A fused Triton kernel decodes directly from the integer codes; with baselines given their authors' kernels where available, it decodes at $1.01\times$ (95% interval $0.98$--$1.05$) the throughput of native SDPA attention on the uncompressed Qwen3-8B-Base at $32\times$ and $1.54\times$ at $97.5\times$. Extreme KV-cache compression is therefore a practical way to extend how much context a fixed device can hold.

title: Dual-Region Slice Aggregation for CT-Based Renal Tumor Classification
abstract: Clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) is the most common kidney cancer in adults. We present a region-aware architecture for CT-based ccRCC classification. Tumor and 0--10 mm peritumoral context are pooled separately from shared frozen DINOv3 feature maps. A shared position-aware slice aggregator precedes fixed training-only principal component analysis (PCA). The resulting representations are fused with radiomics using two scalar feature gates. Evaluation on KiTS23 and 111 external cases yields internal test and external AUCs of 0.8078\pm0.0154 and 0.9094\pm0.0015. Compared with matched single-tumor readout, mean AUC increases by 1.50 and 2.34 percentage points, respectively. Early-PCA and reconstruction controls yield lower internal mean AUCs, while external AUC is similar for early and late PCA. These findings highlight the joint role of regional readout and slice aggregation in adapting frozen visual features to renal CT.

title: Coresets for Capacitated Clustering via Dual Concentration
abstract: We study coresets for clustering problems, focusing on the classical $k$-median and $k$-means objectives. A coreset is a small weighted summary of the input data that approximately preserves the clustering cost for every choice of centers. Such summaries are a central tool for scaling clustering algorithms to large datasets. In this work, we consider the capacitated setting, where the clustering is subject not only to choosing centers but also to respecting prescribed cluster-size constraints. This model is a natural generalization of standard clustering and has been widely studied, but its coreset complexity is less well understood. For finite metric spaces, we obtain optimal-size coresets; surprisingly, these match the best-known bounds for unconstrained clustering. We also give improved coreset bounds in Euclidean space, notably the first coresets with near-linear dependence in $k$ while being independent of the dimension and input size. The main new technical ingredients are concentration bounds for the dual solutions of min-cost flow problems, which allow for both significantly simpler and tighter analyses of the underlying sampling distribution used in the coreset construction.

title: A Fast and Accurate Algorithm for the $p \to q$ Norm of Sparse Non-Negative Matrices
abstract: We present an algorithm that computes the $p \to q$ norm of a non-negative matrix with $s$ nonzero entries to accuracy $\varepsilon$ in time $\widetilde{O}(s^{3/2} \log (1/\varepsilon))$, for any $p \ge q \ge 1$. The fastest algorithm previously designed for this problem has running time $\widetilde{O}(s / \varepsilon)$ (Objois and Vladu, 2026), which is slower when high accuracy solutions are desired. Our algorithm employs a surprising application of Laplacian solvers inside an Interior Point Method (IPM). We formulate the problem as a linear optimization problem over a product of power cones, and show that the Newton updates of the IPM can be computed by solving a Laplacian system in a Schur complement after subtracting a rank-2 matrix. We also discuss an implementation of our algorithm, showing that it is practical and it outperforms optimized solvers such as MOSEK by factors of up to $20\times$ on a variety of tasks.

title: An extension of the notion of algebraic entropy
abstract: The definition of algebraic entropy presents a difficulty in the general setting of filtered algebras, which makes it necessary to distinguish between filtered algebras and finitely filtered algebras. While algebraic entropy is well defined in the finitely filtered case, extending this notion to arbitrary filtered algebras is not immediate. To address this issue, we realize a filtered algebra as the limit of a strict direct system of finitely filtered algebras and define its entropy as the supremum of the entropies of the algebras in the system. This extension is consistent with the original definition, when the algebra is finitely filtered, the extended entropy agrees with its algebraic entropy. This new setting allows us to extend the definition of the algebraic entropy to path and Leavitt path algebras of infinite graphs.

title: Simply connected quotients of fake quadrics
abstract: Fake quadrics are minimal complex surfaces of general type with $b_1=0$ and $e=4$. The paper gives a short introduction to their arithmetic construction, aimed at low-dimensional topologists, and studies their holomorphic and antiholomorphic quotients and their fundamental groups. The running example in the paper comes from a quaternion algebra over a totally real cubic field. The lattice is generated by three explicit pairs of matrices. A holomorphic involution gives (after resolving the singularities) a simply connected minimal complex surface of general type with $p_g=0$ and $K^2=4$, a smooth $4$-manifold homeomorphic but non-diffeomorphic to $CP^2$ blown up $5$ times. An antiholomorphic involution gives a smooth four-manifold homeomorphic to $S^4$, with a knotted torus as branch locus.

title: Quantum subsets discrimination and key sifting with success probability one
abstract: Non-distinguishability of non-orthogonal quantum states is the essential feature of quantum mechanics. In particular, one cannot deterministically orthogonalize the set of quantum states, while probabilistic orthogonalization is possible, including unambiguous state discrimination and discrimination between the subsets. Here, we propose a method for error-free subsets discrimination with significantly increased success probability, which may reach one even for non-orthogonal and linearly dependent input states. This method may be applied in quantum cryptography: An alternative basis reconciliation procedure is described, which may provide unit sifting probability even for a large number of bases and for non-orthogonal states within each basis.

title: DKWBC: Decoupling Motion Tracking and Balancing for Humanoid Whole-Body Control
abstract: Humanoid whole-body control requires a robot to track diverse reference motions while maintaining balance under gravity, torque limits, contact switching, and external disturbances. Existing reinforcement-learning-based trackers typically learn control outputs that jointly address motion tracking and balance. However, similar reference poses can correspond to substantially different dynamic demands, requiring a unified policy to learn motion-dependent control requirements alongside balance corrections. This can complicate learning and lead to high-frequency fluctuations in control outputs. We propose DKWBC, a dynamics-informed whole-body control framework that combines explicit model-based tracking with a learned balancing residual. Inspired by the model-based and environmental-wrench contributions to joint torques in floating-base dynamics, DKWBC uses inverse-dynamics feedforward and joint PD feedback to supply tracking torques, while a residual policy learns additional joint-torque corrections for balanced execution. By explicitly accounting for motion-dependent torque demands, this structure simplifies the policy's learning task. Experiments in simulation and on real hardware demonstrate that a single learned balancing policy generalizes across motion datasets while maintaining accurate motion tracking and balance across ground support, attached payloads, and physical interaction. Project page: https://robbyant-research.github.io/DKWBC/.

title: Quasinormal modes of Kerr--Newman--de Sitter black hole: Linear stability and strong cosmic censorship conjecture
abstract: We present an alternative formulation of coupled gravitational and electromagnetic perturbations of Kerr--Newman--de Sitter black holes, yielding decoupled radial and angular equations with a well-defined $Λ\rightarrow 0$ limit. We compute the quasinormal mode spectra using spectral and direct integration methods, finding excellent agreement. All of these modes are consistent with the linear stability of the Kerr--Newman--de Sitter black hole. We investigate the photon sphere and near-extremal modes, revealing a non-trivial interplay between rotation and electric charge. We further explore the implications for the strong cosmic censorship conjecture and find that the photon sphere modes predominantly determine its validity within the parameter space considered. While increasing the rotation of the black hole generally favours the strong cosmic censorship conjecture, increasing the electric charge can promote its violation. We also find that the region of parameter space exhibiting a violation of the conjecture is comparatively smaller for gravitational perturbations than for electromagnetic perturbations. These results highlight the important role of rotation, electric charge, and the nature of perturbations in determining the validity of the strong cosmic censorship conjecture in Kerr--Newman--de Sitter spacetimes.

title: ReplayAudit: Auditing Outsourced LLM Fine-Tuning via Sealed Records and Selective Replay
abstract: Auditing outsourced LLM fine-tuning requires checking an untrusted provider's training while controlling verification cost. Uniform sampling ignores training-time signals, while checking a suspicious record can require replaying several preceding steps. We present ReplayAudit, a telemetry-guided auditing system that seals training records before challenges and independently replays sampled intervals from sealed checkpoints. Loss changes and parameter-update norms guide stratified random sampling; replay determines whether the selected computation agrees with its records. We relate sampling probabilities to replay work and evaluate the system on real LoRA training. A 7B BF16 prototype rejects a false update-norm report during a random audit; targeted checks also reject false loss reports and skipped updates. We calibrate sampling budgets offline to at least a 90% probability of directly selecting an injected step. For two learning-rate deviation settings, executing these budgets on the same honest 1.5B trajectory reduces median complete-audit wall time by 49% and 67% relative to uniform sampling. When skipped updates evade the high-anomaly stratum, the corresponding audit instead costs 38% more. These results show how deviation capture and actual replay work jointly determine the cost of telemetry-guided auditing.

title: Topological Mundici Adjunction and Its Applications
abstract: We establish a canonical topological lifting of Mundici equivalence, representing every topological MV-algebra as the unit interval of a topological $\ell$-group and extending the correspondence to a categorical adjunction. As applications, we give a direct group-theoretic proof of the equivalence of $T_0$ and $T_{3\frac12}$ and show that every topological MV-algebra is a retral space. We further extend the lifting to topological Riesz MV-algebras and identify the canonical topology with Wiweger's mixed topology under suitable assumptions, recovering the strict topology as a special case. Finally, we obtain a unit-interval formulation of Koopman representations for continuous-time dynamical systems.

title: Not Your Diary, Just Your Topic: Grading the Wrong-User Control
abstract: A common test of personalization replaces a user's history with someone else's and measures the drop in accuracy. But this swap also changes the topics in the history, so the drop may reflect topic mismatch. We examine this problem with a frozen language model on LaMP-2 news categorization, using histories from similar users and synthetic histories assembled from other users' articles. The user's own history improves accuracy by 2.3 percentage points over a model trained without history. Removing history only at evaluation makes this gain appear larger, at 4.8 points. Category labels alone reproduce 86% of the accuracy gap between the user's own history and a random user's history. With synthetic histories matched on labels and text similarity, the gap falls to 0.9 points. Across two user splits and three training seeds, the advantage over a similar user's history is 3.2 points for users seen during training and 0.65 points for unseen users, where the evidence for an advantage remains inconclusive. A small movie-tagging experiment with one training seed also finds no advantage over other users' histories. These findings show why personalization should be evaluated on unseen users, with histories of similar content and a model trained without history as comparisons. We also find that adding gated cross-attention improves on a prefix-only model under our training setup; whether this holds more broadly remains open.

title: New persistent chain spaces: identifying and computing the relevant persistent Laplacians of a filtration
abstract: Persistent homology (PH) summarizes the topological features of data that persist across scales, but it is insensitive to many geometric properties. Persistent Laplacians (PLs) address this limitation: for a pair of simplicial complexes in a filtration, the kernel of the persistent Laplacian recovers the persistent Betti number, while its non-zero spectrum carries additional geometric information. However, PLs are defined for individual pairs of filtration values, so analysing a whole filtration requires evaluating many operators that largely contain the same information, and the result is hard to summarize and interpret. In this paper, we show that this redundancy has a precise structure. For each pair of filtration values, we decompose the space of chains underlying the persistent up-Laplacian into the contributions inherited from the neighboring pairs and a remaining part, which we call the new persistent chain space. We show that the new persistent chain spaces of all earlier pairs form a direct sum decomposition of this space, so that every persistent up-Laplacian in the filtration is determined by them. Moreover, the new persistent chain spaces are non-trivial only at pairs given by the persistence pairing in the same and in the next homological dimension, so that the persistence pairing determines exactly where the persistent up-Laplacian can change. Experiments on several types of point clouds show that evaluating persistent Laplacians only at these pairs reduces the computation time, both for our implementation and for existing software.

title: Online Timely Bin Packing Revisited: A Simpler Algorithm with Optimality in Special Cases
abstract: Online Timely Bin Packing is a variant of classical online bin packing in which items arrive over time with sizes and deadlines. Packing an item may be deferred until its deadline, but once a collection of items is packed into a bin, the bin is closed and cannot be used again. The objective is to minimize the total number of bins used. The problem was introduced by Khattar in 2023. In 2025, Aminian proposed Discrete-Greedy, a deterministic online algorithm with a competitive ratio of exactly $2$, which remains the best-known upper bound. Its analysis is particularly simple; however, the algorithm requires maintaining a fractional simulation internally and may leave usable space in some bins unfilled. We propose Thrifty-Greedy, a simple deterministic online algorithm that does not require a fractional simulation. We prove that its competitive ratio is exactly $2$, matching the best-known upper bound. At the same time, the algorithm automatically achieves the optimal competitive ratio on two natural classes of inputs: it is $1$-competitive when all items have the same size, and $1.5$-competitive when every item has size in $\{1/3,2/3\}$. In contrast, Discrete-Greedy has a competitive ratio of at least $2$ on both classes.

title: Kernel-Based Learning of Analytic Operators and Parametric PDEs
abstract: We study kernel-based learning of analytic operators from finite samples, with a focus on how the regularity of the target should determine the choice of the kernel. We establish embeddings of analytic operators into vector-valued reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces and derive finite-sample, high-probability guarantees that quantify the uncertainty due to random sampling: in the noiseless setting, suitable analytic kernels yield rates exponential in a fractional power of the sample size, while Sobolev-type kernels yield polynomial rates. We apply the theory to the solution operator of a parametric elliptic PDE, where the training data are themselves finite-element approximations, and obtain bounds that separate the sampling and discretization contributions to the error and prescribe how the mesh size should be coupled to the sample size. The results are illustrated numerically.

title: Some normal abelian surfaces in $\mathbf{P}^3$
abstract: Every complex projective surface is birational to a singular surface $S \subseteq \mathbf{P}^3$, but it is unclear whether one can ask that $S$ have only isolated singularities. In particular, it was a folk question as to whether an abelian surface could admit such a model. We present examples to show that there do exist normal abelian surfaces in $\mathbf{P}^3$. One of these examples deforms in a one-parameter family.

title: Know What You Need: Efficient Activation Checkpointing
abstract: Large Language Model training is increasingly constrained by memory capacity. Activation Checkpointing reduces activation memory by avoiding storing selected activations during the forward pass and rematerializing them during backpropagation, thereby trading memory savings for additional computation. Although this technique is essential for scaling model training, rematerialization can be prohibitively expensive, particularly for Transformer linear layers. Approximate computation could reduce this overhead, but conventional approaches either introduce errors that accumulate over the backward pass or fail to exploit information available from the initial forward pass. We introduce a novel approximate rematerialization method that can yield unbiased gradient estimates: using information collected during the initial forward pass, the method selectively recomputes only the most important layer components, either through greedy selection or randomized sketching. Ablation studies show that the resulting gradients closely match the exact gradients. When applied to feed-forward layers, attention layers, or both, our method can recompute only two-thirds of the layer components in a Llama-488M model, while increasing perplexity by just 1.7%, 1.2%, and 2.5%, respectively.

title: Contextual Search and Bilateral Trade with a Trace-Square-Root Potential
abstract: We present a unified potential method for contextual search and bilateral trade with one-bit feedback and obtain order-tight algorithms for both problems. Our framework starts from a Bayesian perspective in which the unknown target (for contextual search) and the unknown pair of valuations (for bilateral trade) are sampled from a known prior distribution. In that model, the decision maker bases its prediction on the posterior distribution, obtained by conditioning on feedback received in previous rounds. For Bayesian contextual search, we present an algorithm with a total loss bounded by $O(\mathrm{Tr} \sqrt Σ)$, where $Σ$ is the covariance matrix of the target's prior; and for contextual bilateral trade, our algorithm's regret is bounded by $O(\mathrm{Tr} \sqrt{Σ_S}+\mathrm{Tr} \sqrt{Σ_B})$, where $Σ_S$ and $Σ_B$ are the covariance matrices of the seller's and buyer's valuations. We then use ideas from this Bayesian setting and adapt a ``dual'' of this trace-square-root potential to the classical worst-case setting, where the target and valuations are chosen adversarially from the unit Euclidean ball. For both contextual search and bilateral trade, we obtain tight $O(\sqrt d)$-regret algorithms. These results match the existing lower bounds up to a constant factor and improve on the previous guarantees of $O(d\log d)$ for contextual search and of $O(d6^d)$ for bilateral trade.

title: SparseModesNet for coupled thermal-hydraulic-mechanical system in heterogeneous porous media
abstract: Coupled thermo-hydro-mechanical (THM) models describe interactions among displacement, fluid pressure, and temperature in geothermal systems. Fine-mesh simulations over many time steps are costly, particularly with heterogeneous permeability and thermal conductivity or fracture networks that alter fluid and heat transport. Proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) reduces the number of unknowns but can require many modes because its reconstruction is linear. We apply SparseModesNet to reconstruct coupled THM solutions using a small set of selected modes and a neural-network nonlinear decoder. Starting from a larger collection of candidate modes, SparseModesNet selects modes to reduce reconstruction error rather than simply retaining those with the highest energy. We compare SparseModesNet with POD on three problems: a two-dimensional heterogeneous medium, a two-dimensional connected fracture network, and a three-dimensional geometry based on Utah FORGE fractures. We evaluate reconstructed displacement, pressure, and temperature fields, as well as pressure- and temperature-based quantities of interest. We also test temporal interpolation by training on a subset of snapshots and reconstructing omitted snapshots within the same time interval. For the same reduced dimension, SparseModesNet achieves smaller reconstruction errors than POD and accurately recovers the solution fields and selected geothermal quantities of interest.

title: CRTrack-Cap: A New Benchmark for Cross-View Dense Video Object Captioning
abstract: Dense video object captioning (DVOC) localizes, tracks, and describes object trajectories within a video. Existing methods process each camera view independently, producing separate camera-local tracklets and captions for the same person across cameras. These outputs lack a unified description and leave complementary appearance evidence across views unused. We therefore formulate cross-view DVOC (CVDVOC), which associates these tracklets into scene-level global trajectories and generates one caption for each trajectory from synchronized views. To support this task, we construct CRTrack-Cap from CRTrack by auditing text-identity links and converting usable referring expressions into canonical captions. It retains 425 global trajectories and 838 local tracklets across 13 scenes, with canonical captions for 335 identities. We adapt CHOTA to the cross-view setting as CV-CHOTA to jointly evaluate tracking and caption quality. Our reference framework combines View-Exclusive Cross-Camera Association (VECA) for grouping tracklets with Conflict-Evidence Gating (CEG) for integrating caption evidence using its reliability and disagreement across views. Against three single-view methods adapted with MvMHAT for cross-view association, our framework achieves CV-CHOTA scores of 83.43 and 33.48 on the scene-disjoint in-domain and cross-domain tests, respectively. Together, CRTrack-Cap and our framework provide a benchmark and a strong baseline for describing the same person consistently across camera views.

title: Quantum-walk measurements with sequential imaging of the same atomic sample
abstract: We demonstrate sequential single-atom-resolved imaging of the same ultracold atomic sample and apply this technique to quantum-walk measurements in an optical lattice. In quantum gas microscope experiments, fluorescence imaging provides microscopic information on atomic distributions but induces motional heating through photon scattering, making it difficult to reuse the same sample for subsequent quantum dynamics. To overcome this limitation, we apply Raman sideband cooling with parameters optimized for post-imaging cooling, enabling sequential single-atom-resolved measurements of the same sample. By optimizing the cooling parameters with machine learning, we achieve high fidelity over multiple imaging cycles. To demonstrate the capability of this technique, we measure one-dimensional quantum walks of single atoms in an optical lattice. By determining the initial atomic positions from fluorescence images, we extract quantum-walk transition probabilities without requiring deterministic preparation of the initial atomic positions. The observed dynamics agree with numerical simulations of quantum walks of single atoms. Our method provides a route toward reducing experimental overhead in quantum gas microscope studies requiring repeated acquisition of spatially resolved correlation data.

title: Beyond Feasibility: Efficient and Robust On-Device Localization with UWB Concurrent Transmissions
abstract: Concurrent transmissions (CTX) enable an ultra-wideband (UWB) tag to range to, or self-localize from, multiple nodes with a single frame reception, significantly improving update rate and energy efficiency compared to traditional approaches. Prior work demonstrated the concept feasibility via prototypes whose real-world applicability is however hindered by many limitations, notably including their inability to directly execute on UWB tags and to cope with interfering UWB signals. We address these limitations in two ways. First, we redesign the core CTX techniques to enable a fast and efficient execution on resource-constrained MCUs without sacrificing accuracy. Second, we leverage the new features in the IEEE 802.15.4z standard to achieve robustness to interference from other UWB devices and enable tags to dynamically select which anchors to use, two crucial and unexplored capabilities in CTX-based systems. We quantitatively evaluate our approach experimentally in two real-world testbeds with different characteristics. We first analyze our new techniques individually, offering an in-depth discussion of design choices and performance trade-offs. Then, we embed all our techniques into a CTX-based system enabling a tag to self-localize entirely on-device, unlocking gains up to 44% in runtime and 85% in energy efficiency compared to traditional approaches.

title: Fourier Positivity and Sharp Poincaré Inequalities on Graphs
abstract: We prove sharp dimension-free $L^1$-Poincaré inequalities on Hamming cubes, a sharp quadratic $L^1$-Poincaré inequality on product Poisson spaces, and a sharp pseudo-Poincaré inequality on finite abelian Cayley graphs. These inequalities use a generalization of the Beckmann boundary introduced by Ivanisvili, Xie, and Zhang. In particular, we prove that the optimal dimension-free constant in the classical $L^1$-Poincaré inequality on the Hamming cube is $\sqrt{π/2}$, answering a question of Ivanisvili et al. Semigroup duality and explicit Malliavin weights reduce these estimates to integrals of first absolute moments of centered Bernoulli and Poisson sums. The key ingredient is a Fourier positivity principle, which shows that replacing the coefficients by their absolute values can only increase these integrals. For the underlying Bernoulli functional at subquadratic exponents, we also characterize the maximizers and determine their exact phase transitions.

title: BiLoGo: Reducing the smoothing of localised responses in Transformer-based neural operators for sheet forming
abstract: Trial-and-error FE simulation of sheet forming could be computationally expensive, neural-network-based learned simulators are used to accelerate design. These simulators should accurately capture localised responses, such as thinning around sharp radii or near ribs, which determine formability. Transformer-based neural operators propagate information efficiently across the mesh but tend to smooth such localised responses. This study develops BiLoGo, a Bipartite Local-Global learned simulator with an FE-guided design that connects local node-element message passing with a Transformer-based neural operator for long-range information exchange. BiLoGo has three modules: a bidirectional node-element GraphSAGE model that learns nodal-elemental coupling on a bipartite graph and predicts each quantity on its native FE entity without interpolation; a dual-stream Transformer-based neural operator that processes blank deformation and tool contact with separate token sets, preventing localised contact information from being averaged with the whole-blank state; and a fusion and element update module that combines global and local features via gated residual fusion and updates element features conditioned on element-node kinematics. Evaluated on a dome-shaped cold forming case and two corner-shaped hot stamping cases (one with ribs), BiLoGo achieves the lowest positional and threshold-based thinning errors on all three cases compared with single-level and hierarchical graph-based models and Transformer-based neural operators. Near the ribs, the smoothing index of predicted thinning increases from 0.41-0.56 for Transformer-based neural operators to 0.94 for BiLoGo-U. Compared with the hierarchical graph network CAtt-BiUGNN, BiLoGo-T reduces mean positional error by 15.5% on the Corner case and BiLoGo-U by 8.3% on the Corner+Rib case, with 66-69% less training memory.

title: On Positive Computation
abstract: We introduce new notions of reducibility for monotone classes and show that a monotone version of Circuit Satisfiability and the Hamiltonian Cycle Problem are complete for $mNP$, even under positive reductions (which are not the same as monotone reductions). If this holds for all (monotone) $mNP$-complete problems - that they are also so complete for $mNP$ -, then $P\neq NP$. We introduce positive models of relativized computation and show that the separation $posP\subsetneq mNP$ does not relativize, even when oracles are restricted to monotone sets. Yet, there is a (weak) diagonalization proof that $posP\subsetneq mNP$.

title: Entering a New Domain in the Era of Generative AI: An Autoethnography of Solo Game Development as a Bioinformatics Educator
abstract: The rapid improvement of generative AI (GenAI) not only increased the efficiency of practice but also empowered individuals with capabilities to explore new domains. However, identity formation in the wake of such empowerment remains understudied. We use an autoethnography to understand identity formation in the context of solo game development as a bioinformatics educator. With the goal of developing a create-your-own-adventure (CYOA) game, we collected data for 73 days through journal entries, interacting with communities of practices. The autoethnographer had continuously reassessed the situation, and closely interacted with communities of practice. Their prior knowledge was used to provide in-game context and to uniquely interpret game development processes. These findings suggest that the autoethnographer made efforts to belong to communities of practice and engaged extensively in sensemaking through the lens of a bioinformatics educator. Although GenAI puts power at hand, attaining a new identity took place at a human pace.

title: TPIC: Energy-Conserving Space Plasma Simulations on GPU Supercomputers
abstract: Artificial heating and numerical damping affect particle energization in kinetic space plasma simulations, even when the numerical scheme remains stable. Implicit and semi implicit energy conserving Particle-in-Cell (PIC) methods eliminate these errors in the discrete energy balance while relaxing explicit stability constraints. We present TPIC, a massively parallel implementation of the Energy Conserving Semi-Implicit Method (ECSIM) for GPU supercomputers. We extend the exact energy conservation in the ECSIM formulation to closed domains with conducting boundaries by deriving and canceling a spurious term in the discrete Poynting flux theorem. TPIC executes the complete particle and field cycle on NVIDIA and AMD GPUs, combining matrix-engine acceleration with asynchronous communication and computation. We validate TPIC in a variety of electrostatic and electrodynamic test cases relevant for space plasma physics applications, including quasineutral plasma expansion, two-stream instability, Whistler waves, Weibel instability, Whistler turbulence, and three-dimensional magnetic reconnection with conducting walls and 12.3 billion particles. We show that in all scenarios, TPIC agrees with the corresponding analytical theory or reference numerical results, and preserves the total system energy to machine precision. On 4,096 AMD GPUs, TPIC advances 1.9 trillion particles with 96.8\% weak scaling efficiency.

title: Encoding Memory in World Models with Test-Time Model-Based Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) approaches have demonstrated strong performance across diverse domains in recent years, learning accurate world models from agent trajectories. However, despite this progress, current approaches still struggle to surpass human performance on tasks that require long-term memory and planning. In this work, we address the problem of long-term memory in MBRL by moving beyond the commonly studied paradigm of architecture design. We introduce Test-Time Model-Based Reinforcement Learning (TT-MBRL), using gradient descent at test time to encode the memory of episode observations into world model parameters. This enables the agent to learn a distinct world model for each episode, improving memory capabilities compared to traditional approaches that solely rely on contextual memory. We first establish a proof of concept on a simplified two-dimensional variant of the Memory Maze environment, which we refer to as Memory Maze 2D, showing consistent improvements across different world model architectures. We then demonstrate the effectiveness of TT-MBRL in the 3D domain, achieving new state-of-the-art results on the Memory Maze benchmark. Finally, we show that TT-MBRL maintains strong performance on non-memory benchmarks such as DeepMind Control and Atari 100k.

title: A Novel Algorithm to Simulate Conductance-based Neuronal Networks
abstract: Conductance-based models are central to neurophysiology and neuromorphic engineering, yet their simulation scales poorly to large networks. We study and analyze an iterative solver that operates in signal space. Each iteration reduces to $N$ decoupled scalar linear time-varying differential equations, one per neuron, which are solved in parallel and in closed form. The solver admits two complementary interpretations: a variable metric forward-backward splitting method, rooted in operator theory, and a waveform relaxation quasi-Newton method, rooted in circuit simulation. We prove uniform and superlinear convergence, with a bound that reflects the conductance structure of the dynamics. The algorithm is illustrated on the classical Hodgkin--Huxley neuron and on networks of up to 5000 neurons.

title: What remains of the planar induced minor conjectures?
abstract: Dallard, Milanič, and Štorgel, and independently Gartland and Lokshtanov, conjectured that for every planar graph $H$, Maximum Weight Independent Set and List $3$-Coloring are polynomial-time solvable in $H$-induced-minor-free graphs. As a structural explanation, Gartland and Lokshtanov further conjectured that such graphs admit balanced separators dominated by a constant number of vertices. Bonnet and Chang recently refuted the independent-set part of the algorithmic conjecture, by showing that Maximum Independent Set is $\mathsf{NP}$-hard in graphs excluding the $5\times5$ grid as an induced minor. We revisit both conjectures. We show that the graphs used by Bonnet and Chang exclude much simpler planar graphs, including several $16$-vertex trees, and we introduce a second, independent family of hard instances. We also prove that $3$-Coloring is $\mathsf{NP}$-hard in both settings, thus refuting the algorithmic conjecture in full, even in its quasipolynomial version, unless $\mathsf{NP}\subseteq\mathsf{QP}$. On the structural side, we identify planar graphs $H$ for which the structural conjecture holds, while the algorithmic one fails. Thus, constantly dominated balanced separators cannot by themselves explain the tractability of Maximum Weight Independent Set and List $3$-Coloring.

title: Fundamental Noise Processes in Pulsar Timing
abstract: The stability of spin rates and emission regions of radio-emitting neutron stars (pulsars) has enabled remarkable advances, including the detection of exoplanets, testing theories of gravity, and stimulating the vigorous exploration of a new window in gravitational wave astronomy an nanohertz frequencies.
